Eventide 3 uses only predictable hidden object game building blocks, but it can easily captivate its players with its graphics and just the right amount of challenge.
Eventide 3: Legacy of Legends is a hidden object game that really starts off on the wrong foot. It never moves outside the most clichéd “rescue kidnapped relative from evil sorcerer” formula and the dialogues are almost humorously bad. On top of that, gameplay has some issues like a practically useless map, hidden object scenes filled to the brim with the wrong kind of distracting clutter, or point ‘n’ click segments where the moon logic is strong enough to force blind trial and error.
It may come as a surprise though that I still think Eventide 3 is fun to play. Not only it is one of the most gorgeous HOGs released in 2017, but also it is chock full of gameplay elements that provide the absolute perfect challenge rating, which goads the player into continuing without ever presenting an actually infuriating or annoying obstacle.
Therefore, in the end, I wholeheartedly recommend this HOG, even though parts of me have no idea why.

I didn't get to do any real sniping apart from blowing away the odd half dozen Nazi Zombies while moving from horde fight to horde fight. And in those horder fights, I just used partial zoom to blow them away, used the SMG or Shotgun when they got too close, or rounded them into a circle and lobbed a grenade at them.
For a series that revolves around sniping and stealth for its main selling points, NZA doesn't even bother trying to include them into its gameplay. Whats even worse is that I had more fun playing the various Call of Duty zombie survial modes.
Going to leave this brain dead game to rot in a dark corner of my library, and go back to the true Sniper Elite roots.

This game is turely a diamond in the rough. It is often overlooked as "Oh just another old game that was a promotion for the Star Wars prequels", well, yes it was that but there is a lot of soul in this game and it actually is entertaining the whole way through. Even if you do think the prequels are a poorly done, such as myself, this game will still make you love it; not because its a Star Wars game but rather for its own reasons ranging from engaging plot to well thought out game mechanics. So now for the pro/con breakdown:
Pros:
•The squad controlls are nice and simple but still feel powerfull because god knows you need them to beat the game
•It is also much darker than most Star Wars games but remains tasteful unlike other installments in the franchise, *cough* Episode 3 *cough*
•It has aged very well graphics wise and will continue to do so
•The characters are memorable and the story is engaging, you will care about what is going on around you (It made me angry, laugh, proud, and scared)
•The controls are tight and the whole thing has good game feel
Cons:
•If you are young you may shy away from this game, on some levels it will push you around and is very linear (which was standard for its time and is still a very valid mothod of design but these days I see people complaining about linear game design)
•I am really grasping at straws for cons here but one is that this game will likely never see a sequil (the devs have all since gone thier separate ways) and leaves you with one hell of a cliff hanger

This game is so hilarious with friends. The spell combinations keep me coming back for more, although after completing the main mission I feel like there's not much to do except re-complete it under a high difficulty with different robe and staff combinations. Still, it was a good 20 hours of fun. Gameplay consists of mashing the speed spell while reviving your teammates (who are the only ones doing any actual work) and praying that whatever abomination is chasing you doesn't finish you off.

Magicka 2 is a lot like Magicka in some ways, and very different in others.  The main difference is that in Magicka 2, you can move while casting (and you are slowed less by conjure weight), so a good number of fights are about casting spells quickly while constantly running around.
The writing is about as funny as the first game, with a number of subtitle jokes and a handful of callbacks sprinkled throughout what is mostly original jokes.  The plot also bears a second playthrough; while I got most of the "between the lines" story my first time, I noticed little details on my next playthrough.  Not because it's insanely convoluted with time travel like the first game, but because they're subtle little details that are only noteworthy on the second go-round.
Overall, I like the game a lot, though it took me some time to get used to the idea that it's very like Magicka, but not Magicka.  I found an outfit that suits me real well and I'm working my way through Hard Mode and Bananas Mode, enjoying every minute!

Fun co-op experience and best played with at least one friend. Combat felt like a methodical hack and slash with brief periods of being overwhelmed.
Controls take a bit of time to get used to and remember. I played with both a controller and mouse/keyboard; preferred the mouse/keyboard. If you use a standard gamepad you'll have to emulate an Xbox pad to get it to work correctly.

I was really hyped for Magicka 2. Too bad it has a sequelitis. At first (pre-update) it seemed to have some features missing, such as combinations of different elements. When I finally got around to playing it with my friend, it was a ton of fun, just like the last part. We played the game through on normal.
There were a bunch of references in the first part, but it's not like the game's humour was composed entirely of it. It was self-aware enough to make fun of itself for those references. Magicka 2 has a ton of referential humour and little else. It builds itself up for a huge gag at the end and suddenly the game ends. The story ends before the game kind of even starts. However, the game is not much about the story. It's about sweet spells and element combos, right? Well, we kind of already saw all of that in the last game.
At least there's a new gameplay element: Artifacts. Or mutators, if you will. You also have to unlock all of them, so you can play the game with them. Sounds kinda awful if you think about it. Play the game a million times to be able to play the game again with something being different each time. It works in a certain kind of game, but here you already have insane amounts of combinations, which you can cheese the game with, at your disposal in the beginning. Also you would be playing the game over and over. The enemies and the places you will see are going to be the same every time. So I don't feel like that would be much fun at all.
Now, I want to stress the fact that I really had a great time. Also there are little puzzles here and there which are fun. However, it was definitely shorter than the last one. Get this game from a Steam sale or something, I can't recommend it for the full price.

Not the litteral kind, I mean the Disney magix and whinsey that the first game gave off... And before you say anything, NO I don't mean clone the first game, I mean take what it gave and improve, not forget HALF of what made is special.
Also, fair warning, this is long. But if you are considering buying this game, I at least recommend you skim this. You have been warned.
I'm not going to go into the controls, art, and basic spells, those are fine. Alot of people are iffy on them, but I have no gripes with them. Also, A+ on the added Poison element.
What I do hate is the basic items you get. The abilety to make your own loadout with your own robes is cool, I like it. But the proble is they are not special anymore. What most of them do is buff/weaken certain spells, or change movement speed. Most of the robes did that in 1, true, but what I'm really talking about here are the staves. There are NO stave secondarys here, they all just buff/weaken. What about the rogue staff that allowed you to use smokebombs? The Scythe that spead poison? The Freedom Staff with grenades? GANDOLF'S STAFF OF LIGHT!!! They COMPLETELY changed how you played with new abiletys, but ushually at some price. If we had THOSE staves on the loadout screen, that would be AMAZING!!! But we have instead is the Skull stave.... It makes life spells suck, but you death better... Yay?
But hey! We have GAME CHANGING ARTIFA- what is this? An item that makes the game black and white? Giving enemys more HP? Why? I got more game changes from starting the game as Dr. Doom than this. How about something WORTH getting? Like a goblet that turns you undead ghost that heals from death, but is hurt by life. That would be a load of fun when playing with freinds, trying to heal you but accidentally killing you instead. Or maybe a bomb bag that makes you Kamakazi the SECOND fire touches you? Some fun stuff like that! And each player could have their own artifact, making the battlefeild MAYHEM!!!
Also, Magicks suck now. All those weird spells you could cast after entering a spell code with good and bad effects? Most of them are gone. Black Hole, the most deadly one, is created by crossing life and death. Most conflicts can now be ended by just doing that over, and over again. It made SENSE it was the last Magick! Now it's a joke! And you get Magicks NOT from well hidden tomes, but from playing the story mode. Instead of a code, you just click a button. You CAN enter the code... But why? Spells like Conflagerate were super fun to use because it was a bit tricky to use, but when you got it working, you felt satified! You murdered ALL those imps by imputing the spell correctly! Now you just hit a button... Is conflag even in this game?.... NO! Cause that was fun! We now have a dragon strike, while better, is alot less fun. You hit a button, and there's fire. Good job, now get back to work. Raisde dead was tricky, and you only got a few zombies, but if you could keep your steak up, you felt like a real necromancer! Summoning armys of zombies to fight!... Now you got a bunch of skeletons you can't spam... Cute.
But the biggest tragety of all is the lack of secrets. In Magicka 1, secret stuff was EVERYWHERE! Like the sword that 1 hit K.O'd one of the final bosses! Or the Sword of Masters hidden beside a creek you would not think to check! I wasted SO much time in Magicka 2 trying to find secrets that did not exsist! Does this lake go anywhere? No. This one? no. This cave? No, this one- Oh hey..... A camo skin....... Neat. And where this is a secret, it's SO OBVIOUS, and the pay out is another staff that does♥♥♥♥♥♥all. Gimmie a reward! Like a staff of Invisabilety! Or something that spits poison! Or the abilety to Charm! ANYTHING WORTH GETTING!!!!!
Also, the Melee is broken, yeah. I keep swinging at an imp, and my blade constantly goes through him like Elsa's hair. Not that Melee is even worth doing. No weapon is THAT neat. It either does more damage, or a little bit of death, or a little bit of.... Life WHAT..... WHY DO WE HAVE SO MANY LIFE MELEES!?!? ARE YOU JOKING!?!? I'm nitpicking, onward. There isn't even any sidearms, like the pistol that one of the original wizards had, or the M18, the Throwing records, the insta-freeze swords! Magicka is about being broken! Cause even if you are god, YOU WILL STILL DIE!!! So much stuff is thrown at you in these games you NEED those powerful weapons to kill the enemy. Magic is not your ONLY tool!
I haven't even gotten to how much less exciting this game's story is, or some of the other flaws. But I hope you see where the problem is. It's just shallow. It's the diffenece between Mario Party 5 and Mario Party 10. They got rid the biggest fun factor for something easier. And no fake difficuly can hide that. Alone, this game is fine, but when your a sequel, you HAVE something to compaire to! And by god, this is not cutting it for Magicka, one of the best bloody games I've played
Paradox, I'm dissapointed, but I'm not giving up on you. Magicka 1 and it's expanchions was incredable, even if the netcode sucked for a while. Take what made Magicka 1 great, and build up. And take some of the things that worked in Magicka 2, and again, build up. This was a flop, but I'm certain you can move on, and make something even better with what you learned from this. Just finished this game in one sitting.
Overall, a brilliant game with fantastic characters, voice acting, and atmosphere.
I thought that both of the main characters, Delilah and Henry, were really well developed as people. The dialogue is written astonishingly well (for a video game). You really do get to see the way their relationship organically develops and the way in which they begin to trust (or not trust?) each other. Being able to pick certain dialogue options, and then seeing those options actively affect the narrative was satisfying as well as engaging.
The voice acting was just absolutely fantastic. They got one of the guys from Mad Men, and the actor for Delilah was just great. There was so much dialogue in the game that had it been handled by VA's who were much less competent, it could have been really forced and cringy. Thankfully, this is some of the best voice acting I've seen in a video game. And the soundtrack was great as well.
The atmosphere was absolutely my favorite part of this game. There are some very beautiful and picturesque moments in this game. I don't think the game fully took advantage of the style it had at times, and wished it had allowed itself more often to indulge in it's unique look. I really liked the New Deal style of art that was going on in this game. They definetly could have taken advantage of that more. There are even times in this game where the atmosphere creates intense levels of suspense. Just play it and see.
I do sort of feel that the writing suffered in terms of the overall narrative. Without spoiling too much, I think that at times the overall pace of the narrative could have been better. Sometimes I felt like I really had to fill in the gaps in terms of my imagination in regards to the development of Delilah and Henry's relationship (I know I said earlier this was one of my favorite parts: it is, however I think they could have done a little better). On the whole I was not upset with the story like many are. I actually sort of appreciated the direction they decided to take. But it felt as though overall the narrative could have been stronger, because they had laid the foundation throughly to explore a lot of different avenues without really doing enough with it.
Sometimes the map design could have been more inspired. By the end of the game, I had become a lot less interested in the sights of the game. It just felt less inspired than it could have been.
The most glaring problem with this game is its technical issues. Buggy graphics at times when vaulting up stones or even walking across landscapes. Stuff like that. Which is dissapointing but not game breaking by any means. But for a games that heavily relys on immersion, this is a problem.
On the whole, fantastic game. It went a whole different direction than I expected (I was a lot more scared than I thought I'd be!) but it was a very rewarding and worthwhile experience. Definetely recommend playing in one sitting. Have fun!

The first half of this game is phenomenal. Mundane slice of life about a middle-aged dude with huge personal baggage (and considerable actual baggage), in beautiful surrounds.
The second half strays from the grounded premise into 'tv drama', though. Never leans into the 'fantastic' but definitely breaks from the mundane 'human problems' setting of the first half of the game.
Dialogue is excellent, and makes up 70% of the game. Rest of the game is spent walking through beautiful but static and linear surrounds. The game is a walking simulator through-and-through. There's some really chewy dialogue choices but very little decisions to be made otherwise, and ultimately even your dialogue choices won't count for much (though the game does definitely pay attention).
Also don't expect to get a perfect happy ending at the end of this. I felt it was clear where the game was going given its tone but I have read a lot of disappointed reactions due to this. The entire game is really about how you can never really escape your problems - don't expect it to tie up neatly at the end.
The game is only about 4 hours long and has limited replayability, unless you play through again with the Developer's Commentary (which I haven't). There's also a 'free roam' mode but by the end of the main game you will have explored the whole park anyway.

This is a sad story told in a very unusual and powerful way.
And this is a bad game.
Completing it, especially more than once, can have a huge impact on you.
But what you get is not a catharsis. Instead you end up feeling terribly depressed and frustrated.
This game tricks you into beliving that your choices matter and therefore you have an instrument to win, and you play it again and again, exploring different choices, only to find out that whatever you do you always lose - there is no good ending, Not even a trade-off kind of ending through wich you can express yourself.
Experience of playing it is a mind state of a person who relives a traumatic experience again and again, trying to figure out what he/she could have done to prevent it, and finding no way out.
I can't recommend playing this game. And you definitly shouldn't do that if you currently have hard times and you are stressed.
And if you are curious, if you still want to play - please, don't do that more than once.

Deathmatch Classic is essentially just a deathmatch type game mode using Quake's weapons (and some of its maps). It feels like it was an experiment to recreate Quake inside Valve's new engine than anything else, because it lacks any sort of content unique to the experience.
Not that there's anything wrong with this game: Quake's multiplayer is some of the best there is. There's a bunch of cool weapons, each for different playstyles and situations, and the maps give a nice sense of dynamic movement. It's quick, fast, and tonnes of fun.
The issue here is that Deathmatch Classic doesn't add anything other than a couple of maps. They're still good, but the issue is that for $5, you're playing a thinned down experience of the multiplayer portion of an 18 year old game that is available on the same platform. As part of the Counter-Strike 1 Anthology, it's an okay bonus, but as a standalone title it's not worth the price.

When you see a story about someone playing a game until they die I immediately think about Factorio. Like Civ or SimCity of ye olden times, Factorio steals time from you effeortlessly.
Hmm, I should probably build out my red circuit array today. Well, before I do that, I better amp up plastic and green circuits. But I'll need to go train in a bunch more oil first, and probably add a bunch more smelter columns. I don't think my two-rail train setup can ramp production, better double that to four-way everything...
Next thing you know, it's two days later.
Factorio, the game, is a choose-your-own-buildventure title with a rudimentary "win" condition and a multitude of ways to get there, if you even bother at all. The joy of Factorio, is in the road traveled, the endless loop of building, rebuilding, expanding, re-rebuilding, and looking down at your first (or twenty-first) megabase and feeling that incredible swell of pride as if you were the greatest engineer on Earth. Followed almost immediately by spotting a mistake you made somewhere that will require half of the base to be re-re-rebuilt.
The team behind Factorio are dedicated, engaged and absolutely committed to making the best possible game they can. They communicate with the players directly and frequently on what they're thinking about, future plans, and HOW they arriving at their conclusions when mechanics change so that the community is never out of the loop.
Multiplayer is a peach, be it you and a few friends or a massively multiplayer map with one of the man active community streamers/youtubers.
Mod support is ridiculously deep, vibrant, and an integral part of the developer's ethos. You will never run out of different ways to play or goals to set for yourself.
It is impossible for me to recommend this game more -- 11 out of 10.

The Real Texas is one of those odd games that I put off playing for ages for one reason or another, then when I finally get to it it becomes one of my all-time favourites.
First off, I guess I should mention that it's definitely not a game for everyone. The pacing is a little slow at times, the dialogue and story is kind of quirky and weird (but intreguing and absolutely hilarious if you share that sense of humour), the world is weird and sometimes confusing, the art direction's papercraft style is very peculiar and unique... And if none of this is offputting to you, it instead gives a ton of charm to a wild ride of a game that you will never forget. Definitely one of the best unknown indie titles to grace the internet and something throughly special, you've never played another game quite like it and probably never will.
If you're interested in quirky, weird, unique, charming, story-driven games like Earthbound or Undertale (though I'm a little hesitant to include that one because -everyone- came around with Undertale), you'll wonder how you missed this one for all of these years. If you prefer a straight-forward RPG or shooter or somesuch, maybe keep looking.
PS: also, the music is fantastic and a -huge- soundtrack for this kind of undertaking. Excellent stuff.

This is a fantastic open-world sort of... Zelda / adventure game hybrid? It's hard to pin down. This game has a special place in my heart. It has some of the best (and odd) worldbuilding, writing, music, and overall feeling of place I've experienced in a game. The graphics, while humble, really fit that world and are abstract enough to make the writing even more evocative.  The unique combat is fun at times, but often very frustrating. I personally recommend playing through on invincible mode to casually explore the world and take your time at the well thought out puzzles and story, but ymmv. [I played through most of this game originally off Steam.]

A quirky gem, if a little rough around the edges, with a unified vision from a one-man dev. Although the tone is unique, gameplay wise it's a little bit of Little Big Adventure, Ultima 6/7, and Zelda all rolled up together.
The graphical style quickly grew on me, and the music is very well done and reminds me of Virt in his IT tracker days (high praise) and I want to say TurboGrafx/PC Engine-era tunes? The writing is clever and witty (though not laugh-out-loud funny), and has depth without getting overly pretentious or full of itself. All three (graphics, music, and writing) come together into an off-beat, yet approachable and surprisingly immersive whole. The exploration is satisfying, and the game is a good length, with plenty of secrets to hunt for, but not so long as to wear its welcome out.
As a one-man indie effort, there's bound to be some imperfections, and The Real Texas does have its share. Inventory management is clunky and obtrusive, and combat is servicable at best, with finicky controls. Sometimes it's not clear where to go next, which isn't a problem in itself, but it can result in a lot of backtracking through the same areas with enemies presenting more of a hassle than a challenge. Unlockable fast travel locations can help but were almost never placed quite where I wanted them to be.
It's not going to be for everyone, but if you can accept the flaws and the lo-fi aesthetic and retro game design, The Real Texas is a wonderful experience.

A delightfully expansive, immersive, and quirky adventure. While the graphics are unabashedly rough, the world itself is beautifully enticing all the same. The game is littered with little short stories and oddball fun among the numerous, well-written characters.
It provides the kind of immersion that happens when you don't have quest markers everywhere. In not searching for high drama or epic scale, the tale unfolds naturally through exploration in a way I didn't realize I'd been missing from other games.
Fun to play and fun to share, The Real Texas is the off-kilter little adventure you've been waiting for when you need a nice escape from a boring work week.
I've had lots of fun exploring this world, glad to see it on steam!

I was really hyped for Magicka 2. Too bad it has a sequelitis. At first (pre-update) it seemed to have some features missing, such as combinations of different elements. When I finally got around to playing it with my friend, it was a ton of fun, just like the last part. We played the game through on normal.
There were a bunch of references in the first part, but it's not like the game's humour was composed entirely of it. It was self-aware enough to make fun of itself for those references. Magicka 2 has a ton of referential humour and little else. It builds itself up for a huge gag at the end and suddenly the game ends. The story ends before the game kind of even starts. However, the game is not much about the story. It's about sweet spells and element combos, right? Well, we kind of already saw all of that in the last game.
At least there's a new gameplay element: Artifacts. Or mutators, if you will. You also have to unlock all of them, so you can play the game with them. Sounds kinda awful if you think about it. Play the game a million times to be able to play the game again with something being different each time. It works in a certain kind of game, but here you already have insane amounts of combinations, which you can cheese the game with, at your disposal in the beginning. Also you would be playing the game over and over. The enemies and the places you will see are going to be the same every time. So I don't feel like that would be much fun at all.
Now, I want to stress the fact that I really had a great time. Also there are little puzzles here and there which are fun. However, it was definitely shorter than the last one. Get this game from a Steam sale or something, I can't recommend it for the full price.

I don't want to hate this game, I really don't. But Paradox forgot something immensly important when making this game, the magic..... Not the litteral kind, I mean the Disney magix and whinsey that the first game gave off... And before you say anything, NO I don't mean clone the first game, I mean take what it gave and improve, not forget HALF of what made is special.
Also, fair warning, this is long. But if you are considering buying this game, I at least recommend you skim this. You have been warned.
I'm not going to go into the controls, art, and basic spells, those are fine. Alot of people are iffy on them, but I have no gripes with them. Also, A+ on the added Poison element.
What I do hate is the basic items you get. The abilety to make your own loadout with your own robes is cool, I like it. But the proble is they are not special anymore. What most of them do is buff/weaken certain spells, or change movement speed. Most of the robes did that in 1, true, but what I'm really talking about here are the staves. There are NO stave secondarys here, they all just buff/weaken. What about the rogue staff that allowed you to use smokebombs? The Scythe that spead poison? The Freedom Staff with grenades? GANDOLF'S STAFF OF LIGHT!!! They COMPLETELY changed how you played with new abiletys, but ushually at some price. If we had THOSE staves on the loadout screen, that would be AMAZING!!! But we have instead is the Skull stave.... It makes life spells suck, but you death better... Yay?
But hey! We have GAME CHANGING ARTIFA- what is this? An item that makes the game black and white? Giving enemys more HP? Why? I got more game changes from starting the game as Dr. Doom than this. How about something WORTH getting? Like a goblet that turns you undead ghost that heals from death, but is hurt by life. That would be a load of fun when playing with freinds, trying to heal you but accidentally killing you instead. Or maybe a bomb bag that makes you Kamakazi the SECOND fire touches you? Some fun stuff like that! And each player could have their own artifact, making the battlefeild MAYHEM!!!
Also, Magicks suck now. All those weird spells you could cast after entering a spell code with good and bad effects? Most of them are gone. Black Hole, the most deadly one, is created by crossing life and death. Most conflicts can now be ended by just doing that over, and over again. It made SENSE it was the last Magick! Now it's a joke! MadSpace runs under DosBox. It is an old title closer to the classic Duke Nukem series than Doom, or in laymans terms there is verticality. However MadSpace is its own distinct beast and breaks a few conventions gamers fond of retro-classic fps may be have become accustomed to. Let's go over my first 2 hours of gameplay:
After a barrage of skippable slide-show text and low-fi cinematics, the player is thrust into a spacecraft rail shooter. Enjoyable but dragged on for longer than appreciated. Jump cut to the real game and it's interface.
Bars, numbers, icons and values. Did I know what any of them were? Yellow and blue bars, were they health? What's the glowing thing up those stairs, an enemy? The bottom left had ammo, but what were the 1-9 shapes, my weapons?
Tapping one and two didn't swap weapons, but I was confident in the akimbo lasers. How could akimbo lasers not be good?
The first steps in MadSpace are described thusly; enemies tend to fly, look like drones and their attacks send you catapulting backwards. Taking damage lowers the yellow bar (as I learned later "Weapon Energy") then the blue bar (System Energy). Getting hit matters, without any yellow stuff one of my lasers was swapped out for a shotgun sort. Being super fast meant the short range was never an issue. This shotgun uses the scrap from drones to operate, and I'm pretty sure damage is its middle name, a quick favorite. Did I mention I still had a laser in the other hand?
Not long after the first scuffle there was a roadblock, the only place left to go was a dead-end. It was at that moment I turned around to a Escher style mind@#$%. Unfortunately, the level design didn't keep up after the initial areas, quickly devolving into a "Press Button - Find Door" style. The design catches itself later on but the buttons and door game didn't leave. It was about an hour before I encountered another enemy type past metal drone and mouth drone. The combination of the two left a "filler" taste in the gameplay that didn't leave. However, I hadn't seen most of what's presented in the store's screenshots, so I know there's more to see still after two hours.
TL;DR
Don't be fooled by the introduction, there some real strange @#$% waiting for you. MadSpace is a flawed novelty.

Have you seen the rating for this game from users? Overwhelmingly positive, and you know what? This game deserves it. One thought explains it, I think; Republic Commando is hugely beloved because it explores things that most Star Wars, and most FPSes won't, and though it takes a lot of risks, 90% of the game is extremely good.

In terms of it as a Star Wars game, it isn't unique simply because it's dark, or gritty. Other games make Star Wars have questionable morals and levels of violence. As a Star Wars entry it's special because it focuses on characters that no one expects to be interesting, and that with the exception of Star Wars clone novels, aren't explored. Star Wars seems content to focus mostly on rebelious padawans, menacing sith lords, austere jedi masters, and suave rogues. As far as the movies go, clones are mostly soulless and alike to the droids in their massive numbers and seemingly unflinching allegiance to their superiors. Republic Commando takes that and flips it on it's head with the abnormal/nuanced clone commandos. Born and raised separately from the fodder clones, the Republic Commandos are BROTHERS with TALENTS. Republic Commando makes 4 family members all you need to tell an emotional story that few would ever hear- a series of covert ops that influenced the entire war. Republic Commando shows the messy side of war full of assassinations, ambushes, casualties, and lots of destroyed infrastructure. Republic Commando shows it isn't as simple as scrambling all the fighters on one target to cripple the enemy, and that a prolonged fight profoundly changes all involved.
As an FPS, Republic Commando is also quite special. Most obviously of course would be the squad orders system. So few FPSes allow you to control a team, and make it feel really meaningful. Republic Commando may not have super in-depth commands, but having even the ten or so various commands you can give are enough. Most areas give a number of tactical possibilities with lots of cover, sniping spots, heavy weapons locations, turrets, trappable explosives, etc. You can order your teammates to scout ahead, you can lead, or you can have the team stick close. You can have your team surround a doorway and wait as the droids march up to it slowly to a grinder of blasterfire. There are a ton of possibilities, of course including the "run through as quick as possible chucking grenades at anyone not easily shot" approach, and they're all so, so satisfying.
Besides the squad commands, the enemy design is also a highlight of this game. The player fights a lot of different baddies, and so long as they don't get stuck on something in the environment (there's a few spots in the game where this happens, but it's really infrequent- once per hour type of deal), they're great fun to fight. Geonosians fly around, jump, and skitter everywhere, avoiding as many shots as possible and then rushing you a few at a time.  Trandoshans try to circle you with SMGs and shotguns, and will cover rooms with mines and grenades to slow you down (or royally ♥♥♥♥ you up if you get hit). Trandoshans also employ heavy troopers with miniguns that will wreck a poorly led team in seconds. Droids come in large numbers and will try to keep you constantly underfire, and spawning more and more until you destroy their spawners. Super battle droids tank a ton of damage and have very powerful weapons too, causing one to adapt to hit-and-run tactics and focused fire. Those are just a few of the enemies, but I don't want to spoil anymore, suffice to say that it's worth experimenting in game to see just how many interesting behaviors the AI can produce. [If you're not satisfied with the AI, multiplayer servers still exist if you look for them too, and the multiplayer is also a lot of fun.]
Republic Commando is just overall an extremely impressive game. In terms of flaws all I can point out are a few bugs where AI gets caught in the environment, if you hit buttons too fast a command might get screwed up, and the somewhat rushed feeling of the ending. Other than that, the squad, story, enemies, weapons, and all around fun of it all stand proud. While the Star Wars franchise has had FPS success in the past with the Dark Forces/Jedi Knight titles, they had never attempted to produce a realistic and gritty FPS experience until Republic Commando. Sure, we've fired plenty of blasters, but we've always played as Jedi or a specific protagonist. In Republic Commando, you put on the armor of a soldier. You carry out missions and blast through hordes of enemies for the glory of the Empire!... uh... I mean the Republic! Yes, the Republic...
Republic Commando is set during the prequels but it carries a much more serious tone than the films. The Clone Wars provide the perfect setting for a modern FPS and Lucasarts did a fine job of creating a decent shooter while keeping the player in their beloved Star Wars universe. It may not be the best FPS but it was made very well. The only things I can think of to complain about are the lack of enemy variety and the lack of a sequel.

First of all, I don't normally leave reviews as I often find it difficult to explain what I don't like about a game, but I feel strongly enough about Firewatch to try. I was ridiculously excited for this game and was prepared to be blown away as story-driven, relaxing games are my jam. Unfortunately, I was seriously disappointed. Maybe it's just me, but I feel like the trailers took the few funny, sarcastic moments the game has in order to make it seem like the whole game is that way, which sadly, isn't the case. The truth is, I found this game seriously boring, and it took me three months to get through it as a result. Yes, the scenery is breathtaking. If you enjoy just walking around looking at a pretty environment and don't care about much else, this game is for you. But I play for the story, and I found the story very much lacking and the ending beyond disappointing. There will be some who will jump me and say that I just don't understand what the story is really about or can't appreciate its realistic approach. The answer to both of those is yes, I do understand what the developers were likely trying to do here. But I still didn't enjoy this game. I am extremely sympathetic toward the main character's family situation. However, I just didn't find either him or Deliliah, the other character, to be likeable. $19.99 just seems like a ridiculous price for this now. It's not even about the short play time some complain about. I'm almost embarassed to say how long it took me to play this. (I spend a lot of time exploring.) It's quality over quantity for me all the way. That being said, I'd advise anyone looking to play this to pick it up during a sale.
DISCLAIMER: I am fully aware that there are many who like this game, and that's 1,000% okay! We are all entitled to our own opinions of games, and what's above is just mine.

As the description of the game itself says, it plays like a blending between ultima and zelda, the game's weirdness can be felt from the beginning all the way to the end. Combat can be extremely unforgiving at times when you find yourself in a headlock from a slime while a midget cyclops zaps you in the junk with a cattle prod, death isn't enough of a setback to make this a real problem though, and if you can look past the simple art style and odd control scheme, there is a LOT to enjoy here, nice soundtrack too.

Hey, you! You there, cowboy! Tired of your fictional life in sunny Texas running a ranch? Why not take a well earned break at Rockingham Castle in 'scenic' Leicestershire, England? Interested? Well step right up, boy...
The Real Texas is an action RPG set mainly in a fantasy world full of bright square blobs and angry lizards which jump at your face if you walk near them. Frickin' lizards. I called one Mr Bitey, and then I shot him in the face, because thankfully in this particular fantasy world you're armed with a gun.
You play as a Texan holidaying in England who steps through a mysterious blue portal into the unknown. The aesthetic is basic but endearing, the controls are simple and responsive, and the mood is light and humorous. The game has been out for four years but was only released on Steam this week, along with the 'Cellpop Goes Out at Night' DLC, which is a more bite-sized sequel. The Real Texas (DLC aside) offers around a dozen hours of gameplay - there's a lot to discover, with plenty of hidden items, clues and NPCs to chat to.
There's some really nice touches here. The writing is pretty good, and the jokes work well for the most part. Think merrily giggling under your breath rather than rolling on the floor crying with laughter. I particularly enjoyed the fact that the characters go about their daily business as you might expect, which involves walking to their house at night to sleep, and then getting up and walking to work again in the morning. Sure, I know that's in Skyrim, but for a small indie title it's extra sprinkles on your Texan cupcake.
Although it's fun stalking the characters around (hey, don't judge me, buddy) they spoil it somewhat by occasionally slowing turning around and staring at you silently, before eventually trotting off to wherever it was they were going.
This game also features chickens in multiple colours! Who doesn't enjoy a game with a variety of chickens in it?
There were a few minor annoyances here and there - you have a very limited inventory size, and whilst you can drop things off in various different boxes, there's a fair bit of to-ing and fro-ing to get the items you need. And going anywhere generally means navigating the face-biting lizards and their blobby friends.
I won't spoil the story, which is fun and inventive, but I will say that a magical tune compels you to dance. On multiple occasions. If you're in the market for a well-written action RPG that won't consume the rest of your summer (I'm looking at you, Witcher 3) you could do far worse than this.

I purchased and put at least 10-20 hours into this game way back in 2012, and really enjoyed finishing it.
I'm a pretty old school PC gamer, but I also enjoy more streamlined console RPGs. To me, this game is the best of both worlds. Some of it feels like the older Ultima games, with lots of freedom when talking to characters, managing and discovering items, puzzling, and RPGing. However many elements are closer to a Legend of Zelda title, with a mostly linear narrative, action based combat, simple character progression, and overworld exploration. Some of the controls may take getting used to. Make sure you have a keyboard/mouse setup to enjoy the game properly.
Graphically it's very stylized. The style grows on you as you play. So does Yesso's amazing soundtrack.
Finally, I'd like to touch on the story and characters. The writing and characters are interesting, but best of all, everything feels like it belongs in the world. The layout of the world makes sense, even as there are many mysteries to discover. There are quirky characters, but they don't spout snarky, self referential lines. After 3 years, I don't recall all the details of the story. But I do remember feeling something *real* as I explored the world of Real Texas.
Highly recommended, and I can't wait to dive back in via the DLC.

The Real Texas is a strange game that's tricky to summarize. It really doesn't settle for doing things conventionally. It has a simple aesthetic that might put some people off. If you don't mind those, there's a great and unique game here.
You're a cowboy who takes a vacation to a castle in England only to find that something unusual has happened. You quickly end up in Strange, Texas, which is probably just purgatory. Obviously, there's a weird sense of humor to this game. While the tone of the game is usually pretty lighthearted, it does take itself seriously when it needs to. Of course, this is a game about purgatory.
The gameplay is a nice mix of exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat. You'll travel between reality (in England) and the town of Strange, Texas (in purgatory). Solving problems in one world helps solve problems in the other. The worlds aren't massive, but there's plenty of detail to make up for it. There are also quite a few side quests to do and secrets to find.
Interactions with objects and NPCs happen via keywords (search, use, talk, etc.). Some are highlighed by conversations, but it's possible to type them out if you want to try something different. This is actually necessary for some things, too.
Most of the progression is based on puzzles and NPCs questlines rather than on combat. These questlines often involve going between the worlds to solve problems on both sides. It's sometimes a little bit unclear what to do next, but I never really found it to be a big problem. These type of segments generally lead into a more straightforward Zelda-ish dungeon with some unique puzzles and combat to mix things up.
The combat is pretty unusual. It's not possible to move while aiming. Shots have to be aimed (somewhat) precisely. The health system is (intentionally) vague. Regaining health happens automatically, but interrupts actions. It's a bit awkward at first, but I think it's interesting. It's not too hard and there's not much penalty for death.
I should also just mention that the soundtrack is fantastic and free to download on the developer's site.
Overall, I just really like The Real Texas. It's a strange, unique game.

I liked this game, though it's certainly not without its flaws.
The concept sounded cool, and the game definitely has a cool visual style, particularly the CG story illustrations and the boss designs -- a bit reminiscent of huke's work on Black Rock Shooter. There's also a great ambient-electronic soundtrack. The meat of the game though is the puzzles, and for the most part the game plays pretty well. The puzzles have a good amount of variation, including a few particularly good ones near the end where the solution is not at all obvious at first.
The game's biggest problem however lies in the physics. Simply put, they're not always predictable. This isn't a problem most of the time, but when you mess up the same puzzle three times in a row because something tipped over in the wrong direction, it can be a bit frustrating. Thankfully dying or resetting a puzzle only sets you back to the start of that puzzle, but it's still not ideal. Also, the English translation is awkward and stilted at best, lending even the human characters a very robotic feel. This makes scenes that seem like they're supposed to be dramatic or funny come off as simply unremarkable.
Recommended if you like puzzle platform games and can deal with a bit of frustration at the physics.

"Emily is Away" has an intriguing idea for its premise, but I was a little disappointed with the execution. In particular, as a player you're offered only the thinnest illusion of choice. Whatever you do, you'll get essentially the same outcome. For example, if you let Emily visit you afrer her break up, she later thinks you took advantage of her; she'll think you're a creep and she'll get back with Brad or Travis. If you don't let her visit you? She'll think you abandoned her in her time of need; again, she'll think you're a creep and get back with Brad or Travis. Do x, you're the creep. Don't do x, you're the creep. Damned if you do, damned if you don't: not much of an interesting "choice". And you're prevented from saying what you might actually say in various situations.
Although "Emily is Away" is actually somewhat immersive on the first playthrough, you soon realise you're just on rails, on the way to an inevitable icky and melancholy conclusion. It's more of an interactive story than a game, then, and that's not necessarily a bad thing; but the story is very simple and a bit... meh... in the end. It leaves you with a vague feeling of futility and frustration at not being able to influence the outcome. If your earlier decisions added up to something a little different each time, this would be a game, and have some replayability value. So I feel like it's a bit of an opportunity missed.

While the Star Wars franchise has had FPS success in the past with the Dark Forces/Jedi Knight titles, they had never attempted to produce a realistic and gritty FPS experience until Republic Commando. Sure, we've fired plenty of blasters, but we've always played as Jedi or a specific protagonist. In Republic Commando, you put on the armor of a soldier. You carry out missions and blast through hordes of enemies for the glory of the Empire!... uh... I mean the Republic! Yes, the Republic...
Republic Commando is set during the prequels but it carries a much more serious tone than the films. The Clone Wars provide the perfect setting for a modern FPS and Lucasarts did a fine job of creating a decent shooter while keeping the player in their beloved Star Wars universe. It may not be the best FPS but it was made very well. The only things I can think of to complain about are the lack of enemy variety and the lack of a sequel.

Whilst this is mostly Sniper Elite v2 with the undead in place of living enemies, to say that's
it is would be really selling it short.
The undead come in various shapes and sizes, mixed together to provide a different pace and challenge. More numerous than it's sequel but with a little less threat due to the map design I feel, it can still be quite overwhelming at times. Sadly as purely a campaign it can get repetitive and lacks that long term replayability (as do most similar games).
What it really excels at is co-op play, and was clearly designed to be played on max difficulty with max players. Potentially a bit easier due to the ability to revive each other, don't let your guard down as you can quickly get overwhelmed by seemingly endless hordes. Sniper rifles versus slow moving targets may sound easy but they do a very good job of shuffling and swaying out of the way, providing some frustration at times.
In single player the music combined with the blood-soaked, corpse ridden environment can get a bit creepy at times, but co-op turns it from more horror to action.

First off, let me say that I love me some Half-Life. Let me also state that it isn't common for me to feel the need to write a review...This game is a total joke. Sure it's free, but it claims to have the original Half-Life in addition to all these player made missions. This does NOT have the original game, and the player made maps are unrealistic in terms of difficulty. Sure a game needs to have challenge to be fun, but these missions are designed in a way that no matter how "good" a player is, they WILL die, many many times. For example. Most of the maps I've tried have "Zombie Gaurds" in them who fire at you with handguns. Sounds harmless right? This alone make even a single gaurd dangerous and any more than that is overkill. Granted, death in this game isn't very punishing because when you die, you can just respawn at the start of the mission (or checkpoint) and all the enemies you've killed will still be dead. So where to begin, State of Decay is flawed and depending on the kind of person you are these flaws are fairly easily overlooked for a period of time until things kick in with force so for now the simple pro's and con's of the game before further elaboration:
Pro's:
- Lots of characters and the DLC only adds to that across 3 scenarios (SoD, Breakdown and Lifeline)
- Good base building actiongs albeit a touch limited
- Weapon diversity, even if it pretty much boils down to guns, melee and throwable
- A fair bit to do if you're a 100% completion person as some of the challenges are more time comsuming than they are hard
Con's:
- Whilst the action is good to begin with and the whole concept of the game is great (in my opinion) after the first 20-30 hours it's very much the same "get this" "save that person" "go here" type of quests
- AI is as dull as a sack of hammers and in the Breakdown DLC (as far as I've seen) the AI doesn't use firearms unless they're in the watch tower at base
- You have to do pretty much everything yourself (see above for partial explaination) as the AI doesn't simply go out in force and search for you whilst you're away over the hill putting a slug between a zombies eyes
- The bugs, whilst not as bad as people make it out to be, I've had some serious "wut?" moments like driving down a road only for the car to hit something and over turn leaving my character hurt, carless and the ensuring explsion luring everything undead in for a good 500 meters
Despite everything this game is easily one of the more enjoyable games I've had a chance to play over the years, whilst not perfect is a solid basis for the series as State of Decay 2 is meant to be in the works. I won't try to play down the bugs as they can be a royal pain or a source of amusement but in literal sense if you're unlucky a bug in game can be the difference between your best survivor making it home goodies and all or being torn in 2 by a freak class zombie. The core game play itself is solid if a bit rinse and repeat after a while, the DLC alters a few things with the likes of lifeline but its very much of a sameness but with a military setting. Breakdown isn't exactly hard as it is trying, as you progress levels you'll get less resources and more zombies / freaks as a result giving what I feel is a false sense of difficulty as they all take the same damage and dish it out but the sheer volume causes the fight or flight moments.
TL;DR
As a whole the game is good, not perfect, but decent enough to keep a zombie fan interested for a while. Anyone with a short attention span may want to avoid it however base builders and to an extent RPS players may enjoy it for its limited RPG like character stats. 7.5/10

I do not recommend this game because it is so ridiculously glitchy.  Being new to the game, I read the reviews, and despite the negative recommendations because this edition should have been a patch instead of a remastered version, I got it anyways.  The indications of poor graphics performance and poor physics were fairly slight in the reviews, while predominant complaints were the former, so I thought, how bad could it be?  Let me tell you new comers, it's that bad.  Let  me break down the problems this game faces.
-sluggish controls;  The action you try to perform may or may not be done on the first button press.  This leads to over zealous and useless button mashing.
-Zombies literally spawn right in front of you and are attacking you before they are visibly spawned in.  This is most notable when the game decides to mess you up, you'll see a few zombies, go whale on them, the music will kick into more serious tones, then you are swarmed with zombies that were nowhere around 2 seconds ago.  You'll start seeing them spawn in right behind a zombie you are executing.
-team npcs are obviously programmed to be more of a nuciance than a help. They are notorious about standing in doorways, not attacking enemies until the last second.  They will NOT help you carry stuff, such as supplies you find, which really makes them pretty useless.  You cannot direct them to move, attack or anything otherwise useful.
-The camera is not your friend.  Half the battle is keeping up with the camera.  Especially while driving.  Nothing says pain in the @$$ like driving with the WASD scheme and rotating the camera manually.  90% of all car accidents in this game is due to blind spots from the camera nemesis.  When fighting, sometimes all you can see is the back side of a zombie or your head.
-Aiming can be a real pain in the nether region.  Scoped weapons aren't truely scoped, as you only zoom in ever so slightly, but the sight is still over the shoulder, and it leads to frustratingly difficult long shots.  Against all survival guide recommendations, spray and pray will end up being the order of the day when you inevitably get swarmed, hopefully you brought enough snacks, painkillers and a backup melee weapon because it's gonna turn into melee when you run out of ammo.
-Vehicle physics seem to have been written by a toddler, because the physics are either as stiff as a board or as bouncy as a rubber ball.  Run over a zombie, you may dent your hood, or you may take your vehicle for a tour of the solar system, you're at the whim of random physics.  On that note, if walking everywhere wasn't a sure recipe for disaster because of materializing zombies, it would be easier to walk.
-Walls and doors may or may not stop a zombie attack or the flames from a molotov.
-Street curb can be an invisible barrier.  Make sure you take a running leap to get up on that sidewalk.
-To search containers, you have to position yourself perfectly in front of it, you can't open that cooler lid standing beside it, because that's IMPOSSIBLE, the same goes for entering and exiting vehicles as well as putting items in the storage compartment.
-Climbing down a ladder can be a perilous endeavor.  Sometimes you'll climb down normally, othertimes you'll swan dive off the platform.  Oh, did I mention how the useless NPCs like to stand in front of doors?  Yeah, they do that with ladders too.  Feel free to push them off, not that you'll teach them any kind of lesson but you'll feel better...
-Last but not least;  the missions are so repetitive, and absolutely pointless...  "<insert name> is in a tough spot." blah blah blah...  The idle NPCs constantly go out, need help, and never bring anything back for the trouble, just a time sink.  You can ignore them, but you'll start having morale problems unless you bring back supplies constantly.  You also run the risk of losing members, especially before you have all your outposts.
Oh, and, whoever decided how much items weigh really needs to spend some time figuring out how much stuff really weighs.  If a person struggles to carry an assault pack filled with a hatchet, 30 rounds of 5.56, a rifle, 3 bottles of asprin, 3 MRE, and 3 grenades, I don't think they would be much use in the military, let alone the apocolypse.  And military trained personel who takes 20-30 seconds' to change a magazine?  I'm looking at you Lifeline.
The game has promise, but I think between the dev's ADD and the DRM (i.e.  lack of any community fixes) it's going to be a broken promise.  Graphically and functionally this game is on par with Xbox1 and the PS2 era, though the concept is there for a great modern game.  Very sad, and I wanted to like this game so badly.  My recommendation, if you absolutely must get it, wait for a sale, but I bet you'll still be disappointed.

After 4 hours of play I already have a love/hate attitude for the game. Concept is good, but events thus far have felt very scripted for an "open" game world. Graphics are decent, love how my laptop is able to stay relatively cool while running. Shooting and targeting objects appears to be fluid for distant combat, but melee combat turns into an inchorent, frantic button mash (there doesn't appear to be any visual targeting for melee like there is for ranged fighting). Had to adjust the mouse sensitivity big time.  My character gets "sucked" into animation sequences during melee combat which kind of sucks (kind of like a RB in an older Madden game getting hit by a defensive lineman, animation sequences once triggered appear to have no way to get out of) There is a dodge button somewhere but there is no tutorial or message on that feature, it's something you'd have to look up in the controls. There are help messages for some of the controls but it's the basic ones over and over again thus far. The death sequences are well done, gets kind of addictive splattering zombie brains. The bad is that zombies tend to spawn in the middle of walls and fences, while also having a terrible respawn script running. You'll be walking in a forest and all of a sudden a zombie will respawn right next to you. You'll clear an area out only to have zombies magically reappear instead of them walking to the area from an offmap starting point. The UI has a good layout but terrible functionality attached to the buttons. Easy to accidently purchase a feature with your influence currency, particularl when you're starting out and learning the controls... which leads me to saving. There is no save functionality. It's all automated. Which doesn't work for the flow of the game. You'll want to be slow and quiet, which means you'll have spent many minutes/hours of playing and need to go do something  in real life yet there is  no way to save except for reaching end of missions and "magical" save points. Getting in a car is no fun whatsoever. The controls are bad, and it doesn't even feel like you're driving a vehicle on earth, it's more like piloting a paper airplane in space. It's been fun to level up a character, but the inability to not switch to other members in the group until the game decides it's ok is very annoying. I would purchase the game again for the $30 price, overall experience has been 75-83 range on a 100 scale, it's just really disappointing that some of the features are the way they are...And probably would have been♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at anything more then that. (Have not purchased played the earlier version which is no longer available, this has been my first experience). If I could give a sideways thumbs I would, but will go with thumbs up, there's been enough good to overcome the shortcomings thus far.

A game called The Real Texas by Canadian game developer Kitty Lambda which is set in England, kind of, and only gets weirder from there.
First off, the game is not for everyone -- if you're put off by the art in the game's screenshots, the rest of the game won't change your mind. That said, the art, like the music, writing, and setting all work together -- this is very clearly not a AAA game, but that's probably why it's able to nail its unique tone.
With a living, breathing world filled with bizzare characters and weird things to interact with, The Real Texas is an incredibly cool and surprisingly complex game that kind of defies any sort of genre classification (though it's probably closest to being an RPG).
Also the music is incredible -- kind of bizzaro Harvest Moon with a bit of Earthbound and just slightly-off, like the rest of the game.
You should definitely check it out if you're a fan of games like Else Heart Break or old CRPG games like Fallout or Planescape (at least in terms of exploration and character interaction, not so much combat as The Real Texas is a stat-less RPG game). You'll know within the first thirty minutes if the game's for you or not.

Recommend but with heavy caveats.
First things first - it's a physics based puzzle platformer, not an action game. Don't be fooled by the action-esque aesthetics.
Gameplay is fun and reasonably challenging, art is fantastic when it comes to stages and NPCs, and beyond fantastic when it comes to main characters, CGs and backgrounds. Seriously, CG and protagonists/bosses sprites can put many AAA games to shame. Story is interesting but is a bit cliche (you're going to predict all beats and twists an hour before they come, let alone revealed).
The only 2 negatives: it's a physics based puzzle platformer with all problems that entails: solutions are quite wonky and imprecise, you can get screwed up by your action missing by the couple pixels or milliseconds, or by just straight up RNG. Second negative - it seems that art and music is where lion share of dev effort was put in while actual coding was done by either B-team or people who didn't make any 2D platformers before. Game has some collision detection issues, some occasional performance problems and extremely wonky physics.
Overall game is great but you might get mildly(/extremely) infuriated during some of its parts.
P.S. Someone on the team had an "ingenious" (<- notice the sarcasm) idea to map "interact" to ↑ button so if you're playing on the controller - get used to a lot accidental interactions. Oh, btw, did i mention that the "reset puzzle even if you've just solved it after spending 10+ min" objects in game do their function immediately upon interaction, without showing a confirmation prompt? Yep, have fun.

So, basically, Paint the Town Red is a fighting game. There is lots of gore, if you're into that stuff. The gore is a bit unique when compared to other games, or actually a lot. I mean, you've probably seen a head get busted and blow into bits... But HALF a head?

Weapons in the game though. You can nail people with pool marbles, stools, even steaks. Anything that you can grab, it's yours to fight with, so be creative with your killing.
Your character has power. Literally. Killing people will give you them. (Don't try this in real life though) If you're in a tight spot, just hold "R" and choose a move. Alien Swarm is a Top-Down shooter with emphasis on multiplier teamwork with four total players. Alien Swarm was developed by Valve and released mid 2010. Many of the initial players were lured to the game by the lure of an Alien hat you can unlock via an achievement on Alien Swarm.
You are a member of a team of space troopers who are investigating the circumstances of a seemingly abandoned/evacuated space colony, and trying to recover whatever data is still available.
Alien Swarm is played from a top-down shooter angle from a 60 degree camera angle, you move your cursor to aim, and can simultaneously walk any direction using the keyboard keys.
Some people have dedicated servers for Alien swarm, however most people will simply host a game from their computer, your latency will depend on the hosts internet settings and physical location.
As you succeed or fail missions you will gain experience, this experience is put towards your level, when you level you unlock new weapons, armor, and tools. There are 25 potential weapons that can be chosen from, including special weapons like sentry guns.
There are 66 achievements on Alien Swarm, after your first level you will get a good grasp of the different achievement difficulties, at the time that I'm writing this review, I've earned 53 achievements, most of which were earned either grinding by myself
, or joining small groups online or playing with a friend occasionally.
There are two types of tough achievements: Beat the game on the hardest difficulties, and speed run achievements, both of these require a fairly coordinated group of players to work together and know what they're doing.
The best part about Alien Swarm is that it's completely free! This is probably because the project was scrapped after the first campaign. It's nice that this game is free, but I would have preferred to pay for the game if it had a single player mode and more campaigns.
The good news is Alien Swarm was released with an “Alien Swarm software development kit” which is also free, so the Steam Community could create their own campaigns! Second best thing to the original dev's picking up the project again.
Story: forgettable, but this game is more about the experience then the story narrative. Gameplay: addicting, fun, best to play with friends. Achievements: Many are soloable, you're better off with a group of pug players the easiest difficulty is your best bet if you want to learn the game. Not an easy 100% completed game. Price: Completely free to play.

I've put a lot of hours into this game on the original Xbox, and I plan to put more into the PC version, and even see if the multiplayer servers are still up (doubt it).

Worth the Buy, if you are a fan of Star Wars, this is a definite buy for your steam library.  Hell, even if you're just a shooter fan, this is a good recommendation, as the mechanics in this game are solid.  So go ahead and try this game out.  You won't be dissapointed.

As a fan of the game Myst and the Choose Your Own Adventure books as a kid, Firewatch was a throwback to the "good old days" with more mature content and modern graphics. It took a little getting use to the controls and gameplay at first, but once it got going the game was a lot of fun. The storyline, plot, and scenery were exciting and got better as the game progressed. Firewatch also made you feel like you had a real connection to the avatar and characters in the game; I only wish there was more content and more maps to explore. As a suggestion I think there could have been a better way to display the map and compass while moving, interact with objects, and toggle auto-run to make the game play a bit smoother. All in all, it was a great game for the price and I would highly recommend it!

The game is short so you the player can go back and connect the dots yourself. By taking in the enviroment as the devs have made good use of it by placing the dots throughout. You just have to find and analyze those dots critically. Then after connect them to all the ideas presented in the game to forge your own supported theories. In most games the ending does that for you, but instead the game allows you to do so and gives the tools to do so yourself. So this ending is not bad game design rather smart game design. So if your the player that just clocks in and that is it this game might be for you but if your the player that is willing to look games critical manner then this game is for you. I myself when I find the time will be revisting this game.

I hate leaving a bad review for a game that is this beautiful, has good dialogue, and is story driven. But I feel I must.
For a team of 50+ working on this title, the "spit and polish" shows. The environment is well-crafted, the voice acting is spot on, and the motivation is good through the first two acts.
But it all falls apart in the third act. The story loses its thread; it's almost like they were told to publish the game *now* and they just decided to end things where they were. They could have done so much more with the main two characters. As it is, there is so much potential wasted. I don't need a "tidy ending" in a game like this, but the mystery aspect of the game doesn't inform your character's motivation at all...and prevents the game from reaching a larger, more satisfying character development for him. If I had a magic wand to wave and could put this game back into development for another year, would the writing have turned out better?
I also wish the choices didn't railroad you so heavily into flirting, but I guess that's what the creators wanted.

I find it difficult to decide whether I liked this game or didn't. The cartoonish aesthetic definitely works well and there are plenty of interesting sights to see. The voice acting is also pretty much top notch. The narrative managed to creep me out, which means it works as intended. I would've liked to see a little more resolution at the end. Maybe I'm approaching this too much as an adventure game rather than computerised fiction (I'm deliberately avoiding the term interactive fiction here, as it's not so much your actions that drive the story). I guess I'm recommending Firewatch by a narrow margin, but think of it more as a work of art than as a game. Not everybody likes the same types of art.

Let's start with positives.  The game's art style is really fantastic, to say the least.  A nice, 'chunky' visual aesthetic.  The open-ended approach to puzzle platforming is refreshing, and very well thought-out.  Honestly, taken from a step back, the game is refreshing to play, and I wish there was more creativity like Giga Wrecker's in modern gaming mechanics.
To quickly summarize what the game lacks.. It feels very quickly pushed out.  The physics of movement feels a little lacking; sometimes you fall through what appear to be solid surfaces.  Sometimes, in the vein of classic side-scrolling action platformers, you take one hit, which causes you to bounce into a second enemy or stage hazard (most notably and egregiously in the Astra fights).  And sometimes, the physics engine just straight-up disagrees with you.  All three of the above will generally result in death, especially in the latter half of the game, with the oft usage of spikes and pitfalls.
Because of the relatively quick loading times, it's not as much of an issue as it could be, but because of the nature of some rooms, you're forced to repeat several sections before you can get back to the segment that caused your death.. only to die to it again because of one of the above, or when you accidentally push the reset button for a fraction of a second.
The music's lacking, and the localization's even moreso.  It's exciting to see Game Freak's name on something considering how much of a mainstay it is regarding my childhood memories regarding the pokemon franchise, so that's what caused me to gravitate towards the game, and, I think, in a lot of cases, it's the same for most of the people who ended up picking Giga Wrecker up.  But genuinely, someone really need to go through these sorts of games with a fine comb before they get pushed out.  I was expecting more, especially after grasping just how intuitive and clever the game's core mechanics are.  Please, make more games like this, but treat them with kid gloves next time, okay?  This sort of result is just not acceptable.

Don't waste your money on this garbage. If you need a screen recording software for games, use FRAPs, or anything else, really. This program is awful. I recorded an hour of raw footage and the recording was corrupted at the end. I tried recording numerous times thereafter and each time the recording was either corrupt or had graphical glitches like greyed out pallets or inverted color schemes. I've never actually wanted my money back for anything that I've bought on Steam, but this makes the first time for that. Please do yourself a favor and do not purchase this program. You will regret it if you do.

*This review has been edited after the voice-recording issue had been resolved, and adjusted further after spending a couple more weeks using it. Lots of info here. This review may not change your mind about the software, but it's intended to provide you with the information you need to make that decision.
This is a great, cheap product, depending on what you need from it. Records audio and video pretty well, and there's a good variety of codecs to choose from, with some additional options for Picture in Picture and limiting your fps if you need to, adding a watermark and such. Little things like that. To compare this to FRAPS, this will provide you with high-quality visuals if you can afford the harddisk space. The default MPEG-4 codec (which it recommends) will eat up approximately 225-250 MB for 2 minutes of footage (varies on how much is going on visually) at 1080p 30fps. You WILL want to experiment with codecs and bitrates to achieve the best performance for what you need out of whatever you're recording. This is something that FRAPS does not do, as FRAPS uses a custom codec that you'll need to obtain again should you decide to reinstall a fresh OS or uninstall FRAPS. I've enjoyed FRAPS a lot, and consider it a beast as it taxes your PC and requires really hefty hardware and lots of RAM, but it's very simple to use. This software requires more fine-tuning than FRAPS. Experiment and find that sweet spot.
To compare this to xSplit Broadcaster/Gamecaster (no, this does not allow live streaming) you can make use of the Picture in Picture functions to place a webcam (adjustable size, but you can only place the PnP in one of 9 spaces, left/center/right from top to bottom, think tic tac toe), This is useful for those of you who may be making videos for YouTube (etc...) and you would like to have a webcam for your face and your voice commentary, and even has Chroma settings for those of you who can use them effectively. xSplit does this as well, but allows you to resize, crop, and place the screens anywhere. xSplit Gamecaster has more of an in-game interface as opposed to xSplit Broadcaster, and there are things in Broadcaster that you can't do in Gamecaster (in regards to window/screen/display positions). Speaking of voice commentary, this brings us to an issue that I had earlier with the software.
liteCam has some audio settings that really need some work. If you have multiple voice recording devices plugged in, you cannot change the order of priority/order of those devices. This is where things get tricky and where the real meat of the original version of this revised review was.
I use a Logitech G35 USB headset for voice recording/capture, and a Logitech 720p webcam with built-in microphone, and I also have the Screaming Bee audio drivers for modifying my voice. My G35 was set as my default voice communication device as far as my OS was concerned and should have taken priority. liteCam was using the Screaming Bee drivers by default when I had placed the check mark (on liteCam's audio settings) to enable my microphone and did not give me a choice in the matter. Because of this, I could record game audio, but not my voice, and adjusting the settings another way allowed me to record my voice, but not the game audio. It was one or the other, but not both, all because it was picking up the wrong drivers. Again, Screaming Bee isn't physical hardware, it's a device driver I can use to modify my voice, and Windows recognizes my G35 headset as the default voice communication device, but liteCam didn't care or give me the option to choose it. This wasn't fixed until I just up and disabled Screaming Bee. The microphone settings work now, but I'm not entirely sure if it's really recording from my headset or my webcam now. A fix or adjustment to this in the future would be nice. Just for clarification, this was all accomplished hours later after thinking about it and writing an angry email to the devs. The product is still new and there was no actual support in the forums here for it other than "send an email to
THX".
Others have complained about stuttering or issues with their FPS. This may be a case by case issue. I've not noticed many problems with my FPS because I'm not running on default settings. My montor doesn't display any higher than 60, so try not to set your settings higher than you can handle. It will give you options to adjust the framerate for your games as well as the recording's framerate. Be sure to adjust both of those values before playing any games.
This software also allows you to edit your videos you recorded but your only option is to trim from left or right. You will want to obtain some decent video-editting software. That's a given though. Unless you're just starting out, most of you who would be interested in this software may already have editing software installed. When recording in xSplit, liteCam, or FRAPS, I'll still be running my footage through Vegas or similar programs.
Last couple issues: Running the program through Steam will make it difficult to invite to multiplayer games. Exiting liteCam can crash some of your programs. I've had it crash ArmA 3 as well as the Raptr desktop app. A patch came through last night, resolved the crashing issues in one area, but caused another issue elsewhere. Again, your milage may vary, maybe they can fix it, but that's all on them. Finally, there's a woman's voice that says "Recording Ready"/"On"/"Off". It's loud, it's annoying, and there's no way to turn it off. You can't even mute liteCam from your volume mixer.

If they continue to update this software on a more or less semi-regular basis until it's perfect, this one is definitely a keeper. Recorded some footage of Grand Theft Auto Online on Xbox 360 using this software in Video Recording mode on my Hauppauge HD PVR2 (1080p @ 30 fps) for 18 minutes. FRAPS used up 37 GB and this used up about 800 MB before running it through Vegas to knock it down further. 24 Minutes of Little Pink Best Buds prototype on liteCam requred 2 GB.
