Wow, how should I start. I just finished the second run through - one normally and the other on the Audio Tour DLC. I have to say the latter was the better experience and it really wrapped up the game very nicely.
Firewatch is a story that explores a trove of human emotions that aren't usually covered in video games. The game explores the regret, pain, tarnished hopes and the very nature of just running away from it all. Despite the depths of such emotions, you see a story of a relationship that blooms between the actors as they were set on a path from a series of mysterious events. I see the main story (the mystery) as a tool to build the characters. It is definitely suspenseful and intriguing on its own but it is emotionally compelling with the stellar character development that happens alongside the 'mystery' side of the story. The choices you make does not affect the ending but that was never the point. The choices you make affects and determines the dynamics of the only relationship you have in the game. If the game spoke to you in an emotional manner, that itself is enough for you to play it a second time to change the way your relationship played out.
Props to the developers for developing an 'Audio Tour' DLC. I have never replayed a game to experience a different ending/story. This was the first. And it was largely due to the Audio Tour. It will give you a vast insight to the story as well as to the technical aspects of developing a game. Not only did it make the game so much more meaningful, it will give you a bigger reason to come back and build your character and relationship in another way. The Audio Tour also gives you 'extra content' by informing you of the little things you can do to that you would most probably have never found out on your own. For those of you who disliked the way the game/ story turned out, I strongly suggest giving the Audio Tour a try.

GIGA WRECKER follows the path of a cyborg girl whose world has been destroyed and now has the power of reconstructing debris and scraps into various weapons in order to find the reason of it all and push back the robot army invasion. There's still a little bit more to it than just this, but I'd like to keep it spoiler-free. Don't expect anything too deep or fancy, though.
As for me the present level of storytelling is fine enough and I enjoyed following it instead of just skipping everything. It's admittedly very anime-like and therefore contains some tropes (as the protagonist's tsundere vibe) some might consider annoying, but I was perfectly fine with it. Not only because I enjoy anime in general, but also because the gameplay/the whole package is the main focus in the end. The story is delivered mainly in rather short dialogues with artworks sprinkled in sometimes.
In the current game state there are still a lof of spelling errors and sometimes the dialogues feel written rather poorly, although it might add up on the game's charm. However, it's been stated already that those errors should decrease with the final release update.
GW is a "2D puzzle-platform action game" as stated in the description already, you probably got that so far. But how good is it really? Well...
vary in difficulty a lot. You might run into very hard ones right after defeating the first boss and run into quite easy ones in a later stage, but to me that's what kept it running, since some of those puzzles (usually physics focused) can be rather tricky and even frustrating at times. Being able to relax (or wreck) a bit after a tough challenge makes you not give up on the puzzles/the game. Apart from that solving those riddles is highly satisfactory, since you get to witness the progress you're making right away, may it be an additional story part, a lot of EXP or a new weapon skin (which are hilarious btw - ever fought with a swordfish/ice cream combination?).
Although there are different ways to approach a puzzle every now and then, (very) few of them didn't make that much sense to me and I pretty much solved them by chance or luck just by randomly destroying my surroundings. This might be intentional, but made me wonder if I actually found the solution and - if not - what the solution is supposed to be. Also some of the puzzles containing lasers seemed pretty unclear to me since they kept changing directions for apparently no particular reason other than placing a block on top of it which should have just blocked it. I managed to solve them anyways, but still a thing to keep in mind. With those few exceptions the physics system works fine.
is pretty decent. Every action takes place immediately and I rarely had any problems controlling the character. I got used to the way it behaves rather easily. Unless the map's design is at fault for making you die by containing a lot of traps, enemies etc, this part of the game is executed smoothly.
focuses on the ARCHE abilities of course. I won't explain them in detail now since they're being presented in the trailer already which gives a quite good overview. You either use those tools to crush everything in your way or in order to explore the maps a bit. The four different weapons (apart from the default debris ball) make these things a fun experience through and through and since it's possible to upgrade them via the skill tree, it's up to you (to a small degree) which weapon's going to be your main tool. Furthermore I never had the feeling of over- or underusing one of them since each puzzle usually asks you to do something slightly different or combine your abilities. (Apart from that you can still just spam your attacks and wreck the map in case things aren't going your way. Way to release stress included!)
Except from a few upgrades or the increasing of your total health the skill tree doesn't feel that game changing in the end. It DOES change things for sure, but since you're improving on your own anyways while the game continues, it became a collectible-like thing for me at some point. Then again it's very easy to farm EXP since you'll never lose those points no matter how often you rewind time to recreate the map (therefore EXP orb blocks, as well). I never farmed them on purpose and ended up with a fully upgraded skill tree and almost 11 points left to spare. Probably the only part of the game that isn't a challenge.
The background music was another factor for me to keep going, even when being stuck at a certain puzzle or boss. While during the stages the music usually has an ambient and relaxing vibe, boss fight themes are uptempo tracks with melodies and beats that kept me pumped for another try. All of the tracks belong to different kinds of electronic subgenres and also feel a bit anime-like (when it comes to boss fights) at times.
Reading through the other reviews the BGM seems to be some kind of ambivalent aspect and I understand that some might consider the music a tad bit annoying after a while, but I enjoyed it a lot (I'd probably even buy an OST CD, but that's just me).
If you despise pixel/2D art or character art as seen in anime and manga, you won't like the visuals, simply put. I do like both, so no downside for me. However, there isn't too much variety and detail to find here, most likely in order to keep the stages easy on the eyes since there is a lot going on sometimes. Characters and enemies, though, are pretty detailed for such a game in my opinion, which leads to a minor...
When the camera zooms out in a few stages in order to give you an overview of the huge puzzle, the character becomes a little bit blurry due to a black outline that somewhat flickers around while moving. Not to a disturbing degree and you probably won't pay too much attention to it, but still.
GIGA WRECKER is a game every platform and/or puzzle game fan should try out for sure. In case you're also a fan of anime/manga, you'll be good to go. There are still a handful of (minor) flaws, but nothing gamebreaking in my opinion, not to mention that this game isn't fully released yet (upcoming patch will be the final one to leave Early Access) and the developers still have some room to act. I finished the game within 15 hours with every collectible achieved (achievements weren't active at time of completion) and a fully upgraded skill tree. There is also a level editor which I didn't try out yet and therefore didn't review, but from the looks of it, some additional hours should be worth spending there, too. I'll be definitely coming back to this title, though, and I'm eagerly waiting for more.

"An incredibly fun and unique post apocalyptic platforming/puzzle/action game from our friends at Game Freak (The Pokemon Developers!) with a green haired cyborg girl as the cherry on top!"
+++Pros+++
+Incredibly fun (the most important thing in any game and this game has fun in spades)
+Great Brain teasing physics based Puzzles (using your various abilities to break structures and move them for stage progression. etc...)
+Enjoyable fast paced combat (and not too difficult either)
+Great fun platforming (which goes along with the puzzles and combat)
+Beautiful art, and graphics
+Bizzarely Beautiful Nanomachine infused post apocalyptic setting
+Entertaining characters (and a fun poweful female main character)
+Great music that fits perfectly with the game's atmosphere
+Your weapons are also used as your tools for puzzle solving
+Powerful fun bosses that are all awesome robot girls
+The game doesn't take itself too seriously or not seriously enough with a great mixture of comedy and drama (there's nothing worse than a "trying too hard" post apocalyptic game or series that has no or very little comedy in it.)
+There is a level editor with pretty much everything in the game at your disposal so you can make your own stages
+Simple and fun progression system/skill tree
+No "lives" system (I pretty much only died to the bosses, but outside of that I think when I died the game simply placed me in the same room close to where I died or at the nearest save point)
+Integration of story and gameplay mechanics (The game explains what the save points function as in the universe of the game, and how the upgrade system works for your character in that world, things like that always a plus for me)
---Negatives (these are all pretty minor to me though)---
-The bosses may be pretty frustrating until you figure out how to correctly fight them
-Some of the puzzles (particularly the later ones in The Mine) can be cryptic and frustrating (most have a simple solution once you figure it out though) I'm also not sure if I solved some of the more cryptic and difficult puzzles correctly, but after getting stuck on some of them for over ten or twenty minutes I was ready to take any solution I could
-Some of the character animations seem a bit weird, I'm not sure how to describe it (like they are stiff or jerky?), but not a big issue, and not that noticeable while playing
-Reika (the main character) has a mirrored character model, her robotic arm is supposed to be on her left side, but when turning left it switches over to her right arm, a very minor issue, but it bugged me a little.
+++Maybe Positive/Maybe Negative---
+-The game is originally in Japanese and has obviously been translated by somebody who speaks english as a second language, some people might find this annoying (since it results in some perhaps unintentional humor), but I think it helps give the game a very unique and entertaining charm, and since it's been done this way you get a more "pure" translation in my opinion.
I'd definitely recommend this game to anybody who is even slightly interested in it, at the time of this writing the game is still in alpha but I had a blast with it and a ton of fun.
Also the developers have said the price may go up for the full version, so I'd definitely recommend buying it if you are on the fence.

I bought this game on release and for years since I've always wanted to go back and play it again, but I could never remember why until I bought it again. Despite having to jump through numerous hoops in order to get it optimised for a modern operating system, Republic Commando is a surprisingly wonderful game given that it is, in many ways, a rather standard corridor shooter.
Whilst genre-wise it may play as a rather standard FPS shooter, the writing of the characters and the missions gives a much greater depth to the world than it otherwise ought to have. You play the commander of a crack team of Republic commandos, and your teammates all have distinct and consistent personalities, and are autonomous enough to make them seem genuinely intelligent. Yes, you will be giving orders for the most part - and their AI is programmed well enough so as to feel like they're an extension of yourself, as they should - but you won't need to tell them to heal themselves, or attack the bad guys if a threat looms, and should you be overcome and you need help, they will be promptly at your side healing you at the risk of their own lives. And this all helps to develop a genuine bond with your fellow squadmates, particularly as the game is much easier when you have their help, further emphasising the importance of your cumulative strength as a team.
On top of this, the missions, whilst comprising of many parts, manage to consistently escalate the stakes until by the end of the mission you feel a genuine and frantic rush of adrenaline as you plunge headlong into the final stages of each operation. And it's the little things that make a difference - for example, whereas most games would have an alert announcement indicating that your vessel will self-destruct, in this case they're serious. And it's these little things that actually make you emote as a player, which is what any experience should do, whether it's a book or a movie or a video game.
And thus, Republic Commando manages to rise above it's state and hold up quite well as a challenging and compelling experience.
I'd recommend it to Star Wars fans primarily, although I think it has a wider appeal because of the quality of the writing.

As soon as I started the game I knew I'd end up having to write a review for it. But even still I feel like words won't do this game justice, you have to play it for yourself.
The envronment and graphics are unique and simple in style but absolutely breathtaking nonetheless. I couldn't stop taking screenshots because every 5 minutes I'd stumble upon a gorgeous landscape I just had to capture.
I really liked how interactive the characters were, I enjoy when the character you're playing actually interacts with others and doesn't just stay silent. And I enjoyed the different options of dialogue you could choose from at different points. The witty comments between your character and Delilah were always enjoyable and light.
The story itself will leave you guessing until the very end, and will make you question whether you think you know what's gonna happen next. I could never be absolutely certain about anything, and I love a game that isn't predictable.
I also felt I could personally connect with the character you play (Henry) on certain levels, and I find that I can't do that often so it was refreshing to have a character I could relate to as I played.
The gameplay is very smooth, and I love that Henry interacts with the environment. Instead of just jumping down a ledge, Henry will actually take his time hopping down. I love games in which the character actually realistically interacts with their environment.
I'm not sure if I appreciate or dislike this, but the music was only used in certain parts rather than a constant soundtrack playing. I do think it heightened the more important points of the story, and the music that was used was simply gorgeous and really helped with the mood in certain situations.
Overall, I thought the game was very well done. The voice actors were incredible, and I just really enjoyed playing it.

What can I say about this that has not already been said? Probably nothing, but as this was one of the games that got me back into gaming after a long hiatus I have to say something.
In a gaming market saturated with zombie survival games what interested me about State of Decay was the clear George A. Romero inspiration.
The zombies are classic Romero, a slow ponderous mass of dead flesh that are all kinds of messed up, and as such they often lull the player into a false sense of security with their weak, slow movements. This is their weakness but collectively this is also their strength.
It is easy to forget than more than a handful of these creatures are much than a match for the average player and often while allowing yourself to get carried away it is easy to overstep and find yourself face to face with a zombie horde. The results of this are obvious and as you struggle fruitlessly for what seems like hours the end is inevitable.
And it is an end.
Once a character dies they are gone for good and if you have not succeeded in bringing in new survivors the longevity of your community is in real question. This fact, coupled with the need to find recourses and protect your borders, can easily overwhelm even a well organised player; leading to ultimate destruction.
There’s a lot good about this game, but I am sad to say it also has a few negatives that grate on the player the longer they play.
Characters are almost non existent, use of dialogue is simplistic and does not allow for much variety and the result of this is that missions can become formulaic and lack interest. This is not as bad as it seems, as the open world provides a great deal of interest in itself; but greater character development would have improved my personal enjoyment a vast amount.
The worst thing about this game must be the pure stupidity of many of the character, partly this is due to the afore mentioned lack of variety but its also because the random nature of the story means that often characters take up residence in the most foolish of places.
This means that the player is sometimes frustrated by the need to protect characters who are simply too dumb to care about. On occasion prompting this particular player to wish I could put them out of their misery (or at least mine).
All this having been said, I enjoyed this game a great deal; in spite of some poor storytelling the game mechanics worked well to instil alternating moments of the habitually mundane and the fight-for-your-life terror that makes the game rather unusual. As in the Romero movies that I feel inspired the game, State of Decay is less about the living dead and more about how we react to them, the terror is not about death but about how we live.
I, for one, am hoping that the poor storytelling and awful characterisations will either be fixed at some point with future updates or will disappear in a continuation of the game franchise.

Six years on, and this is still a blast to play. While Battlefield: Bad Company 2 polarised Battlefield veterans on launch from being more simplified than Battlefield's traditional 64 player large scale firefights, Bad Company 2 is the perfect combination of arcadey shooter gameplay and co-operative teamwork.
The map design is specticular, and you can have a blast of fun just playing in the few maps you're used to, but every map has their strategies and possibilities for experimentation. Maps with open areas will require a greater focus on land vehicles, while ones with more buildings will require a greater use of the game's extremely satisfying destuctive physics to be utilised.
The class system has been retuned from previous Battlefield games, with only four classes instead of the seven featured in Battlefield 2. This, however, works very well, and each class has their own specific features and tools to be used in different scenarios, creating a more "rock-papers-scissors" approach to the battlefield, which I honestly prefer, as it puts more weight on each class.
As of early 2016, there is still plenty of both conquest and rush server up and full, so I highly recommend a purchase. Fans of Battlefield 3 and 4 who were unhappy of the progression of the series will be right at home here. Perhaps my favourite Battlefield game.

Firewatch is more of an experience than a classic game, as the story is quite linear and failing is impossible. It may belong to the adventure genre best.
You play as Henry, a decent guy, who seeks out the loneliness of being a look-out in the wilderness of Wyoming in order to escape his adverse situation at home. For the first half of the game, this works out somewhat as it seems to be an enjoyable experience. I actually felt like being in the woods, enjoying the great light effects and the mellow sounds of mother nature, including this ever-liberating wind sound.
However, things take a mystical turn, but the resolution of the plot isn't mystic at all - it reveals Firewatch as an anti-game. Sort of like Spec Ops: The Line, the game doesn't serve diversion or escapism; no, it made me come back to reality in quite a harsh way. Turns out that the end is quite realistic, depressing and mature in a sense that it's not your usual hero-antihero-story, and neither a story of survival nor extraordinary events after all.
Firewatch left me with a lasting impression, which is basically the most important thing what art can do. A game you'd just forget can easily be regarded as a waste of time. However, it makes me feel quite blue.
And now a bit more profane:
Pro:
-unique, at least in my experience
-good voice acting
-very lovely graphical design, especially the light effects
-an adult story
considerable:
-if you play super-slow like I do, you're finished in 8 hours, but most people probably need no more than 4-5 hours. I wouldn't spend more than 6$ on this.
-your expectations regarding the story may be hurt. If you don't like surprises (the real unexpected ones), you will probably get angry.
-Gameplay is reduced to the minimum, it's basically walking, talking and navigating (no fighting, crafting, real puzzle solving etc.)

You could probably sit and play this game with your kids, enjoying the interactive education of learning random new facts.
You can also do what I would do - and play it as a drinking game. Get a question wrong? Take a shot. Bored of strip poker? Remove a piece of clothing!
So I guess I could describe this game as fun for the whole family, in one way or another...
Really though - it's free for the first 200 questions and then a couple of bucks for 500 more if you want them. I personally don't think it's worth extra unless the cons listed below are addressed. They're all facts you could get from google or reading wikipedia, but this game gives a fun way to explore completely random subjects, with a cute and simple presentation that definitely makes this game suitable for younger gamers.
It does have some issues that such a simple game shouldn't and I hope will be addressed in the future as I think really impair it. Some of the achievements seem bugged, and one of the questions I googled and I'm pretty sure they have the wrong answer. It would also be really nice to have an extra explanation as to WHY something is true or false, rather than just giving an answer. If you're interested in finding out the details, you then have to move over to google. It has no scoreboard, no way of tracking how well you've done in the past or anything like that, so no real competitive nature unless you're keeping track yourself. There were also some obvious English language mistakes that make me think that it wasn't created (or spellchecked) by an English native speaker. The animation is also slow, so if you want a fast paced game this is definitely not it leading to it being a little bit boring if you're not 5 years old or in the process of downing a bottle of vodka.
So in short, good for kids, drunks or alleviating a brief bit of boredom. Simple idea, but not a perfect execution. It gets a tentative recommendation because it's free and certainly still enjoyable in the right situation, but it's a shame that it really doesn't reach its potential and isn't as educational as it could be.

As one would expect with an Early Access title it is very rough. Gameplay doesn't flow as well as it should and hopefully this will be fixed later on. Animations themselves are quite rough and don't read well when the camera pulls out. Despite the camera pulling in and out appropriatley to match what's happening on screen an adjustable camera view would be preferable. I'm only 40 minutes in as of writing this and will update as I continue playing and updates occur, but I can at least say that even this far in I'm still not out of the tutorial and that everything in the core gameplay is rough and clunky. Sometimes the jump button will result in the player character jumping and it's not eactly uncommon for them to fall through walls and floors either, especially when in mid-air.
The biggest fault so far has been the game's hook of creating and distorting platforms with the rubble the player obtains. It presents interesting ideas, but the game is very picky about using them for combat and they generally only work half the time. In certain tutorial segments the player is outright restricted from using any attacks or skills that aren't the one it asks them to use, despite levels being designed to allow for other skill usage. Levels are actually designed with reset markers in case the player somehow screws up a puzzle and needs to reset the entire screen. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it helps highlight the faults in design when you have to reset a puzzle multiple times as a result of the physics acting up.
So far there is little difference in visual design, but I'm hoping it changes in the later levels so I won't really count that against it unelss that is the case later on.
Wait for a few updates and see how reviews have changed. I've no doubt the devs will turn this into a fun title by the end of things, but for now I'd advise on waiting before you pick this up.

I'll start off by saying that I got the YOSE edition during the steam summer sale and it was worth every ~$8 that I spent on it. At this point I have 38 hours into it after beating the storyline, I haven't even touched the DLC yet. The best thing about this game is the gameplay, I would compare it to Left for dead with a little bit of GTA mixed in. I'll make list of my pros and cons so you don't have to read a wall of text.
I'll write a bit more on the cons after
I think a lot of the cons boil down to the fact that the game is a console port. I have a beefy gaming PC with a brand new Nvidia 970, 8Gb of ram, and an i5 @3.2 which can run most games at 60fps on the highest settings. That said I had a lot of issues of texture and environment pop in, really poor draw distance, and just overall very poorly optimized for PC. In fact I turned on Fraps to check my frames per second to find out that if Vsync is enabled it locks the fps at 30. The biggest problem that I had was when driving, when moving at a higher speed the draw distance issue was really obvious and the game itself would lag witch made it even harder to drive giving the amount of invulnerable objects that there are to dodge.
The other big issue that I started to notice after playing for a few dozen hours was how bad the menu and management system is. There is absolutely zero character management if you are not playing a given character. In a game about survival and asset management that seems like a big oversight and missed opportunity. I imagine it was partially planned that way since many of the missions revolve around helping out or rescuing the other survivors that have left the base but it would have been was more fun to designate certain characters for scavageing roles or to be able to lock more important characters to the base. Special characters actually fill roles in the base and give your base bonuses if they are manageing the kitchen, farm, etc so it sucks to have them go out. I think I logged in one day to find all my neighboring survivors had died while I was out which kind of sucked. But realisticly in my playthrough I think I only noticed one of my survivors dieing and that was because we were on a mission together and he was torn in half by a tank mob.
The last think I would mention is that there really isn't a lot of explination for the dynamics of the game. There are a lot of things happening on the map at a given time and the dispatch character will constantly be reminding you that your running out of time to take care of certain things but for the life of me I couldn't tell what the consequences of my action or inaction were.
Anyway, the cons seem big but the gameplay is fun enough that you should be able to make it through the campaign without too much work. Also there are some fixes out there for for some of the problems that I pointed out, if you tweak any of your PC games then you should be able to find them. I would highly recommend picking this game up if its on sale and it is probably still worth it at full price. It certanly scratched that Left for Dead itch that I didn't know that I had.
p.s. - If they skinned this game with The Walking Dead and fixed some of my cons it would be the ultimate zombie game.

I associate this game with the PS1 game Onimusha. It's very short, it's very fun, and it's very well made. This game has some of the best team AI I've ever seen. As squad leader you can give them contextual orders such as planting explosives ("Let's re-arrange some architecture"), commandeering turrets, setting up sniper points, and such like. It's all very tightly engineered and makes for a unique single-player experience. I don't even care that the entire game is linear. You aren't really ever given options about how to approach a situation besides the given tactical options and there's always an optimal way you're meant to take things on. But honestly, everything runs so well that I didn't care. It's a joy to watch your squadmates breach and clear a room, every time. Actually, if this game was any longer it might all start to get repetitive. As you complete missions little Behind the Scenes extras get unlocked. The game designers got a real Special Ops instructor to give them some squad combat training so they could have a better idea of how a real commando squad operates, and it shows. This game's multiplayer support dried up long ago, but I never utilized it so I don't miss it. I bought this game as part of a 4-CD pack of Star Wars games several years ago. As of this writing Humble Bundle is selling a Star Wars themed bundle including this game. Normally, I'm not a fan of buying something twice but I like this game so much, I bought it again so it could go into my Steam library. That's gotta count for something, right?

Walking simulator. In gaming as we know it today that term has a rather negative connotation stuck to it, normally associating the game with three things: that it’s going to be short, extremely linear, and almost entirely narratively reliant. The genre used to deserve this connotation, with the majority of its games containing extremely poor stories and relying wholly on their perception as “art”. As it stands though, I fully believe that the title of walking simulator is now as valid a genre as any other, and that it’s finally outgrown the previous negativity surrounding it. Now, in stark contrast to previous associations, recent walking simulators have more positive implications: that they’re going to have exemplary stories, gorgeous worlds, and some of the greatest characters and dialogue possible. Firewatch perfectly compounds all of that, and really is symbolic of these new walking simulators that focus on actually trying to create an unforgettable experience instead of seemingly playing the “games as art” card to excuse their mistakes. Firewatch wastes no time creating said experience and right from the get go you start forming attractions to the two, arguably three, main characters. First off is Henry, a gruff boyfriend-turned-husband with an extraordinary personality who you’re going to be playing as all throughout your journey. Second comes Julia, not a main character but included anyways since she plays an important part in the story as Henry’s wife. Sadly, before the game begins you find Julia is beginning to show symptoms of early-onset dementia, slowly killing her and stressing Henry out to the point he takes on a job as a Forest Fire Lookout in the Shoshone to get a break. Lastly comes my favorite character Delilah, your supervisory lookout who you never actually see, but can visualize better than any other. Again, there’s really only two main characters, as Julia is more of an idea used to push the game forward than an actual character, which might seem a problem but instead is a unique way to focus attention on character development. When you only have two real characters, it’s a lot easier to flesh out their dialogue and make every conversation have value. I appreciate that they didn’t become too ambitious and try to have a full cast, because there’s something indescribably serene about interacting exclusively with Delilah for something of four hours. It’s intimate. It’s personal. It’s Firewatch.
I'd argue that Firewatch’s two strongest features are the exceptional artwork and the absolutely unparalleled character development/dialogue, though not the only two strong features, these two were just the ones that stood out from my first playthrough. Artwork is one of the most critical aspects to a game’s success, though plenty of people would love to claim otherwise, and is intertwined with many other gameplay elements. For example, environment design and immersion are both nigh impossible with poor graphics, and if there’s no immersion or decent environment design then gameplay suffers, causing a catastrophic chain reaction. While there may be other games that have to worry about sub-par artwork, Firewatch is absolutely not one of them, having the most unique and attractive aesthetic I’ve ever seen. Artwork is an important part of building atmosphere and can heavily influence how you feel about the game, and I think Firewatch’s serene and peaceful air is built heavily on the fact that its art is so calming and beautiful. While this may have just been me, I found the game about an hour longer than expected, and I feel that can be attributed to me taking my time and genuinely wanting to just enjoy the scenery. I’ve never experienced anything like that before, Firewatch wholly immersed me in Henry’s character, as if I’m actually living in the Shoshone, with my only link to civilization being a small orange walkie-talkie. Looking back at my experience with Firewatch feels more like reminiscing on the past than it does playing a game, and I think that's caused by the various gameplay mechanics that pile even more immersion on top of what’s already there. My favorite one is the disposable camera you find about halfway through the game, allowing you to take pictures of the various parts of the environment. While that would be pretty neat on its own, the ability to upload your pictures online and to purchase high quality prints of them on the Firewatch website takes the feature from being neat to being unforgettable. What’s more, this literally gives you a physical way to remember and reminisce on your playthrough, an innovative idea that works well with how walking simulators tend to feel closer to experiences than games. I appreciate that, the small things put into the game to add detail and make this feel like a genuine world, I really do.
Now story quality is irrelevant if you can’t experience it due to horrible gameplay decisions obstructing the narrative with pointless or poorly designed mechanics. Firewatch has none of this and maintains a simple method of interaction with your environment, really only requiring you to press a button to interact with whatever you’re looking at. I enjoy this simplicity because more often than not complex game design, especially in walking simulators, tends to focus attention on the mechanic instead of the atmosphere, shattering your immersion with mechanics that seem out of place. Firewatch however has an extremely minimalistic UI that borders on pretty much none, only really showing up when you interact with the world or talk to Delilah on the radio. The gameplay is simple enough to where it’s not like you’d really need any UI at all, it isn’t particularly hard to just go around pressing E on different things you find in the environment after all. I am however glad that they didn’t make this entirely devoid of gameplay because it gives you something to do, even if that something is just pressing E on a door or radio, it still makes you feel involved without breaking immersion. Gameplay isn’t really what you’re playing Firewatch for though and ,while it’s extremely well implemented, it isn’t the game’s main focus, that would be the story. Firewatch has a story unlike most others that I’ve seen, because it tries to avoid telling a story of aliens, heroes, or what else could have been, and instead focuses on being real. Firewatch has a story that, to me, feels like a retelling of a friends vacation, all believable and real, but with a few minor details embellished or twisted to sound better and build suspense. Many people have a problem with the game's ending and honestly I’m torn: on one hand, they really built the ending up in a direction it clearly never had any intention of going, but on the other it’s a story of Henry and Delilah’s real suspense, and real mystery. It’s not the satisfying conclusion that I was hoping for, but it’s symbolic of the whole journey, it may not be the greatest ending in the world, but I think that it still has significant merit to it and ties in well with the themes all throughout Firewatch.
Firewatch has the most intimately personal dialogue of any game I’ve ever played, with characters to match, and provided a beautiful, if short, experience I’ll never forget.

Like strategy games, but don't want to deal with all the complex mechanisms present in 4X games or battle non-stop "Zerg rushes" in RTS?  If so, you might actually like this game.
It's basically the classic game RISK, but the "Factions" version involves playing one of five different groups: humans, robots, cats, yetis and the undead.  The only differences are visual (i.e. no faction-based special attacks or anything), but it adds a lively -- and often quite amusing -- flourish to what some consider a boring game.  The classic version is available, as well.
The single player campaign is rather short, although the AI is cheap.  You can beat it eventually, but doing so relies more on luck than anything else.  Multiplayer is online or hot-seat.
All in all, it's an inexpensive strategy game that's easy to learn and visually more entertaining and accessible for those not normally inclined toward this genre.

This game is maybe one of the most addictive time-sink games I have ever played.
I originally played it all the way back in 2014 on my old computer, which soon after died, taking the game with it. When I heard it had come to Steam, I bought it as soon as I could, and I don't regret having to pay for it all over again.
While this game doesn't look or sound particularly great (in reality, everything is sort of dirty and quiet, which sort of goes with the atmosphere of the game pretty well), the gameplay is the stand-out factor of this game. I can very easily spend the whole day working on a factory, building it up and researching into new technologies to improve it. I can very easily stay up until 5am expanding said factory and basking in the glory of it, watching in satisfaction as everything is done for me by machines and conveyor belts.
Having said that, the game is pretty hard on new players, it's not the easiest game to get to grips with and move through (especially if you're like me and don't like doing tutorials) but it's extremely satisfying to work it out. Some of the later factory building is pretty difficult to understand, and will probably leave you feeling a little overwhelmed by it all. Using guides online to tell you how things work is usually the way I go.
Overall, this game is a gem amongst a lot of rubbish that's out there. It's fleshed out, fun to play and is very much worth the price tag for the hours you can lose in it. Recommended highly.

Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army uses the same weapons and shooting mechanics as Sniper elite V2, but plays very differently.
Sniper Elite V2 is a slower paced game based more on placing a few key shots on enemy snipers and footsoliders while physically isolating yourself from being rushed.
In Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army, you'll find it's impossible to segregate yourself from the enemies, as they come en masse and don't play around with cover or any other such distractions. This leads to high-octane action filled firefights that require basic teamwork and good accuracy to survive.
The shooting distance is generally under 50m; compare this to the base game which typically has 80m-200m shots. You'll often find yourself to not be doing a lot of sniping.
Playing through with three friends and on Sniper Elite difficulty(default enemy spawns), we had very few problems throughout the game. We had to restart from checkpoint all of twice.
There's not much for enemy variety, but assuming you don't have to restart too many times, it shouldn't be a big problem.
The Good:
Enemies and bosses encourage teamwork
Working netcode (Playing with people 3000 miles away is fine)
Interesting and engaging shooting mechanics (Taken from V2)
Good variety of weapons (though only a few new from V2)
Runs smoothly on moderately old hardware
The Bad:
Little enemy variety
One game mode
Short game length (5 missions/2-3 hours per playthrough)
High cost to hour ratio ($5:h)
No custom difficulty (as in Sniper Elite V2)
Most maps are reused from the Sniper Elite V2 campaign
The Ugly:
Can get stuck perpetually alt+tabbing
Steam community can cause rapid screen flashing if enabled
Poor voice quality and high latency for in-game voice chat
Players can occasionally fall through world geometry when knocked out
Bullet drop is insane at close ranges for all rifles
hit-detection can be broken at times
Buy it on sale/10

DISCLAIMER: I played the original State of Decay, on PC, and loved it despite all its flaws.
So what about SoD:YOSE? Well, it's more of the same minus the most obvious flaws, that's mainly  the weirdly behaved renderer, which seemed to render at 720p internally, then upsampled everything to whatever resolution you had chosen, doing so without any sort of filtering. So it looks a lot better now. Still no antialiasing option in the game's menus, but you can always force that from your video-card control panel.
The engine still isn't very good at streaming the world geometry in a fluid fashion, so the fps still drops significantly at times, slowing the gameplay down A LOT in the process, but that usually doesn't last for more than a second. Might also be a lot less noticeable on a SSD, I'll have to give that a try...
Lastly, the quests' progression will still get stuck when some random zombies forget to get into the quest area and you'll still have to either chase them down or wait for them to despawn in order for the mission continue.
In conclusion, I'd say it's not exactly the facelift I was hoping for. The graphics still look sort of dated, the engine still can't handle the size of the map (I could fit the game 8 times in RAM, but the engine insists on swapping and streaming from the HDD like it's 2008), the zombie AI still gets in the way... But you know what? It's still a great survival/resource management game, probably the best in the zombie flavor: numerous quests, some generic, some unique; nice story; great character management/progression system. Plus you get all the DLCs, which are pretty good. I'd say you get a lot of game for your money... even if some small part of me still wishes it would have been released as a free update for those who already had it, because if you only sort of liked the first iteration, I'm not sure what little changed can justify buying the game a second time. Me, I had a great time with it, and I'm having an even better time with this one.
TLDR: Is it worth a buy? If you like the zombie survival genre and didn't get the original game, yes. Definitely. If you already have State of Decay, you may give it a pass, unless you really liked the game or you feel the horrible upscaling-with-worst-possible-filtering engine prevented you from truely enjoying it.

In one sentence: "it's THE squad based shooter of the Star Wars franchise".
Graphics: The design and fidelity of this game still look and run very well to modern standards. Every vibrant blaster bolt feels impactful, the onslaught of A.I. and explosions around every corner feels climatic in scale even in tight quarters. Being it's so dated, it's really not that hard to find a computer that meets up to specs with the game. So you shouldn't find many frame rate drops, clipping, major bugs, or anything that would ruin your immersion. I wouldn't say it's the "best looking" Star Wars game but it's defintely up there.
As far as I can tell everything ran smoothly until a climax in the second chapter where some 4 turrets, 3 Super Battle Droids, and at least 8 regular droids were all firing missiles and potshotting around the room, meanwhile the environment was shaking and exploding. That's when I felt a minor drop in framerate but that's mostly due to my system specs which are REALLY not up to par.
Gameplay: It does indeed get a little repetitive as you progress but nevertheless EVERY firefight is challenging. You're well equipped for war. With a the cliches of pistol, assault rifle, sniper rifle, and grenade launcher as standard Republic Commando weapons you eventually find shotguns, bowcasters, beam weapons and more. But the thing is, you're always on the brink of running out. With that and maintaining your squad of fellow Republic Commandos by giving them orders such as taking sniping positions, blowing up objectives, and maintaining their health the game is always tense and still is challenging to this day.
Which I’d like to clear up and say, commanding your squad is not only vital to even remotely completing the game but is the best thing about it. You’d be retreating from rounding around a corner barking out order after order. “Get ready on your sniper, get yourself some bacta, defend this position”. All one command after another, like clockwork.
This factor really kicks into high gear the second you have your squad together. There’s a couple solo missions which I’m going flat out say, “you’re going to miss your team”. That mechanic and sort of “security” you feel with them is the core of the game. The second it’s ever taken away either through the story mission itself or if everyone dies, it’s pure trouble in the best way possible. You feel vulnerable (well equipped, yes, but very vulnerable).
There aren't any vehicles beyond turrets so this isn't to the scale of let's say, Battlefront. The maps are linear but massive to what its worth and there's an appropriate onslaught of enemies to keep fights interesting. There are indeed a couple repetitive moments where you'd rather have a boss fight but instead have to bunker down and mow through a dozen some enemies to blow up their spawning zones. From Geonosis to Kashyyyk to abandoned warships the game has enough variation in map design to also keep you invested.
Sound and Music: This is arguably THE best soundtrack I’ve EVER heard of in a Star Wars shooter. It’s not always a rehash of John William’s sweeping scores, but it also includes Mandalorian chants and war songs which make it VERY invigorating.
It’s worthy of keeping on your music playing device!
The sound is crisp, clear, and full of sheer power. Every explosion feels impactful and every blaster shot feels like it would kill you if you stood in front of it (which some will). From the “thunk” of a grenade launcher to the clanking fall and explosion of droids the game “feels” so close to the Star Wars franchise it’s ridiculous and most of the new weapons have proprietary and unique tones which weren’t featured in the films. So you have a unique mix of sounds, some amazing original scores, and overall a fantastic auditory experience.
Story: It's your typical war story in a video game where you're tasked with several missions that boil down to a climatic conclusion where it would allude  to another conflict. But that's the problem, there's NO direct sequel to this beyond Karen Traviss’ books (which were considered canon back in the day and were a FANTASTIC read).
So if you want to know about the fate of the team beyond this game, you need to read the books. Nevertheless, you may complain, "why does every clone sound different to one another" but again this is explained in other media. However, the biggest delight (story-wise) is the characterization and personality.
Every team members has a (albeit cliche) personality. You have the wisecracking demolitionist, the serious brutal sniper, the "by the book" technician and you the leader. However it's the banter when you go between objectives that's memorable, funny, and even looks at a different side of clone troopers that you'd typically don't see in the films.
I will say though it's a shame to have a story that really is asking for a sequel but, it never did or will happen. Which normally, I would slander much like how Rage by iD was going for; however, in this case, given there is other media that reinforces the best qualities of this game, I'm actually very fine with it.
The voice acting is great with Temuera Morrison embalming your playable character, Andrew Chaikin as "Fixer" (who was Grendel from Wolf Among us), Raphael Sbarge as "Scorch" (who played as Kaidan from Mass Effect), then Jonathan David Cook was "Sev" (who played Earl from StarCraft 2 Wings of Liberty). You have a great cast who execute their characters perfectly.
Concluding thoughts:
If you're looking for a great FPS with excellent characterization and want to know more about the culture and philosophy of the more elite troopers, this is the game for you. It's been a pleasure despite only playing through this once.
I'll definitely come back but the only reason why I have yet to go back to it is simply because I play other games beyond what's in my Steam Library. Nevertheless the experience was SO interesting to the point I bought and have read every single Republic Commando book that DelRey offers and to a fault the books expand the game so much that it's more pleasurable.
I don't give out a number rating but rather a "buy immediately, consider buying, do extended research, and don't even bother" sort of scale. I say "consider buying". It's not THE FPS of the century but it's up there with the more memorable ones. I gotta say I remember more character dialogue from this squad of 4 compared to ANY AAA military FPS's that came out in the past 4 years. If you love clones, want to know more about them, and want a challenging FPS with some minor squad commands consider picking this one up. For the price? It was worth every penny!

I don't normally do reviews, but I wanted to review this one.
To start, this “game” is a 5-6 hour story driven walking simulator … I’m not even joking.  BUT, with that said, I really didn't mind it at all.  It is important to realize that this is not a game in a traditional sense.  It is closer to being an interactive short-story than a game.
The year is 1989 and you play Henry who takes a job as a fire lookout in Shoshone National Forest for personal reasons.  Then slowly, things start to get a bit creepy.
I might be wrong, but I felt the developers were purposefully striving to make you feel like that you were actually in the story in a way… and for me, they succeeded.  I got a sense of hiking and being in the wilderness.  Plus, I got the occasional feeling of being vulnerable and confused.  I found myself looking over my shoulder a few times.  And honestly, I thought it was cool that I felt compelled to do that.
The story hooked me and ultimately left me feeling a bit melancholy in the end… like I had just watched the movie "Stand By Me" (if that makes any sense).  The story also felt realistic in a “this really could have happened” sort of way.  And much like real life, the ending will not tie everything in a nice pretty bow for you, but I had enough closure that I was satisfied and didn’t feel cheated.
The visuals and ambiance were great and the occasional background music set the tone when needed.  The pacing of the game was good.  And the voice acting was VERY well done and is simply what makes this game great.  I guess this is why I didn’t mind all the in-gaming walking.  The game simply never got boring to me. Doesn't really need saying at this point(Dec 2017), but this is very much an evolution of the walking simulator genre.  Some people treat that term as an insult, but I think it's an endearment at this stage.  But anyways, this is easily one of the best there is.  Walking simulators obviously have little or no skill-based mechanics and so are *much* more reliant on everything else holding up the game and this one succeeds in pretty much every possible way.  It's not flawless, but the issues I have with it are mostly nitpicks.  Outside the ending, which, well, I cant say anything about it without spoiling the story, but I'm sure plenty of others have brought this up as a contentious issue as well, so I'm not saying anything new or interesting here.
All in all, it's a rare game that I get *truly* emotionally invested into characters and the plot, the way only a good book can usually do.  This sounds like simple praise, but that's really something I consider very notable as I typically consider gaming to be one of the poorest mediums for these things, not inherently, just in execution.  Yet Firewatch succeeds.
I really loved it.  It's one of those games I feel will leave you thinking about it for days(or more) after finishing it.
And before I leave it, I feel it necessary to spread praise on the art and graphics programmers as the game is just gorgeous, not that this is any secret.  The music is also lovely, though maybe just a *touch* short of exceptional.

This game is really fun. The atmosphere is super creepy and desolate. The sounds of the environment to the sounds of your gun shooting is very nice and distinct. The funnest thing about the game was the different kind of zombies.
-You've got your standard nazi zombie. He's very weak but always attacks you in large groups.
-Then you've got skeletal zombies. These guys aren't much different then the standard zombie, however, they are immune to headshots and instead must be shot in the heart. There attack speed is slightly faster as well, but also do less damage then the standard zombies.
-The 3rd class of zombie is a suicide grunt. This guy will rush towards the survivors at an eerily creepy speed. Once he reachers his target he then explodes violently, severely damaging anyone near him.
-And then there's the heavy MG zombie. This zombie is a boss zombie. He can deal a massive amount of damage at short to medium range. He is also slightly immune to headshots. His head ,however, is his weakspot, and he can be brought down with consistent accurate headshots.
-Now, the fifth zombie is a sniper zombie. These guys never directly engage the survivors. Instead they harrass the survivors from afar while jumping from building to building like a kangaroo right out of Austrailia. (Silly, I know)
-Then for the final zombie you've got a giant phantasmal like entity. He is a boss zombie. His unique ability to summon the undead horde makes him the hardest to deal with. He also emits a shield that deflects all incoming bullets from the survivors. This shield can only be brought down by shooting the skulls that flost around this zombie.
I had a blast playing this game just wish the game had more levels(only 5), but for 15 dollars one can not really complain.

First of all, if you already own the original game and every available DLC then don't bother buying this unless you are looking for slightly better graphics, a few new weapons and vehicle skins and bug fixes (and new bugs). The game is still pretty much the same experience.
If you are
to this game and interested, then I'd most likely recommend buying it. Don't mind the negative reviews on this edition of the game. Instead read the ones on the original one (which is no longer available for purchase at the moment) since they tell more about the experience than these on YOSE. Why? Because most of these tell about how this edition was released only to make money out of small updates and about the bugs that make the game worse. The worst thing is that the original game is not receiving any of the new content and updates that are included in this edition. I can understand the pain and I agree that it's a horrible move, but I'd like to direct this short review specifically towards everyone who has no experience with the original game.
I'll let you know about the game's basics and the good and the bad in short.
+Looting and managing inventory is easy
+Combat is alright
+Base management is simple and clear
+Vehicles are easy to control (most of the time)
+Moving alone can actually be really dangerous (it's good to have someone with you)
+Graphics are nice...
-...but they can get a bit ugly (for ex. in the woods)
-Fighting with melee weapons gets repetitive
-Missions also get repetitive
-Simplicity is a minor impact
-Voice acting is propably the most repetitive thing in the game and needs a bigger variety
(same sentences are repeated alot)
-Vehicles feel a bit too fragile sometimes
-The game is still screaming for co-op
-Minor bugs that are close to breaking missions
-Performance needs tweaking (fps drops)
Gameplay: 7.5/10
Graphics: 8/10
Sounds: 7.5/10 (Including voice acting)
Performance: 7/10
Story: 6/10
Yes, State of Decay: YOSE Day One Edition was propably made only with money in mind and so it should propably be avoided by veterans unless you need this new content and bug fixes + the upcoming fixes for the new and old bugs. In the other hand, this is something that fans of survival games should look into. You can spend alot of time while playing this game. Even I spent over 12 hours on the base game and tried out one of the DLCs (Lifeline) that I have not played before (I did play the original game and the Breakdown DLC back in the day). The other DLC (Breakdown) will leave you with even more hours on your counter. All in all I had alot of fun playing this game. There were quite a few intense moments that are something I've never encountered in other survival games. I played this with a controller and I recommend you doing the same if you happen to have one.

PanGEMic surprised me. I actually only downloaded it, to check if Steam downloads work properly for me (I am living in China right now) but I was pleasantly surprised by panGEMic's quality.
It's an oldschool 1-screen platformer where all you do is avoid enemies and collect gems. That's the simple premise for a really engaging experience, due to tight controls and great level design. It seems so easy, so simple, but it's actually quite difficult to collect all gems. If you fall of the screen you respawn at the top and if you leave the screen to the sides you end up on the opposite site. This makes it actually quite difficult sometimes, but always gives you the feeling that it's your fault, if you die.
It really is the essence of what made games so fun back then. A simple premise executed and polished very well provides hours of fun. Highly recommended!

In Star Wars Republic Commando, you play as Delta Three-Eight, lead of Delta Squad. This means that you order your fellow brother around the various battlefields, keeping them alive- and developing a real connection with them throughout the game. Sev is the tough guy, always making remarks to boost the squad's confidence. You, the designated leader, have inherited Jango Fett's accent and his skills. Scorch, my favorite, is always there to make jokes and lighten the mood. Geonosis, the Assualt ship, and Kashyyyk are all wonderfully crafted and are great to explore if you are interested in them. The gunplay is great and commanding your fellow commandos is almost always flawless. The music is fantastic, some areas using the movies' music, and some areas (and main menu) using a darker score. The enemies are diverse and have their weaknesses. Some enemies are annoying, but most are fun and challenging to battle. You really see why clones are intimidated by Super Battle Droids and Droidekas and Spider Tanks, something that was never felt in Star Wars Battlefront II. Also, it has AWESOME breaching, hacking, and grenade gameplay. You also get a new perspective on various battles in the movies, such as the Battle of Geonosis and the Battle of Kashyyyk. I am a huge Episode I-III fan and think this is the second best Star Wars game of all time besides Star Wars Battlefront I/II. I have the first Republic Commando  book ready as well. So, what are you waiting for? Play it!

I liked Magicka 2. Was it shorter than Magicka 1? Yes. Was it less fun? No.
Me and my girlfriend appreciated the new control scheme, even though it took a few flaming rocks to the head to get used to it :) We played with logitech controllers and it was a much better experience than Magicka 1.
Here's what I liked:
- Same awesome friend killing, enemy slaying coop.
- Nicer graphics
- Better control scheme for controllers
- Harder difficulty (Magicka 1 was pretty easy)
- More enemies
- Enemies were though out better so you need to make a strategy about how to kill them
- Jokes and references still abound
Here's what was off:
- High difficulty playing alone. I tried. It didn't work out so well :) All of the enemies quickly surround you and then you die. Then you get revived back in the mob. And then die :)
- Not as long as the Magicka 1
- Difficult to find unlockables. Went through the first level a few times and couldn't find more than half of the secrets.
But all in all, when your girlfriend tries to heal you and instead casts a death bomb at you and you both die laughing, it's worth every penny.

This game is up there with Metroid Prime and Unreal as being one of my favorite FPSes ever, plus one of my favorite Star Wars games. I just wish it was longer.
Unlike most FPSes I've played, where the combat's attempt at a frantic pace just makes it an annoying mess of white noise, Republic Commando's squad-based gameplay forces you constantly calculate battlefield tactics as opposed to just trying not to get shot.
The game's biggest weakness comes in a few brief segments where you're forced into a tactical situation by yourself, where one stray bullet can drop you; or when you're given a time limit, which in one case resulted in me finishing a level with literally a second or two left on the clock. The intensity of the firefights makes completing your objectives in time an incredible strain.
Besides that, the game is only three missions: Geonosis, a deralict Republic battlecruiser, and Kashyyyk. Thankfully, each of these missions will last you a good three hours a piece, so I wasn't left feeling like I'd played an unfinished game. I was, however, left wanting a lot more. In particular, the notion of this game's encounters playing out organically, with nonlinear level design (and a lot more levels), sounds like the workings of one of the greatest FPSes ever.

I highly recommend this game, in short.

Theres a lot of griping of how horribly "broken" this version of State of Decay is compared to the original. As someone who has been playing SoD since launch day (on the Xbox 360) I can honestly say that this version is perfectly acceptable. Its not a massive upgrade over the original version, but there are some marked improvements. Ive noticed next to no bugs not present in the original, and my only issue with starting it up is I had to go into properties and add "-fullscreen" to make it fullscreen.
State of Decay has never been perfectly polished, its janky and funky looking and its physics are strange and kinda broken. But it does what it sets out to do in a way few other games can match, and compared to my experiences playing the 360 version on day one, this is a huge upgrade. Fun for the whole family.. If your family is a bunch of sadists. Paint the Town red is a great stress relief game, and is super addicting to play. The objective of the game is to kill everyone else in the level and become the only one, then walk out all cool with a mess of blood and mutilated bodies behind you.
The combat is great, and it has to be, considering this game is all about fighting. You can pick up most items around you, including bar stools, mugs, chairs, pool ques, pool balls, knives, bats, nun-chucks, katanas, throwing stars, shot glasses, tire irons, pimp cains, and more. They usually break pretty fast though, which forces you to run around constantly grabbing things to use as weapons and gives the combat this improvisational feel. You can do light punches if you tap, and heavy punches if you hold. There's a block button so you can take reduced damage, but generally I see little use for it when you can just dodge very easily by backing up. Unless you're cornered block really has no purpose. Then theres kicks, you have a knock down bar that when full lets your kicks knock people over, it depletes entirely once you use it and constantly fills back up at a quick pace. One of my favorite things with kicks is dropkicking, if you time your jump and your kick just right you can do one, but it can be pretty hard at times. As for weapons they use the same mechanics as punches, but light hits are jabs, heavy hits are swings, and you can throw them. Sometimes your hits stun opponents letting you just wail on them until they recover or go down.
There's three special abilities that use a blue bar, which charges up when you kill people. The first one costs a third of your bar and does a shockwave knocking anyone in your immediate area down, it's called shockwave. The second ability, berserk, slows down time, and lets you explode peoples faces in prosnorkulus style fashion with your punches, using two thirds of your bar. Smite, the third and final ability, using a full bar, slows down time and lets you shoot people with your hand spirit gun style, causing them to be obliterated into nothing with a beam from the sky. The second and third ability sometimes dont work, which is really annoying, and they waste precious slowed time doing an animation. Sometimes due to this you'll only get to kill one or two people with berserk or smite, sometimes none at all, which is just a total waste of your bar, and can be really infuriating.
There's a boss or two on every level, of which there are only two right now (The Bar, and Club beatdown),  but there will be more to come. These guys usually carry a super deadly weapon, and have some ridiculous durability. They're unaffected by your special moves and your kicks, and they can take so many bottles to the face it's hilarious. You can fight them at any time you find them in the level, and usually they come right after you once you do. As for their ridiculous durability, these guys will generally have half their skull hanging out their head and still come at you. But once you get their weapon it usually one hit kills everything you come accross until it breaks. Boss weapons have slightly more durability than others but still break pretty quickly if you have a bunch of opponents left. A nice detail for the sadists out there, your weapons take zero durability damage from smacking corpses so you can mutilate things as much as you like.
Overall I love this game, and despite a couple issues with specials, and lack of optimization, I can see me and my friends taking turns on this game for hours just in its current state. Which kinda makes me wish there was some local coop/deathmatch support in the future. But anyways, if you like senselessly gorey brawls, and/or your looking for a way to outlet your rage, then I recommend you [try] Paint The Town Red.

Alone in a watchtower, guarding the forest and the entire park for fires and troubles. A quiet work, appearently, until odd things start to happen.
It's 1989, you're Henry and you've just reached the watchtower of this park. You will be alone watching over the forest and your only human contact is Delilah, your supervisor that will give you tasks and advices. Job starts quietly with small trips from point to point, some nice chat with your boss and so on, but soon you will witness odd events and notthing will be the same.
Sounds generic, I know, but you will get to know Henry a lot more than it sounds, understanding the reason that brought him to this hermit life, the only human relation you're about to have will grow and evolve, and what you are about to see will involve you, make you suspicious, paranoid and worried. A story that seems incredible but not impossible.
Made with Unity, the map (the park) is quite big, but you will obtain the necessary tools to reach all places along with your playthrough. The aspect is almost ALMOST cartoonish, with simple textures but no cel shading, yet the landscapes and places are simply marvelous. A canyon, a lake, planes, caves, the forest, everything is worth admiring for a second even though textures are quite essential. Locations have been realized with great care for details resulting in the beautiful park you can walk in.
You will rarely hear music during the game, but what you hear is simple yet very effective, simple movements, some classic guitar. Few tunes only during the right moments. Gives a stronger sense of loneliness walking through the park without hearing anything but nature and your own steps.
Walking simulator. Nuff said. First person, you walk around, you can interact with specific objects and you can pick up a handful of items to use around in different specific occasions. The most interesting part however is the radio. You have a radio to communicate with Delilah. Sometimes she'll call you and lots of time you can call her... Mainly to report things and objects you find or need help with. And you can speak with her, chosing answers, or sentences according to the tone you want to use or the matter you want to talk about. In this lone place it's natural to be willing to speak with Delilah about as many things as you can. And it's made on purpose...
Nothing I guess. Unless you're looking for action but then I'd be surprised you're giving attention to a Walking simulator.

Magicka (the first one) was recommended to me recently based on enjoying Castle Crashers. I enjoyed it immensely: the spell combination system is fun, the invented language is brilliant and funny, and overall it's a great game. The follow-up (this one) is somewhat of a disappointment. In summary, it seems like the developers made a sincere effort to address some of the weaknesses of the first game, the primary one being that once you figured out the most powerful spell combinations, it was a little too easy.
Unfortunately, this effort seems to have focused mainly on the kind of frustrating pseudo-difficulty that basically consists of being overwhelmed by numbers and speed of enemies. For example, I frequently died almost immediately after being resurrected by my Familar; unlike the first game, there's no period of invulnerability after resurrection. I'm sure someone will have a way around this, but it's meant as a representative example, not the sum total of my complaints. The bottom line is that if you play this game, be prepared to spend a lot more time boiling with frustration after you die without a chance to react.
Pros
- Better graphics
- More challenging
- Artifacts allow custom difficulty
- Changing Arcane to Death and adding the particular related effects was a good idea
- Having the Magicks in their own control bar and automatically gained as you advance is, overall, better than the first game
Cons
- Shields over-nerfed. The problem is you spend an inordinate amount of time running around just trying to get position so you can fight back. Enemies are as fast as you and are often either unaffected by or can block Frost slowing effects. Some people might like this, but I just found it aggravating.
- Controls changed; takes quite a bit of getting used to and I don't see the benefit. In particular, making the center mouse button involved in both self-cast and AoE cast causes an awful lot of inadvertent self-casting of harmful spells.
- Doesn't seem like as much effort was put into the language in this one, which was a big part of my enjoyment of the first one.
- Not enough levels in the Adventure; even with all the difficulties mentioned, I finished the game in 12 hours, and to be honest even the customizability doesn't make me want to play the same levels again.
Overall, it's a decent game on its own, and I think it's going in the right direction in terms of addressing the issues mentioned. But the fun / challenge balance needs to be fine tuned and it needs to be longer.

Compared to the first instance of Magicka, Magicka 2 is very disappointing.  While graphics are nice, the gameplay is horrible.
For once, controls are more difficult to handle (e.g. once clicked on where to go, it follows through there until clicked elsewhere), which much easier leads to running into enemies or other obstacles as the controls are more indirect.
On the other side, and that is the most annoying part, you get into situations where you are locked into a section of a level unable to escape and get uninterruptedly swarmed by enemies while simultaneously having to trigger something in order to leave the area.  This is very frustrating and makes the game impossible to achieve, at least when playing alone.  Not sure, if there are greater odds surviving such menaces with 3-4 players, but the game offers single player mode as well and it should be achievable without resorting to extreme keyboard and mouse-wrecking.  It is meant to be a game afterall.
I do not mind challenges, but they should be achievable through normal means.  If required to frequently go through extremes, the game loses appeal and misses its goal.
There is a reason games are considered entertainment material.  It should be enjoyable even for the average player.  Putting up impossible odds is sacrificing the game to become work.  For anyone looking for work, I would recommend the nearest work agency.  They will give you work where you even will earn money.
Conclusion
If you enjoyed playing Magicka (the first game), do not waste your time and money on this game and stick to the original title.  Much more fun that way.

This game is up there with Metroid Prime and Unreal as being one of my favorite FPSes ever, plus one of my favorite Star Wars games. I just wish it was longer.
Unlike most FPSes I've played, where the combat's attempt at a frantic pace just makes it an annoying mess of white noise, Republic Commando's squad-based gameplay forces you constantly calculate battlefield tactics as opposed to just trying not to get shot.
The game's biggest weakness comes in a few brief segments where you're forced into a tactical situation by yourself, where one stray bullet can drop you; or when you're given a time limit, which in one case resulted in me finishing a level with literally a second or two left on the clock. The intensity of the firefights makes completing your objectives in time an incredible strain.
Besides that, the game is only three missions: Geonosis, a deralict Republic battlecruiser, and Kashyyyk. Thankfully, each of these missions will last you a good three hours a piece, so I wasn't left feeling like I'd played an unfinished game. I was, however, left wanting a lot more. In particular, the notion of this game's encounters playing out organically, with nonlinear level design (and a lot more levels), sounds like the workings of one of the greatest FPSes ever.
I guess I expected too much...
