text:
I felt the need to review this game since I bought it based on all the glowing, positive reviews it got. After actually playing it myself, however, I can say that most of these people must be delusional or something.
Let me just start off by saying that the game IS really fun. The squad dynamic (when it actually works) is great to play around with in strategic situations and the characters are all interesting enough to make this come alive in some missions. The game also, apparently, ties into some of the books by the same name.
While I would recommend this game to fans of Star Wars and the FPS genre in particular, it's ten years old at this point and has not really aged very well. Aside from that there are bugs and glitches everywhere on top of just poor design choices and lazy coding.
Let's just got down the list, shall we? First off is the bugs. Oh the bugs. Enemies can sometimes shoot you straight through solid walls or between tiny cracks in scenery that you are unable to fire back through yourself. Trying to throw a grenade into enemy formations from behind cover will frequently have your grenades bouncing back at your own team often off of what seems to be thin air. Needless to say the hit detection sucks a fat one.
Next thing is the AI, which is pretty bad for a game that revolves around a squad dynamic. I've lost count of how many times I've had to solo an encounter because my super elite delta squad members charge out strait into both mine and enemy fire or stood directly on a grenade that I just threw only to have other squad members rush out to try and revive them and also get obliterated. I had two instances where a squad member got stuck on map details because of bad path finding. The first instance had a squad member running straight into a rock trying to get to some waypoint or something and no command would pull him back so I had to fight a boss with just two squad members. The second was a bit later and a single member got stuck under a ramp of some kind because whatever command I gave him made him try to walk straight into the ramp so I ended up reloading. The enemy AI is a bit better but there's been a couple times where they've ignored a turret or something blasting away at them while they try to charge straight at me or a squad member.
Next is the difficulty. I played on normal and I was basically quick saving and quick loading for every, single room. Some enemies can kill you in a single shot while others are just difficult to spot, will dodge out of your targeting reticle when you aim at them and never miss. There's also a strange disconnect with weapon damage. The Trandoshans in particular can often take an entire clip of ammo to the chest and keep coming but are supposed to just be regular enemies. They have this shotgun weapon you can pick up that you use to kill them in one or two hits but you have to basically ram it up their noses, at which point, you might as well just melee them. They however can use it to take half your health in a single shot from across an entire room.
Last of all is simply that the game design itself is somewhat flawed on a fundamental level. Each mission has only a single path that you will ever go down. Sometimes they make it LOOK like you can maybe try different approaches or go a different way but there's really only one direction that is the "right" way and all others will lead to certain death. On top of this the core idea, squad command, just doesn't work properly most of the time. For example: I give the command that I want someone to take up a sniper position so my demolitions or close combat squad member will take up the position and gripe about how they're not a sniper. Then enemies will show up and they'll snipe the crap outta them no trouble while the actual sniper character just stands next to me looking rather stupid.
In the end the game is actually pretty fun to play. I mean I'm certainly determined to beat it despite all these glaring issues but then I'm also a huge Star Wars / FPS fan. I'm not very good at writing reviews but, again, I felt the need to do so since everyone is recommending this game and not bothering to mention any of the very serious problems that absolutely plague the gameplay. Although seeing as I'm just a single voice surrounded by hundreds of other reviews, I doubt anyone will see this but, here it is.
If you love Star Wars and FPS games get this one on sale. Otherwise, give it a miss.

What to say about this game? Well, if you decide to buy and play it, make sure to contact your local addiction care center beforehand. Even if this game looks simple and old school, just the unmodded vanilla game provides enough content for hundreds and thousands of hours of game play. I mostly play the DRM-free version of the game, so my steam play time is just a small fraction of the overall time I have invested into this game. You will find yourself rebuilding every aspect of your base many times, starting game after game to build better, larger and more efficient factories. If the vanilla content starts to bore you, choose from hundreds of mods which add even more products, buildings and scenarios to the game.
Even if the game is still in early access, the developers are frequently adding new features and better graphics, fix bugs and listen carefully to the community. In the last two years, just a few bugs slipped into the unstable beta versions, but even those were mostly fixed within a day.
Multiplayer is also fun, but requires either a local area network or a very fast internet connection (specifically upload speed for the host) as larger factories require a lot of bandwidth. I highly suggest to use voice communication to coordinate the players, otherwise your factory quickly ends up looking like a bowl of spaghetti, sauce included.

I bought Magicka 2 for 4.99 USD when it was on sale, and, I'll admit, I was riding the hype train. While it was installing however, I realised that I hadn't read any reviews for it, or watched any gameplay videos. I'd just gone out an bought it. What an idiot. I booted up the game, preparing for a mediocre game. It was amazing. Even the menu screen is well done. Rather than a still picture or a looping video, this was a 3D overview of the realm of Midgard, complete with a comicly oversized ferris wheel and undersized mountains. As you mouse over the different options in challenge mode, the background changes to suit this. Going to battle Orcs in the Highlands? The camera pans over to them. Planning on fighting goblins in the castle of Aldratraz? The ruins rebuild themselves. Although little touches like these make no difference to the gameplay, they make the game feel more... fleshed out. The summoning and casting of spells is awkward at first, but it soon becomes natural, and their's nothing more satisfying than you and your friend combining a life and a death beam to create a miniture black hole. Couple this with great background music and the ability to play multiplayer on one PC (If you have a controller), and you've got yourself, in my opinion, a perfect game.
A defining part of the Magicka franchise is the ability to create your own spells, resulting in a playstyle perfect for you. Here's a good example. Before I fight, I always selfcast Sheild-Stone-Stone-Stone-Stone, which gives my wizard a suit of rock armour. Next, I move so the enemies are
visible on the edge of the screen. Then, I summon Water-Cold-Death-Death-Death, and hold right-mouse, which charges up the attack. After a couple of seconds I let go, firing 3-5 shards of ice, infused with death magic. Then, depending on the situation, I either cast Cold-Water-Cold-Water-Death and right-mouse charge, which does the same as the previous spell, except it shoots 7-9 shards that do less damage. In all honesty, it's like a shotgun. If their are too many enemies, I summon Lightning-Death-Fire-Death-Lightning, and Shift-middlemouse cast, which sends lightning bolts in all directions, which do extra damage (Death element at work) and light the enemies on fire.
I can't even begin to describe how good this music is. Just listen to preveiws of it on iTunes

This game is a huge disapointment. After all the hype building with the comical trailers and pre-order rewards, I was expecting the next big adventure for the Magicka series. Instead, what I got was a short, shallow and frustrating Magicka game that fails to understand what made the first game such a blast to play. Magicka 2 lacks content, magicks and even spell combinations from the 1st game and it doesn't replace it with much else. There is less of everything in Magicka 2 which wouldn't be a big deal if what was there was any good.
However, it's biggest flaw is just how unfun this game is. Some of your basic defenses have been dramatically weakened and your health decreased causing you to die within 1-3 seconds of being spawned in the more difficult areas if you are not lightning fast with your wards. You will die over and over again and barely achieve much during your short lives. To make matters worse, arcane (death) deals the best damage now but is crippled by causing huge explosions when an enemy is killed with it and that explosion can deal great damage to you and your allies. Often killing them which gets really annoying. They ramped up friendly fire to the extreme here.
Now the game being harder isn't necessarily a bad thing conceptually, it's more of a problem due to how they increased the difficulty. The new difficulty modes aren't any fun to play at all. All they do is give enemies more health, the players less, and allow enemies to regenerate health, as well as other adjustments. Anyway there are plenty of other reviews that go into more depth within the game's mechanics but I think you get the jist of it here.
Ultimatelly I cannot recommend this game. It is much less fun than Magicka 1 and if you are a new comer to the series, just go play Magicka 1. If you are returning from Magicka 1, this game is most likely going to disapoint you more than anything else. If that's the case, lower your expectations and perhaps buy the game on sale and approach it as DLC to the first game and then maybe you'll find a tiny amount of entertainment here.

Blanco already looked like a game I would fund for the heck of it, but once I got my hands on it things fell into place. Blanco is a platformer much like the ones in the days of old. Levels with different themes make up the ones availible, along with little collectables sprinkled across the levels. In a way, the way Blanco moves and jumps reminded me of the simpler days when I watch a certain plumber do flips and tricks, of course now our protagonist spins as he jumps higher. Playing this game brought me back to a time where I just played the game for being a game, not some complex combat system or overblow lore context. Much like Blanco's desgin, the game is simple. It has an objective, a bit of an exploring element, and some catchy music to go with while you go around looking for the Super Gems. Simply pleasing.
Now on with the down sides, Blanco does manage to feel a bit stiff when you handle him. Trying to quickly turn around when you were running the other direction feels a lot different compared to other games and it feels pretty stiff, much like his traction(which feels almost nonexistent). Also kicking enemies does feel a bit difficult to do at first. It does get easier with time, but even near the end I still found kicking to be inconsistent. Usually I would just run around and drop bombs everywhere because kicking was to frustrating in some parts(maybe this could be fix by making the dive act as another type of attack for certain enemies?). Also there are some oddly place traps and with some cannon placement latter on, it does seem to act as a sinister way to make a challenge for one part of the level. Since cannonballs can also go through walls, I often found myself getting ganked and falling off into pits because of it. Luckily these moments don't happen often, which is good. The platforming is also a bit weird, since it wants you to be fast enough to make a jump, but percise enough to not fall from great heights, Blanco start up speed makes it a bit odd to do this and I often found myself double jumping over tiny gaps just becaue I was afraid I might fall and have to do a section all over again. Sometime the platforming begs to be ran through, but then halfway through it makes you halt before you can keeping going again.
However, you can overcome these little details like I did and appreciate the world created around Blanco. For every place that contradict your instincts, there's another that compliment it very well. Any cracks in the overall storyline are filled in well with humor and character, not that a ROUGE-like (nethack anyone?) has a whole lot of story in general, this game captures the atmosphere and humor to filll those cracks.
While ROUGE-like in pilot and pattern generation, it is not at all a time and place to be thinking about the best possible move. You MUST continue against the odds, constantly. It's a throwback to all those coin-consuming button-battering andrenaline-assaulting arcade shmups of yesteryear, with very beautiful, but somewhat confusing HUD elements, amazing backgrounds, fantastic soundtrack, and simple controls. The gameplay is rock solid, and rock hard, but amazingly compelling.
It also has an amazing dash of humour and zaniness that I just love.
I had a pilot yell out, in a thick scottish accent "You missed! Of course you missed! You couldn't hit the broad side of a barn!...WITH ANOTHER BARN!!"
That alone should tell you everything you need to know about the humour of this game. If you need further convincing, the Cat Admiral (yes. your fleet admiral is a cat) yelled out "I could use more wet food! It's WARTIME, soldier!" at the beginning.
Issues however are that it takes almost forever to load the game at the start, but once it has, you can just keep playing until you need to quit. Also the mechanics of the game are not especially well explained. It's easy enough to get to grips with them but some kind of guide or tutorial could be helpful. I'm guessing this is coming later when the game is closer to completion.
Finally due to it being roguelikey, it seems if you quit the game you lose all progress. ALL of it. This can be somewhat frustrating but there's no unlock progression at the moment it seems, that I can tell anyway. Again, could do with a guide I guess. Coming later I assume. I can wait. :)
In any case even though it's still in early access, the game is INCREDIBLE and exceptionally well polished for its state.

This game, even in such an early access build, is really, really good. It's an addicting platformer that brings the players back to the days of what shaped modern gaming. Inspired by classic games like Super Mario Bros., Blanco has the (near) perfect tinge of difficulty, exploration, and fun overall. Just one world out of the many to be added, at least an hour is supplied, and that's not including finding the many secrets that are soon to be added to this game, collecting many gems, and taking in the retro beauty this game has to offer.
Of course, not every game is truly perfect, especially into this early state. The game lacks any indication of the time you've spent playing levels, it lacks a pause menu, there are still bugs here and there, and is still in an early design overall. However, as stated above, this game is in an early build, and for such a cheap price (3$, the creator says) with a dollar off the first week, I'd say that this game is absolutely worth it, a steal even. If you want a 3D platformer that gives you a challenge, feel free to sell that hat or gun for a game that will supply you with soon to be hours of fun. Just remember, at the moment, the game is in early access, so you might have to wait some time for more.
8.5/10, for the early access build. Will be updated upon final release.

A poignant mix of walking simulator, explorer, and eBook, Firewatch pulls you in to a continuously deepening mystery with an emotional undertone, all whilst expereiencing the joys of forming a new relationship with a stranger via the radio.
The dialogue is repeatedly funny, appropriate, and the options usually cover all trains of thought - the one cavét being that you can never start a conversation, only respond to the messages you receive.
You can, however, comment on what you encounter in your environment, and it is this aspect of exploring the world and discovering objects that brings Firewatch in to its own.
Firewatch begins by giving you tasks to familiarise yourself with the world around you and how you can traverse it. As you progress, more of the world opens up through different objectives and tools which grant you access to previously cordened off areas. While this sounds unfavourable, the game is short (by modern standards) and the world is sufficiently detailed and expansive to the point where you never feel confined or bored.
As some have pointed out, the gripping mystery that unravels is what motivates you through your days on Firewatch which mainly focus on the begininng and end. While the ending may be anticlimatic for some, I for one believe we have become too used to twists, big surprises, and massive plot shifts in our media, and happily welcome a nice, neat conclusion that doesn't quite resolve the problem at hand theoretically, but does practically for the player.
Firewatch is well worth the ~5 hours of playtime and, combined with the art style and auditory accompaniments, will leave you happier for having experienced its world.

On paper, it sounds great: HD re-release of 2013's State of Decay, all DLC included, bonus missions and new characters for the Breakdown DLC. I got the original State of Decay around the time it came out of Early Access back in late 2013 and it was plagued by bugs that eventually got patched out. So, imagine my surprise when playing the re-release only to discover they brought back the same bugs. To list a few:
- Opening up the journal will running or driving will lock your character in that direction infinitely until you press the same direction key again.
- Incorrect character voices. A female character will use her own voice to say one line, then switch to another female voice, and then cheer in a deep male voice.
- Issues with map geometry, i.e. with a horde right on your butt, you'll sprint across the street only to hit what the game thinks is an invisible wall because the curb is like half a foot above the street.
- Wonky car physics, meaning that driving over what you think is a small rock will rocket your vehicle into the stratosphere and kill your character.
- Worst of all, the infinite loading screen glitch is back. Anyone who played the original SoD at launch will remember this, where if you switch between characters, the game will load in as the new character, but the loading screen will float in place forever. It's easily fixed by exiting to the menu and loading back in, but this shouldn't be an issue in the first place.
It's almost been a month since launch with no patch (other than one to fix the import save function). Until YOSE gets fixed or falls to a price you think is reasonable, I say skip it. If you've not played the original, you can get that and all the DLC for less than $10 or $15 during a sale.

This is a great puzzle game. A lot like Sudoku in which you can only have a number appear once in every column and row. However, from there on out it has way more mechanics. In Sudoku, the 9x9 Grid is divided into 9 Boxes of 3x3, the Boxes themselves are arranged 3x3 as well. In SquareLogic the Boxes are called "Cages". And the cages aren't restricted to only on Mechanic either. In Sudoku, that Mechanic was that the 3x3 Box has to have 9 numbers in it, none of them repeating, and the Box had to be 3x3. In SquareLogic, the Cages can be any number of squares and in any shape. As for the Mechanics, there's a lot of them: For example, a 3 Square Cage has to have those 3 numbers add up to 8. So those 3 numbers(for the 3 squares in the Cage) could be 1+5+2, or 2+2+4, etc. You still have to make sure that numbers don't repeat in the same column and row, but numbers can repeat in the same cage, just not column and row. There's other Mechanics for cages too, mostly math, like all numbers subtracting to a certain value, multiplication, division, have number 3 numbers in consecutive order, etc.
The game introduces the Mechanics slowly, so you're not overwhelmed. You start with a few Mechanics on a 4x4 Grid, and work your way up to a whopping 8x8 Grid with a large amount of mechanics. There's plenty of convenience mechanics too. To make it easier to narrow down numbers, all numbers are listed in the Squares so you can just left click to input that number as the Squares choice, or right click that number to cross it out. You can use your keyboard as well. And when you input a number into a square, that number is automatically crossed out from all the other Squares in the Row and Column.
The hint system is great as well. It starts off with simple hints, then get's less subtle, then blatantly tells you the answer or just crosses off a number. The game can be solved with purely logic though. The Hints do a very good job of not making you feel like a moron and just nudging you in the proper direction.
As I'm sure you guessed by now, there's math involved. But you don't need to do any calculations if you don't want too. Let's say for example you're playing on a 8x8 Grid, which means you have numbers 1-8 to play with. Now let's say you're working on a 6 Square Cage in which all 6 numbers must multiply up to 560. You don't need to do any math at all, because when you highlight that Cage, the Solution List Mechanic pops up on the right. This list will show all possible combinations(remember that numbers can repeat within a Cage, just not row/column) in one easy to read list. If you've crossed out numbers your self or done automatically as you've filled in the rest of the puzzle, the Solution List will automatically factor out all numbers that can't be used anymore in that cage, whether it be due to crossed out numbers or simply because the Cages arrangement means numbers cant repeat themselves without being in the same row/column. Solutions that are still possible are Green, while Solutions that are no longer possible are Red.
Another thing worth mentioning is the ridiculous amount of puzzles in the game. The game is divided up into 5 Regions. Each Region has around 6-8 Locations that must be done in order. Each Location has 12 Practice Puzzles and 1 Challenge Puzzle, in which completing the Challenge Puzzle Unlocks the next Location, and finishing all the Locations Unlocks the next Region. Usually each Location gives you a new Mechanic to play with, and once you complete a Locations 12 Practice Puzzles + 1 Challenge Puzzle, you unlock an additional 787(That's right, Seven Hundred and Eighty Seven) Puzzles that all include the Mechanic learned at that Location plus all previous locations. The 787 Additional Puzzles are divided into 3 difficulties settings: Easy, Medium, and Hard. So if you're having trouble with a Mechanic, there's PLENTY of puzzles to practice with. If we just go with a basic 6 Locations per Region, that's 30 Locations. 12 Practice Puzzles + 1 Challenge Puzzle + 787 Additional Puzzles = 800 Puzzles per Location. That's a bare minimum 24,000 Puzzles in SquareLogic.
There's more stuff to the game, such as other fun mechanics and convenience features, but I'll let you discover it. If you love puzzle games, I definitely recommend SquareLogic. If you love Sudoku I ABSOLUTELY RECOMMEND SquareLogic, especially if you're looking for more in your Sudoku.

Alien Swarm is beloved modders-made game that was never quite finished; it consisted of only one campaign, but received a huge following nonetheless... so huge and faithful that seven years later we've got a much deserved sequel (completion of original title?) .
Alien Swarm: Reactive Drop extends the original Alien Swarm, but let me stop right here and give you a clue what the original game is all about in case you haven't played it (it was one of the first titles I've played on Steam).
Basically, it's class-based Left 4 Dead 2 with top-down camera, Starship Troopers / Aliens (the action sequel!) vibe and free mouse aiming that causes a lot of swearing and anarchy. You pick your marine, equip it with weapons, tools and items and move from point A to point B. You're not gonna be merry trudging down the deserted space stations and secluded laboratories because mother♥♥♥♥ing aliens will attack in swarms and you'll need to be precise while being trigger happy at the same time.
Classes have their own roles and stats: soldiers are stronger and can pack a punch, medics keep everyone alive, while techs are most precious members of the team working computers and hacking minipanels via simple, yet tense minigames. Remember those moments unlocking doors while being hunted in Alien: Isolation? Now imagine being overrun by tens of fast and hungry aliens all coming for your♥♥♥♥♥while your team is basically murdering themselves by having their accuracy locked at 9%. It's like solving a Rubik Cube in the middle of Zerg nest.
Alien Swarm (therefore, Alien Swarm Reactive Drop's) fun factor comes from what I call a complexity of simplicity - it's an easy to understand game that proves to be really challenging, counting on you to ♥♥♥♥ yourself over and over again. People will panic, act as unruly bunch and kill themselves whenever possible.
Now, ASRD is dream come true for the fans of the original; the game has been updated with bunch of new content and the old one has been polished. Reactive Drop includes new campaigns which have been balanced and polished for this release. New weapons also made their debut, with additional weaponry coming, according to Reactive Drop development team. Along came the baddies as well: Reactive Drop introduces additional alien types to raise havoc.
Alien Swarm goes from co-op to PVP in this edition, by introducing several different PVP events: from simple deathmatch types to Gun Game which is similar to CS:GO Arms Race (which is actually based on original Gun Game mod) where you progress through list of weapons and you need to kill with every one of them. Challenges are mutators that spice up gaming experience, usually by making it harder (as if we need that).
Reactive Drop is extremely Steamistic in a good way: there's a Steam Workshop support and lots of new achievements. Stats are available and there's a sense of progression as the time passes because leveling up unlocks additional weapons and equipment.
However, there are downsides to Reactive Drop as well: PVP games are hard to be found, the servers disconnect from time to time and animations cause players to get stuck in the worst of times, often costing you a match. I wouldn't probably mind if I haven't been playing Helldivers, its smoothness spoiled me.
However, Alien Swarm Reactive Drop's price of ZERO BUCKS can't be beaten. Without price tag on base game, no paywalls, DLCs and hidden expenses, Reactive Drop is work of love and truly free game worth trying.

I may upset some hardcore Star Wars fans but at it's core Star Wars: Republic Commando is a pretty straightforward shooter with some tactical commands.
It doesn't mean it's a bad game because I had a lot of fun with it, I'm just not as positive as most people.

I remember playing this game way back on the original Xbox. It's not through rose-colored glasses that I say this is the greatest squad-based shooter I've ever played.
Let's start with the atmosphere. It's spot on. Any casual Star Wars fan will recognize most of the enemies and locations. The level and character designs are grittier than what you see in the movies, and that fits the tone perfectly. The HUD is one of the best I've ever seen, because YOU SEE THE BORDERS OF YOUR HELMET! Such a simple design choice affects your immersion immensely.
So everything around you is cool. What about the combat? This game FEELS great. The modular weapons system is genius.  The squad commands are easy to learn but hard to master. The difficulty is pleasantly challenging; don't expect yourself to be repeating tons of levels, but do expect to be constantly searching for health and ammo. The weapons feel rewarding to use, and above all, the squad-based combat is amazing. You FEEL bad♥♥♥♥♥ You FEEL like it's you four protagonists against the world. And you WANT to take 'em all on.
Your three Clone Commando compatriots, Scorch, Fixer, and Sev, are exceptional AI companions (especially for 2005). They are effective in combat, respond to commands instantly, and generally don't make the kind of dumb decisions that make you rage at AI companions. They don't talk much, but you can still feel personality emanating from them.
On the note of character, the one category where this game falters is story. You know where you are, and you know why. You have objectives. But that's about it. The characters don't change over time. There are no plot twists. There is an instance of tragic loss (I won't spoil it for you), and it hits you hard. But there is room for improvement in that area.
Besides the story, what other improvements could be made? I won't comment on the graphics, because this game is coming up on 10 years old, but I will say they've aged well. The only thing that springs to mind is the level design. Don't get me wrong, the levels are designed fine, but it gives away what's to come. When you see a spot where you can issue a sniping command, you know there's enemies directly ahead. Health and ammo are always located directly behind large groups of enemies. It's textbook old-fashioned level design, but you always know what's coming.
One final point: because this is an older game, a 1920x1080 aspect ratio is not an option it offers. It's a minor detail, but an important one.
In conclusion, ten years later, this is still an incredible game. Although the story is never going to be a selling point, everything else about this game is great. It feels like you're taking a first-person trip through the summer action film spectacular that Star Wars never had. I highly recommend it to anyone who puts gameplay ahead of graphics. Amongst the vast troves of LucasArts treasures, this gem certainly shines bright.

Republic Commando is an FPS with tactical elements added to the gameplay. You control the leader of a squadron of elite clones and you can direct them to perform many tasks on the battlefield as the situation requires, from blasting walls, opening doors and hacking computers to providing cover fire from a safe position while you attempt to do the tasks yourself. They even get discapacitated if they lose too much health, and they can help each other as well as helping you if and when you go down. There are no vehicle sections in the game, the missions mainly consist of the team pushing forward against the enemy forces (sometimes stealthily, others guns blazing) with a few turret sections in between.
The plot follows the squadron (perhaps the other way around should be more appropiate) as they aid the war effort against the Separatist forces, starting with the battle of Geonosis, then moving to recon a seemingly abandoned Republic spaceship, and finishing just before the republic campaign starts on Kashyyyk. Each scenario is divided in several missions with very different objectives. The game is not short in any way, as it still took me over 10h to beat it on the hardest difficulty and will require trial and error strategies during the hardest sections (especially when timers are involved).
The soundtrack in this game is very much Star Wars, it will sound very familliar to anyone who has seen the movies or played other games. The sound effects are beautifully put together, from the laser weapons to the mechanical sounds of the droids and the environment (this is best appreciable during the spaceship section). The squadron will talk and communicate among themselves very frequently and will use the information as best as they can. They each have a distinct personality that will affect the responses they give to any order or situation. Even you as the leader will speak to them too.
The graphics are obviously dated since this is an old game. It lacks many important options such as the resolution and you will have to do some searching yourself on the internet in order to make it enjoyable to watch, but it is well worth it. The enemies are for the most part varied and the environments are more than just corridors of gray and brown (well, bar Geonosis of course. Even then there are indoor sections).
Overall, a very recommendable game with an interesting twist to the FPS genre and likeable characters.

Unfortunately State of Decay Year One Edition has let us down. What was supposed to be, in the developer's own words the "definitive edition" of State of Decay manages to be worse than the original. I could tell the original SOD was unoptimized, having to play it on medium settings on a beast PC just to maintain 60+ FPS at all times. (And this is for a game designed from the ground up for the 9 year old X-Box 360) Well YOSE is far worse in that respect. YOSE has a terrible stuttering/frame drop problem that occurs regularly even on the lowest graphic setting. In a game with unforgiving perma-death of characters you have spent hundreds of hours to build and level, it is unacceptable to loose a character just because a long heavy stutter skip made you die in the middle of intense combat. Also the game just feels like it will crash if you bump into your PC lol. What I mean, if you bring up the steam overlay, minimise the game, someone on skype calls you while your in-game, doing almost anything in the background will cause the game to crash. I have found that even if you manage you unminimise the game by some miracle, the performance will be bad until you close and reopen the game.
All the old glitches from the original SOD I remember are still here, including the ones that glitch your save file, requiring you to start over.
I admit is was pretty cool to see higher resolution versions of all the old art assets as I was able to see and read things on signs and posters that I never could in the past.
Overall I find the original version of SOD to be better overall. Performance is way better, has better load times, and I'd rather not have the gimmicks of YOSE that do not add anything to the experience. I'd rather keep my 60FPS gameplay with minimal stutter over higher res textures, non stop stuttering, and having to exit completely out of the game in order to respond to a Steam message. Also the flashlight has no purpose anymore in YOSE as every playable character magically emits light from their body.

Most of the reviews are talking about the surrounding controversy so I thought I'd write an actual review of this game.
This is a normal shoot em up game like Gradius but what differentiates itself from other games of the genre is the roster. Once you die, you will then move on to your next ship with different stats (Chance of death on hit, ship speed and Carbomite attraction) and weapons. The score you get in the game from collecting Carbomite also acts as a currency. You spend your currency on more ships and you could buy one really high powered ship for 100k + or loads of different ships to have many lives but will generally be less powerful. The different ships also have different pilots. The pilots don't really do much but add character to the game. All characters have been voice acted but the voice seems to be randomly assigned to a pilot. Sometimes I will see pilots who look like a young girl but have the voice of an old man which is odd. Hopefully each pilot could properly be assigned a voice during development.
There are many different types of weapons from single shot high damage guns to rapid fire machine guns or spread shot guns and more. These weapons wil be automatically upgraded when you collect enough Carbomite which drop from enemies. There are 3 levels of upgrades for each weapon. One stat you will see on different ships is Carbomite attractor. This determines how well you pull Carbomite towards you. This is important because you can pull two pieces of Carbomite together to make a bigger piece of Carbomite for a bigger boost to the upgrades of weapons and a bigger score. Bigger score means more money. More money means bigger and better ships on your next run.
The controls are ok but can be very painful after the first level. Due to the movement acting like a digital input even when using a controller, this means that you can only move in 8 directions and always at 100% speed. This is only a problem when trying to manoeuvre through a barrage of bullets and it feels so much more difficult because you can't make small adjustments well. The HUD doesn't help with this since I have tried dodging bullets and flew in the top corner of the screen but I went behind the HUD and I couldn't see where I was and I got hit.
Once you lose all your lives, you start back at the very beginning of the game but you keep your score to buy more ships. This is a really cool idea which I would be ok with if I could save my game somehow. I love playing the game but I have this small amount of dread when playing it. I would get to level 3, die and start from the beginning but with a huge score for better ships to help me on my next run. But if I want to have a break, play something else for a bit, I will lose my score and I will have to grind my score back up again every time I open the game. I could play for 10 hours and die but feel like I have to keep playing even when I don't want to just to keep my progress. If you aren't prepared to play the game for hours and hours non stop, you might as well just play something else which is a huge shame. Please save our score once we quit the game.
The levels are very VERY difficult, at least for me. I have only made it to level 3 once, and I do not know how many levels there are. Once I reach the end of a level, it feels so satisfying despite having done the first level around 10 times.
Despite the negatives, the game is still tremendous fun due to the great soundstrack and sound design, the varied ships and weapons, the cool enemies that work really well and the unique way of buying lives and ships. I think for £7 though, it's hard to be dissapointed.

tl;dr: This is a solid shump that has a fairly narrow scope and executes well on it.
This game is a standard shump where each of your lives has been replaced with a unique pilot which have their own stats and ship loadout. When you lose a life that ship explodes in a blaze of glory and is replaced with your next pilot. Once you have lost all of your pilots your score becomes money that you can then spend on a new batch of pilots.
The graphics and voice acting are well polished in a rough, retro way. The controls are tight and responsive and the hit boxes are good. The mini game of combining crystals and managing your energy add some depth to what is otherwise pretty simple gameplay.
My one major complaint is there is no way to save your progress and that makes the game less conducive to short sessions. There have been a couple times I've wiped and ended up with a good number of points and realized I didn't have time to keep playing. Exiting to menu loses all your progress, if I was to sit down to play this some more I'd make sure I have at least 30-45 minutes to give myself a chance to complete the mission.
Overall this is a solid game with an interesting mechanic, if you are a fan of the genre it's worth checking out.

After giving it some thought, I decided I'd purchase this game despite it's £39.99/$50.00 price tag. I'm an incredibly big fan of the Sword Art Online series, although it's been a couple of years since I've last gotten involved with the franchise. After discovering this being available on the Steam marketplace, I knew I had to try it. Sadly, I was disappointed.
The game starts out with a character creation that's not the greatest. Sure, you could argue that there's multiple options and that you can even alter the color of both eyes individually, but when I checked the skin color, there was hardly a spectrum, and the difference in colors weren't that far apart. Also, don't think that changing your gender to a female will alter the dialogue, because it doesn't. This was a red flag already for me: the developers of this game didn't take out the time to change DIALOGUE for the option of a female gender. That in itself is ridiculous for the price tag they're selling this game for.
Now I move onto my second issue, which I'll paraphrase in my last complaint about the game: DIALOGUE! There's TOO much of it, and the beginning of the game is filled with it. It's a horrible experience at the beginning, you'll face more dialogue than you would gameplay at the start, and while that can be okay in some cases, this one it wasn't.
Thirdly, the skill tree is poorly done. The overall layout for the game's menu is lacking and doesn't really replicate the same feeling as the menu you'd see in Sword Art Online's series. Are you looking for a menu just like in the manga or anime adaptation? Well, forget finding it here, because you won't. You can hardly call it effort, it felt like they put no love into the GUI interface.
Fourthly, the affection system is actually really, really bad... You start off with Asuna being your girlfriend, but when you try to hold her hand, she freaks out... what? How do you make sense of that? Try and wrap your head around that one. You start a game already within a relationship, and yet your "girlfriend" is considered only "close" to you. Yet, even though she's apparently close to you, she negatively reacts to you choosing to hold her hand? None of that makes sense...
Lastly, the game is TOO EXPENSIVE FOR THE GENRE.
The only thing I will say that's good about the game is the combat system, and that's with a stretch. They did a very good job at designing the combat experience. Unfortunately, this is not even remotely close to a reason to buy the game with its full price tag. Absolutely RIDICLOUS. It feels like the overall reviews are paid actors.
My recommendation? Don't buy the game, seriously. And I'm saying this with a broken heart, as a SAO fan. Disappointment awaits you ahead if you do.

I was planning to write an elaborate review on why I like this game so much, but I don't want to come off as airheaded. As you can see, I don't recommend this game. I'll keep playing it because it has personal value to me, both as a fan of SAO, and as a gamer. Objectively, the game is very flawed. Here are a few frustrating tidbits I've picked up in my playthrough thus far:
- ♥♥♥♥ing expensive. This is the biggest reason why I can't recommend it. For the amount of problems it has, I can't recommend it for 50 dollars with a straight face.
- Translations are iffy and sometimes straight-up wrong (voice actor says something, text at the bottom says something else)
- Myriad of typos in the text, starts to become especially obvious in the late vanilla game
- Enemies get stuck in walls
- Enemy balance is way off. Some bosses are level 200 and have a 10-ish minute fight, others are level 90 and have a 30 minute fight and do way too much damage (not all bosses are created equal, I suppose)
- Most maps/zones are forgettable, I can only remember a few
- Loading screens ♥♥♥♥ing everywhere. This is probably the biggest personal disappointment of the bunch. I have a beefy PC, there's no reason other than console limitations to have loading screens on 2 areas that are 100x100 feet
- Horrid FPS in some late-game areas, especially in the DLC
- Soundtrack is good, but it ends up being repetitive, so I usually just turn it off and play with my own music playing
- Party members often get stuck on terrain, causing things like skill chains and switches to ♥♥♥♥ up
- Party members often can't do anything on their own, they are probably 20% of the total DPS (I end up doing the remaining 80%)
- Party members have the same barks and they get really repetitive to see after a while
- Quests are lazily designed, bare-basic fetch and kill quests
- Events are either glorified kill quests or stealth quests
- AI aggro range is ridiculously small, making dashing by them a viable tactic
- Most enemies die in 3 seconds, making enemies feel like cannon fodder instead of posing a threat. Alternatively, in the DLC areas, there are far too many enemies that can wipe the floor with your party because they do ridiculous damage and have a ridiculous health pool
- Controllers aren't directly supported, you have to hook up a controller through Big
Picture Mode
- "Dating" elements are actually grindy in their own special way
- Tutorials explain things like combat and skill chaining in weird ways
- Bosses are way too easy to be intimidating
- Fanservice becomes grating at times
- While using (SPOILERS)
I often get stuck inside the enemies hitbox, resulting in me having to either ALT-F4 or find a workaround through divine intervention. Either way, incredibly frustrating
- Vanilla game has a little too much handholding, while the DLC has too little handholding. The DLC expects you to get the lay of every millimeter of the land, remembering finite details to come back later. It makes the core gameplay loop of exploration tedious if you end up getting stuck.
- Enemies end up being reused too much, with random placement, making some maps look like they were built by an 8 year old using unity assets for the first time
- The dueling system in the DLC is god-awful
- Cutscenes using in-game footage without voice acting are rampant, making the game feel like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ source-engine visual novel at times
- Solo play feels discouraged
These are the negatives I could come up with writing this, but I'm sure more will come to me after I go back to playing it. The game feels unfinished at times, and the DLC feels lazily put together, aside from the story (which I'll get to in a second). All in all, it's a timesink. If these flaws weren't offputting, I commend you, because now I'm going to get to the things that I actually love about this game.
+ The story is very enjoyable, even the DLC's as well
+ Combat can be an absolute riot. Racking up skill chains and combos with your party can be immensely satisfying, watching a light show of sparks and flares as the enemies HP bar empties feels great
+ Voice acting is top notch, as always with SAO
+ New characters introduced are very likable after exploring their personalities
+ Visual-novel style companion quests are often just a good time
+ Soundtrack is solid, especially the main menu theme holy
+ Armor sets are varied and colorful
+ Has replay value if you want to try different builds and party setups
Objectively, I can't recommend this game because it can be a buggy, crashy, typo-filled mess of lazy iterative content. For the asking price of 50 dollars, this is a resounding no from me, dog. However, if you can pick it up for 20 dollars or so, I think the pros would outweigh the cons. The story really is good fun, the combat is fun as well, but there are a lot of smudges on this game's smile.

There's not really much I can say that others already haven't, positive or negative.
So speaking purely from opinion, I personally enjoyed playing through Magicka 2, possibly more than the first game. The movement system and being able to cast while moving took some getting used to, but it works great. They balanced the spells in comparison to the first game, so you can't use Steam/Lightning beams anymore (Lightning cancels out the water in the steam), and even if you could, some enemies are resistant to, immune to, or they absorb the elements used in some combinations. Magicks have been reduced down to a few, more potentially useful offensive spells instead of having a lot of AoE spells that you probably never actually used. I mean, why bother with Blizzard or Time Warp when it's easier to Raise Dead, teleport across the room, and hit something with a rock? You also can't hide behind Shields anymore. Whether you think it's good or bad, Shields have been balanced to only block beams, but any other attack, as well as enemies, will pass right through them.
There is some bad, though. While the game is more polished, it still has it's fair share of bugs and glitches. For example, a few times I've went to launch a Rock but it doesn't respond. This left me in a state that still acted as if there were elements waiting for use until I tried to cast a separate spell, and unfortunately this caused the rock to launch at that point instead (and sometimes they were exsplosive).
The only summoning Magick I've found isn't as useful as Raise Dead or Summon Elemental, only summoning some fairly weak skeletons that every strong enemy and boss can just tear through. Maybe this was part of balancing, but the Magick in question is only really good for brief distractions.
But my experience was overall positive. At least when playing with someone else. I've been playing Hard Mode solo, and it's a long, hard slog. I played normal mode with my brother and it was great, but not having anyone else playing on Hard Mode is a pain.
Like I said, this is all personal opinion. I don't know how you might feel about it. Maybe if you're not sure you could wait for it to go on sale at some point. But I reccomend giving it a fair shot at some point!
UPDATE
Some changes were made to the game recently.
They reworked the element combination system to be like the original game, so we get our Steam Lightning beams back! They also introduced a new element combination: Water and Death creates Poison. You can modify the movement controls too so that you can move the way you did in the first Magicka. Shields still only block beams and nothing else (besides other shields) though.
I think these changes make it much more worth it, personally.

You and up to three of your friends (or strangers online) play one of several characters in a squad. This is a class-based top-down shooter from Valve. For some reason this game did not generate much buzz despite being really good. Think of it as a small-scale Left 4 Dead in a sci-fi setting. Exterminate the aliens or "bugs" with lots of weapons.

The creators of the original mod which inspired tons of other similar games on Steam work at Valve and they made this game to be 100% free and released it with all the resources needed for mods and levels made by the community. For some weird reason it never really caught on. I guess that's because this was released before the Steam Workshop became big and it still doesn't have Workshop implementation which is a crime. You need to find the community made campaigns somewhere in the internet yourself.

It is completely FREE, so what are you waiting for? Get some friends and play the campaign! And if you are hungry for more, download community levels or unlock weapons for all classes!

Like a swift kick to the stomach, this game will leave you doubled-over and gasping for breath hours after you finish playing. How many times have I been forced to kill a spider droid on my own with just a pistol because I ran out of ammo and my entire squad is incapacitated, or how often have I encountered a droid dispenser pumping out SBD's only to realize I've already used up all my anti-armor charges? These kinds of situations force to think ahead and plan & execute your strategies quickly. Keeping your squad organized is key. It's a beatiful thing when you give your squadmates commands and then find out that what you've decided for them to do is the perfect strategy. Good ol' Delta 38... he always knows just what to do.
Squad control in the game is easy as pie, and the friendly AI is okay, though at times a bit frustrating. When they're given a command, the squad will go do it no matter what, even if it means doing something dumb like getting killed because they don't think to kill the things in their way first. Enemies are pretty stupid, but you don't need to be smart when you're a Super Battle Droid. The graphics and landscapes are dated but still amazing, from the windy, dusty canyons of Geonosis to the dark and foreboding forests of Kashyyyk. Except for the commando armor, everything is dark and gloomy. Gameplay is also awesome; everything is fast-paced and keeps you on the edge of your seat (and sometimes out of it completely). Whether you're desperately trying to hold off an endless stream of enemies as one of your squadmates plants explosives on a droid dispenser while another hacks into a security system while under fire, or you're clearing a path through a group of fat Trandoshan slavers in the maze-like corridors of an assault ship, there's never a dull moment in Republic Commando, and the hard difficulty mode is just right.
The Squad:
Delta 38, the main character. A tough-as-nails commando, 38 don't take no crap from nobody. Even when under heavy fire, he calmly gives commands like he's ordering food at a McDonald's drive-thru. He's the voice of reason, keeping everybody under control.
Delta 62 (Scorch), the Demolitions expert. Scorch likes explosives. That's all there is to say.
Delta 07 (Sev), is a fierce hunter. His best use is as a sniper, providing amazingly accurate covering fire for his squadmates. His only job is to kill, kill, kill.
Delta 40 (Fixer), is just a good old-fashioned soldier. He's uncomplicated and a great fighter, and always follows orders. Other than that, I'm not quite sure what his deal is... I guess he's the "computer expert," though any commando can slice any console.
Each commando has his own personality. Scorch can be quite humorous at times, and Sev has some pretty disturbing things to say. One thing I don't understand is why do all have different voices? I though they were all the same clones...
Trust me when I saw that even still to this day this game is worth every penny. The only thing I wish is that more games could be like this.

Back in 2005, Star Wars: Republic Commando was an unsung gaming classic, since then it has aged incredibly well in the gameplay department, standing defiant against both the tides of time and the trends of cover-based shooting and regenerating health. The gameplay, weapons, squad mechanics and even the graphics are still appealing even after all this time. The Steam release of Republic Commando is the third time I have bought this game, and I still love to play it now and again.
The first thing that LucasArts got right with this game is making the Commados feel just as bad♥♥♥♥♥as the Jedi, while at the same time making them feel like soldiers. This is accomplished simply with the squad commands and context-dependant actions such as sniping and grenade positions. The scripted animations are icing on the cake like tackling droidekas or killing a kamikazi trandoshan with his own knives.
But while each member of Delta Squad is comprehensively a one-man killing machine, they are not as invincible as a Jedi Knight, you need your squad, and again this really enhances the military feel of the game. Performing door breaches, setting up entrenched positions, and setting up covering fire while you outflank the enemy do a great deal to give Republic Commando a military feel that few modern military shooters can match. Putting you in command of Delta Squad was an awesome idea.
Atmosphere is another area where this game shines. You start out being dropped behing enemy lines onto Geonosis, fighting your way into a Geonosian hive complex, down through a droid foundry and into a trade federation droid control ship. Then comes the genuinely creepy ghost-ship mission where you will be reduced to being hunted, alone by scavenger droids, and finally you will form part of the first wave in the republic's campaign on Kashyyyk, each location feels unique, and the game manages to capture the frenetic pace of a battlefield, the isolation and helplessness of a horror game, and the epic scale of a megaflora jungle.
While some games start to feel dated and klunky as technology and design practices roll on, Republic Commando was at least 10 years ahead of its time. Everything about it shines, and the few flaws are minor and easily overlooked. Even when it's not on sale, this game is a bargain at ten bucks, the only negative point I can hold against Republic Commando is that it wasn't long enough and never had a sequel.

Definitely a great little puzzle game. Don't be put off if you're not someone who loves Sudoku--even though the layout is similar, this isn't a straightforward Sudoku game, and there are many aspects of the game that make it easier and more interesting than regular Sudoku. For example, the game automatically removes numbers that will not satisfy the requirements of the grid, and notifies you if you have made a mistake. It also offers the option of displaying all of the possible mathematical operations that satisfy the conditions of the grid, but you can turn this off if you like more of a challenge.
The first puzzles are very easy, but the challenge gradually increases, and there is a variety of puzzles to keep things interesting. Sometimes there are "Hidden Cage" puzzles, where you have to work out for yourself which rules apply to which squares, and sometimes there are "Double Board" puzzles, where you work out the solution by comparing two boards. You're not always doing the same puzzle over and over. If you want to do that, though, there are literally hundreds of similar puzzles to keep you occupied if you don't feel like grappling with a new puzzle type yet. Each type of puzzle is available in Easy, Medium, or Hard.
One of the best things about this game is that it lets you take a "challenge puzzle" to unlock the next set of puzzles whenever you like. You don't have to complete all of the puzzles on each level before being able to unlock the next one. This is helpful if you find the first few levels too easy--you can keep skipping ahead until you find a level of difficulty that you like.
Overall, a very good puzzle game that should offer hours of entertainment for a small price. Definitely worth the money.

With a true western vibe, Firewatch provides for an interesting and worthwile playthrough. The game (and subsequently the map) progress in a linear fasion, which might not be to the taste of players looking for a truely open world experience. Overall, the mechanics are quite good, however, some of the climbing actions are quite baffling, given real world climbing experience, whereas there are multiple points in the game where the character willing jumps off a ~10ft+ cliff in the middle of the wilderness (a suprising risk when you are supposed to be miles into the wilderness), but struggles to climb over a few stones on a valley floor. Regardless, Firewatch is worth a play through, given a Steam sale and the time.
A thrilling story accompanied by absolutely beautiful artwork. Ever since you start playing the game it will be hard to put down. The conversation you have with the other character is never boring.

Firewatch sets out from the get go to be a unique game. And in many ways, it is. What it promises, it delivers. 4-5 hours in the beautiful Wyoming landscape through amazing art direction, a sparingly used soundtrack, and incredibly convincing voice acting.
Let me get the technical side of things out of the way, first. The game doesn't run very well. Yes, the landscape is lush with many shades and rich shadows, but overall it felt choppy, there is that occasional pop in, and this generally isn't the sort of game you'd expect to run into problems with, but given the size of the dev team, and given the pace of the game, I guess this could be excused.
So is the ending as bad as they say it is? Well, the game does kick you in the gut, but it depends on how you let it sink in based on your connection with the protagonist.
It is a game that will make you feel a sense of adventure, romance, dread, discovery, and longing. Could it have put forth its true ideas (which again, appear only if you wish to acknowledge them) in a better way? Sure. But this trek through the wilderness, the way it is presented and unfolded is definitely worthwhile.
Is it worthy of the full price? Prolly not. Pick it up on a sale. 7/10.

In a way, the spurious and temporary takedown of this game was the best thing that happened to it, especially since it would have flown under my radar. Tracking the increasingly baffling story of an ex-contributor's copyright system abuse via SidAlpha's coverage was something to behold.
And the game being shown in the background of his vids, this game, looked really fun. After playing it for myself, I can say that it is really fun.
What you have is a difficult but fair sidescrolling shooter in the Gradius/R-Type vein where you're trying to mow down an invading alien fleet through space pilot after space pilot, each with their own weapon configuration. This really is a game that's meant to be mastered, dodging bullets and incoming enemies left, right, and center. I was at the edge of my seat maneuvering around deadly projectiles and ships.
The health system for your ships is also interesting and fun, letting you survive taking hits if timed just right. It's an interesting mechanic that I haven't really seen before in other games, and adds a little bit more fun factor to the game.
But if you do run out of ships, you start anew with another fleet. You do this by opening packs and paying for pilots with your score. With randomized pickings, you'll have a lot of variety to choose from, and different ways to play. Maybe you'll rely on a few strong and expensive pilots to carry you through the game, or maybe you'll recruit cannon fodder by the dozen in order to push back the invasion - hey, it's what you gotta do in an alien invasion. It's a very fun implementation of the trendy "roguelike" elements that fits this kind of game.
Add to that a good pixel aesthetic and really nice musical works, and you've got a good package.
My only complaint is that there's no good save feature, I'd like to space out my sittings for playing this game. I've also played this game with a controller, so your experience may vary if you use a keyboard for this game.
That being said, this is very playable as a complete game, let alone a Early Access title. This is a very fun game, and I'd easily recommend it to anyone hankering for a shump-style game.

I bought this game primarily in support of the creators as they mount a legal battle against their former employee due to her claims of copyright on assets she was contracted to create. That being said, it is a pretty fun game, and well worth the purchase. I haven't played it a ton yet, but I feel like I might play it quite a bit on occasions in the future.
There are only a few small issues I have with it so far.
One is the music. I don't know what it was like previously, with the original music, but I'm not a huge fan of what they have currently. The current music uses a lot of semi-high pitched 8-bit like sounds. I hope they will change it in the future, or provide other options. Of course, one can always just mute the music and play one's own. I might try to do that myself in the future, perhaps by trying to create some sort of game-type music playlist for it.
The voice-overs are pretty entertaining however. Although occasionally they can get repetitive. They make plenty of pop-culture references, and a few jokes about being cats or such, depending on the character. I was pretty surprised they managed to get so many sounds into such a small game. Definitely a much bigger fan of the 150 meg sized game, versus what some others have started to make quite common, of a few gigs.
An issue I had when I first started it was that it says nowhere in the actual interface what the keyboard controls are. I couldn't even find what they were online very easily. Hitting space brings up options, which is really counter-intuitive. In many games when I was growing up, space was fire, with all sorts of different choices for alt-fire. Esc also brings up the options menu, which is pretty standard. I literally had to press almost every key on the keyboard to find that 'X' is fire, and 'Z' is or alt-fire. Really, you're better off using a controller.
This game really doesn't spoon-feed you anything, not even what the keys are to control it. It's kinda old-school in that it's like "Here's the game, you figure it out." It's not overly complex such that you can't figure out the basics of the game if you've played anything like it though, so it's not a huge deal.
I'm also not a huge fan of the pacing of the game, but that's personal choice. It's very fast paced from the second you start it. Enemies buzz into the screen, and back out, and you blast a seemingly infinite supply of laser fire at them. Does every ship have a black hole reactor at it's core or something? Must be, because it seems like a single hit will kill any of your pilots. Not sure how much this changes with pilots you can afford later in the game.
One of the coolest things about this game is the method for obtaining extra lives. Rather than having extra life drops during the game, as is pretty standard in a lot of old-school games, you actually purchase pilots with the score that you obtain with the previous ones. What all the data means on the purchase screen however, I'm still figuring out.
My review might seem mostly negative, but those gripes are really small compared to what amounts to an extremely fun and enjoyable game, that's already very playable, despite still being in early access. Even though I am not a huge fan of the music, I have to hand it to the creators for their ability to bring it back to Steam with new musical assets. I do hope they will either get better music though, or more options, but it's definitely playable. The pacing as well is only my personal choice. It is definitely in line with a lot of old school shooter type games.
If you like old school side-scrolling shooters, get this. It is very fun, and you'll be supporting a small development group, for a very worthwhile price as it is currently. I can't promise you'll survive long on your first few plays, but it's a great addition to a Steam library, to play during those times when you're bored, and won't get mad when you find that you accidentally just played 3 hours when you only meant to play 15 minutes.

In this game, set in the far future, the class system has been reinstated. Instead of the nobility leading us into battle however, it is our feline companions that do so in the search for wet food.
I can only assume that the war you are fighting was caused by our feline overlords insulting the alien race known as the G'rell for their beautiful fireworks. As it stands, you fight against hordes of seemingly automated drones sent by the aforementioned G'rell to bring colorfoul displays of burning plasma to the skies of your home planet.
The act of war has become a very unusual affair in this future. While you are allowed to hire mercenaries, no common armed forces seem to exist anymore. Such are the rules of engagement, that the defending party (You, humanity) has to send their combatants (Space pilots in this case) into battle in successive order of their hiring. No more than one fighter for humanity may be active at the same time ever.
These rules do not seem to apply to the G'rell automated army however. Two theories exist as to why. The first being that these rules of engagement do not apply to automated drones, the second one that the G'rell are still unaware of the fact that this is war and they are just sending out more unregulated fireworks equipment.
The universe is also stuck in a weird form of timeloop. The same, endless battle against the Grell is taking place over and over again, but a certain mineral which is also used as a form of currency in this world is unaffected by these temporal fluctuations. This allows you to keep any such minerals collected during the last unsuccesfull suicide mission of young pilots to hire another team, or even your last team all over again to go back into the fray.
This gruesome tale of feline dictatorship and misunderstandings is accompanied by a very upbeat, synthetic soundtrack and very colorfoul ship and world design on the part of both armies. The pilots on the way to their doom are chipper in their own right, quoting from the great works such as Firefly and Duke Nukem as they go about their hopeless mission of death.
All in all I would recommend this game despite its frustrating aspect of having no possibility to even freeze your progress for later use, an aspect that is sure to discourage people like me that wish to provide their families with food. While this may be unwanted by the developers, the second missing aspect for me is one that was necessary for me to even consider putting my hard-earned lawnmowing and dog-sitting coins into the magical entertainment machines of my youth - A Highscores list is painfully absent.

I am loving this game. Each pilot has so much character both in terms of writing, voice acting etc but also in terms of gameplay. I love the slow firing weapons that pierce swarms but against single strong enemies it becomes a long duel dodging shots and counter firing.
When you have a fast firing ship you can tear throw strong single targets but swarms overrun you like the defence of Zion in the Matrix films. Every ship has its own niche so it never becomes too easy and if you die, your next ship may be better suited.
Your score is your currency to buy pilots, which perform double duty as loadouts and lives. Do you buy lots of cheap pilots and use them their dying explosions as a way to forcefully plough through or do you go for a single good ship and just 'git gud'. When you fail and have to replay a section it doesn't feel like a punishment or a waste of time. Your great run that just failed will buy you an even better squad to make this next run better. Death as progression and reward scaling up with performance. The better you do the better you can do.
The chance to survive thing is interesting too, sometimes you mess up but get away with it. Instant relief then immediately back to tension. I assume if you get hit whilst the yellow the line under your portrait is in a green section you live since it seems different for each pilot (Think Tidus' limit break in Final Fantasy X). If so I can imagine advanced players will be able to use that tactically for some crazy skill depth.
This is very much a modern game with a retro aesthetic. The controls are spot on, the game is beautiful in motion (screenshots don't do it justice). Instantly playable with skyhigh skill ceiling. This feels in no way like an early access game. Usually you have a mess of a game that needs refining all over. This is more akin to a playable demo right now. It seems mechanically finished and the production quality is great accross the board, but only the first act is available.
I look forward to the inevitable design decision discussions about his game in the community.

It’s just one of these days. You wake up late and rush to work. Of course you’re stuck in traffic. Great. You arrive at work , too late, and you get fired. On your way home your car dies for no apparent reason. Literally everything has gone wrong today and you have this urge … this urge to …
There’s no apparent story. You can make your own.
What we do know is that you’re in control of a bad♥♥♥♥♥ one could even say, Chuck Norris.
But other than that the game’s focus isn’t story driven in case you were wondering.
runs pretty smooth. I haven’t encountered any apparent problems or bugs other than enemies ignoring me just because I’ve turned the water on in the public bathroom and decided to jump onto the sink. They just looked at me in disgust, while they were severely bleeding and looking at me with hatred in their eyes. Couldn’t care less to be honest.
Anyway.
is a truly chaotic, first person, voxel based melee combat game. You’ll fight your way through different time zones and locations.
The default level is a classy one. It’s a Biker Brawl in Bitter City.
It’s tuesday, february 4th in 1992. One man vs the world. Well vs the everyone in the bar.
The next level is a truly funky one. It’s Saturday Fight Fever and boy it’s on!
On sunday , june 11th 1978, you’ll get just a tad too funky.
So you see you have a unique location and enemies through out the levels.
The goal is to beat the ever living shi … well is to pain the town read. That means that you have to defeat every enemy in the location.
You might wonder how? Well however you want! That’s the true beauty of the game.
You can use cups, a stool, a chair, a knife, a guitar … literally everything that’s lying around or being held by someone. A dude has a bottle that you want? Kick him in the face and send him flying because that’s
bottle! You want a knife? See those chefs over there? Just beat them till they drop it.
You can kick, jump, stab, punch, throw, block … You can do so much. Hell if you want you can watch some people fight to the death if you’re tired or need a break.
Eventually you’ll run into an enemy that you can’t kill that easily. Lucky you! You’ve found a boss.
Those guys are just a tad tougher but fear not! You have more power than them. I’m not kidding you literally do have powers. There’s a blue bar in the upper left that fills with each enemy that has been defeated and there’ll be a message on the screen once a power’s fully charged. So let’s talk about the fun stuff.
For example the shockwave! As the name implies you’re able to slam your knuckles together to create a shockwave that’ll send enemies flying. Best to be used if you find yourself in a tight spot.
Next up is Berserk! Boy that’s a bloody good one! Everything slows down and you turn into a one-hit-one-kill killing machine. Seriously. If you punch their head like once it just explodes. Kick the enemies and you obliterate them. Bloody good fun! Literally!
Last but not least is a truly god like ability … Smite. No not the game. That’s pronounced SMITE you doofus. I mean smite!
Well you point with your finger at someone and then you smite them. Basically a blueish light will shine on them and, as the name implies, smite them. Best part about it? You can use that from any distance. Not to mention you get to play god for a few seconds before your power runs out.
Overall the gameplay is bloody good fun!

It's basically the original Alien Swarm, just with a few more weapons and a few more campigns. An all-around great game still, and if you liked the original you'd be hardpressed not to like this one.
If you've not played the original, basically it's Helldivers (before Helldivers, of course), but much more based around survival instead of big guns and explosions. Everyone has one life (not matter what your difficulty), and a single death can easily screw you over for the entire match, because of how important every role is. No medic means no healing, no special weapons person will mean you'll lose important firepower, and having no tech will often times mean a straight up restart because of the locked doors only a tech can open.
Friendly-fire, like Helldivers, is still a thing, but it's generally much less deadly in Alien Swarm, unless you're putting friendly fire to the highest difficulty. Most of the time, you won't have to worry about getting killed by friendly fire, but it's still quite annoying.
Things are behind level locks, but it's not too terribly important because most weapons aren't that widely different, so a lot of people stick with the basic weaponry for quite some time.
Overall, it's a fun co-op game from a few years back that I'm extremly happy got revived.

1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Although at first glance this game seems like it is a waste of any money at all, especially coming out near the attack of the clone game, it is one of the best star wars games I have played. This is my second favorite star wars shooter, barley falling below BattleFront 2. The Story is amazing, the atmosphere makes you feel like a badass, while at the same time feeling so weak and fragile. (Especially when fighting Super Battle Droids) This game is a must with either friends or being alone, as the AI will follow orders and even in today's standards are smart and think well. The HUD idea is great, it gives the look as if you are the clone itself. The graphics hold well, and the combat is spectacular. After playing this, you will have a craving for a sequel, and want to have a higher standard in today's shooter games. 10 out of 10. I enjoyed getting this game while being on sale.

Great FPS by itself, plus add in the ability to command you team mates where to go and what to shoot, got lots of weapons, great storyline, and options to destroy or hack a door. Both can be good or bad if used at the wrong times. Honestly one of the best AI for a FPS I've ever seen. (Well at least for your team.) Love the music, the atmosphere, and the battles. In every mission there is going to be a new battleground and new things to take into account. Maybe they have turrets, maybe we have turrets, maybe we have different sniping positions (did I mention you can tell your teammates where to snipe from?), maybe they have a spider droid, what weapons/ammo do we have? Maybe one of my team mates isn't with me right now. All of it comes down to a very fun and stratiegic game. This game really is the defenition of an awesome FPS. The one complaint I have is the storyline is a bit short, but 12 hours campaign for first time play through isn't that bad. 10/10. I would recommend it to any Star Wars or FPS lover.
Also it had hidden wrist blades before Assassin's Creed came out. Just sayin.
