While I support everyone's cause to end developers with the $$ in their eyes, this is clearly not the right title to be doing it on and the people doing so are misinformed.
I'm sitting here reading these "most helpful" reviews from people with much, much less than even 5 hours in the game (a lot of them ironically saying they 'haven't seen anything different or new content-wise yet'), while reviews that are simply people saying they can't start the game (likely because their graphics setup doesn't support Dx11/isn't updated) somehow got upvoted to the most helpful page.
Meanwhile, it doesn't take much to see the shameless squad of review-skewers operating out of the vow to upvote every single negative post no matter how meaningless it is and downvote the opposite, so right now it's pretty hard to view an actual, thought-out review of this game (Obviously, don't pretend I'm somehow 'unbiased' or 'more correct' in this situation). I'm going to predict that the amount of people who downvote this post within the next several hours will prove those previous statements (update - accumulation of 247/1053 as of Oct. 5th 2016).
For further thought material: For a brisk while post-release, critic reviews on Metacritic for this game were definitely positive, and the problems those reviews mainly have with the game are more about a lack of polish and the fact that it wasn't a complete 'overhaul' like they hoped for, rather than it being a bad purchase or a bad game. Of course, by now, even some of those are under the impression that those "darn corrupt devs" made this to rob us thanks to the keyboard-activism.
The issue with the talk of business practice is how obvious it is that nobody is actually looking into the validity of what they are saying - Undead Labs is not in control of the business practice. They are the dev team, it is their concept and ideas that built it, but ultimately, they signed it away to Microsoft for publishing with the XBLA system back in the 360's development stage.
Before you assume that it's their fault anyways - remember that the XBLA program exists for small dev teams to have a place to release their game to the console market, and rules must be followed and UL would not have had any choice in the matter (being as small as they were with no resources at the time). Nobody knew the game was going to succeed how it did.
What does this mean? Well, it certainly doesn't mean that Undead Labs even had the authority to "screw the customers" if they wanted to (which anyone with half a brain for PR can assume that they didn't). Rather that this is the PC port for the
version of the game, which sold for the simple reason that SOD otherwise did not exist on current (XB1) gen consoles at the time. Undead Labs has also stated that they cannot update the port without the go-ahead from Microsoft, which does not care about the PC port in terms of promoting their console-heavy
.
Now, if you actually care about what's in the game and how it compares to the last version, here is actually new content-wise in YOSE:
-New knife-combat (which comes with a bunch of nice badass moves) (One of the bigger changes in the game)
-New difficulty arch for Breakdown that extends far beyond the previous 12 levels.
-30 minutes of new music
-The amount of cars has more than doubled (although most of these come from new variants of already-existing vehicles. There is a classic 80's sedan, SUV, a non-customized version of the modern muscle car, some new tuners, a new classic muscle car and a bunch of new colors and variants for all of them.)
-Some balance and physics tweaks
-Fleshed out car repair features
-New facility options (you can now do stuff like make coffee and convert ammo and stuff like that)
-A bunch of new guns
-A new type of mission (which is acts as a really nice reward occasionally in breakdown)
-New Breakdown Heroes/survivors (including a returning-player bonus)(Milo Eldrige is an example of a new generic survivor for those misinformed souls that think Gurubani is the only change).
-Slightly sharper graphics and frame rate (Not even close to a big change)
-New visual ground effects, actual fog, etc
If you are a new buyer to the series, then yah, buy this. State of Decay is a great game, and this is definitely the better version to get. There is more content, a bunch of smaller features the previous did not have, more community support for it.

). Keep in mind that in that same thread the developer can be quoted as saying that something new might just be in the works as well for the game.

(This comes from the point of view of someone who played magicka one, and wizard wars.)
Pros.
The new ai is great. faster paced monsters and battles, makes for an exciting expierience. There is a decent variety of monsters for the relatively short campaign.
Similar yet different humour than magicka 1. Laughter may vary, but I enjoyed it.
Not mentioned a lot, but i like the method for changing difficulty by adding different talsimany things. bananas difficulty looks like a hell a lot of fun with 300% friendly fire >:)
Lots of fun easter eggs to find off main path.
Graphics are awsome. A lot of attention to detail in every level.
Casting while moving was carried over wizard wars. 10/10 would kite again. Opens up new strategies, but came with a longer charge on projectiles.
Cons
Campaign felt kind of short and wasn't as convuluted and strong as magicka one. With that said I will probably play through it multiple times at different difficulties with different people. (just completed a solo run). (also the unlocking of new items, and challenge levels give the title a little more meat to chew through).
Just like Magicka 1 the expansions will probably all be paid dlc, which sucks.
The higher level magicks are given a coolsown, andcan be activated through a button. You can still qeue elements to cast the spell, which effectivle gives you more spells on your hotbar and can be faster or add more of a challenge. The cooldown is honestly short enough where I didn't notice it (except for revive) but I rarely used magics in either magicka.
Other comments
The spell system changes for magicka 2 are not as big of a deal to me as made out by other people.
The big difference is you cant combine steam and lightning or ice in the same spell, so comboing spells is more important now than finding your favorite op spell.
The companions don't get in the way and are basically only there to revive you. Solo run became a lot easier when I realized I could revive them after they used up there rivive on me.
There is this one battle early on with a jamming song replayed in the credits, best part of the game. I wish the song and the battle lasted forever.

I can see how other people might be dissapointed by change, but I'm not. Nostalgia got in the way of other people, but the mechanics are solid and my biggest complaints are with the plot and the campaign itself.
9/10 would kill myself and my friends over and over and over and over and.... I think you get the point.
Despite the nerfs and changes, this game is still a lot of fun with friends.

A lot has been covered about this game already, so I'll contribute what new points I can.
First off, I was hesitant about this game.  Seemed too simplistic, wasn't sure if it would offer enough of a challenge and thought it might, maybe sit on my list unplayed and forgotten.  Months later, this has become my most played game on PC.  (Don't trust my 'hours played' number: I mostly play it on my laptop when I have no connection.)
There are THOUSANDS of puzzles for you to take on in this game.  They all work off of the same basic concept, with some fun little variations (such as working with two interconnected boards that share the same answers, but different formulas).  Each one offers a new challenge though and with time you pick up on the patterns and logical shortcuts that you may have missed before.
As for difficulty, you really can make it as easy or difficult as you want.  There is no "real" penalty for just guessing every single box.  So, if, for some bizarre reason, you want to just barrel through guessing the whole way, you can.
Or, if you're like me, you can aim to finish each puzzle WELL below the Par number of moves with no mistakes and only the bare minimum use of the right-click-to-hide-invalid-numbers function.
If you're extremely sharp and/or have too much free time, you can also hide the box that shows the possible solution combinations.  Not an issue when you're dealing with two or three boxes, but at five or six it becomes a little more impractical; even with the solutions, you still have the challenge of figuring out the logical placement of everything.  You could be at a single puzzle for hours.
If you use a laptop like I do, you'll also probably appreciate the low demand it will place on your battery and system resources.  Makes for many hours of what we nerds consider "fun."

The interface looks a bit odd if you just look at the screenshots but it works remarkably well when you're using it. All the numbers are big enough so you can fully concentrate on the math/logic in your head and not on having to pixel-perfect click on the right numbers. Very quickly you'll find yourself in "the zone" clicking away and moving to the next puzzle.
The game mechanics are simple, just click on the number you know must be correct and the same number will disappear in the rest of the row/column.
When you know a number can't possibly be in a certain square you can right-click on that number to hide it. Eventually you’ll end up with all squares filled with the correct number.
These are fast-paced math puzzles (don't worry, without a timer) and you have
of puzzles to choose from in a variety of configurations, all organized in groups from easy/medium/hard. You will not run out of puzzles any time soon and it's a great way to pass the time doing mental gymnastics.
p.s. The solutions on the right hand side can be turned off in the settings in case you also find them to make the puzzles too easy, at least in the first couple of locations.

One hell of a game. I've been playing Republic Commando since I owned it on original Xbox. This game beats all other Star Wars games in my books.

Definitely one of my favorite games of all time; when I'm feeling nostalgic about the old days of FPS games, I turn back and replay Republic Commando a couple of times. The story is short but awesome (if you read novels, the book series by Karen Traviss is very, very well-written, I HIGHLY recommend it), the combat remains challenging, and the graphics, although nothing to write home about in 2014, are still decent. All in all, it's right up there with KOTOR and Battlefront II for the "Best Star Wars Game Ever Released" award.
*Edit* I don't feel like I elaborated enough on the combat, in retrospect. In a nutshell, the singleplayer combat has the effeciency, tactics, and overwhelming numbers against expert tactics and firepower that many FPS games, including most of the Call of Duty, Battlefield, and Medal of Honor titles, have sought (and failed, IMO) to match. It's truely one of the most dynamic, immersive FPS games out there, hands down.

Fantastic, only one advice: get it on discount. For a 50€ game, I expect at the very least some international dub
EDIT: As I made more progress through the game, I must say that it's worth every penny, the amount of content is really making up for the price, considering there are 3 already-included DLCs.

Though I would recommend this game, I would only do so at a lower price. The game is solidly built and runs smoothly. It has nice graphics and the combat is fun and fast-paced. The story is not anything noteworthy. I found the controls horrible on the keyboard but they work well on an Xbox One Controller.
Though the game has good combat mechanics, a lot of it is made pointless by how easy the game is after the first two or three mini-sections of the first area. Dodging, healing, debuffs, and  buffs are not needed as you become practically invincible a short time into the game. Either it is far too easy to overlevel or the monster's levels just progress too slowly - eitherway, this results in you constantly being overleveled (You can reduce this by not doing any side quests but it does not completely prevent it - this also shortens the length of the game quite a lot).
Another issue is the over-powered stats on some of the weapons you get in relation to the level you are at. On top of being overleveled you can also gain weapons that can increase your HP by a ridiculous amount - especially when you can upgrade them. With this and overleveling, the only you can really die is to just by standing there.
This is a shame as if the game was more difficult you would actually be able to put the fighting mechanics to full use, making this a very good and fun game. As it is, this allows the game to grow stale as there is no challenge.
The worst problem with this game is how the story is told. It is boring. Everything is told in custscenes including travelling and fighting (though sometimes you do actually get to fight in a designated area), The only interactivity the story has is clicking to continue the conversations - some of which seemingly go on forever and are not at all interesting.

Maps - Literally just a retextured version of Sniper Elite V2
Gameplay - For being a sniper game, there isn't really any actual proper sniping, like shooting a target 200 metres away. There is none of that apart from shooting the occasional bottle for and achievment.
Variety - A large choice of rifles, sub-machine guns and pistols, although it gives minimal information or stats about each gun so you don't know which to choose for the way you'd like to play (fast but not much damage, do lots of damage but slower paced etc.) In terms of killing things, there isn't alot of variety in that either. You get the zombies with the special abilities (e.g. suicide bombers, ones with more health and such), but apart from that you're basically doing the same thing over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. Also very short game.
There's sweet kill cams like in every sniper elite game, but If you want kill cams, go for Sniper Elite 3 or Sniper Elite V2 as these ones aren't really that good. Plus it's not as satisfying when you get a bullet cam from 2 feet away. But when playing Sniper Elite V2, shooting at an enemy sniper a mile away and then instantly getting the bullet cam is so much better, since
you kind of actually earned the bullet cam instead of getting it every other kill.
Story - There is no dialogue in cutscenes. It's literally just 4 blokes standing around with the same facial expression for each character. Also there is no story
Conclusion - Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army isn't a very good game, since they basically put no effort into making it a different game to the others. It's basically an expansion pack displayed as a whole new different game (when it isn't).
If you like to mindlessly kill zombies over and over again and like to watch bullets penetrate various internal organs and testicles, then this game is for you. But if you want a better Sniper experience, then I would go for the actually sniper games (Sniper Elite V2 or 3)

A suprisingly fun and truly addictive arcade shmup with a twist.
This game sets itself apart from its peers with its mechanics; lives-per-run are represented as distinct, procedurally-generated pilots - each with their own stats, weapon loadouts, ships, and voice acting. Stages feature procedurally-generated enemy formations to compliment the pilots.
The music, effects, voices, pixel art, and gameplay all come together to create an outstanding experience; I have a handful of much more expensive shmups in my library, and none of them are this fun. For ten bucks, this is an absolute must-buy.

NOTE: Steam review system is dumb. I wish I could take a neutral stance rather than having to go with WHOLLY RECOMMEND or WHOLLY NOT RECOMMEND, but I chose to not recommend the game for reasons stated below. However, this review is more positive of the game than negative.
NOTE2: I'm a derp that doesn't know how to look for more megative reviews on Steam.
I typically don't buy side-scrolling shmups, or shmups in general for that matter. I have several reasons for this, three major ones.
First of all, I've already spent years of my life playing Touhou and Mushihimesama, enough that I feel like another shmup just won't give me the same amount of satisfaction.
Second, this is a side-scroller, and having played a lot of Touhou, side-scrolling just felt very... awkward to play.
And the third is that this is a shmup. You play one or two or ten, and you've played them all. I wasn't going to put down money for a shmup that probably have mechanics that aren't new nor fresh. It had to be for a good reason.
And then that reason appeared. Its name is Alexander Thomas Mauer. You guys already know what's happened, so let's keep it short. Found out about the 'situation'. Decided to take a side by choosing to buy this game (and planning on buying more copies of it to give to friends and family) as soon as it reappeared on the Steam Store.
And what did I get from buying this game? Unfortunately, a pretty generic shmup, in my opinion. There's nothing specific in this game that's bad. And I guess you can say that's a good thing. It's just unfortunate that the shmup genre is one that's really hard to innovate. There's a set formula to this genre and it's hard to make better.
There's very little good I can say about this game. It's challenging enough, though probably higher than expected for newer players of the genre. It's visually pleasing. The little bits of voice acting from the pilots are hit-or-miss for, more on the miss side though I guess I can just turn them off. I can't really say anything about the music, because this isn't the original music. While I can say that the current music fits the theming of the game, I can't really call it excellent. And I can't really compare it Alexander's original music either.
The one thing this shmup has going for it is its drafting system. Long story short, every round you use the points collected to in that round to draft a set of pilots for the next round. If anyone here plays Magic The Gathering (not the online version, like the actual cards and booster packs you OUTSIDE to play with other people), this system reminds me a lot of the Booster Draft mode of play, where people don't start with their own decks but rather open up booster packs to form the decks that they will choose to play with. Of course, DSP's drafting system isn't as thought-inducing as MtG's (unless there's that one type of bullet fire that YOU REALLY LIKE AND YOU ONLY WANT TO PLAY USING THAT BULLET TYPE), but this system is really the only thing that separates this game from the other shmups in the market. As with any opening of booster packs, there's a chance of finding a pilot with a new type of bullet fire and acquiring said pilot for the next round will enable the possiblity of using that bullet fire type for any other pilots afterwards (please correct me if I'm wrong). This is enjoyable to me, who has spent a lot of time playing gacha games. Acquiring a rarer character/pilot and being able to employ its nature later is a rush of dopamine to my system. But even with how much I enjoyed the drafting system, this is still a generic shmup.
Regardless of its misfortunes of being a shmup, I still had fun with it. A game doesn't have to be excellent, primo material for someone to be able to have fun with it. I will be returning to this game when I have more free time. Unfortunately, this game just doesn't do enough as a shmup that I can really recommend to anybody personally. While I will recommend to people that I gift the game to play the game, I most certainly can't recommend to those same people to buy it if I wasn't gifting the game to them. Sorry Imagos Softworks.
tl;dr I don't buy shmups because I've already played a ♥♥♥♥ton of them, but I bought this one because I wanted to show support for the developers during this Alexander Thomas Mauer debacle. As expected, this game is pretty, but gameplay is generic. It's a side-scrolling shmup. What more are you asking for? The game employs a round-by-round pilot drafting system which really feels like the only thing that separates this shmup from other shmups. I still had fun with it. But the game doesn't do enough as a new entry in the side-scrolling shmup genre, or at least not enough for me to recommend people actually buy this game.
NOTE3: I get that this is Early Access. I would like to reiterate that this is still a side-scrolling shmup. I feel like innovation is pretty hard to come by in any form of shmup because a lot has been attempted. I mean, look at some of Kenta Cho's works (that should still be online) as an example. A lot of things have been attempted with the shmup genre, and thus I'm not expecting Imagos Softworks to be able to whip up something great enough for me to change my mind of not recommending anyone buy it.

Omikron: The Nomad Soul has a very in-depth plot and constantly tries to break the fourth wall (whether it works or not) in order to convince you that your soul has been trapped inside the world of Omikron and that your soul and very existence outside the game is at stake in regards to the antagonist, the demon known as Astaroth. The characters you interact with in the main story are fleshed out in their own rights, some more than others. The player is able to interact with certain people at certain parts of the game and depending on what you say will determine what the character will reply with.
I'D SUGGEST NOT USING WASD OR THE ARROW KEYS TO MOVE AROUND, IT MOST LIKELY WON'T WORK FOR SOME REASON.
Gameplay:
The gameplay hasn't really aged well. Some controls are very stiff, and the parts of the game that works really well in regards to the controls would be the first-person shooting sections. As for the puzzles you need to solve,  the majority of them can be pretty cryptic and you'd need to pay good attention to it all. I'd suggest having a notebook by you at all times to write information down. I would also not recommend playing this game without at least some sort of guide. It rarely ever explains what you need to do in order to progress within the story (for example, how to get to the classified police report after KAY'L returns from being "missing") and without a good amount of wit or even luck, you're basically screwed. The fighting sections are also a bit stiff and it's good to know how to do certain combos (I'm a button masher, personally).
Presentation:
The presentation has also aged VERY poorly. The use of facial recognition technology was revolutionary at the time, but now it just looks awkward, especially when the character stops talking. They just give a vacant stare with their soulless eyes and their mouths are slightly open and unnatural. The way characters' arms would move in certain scenes make it appear as if they are made of rubber and it's quite distracting. It's perhaps the worst when you go to any of the in-game concerts with The Dreamers. The way the lead singer appears to have violent seizures on stage can be very distracting when enjoying songs from David Bowie. The lead dancer also moves and twists unnaturally from time to time. The only Dreamers member that is animated the most "realistically" is the guitarist who doesn't move nearly as much. Certain textures within the game could also have been more clear or more interesting. A lot of models of people/items can also appear pretty blocky for 1999.
Music:
I adore the music, especially the songs written and sung by David Bowie (probably because I'm a big fan of his work), and there's a good handful of instrumental tracks by Xavier Despas that I love to listen to. Jaunpur, The Awakened and the Tetra Factory Assault are only a few to mention. A lot of the songs try to go for a cold, futuristic style in order to represent the society of Omikron as corrupt by the government they follow. I believe Despas has done well in portraying that type of lonely feeling throughout his soundtrack.
Final Word:
I'd say if you're curious, it wouldn't hurt to play it. The story can be very intriguing and it keeps you on your toes with helping the Awakened and saving your soul from the demons that roam Omikron. The more time you spend in Omikron, the more you become a part of their world and the more you can appreciate it for what it has.
To David Bowie Fans:
It's definitely worth checking out if you've never heard of his involvement with this game! If you're familiar with his 1999 album, "Hours," you'll find most of the songs from it within this game either as concerts with The Dreamers or as transcripts you can "purchase" to listen to whenever you'd like. He also voices and lends his appearance to the character, Boz. Boz is the leader of The Awakened, and unfortunately you only get to talk to him once, not counting the ending. It's quite surreal to see Bowie in a video game, so if you like him, definitely check this out!

First off: It astonishes me that this game has had such a long shelf life. I've been playing for years (prior to purchasing it on Steam), and the discussions board is still pretty active. Those who play it, generally keep playing it.
So, with a name like "Everyday Genius," it's pretty easy to be scared off; one could be forgiven for thinking this to be a hardcore math game. It isn't. It's more logic puzzle than anything else, although it remains unique. It is not like Sudoku, except that it uses numbers and the process of elimination to reach a solution.
Simply put, you're presented with a single grid (to start). Inside each grid is a series of puzzle boxes that contain different mathematical symbols along with the numbers 1 through 4 (I said math isn't really needed, and I didn't lie; keep reading). An equal sign (for example "4=") inside a box simply means the answer is the number 4. Two boxes reading "3+" means that the answer will be 3, and it is achieved by adding two numbers together (1+2). Like Sudoku (which this really isn't), numbers can only be used once in each row or column. Each puzzle within the grid can be several boxes, and they are painted the same color so that you know they are one puzzle (for example, 1x2x3=6, might all be painted green). You get the idea.
What keeps it from being less math and more logic is that mousing over any box will automatically show you all possible combinations for the solution. As you solve more puzzles inside each grid, these possible solutions will also change, due to process of elimination. Eliminated numbers will automatically disappear from each puzzle, and you can also manually remove them by right-clicking. Because of this, it really is possible to solve each grid without much math skill.
The variety offered here is stunning. You will use greater than and less than symbols; straights (3,4,5,6, etc); even / odd numbers; multiplication and division; and more. The real creativity comes when boxes arrive unpainted, leaving
to color them in with the correct colors. Color them incorrectly, and you'll be solving puzzles that don't exist, meaning your entire grid will be incorrect! Some times, you may have puzzles without any equations; other times, an entire 9x9 grid may
! The difficulty level amps up until you are solving two grids simultaneously, with factors up to 9.
There is no time limit, the colors are vibrant, and the music that is here is soothing and ambient. It's casual puzzle solving at its best. There is truly nothing else like it, and it remains a classic...for those of us who actually know about it. Some people, like myself, are still playing it years later, and you'll not solve the 20,000 included puzzles (not randomly generated, by the way) any time soon.  Even better, it can be played with one hand, for those times when my grandson falls asleep on my lap!
At less than $5 US, there is not a single puzzle game on Steam that offers this much game time per penny. Highly,
recommended.

In a previous review I called Hexcells "Minesweeper on steroids" (an assessment behind which I gladly stand), and in the same vein I'm going to introduce SquareLogic as "Sudoku on steroids".  Again, you have a game inspired by an original, but taken to wholly higher levels with new gameplay mechanics.
With "Pretentious Title: SquareLogic" (thanks to
for that one...I had to stifle a giggle) you're taken beyond the scope of regular Sudoku as the board gets divided up into arbitrary sections, each with its own independent ruleset.  Then -- in contrast to Sudoku which starts you out with some cells already filled in -- you fill out the entire grid, using the rules for each section (in the game's terms, each "cage").  The result is a wide variety of puzzle times that don't get stale like regular Sudoku (for me, anyway).
The other nice thing about SquareLogic is its wide variety of assists.  You can configure it to immediately highlight errors, show you a list of possible combinations for the "arithmetic cages".  (SquareLogic is not a math game, but some basic arithmetic does organically result for this particular cage type.  We're talking adding and multiplying single-digit numbers.)  These two features can be turned on and off independently, and there's also a hint button (which you can choose not to click).  In addition, it's possible to "cross off" candidate numbers (for example, if you know a particular cell cannot contain a particular number); for an additional challenge, you can solve the puzzles without using this feature (easy enough in the beginning, but try that on a 9x9 grid!).
The background music -- I mean, it's not really music per se, more ambient soundscape -- suits the "deep thought" premise of the game nicely.  However, the audio is never part of the gameplay, so you can definitely play with any other tunes you like in the background (or silence).
At the end of the day, this seems like an obvious choice for a Sudoku fan who's looking to grow into something more -- I won't say more challenging, because the harder Sudoku puzzles I've found are certainly more than challenging enough for me at least -- varied.
As for replay value, if anybody ever finds out, let me know.  There are 20,670 puzzles in the game, so I'd hazard a guess that once you've completed the set, you can probably start over from the beginning and not remember the ones you've already solved.  :)

The concept for this game is great, but the execution is downright awful.  This is a racing game (with flying cars, I might add) where you have no speed indicator and the controls essentially prohibit precision braking, accelerating, and turning, making it extraordinarily difficult to stay on a track that has a lot of tight corners.
The track is created by the player currently in first in this racing game.  That player can create sharp or gradual turns, straight track, and occasionally loops or jumps.  I expected the lead player to have some extra controls to cycle through track choices for the next leg, but instead the track is generated based on where the player drives on the course.  If you drive on the far left, you create a sharp left turn.  If you drive slightly left of center, you create a gradual left turn.  This is  pretty much the worst way you could possibly build track, because anyone who has ever played a racing game knows you start sharp turns from the opposite side, so the lead player has no incentive to ever make the track turn because it would cause him to crash into the wall!
This horrendous oversight in game mechanics all assumes you could even play a multiplayer game.  I have sat for over 30 minutes on the  “Waiting for Players” screen and only once got a multiplayer game going, but the player dropped out of the race shortly after it began.  This is probably because the stupid controls are unmanageable and the cars are all identical, thus there is no way to catch up when you inevitably fall behind unless the other player also makes a grievous mistake.  There are no power ups, no speed boosts, no anything that could give you an advantage or help even the race.  I’m guessing multiplayer would be a lot more fun than solo, but it seems this game isn’t nearly enjoyable enough to keep enough players interested in joining multiplayer sessions.  Perhaps it might be fun if you and 3 of your closest friends collectively waste $$ on this game, but probably not.
The solo levels are also garbage.  The game forces you to earn a medal on a level before the next one opens up.  This means that sooner rather than later you will get stuck and be unable to progress.
The Cars-with-wings aspect is kind of cool, but flying slows you down to about half normal speed, so you have no reason to ever fly unless there is a jump in the course.  Also, the car constantly veers in a completely unexpected direction when you attempt to steer while flying, so that sucks too.

You have two main vehicles: a car, and a car with wings.
You drive an abstract vehicle on an abstract track floating on an empty abstract world.
However, for a racing game, this game has several flaws:
- No HUD for the target times (gold/silver/bronze). The times are only shown AFTER you complete the race. So, there is no way to see if you are doing well or if you should restart the track early. In other words, the game forces the player to waste time.
- No HUD for the current speed. I can't know for sure if my strategy is better or worse, nor can I know if I am too fast for the next turn, just because I have no way to measure it. This quickly becomes a blind trial-and-error, wasting your time.
- Upon the start of the race, or after hitting the RESTART button after finishing a race, there is a 5-second waiting time until you can move. Again, this is the game forcing you to waste time. Fortunately, if you hit Backspace (or gamepad Y) while racing, you get a "fast restart", where there is only a much more reasonable 1-second delay.
- You have to beat the Bronze time in order to progress. However, the times are pretty tight, so most (casual?) players won't ever beat those times.
- The wings of the car, when retracted, fold up, obscuring some essential portions of the view area.
- Although the game can be controlled with an analog input device, the control itself is digital. It doesn't matter if you slightly turn your analog stick (or racing wheel), the car will either go straight or fully turn the wheels.
- The settings screen only has the predefined Unity settings. No way to fine-tune the graphics.
I want to support indie devs, but I must be honest: I didn't like this game.
Overall, my feeling while playing it was: "Why am I playing this inferior game? I should be playing TrackMania instead."
Sure, TrackMania doesn't have a flying car, but it is a much more enjoyable, much more polished, and a much better experience. Go play TrackMania instead of Krautscape.

Devilian is an ARPG that fills a unique niche in the ARPG genre. Replayability is a major factor for me in any ARPG, which is why I rate Path of Exile and Diablo 3 at the very top of the pack. PoE and D3 accomplish this, in large part, by regular seasons and new leagues, which gives people a reason to come back time and time again. Of course, fun game-play is ultimately paramount. Devilian is a fun game. Combat is very enjoyable and character progression and gameplay is fairly deep and varied. Devilian can be enjoyed solo or in groups. The biggest concern I have is longevity. Given that Devilian has no seasons or leagues, I feel that once you hit end-game and grind out "the perfect character", you will quickly find the game becoming monotonous. Also, word to the wise: turn off in-game character speech, unless you like hearing the exact same phrases uttered ad infinitum.
Outside of that, Devilian is still a solid game at its core. Overall, I would rate it a 7 out of 10. I would encourage anyone who enjoys ARPGs to give it a try.

I've begun doing early impression reviews.  I'll play the 2 hours we're affored before a potential refund and make my descisions of a game based on how it starts off.
Starr Mazer does this wonderfully, it knows what it wants to be and throws you into the action to learn off the bat.
This game is sink or swim done right.
So let's talk gameplay-
The gameplay itself is fluid, you learn quickly how to play and what to do .  there's no hiccups or confusion as you progress and any sort of significant shift or change in either scenery or enemy formation is broadcast by voiced lines.
The emersion is fantastic, not once was I pulled out of it by any unusual stutters in either gameplay or character.
You'll be shooting down heavy waves of foes, pressured on every front and challenged differently in every level you reach (I only managed the 4th stage before this review).
The game is challenging, but in no way punishing, if you die you know you're the one to blame and beter yet you'll learn form it.
The bread and butter of the Game is Carbonite, dropped by enemies you slay and better yet able to be combined by luring the floating particles together for increased bonus and point score.
this directly relates back to my "Sink or swim" comment as this itself can be a gamble, you need to navigate around this stuff and lure it together as it slowly follows you like a powerup, but the enemies will not be keen on letting this happen and do not slow down.  Bide your time and keep an eye out on enemy fire, a bonus means nothing if you're dead.
BUT Carbonite does more than just fuel your point score, it fuels your WEAPONS!  While your Weapon doesn't peter out it will become a pea-shooter if you let it, you can't waste shots and avoid enemies or you'll find yourself slowing down and struggling.
Don't cover, show no fear.  Be bold and you are rewarded!
This doesn't even cover the enemies.
No game can excel with boring repettitive enemies or overly powerful ones.  Lucking for you this game has niether!
Enemy patterns aren't predictably scripted, sure you'll run into similar mashes of them each time you play the level, but there are always a few variations to keep you on your toes.
Better yet each stage will feature new enemies with new attacks and challenges from stage hazards to enemies that will even abuse it to thier advantage.
You aren't helpless though, there's an excellent variety of weaponds and specials available in a random mash when you select your pilots.
You'll earn your Pilots by playing the game, the better you do the more Pilots you will be able to purchase for combat, but it goes beyond that with different packs and playstyles.
Mix it up!
Scenery and Music-
The transitions for the background are fantastic.  The color blending isn't too loud or vibrant and won't distract you from the matter at hand which is kicking Alien Kiester.
You'll go from a Planet in ruin to space and the hazards beyond as you progress fighting off the Gr'ell fleet ensuring you'e never too bored of what you're passing through.
As for the music, it's beautiful.
My favorite is currently in the first stages second act once you've entered the stratosphere.  You'll fiond the tracks always match your location and keep you rocking as you punch holes in alien cockpits and make scrap of fine engineering.
Voice Acting-
You may find it surprising that this game features voice acting, unusual for a sprite-based shooter.  But as you recieve your orders from a deep-voiced smart-mouth Cat General you'll chuckle.
The pilots all differ in personality and gender (and possibly species?  I think I hired a lizard but he died a little too quick with an experimental weapon) from fast talking city-slickers to rural homegrown farm-girls.
Overall I feel it gives the game good character as you get slightly attached ot these people only to see them die horrific explosive deaths.
So yes, I do recommend this game.  For an early access it's on track to becomming a fantastic release.

After hearing about one of my favourite games getting a sequel, I could not have been more thrilled. Its such a shame that many issues from the original game were not only carried over but amplified in this one. I am not going to lie, from playing the game for over an hour I can tell how much the fact that the game was developed with the PS4 in mind affected the game.
The Good:
-I know that graphics don't make a game by the cartoony artstyle of the first game was not only fully captured and encanced in this sequel. The game uses some great new effects that make the world feel more vibrant and lively.
-The controls have been refined. The game does not feel as loose as the first one. It is easier to control your character and cast spells with the new UI that makes it easier to navigate your spells.
-Unlike the first game, Magicka 2 uses progression to unlock new types of robes and weapons. This might be seen as a negative however it might decrease the amounr of DLC released in the future and makes the stages more challenging for the player.
-The "Artifact System". This new system allows you to customise your difficulty by using artifacts which can create an experience right for you.
-The Hotkey spells. Unlike in Magicka, this time around you can bind spells to hotkeys which allows for their faster cast rate. It is different and I find it a great addition as it speeds up the gameplay. I do see how this change can be a detraction from the experience.
While Magicka 2 imrpoves several gameplay elements, I am affraid outside of game you will not have much luck. This game had been clearly designed with the PS4 in mind and therefore, the matchmaking is reduced to creating a game or joining a random one. The game lacks any sort of proper server making or Steam integration which does not work well with the lack of voice communication in the game. Unlike the first game, in here the difficulty spikes at a faster rate creating a really harsh experience for lone players in the game. To add insult to injury, the community currently in the game is nothing but atrocious, I had people join my game just to try to kill me so they could play alone, or people trying to kill me to get me out of the game. The lack of voice communication makes it almost impossible to teamwork with strangers and the community does not help. This issue was already present in the first game, with the ingame matchmaking being pretty poor however, this game makes it dozens of times worse by removing lobbies or servers.
Therefore, I would say that if you have at least 1 but prefferably 3 friends to play with, get this game! You will surely enjoy it in one way or another. If its because of the humour, the spell systems or the challenge. However, if you are looking at this game as something to play alone or as a game to find new friends in, stay away from it and try the other 2 games in the series.
I hope you find this helpful and contact me if you'd need someone to play with.

Omikron: The Nomad Soul is weird. Not in the "cats riding bacon through a marshmallow sunrise" sort of way but in the "this thing had a BUDGET" sort or way. You see, you don't play as the main character, or even a side character; you play as a computer spirit whose been invited to possess someone from an alternate dimension by the person its possessing. For all intended purposes, you're not "yourself", or even the person you're roleplaying as; you're roleplaying a spirit roleplaying whoever it is you're controlling.
I'll give the game credit, it nails the sensation PERFECTLY. It's like that one Japanese film from last year, but instead of becoming a country girl attending high-school, you're a police officer with tank controls. Regardless, just like in that movie, you have no clue what's going on and you learn the universe as the day goes on, and you have A LOT of learning to do.
Omikron's world is apparently the brainchild of David Bowie and David Cage. David Bowie makes music, and David Cage made Heavy Rain on the PS3. Both their talents come together to create a universe to get lost in, and I don't mean that in the immersive sense. YOU WILL GET LOST. Consult a guide might as well. There was a point where I couldn't figure out how to make progress long ago, and I tried really hard to figure it out, but the game is of no help. Turns out I had to DRUG my Commanding Officer to obtain a key?! She asked for a soda, and I gave her one. Turns out DRUGGING the soda was the solution, and I thought I had to earn this key from doing a quest or something to earn her trust. That's how most games would have worked, but Omikron is special. Yes: Firewatch doesn't tie up loose ends in a way that is completely satisfactory. I don't mean just the obvious character relationship at the heart of this game, but the emotional journey of the protagonist gets lost when the plot starts to pick up its pieces. Is this a story of connection, redemption? Or coming to peace? None of those things? I just couldn't tell. It's one of those times when I wouldn't have minded if the story's themes were a little more overtly presented.
But it doesn't matter. Firewatch is both quiet and roaring, superbly acted, stylish, and emotionally engaging, and it only took me a little over four hours to complete. It's the best example of interactive fiction I've seen in many years. If you're into this whole "walking simulator" thing, which I am. This is one of the top examples of that, up there with What Remains of Edith Finch and Gone Home.
Rich Sommer's performance as Henry might be my favorite game voice-acting work in a game.
While it is not a long game, it draws you in with a gripping story and a breath-taking environment. Firewatch does not disappoint

text:
Bad Company 2 is a first person shooter game created by DICE and published by EA in 2010. The game features both a team-based multiplayer mode and a singleplayer campaign. The singleplayer campaign has you playing as Marlowe, a member of an elite American special ops team. You start the game,however playing as Thomas Wyatt, coincidentally also a member of a U.S special ops team,though this time you play back in the WWII era instead of in the future. You start out going on a secret mission to meet up with a Japanese Scientist who wants to defect and claims to have valuable information on a new super weapon. Things quickly go to hell and your entire team is wiped out after the Japanese discover you and proceed to make you bear witness to the test firing of the weapon,killing you and your team.
You begin the real campaign after that and you start playing as Marlowe,though the campaign is in a futuristic setting now instead of the bleak hell of WWII. The campaign features 13 full levels with each one ranging from 10-20ish minutes to complete,with some more long or difficult missions being around 30-40 minutes at most. For the most part the missions are all quite linear,although they give you open fighting grounds to fill with corpses as you make your way to the objectives.If you came to Bad Co. 2 for a story that would blow your socks off you will be suprisingly (or maybe not suprisingly,depending on how you feel about Battlefield) dissappointed. The story isn't poorly made nor is it poorly done at all really. Problems arise when you have a story that is incredibly average and is only being held up by the unparalleled gunplay. When you get into the thick of fighting it's easy to get lost in the heavy smoke of the fresh gunpowder and the whump of your rifle as you mow down entire squads in your quest to save America from Soviet invasion.
6
Into the Fire . . . With Some Help
The campaign may not be anything special but i'll be damned if this isn't one of the most fun MP modes I have played in quite a while. The destructibility is astoundingly fun to play with and actually has some serious strategic value. Enemy sniper hiding behind a window? 40MM Grenade launcher solves that real quick. Enemy soldiers crossing a bridge into your base? Blow that bridge to hell and back! Being able to just destroy pretty much anything at anytime you want is an incredible idea in both the campaign and the multiplayer. The multiplayer itself consists of 5 different game modes each with varying degrees of difficulty. The first one is Conquest,a mode where each team has a set amount of tickets,dying will of course drop this ticket total by 1 per death,and the goal is to drain the other teams tickets before they drain yours. There are also multiple flags you can hold that will give you a constant ticket drain if you hold the majority. Other than that you just need to kill them faster than they can kill you.The next mode is Rush,a gamemode where you have two teams,attackers and defenders each trying to attack or defend multiple M-COM stations respectively. Attackers are tasked with setting C4 charges on the stations then defending them until they explode. Defenders,of course are charged with defending the stations until they finally bring the attackers' ticket count to zero.After that you have Team Deathmatch which,if you have ever played a multiplayer FPS before, just consists two teams each trying to end the game with the most kills. Next you have squad rush which is just normal rush but with no vehicles,smaller maps,and a max of eight players.Finally there's onslaught,a co-op DLC mode where you try to play against AI and capture flags. Vehicles spawn at certain points and there are multiple levels of difficulty to fight against. Generally all the MP modes seem fairly balanced and there were no glaring problems with the mode that I noticed during regular play. The matchmaking system is completely broken and will either not find you a match,even though plenty are available,or it will put you in a match with just yourself; so make sure you just use server browser.The Multiplayer is what you really would be buying this game for as the campaign was pretty much overlooked due to more people wanting MP than SP.

If you want to play a game and have fun, personally, I have a lot of fun with this game (I have and also play another seven BF games).
At the time of writing, number of players online range from a few hundred to over a thousand. To check current numbers:
To check where the servers are located:
Do check at different times of the day as the population in servers drastically change (obviously), and just one 'snapshot view' won't tell you much about the online numbers and locations of where the players are.
Depending on the location, some people may only have more distant servers to play on with higher pings - different people feel differently about higher pings.

With all the negative reviews, I feel I have to do this release some justice.
I have spent 110 hours on the original and 35 hours on this remastered version already.
For newcomers, State of Decay is an innovative zombie survival with an open-world "GTA"-esque vibe to it.

As for bugs, there are a few minor which are common to the open-world genre, but there has not been one instance where my gameplay or immersion have been interrupted and there are certainly no new bugs with this release.
Having said all that, for those who did not enjoy the original State of Decay, this release will not change your mind.
I advise prospective buyers to read up on the new features and watch some gameplay before deciding whether to purchase.
Do not be too easily put off by the negative reviewers who were disappointed after asking Santa Claus for too many presents.

I played the first  State of Decay and the expansions for over 400 hours because I really liked the game. I admit that much can be improved and I was hoping YOSE would be a step in the right direction so I bought it even though they only gave a 33% reduction for a game that was only marginally improved.
However I can't play YOSE because the game crashes my pc.  I play for a random timespan then the screen goes black and poof the pc reboots.  I tweaked settings, updated the drivers and checked everything. No matter what: my pc crashes.
My pc is 3 years old and made for rendering movies, which is a pretty intensive process but even when rendering, playing a game, running you tube and various programs at the same time my pc won't crash. I also played a wide range of games  such as Skyrim but only State of Decay causes my pc to crash.
As this takes the fun out of the game and  I don't like my pc crashing to the point of no longer functioning I can't continue to tweak and play this game in the hope it won't happen again. And since most reviews confirm that the changes are superficial I can not recommend YOSE based on my experiences.
I would also remark that selling a game with almost no viable changes for almost the same price is tantamount to a rip off. But we are now doggy trained to the anything-for-a-profit argument so I guess this signifies the normal pattern in game development. You can see this with the early access  games that never get into full release. At first the idea was to give players the chance to help develop the game, but people quickly saw another way to make a profit: selling unfinished software that does not get into finished state because "it is still under development". Examples are such games as  DayZ and Take on Mars from Bohemia Interactive Simulations, both almost 2 years in early access without a release date.
I would advise people not to join the early access release racket. It gives bad companies methods to rip people off,  it makes good companies lazy: they use you for what they should do themselves: properly develop software. And then  finallly they charge you again when the game is released in full.  Yes, people, the game you helped develop, for which you did not get a dime but for which you are charged twice. Come on, people.

Krautscape is a racing game in which you build the track as you drive. Also, your car can fly. It's a neat idea, but it's so terrible in practice. The physics are the worst I've ever seen in a racing game. When you're flying your carplane will veer off in the wrong direction for no apparent reason. I can't tell if it's just buggy or if the game is supposed to be simulating wind, and doing a very poor job of it. Even on land the car controls like a giant icecube with a steering wheel attached. The trailer shows the car flying gracefully into the air like a bird, and doing sweet drifts to send the track exactly where they want it to go. None of this ever happens in the game. Attempting to drive around a corner is a horrible experience. And if you fall off the track (you will) you get sent right to the back. Not behind the last racer, right at the start of the track. The track does disappear when you drive over it, but if you're in the air, this doesn't happen. So if you attempt to skip a section of track by flying over it and you mess it up... you're gonna have to do it all again.
I should explain how the the track building works. It chooses the next piece based on which part of the track the leader is driving on. If they drive on the left, the track curves to the left. But there's absolutely no reason to do this, it only makes your opponents more likely to overtake you. If you curve the track, you're gonna have to slow down to make the turn without falling off, giving your more reckless opponents a chance to zoom past you. Or you can risk falling off and waiting for your car to slowly respawn. Plus, it's probably just going to put your section of track closer to previous sections, making it easier for other racers to fly over and catch up. If you just drive in a straight line without curving at all, there's nothing the other racers can do to overtake you. There are no items or boosts that might help even things out. All you can do is keep driving and hope they somehow ♥♥♥♥ up. But because the leader never has to fly or make unexpected turns, their chance of ♥♥♥♥ing up is much lower than yours. When someone gets in the lead, they tend to stay in the lead.
And then the final nail in the coffin: the multiplayer is dead. I have never seen a multiplayer game this dead. I could only find two people playing it, and they were just repeating the same mode over and over again. And of course there's no map variation to keep things interesting. There's a single player, but no AI racers. All you can do is drive the tracks on your own. Not much fun.

Talk to your contacts, get clues, solve the mystery and find Emily!" You know, kind of like Gone Home, but in AIM form.
This game is not Gone Home.
Instead, this game has a very powerful John Green-esque feel of "Gosh I sure do regret not being more proactive about chasing my high school crush, I guess I'd better write a novel about it." I've played through the game several times trying to see if there is any way out of the inevitable ending of wussily deleting any comment that might break ground before even sending it, and looked online as well, nothing. This game is basically the ultimate wank about the so-called "friend zone" which ironically seems to miss its own point, that the player character is putting their own dumb self into the friend zone by not being honest about their feelings.

I waited with bated breath for this game to release. All Trion did was localize yet another popular Eastern MMO for the Western market with a several QoL changes. I had high hopes for this game and played the beta and then the full release.
The fact is, this is a p2p masquerading as a f2p. Eastern gamers are much more accustomed to and forgiving of micro-transcactions; think of it as an extension of the arcade quarter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. In most cases, Eastern gamers enjoy PC games in cafe atmospheres or cubicles, pumping card time in to continue playing their character every day. They see it as a service more than anything.
For Western gamers, we pay for a product and expect a full experience. In Devilian's example, we get neither. Granted, you can start leveling for free, but to really enjoy the full breadth of the product, you'll have to pay a monthly fee. Which, though not unheard of, grants you next to nothing in this case. This isn't World of Warcraft. There isn't a huge community here. There isn't a lot of support. But most importantly...
The game isn't fun. I'm speaking as a huge ARPG fan and frankly, there are several other options I'd rather spend (read: waste) my time on. It goes without saying that Diablo 2 or 3 is better than this game, but even more modern outings fair WAY better than Devilian. Honestly, spend some time in Grim Dawn, Path of Exile, Marvel Heroes 2016 (yes, even Marvel Heroes), and you'll find a lot more to enjoy from those games.
Obviously, it's free. So you lose nothing but time and bandwidth to give it a try. But don't be surprised when you end up deleting it to save a few Gigs of space.

Anonymous Review 1 - *Blablabla Magicka 1's better than 2*
Anonymous Review 2 - *Blablabla Magicka 2's better than 1*
Look, if any reviewers feel targeted to those lines, you better to look what I would need to write for this game, okay?!
I only played mostly 4 hours total, ALONE (no team party), in this game, so my experiences with others players is considered to be absent. Due to the lack of a few hours, I do write this review only about what I got with my experience only in this game and testing it. Are we agreed on that? Yes (I know people will say "No" there)? Then let's continue!
Magicka 2 has its own similarities with Magicka 1: You play a wizards which you go in an adventure armes only with your staff, a melee weapon (usually) and, off course, your elemental spells.
The spell mechanic got a change if we compare between the first and second game. I could even say quite a nerf too. For me, I really do think it was needed. Why? Because, with my whole experiences  with Magicka 1 with both Solo and Multiplayer modes, that 5 element casting (Ice (Frost/Water), Lightning, Arcane, Defense and Frost - For example) was, in sort, ultimatly destructive, overpower (i mean it there) and a royal friendly killer. It was so powerful to the point that if you barely touch those ice spikes, it means a certain Death to yourself too. I don't count about doing that to your friends either.
Anyhow, with that nerf kinda fusion spell, us, the ancient players from Magicka 1, needed to see the new functionality with the spell system. Even if the title seems like a joke, "Learn to Spell Again", it litterally puts us to learn the new system, re-experiencing anew. Some players enjoyed it. Some others don't. For me, I liked it. It was a good thinking to check and learn new possibilities of spells, to be more effective while doing something less harmless to your friends! I think this is where the Paradox Team wanted us to do. I know when I played Magicka 1 back in time, I made one of my friend to rage quit the game fully because of those combinations. I think the nerf would simply to make that everyone needs to do something together to win. Isn't what Coop means, by the way when you do play this game?
What about Solo then, if ask about it? Remember that sometimes, you need to go more on the defensive rather than the offensive. You can, with your spells, to go in an aggressive defense: Using harm spells to protect yourself. Make a barrier of rock or a wall of cloudy frost! Do something to try to stop your enemies (Crowd Control everyone?). That system puts us to think which kind of spell we need to cast and that is, for me, an improvement. We do get out of the 1-2-3 button combo build that it was in Magicka 1, in sort.
Another thing I think it is an improvement is the equipements. At least we can equip our wizard with the stuff we unlock by playing the game. Quite balanced, you can make a wizard of your own thought: You can be a wizard that it is good with Arcane element but your Life element will be reduced for its effectiveness. They, the Paradox team, really don't want to see us becoming an overpower Rambo wizard (Yes we kill everythings on sight, but that's not what kind of Rambo I mean there). Then again, you need to play the game fully to get everything unlocked, even the support spells too. They are maybe less, but I am sure Magicka 2 will get more with the DLC like Magicka 1 did.
The humor between 1 and 2? The difference? Still there!  Both new and old, we can't miss those ones. What could I say more? They bring me a smile when I find one!
Bugs? I encountered some but not too fancy too. Like if I would not care about them seriously.
Difficulty? Now we are talking! I would say yes about the difficulty to be increased if we compare between the two games. But for me, it really needed. I really do think the difficulty from what the other usually encounter is by the number of enemies coming at you, versus the nerf on the spells. This is where I want to point out that the Magicka 1 players, usually, must get out of this "area of comfort" of the OP spells and try to do something to experiment with.
To be honest there, even myself I got surprise with the difficulty while playing solo. Yes, I died quite alot too. But each time I died, I tried a new combo to beat my enemies. It is by experimenting the elements that I discovered how to "play" with them. Just to give an example for one part in the game there: There is a watermill that you need to turn by using a water spell, but the enemies constantly spawns to go to kill you.  To counteract the enemies, I did created some walls of frost, lightning and arcane to slow them, damaging them. Even some creatures arrived from the water, so they got heavely damaged by the lightning whenever they entered in the wall. It did gave me time to use my water spell and also preparing another spell to finishing them off.
It was challenging and fun, despite I got killed so many times. But I learned my stuff there.
In the end, I do think Magicka 2 is a game that we are related to "Death and Learn" turn off, like previously the 1. But the first one was less present, I must say. So will I recommend this game? I will say "Yes", definitively. I would even suggest to buy the first one and see the difference between them. Either the first or second, Magicka is still Magicka: The serie is about Death, spells casting, laugh, anger and friendship killing.... mixing them to make two words to describe both games : "Have Fun!"

Yes, they changed a few things, and yes, you're not as powerful, but overall, this game is great.
We'll start off with some new things I really enjoy about the game:
-The new customizable robe system
-The fact that you can pick your weapon and staff for when you spawn
-The easy use of the focus-based magick system
These new features help add to a more costumizable system that is much more enjoyable than the simplistic system of the first game. I really enjoy the way which you must unlock new robes and skins for those robes, as it allows for you to "show off" to your friends your skills in prior adventures, rather than the amount of money you're willing to spend, like the first game had it. The new focus magick system is enjoyable for its convenience more than anything, though I do wish it was any four magicks rather than the "tiered" system they currently use.
Some problems I've had:
-The game is still quite buggy, (earth spells will charge without casting, I take damge from my own death spells while I have a ful death ward active, the disruptor magick won't block lok's beam sometimes, etc) but we can assume they will fix that
-The game is extremely hard without friends (I have entered full rage far too many times, and have beaten everything on bananas difficulty except the final fight against Lok, which I haven't been able to beat on any difficulty)
-The final boss fight is insanely hard, and truly unbeatable without teammates
Most of these problems lend themselves into the category of the sillyness of the game, though, which is truly its defining feature. The fact that I am playing the campaign on solo is the main problem I have with this game, but truly that is not the way the game was meant to be played. I would wholeheartedly recommend this game, but I highly suggest you get some friends to play it with and all get the game, otherwise you will have a mind-crackingly furious time!

Magicka 2 was a decent follow-up to Magicka.
Pros:
+ Graphics are greatly improved.
+ You can now choose to spawn with your preferred staff and weapon.
+ There are now quick buttons to cast magicks. This takes away some of the game's difficulty, however.
+ Familiars. These feel largely unnecessary but I suppose one could consider this a pro.
+ Monsters seem stronger and have better AI.
+ Some new and cool magicks.
Cons:
- Campaign feels very short.
- Some magicks are only unlockable in challenges. This makes little to no sense to me.
- No active staff abilities.
- A lack of enemy casters. What happened to druids, disciples and goblin wizards?
- Very easy boss fights.
- Can't see where you can unlock certain magicks, weapons or staves.
- Cringeworthy references.
- Questionable balancing changes. This is only my opinion, but I sure will miss some of the fun combos. The problem lies in that they deliberately wanted to limit possibilities.
Why not recommended? Mostly because of how short the campaign was. It doesn't come off as an improvement to the first game at all. The enemies are less varied, the weapons and staves to pick up seem less interesting. Maybe Magicka 2 will have some good DLCs in the future, perhaps then it'll instead be recommended. But as of right now, it doesn't offer much entertainment.
EDIT: Additional pros and cons!
+ New movement system. You can cast spells while moving. This is a really nice feature, to be fair.

this is a pretty fun shmup game
the gimmick of this game is that every time you load up the game you're given three randomly generated pilots
you collect "carbomite" from shooting enemies down which powers up your weapon and allows you to charge a super bar
the enemy patterns are slightly randomised each time, too
THIS GAME IS HARD
you WILL die - but here's the thing
when you lose all three of your pilots, THE GAME IS NOT OVER
instead, you cash in the score you've gained up to that point in exchange for more randomly generated pilots, each with their own attributes and weapons
some pilots have a higher chance of surviving a hit - some pilots can collect more carbomite
obviously the better pilots are more expensive which gives a risk-vs-reward scenario
do you go for more of the cheap pilots and end up with less firepower but more lives, or do you go in guns blazing with the best pilots at the risk of losing it all in one hit?
as far as I know, there IS NO game over screen - you just keep buying more pilots and going back to the first stage
the actual gameplay is fluid and fun
the graphics are nice and I LOVE the pilot chatter - while the pilots are randomly generated there are only a few voice banks, but all the different voices are endearing with their own personalities
what I would REALLY love to see is more time and polish put into this game - while this is an early access game it doesn't quite have that alpha/beta feel - but it doesn't quite feel like a finished game either
perhaps the difficulty could be turned down a bit - or give the player different difficulty levels to choose from as the game is very challenging from the start and it is very unlikely that a first-time player is going to beat it quickly
one criticism I have is that the game takes a very long time to load on startup
ultimately this is a very fun game with a LOT of replay value
I look forward to seeing what future updates will bring
I also look forward to seeing the actual main Starr Mazer game (of which this game is a prequel spin-off)

after 40+ hours of game play, i have come into the conclusion that this game is a wasted potential.
note that i am not a SAO fan, as i have only read the first 4 novels( roughly the 1st season of the anime), and sadly the majority of the cast only appears in SAO progressive, so i was and am unfamiliar with, but as you'll see that won't affect my wordy review.
objective stuff:
plot:
the very large cast of kirito, his harem and klein play a new VR game.
they meet a null AI, a jerk and they save the game. no death IRL.
gameplay:
the game is a typical action RPG. you go trough each stage, fighting lots of mocks with the occasional boss.
the game is separated to 2 parts - the field and the town. in the town you shop and mingle with your friends, while in the field - kirito smash.
you can choose from a multitude of weapons, each having it's own skill tree (sadly the trees are rather small).
you can hit, you can block, you can use special attack, you can parry and you can dodge. you also gain levels from killings enemies, which in turn raise your attack, def and such. very standard
design and graphic:
the games looks nice. thats it.
the locals are very standard and aren't anything new.
pros:
- the music is awesome. while not breathtaking, it is still great (especially area 4 night time)
- you can befriend and party with the hundreds of NPCs in the town. and no, they are not lesser in anyway than the main cast
- there are a lot of voiced cutscenes about the main cast. they study, party, eat and more. it provides a lot of character development.
or rather it would if not for...
cons:
- the main cast has 0 personality. you don't care about any of them. at all.
each does have a quirk or 2, but you'll still need the whole cast to make one enjoyable character.
- in addition, the story is extremely simple and un-engaging. basically, boring.  the only motivation i had is to end it already.
- no sidequests. nothing. just the main campign and generic missions you take from a board.
- this is the big one:
-the game is too easy. i 1HKO enemies 30 levels above me. even against bosses 40 levels higher i didn't bother to dodge nor block nor buff nor do anything except press the attack button. if you have a healer, you are invincible.
due to that, i very quickly lost interest in the game. levels meant nothing, neither did enemies.
with bad story, boring characters and fighting enemies useless, what is left?
after you finish the main camping a new play mode is unlocked, which looked nice and not too easy, and most importantly fun, but i was already burnt out.
in conclusion, although the devs made a lot of effort to make the game feel like an MMO, and quite a lot of love was put to the game, in the end the failed some of the most important aspect - balancing and characters.
it is very possible to find a lot of enjoyment out of this game, but first you got to go trough a lot of boring stuff.
i give this game a 4/10 due to some truly good content covered by a lot of bad content

This game takes place during the prequel films, in-between episode 2-3. You take the role of 38, who leads an elite unit called Delta Squad. The three other members of your squad are named Sev (Delta 07), Fixer (Delta 40), and Scorch (Delta 60). The character you assume the role of doesn't have a name, but your squadmates refer to you as boss. Speaking of your squadmates the one thing I love about them is not only their A.I, is their distinct personalties. Like Sev being cold and calculating, and thiers Scorch who has many funny lines. Which is kinda werid because aren't they clones? I love the banter with your squadmates, even the voice actor for 38 did a good job too.
Since you are a leader of a squad you're able to give orders to your companions. Like set up sniper position or breaching a door. It's said that each member of has a specialty, like Sev being a deadly sniper, and Scorch whos an explosive expert. Which is kinda pointless becuase all your squadmates can snipe for you, can hack a door, and set up an explostive. You are supposed to be a jack of all trades while the others have distict skills, but no everyone is a jack of all trades. It would've added some urgency to having a squad mate go down. Say for example Fixer goes down and you needed him to hack a door. But nope. Makes me wonder why 38 is even the leader anyone of them could lead the squad. The only thing that sets them apart is their personalities, but I digress.
The graphics are pretty good, they hold up pretty well, it may not look that great today. But it does make you think of star wars, nothing seemed out of place. Overall I think this is one of the greatest Star Wars games out there, Lucas Arts made the best Star Wars games without a doubt and did Star Wars justice in the video gaming medium. And it's a shame they closed doors at the hands of Disney. It's becuase of this I think, without a doubt the newest Star Wars films are going to be a cash grab. Since Disney got Dice to develop the upcoming Battlefront, i'm a little worried about the Star Wars license in video games. Initially, I liked Year One, but I cannot recommend it now that I've seen the bugs and how little content there was.
tl;dr - almost every old bug still exists in the game. I paid good money to improve the game experience and all I got was this reskin (and some NEW bugs!).
I enjoyed the base game with the upgraded visuals. There were also some mechanical tweaks (mainly the vehicles now handle according to Earth gravity) and lovely additions to the soundtrack; it wasn't a new experience, but an improved one. The Freaks got balanced, you didn't get as overwhelmed with tasks, the CLEO drops and reskins brought a little spice into things - it was quite nice revisiting the game I love, warts and all.
The new content ran out a bit too quickly, however, and the endgame was boring with the last stretch of missions and looting a little flat as usual, but I felt it was okay value for 24 hours of gameplay. After all, I was getting 2 refreshed DLCs too,
But then there's Lifeline. My first three playthroughs had major game-breaking bugs, and the whole 'refreshed' DLC is riddled with
.
has been fixed, and there is very little additional content for Lifeline - the reskins are lame and there are no new weapons (the CLEO ones suck compared to army stuff).
I felt utterly cheated, still do after 8+ hours of gameplay.
When Fighting 7/Bladed 7 Kung-Fu Vince falls through a bridge after exiting your vehicle and gets killed by a solo Feral under said bridge, you know your game is ♥♥♥♥ed. Never mind the CLEO missions that don't spawn, zombies that spawn inside the ground, disappearing items, worthless AI, Journal glitching out, wrong voice clips playing for your player character etc.
This really put the base game into perspective for me, too. In the end, the improvements were marginal at best and left a lot to be desired.
This remake is way overpriced for what it is - reskins and some extra tunes. The mechanical tuning should have been done for the original, it was borderline bugfixing! I paid good money thinking I would get actual content and bugfixes/polish too, but
. I still love the base game for what it is (it's complicated with Lifeline...), but if you're an old player, don't buy this for the full price, about 70% off would be fair.
New players? Buyer beware. The base game is still one of the better zombie survival games and has unique mechanics that are quite enjoyable, but the devs don't seem to be interested in fixing and expanding the game - and that is a bad, bad sign.
