If you don't already own State of Decay, then yes, definitely pick up one of the best single player Zombie group survival games there is.
If you already own State of Decay - read up on what this edition brings to ensure that it is worth your time. The original was a PC port of the X-box 360 version. This release is the same as the first game + DLC, but Microsoft had Undead Labs update it for the X-box One and this is the port of that version. So it is primarily minor visual improvements (imo) with a few tweaks that may not be worth your extra cash at this time.
Lots of bugs, crashes, and mostly bad gameplay.

For all of you looking for a true zombie survival game, you've come to the right place. You're going to spend a ridiculous amount of time having stories to share with your friends unfold before your eyes.
The base game has an enjoyable story, though it's the sandboxy feel that goes along with it that makes this game an excellent one. You are continually capable of working toward your next story goal at your own pace, though if you're like me you'll find the majority of the game is spent exploring, collecting supplies, building up your base, dealing with other survivor groups, gaining skills for you survivors, etc. Every character has a unique backstory and there are -a lot- of survivors out there that you might run into and have join you.
The base building is simple, yet very enjoyable as well. Depending on what skills your survivors have, different options are available and you have plenty of options available to you. Do you want to be able to support more survivors? Build a bunkhouse and a garden so that they have a comfortable place to sleep and food to eat if your scavenged supplies run low. Looking to cut back on the sneaking around and really take the fight to the zombies? An infirmary will keep your survivors healthy and a munitions shop will keep them well armed. Just remember, even healthy, well armed survivors might run into a challenge when facing off against the 'freaks' or special zombies.
The Breakdown DLC removes the deep story aspect of the the vanilla campaign, though it adds a brand new achievement system that unlocks 'hero' survivors that, more often than not, are more capable than your average survivor. This mode also has 'Breakdown Levels', each time you complete one you move on to the next, more challenging phase, with new survivor achievements to unlock.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the zombie survival genre. I'd been looking for a game like this for a very long time and was extremely happy when I installed it and truly learned what it was all about. Enjoy and I'd love to hear your stories!

A very interesting Shmup with cool Roguelike elements. It hits you with this beutiful 80's influenced pixel art and music. Then it has such quaint dailog going on some of the time. You have to laugh at the terrible puns the cat general says. At first start you are given three pilots. This game doesn't use lives or lifebars. Instead you buy new pilots with your score. Each pilot is randomly generated. From their cool little UN Squadran avatar in the upper left hand corner to that forementioned quaint dialog(which is spoken in stereotypical fashion).  Each pliot has a different type of ship which has different types of weapons. You power these up with stuff that comes out of exploded ships called carbonite. You can craft higher grade carbonite for greater powerups if you fly around them and use airdrafts to make them collide. Unfortunately you are constantly losing that power up as you use the weapons so it is a battle to keep that energy coming(I think this is the only flaw in the game.) Also each pilot has a bar under their avatar. The bar is randomly filled with grey. During play a line scrolls back and forth on that bar. If you are hit while it's on grey, the pilot will juke and jive. Thus he will escape from exploding.  When you lose all your pilots you are send to a screen where you can use your score to buy more, then you go back in and start from the beginning again.

Pretentious Title: SquareLogic is an abstract puzzle game that takes the concept behind sudoku and twists it to create something far more interesting and engaging.  Like sudoku, the goal is to fill a square grid such that the numbers appear only once in each column and row.
SquareLogic's twist on the formula is in the cage system.  Instead of prepopulating the grid with enough numbers to solve the puzzle, SquareLogic divides the board into arbitrary chunks, called cages, and assigns a mathematical rule to each.  For instance, one cage may require its content to sum to 8, another may require its smaller value to divide the larger value 4 times.  Other cages impose inequality operators on the divisions between cages, indicating that one square must contain a larger or smaller number than its neighbor.  The puzzles have extra mechanics beyond the cages as well, including double-puzzles, where two grids contain the same solution but different cages, each providing too little to solve on its own, but enough to solve when paired with the other.  Other puzzle types may leave some cages unfinished and require the player to paint them in as they go.
This formula would likely be overwhelming and tedious, especially on full-sized 9x9 puzzles (the game ranges from 4x4 to 9x9).  However, the game automatically removes numbers from tiles when that number is used elsewhere in the column/row, and players can right click any number to remove it as a viable option.  This effectively automates the more menial part of the puzzle, leaving the logical problem solving front and center.  The game also highlights possible valid combinations for cages in a small window, so you don't have to constantly keep a calculator by your side to determine what factorizations are possible for a number set.  Because of these features, the puzzles go by quickly and rarely feel like they're ever wasting your time.
SquareLogic isn't flawless though.  The 4x4 puzzles are almost comically easy due to their small size, while the 9x9 and some 8x8 puzzles can become frustrating and tedious because there is simply too much information to pore over.  It becomes less a game of applying logic and more of a mindless search for the next clue you can use.  Luckily, the game still has plenty of 6x6 and 7x7 puzzles, which feel extremely well paced.
Another problem is the immediate error highlighting feature.  When you first boot up the game, go into options and turn this setting off immediately.  This setting causes the game to tell you the very instant you make a mistake.  It's a feature that is quite literally too helpful, as it quietly encourages you to start guessing whenever you begin having trouble.  With this disabled though, there's still an incredibly nice hint feature to help you out of jams.  Rather than openly tell you what's wrong, it simply highlights a section of the grid where you should be able to either eliminate possibilites or find a correct number.  It's especially useful on the large puzzles where it's easy to have too many options to pore over.
The one last problem is somewhat debatable.  The game simply has too many puzzles.  It has 6 regions, each with a staggeringly large number of available puzzles.  The first area alone contains 4800.  That is not an exaggeration.  While it certainly means the game has incredible value, it can be a little disheartening to know that you're not likely to ever even come close to finishing all of the puzzles.  Oh, and anyone obsessed with achievements would do well to avoid this game for that reason, unless you want to solve all 4800 puzzles in the first region for a cheevo.
Overall, for anyone who likes abstract logic puzzles, SquareLogic is pretty much top class.  It's fun, mostly well paced, has a ton of puzzles and lots of good mechanics.  Well worth the $5 asking price.

Very nice! The game controls great, overall. You have a very plesant sense of inertia and freedom of movement that's best comparable to Mirror's Edge, but the overall momentum and sensation of Jet Set Radio. I know a lot of people compare Hover to these two, but it's really the best comparison for the movement. It feels great to control, and it's an improvement on the two inspirations overall: It removes Mirror's Edge's slow-moving climbing and occasionally hard-to-maintain momentum, and it removes JSR's lack of precise control. Also nice are two new mechanics to help ease the frustration of JSR-like gameplay: A bounce and a rewind. The bounce is especially nice in the main (incredibly vertical) hubworld, because it ensures that falling down is not an instant kill of your current momentum, and the rewind alleviates those moments where you
missed the jump.
However, the game as a whole needs some polish. Most textures are pretty plain looking, colors are a little
high-contrast, everything's pretty undecorated (yall aliens REALLY need interior designers), and a lot of assets are reused. The paint's all there, now you just need some varnish.

Having played this game for a good while, I can tell you that Hover: Revolt of Gamers is fun. The open world is lively, if a bit bright, and the controls are pretty darn good. I'm not the biggest fan of the leveling system, for it's heavily based on luck rather than skill, but it gets the job done. The graphics are pretty nice, especialy if you're into that cel-shaded look, though I feel like its... empty. There are hardly any NPC's, and the ones that are walking around don't do much else but walk and get shoved when you move near them. But besides that, the world is pretty solid, although it can be very confusing for newer players to reach the upper, more fun levels of the game due to its complexity.
But, and that's a very large but, there is one thing about this game that I can't stand. It has no story structure. Seriously, Once you leave the incredibly boring and straight-forward tutorial, you're shoved into this world not knowint anything other than, "STOP THE BAD GUY! HE DOESN'T LIKE THE VIDEO GAMES!" The only hint you get is on the top-right hand of your screen, which is pretty much useless since haff of the stuff is cut off anyways. A story has to grab you right away, and guide you in the right way. Seeing how I have played over 25 hours and still can barely recognize the main characters of this game, it really makes it seem like the game doesn't want you to do the story or learn the characters. Also, whenever you talk to someone, they always seem to have a paragraph of info for you to read, and unless you're a Fallout game or something, not many people are going to slow down in a game that emphasizes speed and agility to read an essay. Going back to the leveling system, there is hardly any direction or help as to what you're supposed to do. You get these hexagon upgrades, but most of the time they don't seem to do much and are confusing to use properly. The animal companions are weird, and not in a cute way, and the player isn't given any information or clues on how to properly use them either. The graffiti, while fun to use, has a few that are bugged, and using it seems unintuitive, seeing how you have to double click to activate. The characters. Oh boy, the characters. They are just... boring. Yeah, some look interesting like Greendy, but the rest are just bland. Hell, the only reason I remember Greendy was because I was bored and saw she was having a race. Mind you, this was after becoming level 10 and getting really good at the controls, so when she said, "Welcome! That tutorial was just the beginning!" I was thrown back a bit. The first essence of story I encountered was after 3 hours of gameplay. I know this is supposed to be a Jet Set Radio spin-off kind of thing, but you have to remember that both Jet Set Radios were story first, free play second. Not the opposite way around. I swear, most of the people who bought this game only bought it because the musical composer for the Jet Set Radio franchise did the music, which is composed of, what, 3 songs? That's all I've heard so far, and while they're good, it gets really boring when you hear the same one for more than an hour. And I know this is gonna sound nit-picky, but weren't the level songs of the original games remixes of their own songs played together? Not just one looping soundtrack? I dunno, just something I thought about.
Ok, so this review has seemed pretty negative, and while it's true this game has many caveots that prevent me from getting into it more, it's still a well developed game. You can tell that hours upon hours have been put into the design, and the movement machanics are incredibly solid. Sure, the flying cars look like they're having seizures, but I can look past that one little flaw. Overall, Hover: Revolt of Gamers is pretty ok. The aesthitic is pretty cool, and the music is alright, but the lack of structure and a learning curve steeper than a skyscraper prevents me from recommending this game to everyone at the moment. It's a good game, and if there are more updates to the game that address these issues, I might consider it to be a must have. So who do I recommend should buy this game? Well, I guess if you enjoy any of the Jet Set Radio games, and have $15 (at the time of this review) to burn, then go right ahead. Otherwise you're better off buying the original Jet Set Radio, which is on Steam.

This game is good at making you feel. For a game that drops you in the middle of the forest alone, that's quite an accomplishment. From the very start you're given a heart-wrenching story and series of questions about loss and the game continues to give you more feels all the way through. With only Delilah on the other end of his radio, Henry has to discover the reason behind disappearances and break-ins happening around his watchtower. The story goes very, very in-depth but I don't want to spoil anything. I highly recommend playing this game for yourself without spoilers. The storyline gives you no hints as to the ending until it's staring you in the face and wrenching your gut the entire time.
For a short but very well made exploration and adventure game, I really enjoyed Firewatch. The graphics, while simple and not the most HD out there work for this game and are still very amazing to look at. You can even find a camera in-game and get your game photos printed out (though Steam screenshots are just as good, honestly), as if you really went on a trek through the woods. Some of the landscapes are downright breathtaking, even with the graphic style.
For the achievement hunters out there, most of them are very easy to get. The majority of them are in the storyline and are awarded upon chapter completion. The others just ask you to explore a little and watch your environement to find (or you could use a guide, if you don't want to explore, but why you would not want to explore in an exploration game is strange in my opinion).
If you want a relaxing experience in the virtual wilderness, if you like mysteries that make you feel along the way, or even if you enjoy a short singleplayer experience, I highly recommend this game.

I bought this game as a stopgap measure; I fell into Assassin's Creed: Origins and burned my way through 60 hours of play way faster than I thought I would, and I needed a game to fill in the gap between that and Xenoblade Chronicles 2. I watched and enjoyed the first season of Sword Art Online and the idea of a fake single-player MMO sounded cool. (It's also interesting that this and
Last Recode came out so close to each other. I actually chose between the two.)
SAO:HR was great fun for a while. There are just a bunch of strange little design decisions that rub together in just the wrong way for me, and I think I'm going to stop playing. I've become impatient with every part of the game, and it's not worth it to me to stick it out.
First and foremost, the storytelling. Not the story -- I was actually enjoying that -- but the way the story is told.
The game is pretty clearly split into two parts, story events and the field. Story events are started in town, for the most part; you get a list of possible events you can kick off and you can do them in any order you like. Story events are basically visual novel segments -- anime-styled character sprites over static backgrounds, voice acting, and text at the bottom of the screen. Combat is depicted as roars from off-screen monsters, battle cries and flashes of light. Since most of the story events are about the characters working their way through quest lines, I ended up wondering why I wasn't presented with those quests and asked to actually PLAY through them. This is made worse by the fact that there are a few story events that break these rules, and have actual fights or in-game cutscenes, which shows that that could have been done. It's much cooler to play those kinds of things in a game like this then to hear them happening just off-camera.
The field is a series of outdoor maps in several themes. (I got to the desert area before I decided to call it quits.) There are quests scattered around the maps, but they are ALL of the "kill this marked group of monsters within this very-generous time limit". Puzzle-solving is all automatic. The battle system is quick and fun, but the same every time. I played pretty normally and my characters were constantly overlevelled for the areas they were in -- and even when taking on minibosses 25 levels above them handled everything just fine. Any storytelling in the field is very perfunctory -- either Kirito flat-out says what you should do next, or he says that you should go back to town and have a story event or two.
None of it is very staisfying, or hangs together the way a game should.
Other rough spots:
* UI and control inconsistency -- buttons do different things in different menus, even if they look the same. There are three buttons you have to use in town to interact with NPCs, and I could never remember which one was which. Sometimes you can use the map to switch areas in town, and sometimes you can't, even when you could in the situation before.
* Lack of variety. There's only a handful of monsters, repeated with slight reskins. There's only a handful of bits of armor, repeated with slight reskins. I never did see a weapon that was all that distinct from every other of its type. Every story event starts with the same song.
* The MMO elements are slipshod. There's a quest board, but all of the quests are either "kill X of Y in the area you just opened up" or "collect Z drops". Apparently all the quests are posted by other players and NPCs, and completing one of them will cause that player/NPC to constantly bombard your in-game mailbox with requests to get together, which only result in ANOTHER "collect Z drops" quest. Worst of all, filling any drop quest burns items you need to upgrade your equipment for a minimal reward. Eventually I abandoned all the quests I had open and stopped looking at it at all.
I've been trying as hard as I can to finish all the games I can this year, but I just don't feel it's worth rushing for the end of the game before starting XC2.

A promising game with some major issues.
Krautscape is an online" fly/race game that tries to get away from the traditional race genre.
You play as some folded origami bird and try to complete a map as quick as possible be it driving or flying. Probably a good deal of both. The track is just there..if you think you can take a shortcut, go for it!
You might be rewarded for your guess or severely punished.
On top of that there is the aspect of 'make your track as you go'. Can't say how interesting that is 'cause I havn't been able to find someone to play online with EVER (and there are lots of people who own/owned this much longer than me who experienced thesame issue..)
It's already a beautiful and interesting game but it needs some fixes and even more a decent playerbase.
The rest I'll give to you in a quick pro's and cons down below:
Pros:
- Native support for split screen and LAN
- interesting gameplay with decent single player.
- beautiful art style
- Challenging handling/steering with a real sense of velocity
- interesting take on race games
What de dev's need to do is:
-Fix the much too often screen freezes.
-Give an option to mute or at least adjust the annoying ambient sounds
- Make user made maps easier to share and make (and by 'make' I mean in the traditional sense of the word, probably with a track builder like Speed Runners or TrackMania, the current thing just isn't going to work)
-NOT GIVE UP ON THIS GAME, promote it! or just cut the online aspect completely..and let it fade into obscurity...

Unfortunately, this game has a huge issue.  First, let me say that if you're looking for the type of action you remember from Alleyway and similar games from the arcade and NES days, Brickbreaker has it.  The problem is (and I can't confirm whether this is a problem with the game's programming or somehow had to do with my particular controller) that the controller goes absolutely nuts whenever you're in the menu, making picking game modes and levels nearly impossible. It scrolls through options constantly and selects things without you pressing a button. I've never had a single problem with my controller on any other game, so it's 99% sure that it's a problem with the game.
If it weren't for this enormous issue, this game would get a positive review from me.  As of now, I've refunded the game.  I hope they can fix this issue in the future so I can purchase the game again, because it did scratch the Alleyway/Brickbreaker itch.
EDIT: just so you know, I was using a regular X360 controller, which has worked with every other game I've ever tried with it (and that's dozens of games).  Brickbreaker has controller support, and the controller works when you finally get past the dysfunctional menus and into the game.  The problem is the menus.

Interesting premise, but the execution fell short.
First part was decent with an indepth story surrounding you as Kay'l, a police officer. You look for clues and follow leads like a detective. Very cool. The events that followed after Kay'l were underwhelming in comparison. You are straight up given tasks that are a whole lot less complex than before.
Controls were unusual and took a while to get used to. It was annoying to strafe during shooting sections because you end up drifting and screwing up your aim (made the final battle very difficult). The brawling system would've been nice with its wealth of combo moves, but it's very easy to cheese it with the same combo over and over (a lot of games have this problem, so maybe not a fair criticism).
The reincarnation mechanism was nifty. You can find certain characters and force your soul into their bodies. Unfortunately, it's pointless to do so because you are frequently forced to reincarnate into another character's body to progress the story.
Not recommended for general play, but might be worth playing as a video game study.

Game came out in a time when 3D open world games weren't even the standard yet. As a comparison: GTA3 was released in 2001, the Nomad Soul was released in '99.
From the very first lines that were spoken by Kay'l 669, it had me hooked.
For its time it was one of the best games and one of the best open world games. A unique soundtrack(part of which by David Bowie, who even lend his likeness to a couple of characters). The game had great ambitions, but did not deliver on all fronts. Story was original, adventuring was great, fighting had depth(which i did not expect), but the shooting was lackluster... but it worked.
Quantic Dream won my heart with this game. I am still waiting on Omikron2 though, maybe it will happen someday.

Solo is rather unforgiving. But after memorizing all the combinations, and drilling them in. I was able to solo every game mode, including Bananas.

This game has been falsely accused for being too "casual".
I'll tell you all the truth right now:
Today I saw guys who were telling everyone to not buy this game because it's bad but actually they've played this game only for couple of minutes and were stuck on chapter 1 at normal difficulty level cause they were terrible noobs and I assume you that most of all the negative reviews are written by noobs like these.
Either they are stuck on chapter 1 because their hands grow from their backs or they've decided to jump on a "bandwagon of hate". Some of those noobs who've played the game only for 20 minutes even dare to say that the game has only 4 magicks...
So, don't be tricked by those reviews and even if some will say that people who give positive reviews are just "fanboys who defend game developers" don't believe them cause I'm not trying to "white-knight" anybody here.
I'm just telling truth and if that's not enough for you to believe that me or someone else whose opinion is similar to mine is telling truth about this game just check my or their profiles and you'll see that they've played it for more time than any of those haters did.
----------------------------------------------------------
Now some review about the game itself:
Most of the people are complaining about removal of overpowered magicks. What they actually want to say is that "it's bad to kill enemies using tactics, thinking, escaping, defending" and they'd rather just use some overpowered magicks on enemies for it to be "1 second job".
Judge for yourself what's better but as I think it's better to have real fun thinking than just watching enemies die in a seconds.
People say "those hotkeys were made for stupid PS users". Those hotkeys got recharge time and that's what people are mostly complaining about. Actually those recharges can be easily bypassed if you'll activate magicks manually.
Example: Pressing 3 to use thunderhead will take 3 seconds to recharge with basic set. But if you'll do FFSAA this'll make it activate right after it was fully conjured so everytime you use thunderhead with FFSAA you can just do FFSAA again and there'll be no recharge time and still you'll get that magick activated.
People say "game is non-beatable on bananas alone". Actually I completed game on bananas alone and even if that's hard it's still manageable because familiars that revive you can be revived too, if you'll not run like mad but watch your step and try to deal with enemy groups one by one you'll get your success.
Only thing that I don't like about this game is that it doesn't have much of a content. Sure there'll be more downloadable content and updates later but for now it's not much.

Reccomended, but only just.
It's a satisfying game for what it is, but I don't think they could have picked a worse engine to implement it with. In and of itself, Sniper Elite V2 is a decent game when its focus is on its trademark: sniping. But even in the regular game the use of other weaponry has middling to no effect on enemies because of the horrid hip-firing style mechanics, and on top of that there's no form of melee attack whatsoever.
Fighting zombies only accentuates these problems because you have an enemy that generally takes many, many shots to the body to kill while having a limited number of bullets (many times when I've been surrounded I've wasted an entire SMG magazine to no effect whatsoever), while it makes it much more difficult to actually pull off headshots with anything other than your rifle. Melee attacks have been ridiculously overlooked for a knockdown kick, which can only be used on one zombie at a time. The implementation of the Shotguns and Webley revolver are the excuses to have a close range power weapon, but sometimes they even just manage to knock over a zombie for a moment or two.
So, what are the pros of this game/sub-series?
Well, it has a fantastic atmosphere. Unlike Call of Duty Nazi Zombies, it delves more into the demonic origins of reincarnated corpses rather than having them brought back by a magi-science aspect. The symbols on the walls, the hellish resetting of the main game's levels, everything is amazingly gloomy and it's a world that you want to explore (especially with the sequel). If you can adjust to the game's built-in aiming difficulty the zombies really aren't that hard to kill, though it may restrict your choices to the more accurate SMGs and sidearms for the remainder of the experience. Just like any zombie game it's extremely satisfying taking down a horde, especially if you've got a couple friends playing with you. It's a fair-length campaign that can be revisited a few times, but is much better overall if you do it in multiplayer.
tl;dr, the engine is crap but adaptable over time, the multiplayer aspect is the best part of it, and the setting and story are fresh for something as specific as Nazi Zombies.

In my opinion Star Wars Republic Commando has to be one of the best first-person shooters made to date. This is because:
1. The combat feels great! running at a group of droids firing away at you with just the right amount of accuracy to be a threat and then dispatching them one by one with your wristblade is one of the best experiences in gaming!
2. The Team. Your team is made up of 4 people (no spoilers, as you find this all out in the opening) you, the elite Delta 38, the sniper Sev (Delta 07), the hot headed demolitions expert scorch (Delta 62), and the trustworthy commando fixer (Delta 40). Your command over them is relatively limited as you only have 4 options, Search and destroy, Form up, Stay here and Do thing (sniper point, grenade point, breach door, hack, etc) Also if you "die" your squad will carry on fighting until finished and then will revive you with half health (you can order them to revive you sooner but that often puts them in a very vulnerable spot).
3.The environments, without spoiling the game for you the envoronments range from full on battles with other troopers present to creepy environments with your enemies lurking around every other corner.
4. The story. The story really attaches you mentally to your squad and by the end you'll be scolding scorch for shooting you in the back rather than cursing the AI, and there are some real moments of accomplishment in the story such as the end of the first "chapter". The ending is awesome too!.
So to sum up, GO BUY THIS GAME!

As JSRF (Jet Set Radio Future) being one of the first games I remember as a child, this game does, to an extent, play/act as a nostaliga trip for me; I wouldn't say though that this game is an exact replicate. It so much more than that. It's its own unique game with differing mechanics and story. For those of you who don't know what I am comparing this game to, I will get straight to the point.
Hover is a game best played in third-person. It's about running, grinding, jumping around, and, if you so wish, completing objectives. The learning curve is slow and gradual, and for those that get frustrated really easily, there's systems that don't punish you for making mistakes (Rewind position button.) You are given only two characters, a boy and a girl, to pick from at the start who are functionally the same, and the remaining characters are earned by doing missions. The controls are simple and multi-purposed. Every character varies in abilites, and upgrades can be added to your character to increase performance in a whole slew of stats. All of the character's colors are customizable. The game is multiplayer and does not require any third party connection services.
The art style is rich and colorful which could brighten any sorrow mood. Storyline is extremely cheesey, but does speak some truth. Characters have their own personalities that make you care about them. The map is cleverly designed for novice, adept, and advance players to traverse. It is really hard to rage at this game.

There are vanishingly few side-scrolling retro shmups on Steam which accurately emulate the look & feel of their arcade counter-parts, in my opinion. And so any opportunity I have to review one which claims to do just that, well suffice to say that I am always quite eager to jump at the chance in doing so!
And thus this brings us to Starr Mazer: DSP, a shiny new 2D shooter developed by Imagos Softworks & Pixeljam which attempts to do the genre justice by striving for accuracy as well as attention to detail in properly mimicking the old-school shmup experience. But have they successfully accomplished this task? Let's find out below.
The premise of this game is that a pacifist group of aliens named the "G’ell" are in a protracted war with humanity, and having lost the previous battle, they have unabashedly returned with blood-thristy revenge in mind, full of contempt for us. It's essentially your typical aliens vs humans scenario, although I am not entirely sure why a pacifist group of them would be at war to begin with, unless the humans initiated the conflict which is quite plausible I suppose!
Even more amusing however, is that the game features quite a vast assortment of ships/pilots to choose from, and furthermore the entire squadron is taking orders from the "Cat Admiral" who provides tactical commentary for you during combat. Yes you heard that correctly, your chain of command is an actual cat who talks...and yet somehow, it breathes a sense of light-heartedness into Starr Mazer to remind us that games are supposed to be silly, simple, and fun...especially the retro kind. There even exists not-so-subtle cat references in the dialogue, and so I can only surmise that the developers have some kind of affinity for them.
In any event, what primarily differentiates the gameplay mechanics from this one, compared to others, is its "continue" system which requires you to purchase one or more personalized fighter pilots upon dying - with your present score being the currency to do so. Therefore in this novel way, the game incorporates a nifty rogue-like scheme into the strategic side of things...while also allowing you test out a wide array of their different ships at varying prize ranges and capabilities, each one offering unique primary & secondary weapon systems.
Speaking of its secondary firepower system, you will be collecting crystals of differring sizes in order to recharge this weapon...which can be engaged by pressing and optionally holding down the button for a sustained release upon your enemies until its bar dwindles down. The game heavily revolves around proper utilization and wise management of this mechanic actually.
Variation in enemy types, their attack movements, as well as their bullet patterns...were all excellently executed. Each segment felt fresh and non-repetitive thankfully.
But even with its very basic & straight-forward control scheme, don't think for one second that this is an easy game to beat in one sitting, because it most certainly isn't. In fact it can be downright punishing since your enemies one-shot kill you the entire time. There is no health bar to be found here at all, and so you'd better be fully prepared for some serious reflex action before tackling this one!
Graphics are intentionally simplistic 16-bit style yet are surprisingly sexy...with an inviting pallette of pastel colours to capture your imagination. Whereas bullets themselves will be sparkling across the screen with pretty rainbow hues. I was especially delighted to see that parallax scrolling was implemented here, which is a crucial ingredient in such a game for proper immersion.
By far, one of Starr Mazer's strongest attributes is its gorgeous combo of faithfully recreated arcade sfx in addition to its hypnotically alluring 80s chiptunes music. They effortlessly transport the player back in time with ease, expertly infusing the game with a satisfying sense of immersion. Furthermore, voice acting here is definitely above par, and thankfully it is present for all characters. What a refreshing treat it is to enjoy compared to so many other such games which only include text-based dialogue bubbles. Best of all, the speech itself actually sounds retro too, like it is being spoken through a pilot's head-set in a slightly distored manner. I'm overall extremely impressed with this category, and I only wish that such a level of voice-acting was used in more shmup titles.
It only partially is, and includes 15 achievements to be unlocked.
There exists no DLC at the present time.
Overall, Starr Mazer:DSP wonderfully exceeds where so many other similar titles fail in one way or another as it pertains to faithfully capturing the true essence of an arcade style shmup. This isn't to say that the game is by any means perfect, vanishingly few are actually. But it does hit close enough to the mark of excellence for me to rate it fairly highly.
The jury is still out on whether or not its purchasable character style continuation system is superior to a more traditionally based one...but I suppose it is worth experimenting with in order to bring something fresh & new to the table. If I have any major gripes about it at all, it is that the game forces you to replay large swaths of it again each time you do continue with a newly purchased squadron...and after a while I can see how this may become somewhat aggravating for some...because it will test both your skill and resolve to their limits. Furthermore, it would have been nice for there to be several selectable difficulty levels included...especially for beginners to hone their skills on first.
But nonetheless, this is a very attractive title for inclusion in one's library...especially so for those who genuinely appreciate properly designed retro-shooters such as myself. And as such...

Pros:
*Graphics are better than original release (albeit not significantly)
**Seems better optimized than the original release (from what I've tested I'm getting pretty-much a solid 60fps on Ultra)
***Very easy to mod (hordes of zombies, zombies do more damage, remove lit-up containers, remove zombie radar icons)
****Mods for the original game work on YOSE too
*****Map is a decent size
******Breakdown especially is very fun, lots of different characters, difficulty increases
*******An abundance of different items, weapons, levelling
********Different zombie types, adds to the excitement/fear without being too far-fetched
Cons:
*No anti-aliasing
**Assisted-aim with a controller can't be turned off
***Lootable containers (wardrobes etc) glow white, which kills immersion. Google: No More X-Ray Eyes to disable
****A hunger system would've been cool, but stamina forces you to eat which is an okay compromise
*****Can be buggy, can't climb on certain objects, etc
******I sometimes encounter a bug where if I die, and start a new character, a sound repeatedly replays which is incredibly irritating. Restart game to fix.
7/10. Not the best game I've ever played, but worth it for a cheap price. I'd happily pay £20-$30 for it. Can definitely get a decent number of hours out of it. Just don't expect perfection.

I read these recommendations and lament; that in a world where hours are measured in dollars, I've owed thousands to this series compared with what I bought.
For two years I've played from Vanilla, to Breakdown, to Lifeline - sweeping the hordes on rusted-steel saddle, with a lasso burst from gunpowder, and a mania forged from clout. I've burned, I've savaged, I've salved, I've saved, I've cried, I've praised. It is the community by which we're raised. It is the loftiness of support, it is the understanding shoulder, the irrevokable lamplight in an otherwise sullied seam...
You can play your other zombie games, with an endless struggle of manacled, aging reflex against a toe-tapping slumber party of shamble crumblies with a penchant for frame-skipping in your general, meandering, stumbling, blathering direction, or you can drop that market wholesale and quaff the star motes of an untapped dream.
---
You take that entire genre, you break it down, and make it drown, then throw it a lifeline. Strip away all the non-essentials and see it for what it is. You take away its pretty vestments, its mini skirts and tube tops and stone-washed jeans. You strip away what society has made it, you strip away the old, superfluous tools of survival in whatever culture's theme, from the drip of alchohol to the baker's creme.
Crushing down all the trappings, enigmatically removing much, towards making whole.
Peeling off its Grecian idealism, its mustered motion of messosoprano Machina (Deus Ex), of lights at ends of tunnels, of softly spoken "It'll be alright."
You take the pseudonym you once knew, you make it real, you care for it kindly, you watch it grow. You slave and love and praise its wishes, you listen to its dreams, you fight you die you live you tell you lie - from the 13th canto do these mountains rise.
Until in nonchalance it's bitten, dragged home, bleeding in your bed. You swallow your tongue crying, empathetic solution's liquefaction - seeping heartward, salting now-ephemeral human wounds.
You stop.
Strike out!
Sweep the cliffs, sweep the shallows for some poultice, for some penitent panacea - an herb, a vial, a bottle, a philosophy - anything...everything...something.
Each footstep first thundered, in passion, now's a noose, each footstep strung in heart sinew, stumble's pounds to bear, whimpers come in volley, tears trailing from trebuchets, splashing hard around the ears.
Til each wail's a windlass - descending downwards with a knell...cranial crevasses calmly creeping, knowing naught is all's been found.
This is your world, is your misery, is your mercy shot against your once-loved friend. This is horror...is honor...is triumph...is survival...is your mind's eye into this world.

It downloaded in a couple of minutes and my first impression was not good; everything felt a little "detached" compared to the original; I think it might have been the camera, but also the controls didn't feel quite as responsive. I played through the prologue and put it aside as it just wasn't as fun playing by myself as it was with others and I didn't want to ruin it by playing through it on my own so I put it aside until a few more friends had bought it.
It wasn't shelved for long as this weekend my brothers and I found ourselves with an evening to spare, so they both picked it up and we jumped on the opportunity to learn to spell again.
We had started on Normal difficulty but because I had already played through the prologue and when I clicked "Adventure" the game decided to start from Chapter 1, so we restarted (on one of my brothers machines) and increased the difficulty while we were at it as we were kind of breezing through the first chapter even without remembering what we were doing. We started again on Bananas and it was a lot of fun, we really felt as though we were battling to make progress, wiping on the first few encounters until we found our rhythm and got our comms back up to scratch. It was quite rewarding on this difficulty level, and while occasionally frustrating it meant that we really felt like we were battling.
There was an encounter in the early chapters involving some crabs. It took us a few waves to figure out how we could stop them spawning, and we beat the encounter. We were also exploring the levels as much as we could, trying to find the inevitable jokes hidden around. We were loving it. Until it glitched.
My brother (the host, unfortunately) had gotten stuck somewhere off the map. There are no checkpoints after encounters so at this point we tried basically everything we could to get him out of that spot. We didn't have any emergency teleport spell at that point, but he was unable to summon any elements anyway so he couldn't have cast anything. The camera for some reason at that point wouldn't let us leave a man behind (while it quite willingly leaves people off screen in other situations, more on that later). All the fun and reward that we were experiencing while we were playing the game on Bananas difficulty was instantly converted into anger and frustration when we were unable to progress in a level because of an engine bug.
Angry, we quit the level and switched out for a mini retrospective while we took a short break.
Oh wait we didn't build this. OK...
And we did.
Overall, we enjoyed the experience but nowhere near as much as we had hoped. The game has a few bugs, and not fun ones. The experience of being a wizard feels nerfed from the original; spells feel less powerful, We had issues with controls, we had issues with stability and we had engine glitches that lost us progress and we had consistent sound bugs.
As a fan of the first game, I feel a little let down. The first game was buggy as all hell, especially in the early days, and this game feels more polished but still has the sort of rage-inducing issues that hurt its overall enjoyment.
If you are playing on a console or have some kind of physical impairment that means you can use a controller but not a keyboard+mouse, this game is probably a better choice than the original as casting has been simplified and you don't have to remember spells anymore. But if you are a veteran wizard who was looking forward to using all 8 fingers on your left hand again, you may be disappointed as it feels as though casting has been nerfed.

The game took place a few years(months?) after Aincrad event in Sword Art Online. That being said, player does not necessarily needed to consume previous products prior to the game such as the anime, novels, and/or previous games as Hollow Realization provides enough content to be enjoyed as it is. The game even provides introductions for characters that will be in your team. They also put da/night cycle, although I can not get my head around them as I have not found if they actually have some impact to the game aside of beauty. They also have weather system although only in certain areas.
The developer tried hard to make the game as close as real MMORPG as they can. I can tell. Virtually every NPCs (let's call them pseudo-PCs as there are some that the game deemed as real NPCs and some as PCs) you meet in the game can join your party. The field built to mimic real mmorpg, you know, the vastness of each area and method of travel between areas. The game is basically hack and slash with lockdown targeting system but every skills must be performed manually by using shortcuts. The best comparison would be Tera Onine, Wildstar Online, and Blade & Soul Online but with targeting system. Unlike real MMORPGs though, maps will be unlocked only after you defeat area boss. Only bad thing is that there is only one town. Seriously, one town.
It provides with healthy amount of customization, so no, you are not forced to play as
even if you can. Do note if set you character as a female you might want to turn off
's voice from the setting, they do not have female voice sets for your character. There are hundreds of weapon choices and models for each types. There are only 10(? I forgot, really 10?) weapon types but each types got plenty of active and passive skills to pick. Almost every skill got a weapon type weapon mastery to unlock. And there are EX-Skills, kind of unique sets in which you can only equip one (you can change it anytime) and hidden EX-Skills. So, plenty of choice and freedom to pick your playstyle. Only bad thing is that the game only got a miniscule amount of armor models. And each models only got a few skins too even though there actually a lot of them considering their names and stats. There are also costumes, like in every MMORPG, but there are not that many choices too. As of now (42 hours) I have not confirmed the existence of unique armors for the MC. Equipments can be enhanced and evolved, and the success rate depends on respective blacksmith's smithing level.
You are provided with a main team rooster. Also, as I write above, virtually every NPCs can be put to your party. But to do so you need to build relationship first with them. You do so by fulfilling their quest, talking to them, asking them for a walk, gifting gifts, eat together, etc. You can also change their behaviour in battle by complimenting them if they do an action you like in battle. Every NPCs can be romanced, albeit will take a very long time. So you can build your own harem if you want to. Events come in the form of conversation very like that of a Visual Novel. So you can expect of a lot of unnecessary chats and events. Actually, way too many for my mental health. Oh, and if you can raise your relationship level with the main rooster to a certain amount you can actually take each of them to your bed *wink wink*. No kinky stuff though, just some bonus screen.
As the setting is a group of people playing a VR-MMORPG, you can not actually found them outside the game they played. Hollow Realization revolved solely inside a game played by MC and his group. The main story start at a perfect time, about 4 hours into the game and the pacing is quite slow as you will spend a lot of your time in fields. And somehow, the side-story feels like they have taken more of my time compared with the main storyline. Both are good and solid nevertheless, but they could have put more effort on the main storyline.
There are minor bugs in the game, all of them can be resolved in seconds. The first one in controller problem. Somehow it won't detect yours if you have not set your controller in steam's controller setting. And as my friend point out, even then if you are using Windos 10 you have to put XBox DVR on in windows setting. Second one will occurs fairly often is that sometimes your PC will just stuck, you can just change one of your equipments and then you can move again. Third one also occurs fairly often is that sometimes monster will spawn in an accessible spots such as inside a wall/rock or below the terrain level, nothing can be done about it. Last one is sometimes the game will stop working and have to be forced close if I change map by teleporting. All that minor bugs should easily be fixed. Developer, what are you doing all this time?
Hollow Realization is a great game. Their system is solid and fun to play albeit a bit too grindy for some people. It tells about MMORPG and feels just like an MMORPG would. Recommended even if it is not on sale.

No DLC, no free2play rip-off, just plain free!
Made by Valve.
(You know, the guys who got this thing going called 'Steam'... Rings a bell? No? Ever heard of Half-Life, Team Fortress, Counterstrike, Left 4 Dead, Portal, DotA 2? You're kidding me, of course you know Valve!)
The game used to be a famous Unreal Tournament 2004 total conversion mod. Then Valve hired those devs to remake their game as a stand alone title in Source Engine.
Replay value:
The game is very open towards modding and community created content. Valve has released an SDK, the 'Alien Swarm Authoring Tools' for that purpose. This kinda makes up for the official campaign having only 7 missions, which might seem not too many but...
...For a co-op game the skill cap is pleasantly high and every mission wants to be perfectly mastered and be played over and over, until you got it right and feel safe to try it to a harder difficulty.
There are some pretty experienced guys out there who can teach you some impressive ways to go about things just by watching them finish, solo, after you and the rest of your team died an early death.
What also adds a bit of replay value is this: Once you grow tired of your unlocked arsenal and have reached level 27, you can get promoted. After that you're back at level 1 and all your previously unlocked gear wants to be unlocked again. Every such promotion earns you a medal that serves as an 'experience indicator' and nothing else. I like it though and find it rather tragic that there is currently a maximum of only 6 medals. So you can't grow your epeen any longer after that :(
On a final note, a few most obvious newbie tips for you:
1) Watch your friendly fire! If you're too annoying with your autogun, your medic might just decide to finish you once you come running for help.
2) Learn your secondary weapon modes! The flamer comes with a built-in fire extinguisher, you know. If you set a teammate on fire, at least be polite and put it out.
3) Stay together! You don't stand a chance on your own until you're more experienced.
That's it from me! Now go get it, it's free!

So, what makes these kinds of games fun for me (Crush the Castle, Angry Birds, Some Math Game I Played During Elementary School That Wasn't Blocked), is seeing everything collapse after knocking down a pillar or taking out a wall. Though I also keep the objectives in mind, seeing a gigantic structure crumble to dust with just a few well-placed cannonballs/dynamite/boulders is what's fun about these games.
In Blasted Fortress, while the cannonballs are tied to physics, the fortresses aren't. Taking out an entire layer to a fortress does not split apart the roof and send it tumbling down, and taking out the bottom of a tower does not cause it to topple. Nothing moves, actually... no matter how much damage you do, every (intact) block stays exactly where it was at the  beginning of the siege. This is my biggest complaint; it's taking away my reward. I don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about making money, or completing random levels, or completing minigames, or whatever other side content the game has to offer. I just want the fortress to be ♥♥♥♥ing BLASTED.
As for all of the side content, it comes completely out of the blue after that short (but helpful) tutorial when you start a new game. It tells you how to shoot, how to block, and where to go if you want to do more shooting and blocking, but for minigames, passive income, monster hunting(?), voodoo magic, penalty blocks (and different block types in general), and whatever else I missed in the ten minutes I played, you're going to have to read a few tooltips. Thankfully, the UI design doesn't make this very hard. Developer, if you're reading this, I would suggest broadening the tutorial a little bit, or have a very tiny tutorial compaign to explain a few more details before the player is thrust into the town screen. Having so much information thrust in front of me at once turned me off from the game more than it excited me.
I won't nitpick any more than this, but really, it should be more like what it's inspired by... Angry Birds.

First off, I ask that anyone who agrees with my review or likes it, please up vote it to help combat the people who're posting negative reviews and downvoting positive reviews to give the game a bad reputation for reasons that have nothing to do with Gameplay.
If you enjoy Zombie Survival Immersion, State of Decay is the game for you.
State of Decay is a Zombie Survival game that focuses on community building and management rather than pure Zombie Apocalypse Horror. You will have a group of survivors and a Home that you must defend and manage. You have to scavenge for resources such as Food, Medicine, Ammo Caches, Construction Materials, and Fuel. But you have to decide, "am I going to be quiet and take my time searching, or am I going to search really quickly and risk alerting every Zombie in the area that I'm in this house!", believe me, this can lead to many quick and painful deaths, which is only amplified by the fact that this game uses a perma-death system. If you die, then that survivor is dead, they aren't coming back. If you have more survivors back at home, then you can continue playing as one of them, but you won't be bringing back that dead survivor in any way.
State of Decay is much more of a casual game that you can sit back and enjoy your Zombie Apocalypse with a few heart pumping moments like when you run out of stamina in the middle of a fight you can't run from.
I personally enjoy this game because it has a higher level of immersion than most Zombie Survival games these days. The fact that it is free-roam while maintaining a linear progression so as to keep you moving, only adds to my enjoyment.
The survivors have their own quirky little comments that can give you a giggle or even a facepalm moment for how much a survivors comment can annoy the hell out of you. It brings to life the fact that each survivor really has their own personality and brings something new to the community.
In the main campaign, you start off up north in the woods, I like to call it Camping Central or Ranger Town. You're rather clueless as to what's happening because you've been outside of news broadcasts and such while out camping. You then proceed to the Ranger Station and things start to become clearer as you go, you will meet new people, and have to decide how to work with them. I'm trying to avoid too much info to avoid spoilers. After you get through the basic intro, you will be at a church with your group of survivors. You must protect them, the church and scavenge for supplies. After some time, it becomes your responsibility to move to a safer location, and eventually, leave the town to complete the campaign.
In the Breakdown DLC, you're in the same town/map as in the main campaign. Only with a bit more freedom as the main campaign missions have been removed. You start in the middle of nowhere and get given the choice on how to proceed, you can start a new community as a single survivor, or you can join one of three communities that are available from the get go. Items no longer respawn in buildings once you've scavenged them (not like they do in the main campaign). And this time when you leave town, you start all over again, so be prepared for it. Because each level of Breakdown, while there's a better chance for better loot, will also increase the spawn rate of Zombies and Special Zombies. Making it harder as you go along. Giving you more replayability to scratch your Zombie Survival Simulator itch.
In Lifeline, you take on the role of a group of soldiers that are trying to recover a means to combat the virus (very Resident Evil like if you ask me). You will be on a new map made up mostly of highways to get you around the map faster due to the lengthy distance for each objective. This DLC is rather fun to play once you've put a bit of time into the main Campaign and Breakdown DLC, it gives you some variety and new storyline and characters to follow.
Each character in this game has their own personality, this has only been improved upon with the Year One Survival Edition.
What YOSE has brought to the table is some old bug fixes for this GOTY-like release plus many other improvements such as:
29 new melee weapons
29 new firearms
Cleo Military Supply Drop Missions
55 vehicles (34 in original breakdown/lifeline)
8,275 new audio lines
30 minutes new music
This is not to mention the higher resolution availability for YOSE compared to the Original SoD.
But the bottom line is, if you're looking for a full blown, balls-to-the-wall action game, State of Decay isn't what you're looking for. I suggest you go and play Killing Floor (Killing Floor 2 is now released as Early Access) or something similar.

I haven't played the original game, but I can understand why people who bought it, and then bought this version would feel cheated. I just found out about State of Decay, and so far the game is quite good. TL;DR The game doesn't really match the complexity of other open world survival games, and the PC-port is subpar.
The game is focuses more on being a sandbox. The story is very light, and dialogues brief. The voice-acting is good most of the time. Graphics are ok, but animations are quite cartoony, and there's never any really scary environments or events.
The world seems kind of small, most locations are just a stone's throw from the base, and distant locations take less than a minute to drive to. Scavenging is mostly about finding special lockers (about 2 or 3 per house) and looting them. There's no way to gather natural resources, or construct makeshift weapons on your own (ie. no crafting). Focus here lies instead on maintaining base happiness, upgrading facilities and managing resources. This is not entirely obvious how it works though - the interface is clunky, uninformative and its far too easy to misclick and start deconstructing rather than upgrading, thus wasting precious resources.
The interface and controls are painfully poorly ported. They do the job, but it's obvious that it was designed for a console controller, and very little effort was put into adapting it to a mouse and keyboard (even Skyrim did it better).
When it comes to zombie survival games, my main go-to game is Project Zomboid. In comparison, this game is easier, more cartoony; but also more immersive with the 3D environments, has some good NPC dialogue and adequate AI. For these reasons I think this game is entertaining enough to recommend, although some better controls would make it easier to recommend.

About the game:
SoD is a third person open-world zombie apocalypse survival game, unfortunately only single-player, where you can manage a small survivor community, build and upgrade base structures, and research new items for your ongoing combat against an unlimited zombie horde. The game has perma-death, some RPG elements, a wide variety of weapons and you can use the environment to fight the hordes too.
The main campaign provides a mediocre story with a good atmosphere, and introduces you to the gameplay.
'Breakdown' is a sandbox version of the main story - you play on the same map, without the storyline. You start in a random location, find and join a community, and then take on its management. When all resources were used up, or you are just bored, there is a broken RV you can fix and use to take a few key members of your community to another area. It will be the same map, with all resources respawned randomly, where you will start in a random point (from your broken down RV) and have to build up everything again. As you repeat the previous steps, the horde gets stronger and stronger, and you will receive new, stronger survivors to reinforce your team. This is my favorite game mode.
'Lifeline' takes place on a new map, is more military-oriented and as such provides a different experience. It is a mixture of the previous two: there is some story, but you can decide to stay and continue saving people at an increased difficulty - with a global leaderboard.
Would I recommend this game?
- If you don't own the original, but like what you have read here, definitely.
- If you own the original and like it, maybe. You won't get much extra, so decide based on what I wrote earlier. Or wait for a sale.

Starr Mazer: DSP
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

It has been fifteen years since the G’ell have been defeated! But they are back with a larger and stronger fleet than before. Mankind faith is in the hands of a few skilful pilots. You are now in charge to select the best fighters for the survival of mankind!
Star Mazer: DSP is an Action/Side Scroller/ Shoot’Em Up game where you take control of a squadron of pilots who fight against the alien fleet of G’ell!
You will start the game in Act One with three pilots in your squadron. Your goal is to clear all Acts with the pilots you have at your disposals.

At first, you are not going to excel at your task. In fact, you are probably going to die very quickly. However, as far as you may go, each time you get rid of a G’ell fleet wave, a green diamond will appear. Just go over them and you will get additional power for your secondary weapon. Oops, I may have gone a step too far with excitement. As I mentioned before, you will be allocated three pilots. Each will fly their own spaceship with a main weapon and a secondary one. Your second weapon has a time limit but will be more effective against the G’ell.
Your first run will most likely be somehow . . . miserable. But do not despair, as you get rid of a G’ell wave, a green diamond will appear and you will get point (money) and build up your secondary weapon.

Depending on how you manage during your first run (and each run thereafter), you will accumulate points (money) and will be able to purchase new pilots for your next run. Pilots will be available in three squadrons:  Dog, Hyena and Wolf. Dog Squadron does not have a fee but the pilots and their ship are not the greatest. Hyena will and Wolf will cost you a fee to access “la crème de la crème” in terms of pilots and ships.
Gameplay-wise, the game is fast, addictive and really fun to play with a good soundtrack, too! What I really like is that each pilot has their own voice-over. In regards to the controls, you must have a gamepad.
This game is currently on early access and I am looking forward to seeing new updates.

Love this game.
Hi Don, Kaz, Vanessa, and the rest of the team.

The first three levels of act one are fairly balanced and took me roughly an hour to beat, the second act seems a bit half baked at the moment. The weapons suffer from balancing issues, some are useless, some are overpowered. This game shows great promise and I love the pilot randomization mechanic, but I think it is a bit early to pick this one up at the moment.

I'm not a great judge of shmup quality to tell you how it plays compared to others, but the core mechanic is an interesting take on the genre.  Rather than respawning the same ship a certain number of times when you lose a life, you get the next pilot in your squadron, who may have a completely different ship style with different primary gun and super weapon.  Your score at the end of a credit is used to buy the pilots you'll use for the next credit (and any extra "SK:ORE" is kept in the bank), but you'll start from the beginning again, losing all progress should you quit the game, so it's better for a run if you keep playing (or tab out if you need to stop).  The carbomite gems raise your weapon/super level but also combine Raiden Fighters Jet style into larger carbomite power-ups for a bigger boost.  Definitely worth a try, though I feel like the randomized pilot element throws a small wrench in the leaderboard rankings (idk for sure tho, since I don't score well at these anyway).
Edit: A cool feature is some (all?) of the ships have a chance of surviving a hit if, when your ship is hit, the slider underneath your pilot graphic stops in one of the highlighted areas. Still fairly random, but it takes away just a little bit of frustration when accidentally scraping a stray bullet.

Unfortunately, there were a lack of mazes, but it is satisfying shooting the g'ell. Voice acting is top notch. Art is great. My one gripe is there isn't as much procedural stuff as other rogue likes so it might get a bit repetitive playing through the first few levels.

I was a lapsed "shmup" fan, but Starr Mazer: DSP brought me back to the genre.
I hate dying in games, but in this game dying gets you the chance to buy better pilots (with the SK:ORE you've collected). The variety in the weapon types and pilot voices really help to give each playthrough a fresh feeling. There are just hints of story for now (the game is in Early Access at the moment), but I like what I've seen so far. I'm excited to see how this game evolves as development continues.
Starr Mazer: DSP is a great choice if you're looking to rediscover the fun elements of the "shmup" genre. It belongs in any fan's library.

This game is not a successful successor to JSRF. This game is watered down and boring most of the time. It is a fun game in it's own right, but it can prove to be infuriating at certain points. Instead of rewarding players for their hardwork they're spit in the face. This game is not a game of skill but of pure RNG and luck. Sure skill is involved, but when you're constantly being chased by robo cops that send you to a hub world that's a maze to get out of the game just gets boring. This game is fun to mess around in, but don't expect this to be a good game. This is boring and incohesive game unlike it's predecessors and other open world games such as Sunset Overdrive.
(I'll touch more on these below)
Pros:
fun open world to mess around in
fun with friends
very well optomized
Cons:
inconsistent design flaws
boring and useless story with an even more useless story unless you have all of the million collectibles
way too many collectibles that prove no point to the game except for players to have more in game time
inconsistent gameplay
it's hard to see objectives ex. the ball while playing because of the abundance of bright neon color. I'm sure anyone with mild color blindness wouldn't have a fun time playing this game whatsoever
boring hub worlds that punish you even if you've beaten the game already
very undetailed map
can't spawn on friends
laggy online and missions will abruptly end (I'm guessing due to connection/server issues)
no way to see progress on collectibles except for a small undetailed list on the pause menu
collectibles respawn if you've picked them all up in that area causing confusion if you want to get them all
boring loot system and players
no daily objective leading to a boring and bland game
boring leveling system with little to no depth
same missions over and over (only thing in this game is races/ball game/fetch missions)
no create a character
very bland features throughout the map that you'll use maybe one to two times
very short game (about 3 hours to complete if you do main missions)
missions indicator is a disaster and you never know where you're supposed to go next
boring annoying music compared to JSR and JSRF
Hub Worlds:
Haven District
This is in my opinion one of the best hub worlds. The races, ball games, etc. aren't the best for this world, but the design is one of the best out of all of them. It's colorful bright and actually looks like time and effort was put into making it.
The Sewers
This hub world has the best races, ball games, etc. imo but it's not very lively. There isn't much to do and it's a very small hub world. There's not much to do here, but what is there makes up for it.
Administrative District
The boring bland hub world that's basically a copy of Haven District with higher up buildings.
Prison
This is the one that makes you want to rake your eyes out and uninstall this game. It's a maze of making your way around cameras and traps that send out cop bots after you. If you're caught you're sent back to the beginning of the hub world to do it all over again. Sure I love some challenge, but this world is just infuriating.
E-Cop Tower
This is the prison on illegal 100% imported steroids. This hub world will make you want to uninstall the game and never get back on again. If you beat the game without getting all the collectibles if you want to come back to where the boss is located you have to beat the 2 missions prior just to get to the last mission again. This place is just another maze for you to move around in aimlessly so that it seems that the game is longer than it actually is.
The difficulty in this game is not fun. There are cameras plastered all throughout the game that send out robo cops if you're spotted. This is just infuriating and unbalanced. Instead of adding true challenge it just adds something that is extremely infuriating and punishes the player even if they're running through the world just for fun. The hub worlds mentioned above such as the prison are just mazes with lazers/cameras etc. that send out cops after you and you're sent back to the prison or back to the beginning of the hub world which is extremely annoying. This is just part of the difficulty scale and it's something that I could go on for hours about because of the ubalanced difficulty of the game. It's not a challenge but an annoying flaw in the game.
The loot system has 10 types of 'chips' to put on your character. You get the rarest chip if you get a 'fluffy' medal in missions which in most missions isn't very hard to do. This brings me to the mission difficulty balance. Some missions you'll have no problem getting a fluffy medal, and others you'll feel like you're on speed trying to complete them even with a maxed out character. The loot system is so bland that it would be pointless to add extra objectives such as daily objectives for better loot because it's so easy to get the rarest chips. Also at the end of the game you have an abundance of bad chips that are pointless to have. The only thing you can do with them is gamble with them, which gambling isn't even a topic I want to get on it's so bad. You get pets in the game which you have to feed and the only way you can get food is by doing missions. The loot on missions is completely random and getting food is rare. In turn if you don't feed your pet it dies. Also pets seem so foreign in this game. It's like seeing a cartoon character in a reality tv show it just doesn't fit or flow. This brings me to my next point.
The design in this game is inconsistent. You have the hub worlds and npc's that walk around that has it's own uniqueness and flash vibe to it. Then you add in these unfitting characters you talk to for missions (most which are playable after unlock) and your character you start with called the 'anon gamer.' The actual characters you speak to and play as don't fit in the world and environment they live in. 'Anon Gamer' is just a guy with a hoodie and glasses and doesn't fit the them at all. This is so boring compared to the npc's walking around which seem to be aliens. The pet's and playable characters do not fit into this world at all. In jet set radio the colors and characters felt in tune and cohesive. It's also hard to see objectives such as the ball in ball game and something as simple as a mission because of the bright neon colors. JSR and JSRF were colorful, but also it was tasteful and you could actually see where you were going. In Hover it's just a rainbow of colors that's almost blinding at some points.
The variety in this game is non existent it's just race and ball game back to back. There are some other missions sprinkled in where you do tricks for points and bring an item to different areas of a map (basically just race) but these are side missions not the main quest. Like I said earlier it's impossible to see what missions you have next most of the time, and there's no quest list. Also missions don't explain what you're exactly doing 90% of the time so you just restart the mission over and over until you find out exactly what to do.
The music is terrible compared to the JSR games. Some songs are just the same thing repeated over and over and they don't fit the asthetic of the game really at all. Sure some songs are decent, but this is nothing compared to JSR.
The end game is terrible. I haven't seen the 'good ending' but the ending without getting all the collectibles is completely pointless. The story is boring and bland without any substance. For all the hard work you have to do you're spit in the face.
In the end this is a fun game to mess around in, but is nothing like JSRF or JSR at all. JSR and JSRF were both cohesive and balanced games. This game unlike JSRF did not build on the ideals and concepts of prior games, instead it's just a money grab. This game is not what it was promised to be.

What is this game? Well, first of all it is not really a game but rather a collection of simple mathematical riddles where you have to fill a field of nxn spaces with the correct numbers, as can be seen in the screenshots. There really isn't much more to be said, the game is nicely done and while all the riddles can be logically solved, they will keep you thinking if you choose the grid size that fits your skill.
This one has so many riddles, if you're into that kind of mathematical casual game, you have something for many hours. If you go however for achievements, it will be a real grind to get the final one.
It can't really be compared to other games, for the reasons given. It rather can be compared to riddles, such as Sudoku, and there it would stand as an own genre.
Recommended: Yes

Oh man I had forgotten about this game, it is a great casual math puzzler similar in style to a Sudoku
Except, as you can see in the screenshots there are a bunch of differently shaped colored areas like someone just won at tetris.  Each colored area has a "rule" associated with it (you can see those in the screenshots also); for example you might have to make a 4-tiled "L" shape's numbers multiply all together and equal 36.  Or rule might be that the area can only contain even numbers.
You have to use each number once per column and once per row; once you fill in a tile it automatically removes that number from the rest of the row/column for you.   As the game gets harder the rules get a bit more complex, the areas get larger, some tiles won't have the color filled in, you'll have to use your brain to figure the colors/rules, THEN the numbers for each tile.
There's really no penalty for putting the wrong number in a tile except for your "shortest number of moves to complete this one" personal best ego boost.  I also feel it does a very good job of explaining and working each new rule/aspect of gameplay as it is incorporated into the rising difficulty.
By hovering over a tile, if the rule for it's area is known, all possible solutions are shown to you so you really don't have to be super good at math; this is a logic game that uses math as a tool not as a requirement to play.  I happen to like math so I never had to use the displayed possible solutions very often but I admit there were times when it saved me a headache and the game doesn't make you feel bad about it, it displays this for every tile you hover over on purpose so you don't have to feel the pressure of MATH.
Overall a fun casual puzzle game that combines simple math, 'sudoku' style numberplay, and logical processes of elimination.  I think the screenshots showing the puzzles will help pull this review together, highly suggest taking another look if this review sounds interesting.
