Before David Cage and his band of merry men decided that an ideal video game should have no gameplay whatsover they managed to rub two braincells together long enough to create what is undoubtedly one of the best lesser known titles the open world/multigenred genre has to offer. Archaic controls and desperately aging graphics aside Omikron takes place in a futuristic cyber punk world drawing heavy inspiration from 80s sci fi movies that really draws the player in both figuratively and literally. You play yourself using your computer to enter the world of Omikron taking over the bodies of a wide cast of characters to solve the mystery of just what exactly is happening to this mysterious world of Omikron.
The gameplay is broken into 3 segments. There is the overworld adventure mode where you take part in an investigation which is where the story mainly unfolds and progresses.
Combat is then split up into Fighting and Shooting. The shooting segments are your standard FPS style controls (though you will what to adjust the controls as the default is the arrow keys and not WASD) and the fighting segments play pretty much exactly like the Tekken games.
All in all Omikron is a fantastic immersive game and while it does suffer from sever early 3D game syndrome such as tank controls wonky interaction mechanics and so on, it is still on of the most innovative and ambitious games I've played to date.
Would highly reccomend

My feelings towards Omikron are very mixed. It is certainly one of the most unique games I've played... but it's a bit too unique for my liking. What I mean is, the game has a lot of variety- but not a lot of variety in it's actual gameplay. There are sections where you walk around and talk to people, sections where you swim, sections where you shoot enemies, and sections where you fight Mortal Kombat style. But there isn't much variation to this at all, and each gameplay has some hick in it; something that makes it really clunky to play around with.
The graphics are fine in Omikron. I have no problem with them. But my problem is the animation. Faces make strange expressions and people over-emote by gesturing wildly. It's almost comical to watch at times. As far as stories go, Omikron's is the most involving I've played. It goes to great lengths to make sure that you know that you are NOT playing a game, but interacting with a very real world with very real consequences... but that had no effect on me, as I would often correct my mistakes by booting my old save up and trying again. And the design of the world and flow of the story is way too vague for me. A lot of the game almost requires you to look up a game guide, as the answers to a lot of the puzzles are borderline impossible. And sometimes just trying to find out what EXACTLY you have to do next in order to progress the story can be a massive pain, as you don't telepathically know what the game is requiring you to do.
As far as the world and lore of Omikron goes, it's fine, but it has the same problem that Dragon Age: Origins only suffered slightly from- reading. A good lore can be told with subtlties between characters and showing in the dispaly of the world itself. I'd rather see mages practice magic than go to a library and study and make my own damn Beshe'm. (And I PERSONALLY want to know the people who knew how to make a flipping Besehe'm with no guide because none of the stuff I did to make it made any sense at all!)
I personally don't like Omikron for it's faults. If it wanted it's consequences to matter, well I'd applaud Quantic Dream for doing a much better job of getting that across in Heavy Rain years later. But as Quantic's first production, Omikron suffers from some massive problems as a game, but it still has charm to it. There is freedom in the open world of Omikron, characters can be fun to interact with, and there is a certain draw I had to the game before I got really tired of playing it really fast- since the missions for The Awakened can get repetitive very quickly.
If you want a gaming experience like none you've played before, Omikron is certainly one to fill that desire. But as far as great games go, I'm pretty sure Omikron won't stand the test of time to become a legend.

Stilton, Pear and Walnut bread
(Makes one small loaf)
Ingredients:
500g Strong White Bread Flour
10g Salt
7g satchet instant yeast
20g Unsalted Butter, diced and softened
320ml water
200g Stilton Cheese
100g Walnut Peices
1 pear, peeled, cored and diced
1. Tip the flour into a large bowl. Add the salt to one side, yeast into the other. Add the butter and 3/4ths of the water, then turn the mixture with the fingers of one hand. Add the remaining water a little at a time, continuing to mix untill all the flour is taken in and the dough is soft and sticky; you may not need all the water.
2. Coat the work surface with a little oil to prevent the dough sticking. Turn out the dough and knead for at least 5 mins, until smooth and no longer sticky. Lightly oil a bowl, return the dough to it, and cover with cling film. Put in fride for an hour, so it has doubled in size.
3. Line a baking tray with grease-proof paper. Scrape the dough out of the bowl and fold it inwards again and again until all the air is knocked out and it is smooth. Add the stilton, walnut and pear peices to the dough and work them in well.
4. Shape the dough into a rectangle 30 cm long, roll it up into a sausage, then flatten it out again and roll it up a bit tighter this time. Tuck the edges under and neaten the loaf by rolling the edges to taper them slightly. Put the dogh on the baking tray with greaseproof paperwith the join underneath. Place the tray in a plastic bag and leave to prove for about 40 mins, until the loaf has doubled in size. Heat the oven too 200C, or Gas 6.
5. Just before baking, gently rub flour over the loaf, then make deep diagonal cuts alo9ng the top, first in one direction, then the other, to make a criss-cross pattern. Bake for about 30 mins, until well-risen and golden brown. Cool on a wire rack.

"Dannazionne!" this is one fantastic game!
Mind you, this is more of a sci-fi noir game, there will be a few twists towards the middle that will have you doing a double-take. But trust me, the game is pretty good for what it is.
It's a little slow to start and it's difficult to grasp the story at times since there are so many characters and side stories to keep track of and there are intervals throughout the game that calls for 'rewinds' and 'fast forwards' in time to portray other perspectives.
However, what sets this game apart from other noir-themed games, is that this is a point & click game - which means it's going to be story heavy and less on the action side, which I personally enjoyed; also, you will be able to pick locks and solve puzzles (some of which can  be maddening at times, but they're a delightful addition).
You do get to interview various characters and while there aren't necessarily any consequences for your choices, you might miss out on some details of the story if you don't ask the questions in a certain way or if you're too rough.
My outlook on the game is mostly positive but I do have a few complaints.
There are a few plot holes, things that aren't explained; and, there's a cliffhanger at the end that leaves room for a supposed sequel - and I do hope that it is completed and released soon because I want to know more about the story!
And, it's a bit frustrating that you have the option to skip lock-picking if it's too challenging, but you can't skip puzzles - I felt that option should've been balanced.
If you're like me and craving the noir genre, I do recommend this game.

First of all, this is a kinetic visual novel. For those of you new/unfamiliar with this, then here is a quick explanation: read the description. Thank you very much for actually taking the effort to do so, and for those of you who did not read the description... Google it. On to the rest of this...
The story follows Ciaran and his close and new friends. It explores his present and past life, albeit rather ambiguously most of the time, in his senior year of high school. You read, you laugh, you get rather confused, then you go to sleep because the game became very complex and it is already very late for you to be up. The story contains lots of humor and references to pop culture along with not-so-pop-culture. I had plenty of laughs and I also did my best to get into the mind of the main character, however proving futile as my very few predictions were proven false, then some proven true, while others still nagging my brain for answers. Most of the questions that may come to mind while enjoying this thought-provoking story are answered, but some are not. And that's what made me enjoy it all the more.
The characters are interesting, most of the time. The music usually fits the situation, however when I was listening to it, sometimes the music, unintentionally, took my concentration as I enjoyed quite a lot. And then there were moments where the music had gone with a beat I did not expect, taking me off-guard yet still being enjoyable. The art is pretty simplistic, but that's not a bad thing. It reminded me of the art of another free visual novel, which is not on Steam at the moment... The story was engaging throughout. It made me curious, happy, somewhat sad, and even more surprised by the plot twists. I may not have an eye for foreshadowing, but I was a little shocked by how the end turned out. Some things as I wanted, others not as I expected. However, if you do play/read it, then stick through with it to the TRUE end. It is well worth what some are hoping for.
I would recommend for anyone who reads visual novels. It has quite a bit of psycho-babble throughout, but if you read through it a time or two, it starts to make sense. I would alse recommend this to someone who doesn't read visual novels, however wants to read a usually sarcastic comedic story with a bit of romance and look into the base of the human psyche. For being something that is free, I had enjoyed it far more than some of the things I had actually paid for.
And who doesn't like a main character who plays pranks/jokes on all of his classmates, especially when the opening (post-prologue) is one of the best pranks.

I really like the concept of truth and lies, especially the ending to this visual novel, where the unexpected is truth. I also sympathise with the main protagonist, Ciarán, and how he approaches writing his stories. They are true works of art.

Just finished this visual novel, clocking in at 11 hours. The story was very engaging, even though it was just a novel! All the characters had their own distinct personalities, and I'm satisfied with what was provided. Your name is Ciaran, and the plot centers around a missing package followed by almost threatening emails from an unknown. Plot twists will arise, and that's what was almost to be expected in a game about lies.. yet, it was all done suddenly, making you want to continue on. Including you, the entire story is centered around 5 people
. If I had to classify the best factor in all this, it's the humor. There are just so many laughs that help you get back to realizing you're all just teenagers. Everyone is living the school life, which could be boring, unless you're a part of this exciting group.
There really isn't much to say as to not spoil the story, just give it a try. It's crazy how much content was provided, especially when it is for free (which was the reason I picked it up). This visual novel absolutely blows all other free ones right out the window. I have played others, but this one is just amazing. The free soundtrack provided is top-notch and a huge plus! HIGHLY recommended to any readers!

While I do agree that this is how the PC release should have been to begin with, I'm not going give a negative review based on that fact as it would be petty.
Because the truth is, if you've never played this game or you own the original, I'd recommend it nonetheless.  Its the only real single-player driven zombie survival experience you're really going to find that delivers on the survival front AND gives you some interaction with the world itself in the form of other NPC survivors.
While I've played 7 Days to Die (and I do recommend that game) and Project Zomboid (another great game but it still has a long way to go) and a few others, I found myself playing this one out of the batch the most.  Mostly because the worlds in those games are...well, empty currently, though I intend to revisit them when NPCs survivors are added.
While the world itself is solid and interactions with it are limited (you can board up houses, establish outposts, rescue other survivors but you can't say, build an entirely new building from the ground up) it delivered what I had hoped and that was a zombie experience with some drive beyond, "I'm going to go on and on and on..." because while survival is fun, it is not inherently interesting if that is all you're doing (in a virtual space, mind you).
Plus, the game gets downright difficult as time progresses; there are some serious heavy weight zombies that you don't even want to run into while you're driving a vehicle.  Your insurance won't cover it, trust me.
TL;DR
Day Z (can't blame you, its a long♥♥♥♥♥deathmatch not a zombie survival game) not your thing but you want a zombie focused survival game? Pick it up.
Already own it? Pick it up on sale because the fix to the draw distance, graphical tuning are good but not worth the full price if you already own the original and all the expansion packs.  I agree with the notion that this is how it should have been to begin with but I disagree that the developers should be "punished" for that, especially since they were primarily focused on a console released way back when.

Sword Art Online: Hollow Realisation has you taking on the role of Kirito in the game Sword Art: Origin. This, to my knowledge, is the fourth game in the series with their being 10 games in total. I will be playing the rest of the games if I get the PS versions or if they HD remake for PC.
As someone who has watched and read the Sword Art Online series from Aincrad arc to Mother's Rosario arc, even Ordinal Scale, I can say I ♥♥♥♥ing hate the anime while I love Ordinal Scale. It's absolute garbage after they introduced Asuna into the story in Aincrad which in return made the "You die for good and darkish" vibe completely dissapear. I generally don't play MMO/RPG/JRPG style games. This was new to me, as it's not an MMO but it's a singleplayer MMO designed game. I do enjoy grindy games, hence my 200+ hours in War Thunder...I can say this game is a wonderful treat to play.
The combat system is great, after you set a few keybindings you can easily play with a keyboard and mouse. Everyone who has issues with controllers and complains about that obviously can't set new keys... Another great thing about the combat system is that it gets better the more you progress. You start of with a bit of hack and slash but you soon start to string together combos and doing massive damage through chains.
The level and skill system is simple and really easy to use. I would have prefered a "level up and get points to up AGI/STR/SPD" system, but that's just me. I personally do enjoy the system still, as a 1Handed swordsman working towards the mastery to unlock skills you may not know exist is a truly rewarding experience. Especially when you just magically get a skill. The addition of EX skills such as Celestrial Blades is great, I love working towards them then aquiring complete new skills because of it. Although I hope I can give NPCs the same skills, such as Yuuki being a Dual as well.
Affinity system, I was really against having the Kirito harem in this game. Turns out you can get close to everyone, apparently there's over a 100 NPCs too. It took me maybe 4 hours of talking to Yuuki to get her rank 6. I don't like the fact I need to get an NPC to level 5 affinity to add armour and level 4 for weapons. It's tedious and not needed. At least you can waifu whoever you want, Asuna is bad for my health.
Okay so I have to completely rewrite this bit.
The story, oh boy the story. It got better. So much better from the first 15 or so hours you spend learning to play. I ended up enjoying the story a lot and I hope the DLCs can keep the great running. I do not like the translations though, they're sloppy even for a Japanese game. Content. This game has a lot of content, almost 100 hours of base game I believe (30 if you're me and rush it) and with the DLCs which are included in this purchase it makes the game have a lot of replaybility. Amour is weird though, a wedding dress is better than actual armour? what...
Online co-op and PvP is apparently lacking, the co-op side is only for boss raids and dungeons while you need to play singleplayer for the story. Not a good move but I can look past that. Having actual players with parties can be a massive help in difficult raids.

Quantic Dream's first game, mostly known for featuring David Bowie, is as wacky as its successors.
After being asked to send your soul into a police officer's body in a parallel universe, you replace him in the futuristic city of Omikron, and try to figure out what's going on in a mysterious alien world. It doesn't take long to figure out that nothing in Omikron is what it seems.
Unfortunately Quantic devs bit off more than they could chew. The game is too ambitious for its own good, trying to do too many things. The shooting minigame is tedious, the driving minigame adds nothing to the game, and the pacing is completely ruined in the last few hours.
Still, go ahead and give it a try if you don't mind imperfect, ambitious games.

Hover: Revolt of Gamers is a fast-paced open-world multi-player parkour game by Midgar Studio and Fusty Game, set in a garish, neon-infused dystopian future.
You begin the game as a fresh clone in a deserted laboratory, with a couple of oddly named people talking to you over some sort of communication link. With the help of some holographs, they teach you the basics of controlling yourself and, in the process, lead you out of the laboratory into Hover City.
Hover City is a walled city built more vertically than horizontally, with the sewers, dump, and lower class hovels at the bottom, and the wealthy, bright, and beautiful houses at the top. Here you meet a number of Gamers, or their clones, and gradually learn to become one of them, joining in their fight against the oppressive anti-leisure regime, led by the Great Administrator.
Hover takes a cel-shaded, cartoonish approach to representing the game world, and it mostly works very well. It's decorated everywhere with bright, garish neon colours and looks like a giant Escher-inspired 1980s video arcade (though without any gravity-bending illusions).
The citizens of Hover City are varied and interesting looking, though they're just there for added flavour; you can't interact with the vast majority of them. Similarly, the various buildings and scenery throughout the different zones of the city are different enough to be interesting, but with a common feel that ties them altogether. And lots of neon. Don't forget the neon.
However, character graphics aren't as impressive. Customisation is limited, essentially involving selecting a few colours from a very garish palette, and all characters seem to have bland textures and simple models. Given the work that's gone into Hover City and the other locales, it's disappointing that the same effort isn't visible in the player character choices. The highlight is the neon trail that follows wherever you go, like your own personal Tron bike.
The animations are quite good, but limited in range, with only a handful of parkour tricks available. They look a bit slippery, too, as if you're gliding along rather than actually connecting with the world, which is a shame for a game that's so much about using the world around you to get to where you need to be.
The interface is good, with nice inertia to it when you fall a long way and hit the ground.
Sound effects in Hover are acceptable, but nothing too amazing. There are a number of beeps and boops from the interface at various points, and some 'whooshes' when you jump or hit speed-up plates, but no footsteps or other impact cues, further decreasing the feeling of contact with the world around you.
The music is crazily eclectic, ranging from a sort of beatboxing title theme, like rap without lyrics; to an electronic version of a funky seventies vibe (my wife asked why I was listening to a 70's porn soundtrack); to frantic, high-tempo dance music. There are some tracks that I didn't like much, and some that I loved, but it's a great mix of tunes, to be sure.
There are no voices.
The core of Hover is parkour. The game presents you with a series of challenges of increasing difficulty, like quests in pretty much every MMO, and after a while they become about as interesting: chase x spy drones, graffiti over y propaganda posters, complete a race in z minutes. There are a few variations, but with no combat and little variation, Hover fills up the MMO quest bucket with running, jumping, chasing, spraying, and collecting.
It all seems a bit confusing at first, and I found myself overwhelmed for the first hour. The tutorial is limited and doesn't explain many of the more complicated game mechanics, but I'm assuming that's deliberate on the part of the developers; part of the game's appeal is exploration and discovery.
As well as racing and solving parkour-based platformer puzzles, Hover introduces gameball: a very basic team game where a ball drops and you need to run or throw it into your small goal, while preventing your opponents from doing the same thing. Once I'd worked out the basic controls, done a few races, made a few deliveries, and won a few gameball games, I realised the game really only has two modes: races and gameball. Oh, and gameball races. But it's a lot of fun exploring the city. It's just a shame it's so repetitive doing the same two things over and over again to make any progress in the story.
The parkour is quite good most of the time, but frustratingly bad for the rest. Walljumps are terrible, with your character just as often jumping away from the wall as up it. To make it worse, the 'auto grab' that is supposed to happen when you reach an edge only kicks in half the time, often sending you falling back to the ground. You can't die from falling, and you have a 'rewind' feature that somehow moves you through space (but not time) to where you were previously. This alleviates some of the frustration, but given that the focus of the game is parkour it's a damn shame the controls are so slippery, and freedom of movement so elusive.
You earn experience points by doing quests and tricks, allowing you to level up. This unlocks a slot on your character, which you can fill with various augment chips that you find or win. These chips alter your base stats -- speed, jump, grind, strength, energy, and hacking -- or other derived stats, such as grind speed, friction, ball-carrying speed, etc. Better chips come from doing better in challenges, or from exploring the later zones in the game. But even in the dump at the bottom of Hover City, you can find some useful chips.
You can also unlock DNA kits of other gamers through completing challenges or following the plot, but you have to restart with a new character to make use of these, essentially increasing replayability through forced repetition. I'm not a fan of this model.
The game supports controllers as well as keyboard and mouse. Keyboard and mouse won out for me in all but the trick challenges. These essentially involve repeating the same few tricks over and over again as quickly as possible to rack up combo points, and ended up hurting my left little finger from mashing left-shift.
Hover is a multiplayer game, and can only be played online, but I'd just as soon play it as a single-player offline game. From my little experience playing with others, I had more fun on my own.
I encountered a few other issues with the game, too. There's no map in Hover City, which is a massive pain for the first few hours of play. Some missions quit with no warning and I haven't been able to work out why. This is especially frustrating when you're doing well in a challenge and it decides to dump you out of it, not even telling you that it's done so. The game crashed on me once, too. And the in-game text really needs some editing.
Pros:
+ Great music selection
+ Wonderful, vibrant graphics in Hover City
+ Leaping from heights is really good fun
Cons:
- Slippery animations and controls; no feeling of contact
- Walljumps are awful, autograb doesn't work
- Disappointing character graphics
- Boring multiplayer
Hover: Revolt of Gamers is an interesting game. The setting is weird, but fabulously realised, and the parkour is a mix of rather fun and infuriating. If the controls were tightened, walljumps fixed, some of the frustrating plot missions toned down, and more variation in the world missions added, it would be a great single-player experience.
As it is, I'd recommend picking it up if you're hanging out for a parkour game. Hover is fun when it gets it right.

While this game has many shortcomings that i'll get to in a minute it's just plain fun to play, the way you can slide, run and grind through the map is really satisfying.
It has a good learning curve and the frequent upgrades your character gets makes the experience even more seamless as you go. Which is in itself a feat for a game mostly made by a team of 3 people. Those things make this game well worth buying.
The main thing i want to complain about is the designs and the aesthetic of some elements. This game aims to emulate the tone of a Jet set radio title but in a more cyberpunk and futuristic universe which is not a bad idea in itself but most of the character designs look like some 13 year old emo teens who buy all their clothes from hot topic which is a huge turn off for me.
This game is marketed towards the people who have played Jet set radio who are now fully grown adults and i don't think this is what any of us can relate to. Even the original Jet set radio designs were more mature than the ones in this game. Not only were they more mature but just more aesthetically pleasing and original overall.
This game does not need to have good dialogue and i wouldnt even mention this if the designs were good but the vapid dialogues and the bad designs are two bad things that compound with each other to form this vapid cringey set of characters that i just wanted to murder all throughout the gameplay.
Another thing that i found was really a shame was some of the level designs. The first district you enter is ♥♥♥♥ing great. It gives you every opportunity to chain together cool tricks and you can really feel the freedom you have and what this game has to offer in terms of gameplay. But some levels like the prison or the final level are simply the antithesis of all that. The game gets rid of the freedom of movement and the flow of chaining tricks together organically and it becomes this semi stealth game that completely goes against everything that is fun about this game.
The alarms are really easy to trigger and the only choice you have in some cases is to cower in air ducts waiting for the police drones to dissapear. That or get caught and get put back at the start of the level or in the case of the last level being put back in the prison (an entiely different map) and having to start the long, grueling stealth stuff all over again.
Those are some areas where the developpers willfully didn't make the game play to it's strenghs and that is a huge shame.
Now on to the music. I understand that the studio didn't have the budget JSR did to buy the rights of songs made by obscure musicians and perhaps had to make the tracks themselves but there is a cruel lack of music in this game. There are only a handful of tracks and some of them are very lazy, minimalistic and unappealing. There are tracks, however, that work really well with the tone of the game and that are great to ride around to and those tracks are the ones made by none other than Hideki Naganuma, the original composer of many songs found in JSR. But even those get old because they get repeated over and over and over due to the lack of other tracks. This game needs a LOT more music and needs to get rid of the bland repetitive tracks.
Now that all of this is out of the way I'd like to say that despite all this, this game is hella fun, incredibly impressive for such a small studio, is still being updated frequently to this day and is definitely still worth buying.

I come from FSX:SE and I was happy there. Yes, it was frustrating some times with freezings, and out of memory issues but I thought, "well, there isn't anything else out there. PMDG planes are in FSX and Prepar3D". Then the IXEG was released. I wanted to try so I bought X-Plane. My first steps in the game/sim were to complaint about the weird camera controls, the terrible UI, the bad scenery and airports... So I started investigating a bit in the forums about how to improve it. After all, I did the same with FSX which doesn't look very good until you add some extra stuff.
So I read, and I start learning about the free awesome plugins like eBag, Terra Haze, Airport Navigator, Enhanced Runways HD... Then I found out how easy was to install those plugins (add ons) compared to how frustrating can be in FSX. I found out there are photorealist environments FREE out there. Really good ones! (yes, it's a lot of GB, but it's all free!) and from different sources, "alpilotx",  SpainUHD, World2XPlane...really easy to set up. And a lot of free airports also free with awesome quality! (how many times I said free?)
The controls are not difficult to setup at all once you understand how the setup menu works, and the views control works flawlessly once you get use to it! (actually I wish now FSX was controlled the same way)  And the IXEG 737 is the master piece of the airplanes in X-Plane (well, now we have even PMDG DC-6) I have almost everything to high rendering quality and getting around 50-60fps. I couldn't be happier.
My advice: give a try, and you won't regret. FSX is going to die anyway once Dovetail releases its new flight sim. (it's sad but is the truth) Until we can compare, X-Plane is the best option out there. Looks fantastic (try to fly over cities during the night) and flies in a very realistic way.

For a free visual novel, this really is a work of art. The character design is very clean. It looks like it's out of an anime with 3-D CG or even a recent P2P VN. The art itself is technically solid. Poses are done well, nothing really looks out-of-place. As for the background art, it's also well done, standing up where it should and laying low where it should. It's clean and bright, adding enough to the story that it doesn't completely take over.
Unfortunately, there are no character voicings, but the dialogue is so well done. All of the characters have well defined personalities and they interact naturally. It's as if they are alive. There interactions flow very well with the plot and each character isn't just a cookie-cutter stereotype, but unique individuals with their own histories, their own problems and their own motives.
The music also fits the scenes that are set. Placement and actual composition are both strong. Often times, Visual Novels that have weak music fail to keep me interested. I'll get bored after about 30 minutes because the experience is just so quiet and bland. None of that in One Thousand Lies.
Overall a very well-made piece. All of the elements tie together well. I didn't notice any bugs during my read-through. If the creators turned this from a kinetic novel into an actual visual novel they could probably sell a good amount of copies, although the writing would likely be weaker for side-routes due to the nature of the story revolving around the lies, how they build, and the one single truth at the end.

It also gets a bit weird and kinda long winded with some questionable philosophical expositions towards the end that are riddled with teen angst. But rough edges aside, it was a very enjoyable reading experience that I could fully recommend to any VN fans out there. The music was decent and fitting and the art style was good enough to not detract from the experience. This game would easily be worth $5 or so, but is free to play, so you can't really go wrong here.

Taking place in an unnamed European country, in
you play as Ciarán Endyein, an average teenager in his last year of high school with a reputation as a class clown. Alongside him are his two best friends: confident ladies' man Ausse Ealdwine and amateur psychoanalyst Ziva Shani. It looks to be a rather boring time as usual for them as school goes on, but a couple of events change things for Ciarán. First, he begins receiving cryptic e-mails ostensibly related to a missing package. These lead him to encounter Luce Aurea, a competitive girl and an aspiring artist. He also runs into Claire Argyris whose conversations only seem to be more confusing than the last.
This game is a kinetic novel, that is, a type of visual novel with no actual player control and only one ending. Instead, the story is entirely linear and the game can be completed as quickly as the player can read it.
Overall my impression of this game is mixed. I suppose I should start with the positive aspects. First of all, I generally enjoyed the writing. There was some great incorporation of humor in this game and many jokes made me laugh out loud. I also found the characters in this game well written. Despite being a relatively shorter visual novel, there was still a good use of the time to fully develop the characters with distinct personalities. Another great aspect of the game was the music which was pretty good and appropriately used. Generally, the art was pleasing enough to look at and the game's interface works well.
Besides the humorous writing, the main aspect of a visual novel is the story. I thought it was pretty good and it does have the potential to make the player think. This is especially true due to the fact that you really have to play to the very end in order for all aspects of the story to really be put in perspective.
However, there were some negative aspects with this game. Each character is represented by only one sprite with a few different facial expressions. Even their clothes always stay the same. For example, one scene takes place during a basketball game where a character is shown wearing ordinary street clothes instead of something more appropriate. With only five main characters represented, more diversity could have been utilized. The other main problem was the addition of filler. It should only take 7-8 hours to complete this game, and yet many scenes that do not progress the story at all just seem to drag on for too long. I understand this was likely done to incorporate some slice-of-life situations, but it was excessive.
Overall, while not a bad game, some aspects hold it back from being truly great. Is it worth the time? If you like visual novels with a focus on story, it would be worth a play. It is a shorter story and available at the low price of free, so you do not have much to lose. However, if you do not like visual novels, this is probably a skip.

It's a sequel, not another expansion. On top it's also by an entirely different development studio than the first, and by the third (fourth if you count the mobile game) studio to work on the series. Therefore it obviously plays differently in many ways past the basic concept, compared to any previous iteration in the series.
However, one thing it has done the same so far as the first game, is the rocky start, seemingly completely void of any practical thought or testing put into some parts during development.
For example, when you start the game for the first time, it starts in 1280x720, and puts you right into the prologue/tutorial chapter. Wouldn't be a big issue, if the options menu wasn't only available from the main menu of the game. Supposedly (can't confirm as I did the prologue as it was), exiting the game into main menu before completing the tutorial also locks you out of the main game, and requires editing config files or reinstalling the game, to have the game run for the "first time" again.
On launch the game was also missing all forms of control settings. As of right now it's only added in the form of including keybindings in the config file to edit. The hastily written guide on how to edit it is missing a lot of details, and has some info plain wrong.
Magicka 2 keeps in various balance changes and limitations made for the PvP spin-off Wizard Wars, which were sensible for a PvP-only game, but hardly so for a regular PvE game. Especially in a series where the draw came from the freedom of doing anything and everything exactly as fast and accurately as you could hit your keyboard keys. There's
which explains a lot better than I can, how the game was simplified and rebalanced compared to 1
The newly introduced cooldown system makes the selection of various staves you acquire during the game rather useless. In chapter 2 you find the Jester staff, which majorly reduces magick cooldowns. Additionally it increases the effectiveness of the shield element, used for both crucial survivability as shields and resistances, and damage, in the form of mines and elemental walls.
The game is very much designed around multiplayer, and when playing solo, not only will it be brutal at parts, you will straight up miss on content, as there are some secrets that require multiple people to open. Fortunately the game does seem to point these out when found, so you don't waste your time trying for too long.
In all, it takes getting used to, if coming from the first game, but
. However right now I'd still recommend waiting for the upcoming patches being put out based on community feedback. Then look again.

This game does everything a sequel needs to do, in the sense that it does everything better than its predecessor.
The controls are tigher, the story more ambitious, and the writing much more hilarious in the *I Did not see that coming* kind of way.
Fans of either Metroidvanias or Shantae will find everything needed to satiate ones needs in this little gem of a game, that offers plently of challenging platforming, creative secrets to uncover, and a healthy dose of Pirate goodness, that makes owning the game worth every single Doubloon.
Arr, Me Heartys, i be proud to use me booty, on this here game, and i be recommeding, ye do the same, lest ye be Keelhauled, ye Scurvy Dogs!

<Audio>
Let's start by saying when I saw "Jake Kaufmann" in the credits for the music, it all made sense. Shantae has some incredibly catchy tunes. Each island (seven-ish of them) has at least 2 completely different tracks, and most of them are extremely well done. I first learned who Jake Kaufmann was after I heard the amazing Shovel Knight soundtrack, and his work is just as good in this game. Where Shovelknight sounded more 8-bit, nintendo-y, this game has a bit more 16-bit era (sonic-ish?)  sounding tunes. Really great stuff.
<Art>
The art is colourful and cheerful, even in the desolate regions of the game. The main character, and many other supporting characters are basically made to be "waifu" material. It lays the suggestive themes on thick, and is unapologetic about it. Curvy/busty females are plentiful, and the game has fun with it. Whatever the "first" game did, this one has more, and again, I'm fine with that. Not every game needs super serious/realistic characters all the time. I don't think a single character in this game isn't some sort of caricature (stupid, goofy, scary, sexy, playful, etc) of something.
<Gameplay>
Another improvement on the first game, but don't expect a deep/complex game here. The game does enough to differentiate the gameplay, with different enemies/obstacles for each island to keep it playable. The level design is fairly plain, and overall the difficulty is relatively low. The boss fights bring the most spice to the games, but each one is "megaman"ish where they have 2-3 attacks/patterns that you'll learn, figure out their weakness, and exploit it. Pretty standard stuff, and it's done well. It's good, not great.
The difficulty spikes from 2-3/10 to 8/10 at the end with some challenging, precise platforming. I would've appreciated some of that challenge throughout the game, as the game has a lot going for it. The devs are fairly competent, and I think they have it in them to make this game go to the next level, and have created a good IP. I think what's lacking for this franchise to be great is to expand a little on the level design, add some items/rpg elements maybe... something. It's an enjoyable experience with alternate endings etc, but for me it stands as a "Good" game, not particularly a "Great" one... perhaps by design, as the game is ported from the Nintendo arcade? (3ds? wii-u?.. one of those), so perhaps they were trying to keep the game more "digestible". Comparing this game to something like Shovel Knight (this game is a bit more "open", but it's not exactly a metroid-vania), you'll know exactly what I mean by "simple levels".
<overall>
So ya, if you want a campy, fun platformer that isn't too too long, this is worth getting. Great music, "fanservice" artwork, and good platforming overall -- just not quite in the same echelon as shovel knight, and now, Hollow knight (different styles of games, but fair to compare overall quality to).
It really is an intellectual property that I think has a lot of promise. I hope they decide to make one of these games with a bit more breadth to it.

. The game is amazing, very well designed, I had a lot of fun with it and length was just ok for this genre. Okay, so, I've played a bit of the Early Access version, and now I'm sitting at the very end of the Official Release version.
I guess I can get off the fence, when it comes to my opinion:
GOOD, but . . .
Pros:
--Cute, cartoonish art style lends a unique sort of distinction
--Music is surprisingly catchy
--Overall gameplay is solid; character upgrading is satisfying
--Unlockable characters add a bit of spice
--Overall story is pretty fun, even if it isn't novel or groundbreaking
--Challenging enough to where it isn't boring
Cons:
--...Challenging, again. Some missions are stark contrasts to what your character(s) might be capable of. Some missions are so unfairly spec'd as to make them like pulling teeth--particularly when it comes to obtaining new Hacking Kits, or playing late-game Gameball.
--Translation! Translation! Translation! The English isn't poor in this game, by any means. But it is obvious that it was translated, and crudely. Yes, the game is French-made--but there are many dialogue boxes that STILL show up in French, and there are many unusual spacing and spelling issues that detract from immersion.
--Physics. For the most part, the physics of this game are well-enough laid out. But every now and again I get an odd glitch that sends me flying in the opposite direction of where I was jumping, or I phase through the floor and fall into oblivion untill I rewind my way out of it (this is particularly troubling, as it occurs every time I select 'Try Again' on any mission). There also seems to be a wealth of objectives that are simply unreachable by the INTENDED means. The most frustrating issue here, though, is surfaces that cannot be scaled even though they are obviously intended to be.
--Animations! Some of the animations for characters and actions are pretty good. Some... not so much. Others have complained about it, but the 'Tricks' in this game are very sad filler. Given the fact that this game was designed by a team of no more than 3, I will forgive this one. Even so, these animations aren't anything at all that you'd think about--until you're holding a Gameball, and can't do them anymore.
--...Gameball itself. Gameball, Gameball, Gameball... I like the Gameball RACES, but the actual Gameball mode feels like a forced, clunky interruption of everything that I'm doing in Hover. It's almost antithetical to what this game does, overall.
--Stat Balancing: To make this very short, JUMP can and will break most parts of this game, if you spec into it. Once you acheive 65-75% Jump, most obstacles don't mean much of anything anymore. The only problems that come with it are keeping lower to the ground for precise heights, and not having Strength for the aforementioned terrible Gameball mode.
It might seem like I'm really nitpicking on my Cons for this game, and understating the Pros--but a good game really doesn't make you "consider" what actually makes it good. It will draw you in, and leave nothing to interrupt your enjoyment. Overall? Yeah, Hover does this for me--but with the few snags I mention here and there.
It isn't so much that these details ruin the game for me, but they're things that I become accutely aware of when checking my characters, or reading the dialogue of the game. The game is good, but needs a far stronger hand when it comes to polishing.
Either way, Fusty Games did a pretty good job on this one. Worth the 20$, and I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a fun little time-burner.

Hover is a fantastic exploration into the parkour genre of video games. You'll often find yourself standing on top of a roof looking down into a futuristic city while other players fly past, their colorful light trails creating streamers in the air. This game does a great job of making you feel like you are limitless in your movement capabilities as you grind cables and frontflip over massive gaps. While I do highly recommend this game, it does have some flaws which I'll cover below.
The Good:
-Fantastic movement system which works flawlessly in all but one specific scenario: vertical wall jumping
-Character customization. While there aren't any cosmetics, there is a pretty broad roster of characters to choose from with more on their way, and you can change every color on a character model to make it your own. Your light color also changes the HUD color to match which is a neat addition.
-Awesome soundtrack. I'm not too into the electro-jazz style of music in the first part of the city, but the thumping electronic in the sewers really matches the game's visual aesthetic.
-RPG stats. You unlock upgrades to build your character how you'd like to, and they can be gathered very easily by opening containers found around the world or completing missions and leveling up.
-Single and Multiplayer. Swapping out between the two is as easy as pressing a button.
-Third/First Person camera views. I began in third person, but after switching to the first person cam, I can't go back. Its such a cool feeling to leap from building to building in first person.
The Bad:
-Difficulty. I really, really like challenging games, but some of this game's challenges are RIDICULOUS. One mistake, even the slightest deviation from the fastest route you can go, can result in the loss of the challenge. Not all of the challenges are like this, but there is a certain race-type jumping challenge that I spent about 2 hours on. If I messed up once I had to restart from the beginning. This may appeal to some and not to others.
-Some of the taller buildings can be very difficult to get on to. With a fully upgraded character it isn't really an issue, but for new players or those who are kitted for speed or some other stat may have trouble achieving the highest heights the game has to offer.
-UI. While I've gotten used to it, the UI can be a bit much at first. Instead of having an open-able quest log, it is always in the upper right hand corner of your screen. Minimized, yes, but still there. There's always an ever-present timer as well, even when you aren't in a race or mission or anything. While free roaming it doesn't do anything, but it still bugs me that it's there when it isn't needed.
-Translations. From what I understand, the company who made this is French. The game is 100% understandable to a native English speaker, its just that some things sound weird and out of place. The sentences are fine, but they use strange round-about ways of saying things some times, which could be bothersome to some.
-Cringe. Everything about this game is beautiful, but you'll occasionally run across some 'rawr XD' level cringe dialogue. Its very very rare, but when it happens, it kind of pulls you out of the experience. Not to mention the 'Revolt of Gamers' part of the game title, which is sort of lame too. But hey, the name doesn't make the game.
The Iffy:
-Mechanical skill required for some of the challenges may turn younger/casual players away
-Graphical style may not appeal to all
-This is a very niche genre of game which may not appeal to all
Overall, I'm having nothing but fun with Hover. It has a bright graphical style very reminiscent of parts of Borderlands and character design straight out of some sort of Ratchet and Clank graffiti on the side of a bullet train. So, is the game fun? Yes. Is it worth the value? Yes. Do I recommend it? Yes.

Greetings, comrades! Republic Commando, what a game. Don't let my hour log fool you, as I've been playing this game for about 5 years straight on the disc version, so yeah. First I'd like to say that if you aren't a fan of Star Wars, this isn't a game for you. It's a mediocre FPS that’s rather short if you don’t have a vested interest in the series. But if you love Star Wars, this IS the game you’re looking for!
Pros:
It’s gritty, and not just for a Star Wars game. Yeah, when you compare it to games like Metro or BioShock, it’s squeaky clean, but outside of that, it really is intense. Compare it to games like Medal of Honor or Call of Duty (the old ones for goodness’ sake), where the idea of friendly AI was something new, and you literally cried when you lost one of your nameless comrades. Take that and multiply it by 10 for this game, because not only do you have a bunch of average clones to fight with, you have your squad, which brings us to our next point...
The squad mechanic. Few games can boast a squad-based FPS that doesn’t feel like your babysitting, much less actually have the squad AI actually be USED for something, but this game does both in spades. Your squad is quite literally your weapon, multi-tool, and med-kit. Not to mention the squad controls are simple and intuitive, whilst still remaining effective for every situation. This is really the game’s strongest point, and will leave you wanting to get right back into the action.
Problems do not solve themselves, and the solutions are many. Any FPS should start taking notes here. The game has many preventable/changeable events that you may have missed going through it the first time. For instance, one section of the game has a hall filled with clone troopers and deactivated turrets, when suddenly an enemy hops out of a vent and starts running for the turret controls. Well, the first time through I just kinda stared at him like a bozo and watched my fellow clones (followed promptly by myself) get mowed down. There was really no indication of what was happening, and you had to use your quick wits and quick fingers to get out of it. The game uses these events quite frequently, which is very much unlike today where problems such as these are solved via quick-time-events. This harkens back to an era that gamers have always dreamed of but never really got to revel in, so take a moment and enjoy being able to use your brain.

Since Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army and its sequel are essentially the same game I feel that one review is necessary.
The concept of Nazi Zombies isn’t anything new. However to have a campaign based completely around a zombified Deutschland did arouse my curiosity. To say I was astonished is a bit much, and to say I was disgruntled isn’t necessary either. There are pros and cons to this game.
The Good.
The series features a foggy, bloodied Germany. Something that really isn’t new in any zombie-based video game. However the rules of double tap, beware of bathrooms and the buddy system are all legible in this game. After striking down a kill if it wasn’t a headshot, it’ll probably resurrect. Beware of anywhere really; zombies either dig themselves out of the ground or were sleeping where they died in their previous life. The buddy system is the most important during cooperative play. Due to the explosive zombies or the rifle wielding ones you will get downed a lot. Something that most zombie games don’t have is slow lumbering zombies and that is what this game has. I appreciate the classic zombie speed, giving there is large quantities of zombies to balance it. Oh and the x-ray vision of a zombie’s skull being pierced is the most thrilling thing ever!
The Bad.
The series is a mixture of Left 4 Dead and Call of Duty’s Nazi Zombies. First thing first is Survive the Siege, where a large group of zombies know where you are at. Which isn’t bad, but when your game is 50% siege survival it does get a little dull. The next thing is Get to the Safehouse which for some reason every safehouse in every zombie game is stockpiled with weapons, ammo, enough trip mines to destroy the fatherland then how is it there are only four survivors?
How do these guys even know where the safehouse is? I know there is two playable german characters but in all the destruction you can recognize where the safe houses are? Another problem is the other generic thing: Zombie Subclasses, can someone tell me why there are zombies that know how to use guns and others that don’t? What about the annoying “Kamikaze” zombies? At least zombies with guns lumber these zombies just sprint at you full force and usually a single bullet doesn’t stop them. The thing that makes me laugh is the demon circles summoning the Spooky Scary Skeletons. The final thing that is bland is the boss battles. Why is every boss battle a Nazi ghost that summons nazi zombies? Sure the one at the cathedral was okay. But why is there more than that? Surely you could have incorporated Zombie Hitler instead of just killing him off.
The Ugly.
Game has more graphic bugs than anything. When turning on Cinema grain effect some zombies have glowing heads. Random textures and bump mapping data screw up as soon as you mess with the graphics in-game. Then there is the broken servers where you just cleared the siege and the next mission starts except for the fact the invisible walls didn’t disappear and everyone is waiting for the mission that never comes. What a challenge this game is. Starting a disease is always great fun and you need to select the type and attributes you will start with. Each disease has different strategies and dynamics. You have a precarious balance between spreading your disease at a reasonable rate, but not having it be too serious to have countries all joining to find a cure and stop your disease. Having those last few areas like Greenland, Morocco, and Algeria, as well as small islands be infected before aiports and harbours are shut down can make or break your efforts.
There are many choices as to how to spread your disease and when to start making it more serious and fatal. Do you choose higher transmission rates? Which ones do you choose? Animal? Sea? Air? Cold? Heat? Do you make your disease stronger and more resistant? Do you choose non-serious or serious symptoms? So many choices. Also, you can choose different scenarios to try and beat. Some of the diseases are vastly different from each other and your choices of where to spend your points can differ. My personal favourite is to tackle the scenarios and maps of the apes. It's like you are in Planet of the Apes. It is very satisfying to infect and destroy every last human. Kind of disturbing, but well you know.
The game has very high replayability with unique storylines that do not happen every game or only in certain games once criteria have been met. You may need to play a map several times to have the right stream of events happen. Some achievements are easier, while some are very difficult to complete.

If you consider that out of the box FSX, with its smaller disc footprint, includes huge numbers of landmarks and fun places to fly around, you would be forgiven for thinking X-plane 10 would, judging from its elphantine footprint, be much better. Instead you are required to spend a week downloading external files just to add the most famous world buildings. X-plane 10 is simply not a finished product. In the past it may have been reasonable to have the community help with developing it, but after all this years, X-plane is nothing more than a scrounger living off the hard work of others.
If you want to fly IFR between far flung places, x-plane is great. If you to enjoy great landmarks of the real world, forget it.
The X-plane community defend this shoddy behaviour like rabid fan-bois - "If you're not willing to spend some time setting it up, then you aren't serious." Well folks, selling a game for £45 (and yes, this is a game, not a simulator!) and not including the most basic of famous landmarks makes X-plane very much a pre-release product. Having read about the main "personality" running the x-plane franchise, I should have known. So, enjoy your "hyper real" joyless simulator. One day you will learn, the fun is buzzing the ground and scraping landmarks with your wings just centimeters from disaster, not flying everywhere at 40,000ft or over a landscape which all looks like Oklahoma - but with less movement and shorter trees.
Oh, and one day you'll try an actual simulator and realised you wasted a large part of your life on a pale imitation.

It's been called a "walking simulator" but in all honesty I'm not sure if I can even call this a game.  See to me a game has to provide some kind of obsticle to challenge the player to be called a game,
While video games often resort to obsticles trying to kill you, a game certainly doesn't need violence to challenge a player, but it needs something.  This game really doesn't really have much in the way of such obsticles.  You pick things up and look at them, you talk to your supervisor, and you walk around, and if you come to what looks like a dead end, your supervisor will point you in the right direction.  So I'm not sure I can call this a game, though it makes for an interesting interactive experiance.
The world is colorful, There are choices to be made in how Henry responds to Delilah that can effect their relationship.  Henry and Delilah feel like actual people and not caricatures.
Furthermore the game does a better job making tragedy believable in the first 5 minutes of play using simple text, then most AAA games do  with visually dramatic opening sequences.  Even those who have never watched a family member go through Dementia will find it hard to fight the feels that the opening gives you just by text alone.
Some who have played this find the ending anticlimatic, but then such is the way of life, and I think that's what the dev's were going for, real people facing situations in a realistic manner.
In closing If your looking for a game to challenge you, you might want to look elsewhere.  But if you're looking for an well thought out and put together interactive experiance that won't make you want to smash your keyboard, you may want to give this a try.

I definitely recommend this game to anybody, especially fans of the Metroidvania sub-genre of platformers. The pros certainly outweigh the cons here.
Pros:
- The graphics are incredible; wonderfully detailed environments and characters, fluid animations, and many parallax scrolling layers. In addition, character portraits in cutscenes are well drawn.
- THE SOUNDTRACK IS AMAZING!!
- Gameplay is fast and fluid; the pirate equipment is a blast to use, while keeping things moving.
- In-game currency is plentiful, allowing you to stock up on items which can help you. However, you don't feel like Gems are being dumped on you.
- Dungeons will test your abilities, but they aren't too overwhelming. They strike a good balance between Metroid-type exploration, and Zelda-esque combat and puzzle solving.
- The bosses are huge and daunting, but fun and well designed, putting your pirate gear to good use in their strategies.
- Encourages replayability with Heart Squids, Cacklebats, and Pirate Mode (starting the game again with all of the pirate equipment - a speedrun mode of sorts).
- Don't like backtracking? Pirate Flares can eliminate most of it, and they don't require too many Gems to buy.
- Lots of secrets and hidden stuff.
- Funny and memorable dialogue and character interactions. Shantae is known for having lots of humor, and this is no exception.
- The game puts the pirate gear to good use in the boss fights and they are required to beat the game so they don't feel underutilized.
- Like mentioned before, the game absolutely encourages exploration and it's fun exploring and finding secrets in the world, like walls you can break through.
- Over the course of the story, quite a few characters get a big dose of character development.
- With things like puzzles, you actively have to figure out the solution, testing your smarts and problem solving skills instead of the game pointing out what to do.
- Platforming is decently challenging, putting your skills to the test, and this is complimented by buttery smooth controls. I always felt like falling into a bottomless pit was my fault, not the game's.
Cons:
- Some areas, like the first part of Mud Bog Island, go wayyy overboard with their enemy count.
- There are a few random difficulty spikes like the aformentioned Mud Bog Island and the Pirate Master's Palace (although the latter is the final level; it's supposed to be hard).
- The game puts items and gear you find to good use. However, a few items, such as the Bubble Shield, still manage to feel underutilized.

The game doesn't overstay its welcome and has a very enjoyable level of difficulty which is engaging yet manages to avoid becoming a frustrating experience. Released in March 22, 2005 this first person Star Wars game is probably the best thing about the prequel films. In this game you are 1 of many clones being trained to be Commando's of the Republic on Kamino. Basically the Republic Commandos are the Navy Seals of the Star wars universe. The game takes place during Episode 2: The Clone Wars and is supposed to bridge the gap between Ep2 and Ep3. I always found this game awesome because of the perspective. What I mean by that is that most star wars games always focus on the Jedi or you are this master sith lord or something that gives you an advantage over the others. While in this game it gives you a soldiers perspective of the Clone Wars, which was greatly overlooked during the films. You play as the leader of Delta Squad; a 4 man expertly trained group each with special abilities and skill sets. Sev is the Sniper, Fixer is the hacker, Scorch is the demolitions expert and you... well you are simply the Boss. Although the game emphasizes that each has special ability sets, anyone of your group can do the task you tell them todo. The game is one of the first games that I know of that puts you in control of AI. For example if you see a vantage point you can call out one of the commandos to snipe over there, or if you notice one member is low on health you may send them off to heal. This mechanic brings a variety of ways to play the game but also makes you actually feel like the leader of this squad. Each of the characters in my opinion each have their own personality that doesnt make them dull or boring and makes you want to care for them. The game starts you off on an assassination mission on Geonosis but then leads to other planets like Kashyyyk and broken down space carriers. I personally loved the campaign because you are only a soldier so alot of the time you are just as curious of the mission as they are. The game has great combat with a variety of weapons and a fair difficulty level that you can change at any time. The grittiness that this game brings to the star wars universe is awesome and is defiantly  a must play for any Star Wars fan that can find a original Xbox copy or buys it for $10 off Steam.
OVERALL:
This game is a great first person shooter that takes place in the star wars universe and should be played by anyone who enjoys that. Also the game has team deathmatch multiplayer so if you are into that sort of thing you should play now before the servers shut down!
9/10

In short, the best zombie game I have ever played, and one of the best games I have played in general. Even when my computer started crashing every 20 minutes or so, I just had him host the game and whenever I crashed he would just pause and wait for me to get back in. Seven hours of a crashing computer, sleeplessness, butt-sore-ness, cramping, aching wrists, and frustration at hard parts, and I would still go back and do it all again. 10/10, for sure. It's extremely strategic at points, where we literally had to make abbreviations just to communicate fast enough to stay alive. "Kami behind." "Skel on right" "Biggy up ahead" "SPAWNING ON US GOSH DANG IT RUN" were all part of our vocabulary all night.
You know the best part?
I'm still not tired of it and am going to be playing with other friends
You know the second best part?
There's still the second one to play
Seriously though, 9.5/10. There's a few things that make it that .5 from perfection, but it's aaalmost perfect. One problem is that is kind of the same thing over and over, but each time there's a different strategy, and I don't know why, but I guess if it's your playing style, it just doesn't get old. Insanely fun. People keep saying it's not optimized, and that the mouse will go slow one second, and swing around the next, but I never had that problem, so I can't say much on that account. Seriously, my computer doesn't even run this game properly, and it keeps crashing, but I still try playing it. Such a sweet game

The game was a fantastic, true to life successor to Jet Grind and Jet Set. I went from, in the first hour, being a freshly born lamb still shaky on its feet to, several races, challenges, and some game time later, a god of the grind that scoffed at the game's many attempts to frighten me with heights or challenges.
It would have been perfect if the final mission wasn't so distractedly BAD. Not hard. Not challenging. But frustratingly terrible and cruel in terms of mistakes, because if you make one you get to do two entire levels all over again from the start, and these aren't a short series of challenges. While I don't find Dark Souls the epitome of difficulty it's definitely more well known and not exactly easy-and it isn't nearly as much as an asshat as this game ends up being when it comes to making you repeat content.
So yes, despite my overall enjoyment of the game I feel so STRONGLY about the final stretch which is more tedious than challenging that I am giving the game a resolute hands down and can't recommend it to anyone until they relook that portion of the game.
I'm hardly alone in this regard which you can see from reading the posts throughout the internet of people who actually played the game (I never understood why people leave Steam reviews after only a few hours into the game..).

Overall this game has much potential, however as it stands right now I would not reccomend it for purchase.
THE POSITIVE:
The animations are extremely fluid and pair with the parkour style very well.  There is little to no jarring moments when moving where animations do not seemlessly flow together.
The freerunning feels good (for the most part, see negative section for more on this).  When running/jumping over objects, it reacts quickly and predictably, and the grinding mechanics are very satisfying and remind me very much of the 3D Sonic games.
The ability to play as different characters and customize their color scheme and light trail.
Gameball is a fun addition and easily the best mode of the game.  Think of it like basketball crossed with a tron light disk fight.
I would love to see a more fleshed out version of this game mode.
The graphics style is gorgeous.
THE NEGATIVE:
The map design is an absolute disaster.  Multiple missions require you to reach the top of a certain building yet there is no clear way to the top. I found myself stuck many times in situations like this, where eventually I was either able to spam jump myself to the top or just had to forfeit the mission entirely.  The main city is a dump (literally) with a rather small futuristic city above it.  Most of the maps size is vertical, however its messy layout can it make it nearly impossible to navigate and a challenge (not in a good way) to reach even the simplest destination. As for the size of the map horizonitally, while standing in one corner of the map you can look across the city and see the other diagonal corner with ease.
The missions are repetitive and boring.  When leaving the tutorial area, the initial races seem new and exciting until you realize that nearly every mission is a race of some sort (with the exception of gameball, which also got old after a bit). The three types of missions in the game boil down to Gameball (as mentioned above), Races (sometimes against oppenents and sometimes time trials), Fetch/Delivery, and Chase (where you are sent to chase a flying robot that patrols the city).  The entire game is just these same concepts copy and pasted around an incoherent map.
The time limits.  Nearly every mission in the game has you racing against some sort of clock.  Normally, there is nothing wrong with this.  However in Hover, the time limits allow no room for error after the inital 4-5 missions and usually have you replaying each mission 4-5 times or more until you learn the fastest route possible. I understand not making the game to easy, but there could at least be a difficulty setting that allows more time for completion depending on the difficulty level.  This, coupled with the completely disorganized map, creates some very infuriating moments while playing the game.
From the start the game is confusing.  The tutorial feels uninformative and you are left completely clueless upon first entering the city.  The UI does not make it clear where to go most of the time and in races and fetch missions I sometimes found myself completely lost.  I have played racing games all my life, and I have not once ever found myself going off track or the wrong way in a race, yet while playing Hover this happened multiple times.
The freerunning, while good most of the time, is also terrible.  Trying to climb up ledges is sometimes an impossible task, with the character either jumping away from the ledge (sometimes dropping you back to the bottom of the map) or refusing to grab it alltogether.  For the most part, this isnt a major issue since you can simply use the rewind feature to try again until the character finally makes it up the ledge, however, when the player is holding something during a fetch mission, the item will drop upon using the rewind feature making it absolute hell to deliver items to tall buildings.
CONCLUSION
The game does, like I stated earlier, have much potential. That being said, I personally don't think that the problems I have with the game will be addressed anytime soon, since they are nearly all very core parts of the game.
I do not hate this game, to be honest I had some fun with it for a short time, but I doubt I will ever boot this game up again. It has little to no replay value, and it is not what I had hoped it would be.

One Thousand Lies isn't a game. If you want any kind of gameplay, then you can ignore this visual novel. If you want a great story, then go right ahead and download this.
One Thousand Lies is the story of Ciarán Endyein, an aspiring author, who with the help of his close friends stumbles into an interesting story not unlike one of his own, full of twists and turns.
The characters are amazing; the two close friends share quirky and fun dialouge with Ciarán, but both them and the people we meet on the way also have many deep philosophical discussions with him.
The characters are drawn in a really nice anime-esque style and the backgrounds, while simple, do their job. I haven't bothered to check if the music is original, but it's absolutely amazing, both on it's own and matched with happens on screen.
In conclusion, this is a must-read for everybody who enjoys a good story, it's no masterpiece, but it's closer to it than what you'd expect.

Custom controls are shown as needed, but otherwise players are expected to be familar with rpgmaker games. For example, players can run holding Shift or toggle full screen with Alt+Enter, but there's no help that mentions this. I really do not understand the negative reviews for X-Plane 10. I can only assume they are from people who have wildly inflated expectations, fail to grasp flight-simulation as a study hobby/application, or they are die-hard FSX users and just can’t let go (“because X-Plane has flat trees”)!
X-Plane’s minor issues are constantly being updated and worked on by a dedicated dev group that updates the sim every few weeks/months. The flight model is simply astounding. You feel the terrifying crosswind on final, you have to kick the rudder and stick in on takeoff. Jets will roll on their own without unrealistically having to provide power. Uneven runways that follow the grounds contours? X-Plane does this. And all of it out of the box. You want add-ons and payware content, then X-Plane is rapidly catching up with FSX/P3D. There are already add-on planes that surpass those for FSX. And the scenery? The freeware design community, especially scenery design, is actually better than FSX payware in many cases.
X-Plane is a modern simulator and therefore performance is also modern. Where you might be lucky to get FPS in the high-teens at best in FSX in a complicated add-on at a detailed airport with traffic with a killer PC, you’ll get double-that, locked at a solid 30FPS and possibly more, in X-Plane. There are no freeze-frame stutters on final. No Out of Memory, No .cfg tweaking required. It just works.
If you want a desktop flightsim experience with accurate modeling of the forces you have to wrestle against when flying, then X-Plane delivers with amazing results. Vanilla it is great, but embracing addons will turn it into as complex a sim as you want it to be. FSX cannot and does not compare, simply because it was released in 2006. And at that, the basic flight model stems from 2002. In fact X-Plane delivers in so many areas that I completely removed my 20 year affair with Microsoft Flight Simulator from my PC.

It has a way to go in areas such as traffic and seasons, but there are workarounds available. Bottom line though is this, if you want to learn and experience flight, and then expand upon that in the same simulator, X-Plane is the only modern player. Note: DCS-World also delivers on a supremely high standard but it’s combat only in limited theaters.
Enjoy!

Omikron is 14 years old, however by no means is that a reason to pass this game up.

The Nomad Soul did a lot, and took a lot of chances. In the current development atmosphere where games must be marketed to reach the most absolute mindless of the massess to get the greatest return, this game hails from a time when developers were trying all sorts of things to break the mold. Keep in mind that this was released 2 years prior to the legendary open world RPG Morrowind, yet managed to accomplish having an engaging open world built off fairly interesting and new concept. All of the dialog is voiced, and the world is huge- to a point where it really starts to be a detriment, a mistake Morrowind did not learn from either.
Omikron is not without it's flaws. It is simultaneously an open world RPG, a fighter, a shooter, and maybe something else thrown in there as well.  It does all of these things fairly mediocrely, but combined, it holds up fairly well- particularly for it's age. The story was very dark and very interesting when I had played it in 9th grade. Looking back and revisiting it, it is still very interesting, although is not immune to some cliches that I may not have picked up when I was younger.
Definitely pick the game up on sale just to experience a different time in game development, a developer who took chances with mechanics and genres, had a terrific new IP, and also managed to get robot David Bowie in their game.

Magicka 2 is a fantastic game from what I have played.  I feel the negative press is from those who expected to be as good at this initially as they were after many hours in magicka 1.   On most of the thumbs down, the justification has been a comparison to magicka 1, usually on THESE grounds:
They say: There's quickcast now! Filthy casuals!

They say: There are cooldowns! This is so toned down.
I say: They do not apply if you do not quick cast, apart from like a 2 or 3 second default cooldown, which provides a
necessary balance to overpowered spell spam in the first game like lightning bolt or summon elemental.  You could rapid
fire those spells as fast as you could type to win any battle, eliminating challenge/balance.
They say: It's like wizard wars now I don't like the controls! I run off cliffs 2 die D:
I say: Controls were improved to allow move and shoot, channeling healing, and other little tweaks, persistent sword buffs etc. If you ran off the cliff its because you clicked off the cliff.  You'll be revived in 2 seconds if you're playing multiplayer anyway, I'm sorry you have involuntary tourettes of the wrist, but your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ spasms do not justify giving poor reviews to the developers and their product.  The only con is nonremappable keys, which I'm sure will be patched soon. Most fans played magicka 1 with default controls anyway, and would likely play 2 as such even given the option, its not really an illogical layout.
They say:  The spellcasting is too simplified, I no longer get combined elements!
I say: So if you wanted 5 steam in the past, you had to hit 5 water and 5 fire, 10 keystrokes. Each icon of fire or water would turn into an icon of steam when its counterpart was added to the queue. Now everything is streamlined to 5 inputs out of 8 elements x 4 cast types, that is to say, icons do not combine into secondary elements now. Spell strengths are mostly equivalent to what they were before but with less keystrokes, and all of the steam and ice sickles etc are still doable. I fail to see the problem.

I say: So the more professional team balancing and creating this game decided to take away your crutch of a press to win button, and now you're crying.  I'm sorry that you can't adapt and play a game with strategy reaction and teamwork the way it was intended?
