Put simply, it's Magicka if Magicka wasn't Magicka.
The form is recognisable, many of the design elements familiar, but so much of the charm, pacing, OTT-fun and even narrative of the first game seems completely absent. It's not frantic, it's not intuitive, it's not hilarious. It's sluggish and balanced with no semblance of character and cheap references that go on too long or seem too random. Playing through this with friends, I was recording, and the first laugh we had was 49 minutes in. 49 minutes of play without a single giggle, in a Magicka game, where the first time the player uses their powers they should die horribly and unexpectedly. It seems like every little alteration to the game was made by chopping out or simplifying one of the things that gave the first game its unique character and it really, really shows. This is a smooth, balanced game, devoid of joy or absurdity and too invested in keeping itself streamlined to immerse you for more than a few seconds at a time (unfortunately, I'm not exaggerating there).
It's ok, sure. Perhaps not to everyone's tastes, but definitely worth £11. It's just not a good Magicka sequel, and if you enjoyed the first one at all, you will almost certainly be heartbroken by this. I wish I could use a weaker word, but honestly, it's 100% appropriate.
Defining moment so far was hearing the Magicka end-of-level tune for the first time amid all the new tracks, and the first words on our Skype call were "you have not earned the right to that music".

Do you like shooting zombies? I do. Do you like WW2 shooters? I do. Do you like games that combine these two elements into a mostly hilarious, sometimes unnerving B-movie/game? I do. If you're like me, you might be interested in this game.
Also, zombie snipers. Hax.

So, you like zombies? Shooting them, I mean.
Well, here's the game for you. It retains the beautiful sniping mechanics of sniper elite with aim adjustment for wind and velocity/distance, you get a satisfying go at popping thousands of zombie heads in gory slow motion (something that you can toggle off in case it ends up boring you after the 4600th kill).
That isn't all you'll be doing, though. Featuring iconic WW2 weaponry with their own benefits and drawbacks, you have plenty of choice when it comes to dealing with the hellish hordes that the führer has summoned. Not everyone is an expert sniper and you can still have a grand old time mowing down the flesheating freaks with a machine gun.
Set at the end of WW2, the nazi war machine is failing and Hitler pursues a desperate method of salvaging his war. An ancient nepalese relic recovered by the Thule society reanimates the slain wehrmacht to devour the enemies of the Reich! It's up to our hero, Karl Fairburne, the great Russian bear of a man Boris Medvedev, Dr. Schweiger and redeemed(?) nazi Herman Wolff to wipe the undead scourge off the streets of Berlin before it spreads to the rest of the continent!
That's it for the plot, really. It's vaugely elaborated upon in the followup Nazi Zombie Army 2 but not by much. If you expect a plot, play something different but it's good for what it is, playing up the nazi occult thing in a way I've only seen the Wolfenstein games explore.
Mechanics wise, it's a third person shooter in which you counter hordes of sluggish zombies (no running here, except for the suicide bombers!) but it's not that easy. Unlike games like left 4 dead, you go down in just a couple of hits and the numbers that spawn in co-op can seem endless at times. But hey, that's what grenades are for!
Single player and multiplayer are pretty much the same deal but with more players come more of a challenge. More enemies will spawn to hinder you and something you thought was a breeze when playing alone can become a nightmare.
The levels themselves are largely remade levels from the sniper elite game, approached from different angles and merged in interesting ways. You'll kind of know your way if you played the main game.
Enemy variety includes regular zombies who are just your typical flesh eating monster, groaning and shuffling about as well as quicker moving stripped skeletons who are very good at overwhelming their opposition, forcing stationary snipers to move about.
The previously mentioned suicide bombers appear in the middle of regular zombie hordes to catch you off guard and rush you and sometimes you're faced with eerily cackling zombie snipers, leaping from building to building to take shots at you while you're trying to handle the horde in front.
There's also the trooper zombies who are gigantic, slow moving behemoths with machine guns, shooting right back at you and demanding dozens of shots to the forehead to finally drop.
Finally, there's the occult general. A very rare, scripted boss creature that summons hordes of every variety and protects himself with a magical barrier of floating skulls, encouraging a different kind of headshot.
That's enough about that. Gameplay wise, it's good for what it is. Hardly a captivating masterpiece of storytelling to share with your grandkids someday but an entertaining go through a strange, strange setting.
I don't believe in scores so I rate this game as fun, entertaining but capable of being a lot more than what we're given. Maybe we'll see the formula brought to perfection in sniper elite Afrika's version of the zombie nightmare?

game includes editors you can create your own planes with, you can then load them into the simulator, this game is good as an engineering tool, you can build your own planes and test them

For more than 20 years I have used Microsoft's flight simulators for training and entertainment, but with very positive reviews from fellow pilots and the flight simulator onine community I decided to give this one a try.
Being a professional pilot, my review will only affect those areas of interest for using the simulator as a training platform. For example, I don't care much for how pretty the graphics are.
The aerodynamic model is said to be generated in situ, like a wind-tunnel model, which makes the behaviour of the aircraft much more realistic than any other simulator I've used before.
The weather engine simulates proper low visibility, icing and turbulece, however the clouds have a huge effect on computer performance (framerates) and a very decent pc is required to run this simulator.
Needless to say this simulator is worthless without a good joystick. My own setup contains a yoke, rudder pedals and a throttle quadrant. The configuration of all the switches, handles and axis are somewhat harder to figure out compared the FSX, but the flexibility is much better in the end.
The default aircraft that come with x-plane are of comparible quality of the FSX default aircraft, and therefore utterly useless. Where FSX has hundreds of good (often payware) addon-aircraft, X-plane only has a handfull. I purchased x-plane mostly as a future investment in anticipation of better add-on aircraft. I am very positive about the Saab 340 from x-aviation .com
The manipulation of buttons and switches in the virtual cockpits are not as intuitive as in FSX and even when bound to hardware buttons, setting radios and instruments can be quite a pain. Especially for flying modern aircraft with lot's of automation this is a bit of a pain.
Overall I would recommend it, when used properly it can be a usefull training tool.

Omikron: The Nomad Soul is the first game of the Quantic Dream studio. It might as well be considered three games in one. For the major part of the gameplay it remains a TPP adventure game relying on the usual stuff:  talking with NPCs and using items. Occasionally it switches to FPP shooter or hand to hand 1 on 1 brawler kind of similar to early instalments of the Tekken or Virtua Fighter series. It is worth mentioning that all of these are made pretty solid and none of them feels like it was forced into the gameplay without a reason (well, maybe with the exception of swimming, but it occurs 2 or 3 times in the entire game, which is acceptable).

An interesting mechanic incorporated into the gameplay is the switching of the protagonist’s bodies. While it is not possible to reincarnate into any NPC, there certainly is a significant number of possible bodies the ‘Nomad Soul’ can possess. Some of these are plot induced – when your actual shell is killed, you will take over the first person that touches the dead body – yes, dying does not necessarily mean  seeing a game over screen.  Later on you acquire a spell that allows reincarnation whenever you find an interesting host – for instance to gain access to a particular area. Or just for fun.
I find it a bit disappointing that, while all of these NPCs have their statistics (eg. Strength, speed, HP, MP) and some information on their background, likes and dislikes, when you decide to reincarnate, your previous host simply disappears. At no point it is mentioned that what you actually do is stealing the bodies of living people. I believe that this theme is not sufficiently explored or developed during the game.
Surprisingly enough, the graphics of this game are not all that bad (considering the fact it was published in 1999). Of course, models and  textures are simple and the viewing distance is obscured by the mist,  but all of the game’s districts have their own style and color palette that catches the eye. Furthermore, the way the districts look contributes greatly to the  game’s cyberpunk atmosphere. On the other hand, it is noticeable that there are very few models of NPC characters on the street (2 – 3 per district) and vehicles (1 model of a hovercraft-car and 1 bike –  that’s all!). If you decide to play, I strongly suggest overriding the game’s settings in your graphic card’s panel and forcing every possible filtering on – it greatly improves the game’s appearance: especially the character’s faces during the conversations.
Quite obviously, music is where the game excels (David Bowie!) . It needs to be said that not only the tracks featuring David Bowie are awesome (look around the city – you may find a concert going on. ) but the entirety of the soundtrack is an impressive work.
In my mini-reviews I usually do not discuss the game’s story line, and this case should not be an exception. But let me tell you that: at some points of the storyline some of the NPCs will openly say that Omikron is a computer game ( while others will tell you that it is not :D) and it is the integral part of the plot.  It is quite worth playing the game just to discover this particular story gambit.
To conclude: I cannot say whether Omikron is a good game or not. It is certainly an ambitious one.  It is noticeable that lot of work has been put into Quantic Dream’s first child. Still, one can’t help but notice that the later part of the game is significantly weaker, just as if authors ran out of ideas in the end. It doesn’t help that the puzzles in the final chapter of the game are EXTREMELY annoying ( For example – AND THERE WILL BE SPOILERS as I am describing two most annoying riddles in the game – at one point you are required to run around one of the districts, without the use of cabs, looking for four symbols – this task takes more or less half an hour, while solving the riddle when you know the symbols – no more than a minute. Ten minutes later you need to find a gem  - in the chamber where you can get it, there are approximately 20 chests with 20 similar gems – of course the game gives you hints as to which one you should choose but these are quite vague and you are not told in any way whether you picked the right one – and the place where you use the said gem is one hour ahead into gameplay. So yes, if you chose poorly you will be running right back. Or RAGEquit. Anyways, SPOILERS OUT).

If you are still planning to finish this game, it should take around 15 hours. It took me some more time since I decided to lose all the battles and check out the outcomes. My recommendation in this case is: buy this game (discounted!)  to check out where the authors of Indigo Prophecy, Heavy Rain and Beyond: Two Souls started. Play to discover that one major plot twist.  After that, there is not much Omikron has to offer. Be warned: I finished this one solely because I loved it OH SO MUCH back then in primary school.

From my view, it has their good and bad sides. and some of them are a matter of opinion.
It's only too bad that the game didn't fit well to my opinion. But the game is worth the try.
I'm overall neutral about this, And I'm very two-sided to give it a positive or negative response.
But I decided to give it a positive view as my opinion differs from the others.
It's however worth pointing out the next things before you buy:
Pro's:
- Great animations, I've really enjoying them, especially Shantae herself.
- Great Soundtrack. They're really fitting to them, some of them are arabic, and sometimes it fits even Castlevania.
- Every character has pretty much their own full body render art during dialogues.
- It has their humor, mostly classic humor.
- Fanservice. That's pretty much the game's main point. There are busty ladies with bra's and bikini's everywhere. Now combine it with the full body renders and you've an anime visual novel in a platformer game.
However, I'm not a visual novel fan, When I'm playing a game I prefer the gameplay over the artwork, and honestly I think it would have been fine enough for me if it were just head pictures. I can't take my time to look at their bodies if they might have something important to tell. Maybe appealing for other people. just not for me.
Cons:
- The controls are ... weird, I guess you'll get used to it, but it's weird for me when everything is assigned to a different button. An example: Attack, talk and confirm has 3 seperate buttons, while it would have been more user-friendly if they mixed it into one. This also takes away a bit of the combat flow.
- Difficulity spikes, The game feels too easy at the start. but later on the game turns out to becomes harsh. (The final area is a huge twist compared to the overall game.)
- Fullscreen seems a bit buggy sometimes when using alt-f4.
- Lack of animations, sounds a little ironic as I also said that they've great animations. But sometimes I've noticed that it looks like only halfway done. Causing a bit of a quality break. It sometimes feels like there could have been some extra animations here and there: The idle animations looks the same every time despite their artworks shows different expressions, it's a bit odd to me as the standard idle animation doesn't really fit with the situation sometimes.
And sometimes when I expected to see an unique animated cutscene by an event, the screen goes black instead. It's a little bit easily done in that term and that's a bit disappointing. Because the animations does look good and I could have certainely see that potential.
My own opinion:
I think this game differs too much from what I'm used to with Metroidvania's. And there have been parts that I don't find logical to happen. I do have played the game untill the end though, including the secret ending as I was pretty close to that. But in all honestly, there has been parts that rather takes me away from replaying it. The game didn't really fit my style, but that doesn't make it a bad game. It also has their good sides, as there were several music, animations, mechanics and upgrades that I've enjoyed.
Overall, I've been really trying to love the game, but it didn't really fit at my end.
The real question is where your interests are at, because for me, it's really hard to tell to which audience this game is really meant.
- If you want to play the game for the difficulity and 'Metroidvania' level design, Then I find the game is on the easy side. Despite the insane difficulity ramp at the end. It does have the Metroidvania feelings though, but I find it done rather simple.
- If you want to play the game for the art design, go ahead. The animations, music, art and most character cast design were enjoyable for me. Just be aware that you'll get a really hard time finishing it.
That's it for Pirate's Curse, It didn't fit my style, but I don't hate it, hopefully 1/2 Genie Hero gives me a better experience what Shantae is about.

Putting it simply this is one of the greatest video games I have ever played. The gameplay blends a mix of third person adventure, first person shooter and even Tekken-style fighting sequences. For a game that's 15 years old, it still holds up. The story has a fairly silly premise, but is executed fairly well, and is fully voice-acted. David Bowie's cameos are fantastic, but the concerts will drag if you're not into his stuff. Even when he's not involved, the music is still fairly well composed. The controls haven't aged poorly, and the only complaint is that it's built for a gamepad, however, the controls are rebindable, so that's not a big deal. The shooting segments are somewhat awkward, but it may just be personal experience, since I haven't played the game for over 10 years. Puzzles are sometimes cryptic, but the solution generally presents itself in some format, as long as the player's been diligent about picking up EVERYTHING. The lip-sync gets pretty laughable, but it's impressive for a game this old, considering it animates the entire face.
The open world is interesting to explore, though it can get a bit tedious since there isn't much to do outside the main story. Variation between the multiple characters is great, and players can always find someone who is fully capable, or at the very least, looks like a badass.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who loves classic adventure games or David Bowie.

I have initially played this game on a Nintendo 3DS screen, so a lot of my experience will be based off that and not the PC Version. However, I would state that both versions play basically the same.
Story: Shantae has been stripped bare of her magic and Scuttle Town is now under the iron treads of Ammo Baron. On the other side of the sea, a terrible evil threatens to rise back up to send Sequin Land to a lifetime of darkness and death. Only through a team-up with Shantae's archnemesis Risky Boots can they both save Sequin Land from this evil. As a game plot, it's basic and slightly cliche'd, but it's still good enough to keep on playing. 8.5/10
Controls: Unlike most other games, where you use WASD to control your character, Shantae actually uses the arrow keys and ZXCASD, which could confuse users more used to WASD. Overall, it would be preferable to use a controller, though unlike its older brother, Super Meat Boy, it's playable with just the keyboard. 8/10
Graphics: As a whole, the pixel art style cannot get any more better than this in sheer quality. And while there are some peeople who may be bothered by how anime-like Shantae and her friends appear, it's still all good and gives people some eye candy. And don't worry, He-Man is there to balance out the waifu scale. 9.5/10
Sound: Both Music and general sound effects are here. Music-wise, Jake Kaufman does amazing job as the composer. (11/10) Sound-wise, we do get to hear how Shantae and Risky sound through their occasional spoken line, though most of the sound is through fighting. The sounds do lend themselves pretty well to their designated objects, though certain sounds don't satisfy the feeling we all have. (7.5/10) Overall: 9/10
Overall and other mentions: This game is THE definitive Metroidvania platformer, where you have to collect new power-ups to go into different areas where you couldn't go before, and go out of your way to get 100% or rush the game to complete it under a designated period of time to get a payday, if you will. This game gets a 9/10, since a lot of the less good elements do get drowned out by the best of quality entertainment. To end it, this game is most certainly NOT for kids, grandma and soccer mums everywhere. Or people who get offended real easily, to be fair.

Slowdown, bugs, and especially lack of ingame options to rebind your keys totally kill the experience. The game doesn't even show up on my steam profile. Never have I seen such a major glitch that the game is invisible to Steam itself meaning no achievements or trading cards.
As for the game itself. I recommend you get Magicka 1 instead. It's the better game even without DLC. Already played Magicka 1 to death, and just really desperate for more Magicka? Then you might want this. Just be aware it's a pain in the butt to play single player this time around since they have nerfed almost everything you have but kept enemies fast, numerous, and lethal.

It's the same ham-fisted approach to balancing that made Diablo 3 one of the shortest-lived online RPGs.
Games shouldn't be designed like this. It never works when the player is balanced; it's only fun when the game is balanced around an OP player.
They've removed steam and ice elements, which means that for each kind of projectile, there are only two-three combos to make. It's ridiculously watered-down. There's nothing to learn. You can hardly even kill yourself in this game.
Completely misses the mark; doesn't understand what made the original game so much fun.

After only playing a few hours, I can tell this game can never replace the first Magicka. It's a very different beast, and not in a good way. Pieces attempted to put together a more challenging experience, however, the result is ultimately a more tedious and less exciting one. This is compounded by the recycling of the design of spells, spell types, and spellcasting from Wizard Wars. During the conversion, much of the character that these things previously possessed was lost. There is enjoyment to be had in Magicka 2, but so far, it's hardly what I was looking forward to.
Looks like I won't be writing a "fairer" review. It's very clear to me that, since the game is in Paradox's hands, nothing that matters will be improved or revised. The elements will always be shallow. Simple spells will always be the best. Spell metrics will always be dull. Melee will always be clunky. Many spelltypes will always be half broken. Most importantly, wizards will always be a shadow of their former, Magicka 1 glory.

I've invested a good chunk of hours into the game, and I feel pretty confident in this review. Hover : Revolt of Gamers isn't Jet Set Radio Future. In some ways, it's actually better. It's a great game and something I'd consider a huge Kickstarter success.
There are a lot of comparisons to be made between Hover (and let's be serious, Hover : Revolt of Gamers is a terribly long title) and the cult classic Jet Set Radio, but I'll get to that in the second paragraph. If you're not familiar with Jet Set Radio, it was a game for the Sega Dreamcast that focused on cartoony graphics, groovy sounds, and spraying graffiti while skating around. Jet Set Radio Future was the sequel to that game with faster paced gameplay, simplified mechanics, and a generally better, bigger, and more featured world. Hover borrows heavily from Jet Set Radio Future and Mirror's Edge while mixing in its own flair, and the result is surprisingly polished from such a small developer.
If you've already played Jet Set Radio and Future, you would know how Future streamlined gameplay and made everything faster, sleeker, and simpler to do. Hover does that to Future. Hover is a really fast paced racing game with graffiti mechanics, a really whacky alien world, sand box gameplay, RPG-like leveling, and other things. It's also a game designed around internet multiplayer.
Hoever uses a lobby-MMO setup, think Vindictus, to drop a few players into the same area and have them do stuff, such as participate in the same races or help each other find secrets (and by the way, there are a lot of tasks and collectibles). Unliked Vindictus, Hover does not instance tasks, so you can watch other players doing their thing or join them instead. The story isn't terribly informative as quests go back and forth, but it comes together later on as a rag-tag group of unlikely heroes overthrow a dictator. The world isn't really at stake here though, and your primary function is to have fun.
Fun is where Hover really excels. The soundtrack beating down your eardrums with groovy tunes, the colorful trails that are left by every player in the game, the non-euclidean geometry of the futuristic landscape, those things really pull you in. Once you start leveling a little bit and improving your character, you'll be vaulting over huge distances, running like a gazelle, and hovering with the best of them in no time. What really sets Hover apart is the rewind button though. At any point you can rewind your character back a few seconds to change positioning or recover from a colossal mistake. It's a simple feature, with one or two limitations, but it's an amazingly welcome one. There is zero frustration for small mistakes while exploring, and I never felt like the game was punishing me unreasonably because I could just rewind a couple of seconds if I needed to.
Back to fun. Leveling is easy if you just do random things as the sandbox gameplay gives the player a lot of opportunity to do just that, and there are a variety of tasks (quests) to undertake. A lot of them center on racing or going from place to place, but there is also gameball, which is like futuristic rugby, bouncing, infiltration, and so forth. Not everything is available at once, mind, but you can always re-do already completed tasks. You can even make your own races! The environments in the game are also pretty spacious, like the main city hub, and I personally spent hours getting familiar with them just by exploring. Hover comes together in a tidy package with a really visible FUN postage stamp, and that's all that really needs to be said.
If you do end up picking up this game, I would suggest you do not rush through the available missions. I think Hover is best played with the spirit of discovery close to your chest; the tutorial leaves a few things out that you have to find out on your own, or ask other players, and as I've mentioned before, there are a lot of collectibles that really push you to look around and explore as much as possible. Hell, you can even skip the tutorial all together if you know how to. As a basic tip, you can "super bounce" if you jump from a really high place, then press jump as you're hitting the ground. And don't worry. Your first character will suck at everything at the beginning, but you can change that within a few hours and then stockpile upgrades for any future characters.
Since I've mentioned the good, I'll briefly mention the bad, because honestly, there's very little wrong with Hover. So first, bugs. There are still a few of them left. Tasks have a tendency to cancel out for no reason while you're about to score a medal, the game can crash, and some graffiti tags throw ERROR instead of showing their contents. But that's kind of minor stuff that doesn't really take away from the overall enjoyment of the game, and I'm confident just about all of it will be patched out or improved sooner rather than later.
I was never really a fan of the character artwork, even during the Kickstarter campaign. Good news for me though, the characters look and animate absolutely gorgeous in the game itself. The CGI models feel plastic in a way, but it's actually a good way. I still don't really like some of the art for the characters, but it's not terribly distracting, and the models completely make up for it. Some things are still missing or need rebalancing in the game itself, as some tasks are far easier than others, with little reason for it being that way, and some characters talked about during the Kickstarter are not available. This is minor stuff though.
To finish off, I'm personally interested in the following:
Being able to friend people in the game! This one is huge. It's hard to tell who is who, since character names are used instead of account names. I think the devs are already going to do something like this, so I'll just wait and see.
Character dancing, like emotes or idle animations. Emotes are already being worked on, but characters in Jet Set Radio had unique dances that really added flavor to the game, and I would love to see this in Hover.
More music or ability to play your own music. I love the soundtrack, I really do. I'm even going to buy it after I wright this review. But having more music, especially from the man himself, Hideki Naganuma, would be amazing. Having the same race music play all the time can get pretty repetitive.
Character customization. This was a stretchgoal during the Kickstarter, one that wasn't reached, and I'm hoping that if the game does well we'll see this in some capacity as DLC. The game does feel like a lobby-MMO, so I would really like to see greater customization aside height and colors. Bonus points if there's some way to designate which tricks you can do.
If you've read my review this far, do yourself a favor and play Hover. I don't think you'll regret it.

I've read other reviews saying that this game is like a mix of Rainbow Six and Halo. I think that's an accurate description.
Star Wars Republic Commando puts players in command of Delta Squad, a 4-man elite commando unit comprised of clones, specially engineered for combat. It's true they have the same DNA but their personalities are very different, which can be seen when the squad members banter.
Each squad member has specialized roles; sniper, slicer (computer hacker), and demolitions expert. They perform about the same as each other in combat and the AI does a pretty good job at this.
The player and the squad members all carry the same weapons, however as squad leader the player can pick up other weapons as well. From the start of the game, you will have a blaster sidearm with unlimited ammo and a full auto blaster rifle (functionally it's like the assault rifle from Halo). This rifle can also use special attachments that allows it to be used as a sniper rifle and grenade launcher. Different types of hand grenades called detonators can be picked up as well, which includes thermal, flashbangs, EMP, and sticky grenades
One of the things I like about this game is the ability to make tactical decisions. As squad leader, you can order the squad to lead the way, form up behind you, defend an area, stack up on doors for a breach or stealth entry, and give commands to each squad member such as placing demolition charges and hacking consoles. You can also order each squad member to take up strategic positions as you advance through enemy territory. Ordering the squad to these positions can be vital as there will be some tough enemies that will take a lot of firepower to take down.
Another thing I like about this game is that if you get incapacitated the mission doesn't end like in Rainbow Six. You can order your squad members to revive you. Squad members will automatically revive each other as well once the area is cleared of hostiles but you can order them to revive their squadmates while you provide covering fire.
The game is action-packed and has humorous moments as well. Squad members will sometimes comment on the hostiles they just killed and even kick or shoot a couple more slugs into a dead hostile. (This reminds me a lot of Halo.)
The only things lacking about the game is the somewhat open-ended ending and the lack of a multiplayer co-op mode, which is strange considering how squad-based tactics are used a lot in this game. I heard about a mod that allows parts of the single player campaign to be played with other players but I have yet to try it out and see if it works.
I got this game for $10 so it's a pretty good deal. Overall, it's very fun to play.

Of the many Star Wars games that I've played, Republic Commando stands out. Even though the campaign is strictly solo, the depth at which the AI responds to the environment makes you feel as though you're playing with people that you trust to have your back whenever the battles get intense. Being able to command each individual squad member and assign tasks is one of the most enjoyable aspects of the game. Your on-the-fly decisions as squad leader affect the outcome of the battles, and in sticky situations, your decisions can lead to resounding defeat or decisive victory. The gameplay focuses heavily on your dependence on each member of your squad and how they depend on you, which gives the game its immersive feel; and adds a very welcome element of strategy. An element that you might not expect from a first person shooter but one that I personally believe is lacking from many modern day shooters that seem to be getting more generic. Generic is certainly not what Republic Commando is all about. The unique gameplay, team interaction, and squad based strategy all set during the pivotal Clone Wars era of the Star Wars universe makes for a game that leaves you coming back for more.

After 46 hours played I can honestly say I've been enjoying the game quite a bit. The leveling curve starts off extremely quickly, and then slows down as you approach your 30's. Not too slow, and there is never a grind. It mixes the elements of a traditional ARPG and classic MMO together well. The only gripe is that it's supposed to be a Hybrid ARPG, but there isn't enough random loot. It's the typical asian mmo in that every piece of gear is tiered by "levels" and they all have the exact same name. Instead of wasting time looking at all the gear, I wish they had an "of the xxxx" to know what kind of stat allocation was on the piece of gear. I really love that each class has 3 tree's to go in and every single one of them have their uses. Being able to respec for free at anytime is amazing, even while out in the field.
So far I haven't found the need to spend any money at all. The negative reviews I read about this game kind of was putting me off, but I don't see anything at all in regards to what people's complaints are. Of course theirs going to be a grind at 52 to get the best gear, kind of part of ANY MMO and ARPG alike. Ever played Diablo and done 500+ gear runs to finally get 1 piece of useful upgrade. It's what draws us players to these types of games. Dungeons are very quick and rewarding, and earning tokens in previous area's don't go to waste if you have extras as you can spend 3 tokens to get 2 for the next area allowing you to progress gear wise while leveling very easily. The bosses in the dungeons while not "hard" have fun mechanics and makes everything seem like a controlled chaos. The animations, and the combat are what make this game flat out amazing. I'm playing with my 8 year old and he loves the game, and my wife who typically stays away from mmo's wants to play. The game draws you in quickly, I just got into the game for the first time a few days ago and already have 46 hours invested.
If you're looking for a great ARPG style game that's also an MMO, this is the game to check out. It seriously reminds me of Diablo 2, but a constant player base running around, rather than having to be on
and find rooms. My only complaint is the chat system, but it's typical for all asian mmo's. The need for microphones to talk in open channels is really bleh. I get why they do it, but I'd rather deal with bot spammers than be hindered when I may have questions. My recommendations for keyboard settings is set to classic mmo using wasd, and remove the ability to click to move and set your combo building to mouse 1. If you don't you end up spamming 1 18 million times an hour and gets very tiring. It's almost impossible with click to move to click on targets and attack on mouse click. The only way I found a way around it was to set shift+click to allow using mouse click without moving, but it's more of a chore than using wasd and removing click to move.

Many of Magicka 2's design decisions seem to have been extremely poor.
In Magicka 1, the characters you played felt dangerous. In Magicka 2, they feel like bumbling idiots. Magicka 1 may have had overpowered spells, but it felt like they gave you as many tools as you wanted and said "here's a versatile spell system, go nuts" and balanced the game via the environment and the enemies. Magicka 2 looks like the developers thought "we made a clunky spell system, if we make it 100% clunkier, it'll sell 100% more".
The game plays like a bad console port. The controls are clunky and incomplete on the PC version - with a controller, you use the control stick to move. On PC, you click on a point and you walk towards it until you've arrived but there's no way to cancel your movement short of diverting your current action and clicking on yourself.
Continuing on the previous point, it's like the spell system was watered down to make the game more console friendly. Everything feels more sluggish than in Magicka 1 - a game where you couldn't move and cast spells at the same time, and feels like it has more pointless combinations than Magicka 1 by virtue of how they altered the spell system to handle repetitions of elements.
Pursuant to the previous point, Magicka 1 didn't strictly encourage a wide vocabulary of spells, but it was fun to see what you could get away with. Magicka 2 just feels frustrating to 'play to win' and to 'play for fun' because the best spells for a situation are often from a tiny, counter-intuitive vocabulary and just spammed really fast.
Overall I think that whoever developed this game has no idea of what they're doing and looks like they blew most of their budget on graphics that look outdated and didn't spend enough money actually making a game.
I don't like change in general, but virtually none of the changes for Magicka 2 feels like it's trying to say "change for the better", and they all feel like they're saying "change for the sake of change".

First Impressions (will update as I keep playing)
IF YOU'RE GOING TO MAKE A GAME THAT PLAYS LIKE DIABLO, AT LEAST MAKE SURE THE GAMEPLAY IS AS TIGHT AND FLUID AS DIABLO!
This is a huge reason why a lot of these "Diablo clones" eventually die. The game that has come the closest to matching the fluidity and responsiveness of Diablo is Torchlight, and that game actually did pretty well. I know this is an MMO and Diablo is not, but that's definitely no excuse for a lack of attention to detail in gameplay.
Let me elaborate:
OVERALL:
Pros:
- Game looks beautiful
- The world is quite large
- There's some customization when creating your character
- It's an MMO with Diablo-like mechanics/camera
- You can "hand in" most quests by just clicking the complete in the quest log, rather than having to run back to the quest-giver, which is great for an MMO and allows you to just keep on moving forward, and so far there doesn't seem to be much backtracking to the main towns.
- Chat isn't filled with spammers... rather, I haven't seen a single spammer so far, probably due to how they've organized chat, and that you get a limited amount of "megaphones" which allow you to do a server-wide announcement, and cost in-game credits (but you get 3 to start off with).
- You can actually get in-game credits without paying real money by trading regular currency to players who bought Devilian Exchanges, which you then use to get credits (though I wager they're quite expensive).
- This is just speculation, but a lot of the trading/auction functionality requires you to make a 5$ purchase, which in my opinion is great practice because it lowers the chance of spammers and farmers since they'd actually have to spend money on each account that will inevitably get banned. Also, you won't be doing much trading/auctioneering at the beginning anyway, and once you've committed enough hours into the game, I'm sure you won't have a hard time giving the devs a tiny bit of cash to be able to do those things, which are always optional anyway.
Cons:
- Can't choose character gender
- While the game looks nice, it suffers from the unneccessarily over-sexualized characters that just takes me away from the story, lore, and the world itself. Outside of a few cutscenes it's not such a big deal since the camera is zoomed out so much. There're games that do this tastefully and with reason, like Bayonetta, but this isn't one of those games.
- While you don't get a lot of XP from just killing enemies, you still have a lot of people in the starting zones AFKing and just spamming spells in one spot, killing enemies non-stop as they respawn. The reason why this is annoying for you is because they tend to do this in spots where quest bosses spawn, though if you hit the boss, you still get credit (that's if the now-overleveled AFKer didn't one-shot it before you can even tag it)
MOVEMENT:
Pros:
- You can move fast, dodging/sprinting feels nice and is satisfying in combat.
- Natural-feeling "click to move" mechanics.
- Since it is an MMO, the Auto-Run feature is really nice and allows you to do other things while your character runs to their objective, like manage inventory, actually read a quest objective (unheard of!!), or talk to people.
Cons:
- You stop moving when you hit the edge of a map and need to almost perpendicular to the edge to move away (not as big of a deal as it sounds but can be annoying).
- Your character stops a few feet before the edge of a map appears to end, which can be a bit annoying.
- Your cursor pings the ground (displays the circle on the ground where you clicked) constantly even while you hold down left-click. Aesthetically annoying, nothing more.
COMBAT:
Pros:
- Combat is quick, Diablo-like
- Satisfying to kill tons of enemies at a time
Cons:
- Holding [Shift] should make you stop moving, not switch what left and right click do!!!!! This is a huge annoyance in combat so far. I hold [Shift] so that I can "spray" my spells without having to target something (and targetting has its own problems), so left and right click spells should NOT move my character, but instead, right-click is now movement.... so I have to let go of [Shift] in order to not move when I right click. This does not feel natural at all. One thing you can do to mitigate this is to not have spells in your click slots but rather on your number bar, but this is going around the problem and not fixing it.
- You can, and will, very easily and frequently click on an enemy, but not actually target it. What I mean by this is that every enemy's target area is much smaller than the actual enemy model. So you can click on an enemy's head/feet/arms/wings, and not actually click on it, so you'll end up moving instead of attacking. Again, very very annoying, and breaks the fluidity of combat.

I played a 100 hours on the android version before I bought this virtually identical Windows game.  This is a super-awesome game.  Since you're playing a disease intent on wiping out the human race, you might think the game lacks social conscience maybe the people who wrote it were anarchists or Ayn Rand fans.  But this isn't the case at all.
I think it's a teaching tool about public health.  Modern people see so little virulent disease that they don't think it's a big deal, but it is.  The Black Plague killed more people in the 20th century than it did in the 14th.  Smallpox, Polio, Spanish Flu.  Just one of these things will ruin your whole day.  And the game designers who seem to know something about epidemiology believe that a new disease could evolve at any time and wipe out the entire human race in less than a year.
Even if we didn't need a strong elected government to safeguard human rights, even if government intervention in markets was inherently bad, public health would be reason enough on its own to have a strong, centralized government.  People can not be free to keep vaccines from their kids anymore than they can free to drive their cars drunk; they're endangering other people's lives.  We need a government to make rules like mandatory vaccinations and enforce them.

Where to begin with this game. I think I’ll start with the story and work forward from there. You play as a parkour rebel working to save your city from the grip of an evil polluting businessman dictator who has outlawed any form of fun. Luckily, there is an underground rebellion of hardcore gamers who also, improbably, are gifted with the most amazing free running skills ever seen. You were created as a clone to have fun and join the rebellion. The tutorial is you escaping from the abandoned cloning factory while learning the basics of amazing athleticism. The controls are simple, although could use some better explanation for controllers. The mechanics boil down to jumping and grinding. Grinding rails helps you build up energy which allows you to run faster and jump farther. One interesting feature is the rewind function, which rewinds your character back along their neon light trail. Very helpful when you miss a jump or fall of a building, which happens pretty often because the controls, at least as far as the controller goes, can be a bit sensitive.
Speaking of the city itself, lets talk a bit about aesthetic and design. Honestly, the city hurts my eyes if I look at it too long. It’s like Sunset Overdrive got together with Wizard101 to create the design of this game. That being said, I like the overall look of the game, I think it just takes some adjustment to look at the ridiculously bright colors. The other thing about the design is that the city is mostly vertical, which makes sense in a parkour game, but provides no conventional means of getting from one place to another. If you want to get up a level, enjoy grinding, wall hopping, and climbing your way because even though citizens walk everywhere around the city, there are clear ramps to take you up. This only really gets to be an issue for me in the missions, most of which involve a time element. You know where you start and you know where you’re going, but it’s up to you to parkour your way there. That’s fine except because of the open nature of the game, and the trouble of gauging what level of the city your goals are on, you fall a lot, and then the mission is essentially ruined. Also, because of the dense nature of everything happening in the city, as well as the fact that the game is online multiplayer, there can be occasional issues with stuttering and frame rates, which is not something you want to see in a time sensitive parkour game.
Speaking of the missions, let’s talk about those. As I just mentioned, some missions involve retrieving objects and bringing them back or running deliveries for citizens and the resistance. Other missions may include multiplayer sports like Gamerball or races. Races were my favorite type of mission and make up a lot of my footage of the game. The reason I like the races so much was that you could follow clearly marked paths through the city, often while dodging the city’s security and patrol systems. And while there are certain sections of the race where you have to do so creative free running to find the best and fastest path, they feel more organized and cohesive than the “just get there and get back” delivery missions. Another type of mission I came across was collection, which were usually missions associated with the rebellion. These included incapacitating and collecting spy drones, graffitiing over anti-leisure posters, and destroying anti-leisure holographic propaganda. Also, you can find “game girls” and chests hidden around the city, which you can collect for experience points and upgrades to your character.
Speaking briefly of the danger factor in the game, there is none. The security bots just momentarily stun you and scold you if you get caught, and they’re pretty easy to avoid, and you can fall from the highest building to street level without sustaining any fall damage. I think that speaks more to the age group this game is targeting, which I assume is preteens through late teens, which may not be looking for a game where they can have all the fun of parkour without worrying about one slip-up or failed wall run spelling death for their character. The upgrade system is cool, although I’m a little unclear on the effects. Most upgrades, which you gain from chests and completing missions, boost different skills like scanning (which is basically how you interact with the world), hacking, jumping, acceleration, grinding, etc. by such and such a percentage point. It’s noticeable in races, but to be honest, the character already feels pretty strong with their base abilities, so I don’t know how necessary the upgrades are unless they come into play later in the game. One cool thing I found however is that there are certain upgrades that give you major skill increases, while also giving you an adorable pet! I don’t think I got any of that footage, but trust me, there is an adorable flying bunny that gives you redonkculous speed and acceleration. As far as quest tracking goes, it seems to boil down one of two ways, either the game will target you to the nearest quest, or, if you’ve just completed a race, it will tell you where to go for the next big race. The quest scanning also points out posters to vandalize, spy drones to take out, and propaganda to destroy when you get close to those items.
Getting around to my final thoughts, I think this game creates a fun light-hearted experience that’s a fun way to spend an hour or two. It doesn’t draw me in and hold me, except for the racing which is pretty spectacular, but any time a game has a parkour mechanic, it’s a great way to feel like a super hero. The colorful cartoonish aesthetic is charming, if a bit much to look at and the story has that vague green fun-loving rebels vs. evil cold corporations that is reminiscent of ToonTown Online. On the whole, I like this game, I just think it could do with some post launch tweaking.

Disclaimer: I kickstarted this game.
So if you enjoyed JSRF or Mirror's Edge, you'll probably enjoy this - it's a game about face paced movement, tight controls, going fast and jumping high. It certainly scratches that parkour itch that those games did.
PROS:
+ Tight controls (once you set them up right)
+ Cool art style, in the vein of JSRF.
+ Amazing soundtrack, almost worth buying the game for that alone.
CONS:
- Not much content - two or three "main areas", and another three to five limited mission areas. Could be completed in a solid day or two of playing. A rather small handful of character choices, and an upgrade system that you can max out within a few hours.
- AI can be stupid at times - certain game modes will have them flailing about with buggy pathfinding, and there are a lot of ways to trick them and exploit your way to success.
-- Level design is really hit and miss: often it can be downright frustrating to get around the main mission areas, as options for traversing heights or long distances are extremely obfuscated. It took me about half an hour to get inside a stadium at the top of a building to do a sidequest, for example. They definitely need to provide some more obvious ways to get around without requiring you to scrabble too hard.
-- Graphics are really lacklustre. I know that it's a cel-shaded style game, but that's not an excuse for poorly made and inconsistent textures, and low polycounts. The particle effects also leave a lot to be desired.
-- Bugs. There are some showstopping bugs left in the game at the time of writing, which I hope the devs get around to fixing. The low level of polish in the game highly indicate that it was released too early.
Despite all my condemnations I still recommend the game, at $15 it's definitely worth.

great art, writing, sprites, and music, so right on the surface this game looks and sounds great. the "dungeons" and their bosses are really well made and the island-based map system solves the previous game's (risky's revenge) issues of the confusing/hard to navigate map.
in terms of controls and fluidity of play, the pirate gear abilities mesh really well with the levels, and it keeps the simple damage/attack speed upgrades that risky's revenge had minus the weird requriement of magic jelly. though this game also draws from metroid's habit of ability-locked secrets that require backtracking (whether that's good or bad is up to you).
lastly, if you feel an indescribable need to unlock all achievements in games you buy, then be ready. amongst the hardest are doing bosses without taking damage, speedrunning, finishing a notably difficult platforming and enemy avoiding sequence without dying, and completing the game without any health upgrades (that means with *two* health!) of course, achievements are exactly that, and it's not like you're being forced to do these asininely hard tasks.

What do you look for in a video game? A rough challenge? A great cast and story? Enjoyable gameplay with solid controls? Well with Shantae and the Pirate's Curse you'll get at least 2 out of three.
The greatest asset this game has it's it's cast and story, even if this is your first Shantae game (it was for me). The only 2 characters that were glossed over durin the game are actually new to this title: the blond-haired duo of Twitch and Vinegar (you never even get their names). The rest of the cast, from enemies to allies, all have their own quirks, personalities, and even worries, ranging from finding a husband, turning orphanages into cannons, and dealing with post-boss syndrome. You know, normal video game problems. The story follows our title character joining forces with the previous titles' main baddie, the pirate Risky Boots, to stop the return of her old master from the grave. As with any good rivalry, plenty of bickering and comraderie awaits.
Gameplay is as resposive as you'd want out of an action-platformer. Shantae can use her hair and a variety of sub-weapons to deal with foes. As she clears the game's dungeons (called Dens of Evil) she'll find Risky's missing equipment, each helping her either fight enemies or explore more areas (often both). The game really opens up once you collect all five, as 3 of them (Hat, Boots, and Cannon) can be used in conjuction to speed through areas and past enemies, and it's at this point that the level design really begins to shine as WayForward obviously designed with this in mind. In fact, the game plays equally well, albeit sufficiently different, between Normal and Pirate Modes (NG and NG+ respectfully).
The one area the game will lack during an normal playthrough is challange, as collecting all the power-ups, Heart Squids (for extra health), and healing items mean that you're never at any real risk of dying outside of a couple boss fights. You could easily by circumvent this by skipping all these things, but it'd been nice for there to simply be a mode where the difficulty is set by the game and not the player.
Overall this is easily one of the most replayable games I've played in years. Pirate Mode is such a pleasant way to play after a Normal game, and the cast and music will always bring a smile to my heart. There's a reason it's a fan-favorite in the series.
PS: If you're interested in getting into speedrunning, then this game also makes a great introductory game if you're new and has a nice Discord community as well.
Score: 9.5/10

Wow. This game shocked me with how good it was.
I DEFINATLY reccommend you play it!
BUT!
This is not a game to start Shantae with! The mechanics are different and it's not a good idea of what the series is.
Beyond that, Shantae and the Pirate's Curse takes place directly after the events of Shantae: Risky's Revenge. If you haven't played Risky's Revenge first, then you should because it will cause some confusting moments in Pirate Curse.
Pros:
- Amazing Graphics
- You constantly feel interested in the game. There's never a moment where you feel bored or want to take a break.
- Just like all Shantae games, there is backtracking, but the other thing about Shantae games (excluding Half-Genie Hero)
is that the backtracking never makes you feel sick of the areas. With the new pirate gear you obtain during your time in
the game, after virtually every world there is things to do in all the previous ones.
- There are a ton of collectables
- The game is NOT linear. This game encourages exploration and has the best use of collectable hunting I've seen in my
years of gaming. You have to go off your path and utillize your arsinal in creative ways to find hidden passages in walls
or hidden rooms to find them. You don't even have to find said collectables and that really helps them feel like goodies
rather than chores like many recent games do.
-  This game gives you NOTHING on a sliver platter. Sometimes I feel I'll be hunting for a secret or a collectable just to find
a key in the chest I found. The puzzles aren't simply laid out in front of you, they require dedication and smarts. This
really protects the game from being too easy and definatly ups the enjoyment levels.
-  Amazing character development. The story is great, all the characters have lovable personalities, you just remember
them all and very few are just one-offs.
-  The game also brings some of the trademark Shantae humor to the table which is always greeted with a warm
welcome.
-  Fantastic soundtrack!
-  Just straight fun platforming
-  You actually use your items to fight bosses. You don't know how many games render items useless by not doing this!
-  Gems weren't jsut coming at you in heaps.
-  Platforming wasn't too easy.
-  REALLY good final boss fight!
Cons:
- Items that you had to purchase and upgrade in RR amd HGH were turned into one-time use items.
- Some items like the Monster Milks and the Bubble Shield I felt were useless.
Just buy this game and Risky's Revenge at the same time and you'll have a good few weeks.

Okay first off, it looks like I spent 6 minutes on it. Kinda. I just wanted to get the achievement. BUT, I did read the whole thing on mobile, which is great, because the mobile version is a lot more convenient and is very user friendly. Not to say the Steam version isn't, I just dont wanna lug my laptop around just to read VNs. Okay, I would, but that's not the point. It's easier with the phone.
On to the actual review, I absolutely loved it. I think this visual novel is great. In my opinion, the dialogue in the game is carried out with brilliant (dark... but praiseworthy... you get the point) humour, the story is built upon fantastic character development and accompanied by an excellent soundtrack. One thing to note though, I'd finished 'One Thousand Lies' feeling absolutely disoriented and I shot to the online forums to seek answers. Don't be a dummy like me. Find the true ending (and make sure you get the achievement) before you spoil it for yourself. I kinda blew my mind on the way. It's free, it's on mobile and if you're interested in visual novels I'd definitely recommend it. It can't hurt showing the dev some love; they're really engaged with the reader-base.

I played this on Android, I think it was around 10 hours. I was about to stop reading this VN at the very initial chapters cause the school-pranks-stories are not my cup of tea, but I always complete a VN before judging/commenting it. So, at the end, I think my vote is something around 7-8 out of 10, that is good.
My pros and cons:
+It's a spanish VN (I like to read VNs from different countries, as each of them has its own style)
+Writing: the english version which I played is written very well
+Music: the music is nice, it has its own style. The theme I liked the most is the wolf's tale theme (Vagabond), it fits very well to the story-in-the-story.
+Duration: not too short, not too long, I think it's balanced
+BG Images: I really liked the drawing style effect of the backgrounds, even though they're not very detailed they gave me the feeling I was watching photos
+Sprites: I liked the characters' sprites, all the characters are well-drawn, even though some facial expressions are a bit too similar.
+Characters: they're ok for me, pretty different from each other, can't choose a favourite one as they all contribute to the story
+Plot: You have to go through thefull story (One Hidden Truth included) to get a whole picture about it, and I think it's nice. I liked the references and connections between truths/lies. As the title says, it's about it.
+I appreciate the fact that you've put notes and explanations near some of the rpy sentences, it's really helpful for translators
-Interaction: it's just a story to read with no choices, alternative endings nor minigames
-CG images: they're ok, but there are only a few of them, I would've liked to see more pics about the protagonists

Supreme League of Patriots is a point and click game wiwth a dash of humor and comedy. The game let's you take the role of both Kyle and Mel as they venture through the world of superheroes and supervillains. The story is a bit slow on the build up but the actual plot is very unique and original. Each issue comprises about 3-4 hours of gameplay depending on how you solve the puzzles in the game. The puzzles are easy and you won't get off track much since Melvin is there to guide you when you don't know/forgot what you should be doing. The dialgoues and voices are great especially Melvin's british accent.
Pros:
+ A great funny story plot
+ Great voice acting
+ Great Music (especially each character's BGM)
+ Good Graphics
+ Narrative guide (Mel gives you a hint when you get lost)
Cons:
+ There's a bit of bugs whenever you make Kyle go to an obtacle-full area
+ There are times that the voices become out of sync with the balloons/text that appear
If you're looking for a point and click adventure game full of humor, comedy, patriotism, superheroes and supervillains, then Supreme League of Patriots is a must try for you.

I finished yesterday the adventure on banana difficulty, here are a few observation :
1- With the right staff, the game is a breeze (except for the constant one shot kill)
2- Robes' effects are negligible, too many things murders you instantly (goblin bombers, trolls)
3- Armors are even more important, a good armor in the right situation can save you lots of problems.
4- I haven't found any way to stop the green type of damage (even life absorb did nothing)
Also, if you can't finish the game on solo in hard difficulty or even normal and complain that it is too hard, then I am sorry to tell you, but LEARN TO SPELL...
As far as solo goes, you can swap robe quickly at each checkpoints (simply reach a checkpoint, quit, change your equips, then go back to adventure).
If you are in a group, you only need one strong arcane user and one strong ice user to wreck the content. Arcane is strong against any living creature, so far, there is no real use of undead creatures, so arcane is strong against anyone except for fire mobs (somehow resists arcane ?). Since fire mobs are weak to ice, then just have a strong ice user. A healer might be a good idea, since many staves reduce life magic. Life + Arcane cross beam is useful too.
All in all, the game is not difficult if you know how it works, you MUST move while casting. The keybinding just came up, a bit rudimentary, but I can live with it for now.
Lastly, I found a single irritating bug, which is a problem with the Y axis (a beam going through an enemy because some derping on the Y axis), but if you using an AoE instead of a beam or a projectile, you'll be fine.

This game as a port is difficult to put it as either "recommended" or "not recommended". On the one hand, the gameplay is just as good as it always has been, because it's literally the same game. On the other hand, it's one of the laziest ports I've seen but ultimately it's still functional.
95% of controllers don't work as intended and aren't remappable, and while the keyboard controls are remappable, when you remap them, everytime you boot up the game afterwards the button prompts that come up on the screen will reset, but your controls will be what you set them to (it will always tell you that 1 is light attack and 2 is heavy attack regardless of what they actually are). The only point in which the game will use the default controls no matter what is the very first screen that says "press 2 to start", but then it'll load up your control profile.
These are massive problems, there's no way you can say otherwise. Also needing to remap the use powers button to be able to assign different powers than the set ones is pretty stupid. But there's no denying that once you've gone and done that and put up with the stupid button prompts, the game is still fun. They haven't changed anything about the gameplay except all the DLC characters are in it from the start - which is a good change.
While I'm recommending it because the game is still just as fun as it always has been, if you are someone who will play on keyboard who won't be able to deal with the control prompts being wrong/won't want to set your controls each time you boot up, then obviously don't get the game. If this game is not on sale, then definitely do not get the game because it's stupidly overpriced. If the game is on sale, or if you're thinking of getting it for someone as a gift, then I would definitely go for it unless the person doesn't own a supported controller (very few of which are), and won't want to put up with the keyboard mapping/prompt shenanigans.
Despite all the negative reviews, there is definitely no problems for me with this game. Really nostalgic and fun

I'm playing both MUA and MUA2 using my xbox one wireless controller (with wireless adapter on Windows 10, Creators Update which is what I'm currently using). If you liked this game on the console, I highly recommend these. I've seen a lot of posts regarding the xbox controllers not working. It didn't work right for me either (A button was actually X button, others not mapped right) until I updated my xbox one controller firmware using the Xbox Accessories app on Windows 10 (download it from the store). After that, both games work perfectly. I love these games, and recommend it if you have the controller, not so much the mouse and keyboard.

MUA1 had too many serious issues at launch, but in its current state, the game seems to work fine now (at least on my PC).
My PC: i7-6700, GTX1060 (6GB), 32GB RAM, Windows 10 64bit
(I read that updating patches for Windows 10 could mess up your controller on some games, so I didn't do it.)
Things that work now:
- Using a wired 360 controller, moving, attacking and using powers work fine.
- Menu and button prompts.
- Saving and loading.
- No crash. There are weird bugs and glitches here and there, but nothing game-breaking.
- Screen resolution. The game correctly detects my monitor resolution (16:10) right away.
- Dual monitors. Playing it on one monitor and watching movies on the other works fine, and I can Alt-Tab without any problem.
- Frame rate dropped a little when loading new area and when there were a lot of effects on-screen, but nothing too serious.
I've only tested the Single Player mode.
I've heard that Online Multiplayer doesn't work, but I haven't tried that and I don't care much about multiplayer anyway.
*** UPDATE ****************************************************************************************
I've finished the first playthrough with most of the side quests completed and started a New Game+ without any issue.
Some reviewers said that the Simulation missions were broken. I haven't tried those missions since I also don't care much about them.
*******************************************************************************************************
Conclusion:
For MUA1 and 2 fans who are still on the fence because of the technical issues, things are looking good now.
(Had it not been for all the issues, I would've paid full price on the release date for both MUAs. They're two of my favorite games of all time.)
P.S.
I'm still not giving any credit to Zoe Mode for cleaning up their own mess, since these functions should have been working from day 1. Even one-man indie devs could do better.

A love letter to 16- and 32-bit platformers.  I knew of these games in their various GameBoy iterations, thought they were for kids then realized through word of mouth they were actually very good.  That's definitely the case here.  The levels are well done, the gameplay and options at your disposal are easy to understand but well-defined, and the animation in this game is fantastic.  The artwork and dialgoue are a little pervy at times, but other than that if you yearn for more platformers in this age of endless open world and FPS titles, the Shantae series will scratch the itch.

great platformer with good characters, designs and styles.

If your monitor is 144hz, this game can't be played because the physics are based on the frame-rate and the frame-rate is based on your monitor refresh-rate (with no way to change that in-game).  You literally need fps-limiting software to make the game playable.
It's been a known issue for years, and the developer has shown no indication that they intend on fixing it.

The more that i play this game and really think about it, this (for a multiplayer game) is going to be as close as you could possibly get to being a perfect game and i've never really said that about a game before.
when you first jump into a game you're greeted with a tutorial and plopped in game where you can instantly run around, jump, grind, wallride, and slide around and get a hang of the parkour system (you're able to play in third and first person which both feel very intuitive and both work very well, which not many games that have both a first and third person can really pull off this level of quality from both so i was quite surprised, first person feeling like mirrors edge, and third feeling like jet set radio so it's just up to personal preference). You then notice their are various missions that you can do around the map that will take the form of race's, deliveries, "gameball" (which is like basketball in a way), etc. and various hybrids of the bunch (for example there's a mission where you vs. some bot's run through checkpoints which count as a point as long as your holding the ball and you can punch and take the ball from each other) and these missions can be played solo, or if you're playing the same mission with friends they can either be played competitively or cooperatively depending on the type of mission, the races feel so much fun to run through (slightly reminisent of sonic generations) and gameball can be extremely intense and fun with some friends (also slightly reminisent of rocket league). not only that but you can make your own missions as well and have your friends participate in them. After completing the main missions you move on to various maps. The starting area being "haven district" moving on to "the sewers" (which is like the hide out for all the rebels), "e-cop prision", the "administrative district", and "e-cop tower", but there might be more i don't know of yet, appearantly you have to get a certain amount of experience (your team rank) in order to move onto these levels, i personally had too much fun messing around to notice this right off the bat so i just walked on in later on when i felt like it, which i saw some people complaining about this but you rank up SO fast and have fun while doing it so i didn't really care too much.
enouph♥♥♥♥♥kissing, onto some cons: the map will glitch on a few occasions falling through the map, flying through it when going way too fast ect. | the tutorial kinda messed with me a bit and made me initially think the game was going to be way more complicated than it actually is, it almost scared me a bit and DID make one of my friends shy away from the game entirely which bummed me out a little so i would really encourage a revision on the tutorial situation. | And finnally the "stealth" this was probably one of both me and my friends' biggest pet peaves, you have certain areas that are pressure sensitive meaning you can't walk on them normally and you can't jump nor land on these platform's meaning you have to hold shift (or i guess whatever you may bind this to) which technically acts as your crouch walking button but this is also the button you use for almost all parkour in the game ie. wallriding, grinding and most importantly sliding which in a game that revolves around parkour to have you suddenly navigate through a maze trying to find your objective slowly and safely is really disorienting so i don't really know what could have been done to make this work but it is what it is.
This game has a whole parkour system and just came out so there are a couple of minor bugs with the whole map glitch thing (which is fairly rare) here and there but they do have an option to report these bugs so they'll likely be ironed out in the future but that is really all i have to say on that front.
That's pretty much all i can cover in words, there is just something about this game that really feels purely fun and is just a blast to play, playing 48 hours in the past 5 days i think is proof enough xD. I hope and pray that more content will come in the future ie. more characters, more maps, etc. which from what i've been able to gather that's probably going to be the case, but don't rush it! There is loads of content and replayability to be had as is, so there is no need to rush or anything like that but i look forward to what the future holds for this game ;)
TL;DR: Buy this game! Hover : Revolt Of Gamers has got something for everyone and pulls almost all of it off tremendously! To put it simply it's fun and will keep you busy for hours! :D

The online components are rough, and I've turned them off for the most part, opting to play solo.
The game seems to have video preformance issues; I have a hard time running this at a reasonable framerate on any settings higher than low/medium. Insert "I can run [ ] at 90FPS on my super neato high preformance RIG" statement here.
Knowing where to go or how to get there can be difficult occasionally, due to a lack of map and no clear indication of the activities available to you. I found that the scanning ability, which is your method of interacting with characters and the environment, also shows you points of interest in the area around you, which helps me find my way, but wasn't explained in any tutorial I've found.
You do get a list of missions you've completed, but only half of the ones I've done I can actually go back to try again for higher scores and better rewards, and none of them are labeled for this.
A minor gripe about the art direction I have is that the 3D art and the environments are spot on for the most part, but the UI and 2D character art seem out of place. I feel like the airbrush shading on most of the character art detracts from the style of illustration, it probably would have done better to do away with value and just stick to the color and line. I also feel like most of the UI could do to fade out when not actively being used.

First of all : when it comes to rate novels, i don't like to use that "10 score" standard system. Instead of it, i just decide for myself whether i liked or disliked the story. "One Thousand Lies" hits the point with it's unique great characters, background music and ,of course, the strongest part of this novel - mindbreaks (i could use another word, but it would be censored anyway). Also, there are some nice reffers to Steins;Gate, Greek mythology and stuff. For the first hours of reading you could think that it's another common tale with another common plot. And you know what? You're just a poor little fish - you've got caught in the nets of a Lie.
My advice is to read it carefully and pay attention to details, because there is so much truth (lie) to uncover. Trust yourself only and don't get fooled by attractive and cute characters. But still, remember one thing : behind one thousand lies there is always one hidden truth.
P.S. "One Thousand Lies." After finishing it, i turned on "30 seconds to Mars - Beautiful Lie". Really, such a beautiful lie to believe in... And then... "One Hidden Truth" - the epiloge. There is not that much to say : after finishing it, welcome to "Discussions" section. There you'll find all the answers and great theories from some experienced readers and even developer himself, if you are interested.
P.S.S.

TL;DR: I can't tell you if the game is worth your money or not since it's free, however I can tell you if it's worth your time. The answer to that is a resounding yes. Whether you're new to the visual novel genre or a seasoned veteran, I think you'll enjoy this one.
First things first, there are no choices in this VN. If you come in with those expectations you may be disappointed, but don't drop it just yet.
I didn't bother reading the reviews before downloading, so judging by the first hour or so I was under the impression that this was just a light-hearted comedy. As the story progressed, I realized just how wrong I was. It gets a bit TOO real and depressing at times. I'd rather not get too much into the story, I think you'd enjoy it more if you went into it knowing as little as possible. I will say that it gets confusing though. The beginning is pretty confusing, the ending is confusing as hell. I'm still not 100% sure about what happened, but at least it left an impression.
It starts out a little slowly in terms of plot development, but just watching the characters interact with each other is a lot of fun. They all have a very distinct personality and way they interact with the main character. This isn't to say the characters are predictable, even if that may seem to be the case at times. Most of the main cast have their own running gag that seems to never get old. I could listen to Ausse's corny pick-up lines all day.
The humor in general was what really got me hooked at first. I don't remember the last time I've laughed this much while reading something. The abundance of references and occasional black humor really appeal to me, that's probably the case for most internet dwellers.
The length and art quality were definitely not what I'd expect from a free title. It took me 8 hours to finish it, and while that may not be very long as far as VN's are concerned, I'd even be willing to pay ~5€ for it. The UI is very slick and functional, something I always appreciate.
I love the character art, it's not your generic anime style. It's a breath of fresh air. The backgrounds on the other hand.. not so great. You won't spend a lot of time staring at them though, so it's not a huge problem in my eyes. Another thing I'm not very fond of is the CG, the characters look very different. I almost didn't recognize the character at all when they showed the first CG image. Maybe that's just me though.
As a word of warning, there is some philosophical, "2deep4me" type stuff not everyone will enjoy. I'm sure you'll live through it.
