A more balanced Magicka. Honestly not getting the criticism for this game - the new controls allow for moving while casting, and makes it so that you don't have to focus on moving too much. The new spell balance feels a LOT nicer, and it's not just "spam one combo to win" like Magicka 1. And the fact that spells don't combine into single-slot new elements now seems mostly for balance than anything - which is nice.
Plus, the new features just add to the experience. 1-2-3-4 Magick casting is great for having newer players get used to the game, while they never removed regular Magick casting (and casting them regularly has less cooldown, anyway!) -- so you can still reactively press W-A-SPACE and A-S-F-SPACE for your revive and haste spells, respectively - while assigning your 1-2-3-4 keys to Magicks you don't quite remember the combo for yet. (I never could remember the combo for Conflagration / Dragon Strike, for instance!)
And likewise, the game is a lot more balanced now. The spellcasting is more focused on casting against the weakness of your enemy now instead of just overpowering them with a single spell combo. The difficulty also seems to be ramped up a bit now - enemies tend to swarm a LOT more. You'll want a friend to play with - although playing alone isn't impossible anymore, thanks to the new Familiar companions. Once you get revived (at the cost of your familiar), you can easily just revive your Familiar back again with a quick W-A-SPACE. Just make sure you're not in enemy fire first. ;D

Magicka 2 is Magicka 1 but with a fresher coat of paint and a tweaked engine under the hood, it may not have the charm of its predecessor, but it runs a bit better and is more responsive. Disappointingly, the game's many enemy encounters do not feel as memorable as the first. Which leads to my biggest gripe with this sequel.
Where this game truly pales in comparison to its predecessor is its Soundtrack.
Almost every level in Magicka 1 was accompanied by an Orchestral Masterpiece that helped make every enemy encounter FEEL like an epic Tolkien fantasy battle interspersed with images of your friends fending off hordes with a weenie on a stick and/or dying horribly.
The Background Music in this game is instantly forgettable save for the few encounters where a remixed "Dunka Dunka" is playing from a radio ingame.
The new artifact gameplay changes have definite potential, though I have not yet tried all of them, I hope the strictly cosmetic artifacts (Sitcom Audience being my favorite, where an unseen audience laughs at you when you die) wont prevent you from unlocking things.
In regards to humor, this game lacks the comedic stings of the original by resorting to in large part awful old memes and Game of Thrones references. But these are easily missed and ignored.
All in all Magicka 2 is an OK sequel, it isnt completely disappointing like sequels are in general, and unfortunately, the spellcasting system is not as complex as in the first, the OP spells of old are replaced by the Shield tactic of spamming rock+ice/fire/arcane while equipping a shield of the same element. There is definite room for improvement, which we may see down the line in ...*groan* DLC. Then again i had a lot of fun with Dungeons and Daemons from magicka 1 so we'll see.

This game is honestly one of the greatest indie gems that has come to Steam in the last few years. I only feel justified reviewing it after playing for over 100 hours. Many a time I have told myself; "I just wanna expand my main bus a little further", or "I've just gotta lay a few more train tracks", and I look at the clock 5 hours later, and wonder where the time went.
The game is a mixture of everything great about logistics and factory building. If you are not interested in spending a large ammout of time optimizing inputs and outputs, as well as reviewing wiki's, then this is not for you.
The primary objective of the game is to mine/extract/refine resources, and then use them to craft items, to craft a mega base, to mine more resources, etc. Your main enemys are the biters (enemy AI which attack you and your buildings and machines when you pollute the enviroment to a certain point), and yourself (if you don't macro manage resources), which impedes your ability to develop your gigafactory. The crafting mechanics are easy to use, even if they are tedious in the early game (this is to encourage the player to automate crafting of all items, as that is more efficient then manually crafting), and the health mechanic is not terribly punishing, but does discourage players from going rambo, and to rely on defensive works for most of the game. Building placement is intuitive, and managing your factory is reletivly easy, until they sprawl over half of the discovered map.
Lets talk about the game world. There is a lot of it, I mean, a lot. It is procedurally generated, so the player never runs out of resources, but it takes a long time to navigate this world (this is a personal gripe of mine, but it shouldn't affect most players). The world itself feeds into the idea of a infinate feedback loop, of which there is no end. This may turn people off this game, but this highlights one of the core features of the game, that of progress for progress's sake. There really is no purpose aside from increasing the size of your factories, as well as researching more technology.
All in all, there is a lot I liked about this game (coming from a guy who enjoys logistics and management), but there are a few issues with it. The soundtrack can use some work. I get that it is supposed to be ambient music, but it falls into a pitfall of repetitive, boring music that really doesn't enhance the play experience. There is a large ammount of walking large distances late game, and one particular resource becomes increadably scarse, and runs out quickly (looking at you, oil!).
All in all, this game is perfect as an idle game, or as a game to spend far to much of a Friday night/morning in, and it has a charming pixilated texture theme that is reminicent of older 64 bit graphics, definatly worth a try and a purchance!

As a returning player of State of Decay with over 300 hours into the original, I felt I should share my feelings about Year One Survival Edition.  For the people who have played the original and want to know what was polished in this edition, here are the definitive improvements I have noticed so far (in addition to the more obvious changes that were made):
-  Ferals are nearly impossible to hit with a car.  They have some very responsive reflexes, leaping multiple times to dodge a moving vehicle and they will jump over your car if you kick it into reverse (so no cheesy brake kills in YOSE).
- Characters you've spent Influence on so they will tag along no longer run back to base when they get tired or injured, and they will continue to help out even if you take on a mission while out.  Previously, a lot of missions immediately forced them to run back to base.  I have run several missions and wiped out half a dozen infestations without my companion heading home.
Edit:  A friend of mine says his follower just ran off after accepting a Scavenger mission, so there may still be some missions that auto-kick the companion.  So sad.  Did some testing of my own and found that companions tend to leave when doing missions for survivor enclaves (scavenge, beseiged, etc.) but stick around during missions for your own community.  I have run several Ally in Trouble, Missing Survivor, Zed Hunt and 'needs a talking to' missions without my companion bailing.  Hope this elaboration helps.
- Juggernauts seem to have less health than before.  I continued my game on BD11 and managed to take one out with less than a clip of .22 bullets to the cranium.  To counter that however, there seem to be more of them out there (at least on higher BD levels) and I had to take out 3 of them on my first Ally in Trouble mission.
- Less Bloaters.  They were everywhere in the original on higher BD levels and they seem to have had a significant population reduction.  The number of Ferals and Jugs though seem to be higher than before.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
And for some of the annoyances that still exist:
- Zombies still clipping through walls.  I can see their heads but I just wasted a couple shots trying to hit them even though they are on my side of the fence.
- Still getting stuck on sidewalks.
- Fighting on hills can still be hazardous to your health.
- Still having some trouble getting companions to get in the damn car.  Just have to drive back and forth here and there.  There does seem to be a semi-fix added to YOSE where a companion who is running in place due to bad pathing will try an alternate route after a handful of seconds and get in the car.  This is only if they are already in motion (doing the running man on the corner of the car).  A companion who is standing still will continue to do so until you can trigger a new response by moving the car a bit.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
All in all.  I still enjoy this game a lot and I hope they address some of the bugs that have existed from SOD's inception.  But for what it is, I still gave a thumbs up because those glitches were annoying, but not nearly as bad as the completely broken companion AI.  If you were a fan of the game and can look past those glitches, YOSE is still a lot of fun to play.
I did have some issues with framerate, but I modified my settings to Maximum Graphics @ 1280x720 and it has become a hell of a lot smoother.  The draw distance isn't the best, but it's still a lot better than the original and the combat is much more fluid, the combat animations look much better and I love the improved variety of vehicles.
Note:  I am set up in the Fairgrounds on my BD11 group so I have not experienced the returning Snyder's Trucking Watchtower problem yet, but from what I have read, it still continues to plague that home site.
Edit:  I have decided to start over from BD1 on a new profile and will update this review as I progress through the breakdown levels again.

You won't be swinging any fancy lightsabers or blocking any blaster lasers, you'll be doing the unsung work of the special forces of the clone army: the Commandos; and hell if it wasn't extremely fun. Usually in first person shooters the character developement is rather shallow, well, there isn'[t much in this game either, but it fits okay! You're a CLONE, your character doesn't matter! Right? Well, yes and no. You don't have much background or sappy stories being told among Delta Squad, and well, it fits with the fact that their clones! The character did however manage to do something a lot of other games can't, make me smile! The characters, who lack personal history due to being clones, express themselves in their witty quips or comments on you. One situation was when I blew up an enemy and my squadmate on accident and one of the other members said "Command, send a replacement for 38." (38 [three eight] being your callsign). Every so often, a game comes along that takes a bit of other, more popular games, stitches it together, and pushes it out into the public. However, just because you can crib from other games, it doesn't make the game fun.
This game tries it's best to be Diablo III with a distinctively Trion/RIFT artstyle. The problem is that the game itself tends to try too hard to cosplay as other games without actually bringing anything new. I know people hate F2P/Pay2Win -- and really, $75 of DLC is a bit excessive, and that's before you even get into the in-game store for consumables, pets, and cosmetics -- but the game IS actually fun. For a bit. Like every TRION game, it's fun as a new experience, but it eventually fades to a distinct "meh." Once boredom sets in, and it will, you'll be glad you didn't pay for it.
The biggest issue, though? Lag and disconnects, and you'll have them in abundance. Within a two hour stint and 25 levels, I've been kicked from an instance three times, and the chat was flooded with others complaining about lag and DC's, as well. If nothing else, this game desperately begs for an EARLY ACCESS tag.

Like most of the reviewers on here I purchased Marvel: Ultimate Alliance on a pure nostalgia kick.
The Ultimate Alliance series along with its predecessor, X-Men Legends, were really fun to play (and replay) with my friends back in the day. All of them are still definitely my favorite style of co-op games, i
appreciated how each player can pick a character to match their own playstyle.
You feel like hanging back and blasting fools from a distance with projectiles? Done.
Wanna mow through 'em one by one like a tank? Go for it.
Oh, you prefer to stick to the skies and rain down haymakers? No problemo!
The flexibility in how you approached each stage was (and still is) awesome, countless hours were spent playing through the story with different combinations of teams and it was cool to see how certain team combos were given boosts i.e. Fantastic Four, Avengers, X-men etc.
Unfortunately, when it comes to this port on Steam, i'm just not interested in spending more hours than the few that i already have on an otherwise great game... as you will see in other reviews, controllers are virtually un-usable due to the button mapping. The fact that the game is still being offered for purchase with this major issue is insulting to the series and to the community. It's like expecting people to pay for a car that they can barely drive and having no issues with selling such a sub-par product... even on a sale it's questionnable.
I hope that Steam will increase their standards for what they allow to be sold on here. With this major issue, it would make more sense that you tell the publisher to fix it with a patch or otherwise remove it from the store completely if they fail to do so within a given time. In its current state, it's honestly not doing anyone any good, and hasn't been for a long time.
Visually it runs really well on high settings with no bugs (so far), but that's pretty much where the pros stop.
I'm being really generous here when i say that i recommend this game, and that's
because i absolutely love this game, especially when the plot takes you to Asgard since i'm a big fan of Norse mythology. More so, i recommend it only because technically it does work on my setup after taking a good 20 minutes to map the buttons on keyboard and peripherals. I bought this game purely to enjoy it with friends again, but since controllers don't work, i'm left playing it on my own which takes a lot away from the game's potential experience that i remember.
If you love this series and don't mind playing it alone on keyboard + peripherals (i don't, game runs beatifully), then this games for you.
If you don't subscribe to the above points, honestly just skip it and spend your money on something else. You

After already 30 hours of gameplay non stop + streaming it, this is what I'm about to say.
First of all, I'm a huge fan of bandai namco jrpg games. Mostly been a huge fan of tales and god eater games and some other naruto game that are hack'n'slash one.
I haven't bought any SAO games in my vita, so I only try AW vs SAO and SAO:HR on steam.
Pros :
- I love how every SAO game aren't 100% the same mechanism with the other SAO games. The game isn't like the previous one that is available on steam, is not like an hack'n'slash only, but they try to make like some kind of a MMO game.
- The feel of being like playing with real players. Since they try to create something that ressemble like a real MMO, is pretty impressive that you feel like you're in one even thought you're just playing the singleplayer for the story. If you get into the game+story like I do, you can threat other npc players as if they were real players. You'll see many in town, and also in area, you'll see them fight in group. Of course is not perfect, you can't really choose a topic you want to talk to since they are just AI. But you can interact with them, and while interacting with them more and more, you can create some kind of bond like a real MMO, that's how you make friend.
- Big and interesting story, like many of bandai namco games such as the tales series, god eater, and even other SAO, you can guarantee that you'll have tons of hours before completing the story (unless you skip the dialogue)
- Good amount of customization for your character, some people will say there isn't enough, but I find it pretty cool. Plus, your clothes change depending on the armor you put. Sadly sometimes you will feel that the armor name just don't fit on how it look xD.
- Japanese voice, I know there is a huge debate in the anime about dub vs sub, both have their advantage, and everyone can have their own preference. In my case, I love the japanese voicing more, which you have here. Is not like many JRPG that you just read...read....read....with some few sound like : "ah", "eh", "oh". But you actually hear the character speak, which is something I really enjoy from the tales and god eater games. Since I'm not a big reader, just listening to the voice/reaction and reading the translate, it feel like watching an anime in subs, way more enjoyable then just reading.
- Amazing map, as expected from bandai namco games. Map pretty detail for a JRPG. Of course is not comparable to many shooter game that require high graphic such as destiny 2 that just came out with amazing view/map, but for a JRPG, I'd say is pretty amazing. The details on a rock or jumping between branch, you don't feel like much invisible wall. Of course there will be some invisble wall, like an island surrounded by water, they won't let you start walking on water or swimming for 1 hours non stop. If you play AW vs SAO, you'll see that the map is gigantic, amazing flight range, you can fly anywhere in one area, the only invisible wall are like the edge of an area. While in many other game even in some online MMO, you'll feel invisible wall while trying to jump on a rock where your character jump higher then the height of the rock...but you'll slide straight down @.@...which doesn't happen in SAO:HR, where you can jump on every rock, even the one stick on wall as long as your jump is higher then the rock height.
Cons :
- Not for players that will just skip the story. If you don't care about the story happening in SAO:HR and just want to play the game and kill monster. I probably won't suggest this game for you. Unlike AW vs SAO where the flight system is something really impressive and smooth compare to many other games, in this game, it will be your average killing mobs and visiting place where you can do in many other MMO or other games.
- Not being use to control (since I suppose most people will be using a controller to play this game), the control can be pretty weird at first due to it not being your average hack'n'slash jrpg, but they try to make some kind of MMO. I use a controller to play this game, and usually MMO are being play with a keyboard and mouse on keyboard. Some that play MMO with a controller might be more at ease when they first start this game. On keyboard you have a lots of button which you can set all kind of skills, while on a controller you have to hold button (which is not new) to do some kind of skill, but mostly the select button open you a bar of hotkey. Now this is where it get a bit rough. In some JRPG game, we use select a lots in the middle of a battle of course, like god eater where you need to use select to use healing or bullet change. But in this game, since an MMO usually have a lots of skill, mostly when you advance on class, in here you can have all kind of skill, and there isn't enough button on a controller, so you might be force to press select for other skill + buff + potion.
- Create your kirito. The cool thing about most of bandai namco JRPG, is that there is voice with the character instead of just reading and hearing some few sound from your character. The problem here is that, unlike AW vs SAO where you actually see the story of Kirito and his friends, and you can control any premade character, in this game you will be able to custom your character (which should be a pro). The thing is you will be kirito, that mean you will be the hero of the story of course. I'm a girl, so I created a girl character, but in the story, your character will be speaking as kirito, so you'll have a man voice which can be kinda weird xD.
- Bad translate, if you understand at least a few decent word in japanese, you'll notice there is many mistake in the translate, including grammar or some few typo.
Question I've receive that isn't part of my pros and con:
Q : Is the game worth the price?
A : I'd say yes, I heard the game deluxe edition was 80$ when it first came out, of course is cheaper now since this game been 1 year old. I always buy most of bandai game in full price, mostly because I'm a huge fan and I would love to see more of their game being imported in the western. It really depend on you if you want to buy it in full price or on sales, afterall steam sale happen pretty often. I buy it full price to support the compagny, and because how big the game is compare to many other games, you can see that they put tons of work into it.
Q : Would you recommend this game for someone that never try a JRPG?
A : Probably not SAO : HR to start with due to the fight mechanism being really different then many JRPG, I'll probably suggest to start with the tales one, or AW vs SAO, due to the flight system being really smooth and easy to control even while fighting.
Q : If we don't like the anime, will we enjoy the game?
A : To be fair, is kinda a hard question, I wouldn't say : because you don't like SAO you won't like any other thing related to SAO. Just like god eater, I started from the game, I was a huge huge huge, a REALLY big fan of god eater, I'm also greatfull I got the chance to meet the creator of god eater as well (THANK YOU BANDAI), but the anime...The anime wasn't as enjoyable as I expected. I loved the character in the game, and I loved the small anime special "God eater prologue" that came before God eater the anime. For SAO, it might be the same thing, just like people loving the VN but hating the anime (but that mostly due to poor adaptation). If you love JRPG game, but dislike the anime, you can always try the SAO games, there no harm, except only harming your wallet depending when you buy it. But I find the game more enjoyable due to me liking the anime + movie + character. But SAO game are mostly story focus, unlike naruto fighting game, you don't need to watch naruto to enjoy playing a naruto fighting game. You'll probably put more time into the story in SAO games, so if you didn't enjoy the anime/LN, there is a huge chance you might not like the story in the game as well.

Brilliant flight simulator. As I am a general aviation pilot I was especially keen on the physics engine for general aviation aircraft. FSX always lacked good flight dynamics. Gladly X-Plane is very good with this aspect of flying. Doing touch and go's on a small airport with a good cross wind component (wind coming from the side) is a very enjoyable experience.
The cross wind landing is a very good indicator of how good the physics engine is. Let me explain by describing the procedure.
When wind is coming from, let's say right, then the airplane will be pushed to the left of the center line of the runway. To compensate this you have to steer into the wind. Doing this the nose of the aircraft will be pointing to the right of the runway. The propeller pulls you back on track so to say. However you'll be flying a bit sideways which is not ideal for a landing procedure. So to make the nose of the aircraft point to the center line again you will need to press the left pedal on your rudder pedals to push the nose to the left.
This procedure can be summarized as 'Stick in the wind, opposite rudder to compensate'.
So in this case your stick or yoke will be set to the right -in the wind- and your left foot will be in the forward position.
Doing this in real life will set your aircraft on a fixed line towards the runway and give you a real good feel of control.
Now it becomes interesting as the touchdown will change too. When approaching the runway in this configuration touching down will first occur on the side of main gear at the windy side. So in this case it will be the right main gear wheel that touches the tarmac first. Followed by the left side and then the nose wheel will gently touch the tarmac.
I never got this to work in FSX. X-Plane follows this perfectly and it tells me that they've got it right.
Secondly the engine is still maintained where FSX has remained as it was when it was released years back. This means that the X-Plane engine makes much better use of your video card and is easier on resources. This last part is important. It is stable. FSX crashed many times. Often when I was flying for an hour which in a flight simulator is very bad because you have to start your journey again. This hasn't happened yet in X-Plane.
Then the graphics. Some reviewers say that FSX is better with graphics but this isn't necessarily the case. Agreed, the graphics look a bit dull when first installed but I found a few tutorial video's on YouTube how to make the lighting different so that shadows are more prominent and colors are much richer.
That combined with a ton of free scenery which can be added makes for a very realistic experience.
Last positive point is that they made it multi-platform so that I can run it native on my Linux machine. The only downside is that some add on development companies just don't want to make a Linux version of their add on. I had a conversation of a representative of
about their SkyMaxx add on. They just don't want to invest their time. And that is a shame as a developer needs less or no extra tooling to build an add on when building for Linux. Luckily most add on packages work just fine.
One last note. It's a simulator. When you are more into arcade this will not be for you. Check YouTube to see what it's like if you are unsure.
Happy flying and try the cross wind touch and go's. The are really fun!
Cheers!

This is quite a good game, once you can get to grips with its quirks. However, it really pays to have some experience with flight simming (or even real piloting), because this game is NOT novice-friendly. Unlike Microsoft Flight Simulator X, which has tutorial missions and a wealth of information in its Learning Center (including detailed information about how to fly its default aircraft), X-Plane basically throws you in the cockpit and says "best of British" to you. There are no tutorials, at least not within the game. It doesn't work all that well "out of the box", either. You have to spend some time configuring it (especially with regard to your controller). This is good in some ways, because X-Plane offers a lot of options for customisation and is very flexible in this regard. But in other ways, it's a bit tedious, especially as the user interface is not very user-friendly. Granted, there are plenty of forums where you can get good information, but it would be nice to have more of the information you really need within the game itself.
The scenery (minus any add-ons) is somewhat of a mixed bag. In terms of topography, X-Plane leaves FSX in the dust. The way in which hills, fields and so on are rendered is every bit as good as high-quality FSX scenery add-ons like Orbx or texture add-ons like REX. Water and lighting are also quite magnificent. Runways are (at least in my opinion) easier to see. Weather is very well done. However, where X-Plane trails a fair way behind FSX (and I think, Prepar3D) is in the way airports are depicted - often just bare runways and taxiways with no buildings at all. This is really very poor. Cities are not very well depicted either. While FSX default rendering of cities is pretty ordinary, it is still, at this time, vastly superior to X-Plane (again, I refer purely to default scenery - obviously, the scenery of both these flight sims can be improved with add-ons).
Another area where X-Plane falls short of FSX is AI aircraft. While it is nice to see real airlines (like United) instead of the generic airlines you get in FSX, the type of aircraft are often wrong for the airport. For instance, at my home airport (which is a major international airport, but has a fairly short runway), I saw a United Airlines Boeing 747. United doesn't fly to my city, and the runway is too short for 747s. Even more absurdly, I saw a NASA 747! Another crazy sight I saw was a Hercules (or something similar) doing all manner of weird somersaults before eventually righting itself and rolling down the runway for takeoff. AI aircraft in FSX aren't perfect, but they never do that! And the aircraft type is usually correct for the airport you're at. So this is another area of X-Plane that really needs some work.
As for your own aircraft, they have nice interiors and decent flight dynamics. More 2D pop-up panels would be helpful though (maybe add-ons provide these, but the default planes don't seem to, except for the Garmin GPS), and sometimes the instruments can be hard to read. Sure, you can zoom in on them, but then how are you supposed to see outside? Things like radios and the altimeter have be adjusted manually, but this is not too hard to do. Autopilots are a bit tricky. By the way, for looking around, I recommend using the mouse (zoom in and out with the scroll wheel, and hold down the right button to pan around). Much better than the keyboard. There's also your joystick's hat switch, but you have to manually configure this (X-Plane won't recognise your joystick the way FSX will), which is not that easy. By far and away the best way to look around, or zoom in and out, is with the mouse.
One thing I enjoy doing a lot in FSX is IFR flights between one place and another. It's very straightforward to create a flight plan in FSX. generate a navigation log and interact with ATC. You can do IFR flights in X-Plane as well, but it's far less straightforward (though I'm sure there are add-ons to make it easier). In FSX, you can search for a depature point by airport name, ICAO code or city. Likewise for your destination. But when filing a flight plan in X-Plane, you can only enter the ICAO codes for your departure and arrival points. I guess it's not too hard to look these up somewhere, but this is an example of how X-Plane is not friendly to newbies. Then too, you have to enter a route comprising VORs, DMEs or whatever (although you can leave this section blank and just fly direct, which is best for short flights). But it's not entirely clear how you should do this, what format it should take etc. There's no navigation log, which I love in FSX and really miss in X-Plane. Another thing to beware of is that X-Plane won't park your aircraft at a departure point the way FSX does. You have to choose your airport and gate/ramp BEFORE setting up a flight plan, and you will be returned to that same spot once you're done with your flight plan.
Interacting with ATC takes a bit of getting used to in X-Plane. Whereas FSX will automatically tune you to your departure airport's Clearance Delivery frequency to get you started, you have to manually find the frequency in X-Plane. Better realism, granted, but it can be rather disconcerting at first. Actually, there is a rather handy trick that can help you with ATC in X-Plane. Go to the "Special" menu and select Toggle ATC (that's not exactly what it's called, but anyway it's about halfway down the Special drop-down menu). This brings up a little yellow box that you can use to "auto-tune" frequencies (select the "recommended" one). When ATC says something to you, make sure that you acknowledge their transmission or they'll just keep repeating themselves ad nauseam. Another thing X-Plane's ATC will do is tell you you're off course when you've just taken off and are flying the runway heading to gain a safe altitude, but are (temporarily) going in the opposite direction to your destination. This is quite annoying and I hope it will be fixed. Note also that ATC won't tell you to change course after you've taken off. They expect you to know where you're going (a novel concept). But when you are getting closer to your arrival airport, they will give you altitude and heading instructions that more closely resemble what the FSX ATC does. And I actually think the vectoring of X-Plane's ATC may be a little more precise.
If you are a complete and utter novice to flight simming, you would be better off starting with FSX or the upcoming Dovetail Games Flight School. Certainly in FSX, you can learn a LOT about the fundamentals of flying. X-Plane does not teach you these fundamentals and frankly throws you in the deep end. But if you DO understand the basics of flying (or indeed have reasonable experience with FSX and/or Prepar3D) and you can get the hang of X-Plane's interface (which is a learning curve in its own right), and if you can live with the weird AI aircraft behaviour and total lack of buildings at many airports, then X-Plane is well worth investing in, especially for its topography rendering, weather and aircraft flight dynamics. So I recommend it, albeit with a few caveats.

Magicka 2 is Magicka 1 but with a fresher coat of paint and a tweaked engine under the hood, it may not have the charm of its predecessor, but it runs a bit better and is more responsive. Disappointingly, the game's many enemy encounters do not feel as memorable as the first. Which leads to my biggest gripe with this sequel.
Where this game truly pales in comparison to its predecessor is its Soundtrack.
Almost every level in Magicka 1 was accompanied by an Orchestral Masterpiece that helped make every enemy encounter FEEL like an epic Tolkien fantasy battle interspersed with images of your friends fending off hordes with a weenie on a stick and/or dying horribly.
The Background Music in this game is instantly forgettable save for the few encounters where a remixed "Dunka Dunka" is playing from a radio ingame.
The new artifact gameplay changes have definite potential, though I have not yet tried all of them, I hope the strictly cosmetic artifacts (Sitcom Audience being my favorite, where an unseen audience laughs at you when you die) wont prevent you from unlocking things.
In regards to humor, this game lacks the comedic stings of the original by resorting to in large part awful old memes and Game of Thrones references. But these are easily missed and ignored.
All in all Magicka 2 is an OK sequel, it isnt completely disappointing like sequels are in general, and unfortunately, the spellcasting system is not as complex as in the first, the OP spells of old are replaced by the Shield tactic of spamming rock+ice/fire/arcane while equipping a shield of the same element. There is definite room for improvement, which we may see down the line in ...*groan* DLC. Then again i had a lot of fun with Dungeons and Daemons from magicka 1 so we'll see.

I have seen a lot of people giving negative feedback in reviews about Magicka 2 because they think that the spellcasting system is a worse version of the first game. This is simply not true. There is a distinction between Devs making deliberate balance and gameplay choices and removing features for the sake of removing features. Yes, there are many things that have changed and that have been adopted from Wizard Wars, but in my opinion a lot of these are not worse or better, they just change the way the player plays the game. Going over the comprehensive list of changes I've seen since the first one and why it's still a great game:
- Spellbar nerfed. The elements that used to combine to one in the spell bar don't. This is the most major complaint I've noticed. However, the only thing this affects gameplay-wise is that lightning no longer works in the same spell with steam (intended effect), and lightning no longer works with ice (side-effect and a combo I actually miss). Nor can you cast 5 of steam or ice. This is obviously a balance choice designed to make it so that you cannot give wet status and deal double lightning damage to a target in the same spell cast. It's essentially a general debuff to wizard damage and makes the max amount of button presses per spell always 5.
- Enemies are are buffed. Enemies move at you faster, are more accurate, have clever skills such as trapping you with walls and can swarm you easily. Noticeably enemies that chill you among groups seem to be pretty deadly if you don't remove it fast enough. There is more focus on finding the correct element to blast enemies with as they all have special weaknesses that take them out quickly.
- Magicks nerfed and made easier to cast. There is now a hotkey system for magicks that makes them quick to cast and works on its own cooldown, and you can still manually cast magicks which also has a seperate, short, invisible global cooldown. The two methods can be used simultaneously to cast two magicks in quick succession. There are also a lot less magicks in the game than the first one. Some are still OP (looking at you dragon strike and thunderhead). You also get a little familiar should you so choose that revives you on death in singleplayer/multiplayer which itself can also be revived with the revive magick, giving effectively infinite lives. Push as a standard move (casting without elements conjured) has been changed into a Magick.
- Movement is buffed. You can now move while casting spells; this can be hard to get the hang of at first, but is crucial for being able to kite and fight the now more challenging enemies. You can also heal while on the go. One of the more effective ways I've found to heal now is no longer setting up life mines but instead standard casting a rock element with four life element no charge at your feet for quick powerful heals.
- Weapon Enchants are buffed. Enchantments that include projectile, beam, and shield type spells work similarly as a one time cast, but spray type and lightning type spells now remain on your weapon no matter how many times you swing with it, unless you come into contact with an element of opposite type or have it "nullified" (more on that in a bit).
- Resistances are reworked. No longer does one resistance level of an element cause complete immunity to it, nor can you give your resistances to others by proximity. It is now on-self and staged in power, requiring more thinking/investment into certain defenses. One resist simply reduces damage. Two removes the harm of status effects, chilled, shocked, burning, frozen, and wet and further reduces damage. Three grants immunity to damage of the type. Four gives you major absorption to the damage type. This means for example should you choose to shield four death, yes you will be able to heal while spamming mines on your opponent, but you will be significantly weaker to physical damage due to not being able to add as much rock or ice armor to yourself.
-Some spell modifiers have slightly less representation. Things such as adding more fire to a fireball, won't cause the radius of the fire explosion after the rock lands to be larger. Similarly AOE attacks won't expand in size. Sprays and lightning retain this ability to grow in range. Other modifiers stay the same, like duration or more damage from adding same type elements.
- Lightning has been reworked. It has increased in spell priority to equal projectile type. Since lightning cannot be used with projectiles rock or ice, there's no info on which is higher. This means that beams no longer carry lightning but lightning instead carries beam element types. It also means that lightning mines are no longer available but instead create a kind of life or death vortex wall. Lightning also causes less stun than before.
- Water knockback nerf. Water element knockback and knockback in general are greatly reduced but still workable. I still use it to keep enemies at bay and for wet status. Mines also don't send you flying nearly as far but some enemy attacks do. This can be frustrating as you can't que spells while in mid-air, something they should change.
- Rock reworked. Charge time greatly extended and distance at low charge reduced. Happens to be a high damage option given that other high damage options are nerfed. AOE Attacks that include rock are particularly powerful since they can be spammed quickly such as water rock death fire (also strong standard cast). Or weapon enchantments like rock death fire x3. Using a single rock in standard cast attacks seems to be best for range and charge.
-Ice has been reworked. Granting yourself ice armor does not cause as much damage with the thorns effect and it also has less damage radius. Ice shards remain powerful. Ice walls and armor now reflect beams, making them much more useful.
- Shields reworked. They now work on a timer that cannot be extended, allow for movement through the barrier, and still protect against beams and sprays, but do not suffice against projectiles which pierce straight through now. The shield dome - shift-middle mouse - now causes a "nullification" effect, where it removes enchantments from your weapon, prevents you from adding more while inside it, and also removing and preventing the effect of status ailments on you, chilled, burning, wet (big bonus there).
- Crossing life and death beams in Co-op. Now creates a 2000 damage blackhole. Able to be resisted with death resistance and a great cheesy damage technique. Risky without resistance. Life, death, and cold elements also appear to have kept the same qualities from the first game.

On a side note, the campaign feels a little bit shorter than the original, and the humour and references, while still great hadn't tickled me as much this time around. As a plus, the boss battles are all more interesting than before, and enemy type design is more creative. It's a lot easier to hop into a game with friends or complete strangers, and playing through in co-op makes it miles better. If you are a die-hard Magicka 1 fan, and these changes don't sound good to you, stick to Magicka 1. If you're on the fence, get it when it goes on sale. All in all, in my opinion these changes make it a more mobile, defensive, challenging, and strategic game. I have a great deal of fun playing it and look forward to future related projects. Highly recommend it!

Well I'm recommending it. I’d say wait for a sale though. There are some good things about it and some not so good things right now.
The Good:
Its Magicka! Despite all the changes it still retains the feeling of the first game.
Its fun with friends and its a great “couch and tv” game.
The gamepad controls are a vast improvement over Magicka 1.
Magic shortcuts are convenient. Just 4 of them and they have a cooldown. I think it keeps things balanced well enough.
Streaming works better.
Multiplayer works without crashing.
The Bad:
They dumbed down the spells a bit (biggest gripe). This is ok for the most part. I don’t miss fire and water combining into a steam element for example. However, there still needs to be a way to cast every single spell from the first game and there just isn’t. This game is labeled “2” meaning it should build on the first game and give players MORE, not TAKE AWAY features and say its just as good. I want Vortex and Meteors back! If not those, then I want some equally powerful visually dazzling spell combos.
The new preformed magick system is awesome in my opinion but should be customizable. You should be able to write in your own combos as you discover them. There should also be more like 50 Magicks like there were in the first game as opposed to the 10 or so you can choose from now…
There needs to be a proper server list. I want to see which games I can join, how many players, public/private, etc. I would also like to be able to join a level at the beginning rather than jumping in right at the last 10 seconds of a boss.
Needs more levels. There are only 9! Thats ridiculous in my opinion. I got through the whole campaign solo in about 4 hours. I understand that there will likely be expansions but there should have been more at launch.
Needs more to do. There is a “challenge” mode but the arenas from the first game seem to be gone. I want to set up a custom match between 1-4 wizards and have us duke it out without waves of enemies appearing. There also needs to be more arena maps to accommodate this.
Should have more players. I like the 4 player thing. Its nice. But I want more. I was kind of expecting M2 to have at least a few massive maps and you could play with 16 players (4 teams of 4) at a time.
Verdict:
Ok so I wrote more bad than good. I still recommend this game. Its just fun. Its dorky and if this is your style of humor you’ll have a good time with it.

I have to say, I went into this game expecting it to be mediocre, and possibly able to tide me over for a few hours. It did a lot more than that. Let's start with gameplay. In all reality despite the fantastic feeling of commanding your squad it's fairly average. I went, I shot, I won. Simple as that. So you will really be playing this game for it's story, along with the atmosphere and characters. It all works exactly when it wants to work, and your team actually sounds like real people, not hastily done voice-acting as seen in some games (a personal favorite line of mine is from Sev, "Boss, hold on to your guts while I rip out theirs"). The story spans about 9 hours (for me at least) and it is very well written, especially since it goes off of only three levels. Yes, you will get that many hours out of three stinkin' levels! Unfortunately it is poorly ended, and while I won't spoil anything it felt like they tried to cram a lot of what could have been another half hour to an hour of story into four minutes, and while it does wrap everything up, it just doesn't work that well. On to atmosphere. The only level where it was really polished was the second, on a ship attacked by Trandoshan mercenaries. It reeks of "creepy" and and really helps the build up of what is going on. Now then, time to talk enemies. Anything and everthing will kill you, except regular Battle Droids and Geonision babies. Yes, babies. Super Battle Droids will become the bane of your exisitance and everything you thought you knew about about them goes down the drain (Sorry Battlefront II players, you're done for). Something interesting is how different grenades I had know use for before became quite important to me once I learned what they good against, and I began cursing myself for using them on a Spider Droid and what-not. Overall, this game gave me a very enjoyable experience, and maybe someday I will get around to playing it again.
My score: 7/10
For as much as I praise this game, the levels did feel a bit drawn out at times, as well as the enemy health bars. But on the other hand, I did kill five geonision babies by electrocuting them into little bits. So thats a plus.

It's only been a couple of months and 2010 is already shaping up to be one of the best ever for gamers. If your wallet hasn't already been emptied, Electronic Arts and development studio DICE have tossed yet another videogame on the pile that can't be missed. Battlefield: Bad Company 2 ups the intensity and visual prowess of its predecessor, while still delivering one of the most compelling multiplayer games around.
If you were to buy Bad Company 2 solely for the single-player campaign, you might come away a bit disappointed. That's not to say it's particularly bad in any way, but it doesn't feel impressive enough to stand on its own as a great experience. Once again, the multiplayer game is the star of the Battlefield show.
Watch the video review.
The single-player campaign follows the story of a rag-tag bunch of soldiers as they traipse around the world on the hunt for a mythical weapon of mass destruction which absolutely must not fall into the hands of the Russians. It's a typical story of unlikely heroes as they attempt to save the world, and it will take you across a great variety of locations that range from frozen mountains to densely packed jungles.
The detail of these gorgeous locales is the first thing that will spring out at you as you begin the fight. The vistas and skyboxes look nearly photorealistic in many situations, and DICE did a wonderful job blending the particle effects and game objects in the foreground with the more static backdrops. The result is a sense of depth that few videogame worlds can offer.
Things become more impressive yet when the action kicks in. Returning from the last Bad Company game are nearly fully destructible environments. If an enemy soldier is holed up in a second-story bedroom taking potshots at you, all you have to do is send a rocket at that wall and he'll either wind up dead or fully exposed. The same line of thinking applies to just about anything you see – send enough firepower at it and you can watch it crumble.
Once you're done ogling the smoke trails or mountain ranges in the distance, you'll start to notice that Bad Company 2 has taken a few cues from the Call of Duty franchise. The last Battlefield game was the first to introduce a fully fleshed out storyline and it stumbled a bit in the process. The humor was goofy and over the top, the open mission design was a bit too open, and everything seemed coated in a dense fog. A lot has changed and improved for the sequel.
The backdrops are breathtaking.
The big change comes with a more streamlined and cinematic approach to the action. The dialogue is less overtly inane, though it does offer its fair share of humor, and the level design feels more straightforward. While the last Bad Company game couldn't hold my attention, this one kept me interested and having fun from start to finish.
It shouldn't come as any surprise that this Battlefield game has some great mechanics. The guns react well, and sound fantastic. The vehicles handle smoothly and really do a great job of making you feel like the king of the battlefield. The instant-respawns and med kit injections of the last Bad Company have been replaced by the more standard checkpoints and regenerative health bar and that makes the challenge of war feel more realistic.
To top things off, the AI squad mates at your side act like real soldiers in battle. They'll press the attack while you flank and hold off the enemy while you duck behind cover to recuperate. Many games slap you in a squad of largely ineffective soldiers and let you do all of the heavy lifting. Bad Company 2 is a refreshing change of pace in this regard.
Of course, if you want to start nitpicking, there are plenty of instances to call out. Some of the details and little pieces of the environment stream into view a bit late. There still are no arms drawn on screen when driving a vehicle, causing a poltergeist-like steering wheel to move on its own. On the Xbox 360 version, slow loading from the disc causes the player to be locked out for as much as five seconds from throwing grenades or using the knife when picking up a new weapon or changing kits (this issue went away when installing the game onto a hard drive).

I was looking forward to the single player campaign, but it only took me 5 hours to play through on the hardest difficulty. Then the multiplayer showed NO servers running. I wish I hadn't spent the $5 I did for this. Back to playing BF4 now.

I loved this game. I'm a bit on the older side and I remember when 2D platfomers were in their heyday. To me, 2D platformers are the essence of video gaming. After all, Mario saved the whole industry on his own back in the day. This game takes me back to those glorious times. There are so few games now that hold my attention for very long, but I simply could not put this game down. I even went for the 100% achievement, where usually I just want to complete the story and nothing else.
The visuals in this game are beautiful, from the sprite work to the full 2D character drawings. Environments are varied and well designed and the enemies are cute too. Wayforward has some of my favorite character design in their original IPs, and I love the designs in this game.
There are small bits of voice acting here and there, but they sound really great. The music is catchy, although occasionally repetitive, but that is to be expected in this genre of game.
Controls are tight and work well. I personally finished it using a Steam Controller and I liked it very much.
The gameplay itself is truly excellent. It is
on the hard side but I'm pretty used to that kind of thing from my childhood. If you really want to 100% the game, it will take a bit of work and occasional frustration. I was actually slightly disappointed by the final boss. I found him surprisingly easy to beat, especially with bubble shields and auto-potions equipped. If I had known he would be so easy, I would have probably tried to beat him without any items.
Overall, this game is quite a gem and you should absolutely buy it. Wayforward is a great company that makes great games that are better than many AAA titles, but with 1/10th of the staff and budget. They deserve your love and money.

I've been playing this game for about a week.  For the most part, it's been an enjoyable ride, but the game has a fatal flaw.  That is the final dungeon.  I find myself totally unable to get past the first spike room as the switch timing and all the spikes makes it nearly impossible for all but the most skilled players to pass with any degree of success.
The massive spike in difficulty that comes with the final dungeon totally ruins my enjoyment of the game and makes me feel cheated that I ever bought it.  Due to the difficulty of the dungeon, I will likely never complete the game and it will remain unfinished.  I feel like I wasted my money with this title.
The final dungeon has a difficulty so great that it feels like it belongs in a different game.  Had I known it would be as difficult as it was, I never would've made the purchase, which is a shame since I enjoyed Half Genie Hero.
On the other hand, it does seem like Wayforward Technologies learned their lesson in this regard as the follow up title had less of a difficulty spike with its final level.  When designing games, there should be a more even increase in the level of difficulty as you progress through the game.  For the most part, this is the case with Shantae and the Pirate's Curse.  However this lesson is forgotten with the final level.  I find the level almost totally impassable, which makes me both frustrated and incredibly angry,
I would ask for a refund, but the game is functional and works on my P.C.  The fault isn't with the game not working but in the fundamentally flawed level design of the final level.  I regretfully must recommend against purchasing this game for all but the most skilled players with the best reflexes.

You know...you think you have found a fun game that allows you to jump in and play with a fried for an hour or so and doesn't feel like a job...UNTIL....*drum roll*...you see the ever popular and much hated, mobile game driven  DAILY LOGIN REWARD!!  This system is one of the worst systems created by game developers and is squarely aimed at driving revenue up by forcing the player base to at least login daily or miss out on gifts and goodies.  Now, the counter argument is that nearly every game has a system like this and I don't disagree.  But what makes other systems not so despised is that they incent and reward, not penalize.  What do I mean?  Daileys of any sort reward the player who commits to doing them, but you don't lose anything for not doing them.  It may accelerate your acquisition of skills or gear, but it doesn't stick a carrot in front of your face to pull it away as your mouth gets within chomping distance.  Devlian's login reward system penalizes you for missing a day of activity.  That is, the 7 day, 14 day or 21 day rewards require consecutive logins.  Work late one night and miss the login...*WHAMMIE*   Get sick and don't play one day...*WHAMMIE*  Forget?  *WHAMMIE*.  Go away on vacation...*DOUBLE WHAMMIE*.
Take a lesson from all top grossing games...none of them has a penalty system for not logging in that is so in your face.  Clash of Clans, the king of mobile games doesn't, but you do stand to lose resources if you don't collect/spend them as you'll be attacked.  Top MMO of 2015, ESO, has daily writs to accelerate your crafting skills and daily Undaunted Pledges (dungeons) but that too just accelerates.  It doesn't penalize.
When devs do this, I leave.  Why?  Simple...they admit to not being confident that their game will hold a player's attention and thus need a required daily login system, the carrot and stick, to attempt to retain a player base.
There are so many games to choose from these days, my time AND money goes to the confident developers who let their content stand for itself.

As a great fan of the first Magicka, I have to say this game is totally different. It is based mostly on the Wizard Wars experience (a poor choice from the developers).
The most disappointing aspect is that the movements look clumsy and slow. The charging time of the spells is sooooo long that you will end up not using certain strategies at all (I'm looking at you ice shards).
The game is designed to be played in co-op, but it's surprising how frustrating can get playing solo.
It's just like the developers are telling you "What da f*** are you doing alone? Go get some friends or get lost".
As a positive note, a much needed rebalancing of some OP combinations has been made, even if some elements are just under powered now (Lightning, Fire, Steam).
You don't feel that great inner satisfaction emblematic of the first game,  when you set off your elemental fury against your enemies....Some combinations look very unsatisfactory and you will end up using them very rarely.
I'm simply devastating my keyboard casting spells that end up being "meh".
I understand that you need to learn making complex strategies, but you would expect a full powered Fire elemental attack at point blank to deal much more damage than silly strings...
I managed to make my way alone through the game until the final boss, but a beginner would definitely not achieve the same results.....
I'm not a fan of the Magick's instant-casting-button, but at least they made it rewarding for people who put effort into remembering the combinations, so is a friendly tool for beginners or an emergency button.
In conclusion, the game is still enjoyable and funny (but SHORT), but you'd better wait until they make some changes or make sure you have some friends to play with, as this game is a total single-players  hater.

Star Wars Republic Commando is a first-person shooter about four deadly commandos, the Delta squad, helping the Republic's war effort. You take direct control of the squad's leader, Boss, while he guides his comrades, Sev, Scorch and Fixer, through their missions against the separatists forces.
The main beef of the game is indeed to issue orders to your squad (set a demolition charge here, destroy that specific target, ...) in order to advance in the levels. Thankfully your mates' AI is quite handy and won't give you any serious problems, aside from some rare instances (it's worth mentioning that you and your clones aren't friendly fire-proof and your comrades have an annoying tendency to lock themselves into place if facing a mine field). The members of delta Squad can even revive each other if put down, which is rather fortunate.
You can access a wide array of weapons (an assault and a sniper rifle, a bazooka of some kind, a pistol, ...) in order to battle several rather challenging enemies. The opponents in Republic Commando are indeed very hard to defeat and range from suicidal infantry units with little sense of survival to very sturdy and hard-hitting mini-bosses who can dish out a lot of damage towards your squad. You don't get to face any real boss, though.
Republic Commando's rather short lenght is a well-known fact: it clocks around six or seven hours of gameplay. Many players tend to overlook this in favor of the game's great atmosphere, good soundtrack and solid gameplay, on top of providing a videogame about Star Wars without the usual Jedi and the Force angle and packed with a more gritty and edgier concept
This game is one of the best sci-fi first person shooters ive ever played, I highly recommend it.

*Full disclosure* - I own this game on Nintendo 3DS and purchased a Steam key for this game through Humble for a buck. Keep that in mind while you read this review.
If you like Metroidvania-type games, you should definitely play Shantae and the Pirate's Curse (henceforth PC). While it doesn't have the slick HD graphics of Shantae: 1/2 Genie Hero, it has far more exploration and item hunting that HGH does. If go into PC understanding that this is a port of a 240p game from severely underpowered handheld hardware, you'll be just fine. Wayforward has redrawn the portrait art and menues as those would have looked horrid on any modern PC monitor.
Graphically, PC, like all Shantae games is a colorfull 3D side-scroller with lots of cute girl characters and art. Look for screen shots to get a better idea, but don't go in expecting DOAX or Senran Kagura.
Anyway, rather than a tradition Metroidvania structure where all areas are interconnected, this game has one "hub" island and another 4 (5?) islands which you travel to via a scrolling menu. I would have prefered interconnected worlds, but the menu makes sense with the game's ship/pirate theme.
Most Shantae games see the main character using her genie powers to transform into various animals which grant powers such as block crushing, wall climbing, swimming, and the like. In this game, Shantae instead gets her powere from Pirate Gear like a hat that lets you float/fly, a pistol that allows, long distance hits, etc.  Like most fans of the series, I feel like the Pirate Gear results in better, more seamless gameplay than Shante's genie transformations.
The game has a very fair difficulty. You may die here and there, but you should learn from you mistakes and be able to movbe on quickly. The exception is one sequence near the end of the game. I won't well you what it is, but you will know it when you get there.
This isn't a long game. Most players should be able to finish in 10 hours or less at 100%.
If you like colorful, mid-difficulty exploration games with cute girls and light story, PC is probably for you. if you're looking for a Dark Souls-level challenge, a 100+ hour game, deep story, or are triggered by cute, somtimes scantily-clad anime-style girls, you might be best served to look elsewhere for you gaming needs.
Highly recommended.

This is a fun platformer game.
It feels like playing an updated version of the old Aladdin game that was on the Sega Genesis.
You start in a town where you can save your game, buy items, and talk to people.
Then you choose which level you want to play.
Only one level is available initially, but more levels are unlocked as you progress.
Each level has a special item that gives your character new abilities.
The new abilities allow your character to reach places that were inaccessible before.
The game is pretty linear overall, but you will backtrack after you get new abilities to obtain powerups that were previously beyond your reach.
The game is not difficult in general but there are parts that can be challenging and frustrating.
Most of the bosses are of moderate difficulty but one or two of them are hard.
The characters in the game are likable and the dialogue is fun and light-hearted.
It seems like the story is a continuation of some previous games, but I'm not familiar with this saga.
The graphics and animation are good, though some of the animations are rather strange.
The character portraits are done well.
The different plot-lines you encounter in the levels are often funny but the storyline is pretty simple and straight-forward.
Overall, it definitely a fun game that is worth checking out.

Improvement over the previous installment (Risky's Revenge) in many ways (menu confirm button, pause/select buttons, enemy variety and boss design, map, not zoomed so much you can't see where you are jumping). The previous installment was alright. This is better. But same general idea.

I must say I'm a fan of the Shantae games after my brief encounter with Risky's Revenge. And by brief I mean that that game was too short. Shantae, her hair and endearing cast of characters come at you strong in this game making for a fun platforming adventure.  This time you have a new unseen but ever present foe in the Pirate King, whose presence is felt in the different locations you travel to and as a big bad baddie after revealing himself.
I would say this game features platforming at it's best with every stage being slightly more challenging than the last. Even though you don't sport magical transforming genie powers in this game you still have a number of accessories that help you along the way in the guise of Risky Boots' old pirate gear. Another big change being she's now part of your quest traveling entourage shipping you off to each new destination in Sequin Land.
The graphics, while very reminiscent of the previous game have an updated look and feel making it familiar yet fresh. The in game UI has improved so that it's less cluttered with usable items separated from the questing ones. Some of Shantae's side moves, like her backdash and recovery jump are added as purchased moves but overall felt less necessary than before. The one roundhouse kick move I all but forgot about most of the time as your primary weapons and accessories are more than adequate for dispatching foes.
The platforming though is where this game shines. There's some areas near the end where you'll have to think a lot about how you're going to traverse the area, especially the last stage on your way to defeat the Pirate King. Level design was challenging without being punishing. Bosses had patterns that were easy to figure out but also utilized any new item you picked up in the dungeons well. I would say this game was maybe twice as long as Risky's Revenge and definitely worth your time if you're into Metroidvania type games even if you're not it's just a lot of fun playing.

It's ok... Someone gifted it to me so I gave it a shot and played with that person for a bit. I wouldn't have bought it but can't deny I enjoyed the time I played it, but now after bout 8 hours I'm losing interest. The following are just some of my opinions on it. Some good, some bad.
Feels much faster than Jetset/grind Radio. Almost like the movement powers in DC Online. Which I actually like about it. Specially after you've equipped some decent upgrades for your speed, jump, etc
The tricks are pretty weak, you just hold a direction and hit a button and it does a quick spin or flip. The flips are so fast you can't even tell you did anything, or if you hold that same button you do a grab. Not a lot of style or flare and not dynamic. You can link tricks but cannot combine them. Extremely meh..
Animations seem clunky. First thing I noticed is when you jump, your left hand clips through your butt and moves awkwardly. However first person view is legit attached to your head so when you flip etc you see it happening and you can see your own body, hands, feet which I thought was cool. BUT the cam doesn't spin with the tricks. Only the flip from holding crouch/grind button when jumping so that's oddly inconsistant.
Upgrade system is cool. As you level you unlock mod slots and completing pretty much anything provides mods that offer boosts to differ aspects of your char like: Speed, acceleration, jump hieght, grind speed, etc. The better you do on any event the better the mods you acquire. Thing I don't like about it is that once you place a mod in a slot it locks all previous mods so if you want to pull them out or swap them then you will lose that mod. Can be frustrating depending how much work went into getting that fancy gold or red mod.
Gameplay works. Frustrating at first but you get used to it. Feel like we should have more control when jumping off walls though and shouldn't bog you down so much. You can bounce off the ground to keep your momentum going, would be nice if you could bounce off the walls too. *Bounce is an actual stat you can increase. It allows you to rebound off the ground if you time your jumps for the moment you hit the ground and allows you to jump as high or even higher than the distance you fell prior to the "bounce".
The extra characters are ok.. They provide bonuses to one stat at the cost of another. I personally rather just use the starting character cause of this and I think he looks cooler.. You can customize the coloring of the characters too including the energy effects which your HUD matches the color of.
There's also no reason not to play online. It's much more interesting seeing the city alive with real people. It doesn't affect your game at all with them being there. You can still go about your business doing w/e you want. OR chase em around and go play with someone else if you want..
After playing it and knowing what it is I honestly wouldn't have bought it even on sale. These kind of games require a lot of style and flare in their tricks/stunts to keep me engaged and this just doesn't have it. Running and jumping off walls and grinding is only fun for so long.

I've been searching for a game like
for a long time. I bought it only minutes after learning of its existence. This game scratches that long-term itch I've had for an open world MMO with fast paced gameplay and fluid movement. Jet Set Radio Future is one of my most favourite and memorable gaming experiences of all time with its super slick visuals and eclectic soundtrack. Does
compare favourably? Yes and no.
There is so much to do in
, as a newcomer I found the first world to be extremely overwhelming but after learning the layout of the map and upgrading my character the world was much less daunting. The lacking navigation system and inability to set custom waypoints really cripples the game, along with my inability to complete certain quests and find collectables simply because I often have no idea where to go next. It can be difficult to track down certain NPCs and carry out their tasks, especially when the quest summary explains very little to the player. If only there was a way to set one active quest at a time with waypoints and to implement a breadcrumb trail system to aide players with the most basic quest route whilst continuing to allow the more veteran players the freedom to choose their own path.
The soundtrack is great but it is by no means any rival to the songs found across the Jet Set Radio games, although I do find myself humming along quite frequently and have developed an earworm for some of the more memorable tracks. The A.I. can often be quite dumb, especially during the basketball like missions, as they will either completely dominate me and leave me feeling hopeless or they will wander off into no man's land and I'll be free to score 10+ times within a matter of minutes. There are a lot of unexplained mechanics in the game, either I missed these cues or they were never presented to me, but learning certain tricks really improved how well I could manoeuvre.
The stealth elements aren't great, they do not belong in a game that spends the first two chapters showing off just how incredibly energetic the game can be only to later force the player to slow down to a crawl yet still retain the same agility across jumping, wall riding, and grinding that makes it so easy to break stealth, especially when stealth and parkour elements share the same keybindings. It would have been much more preferred to have a toggle for stealth that limited how high the player could jump and disable the parkour abilities.
The multiplayer is inherently broken, it works well but its implementation is lacking. There is no grouping or invite system which makes it incredibly difficult to team up with other real players before either they or the player activate the mission, which then requires a waiting period before the quest can then be activated by others. I have spent the majority of
completing missions alone while watching players whizz by, so it's not as if the servers are empty, it's that the game does not provide the means to make multiplayer an easy option. Something similar to GTA: Online's instanced group missions would do wonders.
is great but it could be amazing. There are many improvement required to elevate this game, especially if multiplayer is to play a big part. I expect that the developers will continue to support this game and make improvements. No doubt I will continue to play for a long time so long as the game continues to evolve, this is such a niche genre and
represents it well.

A cute heartwarming romance gives way to pages upon pages of note-taking, literary deconstruction, phenomenology, post-structuralist and metamodernist philosophy and post-Derridian ethical musings in the epilogue. 10/10 changed my life.

The story, like many good novels, takes a while to really dig into at first, and a few portions run a tad longer than you'd like or take too long to click through (less clicking through the story-within-a-story about the wolf seeking the Sun might help with that), the philosophy can get a bit overbearing at times, and the rating for nudity absolutely confuses me (there isn't any, so why was the story flagged for such?), but overall it's an exceptionally well done story with a superb soundtrack.
Especially the ending. That ending was well earned, and it didn't fail to satisfy (though I must admit to some confusion regarding the ultimate fate of the protagonist's relationship with Claire).

PRO:
Well written and deep storyline will make you question your life choices,
Interesting characters that the vast majority of people can relate to,
Realistic dialogue that real humans would converse with,
Great comedy and an abundant amount of references,
Above average art style + sleek UI,
Decent music, as Visual Novels go,
And above all, great comedy and an abundant amount of references
CON:
First few hours are a bit sloppy compared to the rest of the story

I recommend this as a free-to-play game only--it's an interesting diversion that plays very similarly to Diablo 3.
There are a few oddities, the first of which you'll encounter is gender-locked classes (and only 4 of them at that). There's very little character customization and the game allows you to freely change your skill trees at will with no penalty, so you certainly won't get too attached to your character.
The quests are straightforward and leveling is QUICK--it'll take you 30 hours or less to hit max level. There are a few interesting dungeon mechanics I haven't seen before but there's nothing groundbreaking in this game. This is an MMO-lite; play for fun, when you need a diversion from a heavier game, or something to play with a friend when you don't want to spend a dime.
I haven't (and won't) spent any cash on this game though I have purchased something from Trion in the past; my understanding is that if you haven't you can't access even the auction house. The only thing tempting to purchase is more inventory space as you start with so little it's almost painful.
This could be a much more interesting game, but as I said, it's an MMO-lite. Light on customization, light on content, light on difficulty. Some strange choices like the gender-locked classes, at will skill changes, and the inability to click on your skills to use them (you must use the numbered hotkeys). Devilian mode is also shockingly weak, making it less of an interesting aspect of the game and more of a strange add-on that the game could do without.
Perhaps in a year this game will have had a lot more content added and become something more than what it is now, but for now, play as a diversion when you're waiting for something else to come along.
