I've never played any other Sniper Elite game before so this review shouldn't be biased by comparisons to older/newer games of the series.
In short, yes, I liked the game. A lot.
Definitely would recommend you to buy it although it would be nice to get the game with at least 10~25% off.
It's a pretty simple and straight foward game, you just need to go from point A to point B and kill the zombies along the way.
There are some little twists here and there, like when you'll need to hold your position and kill hordes of zombies trying to siege your position or some boss battles.
Even though all the levels are pretty much linear I really enjoyed how they were crafted specially for the use of sniper rifles. There are lots of open spaces, long corridors and high places where you'll find yourself being able to effectively shoot zombies in the head all the time.
By the way killing zombies, the central point of the game, feels nice. You may get sick of it if you play the game for more than 3~4 hours straight, though. But overall killing zombies in this game is really satisfying.
It took me about 10 hours to finish the game on normal difficulty on single player mode. The game has a lot of replayability and also a focus on co-op with 3 other players but unfortunately I don't have any friends so I can't say much about the co-op.
I'll definitely play through it again in the future.
Summing up: In spite of the game feeling incomplete, it is a great game with a lot of replayability. It may get monotonous after a while but I definitely recommend it, mainly if you enjoy sniper rifles or games like Left 4 Dead and killing floor.
If possible, buy it when it's in sale.

I got this game expecting it to be terrible, but I was pleasantly surprised.
One of the things that worried me the most was that they were changing the magick system; I thought that because magicks are so critical to gameplay, having a cooldown or being limited in the number of magicks would change everything too much, but you actually have all magicks available at once, the hotbar is only there to aid in quickcasting certain things, this way you can cast resurrection while wet etc.  Secondly, the cooldown is actually very low, especially if you do the magick the old fashioned way.  The hotbar cooldowns are independent of the normal input cooldown, so you can use the two in tandem to let off magicks really quickly.  I understand how the cooldowns can be seen as a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ but keep in mind that you get very powerful magicks from the start, so if you could spam like you could in Magicka 1, the game would be too easy.
Another thing that can be upsetting is the fact that steam and ice are not separate elements anymore, but this is honestly for the better, as the old steam-and-lightning-ray from the original Magicka made the game way too easy.  In Magicka 2 you actually have to be adaptive in how you play and use different spells to take down different enemies.
As a result, the game is much harder than the first, but I think this is honestly a good thing.  They send more varied enemies at you so you have to selectively shield yourself from different elements and you absolutely have to make use of your ability to walk an cast at the same time in order to survive.
The new system of robes and staves is also good because there aren't any overpowered robes like the cyber robe from the first game.
I actually think that despite some of my favorite things being missing, this game is actually better than the first one.  The tagline "Learn to Spell, Again" is very accurate, as this game plays completely different from the first.  One of my only complaints with the game is the number of meme jokes they put in the game.  They retained their good comedy from the first one, but they added way too many pop-culture references in between.

Full disclosure:  I'm a '70s kid.  I had superhero Underoos.  I can't really explain why, but this is my favorite video game.
First things first:  Let's discuss how terrible a port this is.  Actually - let's not.  Just scroll through the reviews and you'll see the reasons.  I do not play with a controller, so I didn't have those issues.  That being said, using the keyboard / mouse combo is nigh unplayable.  It would be great if you could map the controls so your left and right mouse buttons could be regular / strong attacks, but you can't.
Here's how I'm playing:  Use WASD to move with my left hand, with my left pinky on the ctrl button to activate powers.  I use my right hand the number pad for powers and attacks.  In my case, I use numpad #1-4, also remapping normal / heavy attacks to numpad ENTER and +.
This control configuration feels clumsy as all heck at first, but it doesn't take long for muscle memory to kick in and I've got a smooth mouse-free way of playing.
Back to the Underoos - if you grew up in the late '70s, you probably had these (or at least knew about them).  Superheroes back then were everywhere then just like they are today, but instead of AAA-quality movies, we had Lou Ferrigno, Adam West, Linda Carter, and Morgan Freeman narrating the Spider-Man skits on the "Electric Company" on PBS.  It was shallow cash-grabs and lunchbox fodder, mostly.
Fast-forward three decades or so, and I picked this game up for my PSP right before a business trip.  Omigosh - I played the HECK outta this game.  At that time, I didn't even know who half of these characters even were, let alone their backstories / origins.  This completely rekindled my interest in Comics, and I started collecting books, reading all about this varied universe, and some of the great stories Stan Lee and The Boys put together.
I then bought this game for my PS2 so I could play with my kids.
Then I bought it for the Wii... because it had a couple of characters not available on PSP/PS2.
When it was time to upgrade my PS2 for a PS3 - you guessed it, I bought it again.
And now it's on Steam.  Yup... bought it again.  Granted the asking price for this and the sequel aren't really appropriate given the game's age and quality of the port (again - all revolving around controller issues and command mapping).  Even the $30 sale package is too much - but at this point, how many times have I bought this?
The game itself plays out in ARPG/Diablo/Torchlight fashion with lots of unlockables, fun one-off comic book missions that revolve around one particular hero, their backstory, and usually of that heroes' iconic villains (Spider-Man vs. Rhino, Cap against Winter Soldier, that sort of thing).  The story spans so, SO many aspects of the Marvel Universe.  Saving the Skrull homeworld from Galactus, helping Namor reclaim Atlantis, the Inhumans on the moon, Mandarin's palace in Asia, hell (!), and the Sanctum Sanctorum, just to name a few.
You enjoying the comic-book hero resurgence?  Like ARPGs?  Want to explore the Marvel Universe and learn more about the characters?  This is your game.  For real.

Pros:
- Fun concept with very unique gameplay
- Open-World and Multiplayer
- Parkour based Indie game
- Original Characters and Worlds
- Original Soundtracks by Hideki Naganuma
- Team and Character Customization
- Leveling and Badge System
- Multilingual Support
- Controller Support
- No microtransactions or paid DLC
- Forgiving and rewarding mission systems/AI Difficulty
- Lenient Grinding system
- Races, Parkour, Grinding, Wallriding, Sliding, and Grafitti!
- Literally the "Jet Set Radio Online" we've all wanted
Cons:

- Movement controls are a bit stiff
- No in-game Friends List system (for example, if you make friends online in multiplayer, you'd have to ask them for their steam profile link in the chat, there's no in-game UI option that directs you to their steam profile)
- No Rollerblades (personal opinion, doesn't effect score)
- No Manual Jukebox Options (This game has a great sountrack, but it seems the music playlist controls itself rather than giving you the option to listen to whatever tracks you want)
Overview (tl;dr about in-depth game details):
This game does contain missions, and a storyline, but it doesn't force you to do any missions right away, hence making the open-world aspect of this game a lot more fun, however, you still need to complete missions to progress the story further. You can create multiple teams and up to 4 characters in each team. You are only given 2 character choices at the start, but unlocking the rest is fairly easy. You can mix and match many color schemes in the character customization, and even after you create your character, you can change their color schemes at any time. Each character also has their own special traits, where they have pros to some attributes, but cons to others. Tutorial is fairly short and simple, giving fundamentals of controls in the game. Every time you create and use a new character, you will have to replay the tutorial. It is not skippable. Thankfully, you can speedrun through the tutorial in about a minute. Your character can level up from 0 to 10 maximum. Every level up, they will unlock new badge slots to use. You can always check your character's Level and XP in the bottom right corner at any time of the game. You can also quickswitch to any of your other characters at any time, but there is a small cooldown when you use it. (About 10 seconds.) In addition to your characters having levels, the game also has a ranking system for your team. The higher the number, the better rank you are. The game is lenient when it comes to mission difficulty and progression, bare minimum requirements aren't too hard, but does put a challenge on you with their medals, which compliments the usage of the badge system more. The badge system allows you to upgrade aspects of your character to fit your playstyle (Speed, Jump, Grind, Hack, Strength, and Energy). There are badges that improve every attribute available, and you are allowed to choose whatever order of stats you wish. There are also Graffiti and Pet badges (so you can spray custom graffiti and have small pets follow you around wherever you go! You also have to periodically feed pets with badges as well. They will let you know when they get hungry.) When you place a badge, you are able to return it to your inventory at any time, however, if you place another badge, the previous badge slot will be locked in, and you won't be able to return that badge slot in your inventory, meaning it will be deleted, but the space will be re-opened for another badge to be equipped. This isn't a huge issue since the game is very rewarding (if you're good at speedrunning) when it comes to obtaining badges through missions. There are also multiple stations throughout the map where you can trade-up 2 to 5 junk badges for better tier badges (usually works most of the time, keep an eye on your % to get a better chance at obtaining a higher badge in the trade-up). If you wish to restart your progress at any time, you can simply delete your team and all of its members, the missions don't really change, making it easier to replay missions for a better time to get better badges. If you're not fond of online real-time multiplayer, there's always an option to change your gameplay experience to Friends-Only (if you only want to play with friends from Steam), or even Solo (and just play the game alone)! Missions have tons of variety and all depend on the person you take missions from. This includes missions such as: Racing, Chase, Delivery, Combos, etc. You can also opt to do missions solo, or with other people. The better badges you are able to obtain the more fun you will have playing the game overall, as well as having an easier time beating missions. The Combo system in this game does diminish quickly, so you gotta be constantly linking combos together for high scores. After the end of every combo, you get a score, which will give you a certain percentage of energy, energy in this game is what determines your speed (low energy = slow speed, hoverheat mode = high speed), there are areas where toxic sludge is, if you run through the sludge, it will decrease your energy and speed temporarily. Another way to obtain badges is through contains that you can scan/hack. Due to the big sizes of each map/area, there are teleporters and lots of spawn points to choose from throughout the map. Any location with a platform you can scan and a door next to it is a spawn point, all you have to do is scan it, and the game will save that location as your current spawn point. You can overwrite your spawn point to a new location at any time by simply scanning a new spawn point location. Any Teleports you take in this game (platforms with blue logos over them) will take you straight to your spawn point. (If you don't have one, it takes you back to spawn.) As you play the game generally, you'll pick it up farily quickly and notice you're already having a good time.
(If you actually read that whole thing, you get a cookie! If you just scrolled to the bottom, you're a potato!) 0w0
Conclusion:
In my own personal opinion, you need this game in your life. It is worth every cent. As a Jet Set Radio fan growing up, this is almost a perfect clone of it, if not extremely similar to it. If you were also a fan of Mirror's Edge, you may like this game, as it is parkour themed. Or, if you're just looking to try out an online real-time indie game with a completely different and unique style of gameplay compared to other games, this is one I'd definately reccomend you'd try out. Other than a few minor issues with options and UI, the gameplay is still very fluid overall. It's still a lot of fun and will keep me invested for a long time.

If you're both a Mac user and a flight simulator player like me then I'm sorry, you're screwed; X-plane is the only major platform flight sim for us, at least that I'm aware of. When I decided to uninstall Boot Camp et al for more drive space, I thought X-plane would be on par with MS Flight Simulator X. After all, most people in the sim community talk about the two games concurrently. And X-plane is very proud of how their aerodynamic models are better than those of FSX. Now, after +240 hours on X-plane, I can say that those aerodynamic models seem to have come at the cost of every other aspect of the game.
Here's the good: most of the time, you can sync real world weather into the game. Also there is a good size community of free- and pay-ware DLC too. Finally, the flight models are great. A note on that last point, from where I'm sitting they are no better than FSX for the vast majority of flying.
Here's the bad: the ATC is worse than useless. The game crashes often. The real weather updates every hour and every new map and the changes are immediate. The UI is a pain. And lastly there are errors in the weather radios.
The ATC is breathtakingly bad. Here's the bottom line up front; you either file an IFR clearance or you don't use your radios at all. There is no in between. If you aren't on an IFR plan, there are no ground controllers, no towers, no traffic, nothing at all. It’s a radio wasteland for anything but weather. When you do want to file an IFR, the overwhelming majority of the time, I cannot get it to respond at all. I've looked up online help and searched the forums, but from where I like to fly out of (KUAO) they just do not respond. It’s a complete failure, and nothing ruins the immersion more than taking off at KLAX without talking to a single controller.
The weather sync is interesting and fun, but it makes the game more unstable. It also makes flying more interesting than it needs to be. When I said, “the changes are immediate,” I meant one second the wind is 030@13 and the next moment, it’s at 240@30. It makes things very interesting indeed. I've had it go from sunny to stormy in as long as it took to read this sentence. And the manual weather UI is, along with a lot of other points in the UI, useless. Random weather? Okay but it'll be 20 degrees C most of the time. Want to see where your plane is on the world map? Okay but click anywhere on the globe and poof, your transported there, oh and at the same altitude. My An-24 (a really well done payware machine I really recommend) responds badly to being transported into the inside of a mountain. Finally, I know at least some of the AWOS channels are wrong, for example KAST gives you the weather for Olympia, WA, which is not near to the airport.
In summary, the X-plane people seemed to have focused on only one part of making a flight simulator: the flight. And it's great, it really is, however, it comes at the expense of everything else in the game. It’s hard to enjoy the flight dynamics when you're on final at KSFO with silent radios and a cross wind that just changed 180 degrees in less than a second. I think comparing X-plane to FSX is like comparing a super car and a sports car for a daily driver, let's say the Porsche 911 GT2 RS to a Porsche 911 Carrera. Both are great cars; fast, fun, and exciting. The first can do +200mph. But the second has air conditioning and a radio. Which do you think you'll use more?

I bought this game because I enjoy biology and thought it would delve into the complexities of a growing living organism and use the surrounding resources to grow and reproduce in a life cycle.
God how wrong was I... This game (if you can call it a game) should only be played if you're an infant satisfied with clicking and clicking and clicking, while you collect water and do some more clickings to get some SEEDS. Woow good job, you got seeds, which is the "currency". Don't think you can even lose or win, you just collect seeds each time you painfully play (erm, click) a level through.

Pros : this fun biologically themed resource management game From Filament is an excellent educational tool for giving students an idea of how resources influence the growth of living things, exclusively plants in this game, though some principles would be transferrable to animals in a learning/ teaching context and even in a metaphorical sense to business and enterprise. It is also appropriate as a basic starting point for discussing agricultural economics with its currency of seeds gained from successful pollinations used to buy advances in plant care to improve yields on later crops. There are two modes, one is real time Classic mode and the other turn based Strategy mode. Both provide fun educational play at faster or slower paces as the player chooses. It has pleasant horticulturally paced music and appealing graphics which successfully replicate some of the beauty of living growing plants. I am glad to see this kind of game being made because creatures like ourselves learn best when we are having fun. If learning can be made into a game we all benefit and if games teach beneficial things likewise.
Cons: the user interface is perfectly OK and works without any software bugs but in terms of pure gaming technicalities there are minor issues with mouse ergonomics in the Classic real time mode interface which restrict the pace of gameplay and can be frustrating. Even so it is quite possible to achieve the game goals with patience but I will detail the issues for this review. Specifically the info popups and animations for game goal achievements frequently interfere with mouse clicks used to direct gameplay in real time because they are opaque to mouse clicks so they get in the way. Also the mouse pointer graphical tooltips are a little slow to appear creating control lag and they also appear to shift the mouse pointer location marginally or delay its movement under user direction, enough to move it off target making clicking on a target an unnecessarily difficult and delayed process which is unfortunate given that the realtime game is played within fairly tight time constraints. This reduces the fluidity of gameplay which is an important aesthetic for the entertainment market and ultimately reduces the range of its appeal which could otherwise be more extensive as a zen timewaster for frugiform tech enthusiasts. Additional examples, grabbing bees for pollinating is a tricky process because some of the time they appear to be ungrabbable and the effectiveness of making a grab seems unpredictable making it a hit and miss process entirely due to the vicisstudes of the interface. In addition there is no way to prevent the presentation of certain tutorial systems which don't need to be seen twice eg the strategy mode info overlay and the sunflower tutorial mode dialogue, but these can be dismissed so are not showstoppers just minor inconveniences.
With that said I thoroughly enjoyed unlocking my Deluxe Toad Lily achievement and if you enjoy games and plants you cant go wrong at this price so I recommend this game for educational purposes and botanical, horti- and agri- cultural geeks.

Gue search di forum dan google, ternyata benar... seri ini bisa dibilang 'tidak terlalu' support dengan laptop. So gue musti nurunin reso sampai 800 dan LOW. Akhirnya bisa stabil di 30-40fps. Grafik: pada dasarnya suasananya bener bener terasa banget perang dunia ke dua. Bangunan hancur, gelap, dan mistis mistis begitu. Banyak juga korban perang dan berbagai macam api dari bangunan yang hancur. Detail nya juga cukup kuat, banyak banget darah dan berbagai macam ornamen seperti ketika zaman tahun 1940an, mulai dari buku-buku tua, perabotan, bentuk gedung, dan berbagai macam alat perang lainnya. Point yang paling menakjubkan adalah KILL CAM. Sensasi ketika lo menembak headshot zombie secara slow motion itu bener-bener-BENER memuaskan banget.
Gameplay: BORING! Dari awal sampai akhir tugas lo adalah mengambil senjata, mengisi peluru, dan menembak zombie. Misinya pun cuman 'disuruh kesana, ambil item, dan survive'. Dari awal game sampai akhir game begitu. Bahkan senjatanya pun tidak begitu berpengaruh. So far gue berani bilang senjatanya mirip semua. Rifle, secondary rifle, dan hand gun. Walau pun ada granade, mine, dsb buat gue gak begitu berpengaruh. Gameplay juga kurang begitu memicu adrenalin karena kebanyakan waktu adalah lo mencari tempat yang aman untuk bertahan, lalu menembaki zombie yang BERJALAN menunu diri lo. Memang sih ada beberapa zombie yang mempunyai kemampuan spesial tapi buat gue... piece of cake. OMG CONTROL-NYA SUSAH BANGET. Entah kenapa aim nya begitu susah. Heloooooo ini game sniping lho... kalau aim nya susah, gimana mau headshot? bukan karena kurang/terlalu sensitif, tapi bener bener... GAK BANGET.
Story: LAME! Cerita dari game ini bener bener sama sekali gak kuat. Gak ada background nya dan narasinya kurang. Seakan akan game ini itu membeli 'lisensi' untuk menggunakan nama NAZI lalu... selesai. Serius. Gitu doang.
Skor yang gue berikan adalah 6.
Kenapa? Karena masih cukup menghibur dengan grafik dan KILL CAM nya. Yup, pada dasarnya cuman dua itu doang yang ditawarkan oleh game ini.
Apakah pantas dibeli dengan harga $14?
BIG NO! Dengan uang segitu lo bisa membeli game yang JAUUUUUH lebih keren daripada game ini. Saran gue, lo sebaiknya membeli game ini ketika harganya didiskon hingga menjadi kurang dari $5.

So Magicka 2 is finally here..
I played through the first few chapters of the campaign, and did some challenges and trials.
Has this game changed a lot compared to Magicka 1? Yes it has.
Is it a good game nonetheless? It very much is.
So the spell system was redone, or rather, they used the system of Wizard Wars, the biggest changes being the secondary elements now taking two slots with the original elements instead of just one, (example: Steam = Fire + Water instead of just Steam) and the priority of the casting type was rearranged, (Lightning has a priority over Death/Arcane) and while this new system needs some getting used to after Magicka 1, I think it's a good change. It takes away the ability to create some of the most overpowered spells I know, and while it was a lot of fun to just wreck everything in your path with the steam beam, this way it is a lot more balanced.
Te controls are different to both Magicka 1 and Wizard Wars. and while I do think this is the best of the three games, (especially the way you can now walk while casting a spell, I'll come back on that later) It would be a good thing for this game series to just be consistent, instead of players from older games having to get used to the new controls all the time. (But hey, at least they didn't change the arrangement of the spells, that would be horrible!)
That being said, the one thing I really missed in this game is the lack of the ability to rebind your keys.. I mean.. come on..
The enemies are, in my experience, a lot harder than they used to be in Magicka 1. This is partly because there's more focus on finding the weakness of an enemy and using it against it. It takes some time to find the weaknesses, but I like this change. There isn't just one spell that kills every enemy for you. Rather you have to use different methods to defeat different enemies. Additionally, ranged enemies have much better accuracy, and I feel like enemies are made a lot faster, which really means you have to always be moving. The movement mechanic helps a lot with this, as you can now keep walking while you're casting a spell. (It also allows you to come up with some "impressive" dance moves) Overall, the enemies are a lot more challenging, and require you to actually adapt to every situation.
The new magick system is certaintly interesting, and I like how quickly I can use them now. however, (and this might just be a bug) I was unde rthe impression that if you memorized the elements needed for a certain spell, you would not have a cooldown. This however didn't work for me, and I feel like, even if not the lack of cooldown there should be some kind of "reward" for queuing up the right elements instead of mashing 1, 2, 3, or 4.
I love the addition of artifacts. it allows you to play the game in so many different ways. I haven't finished the campaign yet, but if when I do, I can do it again with the artifacts I've unlocked, and I would experience it in a whole new way. I like the trials a lot too, though similar to the challenge mode, it sets different goals, for example defeating an enemy within a  certain time span. This further allows the game to remain interesting even after the campaign is beaten.
Finally, how can you talk about Magicka without mentioning all the hilarious easter eggs? In my opinion they're just as fun as Magicka 1. And I've had a lot of fun finding them. This really brings a lot of humor to the game, and makes it that much better!
So what do I think of this game?
Pro's:
- Great spellcasting mechanics which balances the game out A LOT compared to Magicka 1.
- The movement mechanics. Especially the ability to walk while casting.
- Challenging enemies which require you to find their weakness and adapt to every situation.
- Artifacts!
- Hilarious easter eggs
Cons:
- Controls need getting used to
- Lacks the ability to rebind keys
- No reward for memorizing magicks
Do I recommend this game? Yes. Although, it has to be said that Magicka 1 players might have trouble getting used to the changes. Players from Magicka Wizard Wars, will have less trouble adapting to this, however, it is still a different game.
As a player of both Magicka 1 and Magicka Wizard Wars I can say that though it might need some getting used to, this game is just as amazing as the other two Magicka games, and I guarantee you will have fun with this if you can look past the changes they made from the original Magicka. and may even come to the conclusion that the changes are not as bad as a Magicka 1 player first getting it's hands on this game might think.

I payed approximately £50 into the game and I was top of the leaderboards for about the first week and was also the first person to own a full set Tragedy, this was mainly due to the amount of time I put into the game and days I went without sleep. But soon the people who had played a lot less and payed a lot more surpassed me on both the leaderboards and gear (which is where i decided to quit). It is true that you can play this game without spending a penny on any microtransactions you will never be able to be competative.
Okay now that that's out of the way I'll talk about some of the other Issues I have with the game and more so the Dev team. Shortly after release the Seadrift server went down for maintanence which was supposed to last for 4 hours, It lasted for almost 24 hours, and when the maintanence was finally over and players were able to log back into their server they were appaulled to find that their characters had been lost. All their hardwork, time and dedication were just completely gone. Seeing as this was a new launch we all expected their to be some issues but when this happened not once but twice in the space of 2 days that was just a joke. After people lost all their stuff they quickly rushed to get back to the end-game content and start working towards their gear all over again just to have it ripped away once more, this is totally unacceptable for a fully released game.
Gender locking. Don't do it game devs...
Although those Issues are awful they're basically the only problems I had with the game apart from the lack of quests, lore and crafting the rest I really enjoyed and felt this was the kind of game I'd been looking for.

I really wanted to like this game. As a fan of the Jet Set Radio franchise since the release of the original Dreamcast game, I LOVE these types of games. However, Hover: Revolt of Gamers is a very frustrating experience.
First and foremost, the game lags badly even though my computer exceeds the system requirements, and for a game that requires split-second button presses and movement, it makes the game near-unplayable right off the bat. The world is very large and could probably benefit from being split into separate areas considering there are missions that make you go to certain waypoints that just show up as some random box somewhere in the world, you may spend many tries just figuring out which route actually leads to the waypoint before being able to complete the mission. I will say that the controls are pretty tight and responsive, and when you find an area where you can do contiguous trick combos, the game feels great. The problem is that the level design is poorly thought out; many of the routes in the game just lead to dead-ends or walls you have to climb up to access other areas, making moving around pedantic, when it's supposed to be the most fun part of the game.
The quests you do with the characters have cringe-worthy dialogue and just make you do repetitive tasks over and over. For some reason the devs thought it would be a good idea to introduce stealth elements in the game which are just maddeningly annoying. You may be running from one place to another, perhaps in a timed quest, and turn a corner and see a security camera which will then block your path for a good ten seconds for no reason. If the security guards or police or whatever they're supposed to be do catch you, you just get frozen in place for about five seconds. Why needlessly kill the momentum in a fast-paced game? I can understand certain quests being stealth-focused, but having these elements randomly scattered around the world is just poor judgement.
Lastly, there are so many tiny nitpicky problems that it makes me wonder if this game was sufficiently play-tested. Scrolling on the menus after a mission is extremely slow, you have to "scan" everything in the game to interact with it (including talking to people), missions will randomly abort right after you start them, the graffiti is completely underutilized and feels like it was tacked on to appeal to JSR fans, etc.

Before I start my review, the movement isn't really that bad. It does move in the direction you go in. I don't see the problem. Anyway, with that out of the way, here:
This is definitly worth calling a good free-roam game.
This is set place in a neon colored city in which has floating vehicles rushing around, and looks very busy. You can also noticed that this has JetSet Radio vibes, considering the style, your character, wall-sliding, etc.
The character designs are interesting, too. Some faces are masked (I don't know if it's from the hood they're wearing or just their face in general but it's pretty anonymous), but you can tell they're robots, but some of which are basically creatures. One of your main priorities is the scanning system. It fits with the style yet you'd half to get use to it for the whole game, which starts to feel a bit tedious and makes you think why it should just be a normal communication system. You can also use it to spraypaint on walls, floors, etc., and you can unlock these by scanning these barrel-thingies or just doing missions. That's another thing too-- the missions aren't half bad. You can race, maybe deliever something for someone, you know, usual mission stuff.
Like I mentioned, what seperates this from JetSet Radio is the futuristic style and the neon colors. There on a lot of things, but no so bright nor common that it feels like you're watching some Nick show. And, AlienWare users, I don't know if this is from the game or what, but when your characters' color changes, the color on your PC changes too. It's so weird. If this is only me please let me know. And, finally, the music is pretty cool too if you're a fan of electro. You can even buy the soundtrack if you want.
As for cons, besides the scanning stuff, the graphics might have some problems depending on how powerful your PC is. If there are frames dropping, and it's pretty difficult to play because of this, you might wanna put on the low graphics setting in options, and becareful for multiplayer if this is the case. Especially in multiplayer, which you can do co-op and stuff.
To end this review off, all I gotta say is if you finished JetSet Radio and you loved the game, I reccomend playing this and giving it a try. And like I mentioned, this is a good game in my book.

Such an old classic that, prior to me getting it on Steam, thought it was virtually not known at all. Played it first when I was young, as my dad had it. I was super happy when I actually saw it come to Steam. Definitely one of the early games of the FPS-RPG genre, if not the original. Graphics like Doom, but a semi-open world to explore and interact with in whichever way you really choose. I'd say this would be like a more sci-fi version of Elder Scrolls 1 and 2, albeit a bit more limited than those games.

It's a good FPS-Adventure that was a nice change of pace from the normal way back when, and still holds up today. Provided that you're fine with the graphics.
Gameplay is your standard Doom 1-style run-and-strafe-and-gun first-person shooter. But it also has some adventure elements, in that you can walk around towns, talk to people, and buy equipment.
The Veteran Version fixes a bug with one quest where, if you accept it & get the item, you're essentially locked out of ~1/3 of the game. I won't spoil what quest that is because of that, to leave it up to you to make your own mistakes.
I haven't gotten far enough in the game to see if some of the robots still attack you regardless whether you've done anything wrong in their general vicinity or not, though.
Still, do be careful not to fire a weapon in town, or else every guard will be after you. A lot of the enemies can and will hit you hard, even on lower difficulties, and your two main weapons (the Knife and Crossbow) are relatively weak.
One thing I found real annoying is that a lot of choices the game gives you are "But thou must" moments. Meaning you're not allowed to say no, unless you don't want to progress the story. At least the Veteran Version doesn't make all the guards aggro you when you say "no," now. That, or they just outright removed the option to say "no," like to the Resistance leader, for example.
Some areas can be excessively maze-like; narrow and off-putting, like the requisite Sewers, but otherwise are open with lots of nooks and crannies to explore for ammo and equipment.
The story is your typical dystopian future kind of setting; meteors, ruling class which hoards most of the world's remaining technology and uses it to enslave the rest of the people.
This version even includes the blurb about your character's role prior to starting the game that used to only be in the instruction manual! Nice touch, there.
You start out helping the resistance, but can switch to helping the Big Bads in charge later on, lending itself to an alternate ending.
The graphics are on par with the original Doom, with several options to make the edges look less jagged and add more detail to light sources and so on. The sky looks a lot better now compared to the original game.
The controls are your standard adjustable-mapping keyboard interface for FPSes, with the option to use your mouse to aim and shoot, or use a controller if you really want one.
I found one thing you need to be careful about is using the Left Mouse Button as your Confirmation Button, as it's also your Attack Button. Almost stabbed the odd NPC or two with an accidental double click.
If you're using your mouse as to aim (which I don't know WHY you wouldn't), I recommend switching the Run key (default: right Shift) to another option. One more... easily reached by your left hand.
The music throughout the game is good. There's a handful of tracks that really stood out for me, but most just kind of blended into the scenery. Nothing stood out as being completely horrible, though.
Overall, I say the game is worth the purchase. If you're not sure if the game's right for you, then do more research on your own. Look at more screenshots, maybe a video or two about it, or read some of the other reviews. Or don't. It's up to you.

Pros:
-> Good and accurate flight model for a desktop simulator.
-> Visual capabilities are much more advanced than other desktop simulators.
-> Informative for simulator hobbyists, hobbyist pilots and students.
-> Navigation system (radio signals, gps simulators, autopilots) work good and feel close to the real thing.
-> Keybinding system is very easy to configure and well thought.
Cons:
-> Sound system and stock aircraft audio effects are mediocre and sometimes annoying (repetitive sounds, cracks and pops). There are plugins that enhance the audio of x-plane but why should the user be forced to buy them?
-> Stock aircraft contain unfinished and lackluster aircraft. The buyer expects all stock aircraft to be in excellent condition.
-> User interface is somewhat unfriendly and there are no built-in tutorials for beginners.
-> The advanced flight model which makes this simulator stand out among others, also needs a powerful system to be simulated perfectly. The flight model is tied to the framerates of rendering and when the simulation time is accelerated autopilot may function wrongly which makes accelerated intercontinental flights dangerous.

I have spend this Friday evening playing Reach for the Sun. I usually like simulators and calm, “cosy” games so I thought that Reach of the Sun might suit me. And yes, I got some entertainment out of it but unfortunately not more than that. You can tell that the game is made to educate and that a skilled gamer is not the target audience. After two hours I had played through the game in its entirety and had nothing left to try.
The main purpose of the game is to teach the player about photosynthesis, pollination, and what the different parts of the plant are used for. They have succeeded well in that perspective. Besides that, Reach for the Sun has a pleaseant appearance, a smooth gameplay and nice ambient music. There are also two modes: Classic; where you click your way to resources as fast as you can, and Strategy; which is turn based and thus works better for the players who need more time to read, think, and plan.
Worth to mention is that the game only has support for English in case you are considering buying it for a younger gamer.
The conclusion? Nothing for me, but maybe for younger players.

What I was greeted with when playing SE:NZA was a ridiculously accurate ballistics simulator wrapped in a suitably gory and satisfying package. I cannot tell you how great it feels to watch a zombie's skull crack open after slamming a 7.62x54R round into its temple. This game has a lot of stuff going for it: Cute artstyle, descent platforming, fun gameplay overall. But the overwhelmingly positive score is misleading.
The game is far from perfect.
The game possessed a number of frustrating bits/design flaws, that really spoiled the engagement.
1) I will start of with the worst: In order to get the true ending (which you definitely should strive for) you need to find all cacklebats (type of secret). Problem is, sometimes they are so well hidden that is seems almost impossible to find them without luck. For example, in one area you have to hit a wall while charging, and the cacklebat drops from the sky. There are no markings on the wall whatsoever and it you can't hear or see the cacklebat. How am I suppose to know that will happen?
2) Enemies appear when they are off screen for 2 seconds. Why? Why can't they appear again once I leave the area? Some enemies work that way, but others don't for some reason.
3) Enemies appearing at the same spot you're at. You're just trying to jump from one branch to the other and a ghost appears right in front of you, giving you no time to react. This isn't a huge problem, but it's just unnecessary design.
4) They don't always introduce new mechanics in the best way (apart from gear). There are some platforms that you can shoot and they will do something. Uhm, since when does this happen? There is nothing indicating that something should happen if you hit them.
5) Backtracking. Remember the small rock in the corner that prevented you from going in that direction? Well now that you have the gear, 2 hours later, you can and must go there. You don't remember because you took a break for a day? Tough luck. Some characters do point you to the island you need to go, but this problem could've been tackled much better.
6) Bog island first 3 screens :P
The positives outweigh the negatives, and some type of frustration is good to have if it makes you get good at the game. But these are mainly design flaws that take away from the experience which makes it a good platformer, but not very very good one.

This is truly an unpolished gem of a game. Putting aside the glitches that the remastered edition introduced, Marvel: Ultimate Alliance had plenty of problems already. There's nothing painful enough to stop you from enjoying yourself, but there are constantly things that just don't work right. Body parts tend to phase through each other, dialogue sound cuts out randomly, and enemies will bounce off the invisible edges of endless pits. I think I even finished the final battle by pushing the boss through a wall. The ridiculousness adds an unintentional layer of humor which fits well in a comic book adaptation. You're already being tossed from one unconnected location to the next with only a paper-thin plot to tie them together, and character conversations seem to be ripped straight from Wikipedia. But none of that matters as long as the action is there, and it is. There's an endless parade of various minions to pummel and an equally diverse list of moves to do it with. Characters can be customized with skill points and abilities as well as costumes that have their own set of boosts, all of which have to be earned and developed. Characters can only have three abilities at a time - not counting the Xtreme move particular to each character which can't be switched out - and groups can only have four heroes at a time, so there's a certain strategy to your choices. Simulator disc missions often place characters alone, revealing their personal strengths. The journey is also peppered with side quests, adding ramifications to the player's decisions which are explored in a cleverly presented epilogue.
Strangely enough, filling the playable character roster with actual Marvel heroes does seem to have acted as a double-edge sword. In many places, the plot would have made more sense if Fury's 'Team' was made up of player-created heroes. When it's mentioned that the X-men have done this or the Fantastic Four did that, it seems silly that Storm and the Thing are standing right there, doubly so when Cyclops asks Professor Xavier who he is. The times when characters do have special dialogue with someone they have a relationship with are pretty special though and the charm of hearing familiar catchphrases or looking through generations-old costumes would be missed.
There's a lot to love here and about as much to hate. For every time Ultimate Alliance endears a player with its respect for decades of background, another AI-controlled character irritates by randomly jumping off a cliff or just stopping in their tracks entirely. If you think you can look past the game's many flaws, there's plenty of simple comic book-y fun to be had.

This game's literally my childhood. Literally.
I remember first playing this game on my cousin's PlayStation 2, back in 2007. I absolutely fell in love with it. Spider-Man was the only hero for me, while my cousin used Deadpool (which at the time we had no idea who he was, but we thought he looked badass). I found a video called: ''Marvel Ultimate Alliance All characters and ultimate team''. Halfway throuh the video, I took notice of some extra characters he had, such as Venom, Magneto, and Hulk. After some more research, I discovered the game had a ''Gold'' edition. Which contained 8 extra characters. Since I owned a PS3 at the time, I didn't have the chance to play with them. Until last year.
Reasons for being the best version out there:
*All DLC characters
*1080p and higher resolutions
*Controller support (I played the whole game with a PS4 controller)
*60 FPS (PCMR exclusive)
I totally recommend this game. Especially if you're a Marvel/RPG fan.

One Thousand Lies is a free kinetic novel, so I thought I would pick it up for the (easy-to-get) achievement. However that eventually became secondary, as the story gave a very lasting impression on its own merits.
It starts off slow, and sometimes launches into large amounts of exposition when the characters were discussing their perspectives. The extensive vocabulary used was sometimes difficult to follow, and I was tempted to skip them and advance the plot, but fortunately did not as they provide insight into each characters' personalities and allow the reader to be emotionally invested in them, setting the context for the later parts of the story. Puns, hidden meanings and references also kept the dialogue entertaining and helped offset the pace somewhat. The music helped to set the tone for the scenes in the prologue but I turned them off afterwards and therefore cannot comment any further.
The conclusion was not satisfying as it still left several loose ends unresolved and raised a few questions, so be sure to read the extra chapter that is unlocked afterwards (which is required for the achievement anyway). However, I had to head to the discussions for the final "truth" behind the story and to fill in certain gaps I had while reading (I did not complete the novel in one sitting).
One Thousand Lies is a well-written story that is almost certain to give some "feels" upon completion. Not requiring any monetary sacrifice makes the novel much more accessible, so you should read it if you like plot twists, humour and mind♥♥♥♥s, and have a few hours to properly give the attention it deserves.

As featured on the Jimquisition, this pathetic excuse of a game is made using the generally unreliable Gameguru engine and is very bare bones in features: for starters, there are only a few levels in the game and they all repeat, all in a sparsely decorated house,  with occassional annoying and often random NPCS popping up in the levels.
Here are a couple of facts about the game that you should know:

Weapons:
In addition to the slingshot with plenty of ammo, you also have access to a pistol and shotgun from enemies along with a bow found in the first level, the shotgun is absolutely worthless due to its extremely short range, with the bow having very limited ammo and being too slow to use effectively. Meaning you'll be relying primarily on the slingshot and pistol for most of the game, with the pistol allowing for precise aim with iron sights.
Gameplay:
The absolute WORST part of the game has to be the overpowered superhuman soldiers that you'll encounter in the game, most often they will be able to detect you through walls and will spasmodically jitter about warping from place to place and converge on your location once you're detected, and they have pinpoint perfect aim which depletes your health almost instaneously, in addition to being able to kick you from afar like they have telekinesis. The only real strategy to defeating these enemies without losing a life is to either snipe them from behind or afar, shooting at their clipped limbs from the wall (meaning the game becomes whack-a-mole with hands and feet) or more tactically, slicing the pie at around every corner and doorway, carefully clearing out enemies. Thankfully there are plenty of health packs avaiable in the levels, but they won't help you much aside from making you last a second longer.
Overall:
This game is just a mere trashy student game that is being charged for 99 cents on Steam and in terms of value, its VERY poor even at that price, do not play if you are looking for a good game, or even for something silly, as this game is just simply NOT fun to play.

Jet Set Radio this isn't, but this is by no means a bad thing.
Hover is a good game - for an indie development studio, I would say even very good. Don't come in expecting million-dollar budget triple-A flashiness and mechanical depth of the Mariana Trench. What you get, however, is a well-polished and solid mechanic for getting around town at blazing speed. The moveset isn't by all means terribly complicated or convoluted, in fact I would actually call it simple - but in that simplicity it just feels natural, in a way, to zip around the open world areas. For what reason? No big reason, it's just that fun to lose yourself to your own personal pathfinding.
In a way, Hover's all about that. Unlike the game that inspired it, the core gameplay loop of this game is the rapid movement and pathfinding. Nearly all things to do revolve around getting from point A to point B in the most efficient (or least efficient and most fabulous) way possible, sometimes carrying something with you. Of course, there are various collectibles, a ton of them in fact, but their relevance is just that - optional. Spraying graffiti will be something done in the spur of the moment rather than your primary objective.
Hover is also
. As you level up and gather essentially "mods" that increase your various stats in different ways (faster movement speed, higher jumps, less sliding friction, etc.), you can optimize yourself for various challenges the game throws at you, but even then earning those silver and gold medals (or simple and shiny, as the game calls them) is nothing to scoff at. You'll find yourself restarting a race plenty of times to nail down the timing to the utmost just to make ends meet and get to the finish line at the last three seconds to spare. Or maybe you'll find another route alltogether? Many challenges are set in the open world with loose frequency of checkpoints, letting you scuttle around alternate paths at your leisure.
To sum up, I recommend this game. It's not JSR, don't expect it to be JSR - but in the modern time, so far, it's the next best thing. Hover is a solid, interesting game that manages to charm people with its varied level design and the plethora of ways to get around.

This is awesome.
I only played Jet Set Radio once or twice, so I can't comment too much on how it relates, but... This game is basically a throwback to the old-school games of PS1, with the difficulty and learning curve to match. The game doesn't really hold your hand, and expects you to figure out how to get to where you need to go on your own. Of course, they do use clever tricks like using mission races to show you around a given area, so that you have to use what you learned doing the race to come back to that spot later.
Graphics are awesome. I read that some people are having difficulty with running it with a solid framerate, but I've got a stock GTX 750ti, 16 GB of RAM, an i7 2600 and I don't have any issues.
Music is just the best. Like I said up there, it's basically 90s racer music - think 1080, SSX Tricky, JSR, Ridge Racer, etc... Or if you're too young for that, think more like Persona 3 type music. And then throw in some DDR in there as well.
There's a lot of things to explore and things to collect, but unlike certain games (cough) Assassin's Creed (cough) it doesn't feel like a chore or like something you HAVE to do. Different areas have different musics, but the music also changes when a race takes place.
One of the more enjoyable aspects of the game is the multiplayer - even if you're not playing directly against / with someone, it's still cool to just flip around and just watch other people. Multiplayer interaction itself is based around doing missions / races / "game ball" games. There are a few missions where having a partner can come in handy, as well.
The game is hard. Really hard. Like PS1 hard, and not because of any control issues. As fun as it is just bouncing around and doing tricks, the game doesn't use kid gloves when it comes to giving you a task. There's no path-finding line to follow - you've got a point to move towards, an arrow at the bottom of the screen, and the rest is up to you. I've found myself pulling off genuinely difficult tricks and bounces just to squeeze an extra 5 seconds off the clock.
... of course, that was before I started using the rewind function. Happily, if you're like me and are repeatedly falling off the edges of tall buildings, the rewind button will save you. It basically works like Braid's rewind function, except that it does not in fact rewind time (and the game will remind you of this, for good reason). Not using the rewind button for so long had definitely taught me the best ways to go about the courses, but using it now pretty much removes most of the utter frustration I was having when I missed a jump and had to restart a mission over. :P
There are a few mechanics that are not explained super well in-game. Or rather, they may be explained, but there's no real emphasis on how a given mechanic comes into play. Certain things like tricks aren't really gone over very well - at one point, a character tells you to do "figures" to build points and then charge a generator with them. I don't really know what they meant by "figures," but they could have meant figure-eights, because you can kind of grind / skate... However, what information / tooltips they DO have is really well done, however.
For example, on the Character mod screen, the game helpfully points out that if you try to stack a certain stat with multiple chips of the same kind, then those chips will begin to give diminishing returns. Good to know, right? You might've also noticed that some of the nodes on the grid are connected in a different way than the other nodes, but didn't see anything else indicating that they're different. They don't stand out in such a way that says "Hey, I matter". But, when I actually hovered over it, awesome, it told me exactly what they meant. Luckily, you can also reset chips. Another thing that helped was having veteran players hanging around, helping out, and answering questions. (Thanks, Y1n!)
I've come across a possible mission bug, a keybinding bug, and a small translation quirk, but other than that, the game has run fine for me. A note about controls - I'm usually a guy who likes to play games with a controller when I can, but the mouse and keyboard seemed better suited to fast movements and look directions, so I used those.
One final thing regarding progression: The game uses a sort of RPG progression system for individual characters. Basically, you level your character up by getting points, doing tricks, etc. Leveling up gives you skill slots. Then you have to collect skill mods to actually utilize your level-ups. It seems like to get the better times, you need better equipment, so it pans out well in terms of progression.
Long story short, it's an awesome game with a retro-modern feel that's a bit obtuse on the finer points, but a fun, smooth experience overall. (Seriously, even if you have no idea what you're doing at the beginning, it looks / feels awesome just running around.)

This game likes to wear the mantle of Jet Set Radio's soul successor proudly. I don't mean that it's a blatant copy of Jet Set Radio, but it dealt with a lot of the same themes JSR did: Corrupt government, supression of freedoms, etc. And this atmosphere also loans itself to the gameplay. Everyone acts like it's Jet Set Radio strictly from the game's feeling. Hover is indeed its own entity though. It plays a lot differently, being more open-world based and with an upgrade system. It also lacks rollerblades and relies instead on a system of running and grinding, and doing aerial tricks. While the aerial tricks and grinding are similar, there's only SO MUCH you can do with that concept.
The game is divided into three factions: Gamers, Breakers, and the E-Cops. The last one is self-explanatory: Cops.
Gamers and Breakers are the two groups who fight these police, with the distinction between the Breakers being a disregard for peace, resorting to violence. The game has a good feeling to it, and is very pleasing in most ways. The only issues I had with the game were as follows:
Dreadful NPCs in some required missions.
Some missions being a massive ramp-up in difficulty.
Some missions being downright cruel with their timer.
Mind you none of it makes the game "Unplayable," but it will provide a great difficulty for some.
Pets also have the annoying habit of being there as stat boosts that you must keep feeding, or risk them dying off. If you're lacking in food to feed your Ultimate-tier pet and retain its boosts, you will lose it permanently. The food meter also drops incredibly quick. I was able to finish three missions within five minutes or so, and had gone from a pet with a full stomach to starving. This was rather annoying as I had to frantically scour the overworld for chests and play a miniature game of "Click twice as fast as you can to navigate the UI." but the pets never really do much otherwise.
The game also boasts a fairly fun gamemode if played with other players: Gameball. Now read carefully: IF PLAYED WITH OTHER PLAYERS. The NPCs have two settings in this game for this mode: Dumber than a sack of bricks, or NBA Pro. Often the ones on your team reside in the former category, with enemies sitting in the circle for the latter. The missions essentially boil down to bumper-cars and keeping NPCs (FROM BOTH TEAMS) away from the ball. I had to spend the majority of these missions scoring as many points as I could for a medal rank, and then play Keep-Away as to prevent the NPCs from making a comeback that would put any pro basketball player to shame.
Ranks are the progression system for the story, but it's fairly easy to keep your rank at the required level, so don't worry. The problem you'll be facing is with what chips you get, but this is also circumvented with the chip traders and replaying of missions.
I wish there was more meat to the story though. The game ends after a certain point and.... Well... It's an ending that I would rather have forgotten, especially after the PENULTIMATE DIFFICULTY the game provides at the end of the line. Story-wise, the game is short. 10 hours is what it took me, and this is with waiting for my turn online or scrambling to find a team to help me deal with the NPC issue as previously stated. It's a good game on its own, but I hope the developers bring more to come, otherwise this game may see a drop in players after they all beat the main story and get ultimate chips for each slot. The game DOES allow players to make their own missions for others, but I haven't seen anyone truly use that system to its full utility.
I would definitely play this game again, start to finish, and with some characters requiring others to unlock, it's a welcomed method by the game. Hover: Revolt of Gamers brings back the vibes that Jet Set Radio begun with, and with Hideki Naganuma's music in the game. (Currently at the time of writing: Only two songs.) But on its own, stepping out of JSR's shadow: the game is also very fun. Hopefully the developers don't stop here and keep bringing forth content! It would be a welcomed venture in my book.
But seriously, Gameball's NPCs will make you grind your teeth.

Strife: Veteran Edition.
A really good game in my book, it's essentially built off of DOOM's engine and has solid combat, story, and mechanics that really go together.
In Strife, you play as a mercenary / soldier / freedom fighter working for an organization known as the Front. See, some years back a gigantic super comet crashed into your planet and unleashed a virus onto your species. Most died - suffering the effects of destructive seed. But those who didn't - became mutated. These mutants now hear the voice and will of some sort of god who helps guide them.
Now, these religious fanatics have revolutionary technology, science, and a God-Emperor who imposes their will onto your people. You now live under the tyranny of mad beings. Your enemies are cybernetic mutants who wear bulking armor and hunt down any who oppose the will of their mad god. They've literally  r ap e d your women to build their numbers ten fold. They've stolen your children so they can be brainwashed into a dark cult.
These vile beings call themselves the Order.
You and your fellow man have been driven underground. But you're not going to go down without a fight. It doesn't matter how many minions they have. It's time for action. Weapons are being built. Soldiers are being trained. The revolutionary thought of Man has been reborn in spirit. It is time for action.
It's time for a rebellion.
It's time for a revolution.
It's time for
STRIFE!
Think DOOM. Seriously, just think DOOM. The shooting mechanics are pretty similiar and solid, each weapon feels impactful and when you hit your enemy it has that same sort of feeling. The animations, sprites, it all comes together to have that idea of kicking alien mutated cultist♥♥♥♥♥and look good doing it.
Your weapons range from a petty knife to a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥i n g god killer. In the beginning you start with a knife before meeting a contact. Then he gives you a crossbow with an electric twist ontop of the arrow itself. It's actually pretty cool and when firing it you kind get a feel for the game's "Physics". After that, you later make your way up to an Assault Rifle that feels pretty good to shoot. When firing it - it has this feeling of rippling through your enemy. Later, you can get a flamethrower and torpedo cannon to raise havoc.
But what the hell are you shooting? Good question. Like I said, they're essentially religious fanatics that have been augmented with cybernetics and mutated by a goddamn comet with a god complex. In other words..., they're the Inquisition.
You'll first notice your first line of enemies:
The Minions. They're the Order's Secret Police and are charged with maintaing the status quo. Usually, you'll see them guard the hubworld and work under political officials who are trying to make it in this oppressive society. They carry large shields that cover half of their bodies and fire assault rifles while firing. They're pretty intimidating and are generally the Order's Imperial Guard but badass. Easily my favourite retro game, and I say that knowing all the classics by ID, Apogee and 3DRealms through and through. It has everything it possibly could - enthralling setting (techno-fantasy postapocalypse with guns, castles and cyborg templars as your enemies - could it ever get more awesome?!) great story (there are some illusoric choices - that's bad, but forgiveable - and some that can block the way for you, which is actually brilliant. No modern game ever did that!), a wide array of cool guns to put your hands on, multiple endings...
And a really, really sexy sidekick. Yeah, she's just a voice in your comm, but man, what a voice it is!
Weapons you get seem gimmicky - among which there's an assault rifle that is a good all-rounder but rips through your ammo reserves like crazy, a plasma shotgun which is cool but even worse in this aspect, a grenade launcher that is really easy to blow yourself up with, a psionic relic that shoots thunder and lightning at the expense of your own health (and gets more and more powerful with each big bad you murder)... And a dagger that in your capable hands is able to turn enemies into red mist. All of these require careful inventory management and take some actual skill to aim and fire.
Managing your health is even more important - you can buy more medical supplies for gold, but there's never enough of both. All in all, on higher difficulty levels Strife really offers a challenge.
It's a pseudo-open world - sort of, as locations are opened to you one by one as story progresses. You are able to revisit, and some of the levels are purely optional. By the end, the game does get a little crazy with numbers of enemies set against you which seems a bit tedious, but the story is about enough compelling to keep you moving forward.
Strife was way ahead of its time, but went through in the shadow of other, louder titles, despite being so much better than most of them. It just isn't right to leave it here, forgotten, unknown. If you enjoy old school FPSes, you simply cannot pass on this one. I beg you - please, wield the Sigil of the One God, defeat the Order, save us all.

It’s especially impressive when you consider that Ndemic Creations, the developer of the entire thing, is just one man.
The premise of Plague Inc: Evolved is as simple as ever: you’re a disease, and your goal is to infect and kill everyone on the entire planet. If you actually stop to think about it it’s incredibly bleak, but it’s executed with such skill and attention to detail that you don’t – you scheme, theorise, and try to predict global responses, whilst ignoring the news ticker that tells you Canada’s government has fallen. It makes a change from playing as the civilised government in question in a common strategy game.
A very unique concept - superbly intertaining strategic title.. and a little scary!!! Absolutely one ne of a kind!

Sniper Elite Nazi Zombie Army came out one year later than Sniper Elite V2. Its working on the same engine, even though graphic is quite different.
The story is... below average, but, do you even need good a story to enjoy shooting nazi zombies?!  Anyway, story goes like this: The WW2 is almost over, allies are closing to the Berlin, but Hitler won't surrender that easily (of course). In his last attempt to save Germany he executes plan Z, that awakens the undead. That's the whole story pretty much.
The gameplay is based on: killing zombies, surviving the zombie sieges, getting some relic, and getting to the safe room to rearm and start repeating the whole process. There is one boss, but you will battle him twice. There are couple type of the undead:
1. zombies- they aren't too dangerous and are quite slow, but can (and probably will) revive if you don't shoot them in the head
2. skeletons- quite fast, hitting quickly, they do quite of damage, but have low health
3. suicide zombies- they just scream and run towards you with a grenade to blow you up (can be dangerous for whole team)
4. gunner- does a LOT of damage with his machine gun and has a lot of health
And no, there isn't zombie Hitler.
Bullet and xray killcam are here, but since this is rather fast game, when lots of enemies show up, you aren't gonna use your scope too much. The whole game has 6 levels and will last somewhere around 5-6 hours on regular difficulty.
pros: different zombies to kill, fun with friends, price
cons: story, often repetition and predictability
So, I would recommend you this game if you plan to play it with friends. Otherwise, you might wanna hold with purchase.

This game has a lot of stuff going for it: Cute artstyle, descent platforming, fun gameplay overall. But the overwhelmingly positive score is misleading.
The game is far from perfect.
The game possessed a number of frustrating bits/design flaws, that really spoiled the engagement.
1) I will start of with the worst: In order to get the true ending (which you definitely should strive for) you need to find all cacklebats (type of secret). Problem is, sometimes they are so well hidden that is seems almost impossible to find them without luck. For example, in one area you have to hit a wall while charging, and the cacklebat drops from the sky. There are no markings on the wall whatsoever and it you can't hear or see the cacklebat. How am I suppose to know that will happen?
2) Enemies appear when they are off screen for 2 seconds. Why? Why can't they appear again once I leave the area? Some enemies work that way, but others don't for some reason.
3) Enemies appearing at the same spot you're at. You're just trying to jump from one branch to the other and a ghost appears right in front of you, giving you no time to react. This isn't a huge problem, but it's just unnecessary design.
4) They don't always introduce new mechanics in the best way (apart from gear). There are some platforms that you can shoot and they will do something. Uhm, since when does this happen? There is nothing indicating that something should happen if you hit them.
5) Backtracking. Remember the small rock in the corner that prevented you from going in that direction? Well now that you have the gear, 2 hours later, you can and must go there. You don't remember because you took a break for a day? Tough luck. Some characters do point you to the island you need to go, but this problem could've been tackled much better.
6) Bog island first 3 screens :P
The positives outweigh the negatives, and some type of frustration is good to have if it makes you get good at the game. But these are mainly design flaws that take away from the experience which makes it a good platformer, but not very very good one.

As a botanist and a gamer, Reach for the Sun makes me feel both sad and embarassed. It's not a fun game; it's not a good learning tool; and the lessons that it does teach are often wrong. Yet, somehow, this game has won multiple awards, and the fact of those awards really does make me sad. To give this game an award is to suggest that this is the best we can do. That suggestion is disrespectful to science, because science has huge potential for fun (e.g. Kerbal Space Program). It's also disrespectful to gamers, and to our proven ability to create great games.
The most obvious problem is that the gameplay is all about clicking - even in strategy mode, it's all about the clicking.
A much bigger problem is that, as a player, you have very little agency. You can't just grow your plant in whatever way you like. Instead, each plant has a predetermined fully-grown shape, a shape that was fixed by the developers at compile time. When you add new parts to a plant, you're really just unlocking bits of that predetermined shape. This means that the game is much more about memorization than it is about botany or tactics. To be successful, you need to learn the shape of the fully-grown plant, and then figure out the series of choices that will allow you to most quickly unlock all of the parts of your plant.
As a botanist, I teach that plants must adapt themselves to their environment by making choices about how they will grow. If a seed lands in an unfortunate place, it can't simply pick itself up and go somewhere else, but must instead grow where it lies. For example, a bush on a rocky cliff may grow short and squat to protect itself from cold and wind; while a bush in a shady glade may grow tall and slim to try and reach above its neighbors, and grab a bigger share of sunlight. Thus, the idea that each species of plant has a fixed shape (an idea implicitly taught by this game) is false and misleading.
Another big flaw in the game is the lack of differentiation among species. While there are several different species in this game, from a gameplay standpoint, they're pretty much the same. As a gamer, I find this boring. As a botanist, I find it offensive. The joy and beauty in life and biology come from from the huge variety of shapes, colors, and behaviors that are present in nature. To teach otherwise, as this game does, is a terrible lie.
If you're looking for a bit of variety in your procrastination, something to give you a break from Peggle or Candy Crush, then you may find a bit of enjoyment in this game. If you're looking for something with replay value or educational value, you should look elsewhere.

This is one of the most criminally-underrated shooters ever made. The game manages to fully immerse the player in the Star Wars universe without using Jedi, force powers, or any other hallmarks typical of the Star Wars franchise. This is a tactical first-person shooter played from the perspective of a Clone Trooper, one of the expendable "mooks" who drop like flies in the movies and are predecessors to the Stormtroopers, the ultimate "disposable bad guy." Each member of the squad is a clone, but they behave with distinctive personalities and voices that make you actually care about them.
The game has a fairly good difficulty curve, with the game gradually spacing bacta tanks and ammo dumps farther and farther apart as the game progresses without becoming noticeable. You will need to use teamwork to knock out larger enemies like spider droids, which are almost impossible to down with the limited grenade launcher ammo you have. To drive the importance of team work home, the game has several sections where the squad splits, meaning you have no one to revive you if you die. And you have at most 6 hits on normal difficulty before you're a goner.
The presentation is fantastic. The graphics have aged well and it runs smoothly on modern operating systems with no compatibility issues. The soundtrack is a masterpiece, with memorable pieces like the Mandalorian chant "Vode An" punctuating intense action sequences, as well as familiar snippets from the film scores. The game will throw in bits of fan-service such as a squad mate quipping "these must be the droids we're looking for" which just make you chuckle even under pressure.
The AI is decent but will occasionally get stuck behind barriers when rushing to revive you, leading to frustration. The cooperative nature of the campaign makes the lack of online co-op campaign play very glaring. If this game ever gets a sequel, this feature needs to be added first. The campaign only features three planets, and is pretty short. None of the multiplayer maps are very interesting. These are probably due to the game's status as a tie-in for Episode III's film release with crunched development time.
Just get this game. You will not be disappointed. It's not perfect by any means but its extremely minor flaws do little to hamper an amazing experience. For a 9-year-old game it's extremely playable and not dated at all.

Alright guys i'm going to go into a pretty detailed review of what I think Devilian is worth since I have not seen anyone do a decent review yet.
I have played 200 hours in the past 2 weeks and have reached end-game content and will give you my opinion on the game.  Please enjoy.
Pros:
-There are literally no bots farming/gathering materials ever.  I have been playing and probably have seen ONE person just standing there probably with some type of mouse macro just killing useless mobs.  Mobs in the game don't give much at all, nearly nothing.  You obtain majority of the materials from dungeons.
-Combat is awesome, it's fluid with a top-down camera similar to PoE and the Diablo series
-Non-Tab targeting of course, it's an Action RPG with MMO aspects
-It's extremely easy to learn how to play
-If you want certain costumes but don't want to pay money, you can purchase in-game credits via gold legally.  There is a system called "DEX" (Devilian credits) which is an item you purchase from someone for gold, and when you use it it will add real world funds/credits to your account for use in the marketplace (cash shop).
-Content is actually difficult end game! Even if you have the best equipment you may not be able to clear the final boss of the Archdevil dungeons (3 man raid).  It is extremely mechanical and needs skill as the boss has certain 1 shot mechanics and multiple boss phases depending on his life total.
-3 skill trees per class so you can fine tune your build to your style.
-Skill resets are FREE.  You do not have to do anything to reset them, you just click the button and it will refund all your points for you to experiment with.
-Dungeon party system is available and although may not be that great for early on level dungeons (nobody does them really), it is great for finding your level cap dungeons (instant queue nearly).
-There are 3 people per party for regular dungeons and Archdevil dungeons (which are insanely hard, mechanically & gear wise)
-Raid dungeons will be available in the future with 9 man raids
-Guilds are available with benefits for being in the guild (Guild dungeons, guild daily quest, rewards only obtained via guild)
-PvP available (3v3 and 20v20 battlegrounds)
-Via daily quests and log-in rewards a free to play player can be just as strong as anyone else.  (Currently near the top of the leaderboard for my class and haven't paid anything except to validate my account)
-Validating account (Could be a pro or con?).  You need to use 5 dollars in the marketplace (Cash shop) and make a purchase before your account is validated.  If you have played Archeage or Rift your account is already validated.  It is a ONE time thing for your TRION account.  This is why there are no botters in the game.  Only mail bots that send you occasional garbage are present.
-Nothing is set behind a paywall, you can be very successful in the game as a free to play character
Cons:
-Currently only 4 classes. Cannonner, Evoker (Mage), Shadowhunter (Rogue), Berserker (Warrior).  There is a 5th class scheduled to be released sometime later, Deathscythe.
-Classes are genderlocked (why?).. Not that big of a deal for me but may be for some players
-5 dollar purchase of a marketplace item must be made before your account is validated.
-Non validated accounts are not able to initiate a trade with other players.  The other player MUST trade YOU first.  Trading is still available though.
-Non validated accounts are not able to sell items on the auction house but are able to purchase.
-Can be repetitive at times, grinding for gear in dungeons and what not but every F2P MMO has some aspect of that.

I'm probably going to get alot of hate for this buuuut: Hover Revolt of Gamers is not a good game were it stands. It has alot of potential for sure, but not enough to stop me from getting a refund. My reasons for disliking this game are as follows:
While navigating around the city is fun, the environments often feel like random boxes just scattered around with no thought or care put into them at all. I look foward to this game getting better, and hope I can re-puchase it one day when it's got a bit more going for it.
