Here's my take on the civilian flightsim hobby as it currently stands: More than ever, it is a period of transition and I believe the future looks good. I have and use both FSX and X-Plane and therefore have a foot in both camps. It's a case of fully realized capabilities versus future potential. From another perspective I see one nearing the end of its 32-bit lifecycle and the other very much in its 64-bit adolescence.
Background: I've been flight simming since SubLogic's C64 release, and have been firmly entrenched in the Microsoft FS camp on PC since FS5.1, although like everyone else in the day I had and used Flight Unlimited, FLY! and ProPilot. We loved the variety and happily used them all for what they had to offer. For me FS2004/FS9 was the watershed, and I was entrenched for a decade in the sim using all the familiar add-ons and a full suite of GoFlight hardware. Unfortunately my computer was firmly stuck in 2004 as well, so I avoided migrating to FSX. I was aware of and had messed around with XP during my biannual pilgrimage to Oshkosh, even chatting at length with Austin Meyer, but I was already too deeply invested in the MSFS camp. I'm certain that many can relate.
I've been a licensed private pilot since 1991, with a multi-engine endorsement and lucky enough to have had exposure and stick time on some pretty cool equipment. Now as most real world guys will tell you, flying a computer is NOT the same - I don't care if the flight models are based on lookup tables or basic real-time elemental calculations, it's just not worth arguing over. Get over it.  Where there is tremendous value in simming however, is the 'process' of flight - planning, procedures, checklist habits, instrument scans, IFR approaches. For true immersion in the system look up PilotEdge and add that to your mix no matter what platform you fly.
I was fortunate enough to finally build a cutting edge computer recently. As a treat, I picked up FSX-SE to see how she'd run on a modern box. Looked good and I was enthused enough to purchase Aerosoft's A320/321 (an absolutely excellent add-on BTW). Then the dreaded terrain.dll crashes started on flights lasting longer than about 60 minutes. While I understand these errors may have been largely addressed in the new FSX-SE beta patch, I am very grateful for them. They gave me pause and saved me the hundreds of $$ I was prepared to pour into the scenery and add-ons in order to bring it up to the available standards: Orbx, UTX, ASN, PMDG, et al. It's a slippery slope most know only too well, and when you finally stop and look back at all the resources you have dedicated, the thought of migrating to something totally new seems not only daunting, but is likely financially unwarranted as well.
While waiting for a decade old piece of software to get patched by a third party so that I could run it on modern equipment and proceed to spend a great deal of money and tweaking time to get it to run correctly, the light bulb went on for me. Here I was at a crossroad and I was prepared to reinvest in the same old song and dance. Yes, it's the one tune everybody knows, but there was an opportunity to learn a new one. Even though I tried and failed to get the X-Plane demo working, I purchased the full version (10.35 currently) in order to give it an honest shakedown, flying it exclusively for a week. What that week gave me was an appreciation for just how immersive, smooth and realistic XP can be.
I spent a good deal of time reading the related forums, familiarizing myself with the tips, tricks and FAQs. I found the stock 172 and Baron okay (certainly the equal of their stock FSX equivalents), but added the beautiful Carenado C340 for some GA flying. (Aside - the C340 is a nice looking package and I'm glad I have it but there are some unforgivable faults that required modifications to actually work - in particular the CDI when tuned to an ILS. Basic stuff. For shame.) Then the FlyJsim 737-200 for some good old fashioned radio navigation at jet speeds. Wonderful aircraft, beautifully modelled cockpit and convincingly realistic performance numbers. Definitely a pilot's plane. The coming IXEG 737-300 looks incredible. And I needn't mention that PMDG is developing for XP with a DC6 to be followed by one or more of their 7xx series...
Sparse scenery? To me it looks far and away better than stock FSX. It's nicely scalable to the hardware you're running, and XP definitely makes proper use of modern hardware. The stock mesh is great, autogen works well, the road traffic is cool, and the night lighting is the stuff of pilot training heaven. But here's the kicker - there's so much freely available from the community. I've managed to populate my XP world with all the airport scenery I will be reasonably using with a few visits to the XP ORG. And if you have a look at what's possible using world2xplane... the future looks not only bright, but incredible. Need I mention no terrain.dll CTDs or OOM errors?
Stock XP weather is in my opinion better than stock FSX. Dressed up with ASN and REX however, and FSX has a strong lead. But based on how close XP is getting with aircraft and scenery, the weather engine won't be far behind.
Stock ATC is crap. But so is FSX's. Sorry, it's just not real. I alluded to it above, but try PilotEdge to see what real ATC is. Full stop.
This has become a rather long piece, sorry about that. I suppose I felt I had a lot to say about where we've been, where we are, and where we're going. MSFS has been how it was, and largely how it is now (I include P3D here). Is it time for change? One platform is nearing a developmental dead end, albeit with some wonderful add-ons, and one is just beginning to realize its potential with continuous and meaningful support.
I'll continue to use both platforms for now, I mean why not, I own both and enjoy each for what they offer. Let me be clear though - I will not be adding anything further to my FSX ecosystem, but will simply enjoy what I already have. FSX will be limited to getting my bus fix with that awesome Aerosoft A320, at least until the sim crashes with the latest .dll or OOM error. For the price of a decent FSX add-on, I would urge you to give XP a fair evaluation.
In the end I see FSX as an old woman all gussied up in makeup and a new designer dress. She looks great and is pleasant to spend quality time with, but be careful if you go out dancing - she may fall and break a hip. Now have you seen the new girl in town? Dances funny, but she's smart, modern, and has some really cool moves. You may want to meet her.
My future in the hobby is with XP. I know I am not alone. Developers take note.

Honest review from someone who WISHED for this to be re-released on PC for years. I played the originals when they came out, still have my original Xbox Gold copy AND I kept my 360 JUST for this game.
Pre-launch - I was super eager at the announcement of this release, and didn't even care about the $60 tag (Of course I was going to get both.) Tried to do some digging about the DLC content, and nothing was announced at all, so I just assumed they'd release it because why wouldn't they?
Post-launch - Bought the game, and turned them on and dinked around for roughly 10 minutes. I'm not going to give the game itself a breakdown, you can play it for yourself (Most likely you already have). Game looks great considering its age, runs silky smooth, and the controls (Wired 360 controller) work very well. No problems whatsoever. I haven't tried the keyboard, nor do I plan to. A lot of reviews are slamming the controls and I can only assume it's for the keyboard or the Xbone controller. I have no issues. Ultimate Alliance, as far as I can tell, does NOT come with -any- of the DLC characters for the Xbox Gold version, the PSP, or GBA. While I didn't even know the portables had exclusive DLC, it was kind of heart-breaking to hear that the console characters were missing. So much so, I considered passing on the games until I heard more news. Especially with the price tag, I'd have expected a more "complete" game to be released. I have no idea if this is a licensing issue or Activision greed, but I don't like it. Even with that, I took the plunge, bought the game, and am really surprised at how well it turned out. It looks and plays great, and can't wait to get online with some friends to punch some baddies.
Pros
+ Silky smooth 60 FPS
+ Graphics have aged well, look sharper
+ Controls great
+ Lives up to the hype I remembered in the past
Cons
- Price
- No DLC characters
I recommend this game, but do so with a heavy heart. I'll undoubtedly get great value, personally, but am very disappointed in the lack of content that SHOULD have been released, and for the price I payed. If I could give it a more medium judgement, I would. That said, the game is just as great as I remembered.

Battlefield: Bad Company 2 is a 2010 first-person shooter video game developed by DICE and published by Electronic Arts (EA). It is a direct sequel to Battlefield: Bad Company and is part of the Battlefield game series. The game is primarily a squad-level first-person shooter based in a contemporary modern warfare setting. Additionally, the game includes a single-player campaign, where the player re-assumes the role of Preston Marlowe, the protagonist of the original game. The game's Frostbite 1.5 engine now allows for destructible environments.
Multiplayer maps, which allow for five different game modes, contain a wide selection of vehicles, aircraft and emplacements. While Bad Company 2 is primarily a first-person shooter, it follows other games in the series by allowing the player to control certain vehicles, including ATVs, APCs, tanks, and helicopters. On foot, players are given access to a variety of real-world small arms such as assault rifles and machine guns. Players can also jump, crouch, and sprint. Bad Company 2 heavily emphasizes destructible environments. Large sections of most buildings can be destroyed by explosives, and some walls and fences break down under barrages of bullets, with the game's physics engine realistically simulating the destruction.
Bad Company 2 features a story-driven single-player campaign. For most of the narrative, the player takes control of Preston Marlowe, one of the members of the titular "Bad Company". Multiplayer is class-based, with four classes: Assault, Engineer, Medic, and Recon. Each class has a variety of unique weapons and equipment, and serves a specific role in combat. There are also some weapons that can be used by any class, such as pistols and shotguns. Each class gains experience and levels up separately.

I'm into Sol 0 about 20 hours now. The verdict? Buy this game. It's a bargain. I'm a huge fan of resource management sims (such as SimCity, Banished, etc...) and it's a tremendous value for the money. Since I'm also a space nut, I also love the theme! It works great on my 4K monitors as well.
A game like this is incredibly difficult to get "Right", so to speak, in everyone's eyes, but it has a lot of the basics spot-on, IMHO. Resources like water and power just happen - you don't have to wire anything up, which would be tedious, nor do you have to provide pipes for water, etc... I've even emailed the developers with some suggestions, and their responses were friendly, factual, and appreciated the feedback. It's clear that they're continuing to work on and improve the game. Can't ask for a better team!
There are a few things I'd love to see in the game:
1) Bigger maps! This is a common complaint on all sorts of resource management sims, but I do find that some of the terrain offered by default is a bit limiting. This can be alleviated by creating your own map with nothing on it. One of the developers said that it wouldn't be easy to make larger, unfortunately, so with that in mind, I have some other ideas:
2) Go vertical or underground with buildings!
3) Sometimes the forklifts and astronauts get stuck where they can't access certain regions to repair or add. Maybe have some tunnels that can go vertical briefly to make small bridges so that forklifts and astronauts can pass underneath them?
4) A way to convert astronauts into colonists and vice versa. After your colony is built up, the use for astronauts goes down, and you have a lot of idle resources sitting there not doing anything and it might be nice to have them "reused" as base personnel
5) More building types - Maybe educational centers, recreational areas, machine manufacturing areas (for making things like rovers, forklifts, etc...)
6) Trade with other active maps. I like being able to share resources in games like SimCity, and it seems like this could be useful when food/water/methane, etc...become anemic
7) A way to shut down units' use of electricity. I have had overbudget situations before on power and there's no way to get things to use less power, and I wound up having a lot of my food spoil and colonists die because I couldn't get a thermal generator built fast enough and it took at least a dozen ships from earth until I finally got enough to build a generator.
Thanks guys! Keep up the great work! I am honored to be playing along side future developments!

Try it if you like colonizing other planets in Kerbal Space Program, and if you're into base-building games.
It's a nifty little strategy game about the first colony on Mars. Obviously there are things that could be better as the negative reviews have already pointed out:
But for all those downsides, there are some definite pros:
If I had some suggestions for the dev (a one-man team operating under the name "Chondrite Games"), I'd say that what is here is good, but it feels a bit like a vertical slice; a demo for a full game rather than a complete experience, much like the early versions of KSP. If there was just a bit more to the end-game, some kind of budget system to incentivize smart cargo management on rockets, or a bit more base customization (the lack of T-intersection hallway pieces is irksome) I would be singing this game's praises from the rooftops.
For players, if you like sound science and clever strategy in your space games, this is worth your time. You may be left wanting more, but you could do a hell of a lot worse for the pricetag (6.49 CAD at time of writing, 5.99 USD). This is a developer to watch.

Strife is a game with a lot of cool ideas that was pretty innovative on release, but made the mistake of being released right between Duke Nukem 3D and Quake, which is like releasing a film between the newest Marvel production and a Transformers sequel and sadly doomed Strife to be mostly forgotten. However, those hardworking guys at Night Dive Studios managed to get ahold of the rights and, in 2014, released this remaster on Steam for all to play. I recently completed it, and I thought it was pretty good overall.
The presentation is great. There're some genuinely excellent cinematics, art, writing, and voice acting. The pixel art has a nice, clean, simple aesthetic that portrays personality as well as clearly communicating what things are and what they're doing. The story's pretty good, and it's helped a lot by voice-acted conversations with NPCs, complete with various dialogue options. This was also one of the last games to be released that uses the then-outdated idTech 1 engine, and a lot of stuff's been added to it, including full mouselook and perspective correction. The environments have a wonderful sense of place, seeming almost like locations where people would live and work. Overall, Strife is just great to look at and listen to.
On the gameplay side of things, Strife isn't quite as good but still does pretty well. The shooting is alright, with eight different weapons to choose from (some with different ammo types; actually, Strife might be the first FPS to have that). A lot of them have easily recognizable DOOM equivalents, but they're still fun to use and have a nice amount of variety. There's also an inventory, which integrates into the game well enough and is even nice enough to auto-use health items when you're about to die. The game is hub-based, but there're only like three hubs total (although it is nice that you can travel to any part of the game world at any time).
Strife also experiments with different gameplay styles, which is certainly ahead of its time. There's a pretty basic upgrade system that consists of two linear upgrade paths to increase health and accuracy, and one weapon that gets more powerful as you progress. There's also an attempted stealth element, where in some areas enemies won't shoot you unless you shoot them or do something incriminating. It's not that well-implemented, though; for instance, some NPCs you can talk to in hostile areas don't have dialogue that reflects whether you're stealthing or not, so you can shoot three guards right in front of them and they'll still tell you not to blow your cover by doing anything suspicious. This doesn't impede the game too much, though, and it's fun regardless.
Additionally, at the beginning of the game areas are pretty simple and easy to navigate, and enemies and health/ammo are well-distributed. Near the end, however, this falls apart to some degree, with levels becoming ridiculous mazes and barely enough ammunition to get past the waves and waves of enemies. I never quite ran out entirely, but a lot of the time I was down to just my starting ranged weapon and my almost-useless-against-robot-enemies flamethrower.
Overall, Strife is pretty good. It looks and sounds great, it plays well, and its flaws, while sometimes frustrating, don't ruin an otherwise great experience. I recommend it.
P.S. Your NPC support is a fun, likeable character, but at the end she becomes a love interest for no reason, because this was gaming in the 90s, after all.

I have backed this game since Early Access and I must say I'm quite impressed with the amount the game has to offer. Though at times repetitive, the challenges are fun and dynamic. The world is extremely immersive and the visuals tell a beautiful story. I am definitely happy with the progress the game has made. There is a rare hiccup here and there within the game, but the devs seem to be paying attention to fixing what they need when required.
The
thus far is the player waking up in a cell in a gamer orientated cyber world. There isn't much else being given or elaborated on at the moment, but there is a police system in place much like Jet Set Radio Future had. The only exception here is that you can be caught and thrown into jail. I had a debate with myself about the
whether it was better than JSRF or not. I do like how this game does follow the concept on roller-blades, but did it in it's own style. Rather than having physical roller blades (which made JSRF quite unique and fun), this game gives the player hover shoes (or what looks like hover shoes). For a game attempting to make their own mark, it is a breath fresh air to see which direction the devs would like it take. Everything is actually quite smooth and grinding on rails or wires isn't as much of a hassle as JSRF. The player can press "X" in this case and be near a rail and start grinding instantly. Whether some gamers will like this or not will be interesting as JSRF did pose a challenge at times to grind on certain obstacles. Additionally, players are still able to perform techniques/moves just like in JSRF. There aren't any major flips or specific technique scheme, but there is a presence of neat tricks available.
The one major difference between this and JSRF is that JSRF required the player to do tricks in order to improve their speed. H:RoG allows players to charge up an energy bar to improve their speed and jump range. Tapping "X" will allow players to charge their energy meter. The more the players jump around, the more their energy bar will deplete. Another major feature within the game rests with character creations. The player is able to create a team and multiple characters with different stats. Where stats/attributes were previously locked with each character in JSRF, the player has full control over the characters attributes. If you favor grinding, jumping or physical attributes, this can all be easily chosen to suit your style. There are no real loading screens unless you go between zones. Zones are quite large and it seems they are split up into different districts. There are a lot of different screens the player may scan, but there isn't any major function with them as of yet. What is predicted to come are spawn points, shops, and graffiti editors. One major feature that is present here (that's not in JSRF) is the ability to rewind time.... sort of. Say you miss a jump or a grind, the player is able to rewind the character back to a previous position. This does not rewind time, but does rewind your player. So, if you are being chased by police, don't expect to make them go away so easily!
the game is quite appealing. I absolutely love what they did with the light tail below characters feet. This feature is not only visually appealing, but helps players to follow AI or other players in cases where tailing someone would be difficult (visual aids/cues, I love that)! The maps themselves are quite vast and give the player a new tone, feeling or emotion when entering a different area. Entering a slum area is not extremely different than a rich area, but there is attention to detail that does make the player feel they left an area and entered a new place. Even though visually the game looks cool, I believe there still is a lot of room to add details such as shattering glass to other objects that look too plain.
The
and
is pretty good so far. There aren't many cinematics or voices, but there is a presence of these sounds. The music is pretty good so far; there still needs to be additions in this domain to make the game immersive. JSRF had a deadly sound track to this day I hear people listening to these songs. I can only hope this game does add memorable music. I would also like to see more cut-scenes to better explain the story. Lastly, I would like to add that there is somewhat of a system in place to show where the next mission is. It is at times difficult to find where to go next as scanning 360 degrees in all directions can be cumbersome. I would highly suggest adding a mini map and visual markers on screen to help the player navigate.
Overall, I am glad I acquired this game and hope the updates continue. I would say full price would seem fair, but of course sales are always around some corner.
FINAL RATING : 7.85/10

Quick Summary: Marlow Briggs is a mix of Darksiders style combat with Shadow Warrior 2013 style storytelling. They also throw in various diversions as well such as manning a turret and shooting down attack helicopters, top down airplane shooting, or puzzle platforming. Overall the game is a lot of fun and since it’s an indie game, it’s also cheap (though not on sale very often).
*Spoilers below*
You play the title character Marlow Briggs, trying to rescue your girlfriend after being “killed” with a magical weapon. Sadly (for the bad guys) the magical weapon turns you into a mythical warrior with a new friend, the Mask of Death. The Mask is a lot like the demon companion in Shadow Warrior, who only you can see, and kind of guides you along while making snide remarks at you. Your mission, aside from revenge and rescuing your girlfriend, is to stop the big bad guy from gathering enough magical power to become some kind of ancient Mexican god (even though I think the guy is Chinese).
The game is played in third person perspective and it’s one of those platformers where you can swing a big weapon and knock around a dozen enemies at once, comparable to Darksiders/DMC Devil May Cry. The combat isn’t that sophisticated, just hit the enemies and dodge when they attack. You also have access to some magical spells, but “mana” in the game is kind of limited and you can’t spam the spells (your mana bar won’t even let you cast 2 spells in a row without picking up more energy). The spells are quite powerful though, and really splash up the screen. Combat is about 66% of the game, where the rest is platforming such as climbing, dodging boulders, double jumping (and later gliding on magical wings). There are a few puzzles to solve, but they’re not too hard. The biggest pain comes from some of the enemies having extraordinary amounts of life.
You should try this game if:
+You are looking for a relatively easy hack/slash platforming game with a decent story. Only a few areas in the game had me replaying over and over (challenge areas with risk of instant death). The game only takes about 6-7 hours to beat.
You should NOT try this game if:
-You’re expecting some kind of grand RPG, or a game with a lot of replay value. This game cost me $2 and after playing through, I deleted it. Had a good time, now I move on to something else.

"Some people just want to see the world burn" - someone, about people that like this game
"This is what happens if you play the villain in The 12 Monkeys"
"Can you come help us improve real disease spread modeling?" - CDC-Center for Disease Control
"Better than WAR" - me, because it just is (and its single player, so forgetting objectives and just conquering the whole world doesn't hurt loosing-side family members)
"NOOO, not Sumatra again! Damn island with those flight and ship bans, this is impossible!" - anyone playing this at any given time
The whole game happens on a strategic world map (like WAR) and an evolution tree (skill/tech tree like on rpgs).
You ARE the disease and your goal is the elimination of mankind through contagion and lethality, which can be improved by mutations.
It is easy to learn but harder dificulties and special disease types are hard to master, plus there are a TON of achievements so it doesn't get boring...
...who am I kidding?! I just can't ever get bored watching the healthy world population hit zero then everyone starts dying, not with the news strip rolling comical remarks like the "iCure" being a flop, and then when things get serious narrating with sheer cruelty how the last people on earth are dying in an unknown cave feeling cold, starving, in pain and suffering from diarrhea. These news are really well in sync with how bad/clueless the world is faring against you.
The balance between contagion vs lethality and the balance between lethality vs symptoms/stealthiness are impressively delicate. There is great strategic depth to this and each kind of disease (each has its special traits) make a world of difference in it too. The best strategy for fungus is certainly not the same as bioweapons.
And all those disease types, traits, available mutations (and the emerging behaviors derived from all of that) are quite impressively real-world-like, which adds to the happy/creepy feelings that come when people start dying in tens, thousands, oh-my-god-millions!
Exponential growth of sick/dead people starts slow and mayu be a bit boring at times, but a fast-forward toggle can be used liberally to solve that.
The graphics are very simple but very clean and well designed, beautiful in their own minimalistic way, all in indispensible biohazard read alert fashion.
All in all, totally enjoyable for those that like strategy board games and dark-humored genocide.

The graphics are fantastic and the platform runs stable, which is what drew me into trying out this sim, but sadly that's where it ends when it comes to out-performing FSX.
Tutorials?  Nope, no tutorials at all.  You can buy some, watch some on you tube, but nothing that introduces someone new to flying otherwise.
This simulator expects that you already know how to fly, and know how to use the instrumentation.  They're not advertising this, so they're basically selling to the masses in order to lower the price and fund the project for those who already have the skills to fly in the first place and just need a bit of practice flying someplace away from their normal zone of avialability.
Customizable, well, yes, in-so-far as assigning function to keys.  Multi-monitor support?  In your dreams!  Mine had an option to utilize some instrumentation on a second screen, but kept moving from where I positioned it to where atop my active screen.  There is also several mods and add-on's to improve the graphical experience (the one feature this application excels at), but my post research into these features left me finding that the developers don't appear to bend to any of the consumers desire for improved support.  I found setup to be very difficult to figure out, plan to write down all your commands as there doesn't appear to be any kind of commend export/print feature other than a look-up while in-simulation.
The simulator AI is about as dumb as they come, at least on the ground.  There was constant chatter between the Tower AI and a taxiing flight AI to "cross runway 32, then hold short of runway 32", this same conversation repeated several times with this exact phrase.  The plane I was following attempted to turn down every single taxi intersection, then turned back onto it's original course.  On the far end of the runway it fell off into the water and began flipping around like a fish, bouncing into the air, flipping, and turning in a single spot, before finally flipping and landing upright back onto the taxi-way, where it turned straight towards me and ran me right over without even causing a crash.
Traffic and trees also have no effect on collision, feel free to land and take-off on any old street.
In summation, I'm "increadibly" dissappointed in this simulator!   While the graphics and feel of flight perform extremely well, I find every other aspect of the simulator to be severely lacking in both realism and intuitive use/functionality.  I do hope they take the majority of negative feedback I've been reading and put some consideration to it for their next release/update.  FSX is so unstable and out of date, but leaves a very positive experience to it's user base that the fine folks at Laminar Research could truly benefit to use as a guide for putting together the next great flight simulator of all time!  I would like to think they're interested in training new pilots in addition to providing additional experience to seasoned pilots, at least that's my take on a good simulator.

TL;DR: They changed a number of small things, freshened up much of the rest, and it's all for the better, so far.
In order to dispell some of the misinformation from the other reviews
Compared to the first:
-Movement is click and go, allowing you to move while casting. You can even start a flame thrower, and then start moving. The part in the beginning of the first Magicka, where you have to stop to cast Freeze, because the first didn't cover? Now you don't have to stop. Much better. But you can hold if you want to, even if that is one of the things that annoyed me the most from the first game.
-Elements don't combine on the bar, but still do when cast, you can still shotgun ice, just not ice + thunder, because the water is still there. This also means some of the combos from the old one are gone, but this freshens things up, forcing you to rethink your spells, and not go with the same old ones.
-The quickcasting. Yes, some of the Magicks (Haste and random teleport), have a one click key, with a cooldown, called focus, on the 1-4 keys. But, this is only for quickcasting of that Magick. If you combine the elements, and press space, it doesn't cost focus, and it doesn't have to be on the quick cast bar either. It's simply for quick casting of some spells. They are grouped. '1' has a force blast option (You can't cast without elements any longer, sadly, this is true), but can be switched with Random Teleport. Neither of those could be put on the other quickcasting. The focus cooldown is also only if use the quickcast, instead of doing it old school style.
-Staffs and robes and swords are now all selectable, instead of having to choose a set, like in the original, and they unlock as you get them in game.
Edit/
Also, it's an online account for online play. You can play without an account for local play, and can play without more accounts on the same computer, using different controllers.
And the controls for the controller are much better than they were in the original. So much better.
But no rebinding options, it seems, makes me a sad panda.
Overall, I think they did a lot of good things. The bad stuff, is the story, so far, which seems like it won't be anything new, but I could be wrong. But if you want to play this with friends, in coop or pvp, it doesn't matter about the story. (To clarify, the story is new, it's not a remake, but it seems to be simply another dig at various existing tropes, which can get a little bit tiresome)

Magicka 2 vs. Magicka 1
+ no more "hold LMB" to move, just one click now (also works while conjuring/casting)
+ no more spamming of the same steam/lightning combo every time
+ absorb shields e.g.(FFFFE + MMB) fire will heal you now
+ more challenging gameplay (you have to observe enemies, shield the right element and attack with the right element)
+ all attacks are useful now e.g. in Magicka 1 I rarely used pure element attacks like (FFFFF + RMB)
+ you can permanently enchant your sword with fire, frost, lightning etc.
+ element conjuring seams more responsive than in Magicka 1
+ more interactive environment (still not nearly enough though) e.g. lots of water so you can shield water and lightning/freeze enemies.
+ the graphics work really well for me / atmosphere is nice
- sometimes I got pushed of screen and killed there (not too often)
- teleport is now random and is only useful when you're surrounded
[edit] fixed: single player can now be played without internet connection, nice
One example why I really like the gameplay:
Early in the game you get attacked by goblins (weak to most elements) and flamethrower goblins (weak to frost / immune to fire)
First I got killed very fast then I remembered the absorb shield from the tutorial and used fire absorb shield. Now the flamethrowers heal you.
I used fire attacks to kill everything while the flamethrowers kept healing me. Then frost the flamethrowers, done.
The game also gives you clues what the enemies resist or are weak against."resist" or "weakness" shows up when you hit them with certain elements.

Gritty, dark, and a heck of a lot of fun to play, Star Wars: Republic Commando is a first person tactial shooter that finds the perfect balance between strategy and action.
Whereas most First-Person shooters take the action route there are still a few extreme tactical and strategy based military such as the Tom Clancy: Rainbow Six series. The Rainbow Six series takes a linear strategy and tactical based approach to military operations. The game focuses on the "How to" rather than the "What to." The problem with games like this is that they combine the complex strategy with a genre that most people prefer to stay focused on the "What to." First-Person Shooters. Therefore creating an issue. You have those who love it because it of it strict strategy focus and then you have those who hate it because it doesn't have enough action.
Republic Commando solves this issue...
It blends (and balances) the action with the strategy. Featuring a one key strategy system you can command your squad members directly and quickly. No sub-menus, no complicated explanation. Just push and play.
One of the games main features is a excellent AI system. And boy is it good...
You squad members know how to fight and how to do it efficiently. They automatically take cover and stay focused on the objective. They eliminate the primary targets first and take on the secondary ones later. The first time playing the game through, I found myself dying more than the AI! Now that is good...
The gameplay is fast paced, frantic, and exciting. It perfectly balances strategy and action.
The graphics are...meh...
In their day they were probably amazing. But now a dated Quake engine remains. Don't get me wrong the graphics aren't bad, but by today's standards they are a little old, but acceptable.
The sound is good and the soundtrack is perfect. The soundtrack by Jesse Harlin is a great blend of dark overtones, action sequences, and excellent buildup. The sound effects in game sound exactly like Star Wars.
The campaign is extremely fun. It isn't even much of a campaign. It is just three big missions broken up into small parts. I have probably played the game's through about 7 times. My only complaint about the campaign is the rather abrupt ending. Now I won't spoil anything but it will leave you feeling like...
"WHAT! THAT'S IT! THAT WASN'T HOW IT WAS SUPPOSED TO END! THERE WAS SOOOOO MUCH BUILD UP! COME ON!"
Then you will go frantically searching the web to try and find if there is a sequal. And you'll find this: Cancelled
And when your all done you can play the multiplayer! Which is fun, but pretty much dead...
So in short this game is awesome. Go get it!

Content Review:
Star Wars: Republic Commando is a tough game to review in terms of content. While much of the game is dark, gritty, and permeated by death, on has tot take int the account the fact that...well...it's Star Wars. This is (so far) the most violent Star Wars Video Game to date. Thankfully, violence is the only category that scores high in this game, in terms of content.
Positive Elements: You fight on the good side. You stand for morals such as teamwork, unity, and justice. Teamwork is essential to success in the game.
6/10 (Moderate) Violence: The game is a First Person Shooter, so some violence is expected. What is different about this game game though in comparison to previous Star Wars games is that it features an extensive amount of blood, gore, and corpses. The Genossian bug enemy's you fight break into bits and pieces when killed. If you shoot an enemy up close blood will splatter on your visor only to be removed by a wiper blade seconds later. When shooting at an enemy you can see spurts of blood flying off. Combat is highlighted by screams, cries of pain, and yelling. In addition to all that, many bodies of human clones are found scattered throughout the game.
3/10 (Infrequent/Mild) Language: D--n and Hell are used occasionally. Insults like, clankers, and scumbag are uttered with frequency.
0/10 (None) Sexual Content: :)
0/10 (None) Drugs/Alcohol: :)
4/10 (Present) Negative Elements: Death permeates the environment. Much of the game is dark and has a bleak outlook on things. Frequently the Commandos quote from their fake rule book which says things like "Rule Number 1: Kill them before they kill you."
Other Moral Issues: The weird mystical Force is mentioned (e.g."May the force be with you.") but never elaborated on. The Commandos are cloned from another human being, as are many of the other soldiers you see in game.
Final Content Rating: 5.5 (Acceptable)
Key Elements
- Violent
- Gritty and Dark
- Death permeates the environment
- Infrequent Mild Language

If you sit down and actually think about our place in the solar system it can be awe-inspiring.
Here we are on Earth, sitting in front of our screens made of glass, that's something we figured out, how to make glass from sand, that's kind of cool all on its own, let alone the manipulation of electrons to power the thing, the LCD's or whatever to display the image you're looking at right now.
It's all very, very cool, all our stuff, our society, everything we have around us that we take for granted, it's all something we, as a species, have come up with all on our own over millennia, we're pretty amazing!
Thanks to mutations caused by solar radiation and some helpful mass extinctions along the way to clear the path for our evolution, we now find ourselves advanced to the point where we are collectively smart enough to make all this "stuff" from the resources we find around us.
But imagine if our planets history, Earths own evolution, had been even slightly different.
What if the Earth had formed a little further away from the sun, say at around the same distance Mars orbits today, would that have been enough to stop life from evolving? probably not.
It'd be colder, things would be different, but as Jeff Goldblum said in Jurassic Park  "Life finds a way."
How about if Earth was a little smaller, say around the size of Mars, that doesn't sound like too drastic a change, would that be enough to stop life from evolving?
Again probably not, but there'd be some pretty big problems down the line because size really does matter.
You see, most rocky planets, like the Earth, are essentially big magnets, there's a super hot iron core way down in the middle spinning around which makes a magnetic field, (that's why your compass works) and that magnetic field also protects the planet from lots of dangerous particles that the sun streams off into space.
The problem is if a planet (like Mars) is too small to have enough internal heat and pressure to keep a molten core spinning, then in time, the magnetic field will weaken and fade away.
Without this magnetic force field those dangerous particles from the sun will start to blow away a planets atmosphere, if you're a life form that's gotten into the habit of breathing then this is going to be a pretty big deal for you.
So four billion years ago, when our sun was still a baby and the planets were shiny and new, things were very different.
The Earth and Mars were similar, both hot rocks orbiting the sun, both with molten cores and magnetic fields protecting them from the particles rushing out of our new star.
Mars was our little brother, and went through the same things  the Earth did.
Both planets were bombarded by rocks and comets left cluttering up the new solar system, each bringing all kinds of things with them, gases, water, even organic molecules.
Both planets developed atmospheres and oceans, we know for a fact that on at least one of them, life evolved from this organic soupy goodness, life which eventually advanced to the point where it learnt to play computer games and read reviews, isn't evolution grand!
The problem was that Mars was just a little too small and a little too distant to keep its core hot and "spinny".
As its heart cooled, its magnetic field faded and bad things happened.
Our little brother started to die, it's atmosphere slowly blew away, lost to space, it's water evaporated away with it, what little was left froze into the ground.
It turned cold, dry and dead. It turned into the Mars we know today.
This is why when we send people to Mars (It'll happen one day) they're going to need to take everything they need with them, at least until they can set up some basic infrastructure, and that's where Sol 0: Mars Colonization starts, with the preparation for the first permanent manned presence on Mars.
When you first fire up the game you'll be treated to a screen showing a rocket sitting on a launch pad waiting to be loaded with supplies.
This will be your first flight to Mars and the first decision you'll need to make in the game, what supplies should you start out with?
The launch window to Mars only opens up every few months (it's an orbital alignment thing) and the weight that your first rocket can carry is limited.
You'll likely be tempted to send an astronaut up to have a look around, but for your first flight this would be a very bad idea, whilst you could send a man up along with all the food and water the rocket can carry, this almost certainly wouldn't be enough to keep him alive until your next launch window, also without any building supplies, his usefulness would be pretty limited up there... it'd be a meaningless death.
Fortunately you can satiate your curiosity by sending up a rover or two, these little robotic friends can explore the surface around your landing area, scout out any mineral and ice deposits and allow you to make a more educated decision about where your next Lander should touchdown.
You should have a little room left on your rocket to load up some supplies to leave on Mars in preparation for your future flights too.
After picking your landing zone and deploying your rover you can set about exploring the surface.  You'll need resources to help sustain a manned mission.
Initially, everything you need is going to have to be shipped in from Earth so the sooner you start producing your own resources on Mars, the sooner you can think about sending actual colonists up there to found your first settlement, but we're getting ahead of ourselves...
Your rover should find several resource deposits on the surface ranging from Ice (for drinking water) through to methane (for rocket fuel).
If the thought of constantly clicking around the map to send your rover searching for resources doesn't appeal, don't worry, you can draw out paths for your little robot to follow whilst you get on with other things.
When your next launch window rolls around, it's back to Earth to load up another rocket.
You'll send more supplies, food and water, maybe even an astronaut if you're feeling brave and ready for things to get really interesting.
Once you've taken your first small step for man, your astronaut will want to get busy with some construction work,  all those supplies you've already dropped are now going to be used to lay the foundations of your Mars colony.
You're going to need to place some pallets to start unloading those supplies, maybe you should send a forklift up to help with that on your next launch?
You'll also want to build a cryotank early on to start thawing out that ice to use as drinking water.
Most of what you build will need power too, in the early game this is going to come from solar panels so you'll need to pick a quiet spot for those as well.
Your first hour or so in the game will be spent building up the basic infrastructure on Mars, greenhouses for food, solar panels for electricity, oxygen generators for... well you get the idea.
Several launches later (assuming your astronaut didn't come to a grizzly end on the Martian wastelands) you should have a rudimentary, self sustaining colony on Mars, equipped with all the luxuries like breathable air, drinkable water, home-grown food and maybe even a bed to sleep on.
Keep in mind that things don't always run smoothly... [snip]

I've never played a game in this series before. Based on the preview images, the sexualization of the characters made me suspicious the game was using that to lure in gamers to compensate for poor quality. And, while there is a lot of sexualization (take that for what you will), this ended up being one of the best platformers I've played in years. Definite must play for anyone that enjoys the classic Metroid and Castlevania games. To start off with the sort-of negatives, there really isn't any character development at all for the most part. By the end, I could hardly remember any of the characters names or anything about them. I found the story also pretty forgettable (at least to someone who's new to the series, like me). The end of the game left me feeling indifferent towards the characters and the world because of that.
That said, this game managed to keep me hooked all the way until the end despite the above. The art design for the characters, enemies, and world is great and takes me back to my Sega Genesis days as a kid. The characters, while pretty two-dimensional, do remain charming when they do speak. But, the real reason to play this game is for the platforming. And the platforming is really, really good with a controller. The controls are tight and responsive and the game introduces new platforming mechanics at a regular interval that keeps the game fresh and encourages the player to revisit previous levels. You start off feeling like the game is pretty slow. But, by the end, you'll (literally) be flying through the levels at crazy speeds.
The platforming mechanics in this game are just so much fun I never ended up caring about the neglected story or character development or how much of a BS difficulty spike the last level was (seriously, it's like something out of Super Meat Boy). It took about 10 hours for me to complete the game 100%, but it feels like a game I will want to replay later on and I'm really looking forward to playing Half Genie Hero.

I can't really recommend this program. (it is not a 'game').   As of 3/3/15, X-plane 10 offers a seemingly decent form of aircraft, flight, and limited airport simulation. This comes at the expense of a UI, a functioning Main Menu, any form of missions or objectives, any form of training or practice.
X-plane 10 is quite literally *just* a simulation of flight, at the expense of any grace or sense of direction outside of what the user puts into it and what flights or flight situations the user creates themselves.
That is not to say that, for experienced pilots this program wouldn't have it's uses, in fact I think that is it's intended audience, experienced pilots who have the basics down quite well already. This is not an introductory course.
Now, this much is my fault and I admit it openly, I purchased this in err, without looking this up. I was looking for an introduction to flight, this was literally my first ever flight sim purchased, I saw how it looked visually, read some favorable reviews, and figured that X-plane 10 is a top notch product.
At the high price of $60.00 USD, I expected things like a functional User Interface, a main menu, some wise setup that would let you set some important factors like controls and video settings, sound settings, etc. before entering the game.
I started up X-plane 10 to immediately be placed in an aircraft on an airfield, with resolution and performance issues. I went about figuring out the controls, setting the video settings, etcetera. I found out this program is nothing if not the raw material with which you, the user, can use to create your own scenarios and flights. I still have annoying issues with camera movement, (I use a controller and have used a joystick setup as well), wherein clicking in some areas will blip out to the desktop for a second, cameras resetting to odd positions into weird directions for no reason, and generally some performance issues (low frame-rate, even with a 64-bit version of Windows 8).
There is zero incentive to purchase this product if you are a beginner, if you're looking for an introductory, learning experience into the flight scenario, if you expect missions, tutorials, a proper main menu, flights, a convenient set-up then you'll have to look elsewhere.
If you know how to fly so-and-so plane, and could probably perform a successful flight and landing with no hand-holding whatsoever if you were placed into a fueled version of said plane in an airport, I imagine this would be a very entertaining program for you, and maybe even a good source of practice. If setting up your own flights is your thing too, I'd think you can enjoy this. For this price I simply can't recommend X-plane, in it's very rough and wanting current form.
Instead, I will recommend Microsoft Flight Simulator X Steam edition. Though an older title, I pull a much superior performance on it, it has a proper UI, it is far easier to work with, has an actual main menu, and also will give missions and challenges, tutorials and training for beginners as well as a place for experienced pilots to work with.
For a program that comes off as rough as this, I just don't feel the price is justified.

I'd like to review mostly the helicopter simulation in X-Plane since I used to have a JAA CPL(H)/IR(H) (helicopter licence) and for me this is the best simulation of helicopters out there, period. The only other that comes close is DCS World, but that's a military simulator.
I used X-Plane 9 to help with my instrument and procedure training and it was closer to the real thing than any other flight simulator out there and I've tried almost everything since the days of the 48Kb computers. From X-Plane 9, the 10 is an evolution with much better features and 64bit support.
Remember, this is a simulator, not a game. You may find it harder to control an helicopter in X-Plane than in other "simulations" out there. If you prefer to experience the real handling of such aircraft, X-Plane is for you, just be prepared to crash a lot while learning, otherwise go for other easier titles.
I like to think that X-Plane is much more a piloting simulator than a button pushing simulation, so smaller and more hands-on aircraft are preferable to big flying computers to really enjoy it, but that's probably just a matter of preference.
Some of the aircraft included in the base X-Plane are old and poorly designed, as is most of the world scenario, but you can find a lot of freeware online. Some of the payware is also nice but it's a pity that only a fraction is in the Steam DLC, maybe some option by the publisher, Aerosoft.
As a downside I believe X-Plane Steam integration leaves a lot to be desired. Laminar Research just took a lazy approach to publishing on Steam and there isn't even correct Steam Overlay integration and neither the much wanted Steam Workshop.
IMHO, X-Plane is the best civilian flight simulator out there and it's still evolving.

Contrary to many negative reviews, I'd say I like this game more than I had expected before. It's a very different game from its predecessor. It's very important to know that Pieces is the developer behind this game, not Arrowhead from the first game.
True, it removes away many of the features and things we love in Magicka 1 (OP QFQFQFAS, QRQRQRQRD, EQRQRAA spells). I'm also a fan of huge combos of complex spells (freeze, stone+fire, and then water, and electric with arcane sprinkles). However, I do feel that at some point, these spells seem to be very overpowered and all I do is just spam these spells to get the crap out to the end of the game. There are things I dislike, much to my annoyance and discomfort, but there are also things I like about this game.
Pros :
- Keeping the atmosphere of Magicka 1. Remember, Magicka 2 is developed by a different company, while still published under the same Paradox we know. So expect a lot of different things and revamps from Pieces. But they have successfully keeping the overall game atmosphere, tone, dialogues, unique humors and overall story intact with the first game. I can still feel the core atmosphere from the first game in this.
- Balanced Spells. Or Nerfed/"Dumbed down" spells as some of people here say. Yes, there are some nerfs I don't like personally. Some of them are long charge times, 5 spells instead of max 10, and few mechanics removal (ice rocks no longer freeze an entire pool). Actually, more strategy, thinking are involved in this game. There is also new 'bomb' from Arcane + LIfe, which I like very much :3.
- Improved, adjustable graphics and soundtrack.
- Manual Magicks. This is my favorite. Devs actually hear our opinions and implement the manual ones, along with 1234 hotkeys (yes, you can spam WA again to revive and then kill your friends).
- Tons of challenge maps (Haven't tried it though, but there a plenty of maps)
Cons :
- "Nerfed" spells. Same with my second Pros point, There are things I don't really like such as long charging time, and no longer ice-electric-rocks to overkill the enemies.
- Removal of several side mechanics. Flying wizards from mines, ice rocks to freeze a pool, Area push are surely removed. I miss launching my friends outside of the screen.
- Shorter overall story (about 9 chapters). But this is tolerable with high amount of replayability (Hard & super hard difficulty, artifacts).
Overall, I'm not disappointed with this game. Sure the devs removed many mechanics, but those are for the balance, more challenging gameplay with "out-of-the-box" thinking (Now i'm learning to often use weapon imbues). Still, I even had great laughs from dialogues, idiocy, and accidents I made with my friends. (Not to mention there's Arnold from Terminator Voice Pack!). I give it 9/10.

Graphic side, it's better than Magicka; or I could say it's almost identical to Wizard Wars.
I know it sucks that they changed how the character moves, but this new method to move a character can be useful at fighting enemies. You could attack while running, or even you could heal while running. At first you'll get annoyed but from time to time, you'll get used to this.

Spells controls using controller is awful. Well, I must also admit that it is hard to get used with it.
The spells itself is reduced. Fire and Water can't be combined becomes steam, but they'll still become fire and water until you cast it. Basically, they are nerfing some OP spells like lightning bolt (QFQFAS in magicka). Well, I wonder if crash to desktop spell still working or not...
There is a new feature, quick-spell-slot. It has a cooldown, but you still can spam the spells manually(you could see the spell's combination by right clicking at the quick-spell-slot).
The multiplayer works flawlessly (Like in their trailer, working netcode lol)
The story is promising so far, and the jokes are funny enough.
The conclusion is : Magicka 2 is a nice sequel of Magicka and it is worth buying.

Sol 0 has been a good game thus far and I've enjoyed what I've seen for the most part. Having played a lot of RTS games, I can say that this one is a bit unique in regards to what it targets. The graphics are pretty good, and it seems to play smooth. There are a lot of different options when it comes to buildings, and you have to really plan ahead in order to be successful, as any good RTS should be.
With that said, and the fact that I do recommend the game, I've ran across some issues which I hope will be addressed down the road. The only reason I state these issues, yet still recommend the game is because it has a lot of aspects that are fun, and fixing the bugs will make the game so much better.
AI Paths
I find that the units will get stuck in an area or will "loop" when told to do something. They will pick up supplies and then walk three steps, turn around and come back. I sometimes have to click on them, cancel what I need them to do, and then re-issue the order. The pathing does work about 85% of the time, it just needs to have some special attention in order to iron out the bugs. I've also noticed that sometimes I can place an oygen generator, and for whatever reason at random points, the astronaut will lay down the first supply to build it, and after that, the building will be ignored by them and forklifts and will never be completed. So in return, I'll have a building half-built, just sitting there. I'll then have to destory things around it, in order for me to destroy that building which is stuck.
UI
Sometimes I've noticed the UI is a bit glitchy. You have to make sure that you click directly in the middle of a building in order to select it, otherwise it will select the ground. And no I don't mean that I'm clicking on the ground away from the unit, I mean that I can click somewhere off from the center of the unit and it will do that.
Within the main menu, you have to "right-click" on the first button so that you can access the workshop custom maps. Their needs to be another button for this, or an option. Had I not just started randomly clicking in order to see where the option was at, I would have never found it.
Bulldozer
The vehicle bugs out quite a bit when it comes to moving rocks. And the rocks themselves will glitch out and actually get stuck in a building and then making it sort of difficult to get them away so you can continue to move them.
Over-all, yes the game has issues, but that still shouldn't detour you from trying it out. It's not bad for the price, and as I said before, hopefully in the next few releases the issues will be addressed. I'd probably end up giving this a 7/10.

It's an old school mascot based action platformer, like Sonic, Mario, Kirby, and the like.  It's self aware and quite funny, causing me to laugh out loud at times.  The controls are tight and the art is well done.
That being said, the game constantly tries to get me to give it a bad review.  There are some absolutely intolerable sections involving one hit kills for no reason, a forced stealth section where you have to start the entire thing over if you're detected, poorly explained unneccesary backtracking, and, oh yeah, if you die the game restarts you at the last save point, even if it was ages ago, there's no autosave or checkpoint system.  It only came out in 2014, it's not like it's from decades ago.  The difficulty curve is nonsense thanks to an extremely generous item system that allows you to fully heal multiple times in combat, as well as double or triple your damage and shield yourself.
However, I'm still going recommend it.  Just know what you're getting into and don't expect the moon.

Pros:
-Tight mechanics allow for very precise movements with a decent array of tools and weapons you unlock that increase the complexity of your traversal of new areas.
-The game will present you with interesting mini-games, like having to run a bunch of levels without getting hit once and stealth levels that change up the way you play, keeping the game from getting stale.
-The visuals are fantastic and the soundtrack is amazing. The visuals are bright and colorful even in darker areas of the game while the music is fast and bouncy. Together they create a great atmosphere for a great game.
-Fanservice can be good or bad depending on your taste.
Cons:
-The game is cheap, meaning it will place enemies in places you need to step or land on to move forward, forcing you to take damage. This will set up an environment that, unless you’re super careful, you will jump on a hidden monster which takes a large chunk of health.
-The in game economy is terrible. You need to grind if you want to have both the upgrades and items such as potions. Going for a 100% run I barely made enough money for all the upgrades.
-Third game in the series. Characters interact and have history with each other. It’s not hard to follow but you are jumping into an ongoing story.
-Fanservice can be good or bad depending on your taste.
General Thoughts:
Shantae is a good game with small flaws. You will be immediately greeted with astounding visuals and sounds which will be followed by tight game play and with all of them working together you will be sucked in, that is until you hit a few of it’s flaws. The game places cheap opponents in positions that will hit you even if you are careful, taking away large chunks of your life. Requiring you to memorize enemy positions in areas if you wanna move between them without taking massive damage. Thankfully, it’s not hard to overcome these issues, but it is frustrating dealing with them in an otherwise good game. The game’s story is good enough for what it presents and the addition of character models will either pull you in or put you off as they involved a good amount of fanservice from the main character and the supporting cast. The game is by no means perfect but it is one of the better 2D platformers with metroidvania elements to come out.

The only thing that I didn't like was the lengthy interactions for the purpose of the story line.  Other than that it was pretty damn fun.  The entire game was pretty easy which by contrast caused the final level seem to be virtually impossible.  It was VERY frustrating.  Never-the-less I would wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone of any age who likes Metroid or Castlevania.

Don't be fooled by the 32-bit pixel graphics or if you're offput by the waifubait anime artstyle, this game is a MASSIVE improvement in every conceivable way to Risky's Revenge and a superbly done 2D metroidvania game. It is difficult to put exactly into words why but it addresses almost every problem, from a MUCH better map, to MUCH less confusing maps, to much faster movement which goes SUPER fast once you get the boots, to much more manageable hidden collectibles, to much less boring, droning music; EVERYTHING is better, like geez. However, if you're looking to jump into the Shantae series from this game, it is not exactly the ideal spot to start, since this IS indeed a direct sequel to Risky's Revenge, story-wise and you'll be left scratching your head, and this game does not use the traditional shantae gameplay of using transformation dances, and instead using these pirate equipment you acquire and can even upgrade to a certain extent. This is probably the BEST shantae game overall, but definitely not the place to start for newcomers, even though it's just so good and fun to play.

I'm not a big fan of FPSers, mainly because I can't shoot strait, but I'm a big fan of Star Wars, so I decided to give this a try... And I wasn't disappointed!
The story starts during the Clone War (before Episode III) and you play as the leader of Delta Squad, an elite combat unit. Your squad members are: Delta 07 (sniper) - code name: SEV, Delta 40 (tech) - code name: FIXER and Delta 62 (demo) - code name: SCORCH. The objective: galactic cleanup.
First, let me say, that the VA is fantastic. It's light-hearted, well-written and performed to perfection. You are in the middle of a war, but it never gets too serious, which is good for someone like me, who are not fans of the genre. Jonathan David Cook (07), Temuera Morrison (38), Andrew Chaikin (40) and Raphael Sbarge (62) must be applauded!
The gameplay is smooth and uncomplicated and the controls are easy. In regards to difficulty, easy really is EASY, and it only gets a little tougher once you progress.
The story is linear... and it works brilliantly. It would hate to see this in an open world environment. It sticks to what it is, a simple fps, that gives you a sense of what you're doing.
If I have to say anything negative about this game, it would be that it is too short. You can complete it in a day.
In conclusion: if you are looking for an uncomplicated and fun fps, this is it! It feels like Star Wars, and that is important to me.

I  absolutely love this game. The way it plays is phenomenal, especially for it's time. The AI are smart and the action is intense. You'll never find a dull moment in this game.
The story is dark but has fun aspects to it, especially 62's witty banter with the rest of the squad.
The characters are great and the voice acting is incredible.
You really feel like a Spec Ops soldier of the Republic. You'll actually step straight into the boots of a clone soldier into the most intense situations you could comprehend, such as facing off against super-battle-droids with your entire squad incapacited and have nothing but a pistol and a few grenades. You feel extremely overwhelmed at times, but that's the fun of it.  Also, the squad commands are well done, yet simple, keeping you from freaking out in the middle of battle with your commands and the action combined, so you can keep your head in the game.
As I said earlier, the characters are great and you really feel the emotions when you see an ally fall, and you will likely try your hardest to keep them safe under your command.
Overall, here's my pros and cons:
Pros: Simply incredible gameplay, impressive graphics for it's time, great cast of characters and their voice actors, Simply incredible gameplay and simple but effective squad commands, witty and fun, but very serious about itself and it's scenarios, makes you actaully think, unlike other games where you can "Pray-'n-Spray" without thinking and rack up kills, like CoD.
Cons: Very short campaign, crappy multiplayer.

Reach for the Sun really feels like a simple flash game made as a proof-of-concept or something similar. Play time is somewhere under an hour after which you have gained everything and done everything.
A shame really. With extended gameplay and more interesting mechanics the game could potentially be a unique little flower, but currently it is just over-priced run-of-the-mill flash game you could find on any website.

This game is an underrated classic and the predecessor to games like Deus Ex, Bioshock, and Dishonored. It is one of the earliest, maybe even the original, FPS-RPG. It was lost between the DOOM and Duke Nukem 3D crazes. Strife was a very innovative idea for the time, adding a jump button, stealthy paths, branching story choices, the ability to switch sides or betray people you did quests for, a simple RPG leveling system, currency and stores that sold weapons, ammo, med-kits, and upgrades, as well as a flamethrower and phosphorus grenades that could set enemies on fire and spread. I played this when I was younger and found it underappreciated and unknown to many people. I'm glad to see someone brought it back and updated it. Thanks to Rogue Entertainment for the original Strife (as well as American McGee's Alice - another outside the box, great game) and thanks to Night Dive Studios for the update and re-release. I have nominated it for the "Underrated Classic" Award for the We Didn't Think of Everything Steam Award. Do yourself a favor a check out this classic that took the DOOM engine to its furthest potential.

Good game.
It's an RTS basically with the pathogen types as factions, and each faction will have a build order. I've already come close to a basic build order that seems to work for most pathogens. I'm sure I'll have to refine it when I move to the higher difficulties or abandon it entirely when I play the fantasy pathogens, but basically the formula for victory predictably follows an epidemiological nightmare scenario.
Focus on spread and resistance and then add lethality once you're already everywhere.
This is especially effective if you can then resell your transmission spending.
The virus model tripped that up because it would mutate and announce to humanity before it was done spreading, and there was no resale.
The solution then was to spend all points on transmission and resistance and let the mutation buy the lethality and while racing the clock.
Certain combinations of traits are objectively more dangerous than others. There's gonna be an optimal path here, that's not really avoidable without starting to sacrifice plausibility. Or constrain the narrative, which is what the scenarios and fantasy pathogens are about, which is 100% fine.
I'm kinda disappointed though, I was expecting to be able to craft a pathogen and then unleash it and see what happens, but with a skill and research tree it's not really like that at all. It's a lot more like an RPG or rogue like in that you do stuff, and earn points and spend them as things get harder till you win or die.
Maybe there's a mode that does that later, or maybe it can be modded.
I have some suggestions.
It's not perfectly visually clear which nations are infected and which aren't. Available upgrades should be a whole different color, not a different shade of red.
Healthy countries should have a more visual indication of this, maybe a light green border that turns red once infection happens.
Showing country name when you hover would be nice, and educational. And showing all the options on the tree without having to unlock the adjacent one needs to happen too.
Some realism problems imo.
Global insanity is way less disruptive than it should be. I recommend the devs read up on SSRI discontinuation syndrome and just imagine what that would do to a society if everyone had it. See also the movie Crazies.
Also the game is way too respectful of borders. We don't live in walled city states for the most part.
And certain nations need to react faster and more drastically than others. As per World War Z. (book, not movie)
Also the plane and boat paths need to be a lot more random. California never receives ships according to this model of the world. And Greenland only ever sends ships to Russia. Heh. No.
I feel like this is a good beginning but I'd like to see a much more serious, less QTE/RTS, version. Something where I can design a pathogen, and unleash it.
Still, I definitely recommend the game.

X-Plane is an excellent flight simulator with a great deal of potential, and in it's current state, it is absolutely worth purchasing depending on the type of flying you're interested in.
Out of the box, it is lacking seasonal textures, and upper-level weather. However, easy to install mods are available for both, including Winter_Package for seasonal textures, and XPGFS for upper-level weather. Wind transitions are fairly smooth, however cloud transitions are less so. Add-on weather engines are currently in development.
Terrain graphics are excellent, and upgradeable with free mods, and paid add-ons. Airport scenery is generally complete as far as runways and taxiways, but buildings are frequently missing. This can also be rectified by downloading free scenery mods, and using the WED tool available from X-Plane's website, it is easy to build your own.
X-Plane is in active development.
Included aircraft vary from terrible to okay, however this is normal for flight simulators. Add-on aircraft are very good.
Before buying X-Plane, FSX, or even P3D it's important to understand that all simulators are underfeatured out of the box, and add-ons, generally paid are needed to reach the sims full potential. The base simulator can generally be considered one part of the simulator 'system'.
That said, with one paid add-on(a Carenado aircraft), and a few free ones, X-Plane surpasses FSX for GA flying, and with an improved weather engine and more add-on airliners will surpass FSX for airliners as well.

I like this game and think it has potential, but there are a few bugs that need to be worked out still. When travelling back to Earth, any tasks or directions given to Astronauts or machines are forgotten by those that are given tasks. Along the same vein, if given a task before leaving for Earth, if an Astronaut is currently building something, the task is half completed and cannot be finished nor can it be destroyed thus becoming a nuisance (ex: a half finished solar panel that cannot be finished nor destroyed is a waste of supplies  and energy and becomes a problem when upgrading to geothermal tech power as it cannot be destroyed to make way for more geo-therm plants). Astronauts get hung up when automated, and only fix one solar panel before they become stationary and more or less useless until tasked again as well, when left to their own devices. When selecting a weather satellite for the first time, if the player is unfamiliar with the rocket's capability, the rocket can only be used for weather satellite transport, despite being capable of also carrying a small amount of supplies (those supplies never reach the martian surface). I would also like to see a larger map in future as the current selections are small, but provide adequate space for colonizing (a nice option would be for the developer to take a look at the game "Banished" on Steam and expand map and resources based loosely along that game's design). All in all as I previously stated this game has potential and despite the bugs is innovative in a sandbox format for those who dream of martian colonization some day (which I think is the point of any game along these lines...for the gamer to be immersed in a fantasy of the possibilities.)

I don't know how i never knew about this game. It's a great platformer with a decent story. The aesthetics were great and each level had a different atmosphere. You knew going into the 4th island mod bog was going to be tough just going through the first screen. The animation is awesome everywhere; Even down to the smallest of enemies. The enemies were balanced pretty well, with the exception of the wolves doing 1 1/2 hears of damage. They were annoying, but had relatively low health compared to other enemies in the area. Two of the bosses didn't seem to be balanced very well though. The dragon (dagron) was quite random with it's pattern and sometimes just went way too fast while the other unbalanced boss the ice slug (I'm not looking up the name) was extremely easy and slow.
In my first couple play throughs, i had a tough time finding out what i was supposed to do (i'm not much for trying everything to complete a puzzle), but after that first time it was a breeze the other play throughs. It especially got fun when you unlock pirate mode (new game with all weapons from the start). Dashing through the easy levels and finding shortcuts in the early levels was very fun and i think I'm going to help make a guide for the 100% and any% speed runs.
And lastly the achievements were challenging. 100% speed run, 2 heart challenge, never get hit... All challenging, but doable when you learn the game enough. All in all I would definitely recommend this to anyone looking for a action platformer.
