BC2 was my first foray into the Battlefield series, and consumed over 200 hours of my life that I don't regret.
Battlefield has always been about multiplayer, so I don't know why DICE even bothered putting effort into making a campaign. It was boring and I didn't play more than 15 minutes of it. Those resources could've gone towards improving multiplayer, which while flawed is a blast that I highly recommend to fans of the genre.
Never before has the game engine technology actually mattered so much for the gameplay, and that's because of the Destruction 2.0 part of the engine. Gone are the days of being unable to kill that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who hid behind a missile-proof tree or wall that even a pistol round would easily punch through in real life. With enough punishment, every building will spectacularly collapse, killing anyone trapped inside and also destroying any Rush objectives if they're inside a building. Trees no longer provide free shields, with small-arms fire easily chopping them down while tanks crush them like ants. The destruction capabilities force players to think carefully about where they want to hold their flanking positions or where they should concentrate their firepower.
There are two main game types - Rush and Conquest. Conquest was pretty much the only thing anyone played in BF2, and is just as fun here. Each team needs to capture and hold positions at specific spawn points until the match is over. On maps with tanks and helicopters, this can get really intense. However many servers start off with too many spawn tickets, so this gametype can feel like a drag.
Rush is significantly more heart-pounding and matches also tend to conclude faster. It's like Counter-Strike's demolition gametype but with vehicles, and more than one bomb. One side controls two boxes which the other side is trying to destroy. The boxes can be destroyed by placing a charge (which the defending team can remove before it's too late), or just repeated attacks with tank shells, grenades, missiles, remote C4, and even kamikaze vehicles. Most Rush maps have 3 sets of these boxes. If the first set falls, the defending team retreats to another area of the map to defend another set, which keeps the game interesting and prevents the match from getting repetitive (since the area changes). All 3 sets must fall before the attacking team can be victorious, which keeps things interesting and allows the defending team to adapt their strategy in case of a bad first round, potentially to victory. I'd say over 90% of my games were on Rush maps.
The class system was simplified into 4 classes which I actually like, as it keeps the game simple and makes it easier for everyone to help the team rather than go lone-wolf. The assault class mainly uses assault rifles, and can drop ammo kits for his friends. The engineer mainly uses silenced SMGs, and can repair friendly vehicles (or sabotage enemy vehicles). The engineer is the only guy with access to rocket launchers and anti-tank mines, essential for taking out enemy vehicles if on foot. The medic mainly uses LMGs, and can drop health kits and revive fallen teammates. The recon mainly uses sniper rifles, and can spot enemies, plant C4, and throw motion trackers for "remote spotting".
As you can see, all classes manage to be super-helpful in some way, particularly the medic. In fact, healing and reviving is the easiest way to score points in a game, which encourages players to select the medic class and actually make themselves useful. I've had matches where I got the highest score on the team despite having zero kills, thanks to the ease of scoring as a medic.
Some players may not like the default weapons for a particular class (e.g. I'm not a very skilled sniper). Fret not, for the game has quite a few "any-class" weapons that can be equipped in lieu of the default weapon type. These include multiple shotguns, the M1 Garand semi-auto rifle, and the G3 assault rifle (one of my favourites).
Every weapon is fun to use and I had a blast getting gold stars for all of them including the handguns. The unlock system is also very quick - everything can be unlocked by level 23, and attachments such as red dot sights are available for all weapons, rather than being weapon-specific. Sadly BF3 reverted to the COD-style system of making everything weapon-specific :(
The vehicles, an essential part of the Battlefield experience, do not disappoint. Tanks, Humvees, ATVs, and the dreaded helicopters all have roles to play. The pilot's seat of a helicopter can be very challenging (to this date I still don't know how to fly one, LOL) but everything else is easy to pick up.
In short, the multiplayer gameplay was one of the best experiences of my time in college, and I still have fond memories.
When this game launched in 2010, the Frostbite engine was quite demanding, and not too well optimized (console port!). Five years later, it shouldn't be a problem for any modern rig. However the FOV can't be changed without editing the ini which is annoying. Latency could be improved for sure (in fact it got worse in BF3). Overall it's a fairly stable game that doesn't have too much console-itis.
Sadly, this game doesn't have mod tools, so no custom maps. EA doesn't control most of the dedicated servers though, so the game will at least last quite a while. Get it and have fun!

No doubt that line has been used over and over, but very accurate. You start of in a sewage plant, after dispatching one or two guards, you emerge in a town. The game works very well, has a range of interesting weapons, boss fights, and even stealth missions, if you so choose to play that way. You have currency, which you can use to buy gear a the local shops, or to patch up those bullet holes in your face, at the doctors. I have to admit that i'd never played Strife in 1996, and hadn't even heard of it. I felt i owed it to the game and the developers to find out why this was.
It turns out, that Strife was using the standard Doom engine, and came out a few years after the first Doom. The game was criticised for not having equivalent graphics to it's competitors, like Duke Nukem 3D, therefore seeming outdated, and never getting the chance it deserved, and ultimately being forgotten about.
In the current age of gaming, with games like Minecraft leading the way for a comeback to an almost lost era, with games using phrases like "pixel graphics" and "retro", to hook players in, Strife finally has the chance to be what it should have been in the first place.
An Instant Classic.

CRUSHING DISAPOINTMENT
This feels like a knock off product or a spin off licensed game.
Less spell variety
Slower pacing
Boring levels
Simplified gameplay
Forced "wacky" comedy
Clear Console focus
The almost traditional bugs
This title doesn't have the same frenetic flow and hilarious (often disastrous) antics. You move, charge spells and heal slower, combined with the new "click once" movement the gameplay feels unresponsive and tiring.
The removal of combined elements limits spell options and cuts down on experimentation, no longer will you res your friends just to kill them all over again with a new combination you just thought of.
Weaker impacts from spells and the inability to decimate enemies with the ease of Magicka feel like a denial of what made the first game so memorable. Spells were not balanced in the original game and that was half the fun, obliterating half the screen with your latest creation or an accidental botched spell. This attempt to balance the game as if it were a competitive title just goes against the entertainment of the original.
Maps are even more linier than the original game and often dotted with pitfalls and terrain to limit movement even further. This creates false challenge from holes in the level you couldn't see, to being hemmed in with enemies upon respawn with no brief invulnerability.
There's a definate push for more DLC opportunities. The original was flooded with DLC too, but now weapons, robes and even just colour options are part of an account bound loadout. I may be cynical here, but I believe this is so they can sell more individual gear and equipment.
The game is cluttered with console changes, quick cast spells that are easier for a controller, constant button prompts, and a UI designed for party play in a living room rather than over the net. With the slower pace and change in movement controls to favour a thumbstick, I keep feeling I'm playing a lazy port of the PS4 game.
I regret my purchase of this game.

Lots of problems with this title. Where to start?:
# You are *forced* to sign up for a Paradox account and link it to your steam account in order to be able to play online. Something that is not advertised prior to your purchase. No reason has been given by the developers as to why they are forcing customers to do this.
# Account creation in game not properly working, workaround of creating an account directly on their website necessary to get playing.
# If you have a widescreen monitor, tabbing out and back in will squash up the graphics other than the UI and you will have to restart the game.
# Client crashes on first spacebar press for some users.
# Fewer spells available than in Magicka 1
# There are now preset *special* spells, some of which seem to be very half baked such as "emergency teleport" that basically always ports you to the left of the screen.
# Seems to be a short campaign, at the time of writing with only 2.4hrs played already 2/3 of the way through.
# The "humour" is entirely banal, and a clear downgrade from Magicka 1.
# Cannot remap keys
# Control nuance removed such as hold down mouse button to move is now just click to move.
# Being used as a vehicle to advertise other titles such as Wizard Wars on the main menu screen, basically giving an impression that they dont really have confidence in this product and want you to play something else.
All in all, pretty much a downgrade from the previous title. Severe disappointment.

Going to say the words which seem to be a theme for this game - "I really wanted to like it..." It has so many things going for it; independent dev, great theme, fun concept...
But.
1: Slow the game down. A year takes about 10 minutes and in that time you can only click so much. This game is built as a strategic building and colony management game, but the pace and speed makes it feel more like one of those "real time strategy" games with no strategy and lots of clicking where the only goal is to make as much resource as fast as possible for war - or in this game's case, not dying. This game needs to decide what it wants to be - strategic building or RTS.
2: A bit of mystery on how things work and what they do is great. But a complete lack of instructions (have fun with the Biology Lab!) is really annoying and destroys any actually planning you might find time to do. I would assume any society smart enough to ship a biology lab all the way to Mars might actually know how to use it. So should the player.
3: Wonky AI and unit automation. On some units this works OK, on others it is laughable. And there is zero consistency on how routing and automation works from one unit to the next. Come on - this is just lazy development and usability. It needs to be standardized and fixed.
4: COLONY DOES NOT HAVE ENOUGH COLONISTS!
COLONY DOES NOT HAVE ENOUGH COLONISTS!
COLONY DOES NOT HAVE ENOUGH COLONISTS!
COLONY DOES NOT HAVE ENOUGH COLONISTS!
COLONY DOES NOT HAVE ENOUGH COLONISTS!
COLONY DOES NOT HAVE ENOUGH COLONISTS!

If you like hearing this every thirty seconds, then you will LOVE this game. Especially if you want no information about what level of colonists would be ideal for your designed base and to have the never ending colonist alert messages hide the really important alerts you need to know about. Again, if this is meant to be a strategic game, give the player useful information and alerts that help them play, I don't know, strategically!
5: The bulldozer. Enough said.
There is more, and yes, there are also many GOOD things. Like I said, I really wanted to like this game. But overall it suffers from a lack of identity and completion. I hope in the future it gets fixed. Would love to come back and be able to support this and give it a positive review.

BC2 was my first foray into the Battlefield series, and consumed over 200 hours of my life that I don't regret.
Battlefield has always been about multiplayer, so I don't know why DICE even bothered putting effort into making a campaign. It was boring and I didn't play more than 15 minutes of it. Those resources could've gone towards improving multiplayer, which while flawed is a blast that I highly recommend to fans of the genre.
Never before has the game engine technology actually mattered so much for the gameplay, and that's because of the Destruction 2.0 part of the engine. Gone are the days of being unable to kill that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who hid behind a missile-proof tree or wall that even a pistol round would easily punch through in real life. With enough punishment, every building will spectacularly collapse, killing anyone trapped inside and also destroying any Rush objectives if they're inside a building. Trees no longer provide free shields, with small-arms fire easily chopping them down while tanks crush them like ants. The destruction capabilities force players to think carefully about where they want to hold their flanking positions or where they should concentrate their firepower.
There are two main game types - Rush and Conquest. Conquest was pretty much the only thing anyone played in BF2, and is just as fun here. Each team needs to capture and hold positions at specific spawn points until the match is over. On maps with tanks and helicopters, this can get really intense. However many servers start off with too many spawn tickets, so this gametype can feel like a drag.
Rush is significantly more heart-pounding and matches also tend to conclude faster. It's like Counter-Strike's demolition gametype but with vehicles, and more than one bomb. One side controls two boxes which the other side is trying to destroy. The boxes can be destroyed by placing a charge (which the defending team can remove before it's too late), or just repeated attacks with tank shells, grenades, missiles, remote C4, and even kamikaze vehicles. Most Rush maps have 3 sets of these boxes. If the first set falls, the defending team retreats to another area of the map to defend another set, which keeps the game interesting and prevents the match from getting repetitive (since the area changes). All 3 sets must fall before the attacking team can be victorious, which keeps things interesting and allows the defending team to adapt their strategy in case of a bad first round, potentially to victory. I'd say over 90% of my games were on Rush maps.
The class system was simplified into 4 classes which I actually like, as it keeps the game simple and makes it easier for everyone to help the team rather than go lone-wolf. The assault class mainly uses assault rifles, and can drop ammo kits for his friends. The engineer mainly uses silenced SMGs, and can repair friendly vehicles (or sabotage enemy vehicles). The engineer is the only guy with access to rocket launchers and anti-tank mines, essential for taking out enemy vehicles if on foot. The medic mainly uses LMGs, and can drop health kits and revive fallen teammates. The recon mainly uses sniper rifles, and can spot enemies, plant C4, and throw motion trackers for "remote spotting".
As you can see, all classes manage to be super-helpful in some way, particularly the medic. In fact, healing and reviving is the easiest way to score points in a game, which encourages players to select the medic class and actually make themselves useful. I've had matches where I got the highest score on the team despite having zero kills, thanks to the ease of scoring as a medic.
Some players may not like the default weapons for a particular class (e.g. I'm not a very skilled sniper). Fret not, for the game has quite a few "any-class" weapons that can be equipped in lieu of the default weapon type. These include multiple shotguns, the M1 Garand semi-auto rifle, and the G3 assault rifle (one of my favourites).
Every weapon is fun to use and I had a blast getting gold stars for all of them including the handguns. The unlock system is also very quick - everything can be unlocked by level 23, and attachments such as red dot sights are available for all weapons, rather than being weapon-specific. Sadly BF3 reverted to the COD-style system of making everything weapon-specific :(
The vehicles, an essential part of the Battlefield experience, do not disappoint. Tanks, Humvees, ATVs, and the dreaded helicopters all have roles to play. The pilot's seat of a helicopter can be very challenging (to this date I still don't know how to fly one, LOL) but everything else is easy to pick up.
In short, the multiplayer gameplay was one of the best experiences of my time in college, and I still have fond memories.
When this game launched in 2010, the Frostbite engine was quite demanding, and not too well optimized (console port!). Five years later, it shouldn't be a problem for any modern rig. However the FOV can't be changed without editing the ini which is annoying. Latency could be improved for sure (in fact it got worse in BF3). Overall it's a fairly stable game that doesn't have too much console-itis.
Sadly, this game doesn't have mod tools, so no custom maps. EA doesn't control most of the dedicated servers though, so the game will at least last quite a while. Get it and have fun!

In my honest opinion, Strife is one of the most underrated games back in mid-90s. Unlike other first person shooters of the same age, like Duke Nukem 3D and Quake, this one is an excellent combination of first person shooter and role playing game. Despite of its Doom engine, you have lots of NPCs to interact, to ally with in order to fight against the enemy, or even to trade with your gold for their merchandises. Every major dialogue with those characters is also come with voices, performed by earnest voice actors. This boosts the game experience with its story and progression in a really good way. Speaking of the story, it also has multiple endings, affected by the choice you make during the progression. Those elements are definitely something that you couldn't see from the first person shooters back in mid-90s, and they make this game really unique.
Action is pretty much something that you might expect from the game with Doom engine. You also have inventory system from other FPS like Heretic and Hexen, so you can stock your powerups and use them whenever you really need. What makes this game more unique is the stealth system. Enemy soldiers in the same sector won't attack you until you do something suspicious. That being said, you can kill the enemy acolytes with your slient weapons, such as poison bolt, and you won't sound the alarm. Though some enemy mechanics don't give a $hi+ about the stealth system and attack you, which is a little bit annoying. But who cares, since it's more fun to mow down the enemies with your assault rifle. This game also has upgrade systems for your accuracy and health, just like a level system of other role-playing games.
What makes this game even better is this HD remastering. Now you can enjoy this game with modern elements like proper mouse aiming, better lighting effects, and perfect compatibility for your modern gaming setting. It even has objective assistant on the automap to help you find the location of next objective, which is really useful to navigate those maze-like levels. Speaking of level design, this game uses hub system like Hexen, making various levels into one giant open world with lots of explorable areas.
In overall, this is a forgotten gem from 1996, a something that ahead of the time. It is not a perfect game, but it's definitely something different from other mediocre first person shooters. A solid 9/10 stuff for me.

I have memories of this working perfectly on another Linux system, but on my current setup, it has several issues. It pains me to write a negative review of a Night Dive title, because they usually do excellent work (I was amazed that their Turok remaster even runs fantastically under Wine -- I don't know if that's because of anything they did, but it was awesome).
The first thing I noticed is that the high-quality renderer "smooths" the sprites even if this setting is turned off. Coincidentally, I also encounter this bug in the Linux version of Duke Nukem 3D: Megaton Edition. It's possibly an issue with OpenGL, but on my system, Shadow Warrior Redux correctly displays "retro" textures, so clearly a well-designed program will not succumb to this issue. I've installed several different distros on this machine (a laptop from System76) and they ALL have this rendering issue. Switching to the original renderer makes the sprites nice and chunky, at the expense of all the other pretty graphical enhancements being removed. This was good enough for me, however -- !
Issue number two: Controller support is all ♥♥♥♥ed-up for me. I've tried hacking together several different approaches, and none of them cause the controller to behave normally in this game. Again, Shadow Warrior Redux (an excellent example of a great Linux version of a remastered retro game) works normally with a controller without any tweaks, so I can't help but feel that this is something the developers could fix.
This is not a well-designed Linux port in my eyes. It's great on Windows, however, and if that's your OS I heartily recommend grabbing this game. However, I've got to cast a "negative" vote to express my dissatisfaction with the substandard Linux version.

This is, for all intents and purposes, a good game that is lacking.
While issues such as UI and rather clunky graphics can be overlooked. My biggest issue is the AI. I don't know how many colonists I have lost because my astronauts and forklifts suddenly take leave of their senses and forgetting to build a greenhouse that would save the colony. Sound is woefully terrible and clearly taken from stock sounds with little effort taken in regards to choice. Dying colonists sound like breaking machinery, cryotanks sound like a battalion of infantry are marching around inside and the soundtrack has a section that will, on first hearing it, make you panic and wonder what's happening until you realise it's just part of the ambient track.
On the whole it's not a terrible game. The mechanics work nicely and the slow progression from unmanned exploration mission to a thriving colony is realistic; albeit as far as your imagination might believe a real life Mars colonisation would be. The requirement to send nearly everything up by rockets that have a waiting period between each launch is a nice touch because it makes you plan ahead and think. This is no gratuitous colony builder.
The challenge of space management and the learning curve kept me interested until the AI astronauts started to become complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Were this issue fixed I would recommend this game wholeheartedly. As of now, I recommend it but only with an 8/10. This is a gem in the rough and despite it's fully released status I hope the devs are doing their best to fix game breaking issues soon.

The pathfinding on many units can be frustrating and requires micro-management, but with experience you will learn the unit tendencies and to toggle off a unit's ability when you want pathfinding to improve. After sinking in a good amount of game time you'll learn to appreciate the lack of excellent pathfinding as it's an attention draining game mechanic that actually improves gameplay.
Aside from pathfinding issues, the game is fun, plays on weaker systems, and can be rewardingly challenging. THIS IS A HARDCORE SIMULATOR! NOT A FLYING GAME!
An unbiased opinion from someone who flies over 20 flight sims.
Being a lover of flight sims I have all the major ones.
If your looking for a game, KSP or Ace combat might be more up your alley.
Ill compare this to Microsoft flight simulator for comparision
Flight Model
Microsoft Flight simulator 10 (FSX) uses a variable chart to determin how an aircraft behaves inflight. So the control surfaces moving in game are more or less jjust eye candy. As a file controls the aircrafts variable movements. Not to bash FSX but it gives a more mechanical feel to flying. Less natural. However it is less processor intensive and easier to learn
XPlane uses an advanced blade theory dynamics. Which models of airflow to calculate how the surface would behave in the air condtions. So moving a control surface actually affects the movement of the air. Giving i a far more realistic feel. Its far more difficult to fly and spin outs are to be expected.
Terrain:
FSX uses real world terrain data. Its a fairly low resolution so it can appear to be blocky in some places. However DSX also uses real world road maps and places large cities with real land marks. So you can easily fly around your home town and VFR flights.
Xplane 10 Uses a simular real world terrain model at a higher resoultion. Making mountains much more realistic. As well as the weather effects acting upon them. However real world cities are absent. Although using satelite images the engine places cities and town in the right places. Just don't expect to be flying over the Sears tower in chicago.
FSX uses the same data files to determine aircrafts ability to move in the weather. It feels very clunky and un natural. Adjust for winds and temputures at variing levels
XPlane 10 again uses blade theory. However it only accounts for ground level and altitude of your aircraft. Meaning a cross wind at the airfiled will affect a plane on land almost as much as one at altiude. However Xplane 10 uses an active model radar. So you can in theory actually fly into a hurricane in real time and watch it on radar.
Aircraft Models:
FSX comes with a slew of highly detailed aircraft. All with 3d cockpits and working insterments. So you can fly that little puddle jumper to an F-18 right from the get go.
Xplane10 does have a lot of aircraft but many do not come default with 3d interiors. Most have some sort of 2d panel that will sufice for flying.
Combat:
FSX sucks
Xpalne 10 Sucks
DCS world is free. You have no excuse to not have it.
Multi player.
FSX has a clean and simple interface that allows you to browse and favorite servers. A modern design thats clean and user friendly.
Xplane allows only direct connect. So I hope your computer skills are alright.
Personal conclusion:
FSX is more about the experience of flying. Weather just goofing off or flying across the world to see the sights. I often will just plot courses to sight see various places and to learn to use the systems in the game.
Xplane 10 is more about learning to fly. Which lets face it. Weather you bought FSX or Xpalne is sorto f why you bought either. Xplane is just more about the feel of flying than flying. Its a great product and why I was happy both came to steam.
And totop it all off most of the advatnges what one or the other sim has can be negated with addons. BOth free or payware. So it really boils down to how serious you are about flying. I often enjoy total realism in Xplane so more often than not its my go to sim.

Alright, I've had XP 8, 9, and now 10. These are serious flight sims and not for kids expecting Ace Combat or an equivalent thereof where you can just load it and start fighting other aircraft, etc. I will break down the pros and cons:
PRO:
+More accurate flight models (i.e. I can finally do Pugachev's Cobra in my SU-35 without unrealistic altitude gain).
+Can target all flying aircraft (for those days where shooting down an airliner gives you jollies).
+Black smoke upon missle hits/Explosions for bombs.
+Better graphics
+Better supersonic modeling (much less computational flutter)
+At full tilt, I can recognize my neighborhood (better world detail).
+Wing flexing! (Finally)
+Faster batch-converting for airfoils.
Mixed:
+/- Better AI for air combat but still no gun usage for OPFOR aircraft or complex manuevers. I know this isn't a combat sim but can someone make a plug-in for this? It'll be great for those bad days at the office when you just want to recreate a battle from the Korean War.
CON:
-Super complicated to get older aircraft up to the new version.
-When you get older aircraft up to xp10, a huge amounts of adjustments needed in planemaker to get these aircraft flyable.
-Air Traffic Control is junk, just worthless. Even if you set your comms right.
-Requires extensive knowledge of previous XP versions to get any custom aircraft airworthy.
-Only diehard flightsim fans will have the patience to figure out the complicated variables needed to fly this sim.
-Generic modern-standard radar navigation systems, older aircraft can see like new ones without scan deflection restrictions and analogue vs digital system limitations.
I love the X-plane series and I'm glad it is on Steam. It makes it easier than waiting for the store to carry the Full version than the boiled-down North American version. Hopefully fixes will be addressed in later patches.
I recommend this only for diehard sim fans. Those expecting Ace Combat arcade action are going to be vastly disappointed.

What happens when you combine an Isometric Action RPG with an MMO? A game that almost works, but not quite. That is because one significant design choice reallt hurts the gameplay: Attacks Always Hit.
There are skill shots in the game, both friendly and hostile, and they are the attacks that hit like a truck, but alongside these skillshots are attacks that follow the target, and automatically hit, If anybody swings a sword, it doesn't matter if the target leaves melee distance, that melee attack hits. If a witch attacks you with a ranged attack, no amount of dodging will stop her homing missle of free damage.
This is a sacrifice made, I am assuming, to combat latency, allowing for the experience of an Isometric Action RPG with many people all over the world. But in my opinion this sacrifice was too high of a cost. I can ignore a bad story: not saying this has a bad story. I can look past an artistic direction I do not care for: not saying it looks bad. But I do not want to slug through unsatisfying gameplay, and to me, the introduction of auto-hit attacks makes the game unsatisfying.
As a Hardcore (Perma-death) Diablo player, this made the gameplay unsatisfying. The rest of the game was enjoyable, but due to my dissatisfaction, I cannot give this game my recommendation.

Easily the best game in the series. This is the standard every Shantae game should strive to meet.
PROS:
-Faster, more fluid gameplay than any other Shantae game (though partly due to the lack of transformations, a very traditional part of the series).
-Gorgeous art style. Whoever Wayforward hired for this one did an exceptional job. I even prefer it over the new HD chibi art style in Half Genie Hero, personally. I also prefer pixel graphics generally when it comes to platformers.
-Extremely detailed animations. This is something Wayforward nails perfectly most of the time. When a character turns around for instance, rather than just mirroring the sprite, there might be an animation where they blow their hair over the other eye (heart squid lady). The attention to detail is insane.
-Difficulty curve: Every island/dungeon is a little harder than the previous, with the exception of the frostbite dungeon.
-Challenging and plentiful puzzles. I actually had to look up the solutions to a few of them.
-Story was the better one of the series so far IMO.
-Jake Kaufman does it again with the soundtrack. Absolutely amazing, there are more tracks I like in this soundtrack than HGH.
Cons:
I'd really have to nittpick to find fault with this game. The only thing I can think of right off the bat is this: The lack of transformations means also a lack of upgrades to find, which the game conpensates for by replacing heart containers with heart squids which you have to find multiple of in order to expand your maximum health. There's plenty of stuff out there to find, just very little variety in what you find.
All in all, if you like these sorts of metroidvania open-world platformers, you won't regret Pirates Curse in the slightest. I only regret beating the game 100% because now the adventure is over and I have to hope a future Shantae game can match what Pirate's Curse has achieved.

Bad Company 2 is an awesome game and in my eyes by far the best multiplayer shooter I've ever played. I played this game for 600hrs on PS3, and I missed it so much after being disappointed by BF3 and especially BF4 that I've purchased it again for the PC.
Unlike the recent Battlefields from BF3 onwards, Bad Company 2 is less complicated and overloaded - and that's what makes it brilliant. I have to admit, I'm a huge vehicle freak and I only play Battlefield to fly helicopters and jets online (although there are no jets in BC2). I never got used to the new Battlefields with all the auto-lock weapons spamming at you and never really enjoyed it much when even jet pilots barely used their guns and relied solely on their auto-lock weapons. In Bad Company 2, there is no such thing as auto-lock. It's all about skill. If someone is better than you, he will get you - not because you run out of flares but because he was faster or smarter. Likewise, if you are better, nobody will shoot you down. That's how competitive multiplayer gameplay is supposed to be, not what the new Battlefields are like. While I concentrate on air vehicles, the same can be said about everything in this game. Every weapon (system) has a certain feel to it and can be mastered in a way that makes you seem overpowered compared to other players. But, since only very few people truly master a class or a vehicle, the game is generally more balanced and predictable, which makes it easier for new players to get a hang of it. You don't just die out of nowhere because someone with a higher rank used a weapon system only unlocked later in the game - the unlocks generally don't make a class better, they just offer you more weapons to chose of and that makes it fun to try out different sets or classes because you don't have to worry being "underarmed" compared to others.
No matter what your style of playing is, wether you're a sniper seeking out your kills from a distance or a tanker supporting your infantry when taking a base - the series rises up to its full potential only when you play as a team. Bad Company 2 encourages teamplay in a way I've never seen in the more recent Battlefield. I can't really put a finger on why that exactly is, I can only assume it is because classes are more limited and vehicles don't heal themselves that players rely more on each other and work together.
Another thing great about this game are the maps. Not only do they work well with Rush and Conquest, they each have strategies to them and depending on which path to an objective you take you will experience very different gameplay. It's not a random arena in that people run around in circles seeking for the next kill, it's a real Battlefield in which you can flank enemies or directly assault them.
Bad Company 2 is what Battlefield really is about. There are less weapons, less vehicles, less gadgets and the maps are smaller -  but when everything works out, when two good teams meet each other and you sit in your attack helicopter being shot at from all sides, evading infantry launched rockets, tanks, enemy helicopters, having to stay back because every player is a threat - even for a helicopter - and you support your team overhead keeping a base clean for the tanks and infantry to take a flag, when you are truly concentrated and the atmosphere so dense you need a break after the match, that's when you will play your best and most exciting multiplayer matches you have ever played.
As this is the PC version, I have to say though that especially the vehicle controls are quite insensitive and everything moves a bit slower than on console. Nevertheless, go buy it and experience the Battlefield feeling for yourself. You wont regret it.

This used to be a mod before it was an actual game, now it comes out. Everyone including myself were waiting for this moment. I've been playing Sven Co-op since 4.8 and i still have it. I wont be needing it anymore now that the newest version is the game itself, 5.0 is out.
Now that is on Steam i'm giving out the statistics. It is a great GAME, a game that continues its way just like the mod did except adding more stuff in it thats not in 4.8. The game is heavily focused on teamwork against bot controlled enemies. Whether its aliens, marines, nazis, you name it. You play as any character based from either Half-Life or any other games (Such as the Doomguy in Doom, Young Link from Zelda, Mario from Mario games, etc.).
The maps are heavily on campaign, so your objective is to reach through it whether by fighting enemies, solve puzzles, or both. Theres a HUGE amount of maps you can play on. If you are suddenly on the loading screen, it means someone has reached the end of the map which causes a new map to load up. Also keep noted the guns you see, sometimes you get different guns depends on the campaign you play (such as the thompson if played in WWII maps).
There is Half life maps, but there are also modded maps. If you are feeling for adventure, you came in the right place.
Give yourself time to try the game when you can and while you still can. Note that low players does not always mean a bad thing, being yourself is whats worst since it'll make the game harder playing by yourself. Having just one person with you is enough, bringing more will bring on the carnage. The game may be too easy for you if you bring on the best team or just simply bring LOTS of people with you. You want a fair fun game where you are fighting through with others as a team.
The bosses also are VERY promising in most maps. Some maps has bosses, some dont. But you will see one at some point depending on the map you are playing on.
I truly recommend this to anyone, its going to be a blast when playing this.
Edit: So I noticed theres ANOTHER mode that 4.8 doesnt have, which is called survival mode. Its WAY harder than normal mode and takes REAL teamwork to get through. Though its in one of the servers which you need to find and I happen to find one, which has a "Survival" or "Survival Mode" on it. The game really improved since 4.8, I suggest checking it out if normal mode isnt enough for you.

This game is already finished, you can play it from a start to an end and first playthrough should take you about 30-50h, depending how fast you progress and understand the new things. What's happening in this early access is just improvements to quality of life and polishing the final product. There's plenty of things that you can mod into the game and make it even more complex than it already is.
Essentially the closest I can compare it to is Space Engineers but compared to Factorio... Space Engineers are nowhere near as complete as Factorio is. At least that's what my feelings are about it (I love both games though!).
The devs have their own site under
which also has a blog where they post what they're working on each week. Those posts also available on the Steam! You can easily track what new features/improvements are being added and what is being fixed.
Regarding the gameplay:
1) Start:
A little overwhelming with all the options you have, takes a second to get into it. Luckily they have a tutorial and furthermore there's few guides where they teach you more about some game mechanics. Those guides contrary to tutorial can be triggered at any time during your singleplayer game to educate yourself about some new things.
Basically - you have the whole world to yourself (or do you?), you are free to take anything from the ground be that iron, copper, coal, water, trees, uranium, oil. You collect the first few bits on your own, then you have enough to create basic machinery, you introduce some automation into the process, you create first electricity producing engines and you're set with new options to even further automate everything. You set up some very elementary research center and develop new technologies.
2) Getting a hang of it:
Once you get into desigining your own factories, you're sunk for good. Placing all the belts in an optimal way, deciding how to make supply chains, your first train delivery system, more automatisation, more progress into the game, newer technologies unlocked, more optimalisation, more ... pollution? It seems that you have an impact on the enviroment and the aliens that inhabit the planet don't like that everything stinks.
Later it develops even further into hardcore logistic problems, defending against ever evolving aliens and trying to get the first rocket off the face of the planet.
By the way, the graphics and even sounds remind me of such classics as Icewind Dale or first Fallouts. What's more it even resembles the Starcraft series, with zerg-like aliens and their spawning grounds!
Speaking of sounds - the soundtrack is very good, sometimes dark, eerie and othertimes perfectly mixing with the sounds of factory working making you really proud of whatever awfully looking factory you made so far.
AND THIS GAME IS AMAZING WITH FRIENDS! Especially once you discover you can place points on the map and name them! First time I played with the friends we were making lots of hubs with different name for each and it just worked perfectly, because we quickly adapted. Instead of saying: Aliens are attacking from the north, you'll just say - Oh no! Aliens are going for the USA Wall again!
What's lacking is probably the diversity in the vehicles that you have and weapons and other means of defence. I also feel like there could be an entire additional tier of technology/items etc fit into basic game making it even longer. The enemies could also have few more additional types providing new challenges, because at certain point of the game you just become a god that's unstoppable which gets pretty boring, really fast. It's much more fun to get angry at the "damn aliens, they broke my water-pipe line again!" and then go bust them up and then take a revenge on their homes.
Very easy to lose track of time playing this game, its just lots of fun. Very open ended gameplay no hand holding; you get to decide how you want to play and how your factory is going to function.

ShadowCaster first attempted to blend FPS/RPG elements back in 1993, and the following years saw other hybrids such as Hexen, Witchaven, System Shock and CyberMage. Yet, the game most often remembered as “the first FPS/RPG” is Strife.
There’s a reason for that. Even the first minutes of Strife feel very different. You start the game, fight a couple of guards and then, instead of killing demons, you walk into a peaceful town, with various shops, a bar and some interactive NPCs throwing gossip.
You’re then contacted via radio by “Blackbird”, who asks you to join The Front, an underground resistance against the evil theocracy of The Order. This isn’t just some throwaway backstory – you’ll actually go to the rebel’s HQ and work with them.
Your first objective is to take over The Order’s base in town. For that you’ll have to perform a few sabotage missions and trade favors with other NPCs – all of whom have charming voice acting and portraits. Once the base’s defenses are down, you’ll attack it alongside rebel troops, kill the enemy general and move your HQ there! It’s a nice, satisfying pay-off.
After that the town’s gate opens and you’re sent to another location, to further battle the forces of The Order. The world is hub-based, with the maps linking together to form an overworld of sorts you can freely explore, thought the main quest is mostly linear.
Some of your missions can also involve stealth, meaning disguising yourself and only killing enemies with a poisoned crossbow. As your quest advances you’ll uncover more about The Order, learn about the mythic Sigil and experience some great plot twists.
You’ll also gain access to new weapons and upgrades, such as a grenade launcher or increased accuracy stat. Just be sure to carefully manage your money between health kits, armor and ammo.
Finally, while most of the dialog options are illusionary, there’s a choice about half the way into the game that forks the game into two different routes, each with different missions and endings.

Strife was the last game to use the Doom engine, which was already heavily dated. But, while other FPS focused on new 3D graphics, Strife instead presented a new path for the genre, with memorable NPCs, an early open world and a cool, branching story
Doom + RPGs = Strife

I keep saying DOOM is a great template for shooters. With Heretic, they introduced an inventory system. In Hexen, they made hub worlds. And the Build engine is basically an upgraded DOOM engine with more possibilities for level design with layered floors, destructible scenery and explosions. So what can Strife add to shooters in 1996.
Story:
Unlike other shooter which just had a story to add context to what's going on, Strife has a story with characters and pacing. Not a great story but an enjoyable one. One day, a comet crashed into earth and a plague killed a good chuck of the population was wipe out. However, many survivors started to hear a voice and made a religous movement called the Order which enslaved humanity and kill the women and children. Now a rebel force call the Front to take down this evil force, once and for all.
So, yeah. Not special but it works and I even have a theory about one part of the story. One thing I do like is the choice you'll have to make which changes not so much the tone but the structure of the story. One path makes the game shorter by making it, just kill the bosses, the other lets you explore a whole other area.
There aren't that many major outside of Macil and the Oracle but most prominent is your radio partner, Blackbird, who mainly gives you commentary and what and who you should be looking for. I'm not the biggest fan of her but I do enjoy her dark sense of humour.
Gameplay:
I want to talk about the weapons first, mainly because I think they're pretty mixed: The knife starts out weak but slowly becomes useful to take out guards later after some upgrades, the cross bow is weak unless you have poison arrows, the rifle is the all-purpose gun, I didn't get much use from the flame thrower, the mauler is a powerful shotgun, the grenade launcher is powerful but hard to aim and the rocket launcher, while a decent weapon, is one of the weakest rocket launchers I've ever used. Then there's the plot important Sigil: very powerful but I don't use that much before I got a new upgrade for it outside of boss fights, then again it uses your health to use and you'll need all the health you can get.

Like Hexen, this game has a hub system where you can explore, and talk to people. That's right. Talk to people. normal people, shopkeepers and even enemy guards who aren't trying to kill you yet. Sure, not everyone has anything interesting to say but it's a nice feature considering the tech. Also you can buy health, ammo and armour at shop scattered around the world and in some area's you can upgrade your accuracy and stamina. Stamina increase your health and how strong your knife is and the accuracy...I don't know, maybe help with aiming, I didn't notice.
Presentation:
While each level does have a different look to it, the colour pallet might make some levels repetitive like the factory section or the fortress and the enemies design are pretty bland and the villagers are just the same guy with different shirts. I will admit I really love the way the whole world is layout. If you put all the maps together, you get an open world that explore but there's properly nothing in it. I still thinks it's cool.
The music is pretty enjoyable but like the music for the town or the power plant and the voice acting is fun in a hammy way. Also, the art for the cut-scenes and character portraits look good, if a bit cartoony but I'm okay with that.
Verdict:
The last "offical" DOOM engine game I'm aware of and definetly worth it. Not my favorite shooter but a top ten contender.
8/10

Reviewing older titles is always tricky. How should you approach them? Should you review them based on how it stacks up against its contemporaries, or should you review it based on how it stacks up against modern titles? Reviewing games you played when you were younger is even harder, nostalgia can make even a kinda bad game seem good. I'm a firm believer in basing my reviews on how good the game is "now" rather than how good it used to be.
Strife is a game I have no nostalgia towards, I had never played it until I got it on steam. It's not even a game I was aware of, apart from recognizing a few still images in the game from screenshots people have posted online in the past.
Strife bills itself as the original FPS-RPG, but the RPG elements are very light. System Shock 1 is more of an RPG than this game, and I would not really call System Shock an RPG either.
Strife is a game from 1996, and from a purely technical standpoint, it does of course not hold up well if compared to any modern game. It uses a modified version of the DOOM engine, that has been upgraded further by fans, which gives it some nice lighting effects, higher resolutions and a few other tweaks, which makes it far better looking than it did at release, but it's still built on old technology.
All items, characters & enemies are 2D sprites. They're nice looking sprites, which makes good use of colours and shapes to give everything its own unique look, which clearly stands out against the background, but they're still just sprites. If you've played any other contemporary shooter, other than Quake, you'll know what to expect. The spritework is quite nice, and the game has a pleasing and consistent art style.
The music is relatively good, but I feel that the limitations of its era holds it back, as it sounds a bit artificial (and not in an intentional way). It's also a bit too noticeable at points, which is not great for background music. Still, I'm glad that it's there. The sound effects are better, and most of the weapons have beefy sound effects, that make them satisfying to use.
The voice acting, and there's a surprising amount of it, is all over the place. Sometimes the voice actors do a really good job, portraying their characters in a believable way, other times they really overact, and it enters parody territory. It does not hold a candle compared to today's big budget productions, many of which hire really good voice actors, but most of the important characters have appropriate voice actors.
The story is a strange mix of sci-fi and fantasy. if you've just looked at the still images that are shown during the game, you could easily mistake this for a generic fantasy CRPG.
A comet struck your planet, and it released a virus that killed a large portion of the population. Many of those infected who did not die from the virus were mutated by it, and started hearing the words of an evil god in their heads. They formed "The order", a religious organization that through superior technology and fanaticism has forced the population into servitude.
You're a mercenary who find yourself at odds with the order. Right at the start of the game you get recruited into a resistance movement, who work to bring down The Order.
For a shooter, the story is surprisingly important in this game. The story is, for the most part, well told, even if it's not always well paced. This is hardly Oscar winning material, but it does a good job at immersing you in the world of Strife, and it remains interesting through the course of the game.
For a game based on the DOOM-engine, strife is surprisingly open. The minute to minute gameplay works like in most other DOOM-engine games, which means that you need to use your high movement speed & ability to strafe in order to avoid damage, while shooting at enemies with a verity of weapons. Like other DOOM-engine games, the game does not expect you to have pixel-perfect precision, but instead  the game does most of the aiming for you. This is a bit at odds with the mouse look that they introduced in the Veteran Edition (this was not present in the original), and it can make some combat encounters too easy.
Most levels in this game are at least a bit maze-like, and you need to run around, looking for keys and switches. The level design is good enough most of the time for it to be quite easy to figure out where to go next, but there are a few occasions where a combination of similar-looking textures and confusing level design gets in the way. The sewer section, which happens early in the game, is the worst offender, but there's one more level later on that's rather annoying.
Unlike most DOOM-based games, this game allows for some stealth. There are times when you'll get enemy uniforms, and as long as you don't do anything obviously bad, like shooting a loud weapon or attack someone in front of a bunch of other people, living enemies will let you get by unmolested. You can even take down enemies with your knife or crossbow without raising an alarm. Robots will see right through your disguise though, but even if a robot is shooting at you, enemies around you won't react, it's not until you attack the robot that it will shoot back.
Also unlike most shooters, this game is a semi-open world game. New parts of the map will unlock as you progress through the story, and you can always go back to older ones, and are in fact expected to do so on several occasions. The world is not all that big, and your high movement speed makes this backtracking rather painless, and it does help the world feel more cohesive.
Strife must have been a really impressive game back when it was first released. These days it's not all that impressive, but it's still a really good game. The fast paced combat is fun and the story is surprisingly interesting through the entire game. It has a few flaws here and there, but nothing that seriously holds the game back, and despite its age, it's still a game worth playing, even for those with no nostalgia towards it. At 8 h its length might surprise people who expect something like DOOM (DOOM was a 4h game on my very first playthrough, on Hurt me Plenty, and DOOM II was also a 4h game, but on Ultra-Violence).

As a simulator it's really good and compared to Flight Simulator, there's access to way more plane controls thru knobs and levers on the panel.
The quality on graphics varies some though, while some things have been done with lots of attention, like the plane models, things like knobs and switches on the panel/dashboard are only 2D images.
The flight setup makes you select your plane from a treeview menu full of folders, it works but a normal list and preview would've been better imo.
You get to choose from a nice variety of aircrafts though, from small Cessna planes to the 747, helicopters and a space shuttle.
Like in Flight Simulator, you can choose to sync the time with your computer and enable real-weather.
The standard scenery looks ok, but I think you'll have to buy scenery packs to get something really great on that part.
In terms of simulation, it seems like a good simulator, though some physics feel a bit off, like I was flying a 747-400 in chase view and tried to go extreme with the steering and it reacted like if it was made out of paper, with super quick responses that simply looked completely unnatural for a plane that size.
Is the game worth its pricetag?
Imo, its worth the -50% discounted price I bought it for and so I don't feel I overpayed.
Regarding price, you also need to take into account that all the DLCs (aircrafts and airports) comes at a cost equal to what you normally pay for a full game.
I guess the conclusion here is, that this game is for simulator fanatics who wants the best and most realistic simulation and to someone like that, it'll probably be plenty worth the full price.

They took the Wizard Wars game mechanics, allowed 2 more elements per combo, made a new campaign and left the rest as is.
You can't combine elements such as fire and water to make the steam element, however, you can still make steam. This is true for ice as well. This removes a great deal of the combination possibilities from the first game.
Furthermore, the changes to how arcane (now death) and life interacts with lightning has removed the, IMO, cool shock beams.
SUMMARY:
If you, like me, hated the changes made to the Magicka series in Wizard Wars, stay far away from this game.
If you found the changes to be superior, buy this, since this is Wizard Wars in single player mode.

A fun co-op game, not as buggy as the original Magicka (which was to some extend unplayable) but it still has a few bugs nonetheless.
It badly requires custom keybindings, and they should rather have released the console version first and finished up the PC version instead. Some cutscenes should have been cut down a bit and they should perhaps have tested the game on PC instead of only focusing on the console version.

As an aside I'm surprised this game has so many negative reviews.
Honestly, Magicka 2 so far has been a great experience so far, though I am only up to the third chapter. This game continues on with the humor and chaos from the first game and even in single-player I haven't felt a death was unfair or unwarranted, even on the Hard difficulty. That said, I haven't played the hardest difficulty (Bananas) yet. That said, you will probably end up dying a lot if playing by yourself, as the enemies are tougher in this game.
The only part about this game that I disliked is the fact that Steam and Ice are no longer their own elements, since the game is built on the same engine as Wizard Wars. However in my mind this is a small price to pay for a release that, so far, is no where near as riddled with bugs.
While I have only unlocked a small number of them so far, the new artifacts system allows you to customise your gameplay experience. I foresee myself replaying Magicka 2 more than the first game because of this.
TL;DR Magicka 2 is a great successor to an already great game. While it lacks a few things from the first game, the new additions more than make up for the losses.

This used to be a mod before it was an actual game, now it comes out. Everyone including myself were waiting for this moment. I've been playing Sven Co-op since 4.8 and i still have it. I wont be needing it anymore now that the newest version is the game itself, 5.0 is out.
Now that is on Steam i'm giving out the statistics. It is a great GAME, a game that continues its way just like the mod did except adding more stuff in it thats not in 4.8. The game is heavily focused on teamwork against bot controlled enemies. Whether its aliens, marines, nazis, you name it. You play as any character based from either Half-Life or any other games (Such as the Doomguy in Doom, Young Link from Zelda, Mario from Mario games, etc.).
The maps are heavily on campaign, so your objective is to reach through it whether by fighting enemies, solve puzzles, or both. Theres a HUGE amount of maps you can play on. If you are suddenly on the loading screen, it means someone has reached the end of the map which causes a new map to load up. Also keep noted the guns you see, sometimes you get different guns depends on the campaign you play (such as the thompson if played in WWII maps).
There is Half life maps, but there are also modded maps. If you are feeling for adventure, you came in the right place.
Give yourself time to try the game when you can and while you still can. Note that low players does not always mean a bad thing, being yourself is whats worst since it'll make the game harder playing by yourself. Having just one person with you is enough, bringing more will bring on the carnage. The game may be too easy for you if you bring on the best team or just simply bring LOTS of people with you. You want a fair fun game where you are fighting through with others as a team.
The bosses also are VERY promising in most maps. Some maps has bosses, some dont. But you will see one at some point depending on the map you are playing on.
I truly recommend this to anyone, its going to be a blast when playing this.

I bought this because although I'm excited to see that Flight Sim X has been resurrected on Steam by Dovetail Games, it's still 8 years old, and I wanted to see how X-Plane has developed over the past 8 years.  I'm sure this is a good product, it sure looks very nice, but I wanted to flag a few things that new buyers should be aware of:
1) X-Plane is the only 3D product I have ever used which isn't capable of changing the display resolution.  I'm running it on Windows 7 installed on a Retina MacBook Pro, which has a screen resolution of 2560x1600.  This is great for desktop work but awful for games, as that high a resolution on a mobile GPU means terrible performance.  This isn't an issue with any other game because you can set the resolution to 1280x720 to boost the performance and it still looks good on the 13" screen.  However, if you set X-Plane to 1280x720, it draws that resolution in a tiny box in the middle of the 2560x1600 screen, which is basically useless.  If you want to run X-Plane at a lower resolution than your monitor, you need to change the Windows desktop resolution before loading X-Plane, which is a pain.
2) Upon launching the game, I was parked on the end of a runway, ready to have a quick test flight to check out the graphics and performance.  However, it looks like there's no keyboard or mouse mapping for the flight stick - I was able to increase the throttles, adjust flaps, and get airborne, but there was no mapping for the aircraft flight controls!  Looking through the settings, I couldn't even see a mapping that I could change for these.  It turns out you can (technically) fly using the mouse - you have to click in the windshield of the 2D cockpit and you can then use the mouse to control the flight controls, but it's pretty nasty.  Also, this doesn't seem to work in 3D cockpit mode, which is my preferred view.
3) To download the scenery, right-click on X-Plane in your Steam Library, and go to View Downloadable Content.  You can then click to download the other areas.  I was going to the X-Plane page in the Library, clicking on DLC on the right, which takes you to the DLC page on the Steam Store, where it was showing all the scenery packs as already in my library and ready to play, which was confusing (this is an issue with Steam's terrible user interface rather than X-Plane).
I still recommend X-Plane, but you should be aware of the above issues if you're in a situation like myself.

There is a term, used for platformers mainly, 'Metroidvania'. It is the result of the games Metroid and Castlevania, that had such impact in the game development, that are used as examples nowadays. Strife is to the FPS-RPG genre what Metroid and Castlevania are to platformers.
It is one of the best titles made on doom engine and it was the first that combined RPG elements to a FPS game, by inserting NPCs, quests and voiced dialogues! A part of gaming history, remade on December 2014, 18 years later than its original release. Strife is a first person shooter with some role playing elements, such as quests, talking with NPCs and some decision making that may, or may not, have direct effect to your gameplay! [spoiler alert: there are 3 endings!]
Truly a hidden gem and a must play for every Doom/Quake/Hexen and even DeusEx (the first) lover. It can be as difficult and demanding as you want it to be with since the Veteran Edition has kept all the features of the Original, difficulty levels included! You can also play the game as its original version (some 'vanilla' bugs are included) or the newer version that has some extras, with or without the newer graphics.
The story goes that after a meteor crashed on the planet and killed thousands, it spread a virus where the affected got mad by hearing a voice and called themselves 'the order'. Those who could not hear the voice where used as slaves or even guinea pigs, as a result a rebel movement is forged, 'the front', to fight the order. You are a mercenary that gets captured by the order and gets involved with the front. The world, while not extremely huge, may still surprise you given that there are a lot hidden items in seemingly empty areas or even hidden rooms, and a lot of different paths or backdoors in the various levels for you to explore! It also requires some thinking in addition of the mindless killing of baddies! For example: a friendly NPC tells me that in X room there are weapons, but the room is locked. The quest continues and after a while I meet an NPC that mentions that he had just finished stocking some weapons. So.... killing the NPC did gave me the key I needed!
The only negatives are, the aiming in regards to different levels (higher/lower) that can be clunky even with the games aim assist, few voice dialogues that do not have subtitle support but are quite easy to understand if you pay attention, and the graphics. Now I did not play this game for its graphics and frankly I like this retro-style a lot more than fully 3D games, but the issue is that on first sight the game is a brick of mud, that once you wash it, the gold sparkles! So sadly, it may not receive the attention it deserves.
I usually don't rate games because I find it hard to evaluate stuff like graphics, however, given that graphics here are not in the question I give this jewel, a solid 10 out of 10 just because it managed to entertain me the entire time I was playing it!

Review-
Battlefield: Bad Company 2 is a great BF game. It has great graphics, the fanbase is definitely still there. The combat system is great. There is a huge selection of weapons/vehicles.
You can fight on the ground with guns, or with vehicles like tanks, ATV's, jeeps, etc. Or you can fight in the air with a selection of a few helicopters. There is always a battle going on around you, with 32 person online battles.
This game has huge replayability value. And if you ever get bored with the base game, you should try the Vietnam DLC. It comes at a cheap price, and it is pretty much a new game. It adds new maps, new guns, new vehicles, and new player models. It is just as good; maybe even better than the base game. Not to mention that this is the only Battlefield on steam.
If you are looking for a good, cheap first person shooter, this is definitely one of the best on Steam.

I did not like this game AT ALL. And usually I love Battlefield games.
First of all, the gunplay is boring and uninteresting. There's no "feel" to a gunshot, and the sounds are very generic. There's no real inclusion in the audio at all. And the game feels so, so terribly scripted, it's hard to suspend your disbelief.
Second, the AI. Jesus F Christ, they are so dumb, they might as well be stationary turrets. The enemies can pop out anywhere without much thought in it. And once they get into their...'position' of what the script says, they'll stay there, forever. Oh yes, your AI teammates will very often call for a supressive fire, but those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s won't budge or flinch from a sustained machine gun fire. Nope, they'll just stand in the middle of the field like a bunch of turrets and shoot away at you.
Third, the guns. They really picked one of THE most boring guns they could. XM 8 for most of the game? Really? Plus the guns you can pick up from the enemies aren't much better. But what I thought was the worst offence was that they give you a sniper rifle later on, WITH A HOLOGRAPHIC WEAPON SIGHT! Nope, you don't get a scope for some of that far-away sniping action, you just have to use the SNIPER RIFLE as a regular ol' Assault Rifle, but with limited bullet count and rate of fire.
Fourth, the destructible enviornment. Yes, yes, I get that Dice wanted to show off their cool new engine with destruction everywhere, but jesus christ did they go overboard. The game is not without its rough edges, ammo can be hard to come by, and enemies can dish out some pretty brutal damage.  But, thanks to the use of the Doom engine, you still get a pretty solid shooter, with a comparable amount of content to other FPS games at the time.
With the Veteran edition, you even get an improved engine, better resolutions, mroe modern controls, graphics effects, and some bug fixes.  If you like old school shooters, this is one you shouldn't miss!
Strife is a blast to play! If you love Doom and Duke Nukem then Strife is for you!

They often rely on mechanics that you don't really have to use anywhere else, so sometimes it takes a while to get any idea how you're actually meant to hurt the boss, and it's usually easy to end up getting juggled or stunlocked. Ok, so i have to weigh in on this debate between what sims are the best.
Firstly, about me, I am a real life pilot, and hold FAA and EASA commercial pilot licences (USA and European), EASA PPL Flight Instructor, and i am a gamer.
About the game: its not a game. its a flight simulation software. do not buy if you are looking for a
"fun game to mess around on and earn steam acheivments etc etc", nor will it teach you how to fly planes or anything of the sort. there is no arcade mode, there are no leaderboards, there are no charachter perks etc.
About the flight simulation programme: I first had my taste of flying a plane on Microsoft Flight Simulator 95 (or 98, i forget) on a crappy little PC with a keyboard and mouse. as i grew up and my interest grew and flight sims developed, i hopped from flight sim to flight sim and i have played ALOT of different ones, and in my proffesional training, i have even used things like lockheed martin's Prepar3D flight simulator with full 737 and A320 cockpit mock ups. For home simming, i dont think anything beats XP10 though. I will be drawing comparisons in my review with 1 other game which this is often compared to - FSX (Microsoft Flight Simulator X/10) (im not even going to compare against "Microsoft Flight", that sim was pathetic....)
The differences
FSX is a flight simulator, and a game in one package. it can both teach you how to fly a plane (atleast the basics) and give you fun missions to complete and rewards you with in game acheivments. It also is able to replicate, rather well, realistic flight dynamics and aircraft performance. however, i feel that FSX is a bit more buggy, alot less "modable" (free 3rd party aircraft were difficult to install in my opinion) and it feels a bit outdated.
XP10 is, i have to admit, a little less user friendly. the menus and interface do not seem as polished etc, but boy is there alot you can do. Free 3rd party aircraft are relatively easy to install, a multitude of plugins exist that you can download, such as ground vehicle tows to push your aircraft back from the stands etc and there just seems to be alot more freedom in the game.
Carrier landings for example. FSX, it was very long winded, very procedural, and a bit tedious if you "just wanted to have a go at planting the damn plane on a deck". and with only the F18 to chose from, it was a bit bland. with XP10, even though the scenario would be unrealistic, i can just load a boeing 747 and click "land on a carrier" and try landing a jumbo on a nimitz carrier.
Weather is very customizable, and can download real time actual weather with a click of a button which is pretty cool.
Loads more stock aircraft to chose from
loads of different scenarios (i believe you can fly on mars if you wanted, that is atleast true of my experience on XP7,8 and 9 so i assume its on 10 too)
You can try and bring down a space shuttle from orbit, and many other things that FSX just cant do with the base programme.
Yes there are issues, yes some of the stock 3D cockpits are a bit naff and not done properly, but i have never really found it such a big deal. and if you want the true realism, be it on FSX or XP10, you wont fly stock aircraft anyway, you would go and buy 3rd party aircraft by proffesional 3rd party Devs that make accurate models and cockpits etc.
you WILL need a joystick and rudder pedals, or at the minimum, a joystick with twist function for rudders. you can play with just a mouse, but lets be honest, that sucks. FSX you can play with a keyboard, but even then, joystick set up rules.
so overall, what would i buy? both. i have both. i use them for totally different things. i use FSX and 3rd party payware aircraft and payware photo scenery to practice VFR aircraft navigation, and i use XP10 to practice aircraft procedures and general handling and flying, or to test myself in all sorts of different aircraft in different scenarious, like finding myself in a middle of thunderstorm in the middle of nowhere with various system failures.
again, i would stress, XP10 is NOT a game. it features "weapons", where FSX does not, but these are only for novelty value. they do not replicate the actual fire control systems or anything like that. This is a flight sim that enthusiasts or proffesionals can use.
If you are looking to buy your first flight sim or you want to learn how fly a plane, go and buy FSX
If you are looking for a world war 2 realistic flight sim where you can fire guns and down planes, go and get IL2 Sturmovik 1946 or Wings of Prey
If you are looking for a arcade combat flight sim, Tom Clancy's Hawx
If you are looking for a realistic combat flight sim with modern fighters, get Lock On
if you are looking for a simulator to practice advanced things on, or experiment, or design your own creations and fly them (basic engineering knowledge required or willing to take the time to research how plane maker works), then this is the sim for you.

Devilian is a Massive Multiplayer Online Action Role Playing Game (MMOARPG) and I loved it.  Take a Diablo 3/Torchlight type of game and mix in games like World of Craft and this is what you get.
There are 4 classes in total at the moment.
1.  Evoker - female mage (range with magic)
2.  Cannoneer - female gunner (range with guns)
3.  Shadowhunter - male melee (melee/range hybrid)(looks like someone out of Castlevania)
4.  Berserker - male melee (wields two 1h swords)
Each class has 3 different specializations that you can put ability points into.  You gain 1 ability point per level once you reach level 10.  You can make a pure 1 spec build or dip points into all 3 specs and make a hybrid.  There's nothing holding you back if you'd like to try things out and have fun with this specialization tree.  Respecialization (respec) is completely free and you can do it as many times and as often as you like.
Max level as of this writing is lvl 52.  After about 60 hours I've did ALL the quests available, multiple PvP sessions and have completed the tier 1 PvE set.  There are a total of 3 tiers at the moment.  Tier 1 is the Falling Star set which is blue (rare) equipment.  The next set tier 2 is the Butchery set which is epic (purple) and the final set tier 3 is the Tragedy set and it too is epic (purple).  When reaching max level 52 the grind starts.  Grinding for tokens to complete tier 2 and/or 3 and get gems to socket your gear.
There is PvP in the game and it's set up like a MOBO (think DOTA).  You pick a lane, capture and hold it while killing off the enemy players.  At the moment it seems very range friendly and the melee classes just feel undesired.  You can either play as your human form and use the skills you've acquired or take on your specific Devilian form.
Devilian form is like your Super Saiyen and when you go Devilian you are stronger, faster and harder to kill.  Very fun aspect of the game.  You can either use this in PvP or in PvE.  In PvE you get devil orbs which will help fill your Devilian meter.  Once full you can morph into Devilian form and wreck havok!
There are over 20 dungeons and all are extremely fast paced.  Each dungeon shouldn't take you 10 mins to complete.  Once you hit max level you can queue up for Heroic versions of the dungeons you've did while leveling and once you feel comfortable with that difficulty you can advance to Hell difficulty.  Each difficulty whether it be Normal, Heroic or Hell has 3 tiers and are named +1, +2 or +3.  Each of these +1 are more difficult by means of monster health and how much damage they do to you, but the benefit is more loot!
The game is free to play and you can enjoy the whole game without paying a dime, but if you choose to support the game you can pay for extra bag space, more xp, more gold, different types of mounts (they give you one free) and cosmetics.  Nothing overpowering makes this a pay to win title and should be classified as a pay for convenience.  Other conveniences are an auto run feature that allows you to kick back and let your character run to either the quest giver or the objectives.  I found this nice.  You can sit back and take a drink or get your smoke on for a min.  There are fast travel nodes all over the world too.  So if you don't feel up to traversing the world to get to the other side of it you can use this, but with payment of in game gold.
The major town hub isn't overpopulated, but has a lot of people there doing quests, the auction house, warehouse (store more stuff outside your bag inventory), chat and enchanting gear.  There are still two major continents that have yet to be opened up and the level cap is supposed to increase by the 1st quarter of 2016.  There are still 3 more tiers of gear and Raids to be implemented as well.
There's also a Paragon system once you reach end game level cap.  Meaning, once you reach level 52 you can no longer gain any more levels, but instead the experience you gained can be dumped into another set of proficiencies like the Paragon sytem Diablo 3 has.  When dumping points into this system all your characters will share extended health, more gold per kill, more xp per kill, more damage toward bosses and so forth.  The system still needs some work and shouldn't be bound to all your characters, but at least all that precious xp is wasted!
Lastly, there's a tower to test your skills at and it opens up around level 25ish called the Abyssal Tower.  In this tower you climb up floors of non stop enemies and bosses until you reach the top floor at 100.  As you get better gear and respec your character to fine tune him you will ascend higher into the tower.  You will get XP for your Devilian form in doing this and making yourself even stronger.  You can only do this tower once a day so make sure you do it for it's totally worth it.  There's even a leaders board for this tower for some friendly competition.
As it stands Devilian was extremely great and I very much enjoyed my 60 hours of gameplay, but once I hit max level I've seemed to hit a brick wall.  Due to Devilian being content starved either you grind out endgame mats (which isn't endgame yet due to not complete) or do countless PvP for PvP gear.
If you enjoy Diablo, Torchlight, Grim Dawn, Path of Exile with MMO characteristics like World of Warcraft or Rift you will thoroughly enjoy this.  Recommended!
