I am the sort of person who becomes incredibly enamored with 90's FPSes. Seeing my favourite genre of immersive media in its period of infancy, where the developers were still learning what works and what doesn't... There is just something magical about it, like watching old black and white movies and insisting they're better in every way to the stuff released today.
Of course they aren't. No movie buff is right when they say Kubrick's works outshine the oscarbait we get in our current decade, no photographer is right when they say pictures just look better taken with their analogue sh**boxes. We see the past with rose-tinted glasses because of many factors; nostalgia, passion, auteur admiration, but none of these make the works of the past outright better. I am saying this to quality my recommendation, because Strife was made in 1996; the games industry has had almost 20 years to innovate since this game was released, and as such, as good as the game is, is just can't outshine IPs such as half-life or the elder scrolls series.
That being said, I now feel comfortable telling you that this game is probably one of the best games I have ever played.
Strife is made on a heavily modified DOOM engine, but it plays closer to 3Drealms' Duke 3D or Shadow Warrior; you can jump, run, fill your inventory with all manner of useful gadgets, and best of all, the game contains the first example of RPG elements in an FPS game; you level up doing sidequests, you can find gold in secret areas to buy additional health packs or ammo, and the game has multiple endings based on a couple of important choices you make as a player. This sort of innovation boggles my mind for 1996, and it's even stranger to me that I had not even heard of this game until a few weeks ago.
The levels are scattered with secrets, the crux of which being 3 hidden talismans that the game makes you work like a dog for... When you finally get all three, your reward is... Well, I wont spoil it, but it was the most immensely satisfying prize you can imagine without being something inherently game ending. Strife also Gives you the option to stealth through most levels, again, one of the first FPSes that let you do this. The stealth is a little bit confusing, and isn't explained well, but hey, back in those days games came with a manual. Basically, most new areas bad guys wont consider you a threat until you open fire on them. A reasonable reaction, in my opinion. You can stop the alarms going off by killing secluded enemies with silent weapons; daggers or poison darts so that the inevitable dog-pile of enemies becomes easier to manage when they catch you being a♥♥♥♥♥♥ You can also... you know... just complete your objective and leave without harming anyone; an option that I doubt many people took in 1996, but an option that is mandatory for the bloodbath difficulty which is as to NIGHTMARE mode what the Holocaust is to a teletubbies marathon. Bloodbath is horrendously difficult. I can finish any level of DOOM on nightmare mode but I cant get out of the first ROOM alive on bloodbath.
The protagonist has a hardcore sidekick named blackbird who, again, in a profound innovation is the first character I have ever heard say the F-word in a video game (chronologically, I mean), which endeared her to me immediately, her ultimate role is a shoehorned love interest but hey it's the nineties, too much innovation and they would have been burned at the steak. The protagonist himself is a relatively nameless, voiceless link character who travels through 20+ levels with a stunning variety of weapons from the humble bread and butter assault rifle to the double-barreled High-Explosive grenade launcher with optional white phosphorous rounds for when you're feeling frisky. Seriously the grenade launcher is in my top 3 weapons from all games, it is an immensely satisfying, unnecessarily powerful death machine.
The bosses are good, though the only two worth mentioning are the first boss and the last boss. The first boss is a hectic fast paced battle that I barely survived, the last battle was a wonderfully cinematic ultimatum. All the other bosses get one-shot by the stupid sigil weapon (think soul cube from doom 3). This is probably the only nit-pick I have with this game. Strife is what you would call a "good old game" from ages long past, and even though it didn't get all the attention it would have deserved, it's still something you can play and have fun with even almost 20 years after its release. Rather than walking the path of the classic DOOM clone, Strife aims for a different angle and perspective on the FPS genre, adding NPC interactions and a variety of different approaches to quests and areas.
This particular version, in addition to what the game has to offer, features improved graphics and controls (including controller support) but stays true to the original title (except for a number of bugs who have been fixed) and even offers the chance to play the "classic" version of the game.
All in all, it's well worth its price (getting it in a bundle is a bounty) and will certainly prove to be entertaining for quite a few hours worth of gameplay. In addition, it's one of the few examples of a "revamped" game that doesn't lose a bit of its dignity or identity, but gets a bit of makeup on and a pat on the back instead: that's about all a good game needs to be back on tracks.

I was pleasantly surprised with Devilian. From looking at the previews and the rumours I had heard from others, I assumed it was just a "ripped off tera wannabe" but with some hack'n'slash added. It turned out to be a pretty fun ARPG with a good MMO aspect. I saw that one of the Eu servers was down considerably during the launch week, but being Trion I left that up to them being Trion and not the game itself.
Levelling up did not feel like a chore, I played all of the classes through the first 10 or so levels and ended up sticking with the Evoker (to max lvl) and Canoneer (halfway there!) as two classes I really enjoyed. The gameplay is fun, albeit easy, hacky and slashy as exected, there are lots of dungeons for you to go through as you level that you can run as many times as you want. After completing a dungeon, you can set it up a level (all the way to +3) for better lootdrops and difficulty, all of the dungeons are easily solo'd all the way up to max level. The skill points are set up so you can reset them at any time for free, making experimentation the best way to find the way you enjoy playing.
The pvp is... an aoefest, laggy and somewhat bland, but it was enjoyable enough for me to queue up for a second, then a third match and so on until I'd spent a whole evening playing 20vs20. I have been unable to play a 3v3 or 6v6 game at max level, so will update my review when I get round to that. You can queue either in Devilian form, or as your normal form. Both are fun enough, and seems to be the only way to gear your devilian form. The queues do not seem that active, but it's a nice hobby in between dungeon runs.
The endgame currently is a little sparse, seems to be enough for me to run until my gear is perfect. With the look of the current map I can see that hopefully a lot of content will be coming our way (also, there is gear in game for level 54!) and with this being a f2p game, it means you can drop in and out whenever you want to.
All in all, I was very happily surprised at how fun Devilian is. It doesn't really bring anything new to the table as far as ARPGs go, but it looks lovely and is great fun both solo and in a group. If you're a fan of Diablo and Path of Exile this is a great game to add into your rotation. I will be happily grinding at max level for a while, and patiently waiting for new content! :)

TL;DR: Devilian's a fun, fremium MMO in the ARPG genre. Chat and trade/auction house restrictions on limited accounts are neglegible, especially if you play to play the game in the long run (since you'll likely sub if you plan on staying around that long anyway).
To compare Devilian to Diablo or Path of Exile probably makes sense for a lot of people, but unfortunately they are not the best comparison. Instead, Drakensang Online is more appropriate as that is also an MMOARPG just like Devilian (and is technically a year older).
The reason I say this is because maps are not instances like they are in Diablo and Path of Exile. By that I mean, you don't see everyone in a town hub and they magically no longer exist once you head outside of town unless you're partied with them. No, you see and interact with other players both in towns and out in the maps - the only areas that are instanced are dungeons.
Being in the ARPG genre, you've got your mob grinding, your dungeon grinding, equipment grinding, and so on from a top-down third-person perspective. Not something that's going to entertain a lot of people for a prolongued period of time, but for those that enjoy the genre you'll be right at home.
Marketplace is currently lackluster in items outside of inventory expansion, character slots, and a small assortment of pets, mounts, and costumes. Much of everything else (XP boosts, talisman box, attribute stones, and megaphones) are gotten through the login rewards tracker as well as Archegemstones from Abyssal Tower and such. More costumes I'd expect to see added as more content from the other regions are translated and introduced, as well as things like additional classes.

Summary: This game has great potential. An open-world Zombie apocalypse survivor-group-management game sounds, and is, in concept, very cool. It could have brought together the best of games like Zafehouse Diaries, Project Zomboid and Fallout Tactics, but unfortunately, the game fails to capitalize on its promising foundation. In fact, I think it should be named Inventory Management Simulator. If you can get past the flawed combat, endless inventory space woes and occasional crashes, it could be fun. Problem is, I couldn't. I might still come back to this game and update my review.
Pros:
-An open world zombie game where you recruit and manage survivors
-Extensive map with lots of locations to loot and random events
-Lots of characters to recruit, with backstories and clashes
-Noise mechanics - you can actually stealth through zombie-infested areas by dispatching them silently and avoiding hordes
-The game doesn't hold your hand
-The feeling of progression as you populate the school and get your stores stocked is great
Cons:
-Poor inventory management system.
-Combat. Controls and interface are too complicated, while the combat itself is disturbingly bland and repetitive. Basically, lure enemies into a doorway and kill them as they try to enter, rinse and repeat.
-Repetitive looting trips (see above)
-It crashed twice in 3 hours, could be bad luck but it's worth noting.
-Human enemies. Depending on the circumstances, they're either impossible to beat or behave like zombies themselves.
The Bowcaster, my God, the Bowcaster. Nothing quite like propelling a trandoshan's head into a wall. A thing of beauty.

An old game (by the time I wrote this review) but a great game nonetheless.
As you might know, this is a Star Wars game based on the Clone Wars era where you are the leader of an elite Clone Commando Unit tasked with some of the most dangerous and most critical missions in service of the Galactic Republic.
+ Story: -Amazing story that places you not in the eyes of a skillful Jedi or a powerful Sith, but in the boots of Clone Troopers fighting the war. The game delivers in terms of story with its superior voice acting by Temuera Morrison (Jango Fett) as well and the various personalities of your squad mates really adds to the experience.
+ Squad Mechanics: -You cannot Rambo (go solo) this game, mainly because the squad is mandatory, BUT also because the game is brutal as hell (like most old FPS games). Enemies are really hard to kill without your squad's support requiring the players to properly order their squads into position and direct their fire when necessary.
+ Graphically pleasing despite its age: -Released on 2005, this game carries a dated visual design, but pleasing nonetheless. Animation is good and the atmosphere is immersive. (I simply love the HUD in this game)
+ Sound: -One of the greatest OST I have ever heard. (Vode An is the greatest of these OST)
+ Gameplay: -Lengthy campaign without getting boring: There is always action around the corner.
- Squad AI is a bit limited: -Although the AI, for the most part, is intelligent and is far more useful than some of the other AI partners in modern games, I feel as though a bit more could have been done. They follow command well enough.
- Bugged Graphic setting in terms of Bump Mapping: -Remained unfix to this day. (can be turned off in the options menu though)

This is a game that could have been absolutely fantastic but didn’t get there. It is still very good and I recommend it, but the feeling of lost potential can detract some enjoyment of it. Overall it has a very realistic feeling which makes it stand apart from other games.
Pros:
The world building. Novel-length text of what happened during and after the apocalypse, with news, emails, texts, etc. The locations to explore and scavenge have different feelings and stories. You can deduct what happened, if they were attacked by random zombies, other survivors, etc.
The survivors you can recruit: There are around fifty different characters you can bring to your shelter. Some will be a godsend, some will be annoying, some will be completely useless and some will be dangerous. Also, you don’t start the game having with you an ER doctor, a ballistic experts and a professional hunter by random chance. You just have perfectly average people. That not everybody is immediately proficient at something makes it all the more believable.
The freedom: If you don’t like someone in your group you can arrange for them to have a little accident, if you want to go that way. You also have a few options in how to deal with other groups.
Cons:
The game has around 100 play days. By the time I was in the 50-60 days I had explored everything and killed all my enemies. I spent around 20 more days fishing and scavenging food waiting for the trigger of the final event. If only there was something else to do during that time or if I could jump to the end, the game would have become brilliant. Despite this drag I still enjoyed it and recommend it.

When Marlow Briggs paid a visit to his girlfriend during excavation work in the Central American jungle he, well let's say 'had an accident' and was impaled on an ancient weapon. Fortunately an old Mayan mask of death turns Marlow into a reborn sacred warrior, ready for revenge and on his way to free his abducted girlfriend. This extremely trashy start of the game turns into a very enjoyable action adventure brawler, that does not take itself too seriously and offers beautiful levels and explosive fights.
'Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death' is not a revolutionary game. It does nothing specifically unique and borrows heavily from other games without ever outdoing them. It's not the most polished game and has a few questionable design decisions. But none of this matters because Marlow Briggs is unquestionably a blast to play.

Like many others, I got this for free. And like many others, I still feel ripped off because time is money.
You're a USMC sniper trying to rescue the president of a war-torn African country. The setting is what you'd expect of a military shooter, so you can't exactly bash the story.
But the gameplay is horrible. Your partner is very dumb. You can command him to "hold position" or "follow", and "fire at will" or "hold your fire". In many tactical games, "hold fire" is really, "do not fire unless fired upon" (and rightly so). Not so in this game. Your partner will not shoot back in hold fire. You have to actually tell him to defend himself. The enemy AI isn't any better either (in fact it's worse). As in, they will usually show no reaction even if their comrades are shot in front of them. You're also restricted to your sniper rifle, pistol and knife. That's right, you can't pick up enemy weapons. Finally, the graphics look like they're from 1999 (it's a 2004 game).
Sure my game time is relatively short, but like I said, time is money. I've seen enough. Buy Sniper Elite 1 instead, which came around the same period.

Good game so far. Definitely far from perfect, but it is still a work in progress. The developer is in constant communication with the player base, and you can tell his dedication to the end user. He is a one man designer, so I am willing to give him time and see where the game can go. Great potential for a great game, especially when the game is made by somebody so passionate about space travel and geology.
It can use a lot of refinement, true. But that is why you buy the game, play, and make suggestions in the discussions as to what you would like to see. Solzerogame will listen to your concerns and offer an appropriate solution. I spent almost an hour before purchasing this game doing my research, and have the utmost confidence in my purchase.
The developer even acknowledged that in a larger release, some bugs came out which did not surface during trials (this is a common occurrence) and will be working on all known issues in a timely fashion.
I am all for supporting such projects. I hope to see more good things to come.
Edit to make my review a little more focused on the gameplay itself, as I have been getting flak for putting my hope in the developer:
All of the above out of the way, I have thoroughly enjoyed my time in game. It starts a little slow, but I believe this gives the player time to acclimate to the experience and learn how to start a base. It will require a couple trial and error restarts, but I love that in a game. I don't enjoy my experience being spoon fed to me from a silver platter. You will also need this time to thoroughly explore your planet and gain a firm footing on where to establish a base. Resources will be scattered and one must take time to make an informed decision in order to have a productive colony.
This game focuses on micro management. I like that you have so much control, but feel as if it could get tedious near the endgame. I am not sure how efficiently the micromanagement will scale up. We will see.
This game will not be for a lot of people, because it requires planning and thought. If you are a casual gamer, maybe find yourself another title. I on the other hand enjoy the challenge. I am big into games like Banished, PlanetBase, etc. So if you like those games, I believe this one will fit comfortably into your collection. Just understand that the game needs a little bit more time to mature. If you are not sure yet, throw it on your wish list and wait a couple months...
Bottom line: I enjoy this game. If it looks intriguing to you based on screen shots and videos, I am confident you will as well.

Strife may have been revolutionary in the early 90's, but it does not hold anything to modern FPS-RPG games.
30-something men will tell you that this game is the coolest, but really it is beyond nonsense. Placing you into a medieval dystopian setting, you are to use crossbows, missile launchers and machine guns to kill soldiers in metal armor. These medieval soldiers fire back at you with, get this, machine guns. You'll run across space blobs and robotic spiders, too. Head on down to "Ye Ol' Weapons Shop" to purchase crossbows and machine gun rounds, or try the armor store next door to buy metal armor so you too can make absolutely no sense, just like your enemies and surroundings.
This game isn't good by any rules today. I thought Wolfenstein was alright, and the old Duke Nukems were pretty good too. This game was just a failure in an attempt to put FPS into RPG elements. The RPG elements consist of randomly placed NPCs who give you incredibly vague (at least early on) quests. It's very easy to kill someone who could give you a huge quest if you don't talk to them first. On many characters, there are no graphics rendering them different than any other peasant, which means you will have to literally speak to every character on the map in order to find quests properly without a guide.
When you speak to these people, a pretty nice cartoon visual of their face will pop up, and then you will hear the voice acting. Oh god, the voice acting made me want to continue playing this game with how laughable it was. You'll walk through medieval times wielding your machine gun, and come upon a peasant with a brooklyn accent who's telling you to get to work before the guards shoot ya.
TL;DR - This game was revolutionary as the first FPS RPG, but revolutionary does not usually go hand-in-hand with good.  This game has poor quests, poor voice actors, and a clunky feel that makes it annoying. After a few hours you might get used to it and if you're a sucker for games reminiscent of something out of 3D Realms, you'll probably enjoy some of it, and appreciate the elements that it paved for games like Deus Ex.

Strife runs off the original Doom engine, and while of course Doom is legendary, I always thought Strife did it a little better.
Gradual stat growth, breakable glass walls, enormous non-linear maps, hubs, customizable weaponry, branching mission design, inventory, and neat contextual death animations. If you accidentally shoot an NPC, it will enter a wounded state before it dies. You can set baddies on fire, or vaporize them. There is often a degree of freedom as to how you approach encounters, but it's when negotiations break down that the real fun begins.
The setting, a sort of post alien-invasion medieval England, is instantly likable and fits the story and unique enemies well. Strife is full of shooter innovations that set it far ahead of the pack. Naturally, it was almost completely ignored by the gaming press while simultaneously being borrowed from for years to come.
This new release is the best version yet, featuring crisp GL graphics, bug fixes, a subtle (and welcomed) map marker system that shows you where you need to go, and a new secret level.
Spoiler Alert: Geoff is the alien.

I've played both this game and the ZDoom port of the original.  Besides a few new maps, the Veteran Edition doesn't add a whole lot to what you get from the port in terms of gameplay.  It also throws in achievements, trading cards, and a couple of new in-game things (Blackbird chiding the player upon death or quiting; three collectible artifacts).
Strife is an old-school shooter; it's built on the Doom engine.  It's not a game that holds your hand, though it doesn't throw you out on the street, either.  Several levels are very maze-like and can give inexperienced players problems.  Also, it's not always clear whether it's a good idea to head to an optional area once it's available or progress in the main story first.  I haven't tested it, but it's possible to render the game unwinnable if certain missions are done in the wrong order (I do know that the Veteran Edition removes one specific way of making it unwinnable).
The levels are interconnected; with very few exceptions, it's possible to revisit every place you've been whenever you want.  Teleporters make travel a bit easier.
The weapons in the game have a nice variety, though the electric bolts are pretty much completely worthless.  It's also quite easy to play through the game and never pick up the Mauler.  In my three playthroughs, I only grabbed it once. It's available in two or three places.
The story is strong, with maybe two-dozen voiced characters.  However, the pacing is a bit odd.  Without giving anything away, this game ends rather abruptly.  After accomplishing a key task, you stroll into a structure which you didn't know existed before, fight through a couple of rooms of enemies, confront the final boss, and that's it.  The time between the penultimate task and the boss is five to ten minutes.
If playing on harder difficulties, this game can be unforgiving.  It's not that the enemies are mercilessly hard (they're tough, but with only a couple exceptions are not overpowered); rather, it's that the health and ammo which you depend upon are available inconsistently.  It's very easy to find yourself low on supplies and in a tough spot.  Sometimes they're scarce; sometimes there's more than you can carry, forcing you to leave them behind.  You could theoretically backtrack and pick them up again when you need them.
Strife is a rare example of an FPS/RPG hybrid.  The aforementioned voiced characters are a big part of it.  You can choose text responses in dialogue.  You don't make too many plot altering decisions, though several of them affect what order you perform your tasks.  It's also possible to miss large portions of the game, either through decisions or just not going to certain places.
Overall, Strife is a very good game.  It has challenge and charm.  If you like old shooters, play this one.

Here's a "what if" scenario for you: what if Michael Bay made games instead of movies?
Silly plot? Check. Cheesy dialog? Check. Something exploding like every two seconds? Check. Yeah, this game is pretty much nonstop Bayhem. And it is glorious.
Gameplay-wise this is a generic spectacle fighter in the style of God of War and the like. Nothing special or interesting in the combat department, it's passable. It's a bit clunky and always puts style over substance, but it all works well enough.
Same can be also said about many of the other features. Camera? Checkpoints? Platforming? You name it, they all work well enough. Some annoyances here and there, but not in rage-inducing amounts.
Where this game truly shines however, is the pacing. Any time when you're starting to get a bit bored of punching enemy grunts in the face, the game throws something else your way, like a puzzle for example. Or a platforming segment. Or a short cutscene filled with explosions. Or a shmup minigame. Or a turret section (yeah, to my surprise even those somehow manage to be fun). There wasn't a dull moment in the whole 7-8 hours my first playthrough took.
So all in all, when you start analyzing all the individual parts the game indeed doesn't sound all that great... but I'll be damned if I wasn't entertained the whole way through!

This game really does an excellent job of capturing the adventure of leading a ragtag group of zombie apocolypse survivors. Unfortunately, it also captures the tedium of a managing the established settlement that those survivors eventually evolve into.
This game is a zombie survivor base-building game. It's got all the features. Resource management, job assignments, base building, structural upgrades and repairs. It's got character levelling and growth options, personal needs and beliefs, both base moral and individual moods, as well as scripted but belivable character interactions. There's even some reasonably sophisticated politics that reacts to situations. Random events, situations with multiple options. Base defense, exploration, scavanging, fighting zombies as well as various human groups (each with their own unique equipment and personality). Plenty of features, the majority of them done quite well.
That said, there are many aspects of the game that are just frustrating. Base management is a pain. You control a character and he/she can only control aspects of the base from certain locations. So there's alot of running back and forth between rooms to tweak the aspects of the base. Alot of scanning the halls, looking for the one character so you can deliver your quest item. You can't access character screens unless they're in your party and outside the base, and you can only access inventory screens from a single place in the base. Items can get lost in players inventories, forcing you to regularly go through characters inventories one at a time, to see if they're carrying anything important.
The missons suffers from a major problem, in that it has realtime sneak/explore/loot mode and a turn-based fighting mode, and transitions are handled very poorly. The instigator of combat gets initiative, which makes it a huge tactical advantage to be able to control position, timing and agro as combat starts. Unfortunately, the transition to and from turn-base isn't handled well, so most of the challenge is learning to navigate the transitions.
An example I struggled with many times at first: you'll be sneaking up behind a zombie, then you trigger turn based combat and move your first character a a little closer... but you didn't get close enough for him to see you. There's no agroed zombies, so combat automatically ends. The game returns to realtime and immediately the team regroups with the first member, alerting the zombie to their presence as they do so. Now combat restarts with your whole team in different positions, and since the zombie "started combat" he gets initiative like you're being ambushed. Now he turns and takes a big bite out of that first survivor, possibly infecting him, and now you may have to spend the rest of the game (maybe 40 hours?) making sure he's got a steady supply of medicine so he doesn't turn.
A different kind of frustrating... the combat is slow. On a big map, you might sneak up and attack one zombie, but the combat system has to process the 50 other zombies all over the map (who are just standing around cuz they're across the map and haven't agroed yet). It's like we're playing a 1998 strategy game... the PC's turns tend to be five times as long as yours when nothing is happening. And if there are enemy survivors are fighting zombies somewhere across the map... then you have to wait for all the animations even though you can't see them. Tactically it's a win, but it takes soooooo long.
Camera angles are bad too. You can spin the camera but not adjust the angle, and walls are high and ceilings don't always disappear when you want them to. I had one battle where we fought under a gas-station canopy where the canopy wouldn't disappear, so I just had to keep spinning the cameara, trying to get a glimpse of what was happening underneath. Thin halls and cramped rooms are difficult as well.
Last gripe: Late in the game, zombies become trival enemies, but their bites can infect survivors, which is an incurable catastrophy. But if you've gotten to this point, you know how to be careful. It's not hard, it's just slow and tedious. Going through a suburb, stealth killing one zombie at a time for routine scavenging operations is mind-numbingly boring, but such a big part of the game.
Anyway, all that said, pretty much everything I haven't complained about is very good. Challenging combat is fun. You need to pick your battles, as different groups have different tiers of equipment. I'll never forget the first time my squad bumped into a pair of Coyote gangsters. It's still terrifying bumping into military defectors squads with my zombie-equipped scavanging team. Monitoring your food and medicine levels is always a little tense, and it's a rush of relief when you find that rare stash of supplies. You love dumpsters, hoping for rotten fruit and scrap wood. Finding a AK47 is not nearly as satisfying as a 10lbs bag of beans (Or that time I found the twinky factory and carried back 120lbs of twinkies and raw sugar. Not sure if they'd worship me or crucify me).
I'm much more patient than most gamers, but this one was too much for me. If you want to finish this game, it will take an extremely patient person (or at least someone who is committed to finishing it, regardless of whether they enjoy it). On the other hand, some people probably play the start, but set it down when it becomes a sea of routine scavanging. If you think you're one of those two types of people, maybe this game is for you, but it was just too slow for me.

Star Wars: Republic Commando is a criminally underrated squad-based shooter.
While I'm not a fan of the FPS genre in general, I had a great time playing Republic Commando. Many zones have interesting tactics you can assign you squad, and every corner of the map is a decision. Nothing stands out as ugly, distasteful, inappropriate or awkward. The squad mate radio chatter is entertaining, to say the least.
The system requirements are *incredibly* low for the experience you get. It's really quite amazing how well this will run on even a terrible computer build. Check system specifications for full details :)
There's something I can't quite find the words for that makes the game special. It's a certain atmosphere or perhaps a combination of comaraderie and personal triumph. Further, players get a fair amount of replayability with difficulty settings (which really ramps up some of the more difficult scenarios).
After finishing the campaigns, special features become unlocked. All the footage and developer commentary about the attention to detail the game received was definitely worth a watch.
When all is said and done, I think the art style is a bit dated, but the atmosphere lives on.

This is a very good Star Wars game, made back in the waning days when Lucasarts still cared about video games. You take control of a squad of republic clone troopers each with his own personality (my personal fave is Sev, the cold, silent, deadly sniper on a hunt for blood). The gameplay is short, unfortunately; I think the 14 hours for my playthrough that is listed here is because I either didn't know where to go many times or my file got lost and I had to start over for some reason. At any rate, this game is a must for any hardcore Star Wars fan and perhaps even people who don't care so much about Star Wars and just want some military squad-based action in a science-fiction setting.
Gameplay-wise, this game is terrific. You fight your way through jungles, heavily-fortified enemy bases, desert-terrain, etc as you carry out your missions. You can choose, in many situations, to go head-on with the enemies or sic your bloodthirsty comrades on them with the press of a button.
The music and sounds are top-notch as usual in Star Wars games. You will hear the familar firing of laser blasters and roaring of wookies, not to mention the authentic Star Wars music we all know and love from the movies.
Cons: Game is short, but by today's standards of 8-10 hours, I would say it fits in nicely. Perhaps the AI is a bit boring with the repeated use of "hide behind rock, pop out and shoot, maybe toss a frag, hide again, repeat", but let's be honest, this is the formula for most games, sadly even today. Oh, almost forgot, if I remember correctly this game has what felt like a moderate cliffhanger at the end. This is a huge con because it leaves the story unfinished I feel. It doesn't take away too much from this great game, but it still sucks. Checking online I see that a sequel was planned and then canceled. However, in 2011 there appeared to be reports that a sequel is still in the works. We will have to wait and see.

Honestly I'd rather the game be shorter than waste my time needlessly, or maybe not a game at all.
They also make a liberal use of jump cuts, which is underutilized in games, but it does it in ways that don't really work. For instance, sometimes they break the tension of a storyline because it just jumps a month into the future, and the thing your character was freaking out about is just a distant memory, or the relationship between the main characters shifts without you really being there or a part of it. I appreciate them trying to move the story along quickly, but the jump cuts should have been more closely scrutinized.

Shantae and the Pirate's Curse is the game I have that has clocked the most in-game hours, and for many good reasons.
While it may have been a straight-up port of a 3DS title, nothing has been dumbed down, save for the 3D portraits, which isn't really something to lose sleep over anyway.
Now for the stuff that really matters.
Graphics are superb. No island, stretch of land, or dungeon gets away without a splash of personality and color. The many background layers set the bar even higher.
Combat is easy to get used to. Attack, attack, and reap the rewards of a hard day's work. Sometimes you will even have to use strategy against some of the tougher foes, for a basic hair-whip just won't cut it.
The map is huuuge. Divided into several islands to help not getting too lost, a palette of enemies and traps await your every next adventure.
Last, but not least, the game is cute. Not much to say about that, but it is.
And that's all I have to say about my choice of nominating this for the Steam Awards. I wish this good luck.

I am quite surprise there are such a large number of negative reviews in the first release day.
But in my opinion, this is absolutely an improved version of Magicka.
Improvements:
1) More Challenging Enemies - You can easily beat the original Magicka by spamming 4~5 combinations of spells. In Magicka 2, you can't. You must learn to use different spells to encounter different enemies.
2) Improved Mobility - You can cast spells while moving
3) Customizable loadout - After you've discovered a new Weapon/Staff, you can bring it to your next game/life.
4) Quick cast magick - Absolutely Great!! Manual cast is still there, with less cooldown than quick cast
5) Easier to get heal - You can get heal even you are with stone/ice armor
6) Improved gamepad control - Keybaord is still the best option for playing Magicka 2, but gamepad is also a good option for playing local co-op.
Cons:
1) Can't remap keybind (Dev is working on this)
2) Staff active ability is removed
3) Wards resistance effect is a bit too weak
4) Rock projectiles take too long to charge its power and travel distance
Opinions/Questions:
1) I don't think the removal of ice&steam elements is a huge drawback, you can still cast ice&steam with less input effort. However, It would be great if ice&steam spells can have more damage bonus.
2) What is the use of life wards? Can't heal and have no poison resistance...
3) instead of ice&steam wards, I think it is better to have WaterCold&WaterFire wards.

Many of you who see all the negative reviews on review section, might wonder if this game is really worth playing? Well to say the least, this game runs really well compared to original magicka even the multiplayer. However there is the lack of steam/ice elements but they can still be used to some degree. The lack of steam/ice causes the game to have less spells than original. The new magick slots are a nice add to the game play and offer you a change to quickly cast same magick twice, since original method of casting them is still viable. Speaking of game play they balanced the spell system by ton which causes the player having to think how to deal with enemies rather than simply mashing buttons and calling it a day. Items and robes add a new layer of strategy to the game and affect how you will want to use your spells and what you will put in your magick slots. Humor is still apparent in game and still gives a good laugh here and there. New controls also enable you moving and casting same time, it takes time to get used to, but it's way more useful than the old system.
Overall i'd rate this game 9/10 despite its flaws, and for 15€ or your regional equivalent, it's a pretty good deal if you ask me.

This game is still in early access, and is far from complete, but has enough content to enjoy it.
It's the first sandbox survival game I've come across where I actually like the research. It doesn't use skill points or equivalent like other sandbox games, but instead you have a technology tree, with each technology needing to complete a quest for. The quests are usually gathering the resources and building a few components of what it is you are researching. There's plenty of blocks and items, but you don't have to research and craft every single one to unlock them, the quest has you craft a few common items and the rest of the group becomone unlocked. Some of the quests are also slightly duplicated, so what I found (I don't know if this is intention or not) is that if you have already unlocked the blocks/items on a different quest, when you click start quest it just completes straight away for you.
The resource gathering and the resource stockpiling are brilliant, you chop down a tree (and avoid having it land on you), cut that tree into smaller logs, which you can then use a crafting bench to turn into timbers (square, round or diaganal), and then further into planks. For the logs and timbers, you can create storage from them that have a visual representation of the amount of logs or timbers placed inside, giving it a little more realism. You can make boxes for small stones and ores, and large containers for large stones as well, each of which also visually fill up.  You can see this in a few other places as well (placing items on shelves and tables, or on the oven etc.).
There are mechanical blocks in this, and you can also make your own mechanical blocks with makeshift timber gears for doing menail stuff (lifts, plowers, etc), but it's a bit awkward and it's better turning to mods for gears unless they get added in the game properly.
My favourite thing about the game is that you can make actuall siege engines peice by peice, there isn't a plan or even tutorial in game for them (with the exeption of making a basic catapult in one of the research quests), so you have to use your own knowledge of how seige engines work (or turn to YouTube) to make them.
EDIT: There are proper angles, I'm just blind.
One thing I have mixed thoughts on is the building, I've not done a whole lot of it yet, but unless I'm just doing something wrong there doesn't seem to be proper angles when making castles, the options are making big square enclosures with circle towers here and there, pretty much. You can't make say, a pentagram shaped castle. There is quite a lot of detail though, they didn't stop at just adding battlements but also added Machicolations, and the like. Unfortunately, unless I'm missing it, there's no murder holes (I'm not talking about the arrow slits in walls), or Hoardings. Fortunately there's a mod for the latter. I do however, like that you can place blocks within blocks, unlike in Space Engineers (made by the same company), where a catwalk stops you then placing anything on top of it, that isn't a problem in this. Another great, but subtle feature, is that you don't have to have anything in your inventory to build, stockpiles when close enough count towards your inventory when building, so if you throw a load of timber, sticks, and planks on a little card to pull around with you, you won't have to keep makng trips to restock on materials.
As for the difficulty, that can depend. Surviving of the land is incredibly easy, and fighting barbarians is incredibly easy to to their crap AI, but building siege engines and castles are incredibly more difficult with structrual integrity being a thing, and you'll find that the tower you spend hours gathering materials for and building ends up falling apart because it got a bit too heavy. Because the rubble from collapsing also has a weight, it'll also probably take down half of the rest of your build as well. It's worth going in creative and turning the option to view structural integrity on and try a few things to get an idea of the limits before doing a big build in survival.
I'm going to keep an eye on this game, but it's definitely far from finished. A few more detailed blocks (like hoardings etc I mentioned above), more variatity of angles, and more options for actual engineering (i.e gears), would be a great additions on the building side, and animals such as horses, donkeys or ox to pull carts would be great, right now you have to push them yourself which is glitchy at best, and doesn't work at all at worst.
For the price, as much as I hate to say it, I don't think it's worth the asking price at the moment, it's a great game but it's missing too much and is too buggy to be worth full price. I got it as 6 quid and was satisfied with that price. At full price, it's 4 quid cheaper than Space Engineers, but Space Engineers is in Beta and much closer to a full game and is probably worth the price, even with all the faults that game has as well, but this games isn't nowhere near as complete. I paid 60 US$ for X-Plane 10.3 in October 2014.
If Steam had a refund-button I would use it.
I do NOT recommend X-Plane in its current state.
If this was the year 2002 X-Plane would be up to current standards, but this is 2014 and today you can find even free simulators that are better than X-Plane.
In fact, there is not much realism to be found in X-Plane (except that it's expensive, just like real flying)
The good:
- The runways. They look good and fairly realistic when you're lined up for take-off at night. Seeing the lights on the sloped runway appears quite well-done.
- The cars on the roads, at night, look pretty realistic (but taxes the system quite heavily, which basically makes it useless)
The bad:
Everything else.
A few examples:
- The clouds look like nothing I've seen on planet Earth = unrealistic.
- The cockpits are alpha-status. Gauges are missing and when they are there some of them doesn't actually work. For example; the heading-bug in the King-air (a default aircraft and not a 3rd party aircraft!) can't go from 350 degrees to 010 degrees unless you turn it counter-clockwise. The NAV1 Locator shows negative degrees (puts a minus in front of the degree number) if you turn it past 360 degrees counter-clockwise. Not even Flight-sim 98 by Microsoft was this buggy (and that was in 1997!)
- The aircraft are not optimized for typical PC-joysticks, so the control of the aircraft does not compare to the same levels of work-load and stress-level that you feel in a real similar type. There also is no force-feedback (not even a simple stick-shaker or runway-rumble shaker which even FSX had in 2006) so you have no feeling for what the aircraft is doing in relation to ground or air-flow.
I also want to mention the menus, although they're obviously not related to flight-realism. When you see the menus... you just can't help but feel it's a crazy person who made this sim. For example; if you want to turn the sloped runways off you get a pretty nutty pop-up text about how X-Plane is so much more 'awesome' (a word the X-Plane author seems to use a lot) than FSX because of these runways. A lot of the graphic-settings also has options such as 'Burn your CPU' or 'Too much' or 'Siberian winter'... it's really a joke to see something like this in a 60$, supposedly FAA-certified, simulator.
So, to sum it up, if you want realism from your flight-sim... X-Plane 10.3 is NOT the best choice in my opinion. It's more than 10 years behind current technology standards for home-PC flight-simulators.
I do feel cheated paying 60 bucks for this incomplete software.

If you were buying this game in 2010 or 2011 this review would definitely read differently but the question is whether its any good now, not when it was relevant.
Obviously things like the graphics and the tech is showing its age. It's not horrible but it's also not going to stand up to anything modern. Honestly though the biggest difference is the speed of play. After playing anything modern, even later games bearing the same title, BC2 feels sluggish and grinding. This isn't always a bad thing, it puts an emphasis on positioning rather than movement and reactions, but in instances when you find yourself across the map from your objective without a vehicle it's pretty brutal. The number of maps and gametypes leave you with a decent variety, if you'd like. As with any multiplayer game of this age, veteran players have found all the chinks and advantages in every map meaning new players will face a steep learning curve and on some maps an experienced team can completely break the balance. Of course with a multiplayer focused game like this, finding matches in your chosen gametype or map can be a bit of a challenge.
The one thing that doesn't really change between release and now is the single player. Unfortunately this was the weakest part of this game, as we've come to expect with battlefield, and is wholly forgettable. Suspect AI, obscure objectives, stereotypical NPCs, and all the gritty brown you can handle, and then some. In full disclosure, the game deleted my save 90% of the way through and I didn't have any desire to start over and finish it. That probably tells you what you're getting into. In the end this game is 5 years old and not getting any younger. The base price point, especially without including the great variety of the Vietnam pack and the uselessness of the SpecAct skin pack, is a bit absurd. Luckily if you're really looking for a slightly older style modern military shooter or need something a little lower end spec-wise for a large group of friends (at the very least 3v3 on the smallest maps with 4 to 6 a side being more reasonable) this title often sees relatively deep discounts.

Dead State takes on a game setting that has been done before: A zombie apocalypse has occurred, and you're tasked with surviving by scrounging up whatever materials and rescuing and recruiting any survivors you can find. While it is a tried-and-sometimes-true genre, I feel like Dead State does manage to make it interesting, at least. The beginning is possibly it's strongest point, when you're tasked with fortifying a high-school that ends up becoming your base of operations.
With a handful of other survivors, each with their own personalities, quirks, strengths and weaknesses in different aspects of contribution, you're supposed to somehow ration supplies, assign objectives, get crew assigned to different items, and find a way to go out a scavenge without becoming a citizen of the new apocalypse. It honestly becomes an interesting take on group management in a strenuous situation, and the experience is punctuated with semi-schedules events that take place throughout the game depending on the survivors present and the situation you're in, even sometimes requiring you to make difficult decision that impact the game in a drastic way.
The other portion of the game pertains to the scavenging, and makes up a sizable portion of the game and is arguably the most frequent portion you'll work with outside of the former. Scavenging sees you moving about on a large map and trying to uncover locations of interest, while also trying to manage inventory and supplies during the journey. Once you uncover a location, you're usually able to enter the area's local map and move about, most often encountering zombies, looters, hostile survivors and friendly units that you can potentially recruit and bring about to your cause. Usually, the latter are the more interesting of these, as they often come with encounters unique to them and often showcase the developer's talents in context clues and storytelling.
Combat takes place in a grid-based movement system where all units take turns and have various actions based on their equipment, and on an AP system which limits the amount of actions a single character can perform in a round. It's nothing too drastically new, so I won't go terribly into detail. It has had some known bugs, however, such as looters being killed by zombies, and taking a rather large number of rounds to turn, before you can kill the now zombified-looter and end combat.
PROS:
-Excellent marriage of Group Management and Zombie genres, with some exploration and turn-based grid-aligned combat, to boot.
-While the game largely follows a set path in terms of major events, it does offer quite a large number of optional, semi-random events that can drastically impact the way the game progresses. Not necessarily to the point of providing several greatly different endings, but it can definitely change the game in a good way.
-A truly great instance of developers with a penchant for character writing. Not every character drips with rainbows of uniqueness, but the situations are interesting and presented in ways that seem believable, which lends a great amount of atmosphere and interest to the cast, where they'd normally suffer from having too many on board.
-Context is done masterfully in this game, as most times you can explore a location and see a story unfolding in front of you without a single written word or moving picture. This is usually most impressive when you're rescuing survivors, as you can often piece together terrible, tragic, or even sometimes horrifying stories simply by looking around the area first.
CONS:
-Unfortunately, as time goes on, the strong start does fade somewhat, and the game can sometimes seem more like menial tasking when you're waiting for the next day to arrive, and the end can seem like it is taking forever to arrive.
-A somewhat weak ending, although there are some slight variations depending on your decisions or the events you took part in.
-Some events are almost down-right secrets, as they can be almost entirely too easy to miss without knowledge beforehand.
Even so, I'd recommend trying Dead State, at the very least. It's an underrated gem that really does deserve more coverage than it gets, and if you're into these genres, you really can't go wrong.

It's Deus Ex's old-fashioned granddaddy, an FPS/RPG built in the most advanced version of idTech 1, the Doom engine. It's fast-paced, the limited RPG mechanics largely staying out of the way, and pretty brutal at times. Also, it's surprisingly open for such an old FPS, especially one built in the Doom engine - anywhere you go, with very few exceptions, you can go back to at any time. You'll want to, considering how much they put in to explore.
Don't worry about the engine feeling old, either. This port is very well done, it feels modern. It doesn't have all the bells and whistles that, say, GZDoom has - but it's also easier to handle, doesn't allow you to do things that would break the game, and has a few very welcome additions. Directional damage indicators and different crosshairs for each weapon help in combat, and objective markers are a blessing on some of the more labyrinthine areas. The options menu is comprehensive, although it does have one problem in that it doesn't actually tell you what your FOV is currently set to.
This is a great re-release of a great old shooter. Buy it, for the Front and freedom. Move out!

I loved this game when it came out. It added story, stealth and RPG elements to a genre that, at the time, these elements were new to.
That said, after playing through it again, I realize that only the early parts of the game (set around the hub of a town occupied by the Order) really stuck in my memory all that clearly. There is a good reason for this: the further you get into the game, the less significant the elements I mentioned earlier which make the game unique really have any effect. By the end, it's just navigating maze-like levels looking for the right switch, mowing down masses of enemies that cross your path with your impressive aresenal of weapons. In other words, it gradually devolves into every other shooter of its time.
Another issue I have is just how little variety there is. All the enemies - save one type - are either acolytes or robots. Most of the settings are either medieval-style castles or technological settings that could have been pulled out of a contemporary Star Wars game. There's a bit where you first leave town and find yourself in the outskirts, where it looks like you'll get a new kind of outdoor setting.
I still enjoyed playing this game, and played it all the way until the end. But honestly, if you aren't someone who played it back in the day and wants to rekindle memories or whatever, I don't really see the point in playing this. It might be an interesting curiosity to see an extremely early example of an FPS incorporating these elements from other genres, I suppose, but you might find your interest waning the further in you get.

Strife is an old-school FPS, made with the Doom engine, that never got much recognition, because it was a bit aged by the time of it's release and, even worse, it came out a mere month before Quake made shooters full 3D, making Strife look downright antiquated in comparison. It's a shame, because it's not only a very good game, it was downright revolutionary.
It was one of the first shooters to actually have an actual story in the game, instead of being just a mindless slaughterfest, before Half-Life made story in shooters normal. And Strife's plot is actually quite good, at least for its time. The story of the order and its underlying secrets is not really anything special, but it's interesting and, along with the gameplay, can keep you motivated for quite some time. It also uses a twist that would look rather bad or out-of-place in many other games, but works here very well and is foreshadowed enough. On the other hand, the plot can also get confusing and it's not always what exactly happened. It feels like the devs didn't think out the story quite as well, as they should have.
The characters are... serviceable. Non gets much screentime and development and they only exist to drive the plot forward. The most interesting one is your invisible companion Blackbird, who is quite chatty and lets out many entertaining comments, that sometimes skirt the fourth wall.
As with any old FPS, the gameplay is the most important part and even Strife is no exception. And as with any old FPS, it's no walk in the park. The enemies take away your health pretty quickly and if you have no healing items (or turned auto-heal off), you can find yourself dead very quickly. On the other hand, healing items are pretty plentiful, so the game isn't too harsh. At least on low-mid difficulties.
There are also light stealth elements, for which you have two "silent" weapons. Very light, though, since it's impossible to finish any area without combat (with on possible exception). For the most part, the purpose is solely to thin out the enemy ranks before the proper fight starts. Other enemies don't care if their companions die near them, expect when they are very close, so that works very well.
At first, it might look like the game is pretty free, not exactly open-world, but possibly non-linear. This is not the case, though. There is not much you can do aside from your current objectives and attempting to deviate from it can potentially make the game unwinnable (although the Veteran Edition makes it more fair in that regard). There is only one time where you can make a choice that affects the story, but even then there is clearly a "good" and a "bad" choice.
There are three endings. Two depend on the aforementioned choice, the last on whether you die in the final battle.
There are a good amount of weapons in the game and everyone is quite useful in their own right. Two weapons have alternative ammo and another one has an alternative fire mode, effectively increasing the amount of weapons. Also, one is modular and fires differently, depending on how many pieces you have. However, it also uses your health as ammo, so it's use is limited (mostly to enemies that can only be hurt by it).
The presentation is pretty much what one would expect from a 90's shooter in the Doom engine. It's 2.D, 3D but with 2D sprites for characters, items, decorations and pretty much everything that isn't the map itself and very pixelated. The music is MIDI only, which is a rather mixed thing. The songs itself are good, though. Important (and a few not so important) NPCs are presented with big portraits in a comic style, which are pretty well-done. They are also voiced, which is a mixed bag. Generally, the voice acting isn't very good, but the way it tends to be overdone and hammy is actually pretty entertaining. The best one is the aforementioned Blackbird, who has a pretty pleasing voice. Which is good, because you'll hear it the entire time.
The Veteran Edition improves the visuals with widescreen support and additional effects. Especially Bloom enhances the graphics a lot and makes it kinda hard to go back to "vanilla" Strife.
I can recommend this game to everyone who likes first-person shooters, especially old ones. By now, it doesn't look very impressive anymore, but it still holds up nicely and is especially interesting for retro shooter fans.

One of the very first First Person RPG's ever made. While maintaining a steep difficulty level, Strife remains as one of the most comprehensive Doom overhauls ever devised.
Full voiced NPC's, interaction menus, side-quests, and amazing map designs make this game one of the penultimate Doom Engine games. While the original Strife was cancelled and hailed as free-ware for being released far too late into the 90s, Veteran Edition includes several bonuses and extra content, such as the re-implementation of "Capture the Chalice" mode, Objectives being marked on the Auto-Map, and a High-Rez mode that makes the gmae look breathtaking.
Strife is not for everyone, and before you decide if you should buy the game, you should hunt down the original 1996 verson on the internet. It's abandon ware, so it won't cost you anything. Veteran Edition remains a beautiful remake, however, and I highly reccomend you support Night Dive for finally bringing the game to Steam if you're looking to experience it on a more flexible scale.

I'm not entirely certain what engine they used, but looking at the source code (included with the game) - it LOOKS like a fork of
. Night Dive's efforts have given us a classic title, truly upgraded to a modern experience. The game looks fantastic - not overly done with anti-aliasing or other flashy features. The textures look a bit crisper, the controls are tight, and there's a few subtle lighting features added in.
Is this something you can do yourself with a copy of the Strife1.wad and a Doom source port? Yes. Though this package is good for a quick pick up and play with minimal to no configuration. Night Dive Studios also recovered/finished some of the original content never included in the original release (Capture the Chalice specifically) - I can not say for sure if this replaced content is embedded within the included wad file or not.
All in all, this is a great port - and I look forward to more of Night Dive's releases.

Strife was a cutting edge game that helped put FPS RPG on the map. I have played the original DOS version once and I enjoyed it very much. New ways to interact with people and the environment were what made the game great. There were only illustrations of people with the voice overs speaking, but it was the beginning of what would later become lifelike interaction. It was the precursor to Half-Life, a foundation for a more real time experience. Strife was the grandfather of the RPG and I am very  glad Steam has brought it back.
The weapons are inventive, thought provoking and very impressive. The story is top notch and the level designs are varied and very imaginative. The spectrum of color is wide and Strife has many charming elements, both subtle and unsavory.

I loved Strife when it came out in 1996, and I still think it's a heck of a great game - although I do notice its shortcomings more vividly on this playthrough.
First of all, I really want to congratulate Night Dive. They've smoothed out many  of the rough elements of the original Strife, added some useful/cool new features, and generally done a great job at making Strife look and play better without really touching the game itself.
Here's a few of the improvements:
As for the game itself, Strife is a FPS/RPG hybrid with a heavy leaning towards the former. The FPS elements are interesting in that several of the weapons can hurt you if you're not careful - especially the grenade launcher and secondary fire mode of the Mauler. If you learn to use the weapons effectively, however, they can make you feel like a total badass. You cannot stealth through the whole game, but many areas allow you to get through with minimal killing if you'd like, and one achievement is based around doing this in a specific area.
The plot involves a couple of twists that you may or may not see coming. There's a couple of major areas that only open up if you take the path to the "Good" ending, and one or two that you can just simply miss by not exploring the levels enough.
The RPG elements of Strife involve branching NPC dialogue trees, (optional) upgrades to accuracy and health, and 3 different endings. This is nothing special today, but at the time, nobody had put all those features into a FPS, let alone a Doom engine game. The spoken dialogue is variable in quality - some characters are believable, others a little over-the-top. Thankfully, it's all way above the quality of many other old-school games.
You have essentially a running commentary from Blackbird (a female NPC who talks to you via your comm unit) throughout most of the game. It's a great idea that often helps to give the game some personality, as well as a reminder of where you need to go next.
Then, there's the secrets. Holy heck are there a lot of secrets in this game. I discovered a few secret areas here and there in my original playthroughs, and was pretty satisfied with myself. When I went about trying to get the "Completionist" achievement in this version, I noticed that many of the secrets I knew didn't even count towards the total. I'm now pretty humbled. To be fair, some of the secrets are not at all obvious, and some basically require bumping into/trying to open every square inch of every level [(The transparent wall secrets are some of the worst offenders in this category)]. Also, Night Dive *added* some secrets to this version of Strife, most notably the Talismans (which are a seperate accheivement). I'm currently running through the game specifically trying to find every secret without consulting a walkthrough. It's not easy.
Okay, so there's also some stuff that doesn't hold up so well:
Blackbird often comments on NPC dialogue - but sometimes she doesn't start talking until at least a second after the NPC's line has finished. If you're used to rushing through dialogue trees, you might miss about half of her lines. I can't remember if this was in the original game or not, but in this version a line of text will show up in the saying "Blackbird is listening", which lets you know she's going to comment after the NPC finishes talking.
The graphics are kind of blocky. This version has done a nice job of subtly filtering textures once they get a certain distance from the player, but this is still a Doom engine game. Thankfully, the overall art design is colorful and far from the bland color schemes of more recent FPSs.
The music is variable in quality, with some tunes adding to the intensity of combat
, and some becoming incredible repetitive after a while; the music in the sewer levels is especially grating (pun not intended).
While the lack of handholding in finding mission objectives is a nice change from modern games, there are some levels where it's very easy to get lost and not know what to do/where to go next. The objective waypoints on the map screen are a nice addition, but the markers are totally static and don't clear when individual objectives are achieved.
The multiplayer is limited to your Steam friends. This is great if you have several friends who like to play Strife, but it would be nice to have the option to play with strangers as well. Yes, I do also understand that dedicated servers are expensive to run.
Overall, this is easily the best "re-release with enhancements" I've played, and really helps to show folks what a cool, underappreciated gem Strife was/is.

This game, much like doom, was a defining title for me in PC gaming.  I still own it and have played the original through dos box, but when I saw it available with an updated engine and supported multiplayer I couldn't stop myself from buying it.  This game is not only a solid piece of nostalgia, but also serves as an example of excellent game design and execution from what I consider a golden age of PC gaming.  I highly recommend buying this game, and experiencing it.  It's aged well, and serves as an excellent mile marker for revolutionary gaming and the growth of the platform as a whole.

Although I never played the original version of this game, but anyone who's a fan of DOOM should pick this up right away!
Think of it like DOOM, but focused on a single-player adventure with fleshed out quests and light RPG elements. The only thing missing is leveling, but money replaces experience ;)
THE GOOD (7):
-Extremely tight controls! If you've played DOOM (which I'll reference a lot), you know how Strife plays exactly! This style of control doesn't exist for shooters anymore and it's too bad because the gameplay is quick and exciting. You'll never get frustrated at the controls :)
-Great story production! Although I'm not very far in the game so I'm not sure about the overall plot, but the game has full voiceover work and even has some cutscenes presented as a stylish comic-book!
-Multiple endings! I still haven't gotten a chance to beat it, but I read online that there's at least 3 different endings (probably more), and when is that ever a bad thing?
-Cool Quests! The questing is never more than what it should be. "Go to this area and turn this switch off" or "go kill this guy for some cash". That's all I want and expect from this type of game and it gives incentive to explore some side maps :)
-The main town! This might seem tiny, but I really like the town! Guards (which are enemies on any other map) won't shoot you, and so long as you don't start killing people at random, you can relax and shop at your leisure.
-Shops provide ammunation and in some cases new weapons, so you'll be hard pressed to run through the game without ammo, but don't go shooting walls randomly ;)
-Surprisingly long. I still haven't found time to beat it! After the first boss (which took me a very long time to get to), I thought it was the end of the game. Instead I was presented with a strange new weapon and told that "there's 4 more pieces to that weapon", so I guess there's 4 more bosses!
THE BAD (3):
-The music is pretty lame and sometimes outright annoying. It had me laughing and I love how cheesey it is, but the music is bad XD
-Keeping track of quests can be a bit tricky. This version of the game has added the ability to see quests on your map, this is great! But the icons pointing you where to go won't disappear once you've completed one part of the quest. It will point to the quest giver and the objective at all times, adding more icons for quests that require you to visit multiple locations. Often I found myself backtracking to an area marked on my map only to find I'd already finished that part.
-Sewers. Once you get to this part, you'll know what I mean.
If you'd like to see the game in action, here's my First Look :)
FINAL THOUGHTS:
What can I say? The Original Strife: Veteran Edition is a tight game that any DOOM fan will love! Most other reviews talk about how Strife was overlooked because at the time there were some huge game releases.
I'm glad I was able to pick this one up :)
-Thanks for taking the time to read this review! I hope you found it helpful in deciding whether to purchase this game!

Star Wars Republic Commando is an amazing game that adds a new and interesting twist to the Star Wars video game franchise. Excellent game. You plays as the leader of a squad of clone commandos. This is an old game, which means its graphics won't be super realistic or anything(and I honestly think its a good thing. too many games try to look like real life). You will play Republic Commando half for the action and half for the story. The characters are entertaining and established. While they don't have much dialogue, it is obvious the squad is very tight knit from the little they do say.
A notable feature of Republic Commando is the squad is your weapon; you can order your squad to take up certain positions, use turrets,ect. The AI is also pretty smart, especially compared to when this was released. That really helps the you get immersed while playing. The micromanaging you do makes you feel like their leader instead of making you rage. My only real complaint is the game feels a bit short(well, that and there isn't an expansion or anything like that.) There are a couple bugs, but nothing gamebreaking really. The most frustrating bug I've ever dealt with in this game is one where an NPC I was supposed to protect kept getting stuck(and hammered at by a boss). Had to redo that part 2 times before getting it right. But that was the first time I've experienced it(in about 11 playthroughs....I only bought RC on steam because disk broke).
Republic Commando is a darker part of Star Wars history/Star Wars gaming. That is a good thing considering how "light" some games are. That and George is getting his hands in everything in an effort to make it more kid friendly/marketable. This is probably the only dark story in the prequel trilogy especially.
I recommend this game to everyone. I'm not a massive fan of FPS games, I'm more into RPGS, but I really liked this. I initially played RC more for the story but the action can get addiciting.

Finally, some external marketing of Star Wars that does the franchise perfect justice.
This game may be older, but it's one of the greatest and still relevant shooters I've played today.
Tired of the jedis? Or massive Battlefront-style unit management? Take control of Delta Squad: an elite group of clones who all have their own specialties to bring to the team, and personalities that play well off one another in the amsuing dialouge.
The shooting feels pretty good. Enemies die in a lot of visually pleasing and hilarious ways, keeping the good cartoon/serious balance Star Wars is known for. While there's a dissapointing variety of guns, the ones you have suit you very well.
As Delta Squad's leader, you take advantage of "squad commands". Split up your three squad members to take up sniper positions, heal themselves, hack consoles, breach doors, blow things up, and a variety of helpful things. All these commands are administered and canceled with suprising ease, and the AI is FANTASTIC at fending for themselves and executing orders.
Almost shameful to say that your team AI is better than most cooperative shooter-style games on the market today.
You only play through three worlds. While the game isn't longer than eight or so hours, it's one long thrill-ride that is action packed with appropriate breathing room. Nothing's more intense than when you're the last of your squad not incapacitated and there's a pod dispensing Super Battle Droids infront of you.
There's multiplayer. It's standard deathmatch and CTF type gamemodes. It's nothing special and nobody really plays it anymore.
TL;DR?
FANTASTIC shooter, very unique, BLEEDS Star Wars atmosphere, entertaining and likable characterss, and holds up as one of the greatest shooters and Star Wars games today. What's not to like?

Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death is an action adventure hack and slash made by Zootfly games released on September 20th, 2013. Is this game just another mediocre God of War clone, or does it rise above that by being a hilarious and self aware budget game? Spoilers: it does.
Story: Marlow Briggs takes place in South America, where your ladyfriend is translating ruins for a crazy businessman. When she tries to quit working for him, our protagonist Marlow is stabbed by a ancient Mayan weapon and killed. He is brought back to life by a talkative mask and goes out to kill the bad guy and save the girl. Pretty normal stuff. Anyway, it doesn't take itself seriously, and I did get quite a few laughs from the magical mask, who acts as the comic relief throughout the game, and gets some good banter with Marlow. Also the evil businessman is absolutely amazing, he has enough ham to feed a West Virginia family reunion (In case you didn't know, that is a lot of ham) It might not make much sense, but I had fun, and that's what matters.
Graphics: Looks great, lots of colors, good animations for Marlow's attacks. Very few options on PC but runs smoothly, so I didn't mind. Not much to say here. One quick sidenote, why are some people saying the graphics in this are bad? It's a budget game, 15 bucks at launch man. Are people comparing this game's graphics to AAA 60 dollar games? Cause that doesn't make a whole lotta sense.
Gameplay: The God of War comparison is easy to make, and it certainly follows the formula. Light and heavy attacks, combos, health and mana items, all of that stuff. Not being an expert at God of War (or any game, for that matter) I don't know the small details, for instance if the 43rd frame of Marlow's combo ruins the game or any super indepth thing like that. I can tell you the combat is smooth and responsive on keyboard and mouse, combos feel very natural to pull off,  dodging works effortlessly, and magic attacks feel very powerful and satisfying. It also has quite a bit of variety, platforming, very basic puzzle solving, and turret sections that don't overstay their welcome. Everything in this game works well, and controls pretty much perfectly. Here's a quick side thing, I didn't try using a controller, because the keyboard and mouse worked perfectly. As a guy raised on consoles, it's rare where I play an action game that feels flawless on Keyboard and mouse.
Length and replay value: The game takes about 7.5 hours to beat, probably less if you don't suck as badly as myself. Not many reasons to replay unless you want to beat the game on hard mode.
Should you get it? If you like fun games, I'd recommend it. If you don't like fun games, buy Call of Duty Ghosts instead. Just kidding! Even if you hate video games, don't buy Call of Duty Ghosts. Buy Marlow Briggs and give it to someone who likes games.
Thanks for reading my review! My friend and I also have a youtube channel called, "CultGamerAlliance". Check it out if you get a chance!
