I have no qualms with the story. No, really, not too much of a problem. I'm sure there's lots of people who have seen friendships lost over time as apathy or an attempt to put more meaning into the relationship result in more distance between you.
Starting with the good: This game hit me with nostalgia something fierce, with a reference to all the good and bad of the early to mid naughts. I never listened to any of the bands popular in those days, but I did like most the movies of the era, so there was that. And who can forget using AIM and Windows XP? Took me back to the days before I became a Linux user and before I am the person I am today. And if the author was hoping to convey that "hopeless" feeling you get when you realize you or the other person basically killed your friendship? Kudos.
Now for the negative, and why I don't recommend this game.
My issue is in the game pretending to have any sort of depth to it when it is horrendously linear and shallow. When I first played this I thought this was going to be akin to Stanley Parable, where each choice you make actually changes the path the game takes you.
Nope.
In fact, literally no choice you make changes anything beyond maybe a few lines of dialog that are usually irrelevant to the narrative as a whole. The game basically lies to you about whether your choices have any meaning such as "Emily will remember what you said." or "You chose to talk about [INSERT THING HERE.]" Ultimately only maybe about three choices have any impact, and that impact is horribly minimal.
Thing is, no matter what you do, the story goes the exact same way: There's a party in high school, you keep in touch with Emily, you get subjected to a love triangle, you may or may not hook up one year, Emily acts awkward, and the game shuts down any hope of a different ending as you get relegated to painful small talk.
Remember how I brought up Stanley Parable? I was hoping your choices could have brought you down a multitude of different paths with Emily. From the good, the bad, the ugle, the weird, the hilarious, the philosophical, SOMETHING, with actual multiple endings to show this game has anything to it.
Again, nope.
The events of the story are pretty much exactly the same no matter what you do, with the same ending, meaning your choices are completely without meaning or impact on the game. Basically, just play this game once and you've pretty much seen literally everything in the game.
For the utter lack of variety or choice impact, I cannot recommend this game. It could have been a highly non-linear, branching experience, but it seems like the author just wanted to tell a single story in which you have no real role.

This game is great!! While clearly still a work in progress, the support from the community, especially modders, has created a very different crafting and building game. The developers actively desire involvement, and are completely willing to implement changes proposed and created by others.
Basic Overview:
In Medieval Engineers (ME), you build houses, castles, windmills, siege equipment, or anything else that strikes your fancy. The basic game has just wood and stone to build with, but several mods exist on the workshop to allow other textures to be applied to the basic materials. Additionally, in "Survival" mode, you can starve to death if you don't at least do some hunting and gathering, and there are some foods you can grow, and some nice additons via mods to the farming aspects. There is also the "Creative" mode, which allows direct manipulation of the graphics to create your own planet or just terraform part of it to whatever you would like.
Resources:
Stones of varied sizes for tool-making or building, including weaponry
Small trees for sticks and large trees for logs, that can subsequently be crafted into timbers or planks for tools, weapons, and buiildings
Ores of several types that can be smelted into ingots that can then be used to make metal tools and weapons and more advanced buildings
Simple foodstuffs that can be cooked together to make more nutitious meals
NPCs:
At the moment, there are only deer to hunt and relatively simple-minded barbarians to kill (with the option to turn the barbs off).
Multiplayer:
I haven't tried to play on a public server myself, but there are several servers running in various parts of the world, and this allows for PvP (or PvPvP...), since everything that can be built is also fully destructible (and deconstructible if you place it in the wrong place. AND you get all the resources you spent to build it back when you take it apart).
Overall, thgis game is well worth the US$10 I spent on it. I recommend buying it now, before the price goes up afrter official release!

However I advise purchasing Hover when it is on a sale, since I cannot reccomend paying $19.99 for an early access game is partially overpriced for what you are getting. On the other hand, the price of which Hover is at  goes towards the development team to improve the game further.<<<
>>> If you are searching for a game that is finished and works perfectly without bugs, glitches and crashes, I suggest you don't purchase this game as it will be a waste of your steam wallet and your time. <<<
Hover : Revolt of Gamers is an early access game; this means that there will be bugs and glitches, the story wont be complete, it will be light on content. However, it means it will be improved. Every update will bring something new to the game, be it a new area of map to search or a bug fix. Steam may publicise this game as an early access game but it is in fact only in its alpha stage, meaning it has a long way to go before it will be complete.
Anyone who has played Jet set radio and enjoyed it, I encourage you immensely to buy Hover : Revolt of Gamers as it is pretty much a modern descendant  to the game and will bring you lots of nostalgia.
Hover is a mixture between Jet set radio and mirrors edge, you get the brilliant music amidst doing parkour in an open world (although at this stage, a small portion of a map that will begin to grow).
The only problem which will deter you from buying Hover is the optimisation. On low Graphics with a resolution of 800x640, my laptop (which has a Geforce GT 635m)  can get roughly 25-30 fps, on the reccommended default I can gather only 12-18 fps.  Also the default is set to a french keyboard- since it is a french game- but can be easily switched to other.
Overall, I'd reccomend this game if you want something new to try, if you can handle the rough optimisation, I would definitley give this game a place on your steam library.  Furthermore it has full controller support and will have VR support in the near future, if you get motion sickness, I wouldn't use your VR headset for this game when it is fully compatible.

Magicka 2 is a huge let down for fans of the first game for several reasons and the game is such a chore solo that it made me take a break after 2 hours (that AND the fact that the game lost connection to the server 3 times and froze on some weird "Better hit ALT+F4" screen).
1) The movement is horrible. While the devs made it easier to move and prepare spells instead of the awful Finger Twister game from the first one; You now must go where you click ALWAYS. Aim with the mouse, judge distance on lightning spells with the mouse, walk right off a cliff with the mouse. Why the devs felt the need to add slippery ice mechanics ON TOP OF THIS I have no idea.
2) The spells were weakened INCREDIBLY. You now need to play co-op in order to deal the same damage as the first game but the enemies have roughly the same health. One of the features I noticed first is that shields are no longer worth casting in any way, never again will your "E" key stand alone. You can't mash space to maintain (which is weird because that sounds like a HUGE co-op feature) and if you try to keep up a personal shield, you won't have time to cast anything else. Your spamming of spells is also gone. I prided myself on my ability to mash out a quick Lightning Bolt in Magicka but now, even without the awful "focus regeneration" on your quick-cast spells, each spell has a cool-down that serves to hamper players who have memorized casting spells quickly since you move slower when preparing a spell and there is no "negate casting" button.
3) Quick-casting is a nice option but you cannot program your own spells. If I could set my "1" key to quick-cast a ward or full strength heal, this complaint wouldn't be on the list. The devs feel like they can tell you how to play the game they just handed and marketed as having all these cooky spell combinations (which you don't unlock quickly nor do the original interactions carry over; instead they dumbed down the game for controller support) by forcing certain spells into the "1", "2", "3", &"4" keys and not even allowing you to rebind those to different numbers.
4) After the devs go and dismiss DRMs in  this article:
You later find out that if you disconnect from the Paradox servers, the game kicks you out.
-EDIT-
Most of the issues listed have been fixed and while I don't think the developers should be let off the hook for their poor decisions, I do think they deserve some credit for their responsiveness. I am once again finding myself enjoying and reccomemending this game and its additions.

Great game with a lot of hours of play time - I'm 50 hours in and not sure if I'm even halfway finished yet. If you like turn-based combat, survival, and base management you will probably like this.
The base management part of the game is similar to "This War Of Mine", but different and with more depth... you don't have to go out alone when scavenging, and the combat system is actually good.
Bring back food, medical supplies, fuel, building parts, bourbon, weed, and other essentials to keep your survivors happy.
Build a workshop, garage, mushroom patch, greenhouse, shooting range, chicken coop, etc... probably about 15 - 20 buildings like that to upgrade your shelter.
Turn-based combat with many melee weapons (each type with its own special attacks - knockdown, cripple, etc.), guns, bows, thrown items, and so on.
Human and undead enemies. You can even use sound to create distractions or lure enemies to fight each other, like throwing a firecracker at some enemy looters so they have to fight the undead who come to investigate the noise.
Crisis events at the shelter and other big decisions that actually have noticeable effects. Even a comment you choose in dialog with people in your shelter could be the difference in them staying loyal or running off in the night with some of your supplies.

It pains me to say that I cannot recommend this game to friends.  I absolutely enjoyed my time in development, but always wanted more.  More story, more locations, more things to build / do, etc.  However, the game ended development, and suddenly, support stopped.  This review comes years after the game as since ended all support and development.  This review will explain the game as is, long after it ended abruptly as the game's ending is.
Dead State allows your to create a character in made up middle of nowhere town, Texas, do a quick air plane crash tutorial, then find yourself leading a group of survvors in a school.  There is an interesting dynamic trying to play sides, or just not giving a crap, ultimately, doing what's necessary for the group and your ability to lead.  You get a team of characters, and there is some story, and it's nice.  I spent a great deal of time weighing options, exploring, and scavenging the map for supplies.  The turnbased combat is fun, so I will not dock the review points in that area.  However, after about 10 hours or so, the game loses all story elements and becomes a grind to the finish.  What I mean by grind is, sleeping until the end because game balancing and actually finishing the story through the designated timeline never happened.
After you have a decent amount of supplies and upgrade your school fort to max, there really isn't much point to doing anything.  I can send out my super SWAT team and roll through just about any challenge, boss fights included.  A little preparation and know how makes the static maps rather easy to beat on all difficulties.  So, after skipping through the last 20 days or so, the game ended just about as fast as it began.  It felt rushed, and a let down.  Having backed the game from the beginning, played the beta, then the final, I can tell you that it's a fun game, for a short time, but then ends abruptly, or just gets boring, and there's no point.
There is almost zero replayability.  No bonus rounds or alternate stories.  You know what happens, and can google how to get the best endings.  Total waste of time.  For a zombie sim, it seemed promising.  During development, I loved the take on turn based zombie tactics.  However, considering Project Zomboid is still being supported, and is older than this title...the developer should be shunned for not finishing what he started.

I'm going to give this game a thumbs up, but there are quite a few caveats to go along with it. Its one of those many situations where a 'mixed' review would be what I'd rather pick, but forced to choose I think I land on the thumbs up side.

First, it is not polished. There is a reason this game has a ~70 on metacritic. It is very sloppy in a lot of ways, and lots of things do not work well. Despite looking like it is from 2005, it still runs very poorly at moments when the environments get at all 'complex' or over-populated.
Second, the combat is quirky at the best of times, awkward or broken at the worst. This is kind of a tie in to the first point on the game being polished, but it deserves its own note. I ended up not beating the game just because the process of fighting the undead, and even humans, became tedious after awhile. It was often necessary to use 'cheesy' strategies, such as screwing up the human enemies on doors (which they could not deal with effectively / intelligently most of the time) For context, I've beaten X-Com 1 from start to finish twice, and I've beaten Divinity: Original Sin. I don't normally tire easily of strategic combat games, but this one took it out of me to the point that, after over 100 hours played, I am throwing in the towel and calling the enjoyment I had of the game to where I reached a victory of its own.
Third, it is not pretty. The character pictures are well done, but the actual models in the game are, as mentioned above, reminiscent of games from a decade older than Dead State. That has never really mattered to me all that much in games, but even I got a little bored with its lacklustre visuals.
So, now that that is out of the way, why am I giving a thumbs up? Well, first off, I clocked over a hundred hours and *didn't beat it yet.* So as far as bang-for-your buck between play time and cost goes, this game is pretty damn economic. And to be clear, I did enjoy the first 100 hours. It was only once I continued to slide past that point, and discovered through looking online that I still had a loottt more to do, that I threw in the towel.
Nextly, and this is the main thing for me, the writing, categories and world-building are phenomenol. Despite looking quite bluch, the game has really excellent writing and a huge cast of characters who are unique in their own way. They do a really excellent job as well of having the characters personalities reflected in their stats and decision-making. Many characters will have unique events and relationships that emerge between one another, even if they didn't know each other outside of the shelter. And the decision-making is far more reminsicent of Fallout 1 or 2 than more recent games that claim to give you a lot of choice. One of the advantages of forgoing voice acting is they can pile on the dialogue and character choice options without as much concern.
So that's dead state in a nutshell. I'm done with it for now, but I think I may come back in a few years and use a walkthrough to try and find / save all the characters that you can (if that's even possible). Last thing I should probably note is this is a pretty cut and dried zombie survival game in a lot of basic ways, so if that's your jam you'll probably like it, but if that's a big turn off, you might find the cons I mentioned even more overpowering, and the pros inadequate.

Dead State Reanimated is a 3D zombie wrecking turn-based RPG that reminds me of Fallout 2(the combat not the story). There is  some base building, scavenging and item crafting, and a lot of fight. You could find a lot of 3-way war in this game, with you fighting both zombies and human enemies, or you could stand aside and watch them fight it out if you'd mastered the art of zombie luring. If the human enemies were killed by zombies, they come back to life as zombies too. There are a lot of weapons and armors to choose from. Objects in the maps are quite detailed. And the most brilliant thing about this game is all the recruitable survivors with their own stories and their own interactions and dialogues between them. Took me around 120 hours to complete it. Very recommended.

This game surprised me. Its far better then most Tactical games out there in this price range. I personally prefer a fantasy setting over sci fi or horror, but this one is an exception. Its actually "feels" apocolyptic, and while most of the gameplay outside of the typical turned based combat is typical loot and scoot,its still done well, and is addictive and fun.
There is a tension in the air as well, as you have a "sound meter" that if you make to much noise, you will attract some unwanted attention in the form of Zombies by the hordes. This meter is even still active DURING battle, so firing off that gun to save your♥♥♥♥♥may actually get said♥♥♥♥♥eaten. Zombies can also tackle a member of your gang of mismatched heros to the ground if they outswarm them, even at full health, leading to an instant kill if you dont hurry and help get the zombies off them. Bites can also infect a person, killing them and turning them into a zombie if you dont give them daily anti biotics. And while it  is not easy to get infected by a bite (unless your being careless or overzealous) it adds to the tension even more.
Zombies are not the only threat. You also need to deal with marauders, bad cops, biker gangs, looters, and raiders, and even other paranoid or desperate survivors who want your resources.
Your "base" is an old school, which you can populate with a WIDE variety of characters. These characters are not cut and paste, as they all have thier uses such as mechanics or soldiers, to meth addicts and doctors. No too are alike, and they dont always play nice with you or each other. But if you handle the situations well, you can keep them all useful and under control. Handle things the wrong way, and one of your characters may be murdered in thier sleep by another, or you may wake up to find one of them stole your resources and ran off in the middle of the night. Its VERY nice to see this much depth in a game I had low expectation for going into.
This hybrid Turn based strategy/tactical game/Zombie apocalypse simulater/social simulator/exploration and plundering game is a MUST for Turn based rpg/strategy gamers and zombie apocalypse fans in general! Would LOVE to see a fantasy game using this same system! Two thumbs WAY up!

Back in the 90's when First Person Shooters were gaining the most momentum there was an abundance of ingenious and ambitious usages of the legendary Doom engine, and while titles like Quake and Duke Nukem were the most talked about at the time there was one debut title from the great Rogue Entertainment whose mechanics influenced an emergence of now familiar and relied on mechanics. Strife finally marks its comeback in a more modern and accessible package for both fans old and new.
Most importantly, this is an incredibly solid port that is consistent with the quality you'd expect from Night Dive and then some. All modern resolutions are included here as well as graphical improvements in the form of dynamic lighting, bloom, and customizable motion blur. Controls have been tweaked to fit the playstyle of modern shooters, and objectives now glow with a circle on the minimap creating a much smoother and seamless quest hunt. Night Dive Studios has given Strife all of the needed customization to allow players of any background enjoy the game however they please, be it in its original intended form or with all the new bells and whistles.
An extraterrestrial meteorite strikes your planet, unleashing a mysterious virus ravaging the brains of those it infects. Society has been split into two, the infected who have become cruel and barbaric rulers over the uninfected and powerless civilians. You are one of the uninfected who have banded together to create their own rebel community and fight this infected authority that reigns over your lives known only as The Order.
Strife features a large and detailed town hub unlike any FPS before it due to its population of many colorful, grizzled citizens and their connected questlines with fully voiced dialogue trees, the exploration within this community feeling fluid and engaging even after all these years. Here you've got all the staple establishments used throughout the RPG medium. The tavern provides you with side quests to perform for cash as well as tidbits of valuable info that comes at a price, the hospital sells valuable potions to heal during combat, and the weapon and armor shop sell the valuable equipment needed to advance through the harder levels found throughout the world.
Once you've met up with your underground resistance group of rebels the game opens up, as you take quests and carry out important mission from the various NPCs you'll find scattered around the sprawling town. Different strongholds and hidden corridors throughout the outskirts of the town play host to these missions following classic FPS action, and will reward you with scavenged loot and money in the form of quest rewards to purchase new equipment or much needed medical kits before delving into newer, harder territory.
While it certainly isn't the first FPS/RPG hybrid to ever be created, I feel it was the best original attempt to really get it right with a user friendly combination of addictive RPG progression within a fast and furious world of Doom-like violence. Fans of the engine and of the era in general will be drawn to the reminiscent visuals and their application to a unique fantasy world, an extremely pleasant departure from the usual bleak and gray environments we're used to from shooters of that period. The nostalgic Roland powered music is especially delightful here, and takes an extremely adventurous turn in composition.
tl;dr
If you've never played Strife there is no better time to discover and enjoy a legend, and if you're an old fan of Strife this is the perfect excuse to go back and experience it again in its most polished form to date.

I remember when I was a kid and we had Strife on our Windows 95 PC alongside many other classic first person shooters like Wolfenstein 3D, Doom 1 and 2, Heretic, Hexen 1 and 2, Duke Nukem 3D, Shadow Warrior and Quake. I used to watch my brothers play these games as I was too young to play them myself. Of all these games Strife seemed most boreing of these all games for me back then, since it had so much RPG elements like talking to people etc., not non-stop action like Doom, Heretic and Hexen.
It was until many years later, I was much older when I started to appreciate this game and like it, as I started to play it myself and got more into RPG stuff in general too. And I realized how unfairly overlooked it is when compared to other classic FPS games and started to wish that it would be re-released someday so it could get a second chance.
Naturally I was very happy when that day finally came to be, as Strife: Veteran Edition was released here in Steam. Even better is how they have fixed and improved many things with the game yet still keeping the game familiar.
My point of telling this experience of mine with Strife is that I do totally recommend Strife: Veteran Edition to anyone, especially to the fans of classic first person shooters.

I love Strife. I love the engine, the overworld, the shooting, the secrets, everything. It's one of those games that just reeks of originality and ingenuity that it's hard to even come to grips with the fact that it disappeared off the face of the planet shortly after it was released. The Veteran Edition, led by Night Dive Studios, is not only a faithful port of the original game, but also offers a re-done version that fixes up a lot of bugs, adds an unfinished game mode to it, and makes the Doom engine look brand spanking new. And it's glorious.
Strife came out in 1996, a month before Quake was released. Graphically, it definitely was overshadowed by Quake. The Doom engine could pull off some amazingly large locations and have tonnes of enemies on screen, but Quake was in full 3D, and it looked amazing (and also the level design was ridiculously good too). Strife faded into obscurity as Quake basically became the hall-mark for FPS standards.
Strife is mostly a first-person shooter: you move around, shoot bad guys, and walk around a map completing objectives. It had an inventory system similar to Heretic or Hexen before it, where health packs and other gadgets could be used. It had a bunch of weapons that could be used, and, in the retro shooter fashion, were completely explosive and amazing. My favourite has to be the grenade launcher, which fires two giant bombs forward, which explode into a tower of fiery death. There's also a secondary ammo for that weapon which fires napalm, and man is it devastating.
However, it also had a few RPG mechanics thrown in. Firstly, the entire game was a persistent overworld: you start in a main hub, and every level branches off from that, interacting with each other as the game goes on. Military bases become overrun, pathways open up between areas, and so on. You can also talk to almost every human character in the game. While a lot of them don't say anything useful, a few give some nice tips on fighting enemies or navigating the levels. Quite a number of NPCs are voice acted, and it definitely brings the game some life.
On top of that, levels have a lot of secrets involved with them. With the Veteran Edition, there are 16 that are marked and count towards an achievement (which honestly is not that many), but there are definitely a lot of other hidden away areas that include items, rewarding the player for keeping an eye out for inconsistencies in the level. One kind of secret actually increases your maximum health and makes your weapons more accurate, which is a nice way to reward the player rather than giving a bunch of ammo.
The story will leads you around a bunch of locations around the world. While it gives the illusion of an open-world game, it's really linear, as you're expected to clear off levels in a specific order. However, quite a few areas allow the player to approach it from different angles, similar to Deus Ex. For a lot of levels, stealth is an option. While the player, in a few areas, can walk around without guards attacking, robots will always hunt the player down, so stealth is more about avoiding enemies than trying to take out each of them one at a time. When stealth goes, the game doesn't make you feel like you've messed up, as your weapons are more than capable of taking down enemies (although on higher difficulties the number of enemies gets ridiculous). A few areas in the game do get quite ridiculous though in terms of irritating enemy placement or level design, but overall there's a lot of good stuff.
A lot of the enemies attack with hitscan-like weapons (or projectiles that move very fast). This can get a bit annoying and can contribute to a lot of deaths in the game. Again, fortunately in the Veteran Edition, a little blip comes up on the screen indicating where you are getting hit from, which makes it easier to react to them. Because of these enemies, your playstyle will move towards a more cautionary stance rather than running in rooms guns blazing. It's an interesting change of pace, but it does get a bit annoying when you die very quickly. Fortunately, hitscanning enemies are also the weaker enemies in the grand scheme of things (akin to Doom), which makes it not as cheap as it could be.
The story has you up against a few bosses, each one harder than the last. They also require to be hit with the ultimate weapon of the game: the Sigil, which upgrades its damage output and attack style after each boss is defeated. The Sigil uses the player's health as ammo, and it provides an interesting dynamic for the fights: where survivability is more crucial than before.
Strife also has a couple of different endings, and, fortunately, it isn't just a different button at the end of the final room of the game. The endings are determined in the last third of the game, and it changes the course of where you go and such. It's interesting to see a game from almost 20 years ago do this and many other elements so well compared to more modern games.
The Veteran Edition release not only fixes the original game's bugs, but it also offers the original game as a bonus which is nice. It also uses a fancy OpenGL version of the Chocolate Strife port, which offers bloom and dynamic lighting, but, again, there is an option to use the software renderer and make the game look as old as it originally did. Also the multiplayer is nice and chaotic as most retro shooters seemed to be. However, the player-base is not quite there yet, so it's hard to get into a match.
However, of course, the game not only includes support for modding, but it's compatible with a bunch of mods that were made back in 1996. While not as extensive as some other games at the time, there's a lot of good stuff that came out of the modding community back then, which will definitely extend the game's life cycle.
If you play Strife, you have to remember that it came out in 1996: well before any other shooter RPG hybrid that was big and popular. And it's sad just how amazing this game was. The Veteran Edition release is very faithful in making the game run well on modern systems, as well as making it compatible with older content. The $10 price point is well worth the content. Strife is a magnificent game, and you'll definitely like it if you're into retro shooters or shooter-RPG hybrids in general, or if you just want to play a hard as nails old school game.

Do you like games like Banished? Do you wish Oregon Trail had a space program? Sol 0 is the game for you. Continuing in the long tradition of base-building games, it's a lot of fun being in at the ground level of a Martian space program - this feels in a lot of ways like The Martian got a game without having let the licence free, which is no bad thing!
The only real negative to the game thus far is that the tutorial, while 'complete' in giving you the means of controlling the game, doesn't give you a great deal of help in figuring out the tech tree. Building requirements and advancement can be a little obtuse in your first handful of games. If you like this sort of discovery pattern, though, you may very well find it a positive rather than a negative. Overall a lot of fun, and I can see tons of replay value already.

When one thinks of zombie shooters, the kind of combat that usually comes to mind are close-quarters and brutal in nature which encourages twitch reactions and allows for some poor aiming. However, this game tried something new by taking the idea of methodical and deliberate long range combat prevalent in the Sniper Elite series with the legion of inexorable shambling Nazis.
And the most amazing thing is, it actually works. The way that the weapons are balanced allows for a wide gamut of sniper rifles that are great for different situations, as well as a great selection of secondary weapons for when things get too intimate. From the PPSh-41 and it's extreme RoF, to the stopping power of the Trench gun, there is always a gun for every situation, and the challenge is executing your shots right.
Being that this is a budget title made by Rebellion, I didn't expect this to be good and bought it for ironic entertainment value. Instead, I got genuinely entertained by the variety of weapons, and the zombies' reactions to being shot. Of course there are a LOT of rough edges to this game, like how hit detection for headshots can be spotty at times, or how the bullet vision can be annoying with how often it triggers.
Do I recommend this game? Absolutely! Especially if you're looking for an alternative to Left 4 Dead 2, it is a blast on co-op.

As far as combat goes, it feels.. off, definitely could use some work on that end. As of now it's just click and spam and the diving function is kind of unneeded it seems.
Questing is generic, pretty simple. Fetch this, kill that, spam some buttons, grab the loot. A classic ARPG element so I wont harp on that too much.. but I did expect some variety.
The UI and Graphics look fine to me. UI's are usually a deal breaker for me because I despise an interface that is difficult to interact with or one that simply looks ugly. I'd love to see the developers allow skin mods for this.
All in all I'd give this game a 4 out of 10. However I still recommend it because I think there's plenty of room for improvement and would like to see what the developers offer to this game. So give it a try, it may or may not be your cup of tea.

I want to state, that writing this review, makes me want to cry. I loved Magicka 1, I put 88 hours into that game and this is unfortunately a massive downgrade.
First off, always on DRM. You lose connection while playing single player? Hope you like having to open the task manager and close down the damn game!
Second, the game play is highly iterative, which is fine. I think we all just wanted more Magicka, but they've made changes to the spell system which essentially mean that not only is there less variety in terms of what you can do, but most of the spells you can create do very little damage, so you're not encouraged to experiment, which is basically the whole point!
Because no spell does decent damage, you're basically keeping to the same ones over and over.
Some might claim this is balanced, but it doesn't feel fun. In the first game, a fully charged rock would blast it's way through a horde of weaker enemies but in this, it not only takes forever to charge, but it bounces off the first one! This doesn't feel fun, you feel weak.
They also removed alot of the "magicks", certain spell combinations that triggered specific effects, such as tornados or summoning zombies. So you have less variety with that as well. They can also be keybound, which lowers the skill requirement and thus, the feeling of success when you pull it off.
So to recap, the magic casting system has been gutted, castrated and beaten into the ground, possibly to get the game on xbox.
Having finished the game, I have to say that I'm very, very dissapointed with the lack of enemy variety. I went through the game and met less enemy types than the original and most of the enemies were cut and paste from the original name. For some reason they decided to dissapoint on enemy variety, yet remove the magicks that had really cool effects, such as vortex.
I will say though, the last boss fight is pretty well designed. It played out alot like an MMO fight and even if it is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥in single player, it has good design.
BUT unlike the first game, it doesn't test your ability to use various magical spells effectively. In the first game, you had a banished demon wizard (if I remember correctly) and if you didn't use certain magicks (lightning bolt and time warp), it was a really tricky fight, but you had the tools you needed.
The last boss fight in this one, is more about timing and positioning, which isn't neccesarily what I wanted.
The humour is still there, but if you're after that, I'd honestly suggest watching a let's play and as someone who played 88 hours of Magicka 1, that makes me weep.

I thought I'd try out X-Plane 10 in the hopes that it would be able to replace the aging FSX. Whilst FSX is great and is the gold standard, it's old architecture places limits on it which we have pretty much reached now. X-Plane 10 is the ONLY 64bit high fidelity general  flight sim and that is able to fully use today's hardware. Add to that the fact that its flight model is more accurate out of the box than FSX and you have a recipe for success. Right?
The flight model is good. The planes don't feel like they fly on rails (unlike stock FSX). The auto-gen scenery and effects are very good. The environment is gorgeous straight out of the box. It runs smooth as silk on my machine. But... I only put a few hours in the sim before regretting downloading it's 50 odd gig of content and returning to FSX. Why?
Part of the joy of sims for me is immersion and level of fidelity to reality. Whilst X-Plane 10 hit the ball out of the park with flight modeling, its "plausible world" just simply isn't. I was dismayed to discover there are very few runways or airports with any buildings on them. Almost all of them are just flat strips on the ground with no buildings, no life, and no feeling of having actually arrived at a destination. Every landing feels like a landing on some remote bush strip in the middle of nowhere. In addition, the various cities and locations don't actually look much like those locations.  You have to go to great lengths with addons to rectify this sitation, and even then it falls short of the mark.
The cockpits of the default aircraft look like they were made a decade ago (I think some were!) and a number of the 3d virtual cockpits just dont work at all. I was so disappointed that I felt the need to drop some money on a plane from Carenado on day one, just to enjoy the experience. This was a major disappointment.
Another area that X-Plane get's let down on is developer support. Compared to FSX or Prepar3D, there is very little in the way of professional addons, scenery packs, and aircraft. X-Plane does have a thriving amateur community creating content... but that is exactly like it sounds.
Oh, the UI is clunky as hell and the loading times are a nightmare!
All that being said, I do enjoy the feeling of flight in X-Plane 10 and it does run very well. If you only care about flight modeling and the feeling of flight, and can live with scenery that doesn't reflect the real world then this is a great sim and I recommend it. If you are new to sims, it's Steam access makes it a great and easy place to start. It's for these reasons that I am going to give X-Plane 10 a thumbs up.

A lot of the reviews I’ve read have said the game was boring to play, the buildup was wasted, and the length was disappointing.
I felt the game itself was enjoyable, regardless of if the entirety of it consisted of you walking from place to place, the game made it dialogue filled, and often had areas or items to observe and speculate about, which helped fill in gaps in the story that are left mostly unanswered otherwise. Beyond that, the game is story-driven, meaning that the whole point of the game is to convey the story, however that may be, so complaining about how the game is basically a walking simulator doesn’t hold any foundation to me. While I was partially disappointed with the “ending” of the story, I felt that it was a heartfelt but realistic conclusion, and anything more wouldn’t have fit with the atmosphere of the game. As for the length, I feel that the exploration factor was ignored by a lot of players, and without it, yeah, the game feels extremely short, and that’s because you missed chunks of the game that would’ve lengthened the time it takes to complete it. On top of that, the motivation to explore is to unveil parts of the story that go unmentioned, and the argument that the game was too short for $20 doesn’t make sense to me, when many people rushed through the game but then proceeded to give this game a bad review based on its length.
As for the game overall, I think it was one of the best games of 2016, and is certainly still worth a play now. If you’re more interested in gameplay than story, I guess a game like this isn’t for you, but if you enjoy a good story, good graphics, good voice acting, good music, or all of the above, this game is a gem.

With a lot of zombie/zombie style games out there.  It is nice to find one that is not the same thing with a fresh coat of ooze to make you think it's new.  So here is what makes this game worth playing.
Charactures you love and hate with nice little stories for each.

LOVE IT !   Played around 30+ hours so far and its everything i ever wanted in a zombie survival game.  The story is great, i love the aspect of building shelter upgrades, assigning building jobs, finding new allies, and the fact that whilst the main story seems the same no matter how many times you play it through - there are always nice little random events that make it seem like a brand new game each time.
If i am being picky, a couple of things id like to see added/improve (i know probably unlikely as game is a few years old but..) :
1) Looting system - either give more looting events or less (i'll explain that).   If you find a car or van, you cant loot it because the game has nothing to give you from it, so then why are they so many "lootable things" like zombies that allow you to click on them but nothing inside.  It shouldnt be that hard to code that an object can only be looted/clicked if it has something to actually loot.
2) Parts seem really hard to find yet there is an abundance of "uncollectable / visual only" items in each area, i get it must be balanced but again i cant help but cheer every time i find parts as they seem so rare, yes i did build recycling but its the finding of parts im talking about.
3) Space allocation - would be nice to have an extra plot of land and you decide what its used for: farm / shooting range / recreation, etc rather than having set plots that then cant be expanded, example lets say you want a farm but you want a huge farm using all available land, not just a little greenhouse on the roof. But you would have to make the choice - if you build a farm you then cant have anything else on that land.  Maybe even the option to expand the perimeter.
4) travelling at night time - i get that the game wants you back in your shelter by 8pm but why cant you say spend the night in an abandoned house then set off again in morning back to the shelter?  If it were real life thats what you would do.  Even if it were just a clickable button on the map next to the house you were at that said "stay the night" and gave you a percentage survival chance of you not being attacked during the night would be good. Then you could pick and choose the best option to spend the night and head back to the shelter the next day.
5) romance options - even if it were just an occasional conversation or two that could lead to an ally getting a bonus towards agreeing with you would be nice.
6) combat movement - the square chess like system can be very annoying especially if you have an injured ally that then cant escape because all spaces are blocked, really there shoukld be allowances for this like maybe when they panic they can run through taken spaces or that moving through a taken space as an additonal movement point/points penalty.
Dont let my above 6 things put you off, its a great game and already has been worth every penny i paid for it.  Buy it !

I've clocked 57 hours into Dead State, it's been a grindy experience but an enjoyable one, and I think now I'm done. 57 hours seems like an excellent return for what I paid for it.
Dead State is an isometric RPG based in a post apocalyptic zombie world. It is clearly the work of people who know and love old school RPGs, and while it owes a lot to the first two Fallout games it develops on them in certain respects. Combat is fun and they have very successfully translated the vibe of zombies not being difficult to kill, but that you can easily end up in trouble when things get on top of you. The balance of risk/reward for gathering food and luxuries is the strategic element of the game and works very well.
There are downsides. Several patches down the line it remains buggy. There is a loss of polish in many respects. Dead State puts a lot on its character interactions, but the manner in which they occur and the general writing appears amateurish. The characters and interactions appear deeply two dimensional and I was no more attached to any of them than the bolts in my crossbow.
Another potential problem that I know many others had, is the long-term play of Dead State. Dead State is, apparently, completable. At the start you can choose to play either Iron Man or with saves. If you're playing on Iron Man, it will be a very challenging experience just to stay alive and you are probably playing until your demise. With saves it is infinitely easier, but the sheer length of the game is revealed. At 57 hours put in, I did not complete the game nor did I have any sight of the end-game. If I had to guess, I would suggest that the designers felt that they wanted to make surviving the apocalypse an unlikely experience. I don't feel terribly strongly about it, since I'm happy to walk away from games than most, but that can be a downside for you.
So its grindy fun, some nice features and some horrible design. I'm unlikely to ever complete it and am zen with that. Horribly flawed but at 57 hours of play it's hard not to recommend.

I loved enough about this game to play it all the way to the end, but it has some major flaws and it's not for everyone. It has a lot of heart, but like the zombies you fight in it, it's missing some brains.
Easily the best thing about the game is the writing. You will meet 40-50 strongly drawn individuals in a full playthrough and, as the leader of your shelter, you will need to manage their concerns, demands, and occasional breakdowns via individual interactions and through more collective decision-making known as "crisis events." This is great stuff. You'll constantly feel the tension of having to manage so many conflicting personalities in order to keep everyone safe, fed, and what now passes for comfortable. Resource management is also a critical part of the game--at least in the beginning. Assigning people to various tasks in the shelter to best use their skills and your scarce resources is an engaging challenge, compounded by the fact that many of your shelter inhabitants have strong preferences about how much danger they or someone they love should be in. Base management and personality management are very strongly merged and if you like that sort of thing, you'll love this part of the game.
Unfortunately, the other major part of the game--scavanging and combat--is much less strong. First of all, ignore any comparisons to X-Com you might see in the promo materials. Combat here is nothing like X-Com; there isn't even a cover mechanic. If you are looking for a deep tactical experience, you will not find it here. It's frustrating because there is a lot of wasted potential. For instance, there is a "noise" mechanic in which using louder (and more powerful) weapons, like guns, will draw more zombies to your location. In the early game, this is very dangerous, but you can also use it to your advantage by luring zombies to attack human foes. You feel pretty badass the first time you manage to pull it off! Unfortunately, zombies pretty quickly become unthreatening once you find any decent armor, and they never "evolve" or become any more dangerous. Yet you will be fighting those same zombies throughout the entire game.
This problem is compounded by the fact that every zombie on the map takes its turn at the SAME TIME, regardless of whether you have aggroed it or not. So aggroing even ONE zombie, when the typical map can have 30-50 of them, means sitting there for 10-20 seconds while the game processes the turn of every zombie on the map who is not doing anything but standing around picking its nose. It turns what should be an incredibly brief and decisive battle against a completely unthreatening single foe into an agonizing waiting game. And the game lags horribly while this is happening. It is excruciating, and you may find yourself intentionally aggroing every zombie on the map by being as loud as possible just to get it over with. So what should have been an interesting combat mechanic soon becomes merely a tool to bypass the irritations of the game engine.
It's also worth noting that if you scavenge every day (and there is no reaosn not to), the nail-biting scarcity of the early game quickly passes and by mid-game you will find yourself swimming in food and supplies, even if you take in literally every survivor that you find, as I did. I thought that playing this way would force me to make harder and harder decisions about how to keep this ever-growing number of people safe and fed, when in fact having more people in the shelter makes the game easier, as you will more quickly be able to complete upgrades that produce more food and parts for you. Soon enough, I actually ran out of useful things for survivors to do around the shelter, and most of them spent their days enjoying the seemingly endless bourbon and bon-bons I was scavenging up for them.
And for whatever it's worth: at least one major and obvious ending was scrapped from the game, and the one I got was lackluster, to say the least.
So that's Dead State. It has a lot to recommend it, but a lot of problems too. If I could give it a sideways thumb, I would--but since I was willing to put up with its flaws because I really enjoyed the good parts, maybe some other people will feel that way too. If you want an open world with strong characters, interesting decision-making, and base management that is engaging for at least half of the game, give it a shot. If you hate reading and want deep tactical combat and a game engine that doesn't feel like it's held together with string and tape, give this one a miss.

(NB - I initially put this as a postscript but I'll put it here just in case: DO NOT LOOK THROUGH THE ACHIEVEMENTS! THERE IS A SPOILER PRESENT! You won't know if you have never played this game before and if that doesn't bother you, disregard but I have so it's obvious to me.)
Many, many, many moons ago, I played a demo of an ad hoc Doom-meets-Zelda game on my cousin's PC. Many, many, moons after (early 2007), when I accrued the cash to buy my own PC and a month or two after that when our house got the Internet, I stumbled across a website named Abandonia which served as a threshold for some of the long forgotten classics of yesteryear, most of which were, as they are today, long out of print. Well, that unusual title happened to be amongst its collective and after a little while struggling to get my head around the Metroid Prime of the mid-90s, a lot of fun and a lot of happy hours were spent playing through it.
Of course, the game in question is Strife and a few more moons later, I discover that a refurbished edition is on sale in the Steam store at a price which slots in at well under ten gold. Needless to say, the cash was parted as a great game is always worth its weight in gold (or something)! As has been said, it's a first-person shooter in the vein of Doom (particularly as it uses the Doom engine) but with a twist: instead of making cold meat pies out of everyone and everything, there are Zelda/Final Fantasy/Shadowrun-like elements of exploration, character interaction and even some (very loose) stealth elements. More on that in a tick.
You start off much as you do in Wolfenstein 3D, in a small room with just you and a guard (acolyte) albeit with no weapon other than a spike attached to your glove. He takes a few punches, but you'll do away with him easily enough. Immediately after exiting the room, and after executing another acolyte, you find yourself in a dystopic village, an unusual hybrid of medieval setting, not unlike Hyrule Castle in Ocarina Of Time, mixed with a futuristic sci-fi world. A small room on the left brings you to a well-spoken character named Rowan, who's vaguely aware of you and what's just happened, and reckons you're just what a friend of his named Macil, the leader of a resistance movement known as The Front (such imaginative names, guys!), needs for their force. After doing a quick chore to prove your allegiance, you're on your way. Sort of.
You start off by acquiring a 'companion', a voice from someone named Blackbird: a tough, headstrong lass who lets you know the score. But there's also a strand of charm to her and a sense of humour and you'll find that she's a very pleasant companion and keeps you interested. After a small bit of espionage, chatting to the barkeep and a couple of patrons at the pub (and another guy, more on that to follow) to get an idea of the place and what's going on, it's time to meet Macil and be sworn into the ranks of the front. There's an option to refuse, as there is when Rowan first asks you, but it's not an option that's conducive if you wish to live. He gives you your first lot of tasks, one of which involves dealing with the Sepp Blatter-like Govenor who's happy to turn a blind eye provided he gets paid. It's all going well..... for now.
But I digress. It all sounds very deep for a game of this ilk and you're right, because it is or at least is by 1996's standards. It's a shooter with a resonating storyline which twists and turns depending on the choices you make whilst playing it. You're out to get the bad guys but unlike its older, Mars-based cousin, you can't go out all guns blazing, you have to think and get a feel for your surroundings, decide what to do and how you do it. Hence the element of stealth, which though extremely inconsistent (as you'll later find out), has to be used and maintained especially in the village and Commons. The gameplay is vastly improved from the original title, which has a smoother framerate and superior resolution in addition to the standard WSAD/mouse control for FPS games as opposed to the fiddly keyboard controls of old (which never stopped me playing, mind). Movement is better, action is more fluid and for me, it takes the edge off of the difficulty a little bit - and this game is tough! Also, as has perhaps been insinuated, there are no levels as such - you go between the different areas of the game, which totals about a dozen with sub-areas to some, as and when you need to.
The paths you traipse and the ending you receive when you're done depend on your decision-making when interacting with specific characters, which usually involves taking their word for it 'cos as there's no real incling to what might happen before you go one way or the other, wisdom does not come quite as conducive. For instance, one of the first missions you receive is optional: a crooked Mafia-esque businessman named Harris who asks you to steal the chalice holed up in the Sanctuary in exchange for riches. Other than his voice actor's DeNiro-like tone which gives you the notion that he sounds dodgy, there's no real evidence he'll lead you to a trap which he does, and that sets the town's acolytes on top of you. Yes, that's a spoiler but trust me, it's one you'll want.
Of course, no game is without its flaws and Strife is no exception, suffering the fate of many other titles of that era. There are a lot of graphically-inept maze-like passages from A to B to C to D with a lot of deja-vu moments (wittingly remarked upon by Blackbird on a few occasions) and even though this version highlights the points of interest on the map for you, it can be frustrating getting to them, sometimes even requiring to exit the area and find another entrance in another part of the game (as the areas are interconnected). The AI is very ropey, as it was in nearly all games up until about ten years ago, which would be fine in most other FPS games but not one where interacting with the enemy and often being forced to keep a low profile are required to progress. And when you do have to fight them - stuff like cyborgs, robot spheres, mechanical spiders and ED-209s - they are quite tough and they take a lot of hits, hitting hard themselves. Add to that they are profuse in numbers and ubiquitous in each area and though the game isn't too stingy on health and ammo refills, there are points where you'll find yourself stuck for one or the other and even both. I'd advise keeping two or three save files, particularly if you're playing on any difficulty past and inclusive of Veteran 'cos you might have to end up doing an entire segment again.
As with something that little bit different than expected, Strife is an unexpected pleasure. A blaster with a storyline, a world to explore and characters who speak is a very refreshing concept, even now almost 20 years after its release. It's not a game for everyone: if you like your shooters to be more about the killing, stick with Doom, Blood or Duke Nukem 3D. But if the likes of Goldeneye or Mass Effect (not great comparisons, I'll admit) whet your appetite and you can put up with the odd bit of RPG-style roadblocking, you'll find a kindred spirit with this underrated, overlooked and very original classic. Macil says it best: "FIGHT FOR THE FRONT AND FREEDOM! MOVE OUT!"

Strife is a game you probably haven't heard of, and that's largely because
. As a result, people pretty much forgot it existed. It's a remarkably ground-breaking non-linear FPSRPG that kind of shattered contemporary conventions, long before the days of Far Cry, Borderlands or Destiny (but following in the footsteps of 1993's Pathways into Darkness and 1994's System Shock).
Notably, all copies of its source code were completely lost and so, modern versions of the game running on source ports rely on reverse-engineering. That's where the Veteran Edition comes in, and it's clear that a lot of care has gone into crafting it. Not only have you got modern OS support, customizable keybinds, along with bells and whistles like bloom, motion blur, high-res textures and so on, but you've also got the original version of the game for purists or curious folk and, on top of that, the reconstruction of unfinished features in the original game, which is pretty damn neat.
The game itself holds up remarkably well to this day. It's far from the highly immersive, airtight, diegetic experiences from nowadays, but exploring it and making gradual progress through the world feels incredibly rewarding. Gameplay is fun and challenging, and the world itself looks pretty good and most environments offer a good sense of realism and sense of purpose.
In a lot of ways, it feels like a lot more than just an underrated game from 1996; it's distinctly ahead of its time and so, playing it feels totally unlike a step backwards in any way. In fact, it feels just as fun, and perhaps more so, than some of the games of today it predated. To sum up, it's a really good game and you should go spend money on it.

When I first looked at the trailer for the game, I thought, "Hey, this kinda seems like Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon; it's cheesy and a little over the top, seems to incorporate humor, and doesn’t seem to take itself too seriously; this should be great!" However, upon actually playing the game, I realized how wrong I was.
Firstly, it is an incredible drag to play; the combat is astoundingly dull, which is says a lot, considering that the game does try to change the weapons you're using and enemies being thrown at you somewhat frequently. The gameplay outside of combat is no better; there are numerous puzzle and platforming sections, but I found these areas just a hassle; I ran into numerous glitches, (character unable to climb up walls, character glitching through walls, etc.) which was only made worse by the fact that the puzzles, I felt, lacked any real challenge.
(I will now discuss the issue of the game taking itself seriously, this is a personal preference when it comes to cheesy games, so you can disregard this section if you'd like, [skip to next paragraph] but I feel it's worth saying) Secondly, and by far one of my biggest complaints, the game takes itself way too seriously. What I mean by this is, the game, or I suppose the creators, really, could not see how ridiculous and cheesy the plot, characters, cut-scenes, and overall feel of the game is; they want us to look at the game as a serious work meant to inspire powerful emotion, instead of a tongue-in-cheek ride meant to entertain. Aside from the fact that this is a serious missed opportunity, as it shows an incredible amount of potential to be a wonderful parody game. it completely broke the immersion; I was never able to get fully involved and feel the emotions the game was trying to invoke, because all the situations were too ridiculous for me to be able to take seriously. It left me feeling disinterested; further worsening how much of a chore playing the game felt.
Thirdly, the plot in this game is heavily bogged down by the fact that I was completely unable to sympathize with the protagonist, and worse yet, I actually sympathized with the antagonists, as technically, they did nothing wrong and it was actually the hero who started the conflict, (I won't go further into this, as I would spoil what little there is to be spoiled). This left me actually rooting for the villains to win, and gave me no drive to push forward through the campaign; why go through the effort if I can't sympathize with the hero or his plight?
All in all, I simply cannot recommend this game. I found it completely unenjoyable, and would hate to see another person buy this game only to have the same conclusion. I only hope that if the developers do decide to come out with another game, they can learn from the mistakes made in Marlow Briggs, and produce a high-quality product for us all to enjoy.

For coming out in 2005 this game still is a thrill to go back and relive the ultimate Clone Special Ops experience. You will be tasked with dealing with the most elite and discreet Republic operations, and leading a group of 4 (including yourself) elite Clone soldiers called Commandos.
To begin, the gameplay is really good for a 2005 game. The shooting action gets really intense in the latter part of the game, and you will have to learn how to manage your squads survival as well as your own. Get too caught up in keeping your squad fit, and your own health will fall and you will go unconscious. Focus too much on your own health and equipment, and your squad will be left without orders and ultimately end up dying. This ends up being a gameplay goal for you as you must balance the two in order to have a successful playthrough (unless you want to play on the easiest difficulty). Although this does end up becoming a problem when your squad completely goes against their own common sense and runs out into a crowd of a bunch of droids, guns blazing, and gets shot down within seconds. Your squad also tends to run in front of you as you're throwing a grenade, which is super annoying because it will take down your shields and your health, as well as your squad member's, and you will still have enemies firing at you. I also feel the game is a little bit too difficult as you will find yourself screaming at your monitor on the Normal difficulty setting. Perhaps the developers could have balanced the difficulties by adding a fourth one (easy would still be easy, add a normal, normal would be hard, and hard would be very hard). But still, the game is still enjoyable despite the setbacks of a few gameplay issues. The guns are also nice. Most of them have decent sounds (other ones being laughable), and they have a good difference in purpose and power. The grenades, with the exception of the flash-bang grenade, are all pretty useful. Although none stand out above the other in the department of usefulness as they're all pretty much the same: aim at your enemy and throw. But still, they're a decent touch.
The presentation is at an average level. With your standard graphics card you can max this game out, and the visuals won't look too bad. The textures are decent, and you won't really see any frame rate drop or texture pop-ins. The game overall has excellent environments that all differ from each other drastically. You'll go from fighting on the sandy and rocky world of Geonosis to the "abandoned" Republic ship in a matter of hours. With the varied environments and average graphics with no presentation technical difficulties, I can confidentially saw this game has above par presentation given its age.
Now, onto the fun part, the content of Star Wars Republic Commando. First off, the story is really good. You are placed in command of Delta Squad, an elite group of Republic Commandos, which essentially are just Clone super soldiers. You will be given a variety of missions ranging from destroying a Droid Factory to helping the leader of the Wookies on Kashyyyk. Along the way you will unlock a few extras, which aren't really anything special, but they're a decent addition. The game is honestly too short. With the edition of another planet this game would have easily felt more complete. But the content that is there is fun and replayable, so it doesn't diminish the game too much. The multiplayer is remotely enjoyable, but will get old quickly. The community is either dead silent or a bunch of snotty veterans who trash talk new players and exploit the more powerful weapons. The maps themselves aren't anything out of the box, and quite bland, which is a shame considering the variety and design of the campaign maps were quite well. You'll most likely end up playing the campaign 1 or 2 times and maybe the multiplayer an hour or two (unless you find the multiplayer really fun, which I doubt most will).
All in all I can say this game was a very good addition to the Star Wars franchise. Although it is a little short and has some gameplay issues and a below par multiplayer, you will find yourself thoroughly enjoying the amazing campaign and its awesome storytelling, environments, and characters. For the current price of $9.99 you should definitely pick this game up and relive or enjoy for the first time one of the greatest Star Wars gaming experiences you can possibly find.

Sol 0: Mars Colonization is a colony building simulation game from one-man developer, Chondrite Games. Humans have at last advanced beyond sending astronauts to the moon, we are now capable of sending humans to Mars. You are in charge of the first mission to Mars, it’s your job to choose a suitable location on the Martian surface and establish a self-sufficient colony. You’ll need to manage your resources while expanding your colony and performing research. If you run out of food and/or water your astronauts and colonists will perish. This is a momentous event for all of humanity, make sure you don’t screw up!
Full Disclosure: A review copy was provided by the developer.
Being a small game, Sol 0 is modest in appearance. The overall appearance of the game is solid, it’s all high quality and the graphics don’t cause any issues with actually playing the game. The individual models all look good when fully zoomed in as well as when zoomed all the way out which is great for those who put their camera close to one of the two extremes. My only real issue with the game’s appearance was the UI, while it does look good I found that the bar seen at the bottom of the screen was a little too small for my liking, especially the small buttons and displays.
Sol 0 is all about building a colony, finding the necessary resources and then sustaining it. The first step is choosing which part of Mars (
) you want to establish your colony on. Each location has a different number of resources to be found and so the less resources there are, the harder the game is. The game contains eight maps (nine if you count the special tutorial location) and the developer has already uploaded quite a few maps to the Workshop including locations other than Mars such as Titan.
Once you’ve decided where you’ll build your colony, it’s time to send the first supply mission. While you can send astronauts straight away it’s best to send up a rover and some supplies on at least the first mission. The rover is what you use to find resources. You can set up an exploration route for it and when it detects resources they’ll appear as different colours and they’ll be shown as different heights depending on how much of the resource is available there (the higher up the bar is, the more there is to be collected). It’s best to survey the majority of the location before sending humans to Mars as resources are drained incredibly quickly and so you need to be harvesting them as quickly as possible in high quantities.
After 120 Sols (Mars’ equivalent to a day) you’ll be able to send the next rocket to Mars. The basic rocket has a maximum mass of 7000kg and since the rocket itself is 6200kg you’re very limited in what you can take. Deciding what to take is possibly the most important part of the game, from a strategy standpoint, as you need to be able to survive on whatever you take up until the next mission. Later on in the game, once you’ve built certain things, you’ll be able to send larger rockets which can carry different equipment as well as colonists (the basic rocket can only carry astronauts).
The majority of the game is, of course, made up of actually building your colony. You’re given access to quite a few different structures, some of which are available right away, some of which depend on the presence of other structures and lastly some that require a minimum population before they become available. Structures are made to fit together in certain ways and the building is completely on-grid, i.e. there’s no flexibility when positioning your structures. Personally I prefer building like this as you end up with a much neater structure and you save on space but I realise not everyone likes it.
Back to those resources you’re managing. The main four are food, water, methane and power. Food and water can both be brought to your colony on your rockets but there are dedicated structures for their production on Mars, their purpose is pretty obvious, to keep your humans alive. Methane is used in conjunction with water to refuel the parts of your rocket which land on Mars so that they can be launched and sent back to Earth. While it’s not hugely important to do this the landing craft does take up quite a bit of space so you will need to send them back every so often. Power is again pretty self-explanatory. While the harvesting of the other resources is fine I wasn’t too happy with how power was handled. Firstly, you can only use solar panels to generate power and they become completely useless during a dust storm meaning everything loses power and so you lose resources. My second issue with power in Sol 0 is that there’s no way to store it. If you could build power banks which stored excess power than my first issue would be balanced out but since there isn’t it feels, to me, like power has only been partially implemented into the game, i.e. you can’t really manage it.
Sol 0 is a great colony building simulation with enjoyable yet challenging gameplay and plenty of locations to keep you busy with. Sol 0 isn’t perfect but it is good fun and for such a small asking price you’d be silly to pass it up if you’re a fan of similar games or want to try something new!

There are only 5 different upgrades to get and none of them feel unique. You get a weak long distance attack (never really worth using), a glide, which is very dull and adds very little bar sections that actually require the use, a pair of boots which allow you to do an equivalent of the Shine Spark from Super Metroid, except you need an even bigger run up and you just run forward, not fly up as well. A down attack, adds very little as the hair whip still can be more effective and only serves to kill a few enemies designed specifically to die to them and lastly a triple jump, which occurs very late in the game and only serves to make you go back and get all the items you saw in plain sight in previous levels.
The biggest problem however is that the game seems designed entirely around these items, rather than the world and the items being designed in tandem.
I can't recommend this game. I did enjoy it, but it was a slog to get through.

I've decided to rewrite my review and change it from negative to positive because I don't want to feed the downward spiral. Screenshot of the old review here:
(please read that first, then the updated one below)
[~] It's been a while since I've played Magicka 2 as I don't have any computer that can run it at a decent frame rate currently. My machine can run the original and Wizard Wars flawlessly though.
[+] The
fixed some of my issues I had with the game, most notably the inability to queue elements while being airborne, the the lack of a halt key and the inability to rebind the keybindings.
[~] I don't know whether they have fixed the issue with elements queuing in the wrong order.
I don't know if they ever will, maybe it's just me. Or maybe nobody else has paid attention to it and that's why it isn't mentioned in any reviews.
[-] No active staff abilities, no cool weapons. So that's still a minus. Though if you've never played the original Magicka you won't notice this.
[-] Unless they accidentally forgot to list it in the patch notes, the damage numbers are still the same. Pure shield barriers are still rather useless. The obnoxious magick cooldown still exists. Wards are still very weak.
[-] Ice and Steam take two element slots now and can't be combined with lightning anymore. So instead of QREASR you can at best do QRESR. For me this is a minus point not because I miss the overpowered spells but because this reduces the amount of possible spell combinations by quite a bit.
[~]Lightning has priority over Arcane now, which means that you can't cast lightning beams anymore. However, you can cast arcane lightning, which is pretty cool too. It's up to you to decide whether this is a good or a bad change. I personally don't really mind.
[+] The easter eggs are alright, though not as funny as in the original
[+] The story is pretty alright. I personally found it to be rather predictable but I know enough people who couldn't tell what would happen next.
[+] Multiplayer works almost flawlessly. But due to the many negative reviews the player base is rather small, so finding a public server can take a while if you don't have any M2 playing friends in Steam.
[+] The equipment screen is a nice addition, now you can customise your character!
[+] You can see your stats now - how many enemies you've killed, how many times you've killed youself, stuff like that. Pretty cool.
People who are new to the Magicka franchise will definitely enjoy this game. If you like Wizard Wars more than the original Magicka, you will enjoy Magicka 2 also.
However, if you loved Magicka and didn't like Magicka: Wizard Wars, you probably won't like Magicka 2. But hey, there'll be more patches!

Great game! One of those, that after you're bored of gaming in general, can still enjoy - which is rare from my perspective.
Pros:
- It's complex and it's unforgiving which is fun and challenging. The social- and base-building-related game mechanics are well performed.
- The characters in the game (which it is full of) are interesting and mostly well written. They make sense when they talk to you. They are not randomized sandbox NPCs which give you quests and hail at you for completing them but the game actually spends a lot of focus on real social interaction between a good diversity of characters. There's a good soul, a preacher, people with challenging mentals stats .... even racists, rapists and murderers. And you somehow need to manage to get those people to work together. I liked that!
- Going out to look for much needed ressources for the rest of the team is fun aswell. The levels to play through are basically non-generic but handmade and not too repetetive. I was surprised a lot by a variety of ideas the developers came up with in order to surprise me. The map is basically open world with a few exceptions, enabling you to make your own decissions on what would be best for your people and letting the game appear less linear which it otherwise would be.
- Combat AI is okay. Not a masterpiece but totally okay.
- Lot's of well written flavor texts - if you're into that.
- Huge variety of items you can possibly find while scavenging.
- A smart yet mostly subtile humour throughout the entire game which made me smile a lot.
- Very cheap game for the time I played and felt entertained by it.
- Developers had a good eye for details in general. I think you can feel that they made this game because they wanted to make a great game and not because they wanted to make the cash flow. That's probably even the biggest plus I give this game. You hardly ever see something like this from the big studios and the big titles.
Cons:
- To get right to the point: After the first half of the game when you scavenged enough food and supplies for the other half of the game, killed the bad guys with the best weapons which you looted and now use for yourself, the game stops being challenging and interesting. The lack of lategame content is in my opinion the biggest flaw. When no enemy gives you a tough fight anymore, you have enough food for months to come and everyone in your shelter is completely happy, the game pretty much loses it's point and becomes a "The Sims" clone with dead rats, some social intrigues and a whole lot of mayonnaise. All that isn't too bad becase noone forces you to actually leave the shelter and go out to look for things you allready have more than enough of but staying at home and looking at a wall is the only other option you have then.
- Combat balancing is a bit off even in the first half of the game. But as mentioned above: Once you have good weapons and armor, the game lacks challenge. Have someone with the best armor and a medkit standing in front taking hardly any damage but your opponents and bring some people with big guns to kill your foes from a distance. Master that and you'll master the game. Other or similar tactics might generally work aswell. Too easy!
- Bugs and crashes. Game crashes around every 10 hours on average on my system which arguably is still okay, but gave me a headtache for a few moments. Similar to bugs where I want to say that the game isn't too buggy, really, but at some points in the game really problematic. For example: Being stuck in a door after appearing in a level and bad guys immediatly shooting at you while you're stuck, unable to free yourself, unable to get to that area from another entry area, only able to fire back from inside that door and hope you win because that's the only way to unstuck yourself. Also: Enemies in similar situations. Door bugs. They are a problem.
- Graphics are a bit clumsy. I personally didn't feel bad about it but thought I should mention it.
- Game gave me nightmares about having to eat tons of mayonnaise in a potential zombie apocalypse. I'm dead serious about it. Dead State serious.
