POST UPDATES REVIEW:
I'm........shocked at how Paradox North managed to pull this together.
Every single problem encountered at launch has been fixed.
The inclusion of the new poison element is awesome, to boot.
TL;DR: Don't read the original review. Buy Magicka 2. Enjoy it.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Magicka (The Original) is a GREAT, AMAZING GAME. BUY IT. Magicka 2 is a *good* game. As in, not AS good as the original, but still good, kind of? Think Diablo II and Diablo 3.
I never thought I'd give a Magicka game a bad recommendation, but.......*sigh*
TL;DR: Buy Magicka (the original). If you have it, buy Magicka 2 when it's on sale and you have nothing else to do.
Magicka 2 feels like 50 steps forward, and 55 steps back.
Magicka (the original) is one of my favorite games of all time.
Nothing comes close to it.
Magicka: Wizard Wars got me incredibly excited......until I realized that they dumbed it down to bare-bones as far as the magic system is concerned.
Magicka 2 was like a dream come true. A sequel to one of my favorite games? Of course I'm happy!
Unnnntiiillll...... I realized they made it more similar to Wizard Wars than the original....
The controls feel floaty and slippery like in Wizard Wars, and the controls have completely changed since the original, and the lack of rebindable keys makes this worse.
Additonal Info/Edit:
I feel like more detail is required here, I'll admit I kind of jumped the gun when I fired off this review, but I meant what I said.
The spell system has changed drastically since the original. Which is not inherently bad. However, things changing caused them to lose value. The earth element is basically useless now, seeing as charging a huge boulder takes WAY too long. This causes interesting combinations like the "Ice Ball of Death" from Magicka 1 almost impossible to pull off. I however, really LIKE that lightning doesn't become a beam when mixed with arcane/death. THAT opens up possiblities that I may not have even discovered yet. Also, the Shield element: There is basically no reason to use it on its own. Shield doesn't block ANYTHING other than elemental attacks? That's a HUGE change from the original that takes away from the chaos that made the original good.
The fact that steam and ice elements do not combine IN the spell queue is a significant change. One that can be adapted to, if it weren't for the fact that those types of damage are impossible to stack against creatures that are weak to it. For example, Steam damage is very effective against the lobster/crab things. However, in any given spell, you can only have a MAXIMUM of 2 Steam elements in queue, leaving very little room for customization.
In addition, the change that makes frozen entities NOT weak to physical damage is honestly pretty lame. I really miss that from the first game. My friends and I loved to tag-team bosses with one of us freezing him, and the rest unleashing huge boulders to shatter them into pieces. A strategy that is now impossible due to the change listed as well as earth element spells being incredibly slow and lackluster.
The quickbar concept SOUNDS like a really good idea, and I'll admit I thought it was a great idea, however I quickly realized that being able to spam magicks with a single button click on a cooldown system really took the fun out of the Magicks themselves. I quickly become aware that I was able to spam-cast dragon strike and haste using a staff that regenerated focus very quickly. I knew how to cast Summon Elemental and Summon Death by memory in the original, and that allowed me to do some crazy things that made me FEEL like a wizard. You actually had to try to do stuff like that quickly.
The controls being similar to Wizard Wars is a VERY minor flaw, all things considered, I would happily adapt and shut up about it if the original gameplay of Magicka was kept intact. It, however, was NOT kept intact in Magicka 2.
ALSO: Including a MULTIPLAYER-ONLY PUZZLE?! Really? I mean, I know its a "co-op" game, but FORCING it is just a bad decision. I don't have "friends".

Devilian is a F2P ARPG-MMO that was made in Korea.
IN DEPTH ON GAMEPLAY:
If you have played other ARPG-MMO's such as Marvel Heroes or Path of Exile then you know what you're getting. Comparing to those alternatives the MMO is much more fleshed out than Marvel Heroes and combat is on par is Path of Exile (perhaps a bit better). There are currently only 4 classes though a 5th is on the horizon.
Action is solid and fast, enemies die with just the right attacks, they don't instantly die with basic attacks but they don't stick around too long either. Skill Trees are customizable and end-game allows for more proficiencies. Overall a very solid ARPG with MMO elements on top.
IN DEPTH ON F2P:
It is F2P, with cosmetics and xp/gold boost in the marketplace. There is an optional subscription perk called Patron that gives no real gameplay benefits, but even it can be purchased with in game gold. You must expand your inventory with store bought items like many F2P MMO's though it is cheaper than many (such as GW2) to do so. Ovreall a very fair business model.
NOTE ON LAUNCH HISTORY:
There was an issue with a EU server where many players lost a few hours of progress. It took a couple of days but Trion has since provided gear and other benefits to those affected. I'd like to point out that this happens even to games that did not just launch. I bought the Mk III pack ($100 for all heroes and storage and gems) in Marvel Heroes and after using the blender (to get more costumes) the server went down and everyone lost some game progress. I lost all the costumes and no one was compensated. Gazillian (the developer) is more well regarded by it's playerbase than Trion seems to be, as the backlash was negligable.
SUMMARY
I have enjoyed my time so far with Devilian, both as a solid ARPG game experience and with nice MMO features (guild raids, guild wars, 20v20 pvp, etc.) as a bonus. If you see the current "mixed" reviews and are cautious, give it a try. It's free and will only cost you a bit of time if you end up not liking it.

text: THE BEST Star Wars Game ever made in the Star Wars Saga. Definetly recommended to Delta Squad Lovers around the world! Have Fun!

The game follows the missions of Delta Squad, one of the elite clone commando units.  You play as RC-1138 or “Boss”, and your team consists of RC-1152(Scorch), RC-1207(Sev), and RC-1140(Fixer).  Each has their own specialties, sniping, demolitions, and computer hacking respectively.  Each is also represented by a color(Red, Green, and Yellow) allowing for easy recognition in battle.
Graphically Republic Commando is still a beautiful game, the models and textures all hold their own to the current standards.  As do the shadows and lighting.  While true, things could be improved, and I’m not going to say they are perfect.  But on the graphic side of things, it’s pretty common for a game to look dated.  Realizing though, that a game only looks dated because of the improved technology allowing newer games to look better.  And no game made today can anticipate what games will look like in seven years, so no game can ever not look dated to a degree.
Now since Republic Commando is a squad based shooter, it only makes sense that I talk a little on the squad based shooting.  And since you play as the leader of Delta Squad, it makes perfect sense that they all follow both your lead(mostly) and listen to your orders.  But it’s in this AI that some of the best aspects of this game are found.  When you tell Sev to get on a turret, or Scorch to take up a sniping position.  They don’t just run straight to the location, they go there with forward thinking.  I’ve played games in the past where you tell an AI controlled partner to do something and they just run Han Solo-esque head first into it.  Without thought of any kind, but you don’t get any of that here.  You tell Fixer to take up an anti-armor position across the room, and he does.  And on his way to the location he’ll stop to shoot who ever is shooting him.  He’ll bob and weave, zig and zag, do whatever he has to to get to that point, and get there alive.
As much as I love the AI and their ability to be smart about things, it’s not perfect.  Sometimes when you want to hold back, reload, heal, and prepare for the next section.  They are already off down the corridor heading for the door.  This can be a problem when that door is unlocked and they get into conflict with some Trandos.  Sure they can handle themselves most of the time, they’re not totally reliant on your orders to survive.  But it can be annoying, especially if you are wanting them to heal.  Or if they are holding a sniping/anti-armor position and someone gets behind them.  Yea eventually they will turn around, but all too often they just ignore the one guy behind them and focus on the guys in front.  They will at least yell for someone to “Get them off me!”
The context-based squad order system is pretty neat.  You can pretty much tell your guys to do anything.  Anything that would be needed while killing Seps, that is.  You’ll see a small barricade in a hallway, put your crosshair on it and get an image of a sniping commando.  Hit ‘F’ on the keyboard and one of your men will head that way and start sniping.  You can tell them if you want to hack a door and go in quietly or just blow the thing and toss a grenade to say hello.  And if you’re like me, and crazy about healing, you can tell them to go heal up.  This they will do on their own, from time to time.  But I’m a little obsessed about keeping my health in the green.
The audio chatter is fun, the guys have a constant chit chat back and forth.  There is enough audio content there that while you will hear things repeated, it’s spaced out enough as to not become annoying.  The voice acting is done by different people, all basically doing their own impressions of the same voice.  So while they are all different, they all have a similar sound to them.  It helps add to the immersion of being clones, without making you confused with who said what.  Because sure, a room full of clones might all look and sound the same to a non-clone.  But to them they all look and sound different.
Sticking with sounds, the music is purely epic.  It’s not just your normal Star Wars John Williams fodder.  Don’t get me wrong, I love John Williams, and every piece he has ever written for Star Wars.  But this game likes to play the cards differently and tasked Jesse Harlin to write a unique score.  Sure, you’ll still hear some of the standard classic Star Wars pieces.  But you’ll also hear a darker, fast-paced, and militaristic score that fits all too perfectly.  Which includes one of my favourite pieces, Vode An (Brothers All).  Have I mentioned how much I love the Mandalorian culture in the Star Wars expanded universe?
The story is solid and ties in well with the movies, mainly Episodes 2 and 3.  It is however short.  While most will complete the game in around 10 hours, which I guess isn’t too bad for any game.  I’m not going to give away too much of the story.  I will say though it starts on Geonosis and ends on Kashyyyk.  And when it ends, you wont be expecting it.  Which kind of makes it a bummer.  The ending screams sequel, or at least an expansion pack, dlc, addon, or something.  There has got to be more to this story.  And yes, you can learn more about Delta Squad in the novels and comics found in the Republic Commando Series.  But you will notice none of them come close to even touching this stories ending.  My guess is that Lucas Arts has made it off limits, for a possible sequel, a sequel that may never happen.  Wikipedia states: “A sequel to the game was already planned…  …however the project only went as far as concept paintings, and was cancelled in 2004.”
And with that I make a heal-turn, and go from the good to the bad.  With some of the more annoying aspects of the game.  For example, the solo missions.  Why is it that every game feels a need to change up it’s gameplay?  I mean you get used to the squad, you like the squad, the squad works.  And then you have to split up?  Okay fine, split us up into two two-man groups, how about that?  And its not just Republic Commando that changes  things.  Every game seems to do this.  What happen to keeping the game the way it is?  We don’t need a change mid game, or a driving section, thankfully this doesn't go that far, but the point remains.  If you want to make a change, save it for the DLC/expansion pack.
There was a small bug, that I’m not 100% is a compatibility issue or just a Steam bug.  Where the game wouldn't start, stating that it couldn't find Steam.  But a quick check on the Steam forums shows this is fairly common, and easily fixed with a Steam restart.  So no points off for that one.  I did see however that some other players were have some issues getting the game to run at all.  That might be a Windows 7 issue, but I’m not sure, as I didn't investigate that matter too much.  Over all it ran perfectly fine running Windows Vista, and outside of the aforementioned had no problems or issues.
To wrap it up and bring this to a close I have to say I was pleasantly surprised at how good a game Republic Commando is after I realized how old it was.  I didn't think it was any where near the seven year mark.  I will admit that 2005 still feels like just a few months ago, times been going by a bit too fast for me lately.  But I enjoyed my time playing as well as writing about it.  Republic Commando is enjoyable, exciting, strategic, and best of all Star Wars.  It is however too short, and has far too abrupt of an ending.

As an update to this review for version 3.0:
* the performance has definitely been improved (pulling about 60FPS on the same equipment; seems capped at that).
* The FOV cap is now 110, and you can alter the distance of the camera from the character, which massively helps.
* It's easier to go up now, but still much easier to go down. That's gravity for you I guess. Still, upward angled rails and such would do wonders in making it easier.
The game has definitely been improved since I originally wrote this, however it's still not quite there. While the aesthetic is as striking as ever, I still can't get into it due to the floaty controls and level design.
JSFR also had issues with its controls; the skating controls were very imprecise and floaty. However, it managed to overcome these limitations with intelligent use of directing rails. Indeed, the worst parts of those games were when you were actually skating around; the best levels were ones that you could lap almost exclusively by grinding, and that gave a much more enhanced sense of speed and control.
I still can't recommend the game as a positive experience in its current form, but it's certainly an improvement. If you wish to support the developer, then it may be justifiable, but understand that this game is still far, far from what most would consider a "finished product".

This game plays like Jet Set Radio had a love child with Robot Roller-Derby Disco Dodgeball, and that love child were kidnapped by Mass Effect. It's very fun to run around and explore, and the races and gameball missions are pretty entertaining too.
However, there are some major issues.
1) The performance of the game is in the crapper; I couldn't pull more than ~28fps between an i5, a GTX760 and 12GB of DDR3 memory, in a game that is primarily cell-shaded polygons. Often, it dipped down to ~12fps
2) The controls of the game defaulted to a french keyboard, which made no sense. The dialog is also a bit iffy, which tells me that perhaps the localisation needs some work. Further, the controls felt very floaty, making it hard to control the character while turning. This wasn't helped by the left and right actions changing the bearing of the player character, rather than strafing.
3) The first-person FOV was capped at 90. For a game that moves this quickly, and that is this dependant on environmental awareness, I'd expect a minimum cap of 110.
4) The tutorial was hard to understand (see point 2), and didn't explain a lot of the systems in the game.
5) The level design needs to be tweaked a little, it was very easy to go down, and very hard to successfully go back up again. This meant I constantly kept finding myself in the same places, hampering exploration.
All in all, I wouldn't recommend this game as it stands. In the future, when it's a bit more polished, then maybe; It has a lot of potential, and I expect some of it to be realised. However, with this quality, this performance, and at this price point? Perhaps not.

First off, I am acknowledging that this game is NOT DONE. In any way, shape or form.
Second off, I'm currently nerdgasming over this entire thing. This game feels like the lovechild of Jet Set Radio Future and Mirror's Edge, which are possibly the best two things you can ever combine.
Character creation is pretty great. You start out with the 'starter' and the color sliders are a bit annoying to deal with, as you can't slide one without sliding the other, and it takes getting used to. You can also change the height of your character drastically, which is a feature I haven't seen on a lot of games like this, and a feature that is heartily welcomed. As you level up, you gain new characters. I believe you get all 4 avalible right now by level 6.
Gameplay-wise, it's glorious. Parkour, races, missions, all the greatest stuff. There are places where it is lacking, such as player-to-player interactions and variety in minigames, but so far in development, it exceeds all expectations.
Visual-wise, it's a bit...glaring. Bright contrasting colors everywhere. It's okay if you can tolerate that sort of stuff, but it gives me a bit of a headache. The movement of the camera is glorious in 1st person, if a bit disorienting when you are doing flips and tricks. Auto is...strange, as it combines 1st and 3rd. 3rd person is great if your character is small. It'd be much better if the camera adjusted with the height of the character, but you win some and lose some. Movement is a tad disorienting and sickening if you aren't used to fast paced, spastic movements, but you get used to it quickly.
All in all, this game gets a 8/10 so far, and I'm sure once it is completed, it will be a 10/10.

The last time I played Dead State, it was a completely different game. The way it looked, played and felt, was differant than the game that is currently on Steam.
To be perfectly honest, Dead State was not a good game, in any capacity. It tried to compare itself to titles such as Fallout, X-Com and Suikoden. The reality was, Dead State did not share anything in common with any of these titles.
Not only was Dead State just one of the most shallow, simple, real time strategy games I have ever seen, it was also completely linear and offered no sense of character growth in any capacity.
As far as programming went, the game was awful. It suffered from long loading times, constant crashing and a wide selection of other bugs that made the game basically unplayable.
One of the things I noticed, that I really didn't like, was that the game is now called Dead State: Reanimated. "Why is this a big deal?" you ask, well that's simple, this game had a terrible score and justifiably so. The developer managed to find a way to toss all of their old, negative reviews in the trash by having the game change it's title. This kind of tactic seems sketchy at best and causes me to trust the developer even less than I did before.
So, what about the new version of Dead State, also known as Reanimated? Well, a lot has changed since the last time I played the game, from the way the game looks, to the way the game functions, so let's discuss these changes.
Players are now given the option to make their own characters, design the way that character looks and assign a number of stat points as well as skill points. I feel as though they were going for a 'Fallout' feeling here, but the lack of skills and reasonable stats just makes it feels like a cheap imitator.
The story and writing has been completely changed. What originally started as a quest for gas and beer now finds the player on a plane that has been invaded by the infected. This scene is rendered by cheap, dull, static, 3D rendered images that look like were done as part of a Middle Schooler's computer lab assignment. The scene is described to you via a text box while drab music plays in the background.. How exciting.
The art assets for this game are anywhere between 'awful' to 'cheap'. A lot of the UI feels unpolished and looks like free assets from a online archive were used. Other times, enviroments like houses or parks look like they were ripped right out of the Sims 2 on the Playstation 2. The graphics are cheap, dull, aged and muddy.
Walking is a simple affair, click to walk, when encountering a enemy, the system changes over to a turn based combat system, which relies on 'AP' (action points) to perform an action. Sounds familiar? It shoud, because it's another page out of Fallout's own handbook.
Dialog choices seem to all lead to the same result, just worded differently to make players feel like they have some sort of control over the flow of the conversation. Obviously I can't confirm that for the entire game, but saving and loading the beginning of the game and trying multiple branches of dialog all lead to very similar outcomes.
You can actually search through the rubble of the fallen civilization now, which leads to a better sense of "looting" (the original game simply had items on the ground with big neon green circles). Unfortunately, since there is no indication on what can and cannot be interacted with, you are stuck highlighting everything with your mouse until you find something to search. Perhaps add in a keyboard shortcut that highlights things you can interact with to give players a better sense of what they can do?
As far as the programming goes, I can't really say if it's better or not. I get the feeling they are using a new engine, but I don't have a older version of the game to compare to. What I do know is that after running this game, the fans on my PC go insane, checking the task manager on Windows, the game uses a ton of resources, much more than what I feel is reasonable for what this game is.
I didn't spend a lot of time with this game, so this is all I can comment on. I don't really apologize for that. It's a game's job, it's responsibility, to grab the attention of the player, to entertain them. When a game fails to do that within the first half an hour, it's failing at it's job.

Admit it.  We all loved God of War.  When those games first hit the market, videos games as an industry woul never be the same.  In a market that constantly demands innovation, development of new concepts and methods of interaction, it can be easy to forget how amazing certain tried and true formula can be.  I STILL love playing God of War...  and this game, is a shameless clone/update, call it what you will.  Graphically upated, and skinned in a different mythos, Kratos becomes Marlow.
This games isn't promising anything revolutionary.  It also refuses to take itself seriously.  The production value is solid, the voice acting well done.  The narrator that is Marlow's "spirit guide" i suppose, is constantly making wise cracks.  I found the game delightful.
Every time I wanted to put the controller down, it kept pulling me back in...  a familiar feeling.  It isn't perfect and it doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it brought back a play style and experience that I feel you don't find enough in modern gaming.  I think someone described it as being able to play a 90's action blockbuster....  fairly dead on.
Get it on sale and you will not be dissapointed.  It's FUN.  Engaging and you will not have to think to hard.  Everyting in it takes place on an epic scale.  An abundance of great Mini-games too.
I am not finished with the game at this point.  I did notice the absence of any MEGA boss fights (Kratos vs the hydra  or kraken) but perhaps those are to come.

This is not just "Devil May Cry or God of War" rip off. It's a full fledged action-packed combat game with dry humor. Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death draws inspiration from several popular media like Devil May Cry, God of War, Indiana Jones and etc. It's an adventure of Marlow Briggs who was killed and then resurrected by the Mask of Death, ancient Mayan mystical artifact, in order to save the world and his girlfriend. The visual and locations in this game are nice and beautiful, giving a sense of archaeological adventure. Combat is challenging and satisfying with a lot of weapons, combos and magics. There are a lot of dry humours along the way to relief you from intense moments. Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death is a worth entertaining addition to hack and slash action genre.

This game is a button masher adolescent power fantasy.
Thankfully that's exactly what I wanted. It's a stupid hack-and-slash with no depth that succeeds because it keeps the pace up and constantly changes what you're doing. It has a dumb-as-rocks story that involves Marlow Briggs, a Regular Guy (TM) getting killed by an Evil Genius (TM) and then being resurrected to take on said Evil Genius by Aku Aku from Crash Bandicoot.
From there it's 6-8 hours of slashing and platforming and rail shooting. You don't do any one thing for too long so it doesn't get boring.
The only issue I have with the game is some of the late game boss fights, which fall into the trap of going like this: dodge to avoid boss's slow attack, dodge in and hit boss once or twice, dodge back out, repeat. This would be fine except that many of the bosses have really large health pools, so, while it's not hard to beat them because you can easily avoid their attacks, the battles do test your patience. This is just bad game design. If I've figured out the trick to beating the boss, let me beat the boss already! Don't make me do the trick 40 times, I already understand it!
Other than that it's good if you want something with that dumb 80s action movie feel.
Performance note: this game has a couple of annoying, but not game-breaking, technical problems.
First, my audio drivers crashed every single time I quit the game, resulting in that loud buzzing noise that you get when your drivers crash. I had to restart the computer to get the noise to stop. Not a huge deal since I beat this in 3 sittings, but it is annoying. I have a dedicated Asus Xonar soundcard and I haven't noticed anyone else complaining about this problem, so it might just be my setup. YMMV.
Second, this game respects the Windows display scaling when it shouldn't. What I mean is, I have my computer hooked up to a 43" TV and I sit about 7 feet away, so I have to set text and apps to 150% size in Windows display settings to make things readable. When I run Marlow Briggs with display scaling set to 150%, the game's menus and HUD increase as well and run off the side of the screen. So I had to toggle my Windows display scaling every time I booted the game up. I haven't noticed any other games that do this, so it makes me think that 505 Games just doesn't know what they're doing.

I was quite shocked when I saw this game on here, considering I last played it in 1996. This game is a truly oldschool PC first person classic, similar to the likes of Doom, Quake, Hexen and more. Don't allow my playing hours to fool you; they obviously didn't log them way back then, but before I purchased this on Steam, I had already completed multiple playthroughs way back.
Get ready to fight The Order, a death cult of religious zealot cyborgs that not only oppress humans greatly, but make humans do their dirty work for them. You are part of a rebel army, doing whatever you can to collect pieces of an artifact which will ultimately help you defeat The Order. How you do that, and the final outcome that happens as a result of your actions, is up to you.
The one thing that makes this game unique from other shooters of it's era, is that you have the choice as to how the story will turn out in small and large ways. The decisions you make when you talk to NPCs, as well as choosing who to fight and who to not fight, will affect the game temporarily, but will also affect it's final, ultimate outcome. You can travel to different levels from a central area, and the levels will stay the same as when you left them.
Overall, I would definitely recommend this to players who prefer the classic shooter types. Perhaps new-generation players could also learn to like it as well.

Strife was the first FPS RPG ever.  It was such a crucial part of the evolution of FPS games that it deserves to be alongside greats like Doom, Duke Nukem 3D, Quake, Deus Ex, and Half Life.
In Strife you get to choose your dialogue, and as such, choose your adventure.
Strife is one of the best FPS games of all time and shouldn't be missed by any fan of 90's FPS or anyone who likes RPG's.  If you want an in depth story similar to that of Deus Ex, mixed with Doom style action sequences then this is the game for you.

Video Review and Impressions:
I loved the original Magicka and Wizard Wars was pretty good for a MOBA and they both had unique game styles in terms of spell casting and control. Although, WW felt like it dumbed down the spell variety considerably compared to the base game of Magicka. This game tries to simplify (I think) the gameplay from the first and it ends up feeling like a mix of Wizard Wars and Magicka's playstyles. There are definitely improvements, for example, the more responsive middle mouse button but it still doesn't feel better than the first game's controls. Oh and it sucks that you can't combine to make ICE anymore. It's cool that you can move while casting now which makes soloing the game easier but the movement can feel really floaty at times or that your character is sliding around on ice so again it doesn't feel as good as the original. It seems they tried waaay too hard to cater to the console crowd.
However, despite these complaints. I believe the game stands up on it's own and is still a great game. Honestly, it feels a so different from the first one, it's hard to really compare it indefinitely to the original. The humor is still humorous, the story is still good, and there are plenty of outfits and unlockables to be found throughout the game... Seriously, I can't get over how much there is to find in the game... from one liners and pop culture references just as hilarious as you would expect and new weapons and staffs dot every single chapter I've played so far.  Another nice touch, is the Artwork for every cutscene and the improved graphics... not that the other games were ever lacking in that department.
All in all, I definitely recommend this game and can already see how much fun it's going to be playing with friends. Now I've gonna go blow up some Yellow Wizards.

I've been flying X-Plane since version 7 and spent countless hours in the virtual cockpit of this simulator. I'm very please to see it on steam now, so that we don't have to carry 8+ DVDs anymore.
X-Plane 10 is what it says on the tin. An extremely realistic flight simulator. I comes with a complete high-res world scenery package and a descent collection of standard aircraft out of the box. Yet it's not a game that takes your hand and tells you what to do. It's a flight simulator that requires some commitment to get the most out of it. You'll literally learn how to fly along the way.
Like with other flight simulators the real power lays in modification. There are tons of free custom airport sceneries out on the web, many of which are quite stunning. The same goes for planes. For a long time free resources dominated X-Plane, yet in recent years high quality payware Add-Ons of stunning quality emerged, so that even the most pampered Flight Simulator use finds very well made airliners, photorealistic sceneries and so on.
My setup consists of hundreds of custom airports, dozens of payware aircraft (mostly airliners) and a small array of tools like PFPX to do the flight planning. With that I conquer the world almost daily. For long flights I often chose the Flightfactor Boeing 777 while shorter hops are a lot of fun using one of Peters Aircraft A320 or A321 models. Looking for a realistic A380? No problem, there's one. More of a Boeing guy? Go forthe 747-8i then. Not into airliners at all? Have fun with the KingAir 200 or a Cessna Corvalis TT. Why not a Challenger 300 business jet for a change. Oh and there's the occasional flighter trip you can do for thrills at supersonic speeds. Too slow? Take the space shuttle for a few circles around the earth.
My point here is that X-Plane 10 is what you make of it. It's an open world, literally, that allows you to fly as close to the real thing as you can get.
It doesn't blow the budget on hardware (I run it with rather high setting on 500$ hardware!), yet doesn't have any limits to what it can take hardware wise as well. So whatever you throw at it, it will only look better.
The weather engine is quite detailed. Weather may be generated at random, drawn out on a map or finetuned. Want the real weather? Just download it and don't forget to check your weather radar (yes there's one!)
After years of using X-Plane I never grew tired of it. If you're looking for a modern, realistic, extendable and smooth running flight simulator, X-Plane is a great choice and I can only recommend it. If you're unsure, check out the official website for the free demo. Check out the community, which provides a lot of useful information and creates new resources, most of them free, on a daily basis.
See you in the skies!

I'm writing this review for people who might not know what X-Plane is and may want the opinion of someone who is new to the program.
X-Plane, is of course, a flight sim. It's highly detailed. People say it's the most realistic flight sim ever. Having never flown a plane in real life I cannot attest to that comment, but this program is known to be used by real life pilots for training.
All the DLC in this game is included in that $60 price. You get the whole world... sort of. Not the world as we know it with the unique buildings we all know, but the land masses are very accurate and the airport locations are also very accurate.
The realism, from my perspective playing many different plane sims, is a great place for any pilot to start. There are few variables to change, but they include what kind of damage you can cause the plane through overspeed or over-g. I've seen more brutal flight models in games like Il-2 Sturmovik or Rise of Flight, but I also must bare in mind that those were a different era of planes with their own set of considerations. The damage modeling in X-Plane is not extensive. This isn't a crashing simulator; it's a flight sim. Don't expect to shear your wings off with over speed or any of the extensive modeling you'd find in Rise of Flight. You'll just be greeted with a message accompanied by poorer flight capability.
I do have to make a few comments about the gear I use to play the game.
I have TrackIR, which makes looking around supposedly A LOT easier. A lot of people have to use the hat triggers on their flight sticks and I hear it's not very enjoyable.
I have a Logitech 3D Extreme Pro or whatever it's called. It's got X, Y and Z axes and a slider bar. I can use that flight stick for full plane functionability, though the flight afficianado might want rudder pedals to go with that mix.
My rig is not super powerful: Radeon HD 7770, 16 GB ram and 2.8 GHz x4. The game runs at about 30 to 40 FPS with dips into 28+ sometimes. It's not optimal for this program. I would suggest something better than what I have.
It's mainly fun for me because I can make my own objectives within the simulation, though it doesn't have the premade missions that FSX had. You can also play it like a rogue-like if you want to. For example, try to make your way going North up to the very northern tip of Alaska using airports as "save" points as a sort of no save scumming/ironman challenge. The plus side to this is that the routes you can take are so varied that you will probably not see the same scenery twice.
I say that I recommend it because you can do what I do and cruise your local airports and have a lot of fun trying to get more proficient at flying. You can pretend that the time spent in this program is actually training you to operate planes. Whether or not that is helpful to you is a matter of opinion and situation.

This is not your normal flight simulator.
This is nothing like FSX.
And that is a good thing.
This gives you a challenge without many bells and whistles while being extremely accurate and difficult to learn but after you get the hang of it, it is very rewarding.
It also has the tools bundled in so you can create anything and see if it will fly.
Want to make a cat airplane and try to fly it cross country? Go nuts. It might not even get off the ground, but this is not going to stop you from trying without it looking weird.
Want to have a tiny Cessna tug a massive 747 into the air via a small tow rope? Yep, totally possible (this is a easter egg though!) but be ready for a challenge to get out of that dive after you cut that tow rope.
Want to dive from 35 thousand feet then pull out of it last second? You better hope your wings are strong enough because they WILL snap off (if you do not break apart on the way down).
Yes it looks bare but there are plenty of free addons out there that you can install. Some are pretty, others fix things in the core game, while others are crazy user creations.
The simulator is very much a platform for you to improve and make what you want and it will give you a highly accurate flight model with minimal effort on your part.
Yes it might be silly to spend 60 dollars on a simulator. But if you are into flight simulators, it could be the best 60 dollars you could spend.
This is not for everyone. This is for people who want a challenge.

Don't let my small amount of played hours mistaken you, I've spent months over months flying this sim and I still do. So let me start straight from the end - It's the best civil sim right now on the market. BUT IT!

Full disclosure: I'm an actual licensed commercial pilot in Canada. I have about 15 hours of sim time in my logbook, 12 of which were on a commercial and Transport Canada-approved version of X-Plane (the other 3 were on Prepar3D, a version of FSX), and 10 of which applied to my license.
This is a simulator, not a game. You can mess around with the fun fighters and experimental planes, but this is first and foremost a simulator. And what a simulator!
If you're like me, you find fun in a challenging radionav approach. You find fun in managing system failures. You find fun in printing out checklists and having them next to you while handling the simulator. You find fun in education and a job well done. And this is where you get it. You can tweak the simulation accuracy, you can go from messing around doing aerobatics in a fictional plane, or you can turn your garage into a full-sized flight simulator. You can do all this in X-Plane 10, and it has the added bonuses of being more accurate, prettier, and less system-taxing than FSX.
FSX is almost a decade old by now, is a RAM hog, hates graphics cards, is 32-bit, and is still slow and unoptimized. On my machine, it runs terribly. But X-Plane 10 has a 64-bit and 32-bit executable, supports multi-threading, is considerate of your RAM, and looks fantastic.
I spent hundreds of hours with FS2004, FSX, and X-Plane 9. Thanks to them, my instrument and radionavigation training was easy. Thanks to them, I passed the infamous INRAT on my first try. This is a fantastic simulator, simply the best on the market, and the only one worth your money. I can fully recommend this for full price, and I'm a pennypincher.

Lost Interest half way through, It is essentially a walking simulator with little gameplay or challenge. The Story is where this game is supposed to shine.  I will admit, It is well acted and the interactions between the two main characters are well written and does feel like two strangers trying to get along. But the problem I have with these interactions is how the game uses them. The game gives you multiple choice of how you interact with each other so I thought the character and games story would change depending on what your choices were. That is not the case; I found the story and characters were set on one  path from beggining to end with my doing little to no change, It also came to my attention after reading others thoughts on the game that the payoff to the story was disappointing for some and since I was already losing interest I dropped it.
Now gameplay wise well its a walking simulator you walk from point a to point b with no enemies and few obstacles to block your path. What few you do come by. Well. Just push the action button to watch a short preanimated action as your character does said action to get through. Such as Jumping over logs, climbing up small ledges, or using items you find in the game.  All while you walk around looking at your map ( and I mean stopping to look at a map not one in the corner o the screen) to find a certain path you can take to get where you need to be. All while interacting with the other character via walkie talkie about the scenery or whatever.
Speaking of scenery this game is really pretty  sounds great and is beautifully rendered as most walk simulators tend to be. While stylized it definitely gives the feeling of walking through nature. A lot of effort was put into creating this national park landscape from the sound and flow of a stream. To the breeze and movement of grass it does not disappoint on that front. just watch a trailer or look at a screen shot.
In conclusion I would say this game would have been better as an animated movie then a game. With a lot emphasis on the story and visuals, and with no real challenge in gameplay  unless you call getting temporarily side tracked cause of a high ledge or hill challenging. Clocking in at just over 3 hours  for most players. With a $21.99 pricetag  and no replay value since it will play out the same story.  I cannot reccomend this game unless you find it on sale for 5 dollars or less.

It knows there shouldn't be so many explosions, but it lets you know right out of the gate that this is how it is going to be and jokes about it the entire way.
I like the combination of solid action mechanics and platforming.  The addition of difficulty settings helps the cause as well.
Honestly, it is a good thing the game only takes about 6 hours to beat.  If it were any longer it would wear you out and get boring.  It is just long enough to introduce the characters and humor, let you get in some good fights, power up, and then it is done, inviting you to come back later on to try a harder difficulty. What do you get when you cross Darksiders with God of War? The answer is... well, lots of things actually, but Marlow Briggs is perhaps one of the least well-known of the various clones that have spawned as a result of the aforementioned combination. It's a budget title with little in the way of innovation or originality, and its lumpen, cheese-tastic story is nothing to write home about, but in here lurks a fun, respectable, though flawed action game.
Perhaps the best thing about Marlow Briggs is that the action rarely lets up, as it shifts from set piece to set piece, never really giving you a chance to get bored as you deal with waves of enemies by using a variety of combos to slice them to pieces. Throughout the 6-7 hour campaign you're furnished with a number of new weapons and magic powers, all of which are then upgraded via XP that you earn from kills and pick-ups. Along the way you'll find plenty of health and mana pick-ups too, helping you to replenish your stock ahead of the next big fight. It's a relatively simple system, and the combos aren't too difficult to master, though you'll probably stick to a couple of good ones and use those throughout. Along the way you'll be taking out human enemies, insects and spirits, along with a few boss battles to spice things up, and all with a smooth, easy-to-learn control scheme.
Honestly, I was really enjoying Marlow Briggs up until around the halfway mark, where the game then insists on giving you incredibly tanky enemies that take far too long to kill, artifically increasing the difficulty and the length of the game in doing so. As fun as it was to slice and dice my way around, I felt like the tanky enemies began to detract from the enjoyment of the game, with spirit creatures that disappear every few seconds, forcing you to spend longer running around as you slice away at them until they finally go down. I began to get frustrated with some of the enemy encounters in the second half of the game, though unlocking some weapons and powers did help to satisfy my desire to finish out the game. These encounters won't kill the appeal of the game for you, but they might make the last few hours of it less palatable.
It's hard not to recommend Marlow Briggs at just £4. You're getting a decent game, and you may even improve the experience a tad by dropping the difficulty level down to Casual (I played on Normal), where the tankier enemy encounters that pop up constantly in the second half might be a bit more tolerable. I was impressed that the game has a bit of gusto, and though I encountered a few bugs and glitches, it was a smooth experience overall. There's a bit of humour and self-awareness to the whole thing, and the game never takes itself too seriously. Oh and James Hong is in it, and he's pretty much playing Lo Pan from Big Trouble in Little China again. So if that's not going to sell you on it, I'm not sure anything will!

My first personal thoughts on this game, are thusly: plenty of potentail and totally awesome! So far, I'm loving where this game is going and I can't wait to watch it develope. Just to make this a little easy and not a jumbled up mess I'm going to comment in category.
Design/textures/graphics/art: It may not have realistic graphics, but I, in a way, prefer that with a game like this. It gives a very nice smooth, technologic feel to the city and the characters, and it really gets me in a video game mood, so to say. I'm sure the graphics will update over time, but at the moment, developing those are the least of anyone's worries. There are plenty of amazing games who's graphics never even needed to be developed for people to be content with the game, and I have a feeling this game is going to be like that.
Controls: Now, I playing my controller, not a keyboard, so keep that in mind. On my USB xbox controller, it handles very well. All I really had to do was turn the sensitivity way up to fit my likings. I like the preset controls and I haven't changed them at all, since they corespond with each other very well. At the moment, two buttons are able to do the same action with a few things, but I have a feeling that won't be a thing once more abilities for parkour (which I will talk about a few times in this) are available.
Free roam: The free roaming in this game is really, really fun, and completely open from what I've expereinced so far. Obviously there are plenty of places not availble since the game is still in alpha, and I respect and can't wait to watch them open up one by one or however the developers decide to go with that. There isn't all that much your character can do, and I don't mean that in a bad way since I know this is early access, but I will get more on that.
Parkour/character abilities: I really like the parkour aspect here, and you can even upgrade your character's abilities. I'm hoping then add more to the parkour as the game goes on. There have been plenty of parkour like games (Assassian's Creed and Mirror's Edge are two examples) and I feel that this game has potential to up the parkour gaming experience with parkour challenges and objectives, and the complete open world ability given to you.
Customization of your character: For an alpha version of a game, there's a good amount of customization. You unlock characters as you, and you can choose your height and colors. I'm sure there will more as the game is developed but for where it is at the moment, I'm eagerly content with the customization.
Music: I know the music is limited at the moment, but, I also know that they plan to work on getting more tracks, and more, so to say, professionaly done tracks. The current music is pretty upbeat, catchy, and definately something that does NOT annoy me to hear through the game. I'm happy with it and it suits the game currently very well.
Reccomendations and ideas: I have many of these, and I hope they will help if seen. One is more parkouring abilities if possible, such as grabbing onto and shuffles across ledges, grabbing onto and swinging from poles, climbing up poles, and things like that. Another thing I would like to see is more customization for your character. Clothing, hairstyle, things like that, but they still use the unlockable templates like they use now. Each character has their own set of clothing and styles and things like that.
A bonus I really like about this game is the 1st and 3rd person POVs. I really like those, especially when doing front flips and backflips in first person, THAT'S really fun and really cool to do. I never really see too many games who take the first person and actually make it like you're doing a back/front flip. It's a bit disorenting at first, but, it's realistic and really makes you feel into the game when you do it. The first person POV in this game is so well done so far and I really, really love it.
I have high hopes for this game and I'm eager to see what it developes into. I have yet to try the multiplayer personally, since I'm more of a single-player gamer, but I'll give a hit at it soon enough. I really enjoy this game, even with it's currently limitations. I defininently recommend this game and I'm incredibly glad I decided to get it!
I apologize for any grammer and spelling mistakes made in this review.

OUTDATED REVIEW!!!
Alright, let me get this out of the way, I am having a ton of fun with this game so far. It's a very colorful, very cool looking, and a very fun game to play. The game gives you freedom to platform and parkour all over (half) a city, with option to do missions (be it races or taking a thing and throwing it into a thing into another thing) to level up and increase the stats of what your character can do. The controls are pretty responsive (I'm playing on a Xbox One controller), it's a bit slippery, but it works because it gives the feeling of momentum, and tells you to slow down if you want to make a good turn or not fall off a building. This game is still in Early Access, and really there are way worse games out there that are in the same catagory, so this feels more complete than other games of its nature.
So it saddens me to say that I cannot really recomend people to pay $20 for the game just yet, or if you do, pay attention to what I have to say so you know what you're getting into. While you can attribute to the game being in Early Access (alpha state), then it's most important that I state these flaws now so the devs can improve on the game before it can be considered a full legit game. Also just because it's in early access doesn't mean I can't criticizes it. I payed $20 on this game, I can state the flaws of the product if I want to, plus I have 4+ hours in this game.
-No story: The game technically has a story, but it's pretty shallow and doesn't really move forward at all. You are a guy and you wake up in a... place. You are told by some other teens that games have been taken away by the government empire society yadayadayada. It's pretty meh, but it can be presented as fun or tounge in cheek, but it seems a bit half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ The 3 members of the revolution are cool looking characters themselves, and each have something of a personality, but it's all told through in game chat boxes with images of the characters. Then some other characters show up with no context and say things, and leave. Really, it seems like the story needs something, like to be there.
-Bad FPS: FPS being frames per second. The game has no FPS cap, but from my experience, it's highest is maybe 40. It could be my computor, but the Frame Rate drops considerdably down a lot, to as low as 15 or 10, and with this speedy game, that is a not good thing. Not good at all.
-Shallow parkour: The gameplay feels a bit shallow. And by bit I mean a lot. The game is pretty fluid, jumping from wall to wall is good, parkouring all around feels nice, BUT it's basic. And the game has a focus on parkouring, it's in the tag! Other then sliding and jumping for tricks, and super hopping after falling for 167 feet from the air and pressing jump, the game feels like it needs more before it gets pretty stale and repetitive. You can do tricks in the air, but that's just pressing a button, posing, and not much happening. I remember the KickStarter having points in the gameplay, which would have actually made the game feel more fun (like the style meter in the DMC games) but because it's not there, there doesn't seem to be any reward for doing cool stuff other than for the sake for it. And really, this game needs some fun tricks, like pole spinning, or car balancing, or something, anything.
-Repetitive missions: I said earlier that there are missions, and I only gave 2 examples. That's because that's the only type of missions of the game. Racing is racing, though there is 3 different types of it. V1 is racing by yourself agaisnt the clock. V2 is you against an AI opponent. V3 is you against someone online. Go through checkpoints, 3 laps, done. They are good in that you have to be clever in figuring out short cuts or how to get to the next point faster, but it's still just racing. The other type is taking an object called the gamerball, which looks like a fat gamecube, and tossing it into an X. You can't do tricks, and you can get lost by following the arrow because stuff can be in the way of the objective. There's also this flying droid that sometimes follows you and shocks you for you to drop the gamerball. It hinders the mission already because what else do I need in a mission where it's easy to get lost in, a droid that makes me drop the maguffin.
-Focus too much on online: The game is obvious to be making you go play online with other people and do stuff, which may explain why the game feels so MMO in it's story approch. You are generic guy, here is noob tube, you train, you out of tube, bye-bye! And honestly, being online feels pretty shallow.  Usually people are doing their own thing since there is no real encouragement to go do stuff with other players other than... nothing. So because of this, there seems to be a lack of single player offline care.
-$20: It's too pricy right now honestly. For $20, I could of gotten a few games off Steam or GOG or PSN or Origin or Wii U or Xbox Live, go out to see a movie with snacks, buy a cool toy, save up for something special, get a magizine subcription, buy some books. Basically get something complete instead of something not even finished.
-Color pallet: If you love/hate orange and blue contrast, you'll love/hate this game. This game presents itself as a colorful throwback to the Sega Dreamcast days, where games were full of color and life. But this game does the cheap orange/blue contrast trick that movies and games trying to be movies do now-a-days. Jet Set Radio did not do the orange/blue trick, it used a nice pallet to give the player something nice and unique to look at. This game sadly does not look unique because of this orange/blue choice.
-Lifeless citizens: Holy heck these citizens barely do anything, other than walk. And call me a racist if you want, but they all look the same.
-No real threats: Remember the flying shock droid I mentioned earlier? Yeah, he's your only threat, other than cameras that make laser walls that not allow you to go through coridiors, even if you can and will find ways around them. I'm supposed to be part in a team of gaming freedom fighters, but never do I feel like I am one since I never fight anything, or at least GTFO myself away from baddies (like in Jet Set Radio, the game that influenced this game a lot, other than Mirriors Edge, which also had enimies).
-Not enough music: Even though this game got some help by the composer of Jet Set Radio, Hideki Naganuma, there is only 2 tunes in this game so far. Basic world music, and racing music. And honestly, it doesn't sound like his style of music. Compare the music in this game to JTS or Sonic Rush, it just sounds way different. Also the 2 tracks have already gotten repetitive. Maybe an ingame radio would be nice, to cycle through songs and stuff.
-Level cap too low: Just 10, and I have like 4 or 5 different types of areas I can upgrade, of which 3 points is the highest I can give to each. I'm gonna focus on certain aspects of the charcter growth over others, and be done with it quick, and regret my desicion later.
-World layout is forgetable: While it looks nice, the game doesn't really have too many places you can say is memorable, other than the rusty metal shack looking places that are next to each other attacheted to the walls and each other through stuff, and the slime waterfall. This is a huge issue for me, because you can get lost easy in this game, and look as if you're going circles everywhere. This game needs more visually more reconizable local, pinpoints that can make you go "oh, I remember that place, I know where I am!"
-Online issues: It could just be me, but after the most recent update, I can't seem to get online. My wi-fi has been acting not goot recenlty though, so it could just be me.
This game has great potential to be one of the most fun and unique parkour games out there to date (what few there are though), but it also can screw that up badly if it doesn't fix these issues ASAP.

Dead State Reanimated has a lot of heart. But I only recommend this title to people with a lot of time and patience on their hand. Dead state combine several types of games into one. It is fascinating to build a community and fill it with survivors of the zombie apocalypse. It is awesome to explore the numerous characters backgrounds and affect how they continue their stories under your leadership. You also get a fleshed out RPG experience, where you get to equip and level up as you go along. Exploration is also done quite well, in that you explore the surroundings around your little community, to find resources, allies and an abundance of enemies to kill. There are a certain beauty to the turn based fighting mechanics, which is done on painstakingly designed locations, which each tell a tale of the zombie apocalypse. There are small random encounters as well, but even those are also quite varied and unique in nature. This is truly where the game shines, as every place you visit will bring a new setting to explore. You even get to collect snippets of the events leading up to the apocalypse, which together tells a rather fleshed out and chilling tale of how society broke down, from numerous points of view.
Sadly this game is not without its flaws. Most prominently, it shows that there wasn't enough man hours to make this game truly stand out in its genre. I really liked that there is a larger story in Dead State, which leads to several endings, depending on what resources you have collected, and how you have interacted with survivors on the map. But the pacing of this story isn't working very well, and it is rather glaring that the development of your survivors storyline simply stop after a couple of weeks in the community. You are also likely to run out of places to explore, on the map, long before the ending comes around. The same goes for projects in your community which simply grinds to a halt. I feel like the developers intended to flesh out this part of the game too, but never got around to it. It is obvious that there were plans for more endings, which was sadly cut out. And the endings we were left with really should have given us more than they did. Basically, this game would have been far better if it had ended around its halfway point. I played this game on the highest difficulty, which should have forced me to make hard choices on where my resources and skill points would be placed, while I struggled to get to one of the endings.
All in all I enjoyed this game. I would definitely buy an expansion, if it came with: More fleshed out dialog and character development. More locations, specifically locked away, until the late game, along with more types of advanced enemies and maybe a bunch of boss battles. More projects to explore along with more ways and choices to improve the community. Make the hardest difficulties a struggle to complete. But most importantly, make the endings more engaging as well as better fleshed out.

Dead State offers a pretty unique combination of turn-based tactical RPG battles (along the lines of Fallout 2, Jagged Alliance, XCom, etc.), exploration, and base/resource/personnel management that makes me strongly recommend this game. It scratches an itch that few other games get near. A good comparison would be to imagine XCom if it had much more primitive, clunky, unpolished combat, but more more involved base management and open-world exploration.
Pros:
+ The game bills itself as an "apocalypse simulator" and it delivers on this. Rather than going off in a sci-fi direction with the zombie apocalypse, the game is almost disturbing realistic is how people interact with each other and the problems you face. Your main threat (after the first few days) isn't the zombies at all but looters, biker gangs, rogue soldiers, decent people willing to do anything to survive, and even your own party members. In addition, you gradually find little "data items" throughout the game which gradually reveal the backstory of the apocalypse. Once again, it is almost disturbingly realistic in terms of how people really act.
+ The presence of both zombies and hostile humans in missions offers the possibility some interesting tactics like luring zombies into attacking your enemies. Also, you never quite know what you will find when you go out exploring.
+ If you like management games, you'll like how you have to worry about your base's food, fuel, morale, interpersonal relationships, and many other things that you need to keep your eye on for your base to keep going. Resources are scarce (at times), and you'll definitely be agonizing over certain decisions. This is often the aspect of games like this that gets cut for the sake of making a more exiciting action-oriented game, but I like having the management aspects there.

Cons:
- A lot of things about the UI, controls, and information displays could have been done better. It feels a bit like the 80s when you realize you've got to have a sheet of paper or spreadsheet handy to keep track of which locations you've explored and where you've left some resources that you couldn't carry home. You'll have some frustrating moments where you accidentally throw a grenade at the wrong enemy or accidentally bandage an ally who doesn't need it due to the clunky controls. You'll be grumbling over how clunky and time-consuming it is to manage your base's inventory and equip your party members. These things sometimes make the game feel like a beta version that should have gotten a full makeover before release.
- The game starts to stall out in the mid-game when you are well-equipped enough that zombies are no threat and you get to the point of just wandering around exploring random locations, and most of the time you don't find anything interesting that you haven't seen before. I can't complain too much about this, though, because it took me dozens of hours of play before I got to this point.
- There are a few small things that are very frustrating in how they were implemented. For example, there is a crafting system to make ammo, but the resources required are absurdly high. Another example is that your main character (who represents the player) has to go on every single mission and is not permitted to heal/craft/build at the base while others go out exploring--effectively meaning you *must* make a combat-oriented character. These kinds of things can detract from both realism and gameplay.

Here's my bottom line opinion on Republic Commando; it's the second-best Star Wars first-person shooter. Just below Dark Forces. It has the unfortunate distinction of being the best game to come out of the prequel trilogy, and doesn't escape the taint of the prequel's legacy. I may even like the ideas behind Republic Commando more than I like the game itself.
Here is what sucks about Republic Commando: the weapons sound weak, and there aren't many different enemies to fight. So what does Republic Commando do right? The intro to the game is great. It details where you and your squad came from, all from the first person perspective. In fact, this game takes a page from Half-Life in that the entire game is played from the first-person perspective. There are a couple of scenes where you are not in control of your character, but they're limited.
The squad AI is not smart but it's competent. They'll kill enemies, heal themselves, heal you when you drop, take cover, etc. There are certain set pieces that you can order a squadmate to take position at for a specific purpose (like sniping or anti-armor) and they're meant to be used. Your squad dies less when they're in one of these ordered positions. The squad also has fantastic vocal banter. Each member is a personality, and I got attached to them as the game went along.
Though the levels are a little cookie cutter, there are plenty of objectives to them and no lack for fights. I was fighting in corridors, in small courtyards and hangers, on multi-level starship bridges, and in trees. They're not as varied as Dark Forces, but each environment is well made.
And now I can get to what stops this from being a great game. They can fix the sound effects and toss in a couple more enemies, but it's harder to change the setting. Republic Commando takes place at the onset of the Clone Wars. It starts on Geonosha even. And though it takes place over a two (three?) year span, it could have gone farther. This was a pre-Episode 3 game and it shows. It feels like a teaser leading up to Episode 3 and, ultimately, suffers for that. It doesn't deserve to be timely movie release fodder. It deserves to be treated like a game that can stand on its own two legs. Something that can be taken out of the context of the prequel release. It doesn't deserve to be lumped in with Episode 1 Racer, Star Wars Starfighter, Bounty Hunter, Obi-Wan, or any other godawful prequel game.
It doesn't carry the same tone as those games. The developers did their damnedest to give this game a fair chance. They go out of their way to make  you know that you are playing an elite soldier. You're no jedi, and you're not fodder either. You see your share of ally deaths and the Clone War takes its toll. But you're fighting bugs on Geonosha. And battle droids, even if they're way more menacing than they ever were in the prequel movies. They may bleed oil, wear a metallic gray paint job (rather than the orange seen in the movies), and the super battle droids may be some tough ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, but they're still battle droids, which are inherently lame. There's a pitiful tie in with General Grieveous in the form of his bodyguards, which flip and hop around like acrobats, with electric sticks. They're not threatening in the slightest, more annoying than anything, and serve only to give General Grieveous an excuse to make an unwarranted appearance.
What I'm getting down to is that in Republic Commando you are playing, in essence, a proto super stormtrooper. I wish the devs would've been allowed to run with that rather than get tied to the time frame that stuck them between the two prequel movies. I hope we can get another Republic Commando game, but I'm not expecting it. This franchise has legs that get cut out from beneath it by the movies it was made to support.

This game was one of the first FPS action RPGs, a genre shared by classics such as Deus Ex and Vampire Bloodlines. Released in 1996, Strife pushed the limits by offering a FPS that didn't involve shooting everything sight. In fact, it was well possible to screw up your game having to start all over by doing something you weren't supposed to.
The Veteran Edition does its best to bring Strife into the 21st century, luckily. As revolutionary as the game was in 1996, it still had quite a few flaws including only having a single save game. In a game where it's possible to make a wrong move and only finding out half an hour later, this was painful so due to the Veteran Edition having several save games, it starts off by eliminating the biggest flaw of the original.
Another annoyance from the first game, was its vague mission parameters combined with maze-like locations (like the sewers). While you have a detailed map, you could still get lost for ages. The Veteran Edition helps you out by marking quest locations - another welcome improvement.
Besides these gameplay tweaks, you have the standard graphic and control improvements including fluent mouse look, bloom, higher resolution graphics, proper shading, etc.
While Strife won't blow your socks off if you compare it to modern games, it's still a rare gem. Back in the day, it wasn't even that well known and has become a cult classic but it's really worth a look for any games enthusiast.

This is an overlooked gem.
I picked this up in a steam sale with no prior knowledge and I have to say it really impressed me. Firstly, I know this game was made for a relatively modest budget but the production values are up there with AAA titles. Graphics are very well done, animations, lighting and textures are impressive & it runs silky smooth. Its very solid with no noticable bugs and its obvious a lot of craft and care has gone into making this game as fun as possible.
The premise is that its a (up to) four player, coop 3rd person shooter. As the title suggests the main antagonists are Nazi Zombies. The obvious comparisons to make are to Call of Duty: Black Ops coop nazi zombie mode and Left for Dead.
While it borrows elements from each it does very much have its own ideas and its own character but if I was summarising it to a friend I would say its COD's zombies in Left for Dead style open levels.
Levels are well designed and although quite linear they do give options for paths to take and for cover and at key points require teamwork and strategy from the coop players with enemies coming in multiple directions. The main weapon of choice is the sniper rifle and this adds an interesting game mechanic. Getting a headshot is immensly satisfying but when enemies start getting in close you can switch to a closer range weapon but ammo for these guns is in short supply. It really makes you think about each shot and makes things very tense when your in danger of getting overwhelmed.
Sniper Elites party piece is there and is a gory and fun idea in a similar vein to Mortal Kombat's fatalities. When you get a certain kind of shot you get treated to a slow motion, xray view of the bullet passing through the body, causing horrendous damage to internal organs and bones. Even after a lot of play it can still be very satisfying to watch after a good shot.
If you and some friends have played Left for Dead to death and want something new and a bit different and a hell of a lot of zombie blasting fun I recommend giving this a go. Im looking forward to grabbing to sequel soon as well

This game allows you the freedom to build whatever your mind can imagine not just slap down pre-made cookie cutter buildings etc.   You can do anything from create a small dwelling, a magnificent castle, a village or an entire city, not to mention have fun along the way mining, gathering, crafting, etc.
I specifically like the ability to work on a project with friends because a team effort and shared vision can result in much more amazing results than any one single individual is likely to come up with alone.  I also like that the game is mod-able and from what I hear from modders it is improving on the code & backbone that allows modders to create better mods & with greater ease.  Take this game & add the available mods from awesome community workshop content put them together and spend some time you can make very detailed life like realistic projects quickly in creative or simulate living the experience in survival.  Like all games it has room for improvement but unlike many that are left stagnant and lost by the wayside the company is making progress and advancing this game forward at a reasonable pace.   This game already ranks in my mind as one of the most enjoyable I have ever played, and has extreme potential for improvement especially if they continue to work on improving mod support & giving modders and players tools, content, and optoins they need.
I will for the sake of providing a balanced & fair review mention a few of the weaknesses or “cons” of the game but since it is a early access game and the company is making an honest effort to progress the product I will not list every flaw or deficit.   One thing the game is lacking a world generator tool so you have a few map scenarios to choose from and that is it unless you get a mod that changes the map.  Biomes are great but on such a small planet can be somewhat unrealistic still & it would be nice to be able to choose a more randomized set of biomes or specific type of terrain for your project or servers needs.    While not as big of deal to me personally because I am currently enjoying building more than fighting, the combat system is still greatly lacking and if you start lobbing projectiles into a building even on the best of server’s things are going to get real funky.   Another thing that will jump out at you right away as missing is animals, there is... "deer" but no horses, donkeys, pigs, cattle, chickens, etc. which are just to glaringly obviously void in the world.
This game is worth every cent you'll pay for it in my opinion and will provide you with many hours of enjoyment single player, multiplayer, creative, survival, let your mind lose to create.

It's not kidding... what you see is what you get (and I have yet to find anything else).
I know they said you can get additional content for the game, but I am having the hardest time finding anything. On the X-Plane’s site, I find options to purchase X-Plane and the USB key… That is all; otherwise, I am just stuck with one skin for my plane. I absolutely LOVE the United 747 (but you’re just suck with that one 747 as an example)  =’(
Okay, so firstly, the graphics, the actual physics of the plane (micro stuff), and the lack of lag are AMAZING (All the things FSX lacks). I have a decent gaming PC, and despite some patches of “not responding” during loading time, the game runs quite fluidly on very high-detail settings.
However, the controls SUCK, the realism SUCKS, and I have yet to find the multi-player (if it exists). Many of the planes I have tried to fly are buggy, or just do not work at all. Like the space shuttle for example, it is not even running on the runway when it spawns, so I tried to add fuel, and it will not even let me do that. Some planes feel like they are loaded to capacity by bricks, meanwhile others are tossed around like toys by the controls. To be honest, I’m terrified that they train real pilots off this game. The controls are never precise and it feels like I’m flying the plane willy-nilly on my tablet.
The X-Plane (Liminar Research) folks need to get together with the Microsoft folks and they could make a TRULY AMAZING game! With X-Plane’s graphics and Microsoft’s UI + Realism, I’d be more than happy to pay a hefty sum for that game.
The user-interface in X-Plane is not user friendly at all. You have to clamor through a whole ton of menus with high hopes that you understand the geek-language and manually set your joystick buttons. I have a joystick, throttle quadrant, and a set of rudder-pedals. I had to manually program ALL the buttons and axes for the game. Personally, I was able to accomplish this part with slight stress, but I feel it would be almost impossible for the average person who is new to flight simulators.
During flight, it is as if the game “forgets” some of my pre-programmed buttons and usually replaces it with something random. The “Lights” button becomes a “Pan-Left” button for example.
At the end of the day, it is as if the game just does whatever it wants. I was en-route to an airport and I wanted to check the map (to see where I was). BEWARE OF MIS-CLICKS!! I clicked “global map” instead of “local map” and all of a sudden, I was in a different aircraft at some RANDOM airport. There is no warning message for things like this, but tons of warning messages for the scenery that you have to spontaneously know how to download as DLC vs. coming with the game as it should. The redeeming quality is that the DLC comes free with the game, YAY.
I am still new to X-Plane, but I have been playing flight simulators for over 10 years, and I "like" this game, but feel VERY disappointed by it!

Have been waiting a while to buy this on steam (heard a bit back that it was supposed to be coming and I had played on an earlier version many years ago), very glad I bought it, not only is it a realistic simulator with a ton of control configuration options (it might all seem a little daunting at first, but persevere) but I am getting great pleasure out of learning to fly with Xplane...
At the time of writing this review I have just done my first proper fight on Xplane 10 from Blackpool (EGNH) to Manchester (EGCC) - not a long flight (chose the route as these are local locations) but after earlier sims which basically gave you heading waypoints and large visual clues after clicking on a destination this was much more challenging. Used the VOR system to navigate to Manchester, during the flight Xplane taught me how several of the instruments worked that I glossed over playing previous flight simulators on PC.
With my plane drifting a little to the left I had to correct my heading a few times (by a small amount) but eventually arrived at my destination. No clue how to use the local air traffic controllers (yet) I just picked a runway and landed...
Learnt quite a bit from that hour playing the game and I can see it teaching me a lot more, I used to love flight-sims and played a lot but this game made me feel a complete novice again (especially after so long not playing any sims). However lack of arcade-game style assists, popup help and hand-holding made me feel like I really accomplished something in the game when I finally touched down. Been a while since I both enjoyed a game and felt like I achieved something.
Worth the asking price? For me yes :)
edit: I have added some comments to this review, including a very short version of how I used VOR to navigate, system specs and controllers being used.
