Describing Marlow Briggs to someone would be easy. It’s an over the top, in your face action and comedic hack and slash. I definitely enjoyed my playthrough of it.
You play as Marlow, trying to save your girlfriend, Eva, after she is taken hostage to decipher some ancient codices. I was quite surprised with the range of environments that you are taken through. They are nicely done too and feel full and rich.
An odd thing to point out, but I will. The game sets up the “camera” to be the Mask of Death following you around. Or at least that’s how I interpreted it. Reminded me of how Mario 64 implied the Lakitu Brothers were “filming you” during gameplay.
Since we are on the camera, there is a love/hate relationship with it. The camera is FIXED and you cannot control it. This can, and is, used to hide secrets and extra experience points that are out of view until you explore a little. Generally, it’s good and doesn’t get in the way. But on occasion, especially during battle, it will not let you see where the enemy is. It also tended to lag behind if I started moving too fast. The multiple rope swinging segments are brought to mind where this happened. In the end, it wasn’t too much of a nuisance.
Marlow Briggs is extremely linear. I don’t mind this at all in games, but I know this is a personal preference. There are invisible walls everywhere and you cannot explore much outside your destined path. I say can’t explore “much” because you can go in little crevices and off camera areas that give you experience. It definitely rewards you for doing what little exploring you can.
Controls feel relatively tight during combat and responsive during the many platforming segments.
It was released on the 360 and it shows. The mouse and keyboard controls are awkward and I immediately switched to a controller. The game switches seamlessly between the two, which is appreciated.
Marlow can upgrade and acquire a few more weapons and magic powers throughout the playthough. You can switch quickly and easily between them for whatever situation you’re in. I tended to stick with the weapon that was on a chain for a majority of the game after I acquired it. It’s the only ranged weapon and felt the most safe using it. It was also easy to break out of a combo and dodge an enemy attack. The magic powers are visually cool, but consistently felt underpowered. They were expensive to use (Mana) and would usually not even kill the smaller enemies. I wish they were quite a bit more powerful or used less Mana.
Saving is spectacular. Tons of auto-saves and you can save manually at any point. I always love to see this in games.
Graphically the game is quite good! I found myself taking a lot of screenshots because of the really nice looking environments I was in. However, there are NO graphics options to play around with. You get to choose your resolution and if it’s full screen or not. That’s it…
Sound and music is good. I felt some of the epic songs got tired since they were used a lot during the cut scenes.
Let’s get to the Pros and Cons
+Awesome, over the top action. All the explosions you could ask for
+Nice graphics
+Great auto and manual save system
+Controls feel good (use a controller to play!)
+Fantastic variety of environments
+Solid variety of enemies. (Possessed enemies are recycled)
+Weapon combos are cool
+Good game length. Not too short or long.
+Rewarded for the small amount of exploring you can do
+60fps throughout

+No graphics options?! (Just resolution and full screen toggle)
+Magic powers felt weak, cost too much Mana
+Puzzles could be more challenging
+Camera at times can be frustrating
+Slightly repetitive
Worth the $5 asking price and a “must buy” if it’s on some type of sale or in a bundle. I had a great time playing Marlow Briggs. The gripes I had are easily overlooked by the crazy action everywhere.

WayForward is an impressive developer, taking up bigger jobs to fund their own series is admirable, and you can tell they put in the love and effort the games deserve. I cannot wait for the next game in the series, while diverging from a pixel animated art style to a full on digital, it still looks impressive. 20$ is asking just a bit too much however, as this game has nothing more to give after completing the game 100% (aside from the achievements for my fellow achievement freaks). Do give this game a try though, WayForward deserves more praise than they get, you won't regret putting time into this game.

Dead State is a turn-based RPG in the tradition of Wasteland and the early (isometric) Fallout games.
It's not a game for everyone. Actually it's a game unlikely to steal anybody's heart in its current state, but it is impressive in some regards and definitely has potential. There is a core fanbase that would like to see a sequel or rather a remake.
To start with the bad: the game's graphics are primitive, and the engine it's built on, the Torque 3D, was already a bit long in the tooth even when they started. Furthermore the game is repetitive, buggy, has performance issues and is hard, especially for players who are not familiar with the Wasteland style of combat.
So why do some people keep playing -- get hooked so to speak, once they have started?
I think it's primarily the way the game engages the player. It does a much better job of this than for instance Wasteland 2, whose absurdist setting makes you feel detached rather than involved, and whose often obnoxious npc's leave you wondering why the hell you bother trying to help them. Apparently because it's your duty or something.
Deadstate doesn't have this problem.
In spite of the fantastical setting of a Zombie apocalypse, the characters are very relatable. You are a survivor of an airplane crash (the pilots got overwhelmed by the infected) and you find shelter with a few other survivors in a local school. You need to repair the fence, find food and fuel for the generator and most importantly you need to keep up morale.
You can assign tasks for the people to repair or build things, like a recycler, a well, a workshop, a roof garden and so on. Gradually you become more and more self-sufficient. You can find new survivors to strengthen your workforce, but you also have to manage their conflicts and deal with crisis events, and maintain your authority.
You can lead a scavenging party of max 4 to find resources and contacts outside the shelter. Zombies are everywhere, and you are in constant danger of being swarmed by them, and even have your people bitten and infected. You may also find armed looters, gangbangers, hostile survivalists, rogue soldiers, and demoralized police on your path.
Right from the start you slip into the role of provider and protector, a difficult but also deeply satisfying one. You feel a real responsibility toward the people who have been entrusted to your care. You feel good when you manage to bring home some fresh fruit or medication for them. And they can also drive you up the wall. Sound familiar?
The graphics and sound effects may be basic, they are nevertheless well-made, expressive and effective.
The game is quite suspenseful, and I can recommend it with the caveat that this game can

Definitely a buy for any 2D-platformer enthusiast, sale or no sale. Action-packed from start to finish with satisfying upgrades that changes Shantae's moveset to allow for some tricky platforming towards the end of the game.

"Shantae and the Pirate's Curse" is the latest and best game released of the Shantae series (so far). Join Shantae as she teams up with the pirate Risky Boots to stop the spread of an ancient curse. Use various pirate equipment and sail on a pirate ship as you explore several islands in Sequin Land. Battle monsters, upgrade weapons and search labyrinths for rare treasures and items.
Like the previous installment, the game stands out with great music, beautiful art, solid controls, lovable characters and a memorable story that never takes itself too seriously. Note that it has more content than the previous games, including an unlockable "Pirate Mode", multiple endings and enough achievements to challenge even hardcore players. The only significant flaw is the lack of transformation magic (and sexy dances) due to the events of the previous game.
I highly recommend "Shantae and the Pirate's Curse" to anyone who enjoys platformers like Castlevania or Metroid. Definitely look forward to the release of the next Shantae game!

You play one match, you've played them all. Pandemic works as a Flash game because it's simple, and casual. You wouldn't play more than a few games at once for a while. It requires a little more strategising and long-term thinking than most Flash games and that's what makes it appealing. It has just enough different options to keep things interesting - viruses, bacteria, etc. and the dice roll of your starting location means you have to tweak you approach a little every time you play. There's a satisfaction in seeing your disease spread across the globe, a list of eerie real-time news updates lets you quietly revel in the devastation of your manuafactured contagion and the actions the country AIs take in response force you to adapt quickly - adding tension and keeping your head in the game.
Plague Inc. takes this simple formula and... does nothing with it, except maybe break it. It adds a strange mechanic where you can click on random bubble pop-ups to gain DNA (used to upgrade/evolve your disease) or smash vials to stall research. Why is this in the game? Not only is there no challenge since the pop-ups are harder to miss than to click even at full speed, you can also pause the game and click on them at your own leisure, even once they've begun to shrink away. Mobile game monkey♥♥♥♥♥♥ What am I playing exactly? Am I God? What exactly is clicking on these research bubbles doing in the ingame world? Am I a sentient virus that targets research facilities? It doesn't make any sense and, worse, it isn't fun to do.

I like to call it. . . Cracktorio . . .
[Early Access Review Nov. 11 / 17]
I highly suggest this game to those with OCD tendancies, those that don't mind simple math, enjoy puzzles, and not looking for an in-depth storyline.  This game is as the name and description states; you build factories in order to achieve the end-game goal, which is quite simply:
Launch a rocket into space.
Sounds easy right? WELL YOU MIGHT WANT TO RETHINK THAT! In my first experience the fun really began when I wanted red circuits; well to do that, you need oil.  Build pump jacks to pump out crude oil. Then you need to refine that oil; well now hook up the basic oil refinement process to acheive a 3:3:4 Light, Heavy, and Petroleum output, which will then need to be fed into a chemical plant that can refine the petroleum gases into meldable plastics.  Finally that plastic can now be combined in an assembler with green circuits, copper wire, and said plastic.  Then the first problem occurs, in order to keep pumping petroleum you need to find a use for the light and heavy oil by-products. Otherwise your storage containers will be unable to pump in more petro because there is no where for the oils to go.  Thats plastic for ya. Which overall wasn't that bad. . . especially compared to the nuclear option.
The beauty of this game is the fact that it always gives you something to do.  Theres never a time where you're waiting for something to finish because there is always a problem to solve, minerals to refine, resources to move, and factories to build.  In my first 3 days after purchase I managed to rack up 44 hours of gameplay time.
PROS:
- Highly Optimized, with low recommended specs. And a puny file size. (Less than a Gb)
- Never encountered any major bugs or glitches.
- Active and openly discussive developers
- Intuitive & powerful GUI; simple, elegant, and very useful.
- Brilliantly executed hotkeys, and multikey functions.  I can run, move inventory, and craft items virtually all simultaneously.
CONS:
- VERY ADDICTING; I highly advise lining up the purchase of this game with a weekend as it can easily consume your mind into solving the infinite amount of puzzles the game provides.
- Math-Oriented. Especially with Ratios, learn your ratios!
- No Train Horn (in Vanilla anyways).
- Fluid Wagon attachment (to pumps) is very finicky.
Bottom Line:
I highly recommend this game if you have the patience, time, and motivaton to work with puzzles in a Real-Time sense.  If you enjoyed playing any RTS or Sandbox game then this game will likely appeal to you.
If you want an in-depth story, cut-scenes, and current gen graphics, fast-paced shooter, or RPG.  I would not recommend this game.
Similar Games:
(please note these might be pretty vague similarities, but overall there is some feature or style that is similar)
Minecraft - (circuits, logic gates, & mechanical engineering)
Space Engineers - (creative freedom, sandbox-style building mechanics w/ mining, refinement, and production)
Age of Empires - (mostly graphically.  Although resource management is quite similar)
Cities: Skylines - (power, fluids, pollution, and math-involved)

Strife is extremely underrated and one of the prime examples of why the 90's was the golden era of gaming, while games today may be more visually advanced, they're pretty much all formulaic, bland, dumbed down and generic clones of each other with no soul or depth except for the very rare exception. How did games devolve from this into brown/gray, linear, cinematic slogfests that play themselves?
Strife is an FPS-RPG hybrid which is said to be one of the original games of the like, set in a world ruled by a tyrannous cult known as The Order in which you play part of a rebellion which plots to overthrow them. The game itself plays like a mixture of DooM and Duke 3D with fast paced combat that relies heavily on maneuverability/skill and the missions in Strife are open ended which allow for a lot of freedom and exploration.
This has got to be one of the best looking games I've ever played to this day, it has tons of rich colours and the textures all fit perfectly with each other instead of the monotonous garbage that passes off for games these days that consist only of disgustingly bland mixtures of brown and gray. The sound is great, the weapons feel heavy and powerful and the game is complimented by what has to be one of the most badass soundtracks in gaming.
Strife is definitely worth the 9.99 asking price (currently 7.49 on sale) given that it is a complete masterpiece in every regard. I wish gaming would return to what made it great in the first place but until then I've got plenty of classics like this to play through again.

The original version of this game is one of the few first-person shooters I have in its original big box in my classic game collection shelves – and the reason is simple: it's just overwhelmingly good! Why?
Well, the game was way ahead of its time, back in 1996. Just think of it as a mission-based, story-driven "Doom"-clone with an open world. This description still doesn't do the game full justice, but it's a good way to at least categorize it.
I've re-played the original game during the Christmas holidays in 2010 and thoroughly enjoyed every second of it. The comic-style artwork and the voice acting really reminds me of the style of the classic adventure game "Beneath a Steel Sky", the faction of The Order feels like a high-tech version of the Hammers from the "Thief" trilogy (by the way: "Thief 2014" doesn't exist...) and the open world has a very unique feel to it. It offers a nice opportunity to experiment a bit with choices and outcomes. Getting your secret "underground rebellion missions" via in-ear radio feels really immersive, too!
Thankfully, this updated Veteran Edition doesn't change the original too much. Just a very comfortable new Full HD engine with complete mouse look, high quality textures, dynamic lighting and bloom and a rich variety of options to customize the game to your liking. Oh, and Steam achievements, too.
This was an instant buy – and I wholeheartedly recommend this game!
Go buy it. It's WELL worth the asking price!

(I'll say that firstly I liked Sniper Elite V2, so I had moderate hopes for this title too!)
Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army is a gothic/horror spin on Sniper Elite V2, featuring hordes of the undead and supernatural. You'll encounter standard zombies, special zombies (brute, sniper and speedy) and various monsters such as the 'ever-so-annoying fire creatures'.
The shooting mechanics are just like Sniper Elite V2's, with the performance being just as good too! Your character is still controlled in exactly the same way, no significant changes have been made.
Visual-wise, the characters and world/levels are still highly detailed like Sniper Elite V2's, apart from this time many of the levels have been laid out and altered to appear more Arena-like. This can be a negative at times because the sniping mechanics become less effective at close range. Like the predecessor, the close-range weapons still fail to 'pack a punch' meaning you'll find yourself spraying bullets everywhere every-so-often.
Apart from the changes to the lighting, enemies (& AI) and some new weapons added, the game is still very similar to its predecessor. The Slow-motion, X-ray bullet cams are still there but because the zombies are 'rotting', the textures for the organs and bones have been changed to look more rotten and decaying. And because it's the diablo 3 combat, it's also a lot more casual. You can just log in and play for 15 min as a break to whatever you're doing and then go back and do what you want to do. It's not like some MMOs you'll have to be on for 1-2 hours for a raid.

Wow, where to even begin with this game?
The voice cast is star-studded.  The hero, unsurprisingly named Marlow, is portrayed by Arif Kinchen (aka Pierce from Saints Row), you've also got James Hong (Mr. Ping from Kung Fu Panda), and Steve Blum (Tom from Toonami, and pretty much everything else in existence with a voice actor). The bantor and the comedy is there, even though the game "acts" like it takes itself seriously, more on that in a bit...
I've never played a God of War game, but having seen some gameplay videos from that landmark franchise I can see where the parallels are drawn from.  I played most of my playthrough with a Steam Controller using the default gamepad template Steam offers for all titles and it felt very natural.  I couldn't comment on the keyboard/mouse input as I have yet to give it a chance, but I also played the intro with a 360 controller just fine, so if you have a gamepad laying around you should give it a shot on this title as it has console roots, both mechanic and development wise.
Speaking of development, where in xibalba did this game even come from?  I remember the tweet for the release going live on the official Steam accounts, but prior to that ZootFly was never on my radar.  Even looking into their catalog, Marlow Briggs seems like a diamond in the rough.  The game launched on PC and Xbox 360 as an Arcade title, but sports graphics that would be at home on most AAA console titles from the 360/PS3 era.  There is a decent variety of enemies, with new variations and additions being thrown at you right until the end.  The settings alternate between Mesoamerican ruins that leave you wondering "how the heck did they build something so ginormous?", and humongous industrial complexes/machines that leave you wondering "why the heck did they build something so ginormous?".  The weapons and powers follow an experience based upgrade system, but the game is plenty generous with xp pickups and you usually end up maxing out your new unlocks not too long after receiving them.
The plot, and even in some portions the animation and voice acting can be received in two different ways-
1. So cheesey and jenky that it circles around to become awesome again.
2. Purposefully made super duper cheesey and jenky, which means it was done with just as much heart, so also making it awesome.
I mean, there are scenes where your goal is to "shoot down all the helicpoters" and the game proceeds to throw nearly a 100 choppers at you.  Who has that many choppers on standby?  Who is that 100th chopper that sees the first 99 explode in front of him that says "Ef it, yolo" and continues to come at you guns blazing?  Also there's a scene where you fly a generic prop plane like Xevious and it somehow has the payload capacity for a bunch of heat seeking rockets AND machine guns under the propeller. I know, I know: What. Even.
Either way, I'm not quite sure Zootfly knows what they've got with this franchise but the cliffhangerish ending demands a sequel with just as much over the top action, explosions, and lulzy dialog.

Sven Co-op...Where does one even start...Well lets explain exactly what it is.
Sven Co-op is an engine overhaul for the original GoldSrc engine used for Half-Life 1 that allows users to play any of the Half-Life 1 anthology stories or user created mods or levels with as many people as they want. You ever dreamed about running through the halls of Sector C with 12 other HEVsuits and gmen? You can do it here. You ever wanted to explore the tunnels in Foxtrot Uniform with other Soldiers armed with M60s? Yup! You want to play the horror mods of They Hunger and Afraid of Monsters with friends? Sven Co-op has you covered, you get the idea.
One of the oldest Half-Life 1 mods in exsistance, Sven Co-op has been in development since 1999 and with this steam release comes it's 5.0 version which has added extra functionallity for map creators to toy around with, such as inventory systems to improve map flexibillity and creative oppurtunity. The Mod itself already has so much content to experience, it tweaks weapons, improves animations, custom models, adds some new toys, comes with it's own library of maps for you ready to play and makes some adjustments to the original Half-Life 1, Opposing Force and Blue Shift maps to acommodate for the higher player numbers, meaning that proper cooperation with your crowbar banging fellows is essential to get past some tough situations. Everybody comes equipped with a medkit which allows it's operators to heal injuired team mates or even revive fallen allies to get them back up and running, you can even give ammo to people if they've ran out of shotgun shells.
So many hours of my weekends have been lost to the vast amount of things to do in Sven Co-op, Nights spent laughing with friends at the brutally unforgiving soldier AI who'll murder anybody who thinks they can withstand a squad of the HECU. Evenings of exploring cartoonish comedic maps where you need to stand on pannels that'll flip you supposidly into a wall where instead it'll just gib you, and of course you can never forget scaring that one friend who for some reason agreed to play horror maps late into the early hours of the morning.
Sven Co-op is the king of all Half-Life mods, new maps are released pretty much everyday on the SCmap database with already over 300 unique maps to download and play and with the improvements to the overall engine, you can hopefully expect some even better maps to soon follow. The potential longevity you can get from this is astounding. It's the ultimate party game for fans of the anthology and you can play it entirely free of charge.

Do I think Hover is a bad game? Hell no. If on the fence, do I think you should wait until the game becomes more stable and polished? Yes.
Has massive potential with great mechanics and a colorful, large open world. Solid character customization and is a joy to play - when it works. A mission editor is also there that I have yet to try.
Where it goes wrong is the abysmal optimization. The game runs at a consistant 20 FPS - I was lucky to get 40 at one point. I personally feel that this is not fair to the consumer. If one's game is unstable to the point where there are constant problems - it shouldn't be sold as a $20 game. Crashing and glitches are also frequent. I've only played this for about 20 minutes and have experienced 3 crashes; refusing to play more.
The devs claim all of this will be fixed - and I'm sure it will be. If you are willing to wait a little to snatch the game 15% off, I'd say buy it. If you aren't that invested into it yet - wait for the much needed pass.
One of the more disappointing Early Access games out right now.
Hover will be a great game - but it will take time.

I approach a race point, my palms are sweaty, and am a little intimidated by the Gamers around me. My HUD pulls up their Experience levels, 2 are max level (10) and the 3rd is a level 9, I'm level 8 not too far behind the others. They are all waiting for me at the start line waiting for me to scan into the race, I do it. The countdown meter begins 3.....2.....1.....We all begin to run, dashing through the neon flashing streets of Hover City, grinding on rails, flipping through traffic, leaping over pedestrians, human, alien, tentacle-man, robogirl, it didn't matter I had only one thing on my mind...to win. I grinded a rail to catch up to the level 9 that was zooming ahead of me, as i gain on her, I cartwheel over her to switch to another rail, and grind through the checkpoint. As i zoom past the lvl9 my HUD plays a sound cue....HoverHeat is activated. The bright blue neon lights on my character glow even brighter, the light trails following my shoes are even stronger, my grind speed gets even faster, I leap off of the rail and dash through Hover traffic leaving, dazed drivers and streaks of beautiful blue behind me. I have the two lvl10s in my sight fighting for 1st place...they had no clue I was coming. I peek at the top right of my HUD and it displays that there is only one checkpoint left, it was now or never. As i round a corner, right on the Red and Green light trails that the lvl10s left behind, a FlyBox manufactured HoverTruck is speeding towards me.."Is this it?" I think.
No.
I slide mid-run, and begin to build up HoverHeat.."Cmoonnnnn" I beg as the Truck gets even closer. The Sound Cue plays, with a split second left,  I leap forward, over the FlyBox truck, and stylishly perform a trick, to maintain my HoverHeat. The lvl 10s had noticed me and look back, amazed with my near-death escape, in fact so amazed they don't see the other HoverTruck in front of them. The Truck knocks the two Veteran Gamers away in an instant and I quickly steal first place from the both of them and fly throught the  Final Checkpoint with the level9 10secs behind me.
Jay Wins, my HUD displays.
In the bottom right corner, a chatbox pulls up and displays a message from one of the lvl10s, Minimumu.
"Great Race!" it reads.
I am a Gamer, and I live to Level.

I don't think I have anything good to say about this "game". I say “Game” because it plays itself more than I do. As a game with a story entirely built on the choices you make (at least on the surface level) you'd expect your choices to have weight. Unfortunately, that is NOT the case. I've played through the game 6 times now taking careful note to play the game as differently as I could each time, and all but one time I got effectively the same ending and was in the same position with Emily.
The worst thing about this game is that things change to the exact opposite of your choices, similar to picking a starter pokemon and having your rival pick the contrasting element. So attempting to learn about what Emily intends to do throughout the playthrough will reap you no rewards as every conversation will go over the same way just with different words swapped out.
For example: There are two men that Emily can fall for throughout the game and they are described in literally the exact same way and the only thing you can do is inadvertently pick which man treats her like♥♥♥♥♥♥and then eventually gets back together with her. This is done in one of two ways. You can either go to the party at the beginning of the game and she’ll fall for the edgelord that bombards her with creepy emails until she decides it’s cute, or you can not go to the party and she’ll go head over heels for the tool of a surfer boy.
Better yet, she’ll respond the exact same way no matter what choices you make regarding her as well. If you let her visit regardless of whether or not you sleep together she’ll say that the opposite of what happened is what should’ve happened. It feels like the entire game is built to make you regret every choice you make and guilt trip you over decisions you can’t control. And speaking of control, at several points throughout the game instead of you controlling a character fully, the coward that you’re supposed to be decides that whatever they typed is not good enough and then totally switch the words around for an entirely different meaning. I understand this from a narrative perspective as it gives you insight into the mind of a person who’s terrified to speak their mind for fear of rejection or inadequacy, but from a gameplay perspective it’s terrible. Either establish a dissonance between player and character to set a precedent for your actions not fully translating or give the player full control. Anything less totally breaks the immersion and makes the player feel like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for what they had no control over.
If you’re a pessimist, an optimist, supportive, dismissive, or entirely self centered all conversations will go over exactly the same. If I wanted my choices not to matter, I would’ve played a Telltale game.

Shantae and the Pirate's Curse is a fun and light-hearted adventure with great music, solid controls, beautiful animated sprite art, and funny reimaginings on common metroidvania power-ups and abilities.  I would call most of the game easier than the classics in the genre, but I would not hold that against it.    That said I found a few specific levels to be difficulty spikes and found them frustrating against the challenge level of the rest of the game.
As the third game in the series I do not recommend it as an introduction to the series;  Risky's Revenge is a better starting point.  Pirate's Curse doesn't really try to introduce any of the returning characters to you, which would make the story beats fly over a player new to the series' head, including that our heroine *had* magic abilities that she somehow *lost* before this game begain, and her history with series antagonist, Risky Boots.
Some folks might be turned off by the fan service.  There is a high number of female characters wearing outfits that show off clevage or belly buttons if not both, and there's an entire sequence poking fun at the "slave Leia" outfit.   To me the game came off as self aware about it as opposed to creepy or skeevy, but other folks may feel different.  I did find it refreshing to play a game where not just the heroine is female, but so are most of the significant cast members.  This is something I enjoy about the series overall.
Wayforward overall does good work, and Pirate's Curse is certainly another example of that.  I enjoyed turning to it when I wanted a pick-me-up with fun gameplay, good controls, fun story, and solid music.

I know what you’re thinking "it’s Space Engineers with castles". Medieval Engineers is the second Early Access game from Keen Software House, and like its predecessor, it’s a voxel building game and physics simulation. The similarities run deep, but two key differences set the games apart.
Where Space Engineers was a game free from gravity push/pull, Medieval Engineers is dominated by it. Things don’t fly, they fall (and they fall hard), and this "learning experience" teaches you how and what you can build. Then there’s the second key difference "castles just aren’t as much fun as spaceships".
a hateful sentence, you might say if you’re a fan of big stalwart walls and mighty towers. Castles are cool. Giant, towering monuments to feed ego . Who wouldn’t want a castle? But you can’t do much with an empty one.
Spaceships you can shoot off into space, weaving between asteroids, launching a barrage of missiles and lasers into enemy vessels, smashing (ramming) into them in a last ditch effort to win a dogfight. A castle just sits there, looking cool.

If you pay $10 for DEX (Devilian Exchance) you can sell it for gold on the AH and buy everything you need. People are selling carries for gear/gems/upgrades. You name it.... It can be bought by exchanging real money for gold.
I was able to get my evoker to the top 15 on the server Asperon without paying more than $5 (to get varified). But on the leaderboards you can clearly see what players were the ones who were able to buy and sell DEX to progress their character.
Furthermore, there are only a handful of end game dungeons that you will need to grind for anywhere between 6-12 hours to get full gear. For me the tedium and lack of variety kills the game. It feels like there is depth but it's in all the wrong places (leveling artifacts/enchanting/fusing/refine). I like the idea of enhancing weapons but I think this game tries to add content where it's not needed but that's just my opinion. I like to be able to find a weapon and know that it is THE ONE that I've been looking for.
Overall I would rate this game 7/10 because it is completely free and you CAN have fun playing it. I still can't recommend it though because it's inherently flawed from having a buisness model that allows players to convert their real cash into progress that would otherwise take hours of tedious and repetitive farming to achieve. As I said earlier, if clash of clans designed a buisness model for a ARPG/MMO I think this would be it.

Strife was one of the last games made on the Doom engine, and it really shows off the strength of Carmack's engine really well.
Unlike Doom, in Strife your objective is not to kill everything in sight and find the level exit. The game is built more like an RPG with mission based objectives. You play as a wandering mercenary who joins the resistance toward a corrupt government of cyborgs known as The Order. All of the characters in the game are really memorable and really well voice acted. It also features multiple endings, and overall the story is really engaging. Especially for a game released in 1996 with comic book cutscenes.
Strife also features hub levels like Hexen, where you revisit a central town location regularly to purchase ammunition and health items prior to a mission. The game also takes place in an interconnected world similar to Metroid. Where you can backtrack to prior mission areas if you so desire to uncover secrets you might have missed. Later on in the game the levels get much more sprawling and the level design in general gets more unique.
Strife is one of my favorite fps/rpg games. While it wasn't the first one to try the concept, it was probably the first one to do it really well. It's a very enjoyable and simple game to play and if you're a fan of games like Deus Ex and System Shock I guarantee you'll like it.
This re-release also includes the original WAD files that Strife shipped with back in 1996. So if you're not a fan of this particular port of the game, you can copy those into your favorite Doom source port like gzDoom or Skulltag. Happy hunting.

Yeah, right, so. With a background in biology I can say, that sicknesses do not work this way.
On the other hand, Plague Inc. Evolved is a great time management game, in which you name, start, spread and develop a disease, with the explicit goal to wipe out (or enslave in some cases) all of humanity. To your disposal are bacteria, and you quite rapidly unlock viruses, parasites, bioweapons, and even zombies, vampires and apes, all of which play very different. There are four difficulty levels, one of which matches your skill level. You also unlock special genes as a loadout per won game to make a rerun different or easier.
A lot of content is to be found here, and you can spend a lot of time with the destruction of earth. The only thing to really critisize negatively here is, that a lot of the rules to progress are not explained. DNA seems to pop up somewhat randomly, until you read deeper into it (in the over 150 guides for example).
Plague Inc. Evolved is a mobile port done right! All important PC options are there, controls work perfectly, no "in-app"-BS except for the wonderful soundtrack. Even on mobile, it is worth it. I have both.

The year is 2002 and AIM is your go to for talking to your friends. Oh hey Emily is online! You should talk to her cause you like her.
Think of a choose your own adventure game about going through your teenage years and through college. Yes even those cringeworthy years where you're still trying to, "figure yourself out". You obviously like this girl Emily, and it's crystal clear that she digs you back. (Even if you're a girl, so don't feel left out if you're a girl as well; Emily is bisexual.)
Every time you try to advance in the relationship it always manages to go the oppostie way.
Now think of that, "Choose your own adventure" game but you have the same ending... NO MATTER WHAT YOU DO.
You can talk about your favorite music together, you can tell her that her taste in music is trash, you can be a typical teen and go to parties or you could break away from the norm and do your own thing. No matter what happens, if you're chasing Emily, or if she is chasing you, she always seems to be out of reach.
See, looking back after attempting to get a different ending in any way possible, this is a sad game. No, not sad in a bad way, but a game that can make you feel sad through its story as you go throughout the years 2002-2006. Probably because AIM was dying out aways but I'm just a stickler for details... Don't pay me no mind.
My impression of this game feels as though Kyle Seeley, (The games creator) may have personally been through this same (Yet oddly specific) sernario, or he really wanted to make a, "Choose your own adventure game" except he either messed up, or made the difficulty too high?
Perhaps he is trying to reach out to Emily today? Maybe he just has a lot of feelings bottled up and he's trying to express himself, or possibly I could be over analyzing the true meaning behind the game? Who knows? Maybe you should give it a few attempts and come up with your own input, instead of being a sheep and blindly follow someones opinion, be a shepard and form your own.
Originally I was not going to recommend this game because there's nothing you can do to change the outcome. But the more I write, the more I feel as though, you should give it a try.
Even though I'm salty that you can't seem to be with Emily, (Or Emma, another girl you meet (Not really)) maybe you can give it a shot and be with her? Or you could just be salty like I am.
TLDR: This game was oddly specific Kyle...Are you okay?

Shantae and The Pirate's Curse is the 3rd installement in the shantae series. This time with the help from IntiCreates ( makers of Megaman zero, ZX , 9/10) , wayforward was able to show us what Shantae was really capable of. The first Shantae game well being the first one and being on the gameboy color had some issues , most of them caused by the console itself, it also didn't know what it wanted to be. The second game Risky's Revenge which you can also get on steam while improved upon a lot of things in the first game still had some design choices that made the game feel unfinished (the map , only 3 dungeons one being a gauntlet etc...) .
With background out of the way lets look at this game.
Pros:
1: The music is amazing. Its energetic and memorable. Same guy who worked on shovel knight also a great game.
2:The controls are tight if you die its your fault and not because of some input delays.
3: The weapons you get are really useful and welcomed addition to the game. In previous games you had to hold buttons certain amount of time to dance and then transform  just to use the power you needed. However this time all you have to do is to just press the correct button and BOOM. It kinda reminds me of Symphony Of the Night in that regard.
4:The bosses are really fun and challanging and the best part is you can beat all of them withouth getting hit. Its actually not that hard.
5: There are lots of dungeons (and 2 of them are secret bonus) and these are pretty fun.
6:The writing is hilarious.
Cons:
1: You can't (to my knowledge ) assign the buttons on your controller. You can do it for the keyboard but not the controller.
..........And thats it , I can't really find major problems with this game.
I recommend Shantae and The Pirate's Curse to anyone who enjoys 2d platformer/metroidvania type of games.

Too early of a release to give a full fledged review, and I do NOT own any level capped players as of now. I can say this.....
The flow of this game just feels amazing to me. Almost diablo-esqueue, mixed with some MMO goodness, and it's own sort of flair. The battle is pretty fluent which is a neccessity to an action rpg (and the lack of this has caused many past action MMOs to bite the dust quick imo). The general "don't stand in fire" rule applies for most boss/super encounters and each class comes with a dodge skill for close calls.
As for the story-line, I don't know...nor, do I care. If you play MMOs for a storyline driven by artificial intelligence you will have to read another review for insight. I play an MMO for group-driven advancement, and player-vs-player competition. I will be basing my review on this (maybe after the game progresses I will review it again with an opinion on this matter).
Instance queueing is another feauture I enjoyed in Devilian. No waiting 2 hours on a tank and healer in an endless queue.... Queue for an instance and usually you will have a group together rather quickly (atleast as of now....). I also love the fact you can queue for a 20-vs-20 pvp battleground  right after you dive into the game and learn the basic controls.
Love the dark devil characters with two states (you can be your normal state or go Devilian (devil) mode). The devilian state characters had advanced/modified skills, and some other powerhouse skills unique to devilian mode. You can trigger this mode after charging it, or some battlegrounds and events force you to use your Devilian state for the entire instance/event.
Overall its one of the very few free to play games I didn't delete after level 20 of character progression, and will re-review once I have put hours into end-game content.... but download me, try me, love me..... you shouldnt be disappointed if you are into MMORPGs or Action RPGs such as Diablo.

The devs have been working a lot on the game since its launch, almost always for the best and sometimes for the worst.
It is a basically a game where you free your imagination creating contraptions of all sorts, may them be mobile (on wheels or otherwise) or anchored to the ground. You can try whatever creation your twisted mind can think of and it somehow shows you how and why such a mechanism is possible or not, since Medieval Engineers uses really good physics simulation.
Of course, it is a game, so there's only a set number of things you can "invent" or create, since there is a finite amount of different "part" types you can use, but the devs are constantly adding new gadgets to enhance the experience while fixing bugs and balancing stuff. It's always fun to check out the new content they put in the game every few weeks or so, as they upload a patch every week, because the new content can sometimes be game-changing.
I can recommend this game for the awsome replayability and the fact that it lets your creativity go rampage while staying really realistic and rewarding.
To conclude, I would give Medieval Engineers an overall note of
, based on several aspects including:
(How active are the devs and how much new content is added regularly)
(How many people are actively playing the game, on the dedicated servers)
Note that I did not base my evaluation on the amount of bugs/game-breaking "functionalities" as I believe those are temporary and will be changed/fixed as development goes, the devs being active and quite close to their playerbase.

For example, when you shoot your teammate (the story is so good and original I can't even remember his name) he responds with "Receiving fire!", or maybe even "Returning fire!", yet he never does. Now, you may ask yourself, "How is this realistic if he never returns fire to you, the teammate who shot him?", when you look at it from a psychological level, he sees you as a father figure in his life, he originally thought someone in the treelines in this dangerous world took a potshot at him, but then when he knew it was you, he realized his mistakes.. He wouldn't hurt his father figure, the one leader in his life, that didn't abandon him, and you, as the player, must assume this responsibility.

Strife was originally released in 1996 on a modified doom engine, it was unique for its time because it combined elements of RPGs with dooms run and gun gameplay. The result was a cult classic that has garnered fan projects and restorations, but sadly it was forgotten amongst the other big PC games like Duke Nukem 3D and Quake. Until this re-release I was convinced many forgot about Strife, thankfully I was wrong as the devs who ported this cared very much about the game. Strife: Veteran Edition is thankfully not just Strife shoved in with dosbox, it is an actual port based mainly off of the Chocolate Strife source port. It contains the original IWADs and the ability to play it as it was in 1996. It also adds a large amount of modern new features and customization options. An optional bloom lighting system and motion blur have been added along with objective/damage indicators and weapon recoil. I'd easily recommend this version of Strife to anyone looking for a good action game, its a very unique experience and this port only enhances it.
It's ♥♥♥♥in' Strife, man. And now it's better than ever.

Ahhh Strife! Back in 1996, Rogue Entertainment made it's debut with the most ambitious use of the Doom engine yet. Strife hit the scene as the first true story-driven FPS/RPG hybrid. Using a hub system quite similar to Hexen, Strife also added in NPCs, voiced dialog, and actual conversation choices that affect the outcome of the game. Compared to the mindless run and gun action of previous Doom-based games, this was quite a refreshing change. And now 18 years later Night Dive Studios has taken this amazing classic, and given it the kind of re-release that quite frankly I wish could be done for every Doom-engine game!
Right off the bat when you start up Strife: Veteran Edition you're greeted with a plethora of options, ranging from enhanced music to widescreen views, FOV, bloom, and all the other trimmings. You want delicious crunchy pixels? You got it! Smoothed filtering your kinda thing? It's there too! Night Dive Studios has replaced the "vanilla" doom engine with a massively reworked version of the hit source port Chocolate Doom. Despite the source code for Strife being lost to the ages, they have managed to completely reverse-engineer the game, and bring it perfectly into the modern age.
Everything that made Strife what it is is completely intact here, and it all holds up very well considering the game's age. From the games stealth elements to its vicious deathmatch mode, this package is just dripping with juicy goodness. The original manual, town map, and field guide are all included as .pdf files, and the Roland SC-55 soundtrack is present as ogg files. Speaking of music, if you want to experience the oldschool synthesizer charms of retro Adlib sound, you can turn on OPL3 music in the sound settings.
As if all of the above wasn't good enough, Night Dive has also augmented Strife: Veteran Edition with a set of trading cards, badges and achievements. They are also planning further additions such as a "capture the Chalice" multiplayer mode, and better automapping. If only id Software would hire Night Dive to give Doom, Heretic and Hexen this kind of epic overhaul. Those games sorely need it as the janky Dosbox setup they have on Steam is just not pretty. Strife: Veteran edition is a shining example of what happens with a game company is passionate about both the game at hand, and giving their customers the best experience possible.

At the moment of writing this review, The Steam page for Dead State Reanimated rates this game as mostly positive and that is how I would rate my experience playing it: For every great thing this game does, it is usually followed by a major flaw that undermines the Dead State’s overall impression. If you like to play modern RPGs like Mass Effect, The Witcher 3 or Dragon Age, chances are you won’t find this game enjoyable. But if you fondly remember old RPG classics, like Fallout 1 and 2, or Baldur’s Gate series, and you’re armed with patience then you will enjoy Dead State… most of the time. Allow me to dissect this game for you (no pun intended):
Pros:
+ Good overall writing and gameplay
+ Tactical and satisfying turn-based combat
+ Interesting noise level, survival and experience system
+ Decent sim management gameplay while in the shelter, with various resources that need to be balanced
+ Lots of diverse and unique allies that will join your cause, each with different personality, wants and demands
+ Strong level design and good, albeit simplistic artistic and graphical presentation
Cons:
- Game has a very sluggish pace with unavoidable grinding
- Quests are far and few, mostly fetch-based and primitive
- Disappointing end game content
- Thrown weapons are unbalanced
- Combat rounds can drag on and game is plentiful with annoying bugs
- Limited lore and zombie tropes make the game world a very uninteresting place to reside in
- UI and inventory are needlessly complex and counter-intuitive
- Minimalistic sound and music design serve to the detriment of game’s atmosphere
Dead State was made by many creative individuals, including Brian Mitsoda who was a writer for the legendary game Vampire the Masquerade Bloodlines, and that means the writing in this game is constantly on a high level of polish. All dialogues in Dead State are well written, as well are many data items you’ll find as you explore the world, which carry poignant and memorable articles to read. Nearly 50 allies you’ll have a chance to meet are all well-rounded characters that will follow you on your adventures or help you build more things in the shelter, if you are on their good side. But the off trade is that they don’t evolve as in other games with fewer companions that are extremely well-written and change dramatically as the game goes on.
You are stuck in a world overrun by zombies, and you’ll need people, resources and the main headquarter to survive. The Shelter you find at the start of the game is an interesting concept, as it can be upgraded in order to provide a bonus to protection or a new type or resource against the overwhelming odds. There are many resources in the game you’ll have collect if you want to survive another day: food, fuel, spare parts and luxury items all grant mood boosts to you and allies, and keeping them well feed and taken care of is very important, otherwise they’ll fall into depression, inner-struggle and violence or will abandon you completely. That is why you’ll have to collect as much resources on your travels as you can.
While you travel on the map, you’ll encounter many settlements that may be peaceful, but usually want you dead. All levels in the game you visit are well designed with many small and welcoming details developers could have easily omit, and add a lot to the overall atmosphere of the game. You’ll have to watch on the amount of noise you make, measured in decibels, otherwise you’ll attract the restless undead to your current location. You can also use the noise to you benefit, by directing zombies to the dangerous living enemies, while you wait out their clash to end and scavenge the remains of the battle. The living are the most daunting enemies in the game, as most of them liberally use firearms that can easily incapacitate you and your allies, and make a lot of unnecessary noise. Zombies on the other hand serve as an obstacle and a nuisance, since they are slow and their attacks are limited. However they can infect you if you are not careful, slowly leading to your doom.
Leveling system in Dead State also differs from other RPGs: you only gain experience by surviving another day, and securing as much resources as you can. Surviving battle encounters yield you no experience, but you do get from it various traditional weapons and firearms that can be upgraded in the shelter to be more precise and deadly.  The combat is similar to first two Fallout games, where your positioning, use of a correct weapon on a correct enemy, and wisely using your skills and setting traps and snares are key to your victory. The longer the combat prolongs, chances of your survival diminish significantly. But there is a negative side to this type of combat: turns can slow down as more and more enemies enter the fray, human enemies can go dumb occasionally and move around not knowing how to get to you. Thrown weapons such as grenades break the careful balance of all weapons in the game as they can be flung so far, that if they are aimed at you, you’ll have no option from protecting yourself from their devastating effects.
Biggest flaw of Dead State is the slow pace the game is developing and the main story is resolving. There are no traditional quests, with self-contained stories to tell and dramatic impact, only simple list of things to do for you or for your allies. And almost all of them involve annoying fetch-me–this and fetch-me-that demands. The number of encounters on the global map is limited and when you discover them all, you’ll have nothing to do but to wait for the end of the game to begin. And the amount of grinding you have to do is staggeringly bad: everything that is not nailed to the ground, you’ll have to pick up at some point. Your and allies’ Inventory will fill up so quickly that you’ll be forced to go back to the shelter to unload everything you’ve found and then return again to the latest destination to haul the rest of the stuff. This kind of pick-up-deliver-pick-up-again philosophy drags the entire pace of the game down and your enjoyment as well. You’ll also struggle with bafflingly illogical interface: how to split objects in your inventory and move them around, how to access the inventory of the vehicle, how to access skills you can use in combat and how many steps you have to take to assign your allies daily chores to do. And if that doesn’t drive you crazy, a letdown of the end content, the final battle and abrupt endings will leave you wanting for more grandiose conclusion. Music is un-intrusive and forgettable, while sound effects are minimal and underused, thus missing the chance for them to aid in building more memorable atmosphere and emphasize the dialogues and emotional bonds you and your allies share.
Still, for me Dead State manages to be an overall mostly positive experience. I wish this kind of game wasn’t settled among zombies, for me one of the most overused and least interesting/frightening horror tropes and it is too bad that the game didn’t try to change and evolve our expectations regarding zombies. But at one point in the game, pressured by many choices, good and bad that I’ve made, and combat encounters I’ve survived and will have to endure, I started to adopt the ruthless survivalist way of thinking without even noticing at first. As I always want to play and do play as a good guy, this game made me aware of how enjoyable it can be to be a bad guy once in a while :D Thus I give it a cautious recommendation to the fans of classic RPG games and zombies, but I’ll also understand anyone who finds the amount of flaws to be a bit too much.

You know what, Marlow Briggs may be a low budgeter, but it truly was an entertaining game.  Sure it copies a decent amount of its tricks from the God of War formula, but in all honestly, that's not really a bad template to borrow from.  Throw in a little bit of Indiana Jones, 70s blaxploitation film-making, B action movies, nonsensical comedy and you've got the vibe for this game down pat.  I actually enjoyed this game more than alot of big budget games from the same genre.
Briggs isn't a perfect game, yet it does so much right that I couldn't stop playing until I completed the hardcore mode today, FINALLY.  In Marlow Briggs you are killed by an evil Chinese magnate who wants to rule the world with a frightening, sort of terraforming magical power.  He kills you and kidnaps your girlfriend, though thankfully Marlow is brought back by a wise-cracking mask that guides him through his journey to save the girl, the day and the world.  The entire premise is ridiculous.  Once you're having fun with the game, the plot hardly even matters.
At its core, Briggs is a hack n' slashers delight.  You arm yourself with several types of melee weapons, magic, long range attacks and acrobatic abilities.  As you fight and explore, you earn experience to upgrade your powers, making you a killing machine on a machine.  You'll explore crazy industrial complexes, temples, caves, jungles and much more.  While graphically, Marlow and the gang aren't the best game in town; he surely isn't the worst looking either.  Levels are solidly detailed with lots to peer at in the distance and the enviroments look good while alternately being a blast to travel.  There's hidden secrets to find and numerous achievements to unlock.  There is also a hardcore mode on hand that will test your skills for certain.  It's not as impossible as Deadlight, but it will put up a stiff challenge and make you sing for your supper.
You upgrade with new equipment at key points of the game while fighting legions of foes that include all sorts of armed guards, giant insects, mythical looking boss creatures, teleporting evil priests, giants, a wolf like Hellbeast and other assorted demons.  The boss fights are a blast, and require quicks hands, strategic use of attacks/abilities and old fashioned pattern memorization.  That's really all there is to it!  The campagin is a decent length with alot of areas to explore and frequent differences in scenery so that you'll rarely be bored and when you're not fighting like a champ there are all sorts of gameplay variations to keep things exciting.  You'll man gun turrets, fly choppers and fighter planes while shooting down everything in sight, use your nimble abilities to platform your way to victory, etc.  The controls were mostly tight and responsive, so it's easy to get yourself in the action and stay there.  While I expected minimal of this game, I got way more than I bargained for and put in 28.7 hrs to beat it twice and get most of the achievements (97%).   Hell, once weakening certain monsters like the club wielding giants and monster scorpions, you can even ride and use them to fight Golden Axe style!
On the downside, sometimes the controls do tend to get a little wacky and combo stringing won't feel entirely accurate, making for a cheap death or two.  The QT buttom presses to hammer down on certain bosses and deal decisive blows don't always register, which also got me slaughtered a couple of times as well.  While not with the frequency of a survival horror game, the camera has potential to get a little rickety and you'll end up taking a beating from some foes you can't even see.  All of the problems with the game were rather minor and I actually thought this game was HIGHLY addicting and entertaining to play.  To be honest...I like it more than some of the God of War sequels.  You can scream blasphemy all you want, but that's how I felt.  Another downside is that the slow-motion cut scenes could have been better executed and the voice acting isn't top-notch (although its rampant cheesiness is rather endearing as this game is straight out of one of those B movie action 4 packs).  Overall, anyone into the hack n' slash genre would do well to check this out for the cheap price.  I hope they make a sequel with co-op!  Good lord, that'd be a blast.
Now for some quick pros and cons:
Pros
-Solid graphics and sound
-Excellent set of weapons, abilities and magic
-90% of the time the fighting is fluid and fun
-Superb enemy variety with tough fights and killer battles with monstrous bosses
-Campy storyline and voice-acting adds to the appeal
-Combos are easy to execute and satisfying
- 90% of the time the controls are response and fun
-Great gameplay variety with everything listed above and even a few puzzles
Cons
-10% of the time the fighting can be a little clunky
-10% of the time some button presses won't register, especially the QT sequences (fortunately they are few)
-Platforming is a beotch when the controls stutter
Overall:  8.2/10

There are reviews out there saying that this game is one of those that is so bad that it's good. I don't know what they are smoking. Sure, given it's low price i can understand that many start the game with low expectations about it. But i found this game amazing, deserving well more than 5 bucks. As soon as you get to the main menu, you are greeted to one of the best epic main menu songs out there. Everytime i started the game, i couldn't help but listening to the music for at least 2 minutes. The rest of the music is ok, but this song makes up for all of them. Now speaking of the game, it's a ripoff of God of War, but a pretty good one. The story surely sucks, but there's plenty of funny dialog. The graphics are decent and the game is surprisingly well optimized for PC. Now speaking of the gameplay, it's mostly an Hack and Slash. There's a light and a heavy attack that you can combo, and a grab, block and jump buttons. There's 4 weapons and 5 magic powers that you collect, and they all play differently. You can also upgrade them. The combat is good, with a solid variety of enemy types and bosses, but blocking feels a bit off because you can't block in the middle of an attack, so you'll be evading most of the time. Besides combat, there are also sections of platforming (those could be better), puzzle solving, evading obstacles, 3D shooting and top down shooting. Together, it'll last about 6 hours, and if you are like me, you'll play right again on the hardcore difficulty, which isn't really that hard except for some encounters later in the game. For it's price, it has a good lenght. And you can also replay some challenges from the story in the menu with leaderboards, but for me only the first time was added. Probably a bug, but didn't care much about it. And there's also a minigame in the credits, which sucks but lets you skip the credits the faster you complete it. It was a nice addition to finish the game. In the end, the game isn't brilliant, but surprisingly good given it's price, and you should definitely get it if you're a fan of Hack and Slash games. Marlow Briggs is the kind of game that knows it is bad and enjoys every last second of it. The corny acting, the even cornier lines, the dumbed down hack & slash mechanics, and the hilariously stupid plot all serve one thing: to let you have a great time.
Steam is full of bad games. And while Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death is undoubtedly a bad game, what makes it stand out in the sea of Greenlight schlock is that it was designed to be a bad game: which suddenly elevates it into so-bad-it-is-actually-great status.
Let me explain.
When you play a bad game, you often get frustrated because of bad level design or game mechanics, or bad controls. Or even worse, the game is downright boring. With Marlow Briggs, you will hardly ever get bored: it is a platformer, a hack & slash, a rail shooter, and a shoot ‘em up– all packed into one explosive pack of joy. Sure, some of the platforming levels are repetitive and the camera tends to kill you more than the bosses, but there are so many minigames and shooter sections that you will never, ever get bored.
The game mechanics are simple as a brick: you have a jump button, normal and a power attack, and a few spells. They form dozens of combos, but they cannot hide the fact that Marlow Briggs is played by mashing two buttons as fast as you can. Combat is strangely satisfying though with good enemy design and one of the most balanced difficulty sliders I saw in a long time.
The cherry on top of this rather delicious action cake is the story. You cannot name a single 90s action movie cliché or one-liner that isn’t here in some form, and there are more explosions than in Michael Bay’s entire filmography. All completed with a voice acting hammier than a pig farm; it is hilariously terrible and you will probably find yourself unable to not laugh at it, just like how the developers intended.

This isn't a game that you'll find everywhere, because it fulfills a certain niche, which is parkouring game, so if you like parkour, and you like Jet Set Radio, I can almost guarantee you that you would like this game. Short premise, it’s a game where you can be a character with genetic modification, or gears that amplifies your strengths and speed, and you’re placed in a dystopian city ruled by a dedicated party-pooper. You can run, jump, grind, wall-climb, and do trick to travel from one point to another point. Basically the description clearly explains what you need to know about the game’s context. If you like what you read, you’ll like the game.
As always, TL;DR on the bottom
Definitely not the game’s strongest point. The storyline itself isn’t bad, but it’s nothing to write home about. It follows the usual ragtag group of rebellion rebelling against a dictator ruling a dystopian city. It’s definitely not bad, but it’s nothing that would keep you up at night wondering what would happen next. It also doesn’t help the fact that the story, or the main mission, can be sidetracked by almost everything in the game.
Personally, the story itself isn’t interesting enough to keep me playing through it just for the story itself, and I wouldn’t actually mind if there’s no story in the game to keep me around. I’ve been playing since the alpha version, where there’s no semblance of story anywhere, and it still keeps me entertained. By no means that I’m saying the story is bad, but it’s just average.
Regarding the characters, they were designed uniquely, and their designs is definitely more on the memorable side, however their character doesn’t get much exposure, and there’s not enough side mission where you can delve deeper and learn about them as a character, because most story dialogue only shows them as ‘tropes’. It’s a huge missed chance, because their character’s design is already quite interesting to boot.
It’s fun, it’s bright, and it’s neon. The world design is definitely one of the more unique worlds I’ve seen. The preview image should sum ups the world design, and if again, if you like JSR, you would like this game. The world itself is designed with the gameplay in mind. You would definitely see some stuffs that just juts out of place, but it’s convenient for you to, say get from one platform to another platform. Kudos to the developer for creating the world the way it is by the way, because unlike, say, Mirror’s Edge, the path you take from one point to another is not obvious. This might come as a cons, but the way the dev places the grinding spot, the jumping spot, etc. felt natural in this world. To put it simply, the route doesn’t just felt like it was placed just for the convenience of the player. The same cannot be said for the closed indoor levels however, because it was clear that those was designed in a way for the convenience of the players, but that just increases the fun you get when you do those race mission
I don’t usually buy the soundtrack of a game for the music. I usually bought it because of the bundles it comes with, and usually to support the dev.
I bought Hover’s soundtrack for the music.
Two of the soundtrack was made, by none other than, Hideki Naganuma, and if you know that name, then you’re in for a treat.
The other soundtracks fits the theme that Hover is going for, and the song never felt out of place from the area you’re around, or the situation you’re in. It felt nice jamming to the tune when you’re leisurely exploring the world, and when it comes time to do some high octane mission, the soundtracks deliver the extra edge to the overall feeling.
The main selling point of the game, and I say it deserves all the money it gets.
Like I stated earlier on my story section, even if there’s no story in the game, I would still play the game for hours and hours. It gives you the freedom you wants from a parkour game; no fall damage, low gravity/high jumping power, seamless transition from running to grinding rails, the high speed running to even be able to outrun car, and the world provides you with a playground that synergizes nicely with the gameplay elements. When you find out those hidden path that the devs made for a certain action, you would enjoy the trip from one point to another.
If you like JSR, Mirror’s Edge, Skate series, or Tony Hawk series, you would feel right at home with Hover. Combining open world with parkour might be hard to pull off, but Hover hits just the right spot to integrate the two of it into a fun and amusing game to play.
That being said, there’s still some flaw to the gameplay mechanics, namely the verticality. This game isn’t Assassin’s Creed, so the grapping onto ledges, wall-climb, wall-run, sometimes doesn’t work properly, and it can be quite frustrating when you’re running around seamlessly horizontally, only to find yourself having to stop for a moment and adjust yourself to climb up a place. It also doesn’t help that the map put a lot of emphasis on verticality, especially on Admin District. It definitely could use a lot of polishing and fine tuning to reach Assassin’s creed level of vertical traversing.
Unlike the alpha, Hover uses grid system for levelling up stats for your characters. Imagine FF-X grid system, but instead of getting to move to the next grid when you level up, you unlocks more slot to put in ‘sphere’ (in FFX) or ‘processor’ (in Hover), and you increase your level by filling the slots. I’d say that it’s not the best levelling system out there, but it’s not too detrimental to the core gameplay. What’s quite detrimental to the core gameplay however is the emphasis on the quality of the processor. The higher rarity of processor you have, the higher the stat boost is, pretty basic stuff, but in certain mission, or stages of the game, it’s absolutely mandatory to have those highest rarity processor to pass. It’s quite the difficulty spike if you doesn’t have the highest rarity, and you will definitely find another people complaining about the difficulty spike as well.
However, finding the highest rarity processor is not that hard, where you have to scale a mountain or something. You’re almost always guaranteed to get the highest rarity processor if you finish a mission with the highest medal possible, and there’s also E-Swap system, where you can place in up to 5 processor for a chance to get one higher rarity processor. It’s quite the, grind, to get all highest rarity processor, but it’s not something that needs hundreds of hour to get it. Again, not the best crafting system out there, but at least it’s something
The online aspect of the game is pretty fun as well, but it’s rather unpolished. Imagine an MMO game where you can just meet with other people and join their mission. The mission itself is ten times better when you’re playing with or against other people, and the community so far is pretty welcoming as well, as long as you’re nice, they’ll be nice. However, some mission doesn’t actually give enough incentive to play together with other people, and there’s still some connectivity issue. It’s not too distracting however.

6:The writing is hilarious.
Cons:
1: You can't (to my knowledge ) assign the buttons on your controller. You can do it for the keyboard but not the controller.
..........And thats it , I can't really find major problems with this game.
I recommend Shantae and The Pirate's Curse to anyone who enjoys 2d platformer/metroidvania type of games.

Honestly, I think the plot here is actually much better than in the previous game. Whereas the plot in Risky's Revenge is at times quite thin, in this game it doesn't feel thin at all - there always seems to be something going on and it's in general much easier to follow.
Gameplay-wise It's a Metroidvania-platformer like its predecessor, but the areas you explore have been expanded quite a bit. Rather than just Scuttle Town and the nearby areas, you have a multitude of different islands to explore, from the tropical Saliva Island to the zombie-infested Spiderweb Island and the icy Frostbite Island, which gives it much more variety with regards to the areas you explore and visit. Compared to the first game, Scuttle Town and the surrounding areas have also been shrunk massively, though in all honesty this is more to the game's overall benefit, since it cuts out a lot of the needless traipsing back and forth that the first game had. The multiple islands also help to mitigate the Metroidvania forgetting-where-you're-up-to problem by giving you much more of a sense of progression as you unlock the islands and defeat the Cacklebats found there. The number of undiscovered Cacklebats and Heart Squids, which you use to increase the size of your life bar, are also shown above each island in the hub screen, making the completion aspect of the game much more accessible too. Because of the way in which it's been redesigned it's also much easier to find your way around Scuttle Town since all the buildings are now clearly labelled, so you no longer have to guess which door contains what.
The base gameplay and graphics are very similar to that of Risky's Revenge, with a few notable differences. In this instalment Shantae is by default able to whip her hair back and forth much faster than before, and as a result from the get-go the action is much less rigid and more snappy and satisfying. The fact that they've also added Castlevania-style knockback is both a blessing and a curse, since it allows the action to flow a bit more, but on occasion can be quite irritating. Unfortunately, due to Shantae having lost her genie powers, her Dancing mechanic is missing, but fortunately this is replaced with a new mechanic in the form of pirate equipment that can be found throughout the levels, for instance a pistol that allows you to hit far-off switches and serves as a weak ranged attack, a hat which lets you glide over long distances, and a scimitar which lets you do a ground-pound attack. These new mechanics complement the Metroidvania gameplay much like the Dances did in the previous game, and arguably even do a better job, since there's much more of them and they allow for a lot more variety in the platforming puzzles than the Dances did. Not only that, but WayForward have also, it seems, managed to add a couple of new spins on the platforming too, with gameplay drastically changing in a couple of sections of the game as you play. One section has you running through the woods, unable to attack, and another is a Wind Waker-eqsue stealth section in which you're stripped of all your items and have to try and sneak out of the area - if you're detected by the guards they will march you back to the start. These serve as interesting, fun little breaks from the Metroidvania gameplay and keep the game interesting in a way that doesn't disturb the flow of the plot in any serious way.
A drastic change from the previous game is the items system, which has been almost completely overhauled. Most of the Magic from Risky's Revenge is gone and the mana system has been replaced with time-limited, single-use items. You're no longer able to hot-switch between different items in quite the same way as in Risky's Revenge but what you can do is use multiple items at the same time - a feature which the previous game lacked. The overall range of items available is also wider and you no longer need to find Magic Jam to buy anything. There's some offensive items, attack buffs, "Fighter's Moves" - extra maneuvers you can perform in combat, some of which can come in particularly handy, and a massive, very variable and on occasion slightly humourous range of healing items (including the new Auto-Potion which activates as soon as you run out of health - believe me they will save your bacon on many an occasion). I found myself not using quite as many items in this game as in Risky's Revenge, but honestly there's nothing wrong with the new system. It's different, but it doesn't really detract from the experience at all and is just as fun to use as the old system.
A lot of the characters from Risky's Revenge also reappear in Pirate's Curse as do some new characters, major and minor, ranging from a new Baron to a walking He-Man parody, and they're all just as funny and interesting as they were before, perhaps even more so. You get to see a lot more of the other characters than in Risky's Revenge and you'll learn more about them as you progress through the game - and you'll be glad to know that the fantastic writing also makes a return, and in greater and even more humourous amounts. Sometimes it'll have you on the edge of your seat, other times every other line will have you giggling, heck, even SIGNS and some item descriptions contain their fair share of weird and wacky humour! All that and somehow you never really lose track of the plot. Suffice to say, this game's writing is top notch.
A fair amount of the sountrack is made up of remixed tracks from Risky's Revenge but most of them are original, and whereas its predecessor's soundtrack was pretty good, Pirate's Curse ramps that description up to "freaking fantastic". Every single track is even more riveting than in the previous installment, and the soundtrack in general seems to have much more "thump" to it than before. As a result it perfectly complements the action-rich gameplay and awesomely-written characters, and not only that, but whilst it does sound modern and upbeat some of the songs seem to remind slightly of its 16-bit forefathers - if you listen to them in the right way they sound a bit like remixes of songs from the days of the SNES era. I really kind of regret that I can't fit more songs from this game's soundtrack into this video, it really is that much of joy to listen to.
Another thing which this game has which Risky's Revenge doesn't is voice acting for some of Shantae's lines, provided by none other than Cristina Vee, who also played such high-profile roles as Homura Akemi from Madoka Magica and Compa from Hyperdimension Neptunia. Whilst at times her voice acting can be a teeny bit grating it certainly helps to build up Shantae's character a little more by putting more of a voice in her mouth, and Christina Vee's performance is pretty good. That said, it is a bit of a shame that WayForward didn't choose to go big and fully voice-act it, because that would have been downright awesome.
All in all, Shantae and the Pirate's Curse is not just a great sequel to a great game, but also a truly fantastic game in its own right. The music is wonderful, the dialogue is stellar, the gameplay is smooth and enjoyable, the 16-bit graphics once again give it a fair amount of charm, and for what it's worth I can say that, even on its own, this is one of the best platformers I've ever played and certainly one of my all time favourites.
